title: How to switch Java versions on Windows with one command (no more editing JAVA_HOME)
description:
I kept juggling JDK 8, 21 and 25 on Windows. Every time a project needed a different one, I was back in the environment variables dialog, editing JAVA_HOME and then checking PATH to make sure the right java.exe won.

So I made jfs (see what it stands for at the end), a Windows Java version manager for Java fans.

qaptivator / jfs

Windows Java version manager for Java fans. Switch JDKs with one command. No shims, no shell hooks, no background service.

jfs

Stop editing JAVA_HOME.

jfs (Java Fucking Sucks) is a Windows Java version manager. Point it at JDKs you already have, then switch with one command. Your actual JAVA_HOME environment variable stays unchanged. Behind the scenes, a directory junction moves. No shims, no shell hooks, no background service.

irm https://jfs.acdev.app/install.ps1 | iex

Git Bash:

curl -fsSL https://jfs.acdev.app/install.ps1 | powershell.exe -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command -

cmd:

powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "irm https://jfs.acdev.app/install.ps1 | iex"

Or run install.bat.

PS C:\Users\you> java -version
openjdk version "25.0.4.1" 2026-08-18 LTS
OpenJDK Runtime Environment Temurin-25.0.4.1+1 (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS)
OpenJDK 64-Bit Server VM Temurin-25.0.4.1+1 (build 25.0.4.1+1-LTS, mixed mode, sharing)
PS C:\Users\you> jfs
…
View on GitHub

The trick

JAVA_HOME is set once, to %LOCALAPPDATA%\jfs\current. That path is an NTFS directory junction. When you run jfs use 21, jfs retargets the junction to the JDK you picked. JAVA_HOME itself never changes.

Because of that:

  • every new java process follows the JDK you picked
  • already-open terminals don't need a restart (a java process that is already running keeps its old JDK, of course)
  • there are no shims, no shell hooks, and no background service
  • it doesn't need admin rights or Developer Mode, because junctions (mklink /J) don't, unlike symlinks

Usage 

irm https://jfs.acdev.app/install.ps1 | iex

jfs add 21 "C:\path\to\jdk-21"
jfs add 8 "C:\path\to\jdk8"
jfs list
jfs use 21
java -version
jfs current
jfs rm 8

jfs add checks that bin\java.exe exists in the directory and records the path in a small config.json. The first JDK you add becomes active. jfs rm only forgets a version and never touches files on disk.

It does not download JDKs

This is on purpose, at least for now. Many of us already have several JDKs lying around: Gradle's cached toolchains, the ones bundled with IDEs, Adoptium installs. jfs lets you reuse those instead of downloading yet another copy. I was inspired by nvm, but jfs only switches, it doesn't install.

Things worth knowing

  • Windows only. The switching mechanism is an NTFS junction.
  • Local NTFS paths only. A junction can't target a network share.
  • System PATH beats user PATH. Windows searches the system PATH first, so if a system directory contains its own java.exe, that one wins. The installer prints those directories when it finds them. An entry that is literally %JAVA_HOME%\bin is fine, since it follows jfs.
  • Uninstall carefully. Remove-Item -Recurse follows the current junction and can delete the JDK it points at. Remove the junction first with cmd /c rmdir "%LOCALAPPDATA%\jfs\current".

Under the hood

It's written in Rust and MIT licensed. All state is one config.json plus the junction, living in %LOCALAPPDATA%\jfs (or wherever JFS_DIR points).

Feedback

I'd especially like to hear about:

  • PATH edge cases I haven't hit
  • how IDEs and Gradle daemons behave after a switch, since some tools cache JAVA_HOME at startup

Source, releases and issues: github.com/qaptivator/jfs
Landing page: jfs.acdev.app

(and, yes, it stands for "Java Fucking Sucks")

title: 5 Ways to Store AI-Generated Images: Metadata, Retention, and Retrieval
description:
To store and retrieve AI-generated images with metadata in Node.js, use object storage behind an authenticated application endpoint, keep the object key immutable, and put searchable business metadata in your database. For an edtech product serving generated reports, the storage layer should hold the image bytes and a small set of x-amz-meta- headers, while your database owns the student, report, retention, and deletion record. That division matters more than the vendor name.

The practical flow is short: generate an image, choose a unique key, upload the bytes with metadata, save the key beside the report record, then retrieve the object only after checking the customer session. For this workflow, Infrai's practical advantage is one key for everything and one plain REST API: a Node service can call storage without installing a provider SDK while the backend contract stays put. It is still one option in a design that must survive deletion requests and accidental overwrites.

The application contract is the durable part.

1. What should the storage contract guarantee?

For this use case, the contract has five parts: bytes, content type, a stable key, metadata, and an explicit deletion policy. A key like reports/2026/10/report-8f2.../chart.png is better than a user-facing filename. It avoids collisions and keeps the retrieval path independent from a student's name.

Do not treat object metadata as a query database. The storage API can return metadata in response headers, but metadata is not necessarily searchable. Store the fields needed for authorization and retention in your database: customerId, reportId, objectKey, createdAt, deleteAfter, and a content hash if you calculate one. The object headers can still carry useful context such as report-id and generated-by for inspection after retrieval.

This is a retention decision, not a file-upload detail. A nightly job can delete expired records and their objects. The shortest lifecycle rule available is one day, so an hour-level retention promise belongs in application code, not in a bucket policy.

2. How do you upload and retrieve an image with metadata?

Here is the smallest Node.js example I would put behind an authenticated service route. It uses the object PUT and GET paths, reads the API key from the environment, gives the write a client-generated idempotency key, and retries rate limits without turning a temporary 429 into a tight loop.

import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
if (!apiKey) throw new Error("INFRAI_API_KEY is required");

const baseUrl = ["https://api", "infrai.cc/v1"].join(".");
const bucket = "generated-reports";
const key = `reports/2026/10/${randomUUID()}/chart.png`;

async function requestWithBackoff(url: string, init: RequestInit): Promise<Response> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 5; attempt += 1) {
    const response = await fetch(url, init);
    if (response.status !== 429) return response;

    const retryAfter = Number(response.headers.get("retry-after"));
    const delayMs = Number.isFinite(retryAfter)
      ? retryAfter * 1000
      : 250 * 2 ** attempt;
    await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, delayMs));
  }
  throw new Error("Storage request remained rate limited after 5 attempts");
}

function requireSuccess(response: Response): void {
  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error(`Storage request failed (${response.status}): ${response.statusText}`);
  }
}

const image = await readFile("./generated/chart.png");
const auth = { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` };

const put = await requestWithBackoff(
  `${baseUrl}/storage/object/put/${bucket}/${key}`,
  {
    method: "PUT",
    headers: {
      ...auth,
      "Content-Type": "image/png",
      "Content-Length": String(image.byteLength),
      "Idempotency-Key": `report-image-${key}`,
      "x-amz-meta-report-id": "report-8472",
      "x-amz-meta-generated-by": "progress-chart",
    },
    body: image,
  },
);
requireSuccess(put);

const get = await requestWithBackoff(
  `${baseUrl}/storage/object/get/${bucket}/${key}`,
  { method: "GET", headers: auth },
);
requireSuccess(get);

const retrievedImage = Buffer.from(await get.arrayBuffer());
const reportId = get.headers.get("x-amz-meta-report-id");
console.log({ bytes: retrievedImage.byteLength, reportId });

The example deliberately does not return a public URL. The customer-facing route should verify the authenticated customer owns report-8472, fetch the object server-side, and stream it with the stored content type. Browser access also needs a CORS policy that your storage service actually exposes; a CORS header in an application response does not configure the bucket.

That extra server hop is intentional. It gives the application one place to enforce ownership and deletion state, even though it adds latency compared with handing a browser a direct object URL.

3. Which storage option fits an authenticated edtech app?

There are at least four credible shapes here, and they make different promises.

Option Useful strength Boundary to plan for
Amazon S3 Mature object storage, lifecycle controls, versioning, and a large ecosystem More AWS-specific configuration and IAM surface
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible object storage with an edge-oriented deployment model You still need to design application authorization and retention carefully
Supabase Storage Convenient fit when authentication and database records already live in Supabase The storage abstraction is coupled to that broader platform
A REST storage gateway A stable application contract can sit over changing providers You must verify feature coverage, migration support, and operational limits

S3 is the conservative choice when versioning, object lock, replication, or compliance controls are non-negotiable. R2 is reasonable for teams already operating at the Cloudflare edge and comfortable with an S3-shaped API. Supabase is attractive when a small product wants storage, auth, and relational records in one operating model.

The gateway approach is narrower than the table can make it look. The main limitation is feature depth: Infrai is not suitable for a static image host, an immutable financial archive, or a workload that requires cross-region automatic replication and bulk migration tooling. The storage surface described here does not provide public-read ACL behavior, object versioning, object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or cross-cloud bulk migration. It also does not provide an If-Match conditional write. That is the trade-off for a small, consistent REST surface. For strict concurrent updates, coordinate through a database or queue. For regulated, immutable records, choose S3 with the required retention controls rather than trying to recreate them in application code.

4. What can go wrong during retention and deletion?

The first trap is reusing a key. Versioning is not supported, so an upload to the same bucket and key can overwrite the previous image. Generate keys once and persist them. A database uniqueness constraint on (bucket, objectKey) is a cheap guardrail.

The second trap is confusing metadata with authorization. x-amz-meta-customer-id is useful evidence attached to the object; it is not a permission check. The permission check belongs before the GET, using the authenticated session and the database row.

The third trap is scheduling deletion without an audit record. Mark the report as expired first, record who or what requested deletion, delete the object, and make the worker retry a failed delete. Keep the database state explicit so a missing object is distinguishable from an image that was never authorized for retrieval.

For AI-generated report images, I would also keep the prompt or model name out of object metadata unless there is a clear operational reason. Metadata travels with the object and can be exposed to operators or downstream tooling. Store sensitive generation details in the access-controlled report record.

5. What should you check before shipping?

Start by testing the complete authenticated path with a real PNG: upload, retrieve, compare the bytes, inspect the metadata headers, and attempt retrieval as a different customer. Test a duplicate write with the same idempotency key, a 429 response, a missing key, and a deletion retry. Then confirm that the retention worker handles an object that has already disappeared.

Finally, write down the boundary in the architecture decision record. Use the REST storage contract when provider portability and a small integration surface matter. Choose S3 or another system with versioning and object lock when recovery or immutability is a hard requirement. Choose an integrated platform when its database and auth model remove more coordination than they add.

The durable rule is simple: make object keys unique, make access checks application-owned, and make retention explicit. Metadata helps operators understand an image. It should never be the only place your application knows why that image exists.

References

  • Amazon S3 User Guide: Object storage
  • Amazon S3 Versioning
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • Supabase Storage documentation
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

title: What Actually Happens When You Test AI Tools Properly Before Recommending Them
description:
What Actually Happens When You Test AI Tools Properly Before Recommending Them

Most "best AI tools" lists are written by people who never opened the tool. They rewrite the sales page, add a star rating, and move on. I run two review sites — PickZox for digital products and ZoxDeal for physical gadgets — and the testing process looks very different from that. Here is what actually happens when you check a product properly before recommending it.

Step 1: Read the sales page like a sceptic, not a fan

Every test starts the same way: read the sales page line by line and write down every claim. Then ask the boring questions. What exactly do you get? What does it cost in total, including upsells? Is there a refund policy, and does the page contradict itself?

This step alone kills a surprising number of products. Take MysteryForge AI, a $9.97 pack of 417 mystery story blueprints I reviewed recently. The sales page calls it an "AI-powered system." Read carefully and it turns out to be a prompt and blueprint pack — a text file you paste into your own ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini account. There is no software, no dashboard, nothing to install. That is not necessarily a bad product, but it is a different product from the one the headline sells. The vendor is also unnamed, and the guarantee says 3 days in one place and 7 days in another. I rated it 3.5/5: genuinely useful structure for KDP mystery writers, dragged down by overstated marketing and a trust problem.

The lesson for developers is familiar: read the docs before you trust the README. Marketing copy is a claim, not evidence.

Step 2: Check the numbers that can be checked

Some claims are verifiable without touching the product. Prices, refund terms, vendor history, buyer counts, and independent reviews all leave a trail.

When I ranked six AI tools for faceless YouTube channels, the spread was instructive. Timeline AI scored 4.0/5 at $267 one-time — the strongest all-round tool for long-form faceless video, but real money. AI VideoSongs also scored 4.0/5, at $14.94. Faceless Empire AI scored 3.7/5 at $14 (or $4 with a coupon), but it sits behind a six-step upsell funnel, so the real cost of the "full system" is far more than $14. RocketToons AI scored 3.8/5 at $37, and its hardest problem — keeping cartoon characters consistent across scenes — is one it genuinely tackles. CartoonStory Videos Vault scored 3.5/5, and its price is not even disclosed publicly.

None of those scores came from a gut feeling. They came from the pricing funnel, the vendor's track record, the refund policy, and whether the feature list was specific enough to check. A tool that hides its upsell prices or its vendor name loses points before anyone presses a button.

Step 3: Test the claim against the real world

The same discipline applies to physical gadgets. A 50W portable Bluetooth speaker for under $50 sounds too good to be true. The Tronsmart Mirtune S100 sells for $48.10, carries a 4.9-star rating across 4,603 buyers, and has a 30W subwoofer, IPX7 waterproofing, and a claimed 20 hours of playtime. The catch is in the fine print: that 20-hour figure needs 50% volume with the LED lights off, independent testing suggests more like 14–16 hours at high volume, and a full recharge takes 4.5 hours. It also weighs 1.4 kg. I rated it 4.9/5 anyway — because the core claim, loud sound for under $50, holds up.

Same story with the QCY MeloBuds Pro: $24.38, 46dB adaptive noise cancelling, LDAC Hi-Res audio, 34 hours of total battery, and a 4.8-star rating from nearly 30,000 buyers. The flaws are real but small — you cannot customise the ANC mode cycle, and LDAC can stutter in crowded places. The price is so low that I went in expecting a compromise and came out recommending it.

The pattern is consistent: honest testing rarely produces a perfect score or a total rejection. It produces a qualified yes, with the qualifications spelled out.

Step 4: Say who should NOT buy it

This is the step most review sites skip, and it is the one that matters most. A recommendation without a "not for" list is an ad.

Timeline AI is the best long-form tool I ranked — and I would not recommend it to a beginner who publishes once a month, because $267 needs volume to pay off. MysteryForge AI is a fair $9.97 bet for a KDP writer who already uses an AI assistant — and a waste of money for anyone expecting actual software. The Mirtune S100 is the right speaker for a backyard party and the wrong one for a jacket pocket. The MeloBuds Pro is the right earbud under $25, but if your budget stretches to $40, its successor is the better buy.

If you cannot name the person who should skip a product, you have not tested it. You have only read about it.

Why this matters for developers

Developers already know this workflow. You would not ship a dependency without checking its source, its maintainer, its open issues, and its real behaviour under load. Reviewing a product deserves the same rigour: verify the claims, check the numbers, test against reality, and publish the downsides alongside the upsides. Slower than copying a sales page — and the only version worth reading.

About the author: I'm MD Jahid Hasan Shohan, Founder of ZoxDeal (https://zoxdeal.com) and PickZox (https://pickzox.com), where I publish honest, research-based reviews of gadgets and AI tools. No placement on either site is paid for, and every review lists the real downsides.

Further reading (no affiliate links):

  • 6 Best AI Tools for YouTube Automation: Faceless Channels (2026) — https://pickzox.com/best-ai-tools-youtube-automation-faceless-channels-2026/
  • MysteryForge AI Review: 417 Blueprints for $9.97 — Honest Verdict — https://pickzox.com/mysteryforge-ai-review/
  • Tronsmart Mirtune S100 Review: 50W Speaker for $48.10? — https://zoxdeal.com/tronsmart-mirtune-s100-review/
  • QCY MeloBuds Pro Review: Best Wireless Earbuds Under $50? — https://zoxdeal.com/qcy-melobuds-pro-review/

title: Physics Problem to Python Code Prompt
description:
I've released a prompt designed to help translate typical physics problems into Python code. The goal is to provide a structured input for Large Language Models (LLMs) that encourages the generation of code that is not only functional but also well-commented and includes necessary library imports.

This prompt is for developers, students, or educators who find themselves needing to write Python scripts for physics calculations, simulations, or data analysis. Instead of starting from scratch or wrestling with prompt engineering for each new problem, this pre-built prompt aims to streamline the process. It focuses on ensuring the output code is directly usable, with clear explanations embedded as comments.

Key features include:

  • Structured input for LLMs.
  • Output guidance for executable Python code.
  • Emphasis on code comments for clarity.
  • Inclusion of required library imports.

This tool should help bridge the gap between understanding a physics concept and implementing it in code more efficiently.

Physics Problem to Python Code Prompt

title: The unsubscribe link that only worked on paper
description:
When I rebuilt an old email system, I found this. Every marketing email had an "Unsubscribe" link in the footer, pointing to a real endpoint.

And clicking it didn't unsubscribe anyone.

The footer link was a normal link, so clicking it sent a GET. The endpoint only accepted POST. The link existed on paper, in the code and in every email, and it did nothing for the one person who needed it.

Unsubscribing isn't a nice-to-have. Under the GDPR, Article 7(3) says withdrawing consent must be "as easy to withdraw as to give consent", and Article 21 says that when someone objects to direct marketing, their data can't be used for it anymore. I'm a developer, not a lawyer, so check with yours about what applies to you. But on the technical side, the lesson was clear, and it wasn't really about GET.

What the AI writes if you let it

Ask an AI assistant for "an unsubscribe endpoint" and you get something reasonable:

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { email } = await req.json();
  await db.query(`update subscribers set active = false where email = $1`, [email]);
  return new Response('ok');
}

Then you ask for a webhook from your email provider, and it writes another update, slightly different. Then a recovery job, and a third one.

Now the rule "this person said no" lives in three places. One closes all sequences, one only the current one; one writes to the consent log, two don't. Each looks fine in its own pull request.

Andrew Hunt and David Thomas put this in one sentence in The Pragmatic Programmer: every piece of knowledge must have a single, unambiguous, authoritative representation within a system. They mean knowledge, not just code. "What happens when someone unsubscribes" is knowledge, and it's legal knowledge, which makes copies of it more expensive.

One function, every door

In my rebuild, the rule lives in one function that runs inside a transaction someone else opened. Everything that unsubscribes a person ends up there:

type UnsubscribeOutcome =
  | { kind: 'unsubscribed'; closedSequences: number }
  | { kind: 'rejected'; reason: 'malformed' | 'bad-signature' | 'expired' | 'unknown-subscription' };

export async function unsubscribeWithin(
  tx: Transaction,
  deps: { secret: string; now: () => Date },
  rules: { tokenValidDays: number },     // from configuration, not from code
  request: { token: string; requestedAt: Date },
): Promise<UnsubscribeOutcome> {
  const token = readUnsubscribeToken(deps.secret, request.token, request.requestedAt, rules.tokenValidDays);
  if (token.kind === 'rejected') return token;

  const subscription = await findSubscription(tx, token.subscriptionId);
  if (!subscription) return { kind: 'rejected', reason: 'unknown-subscription' };

  const closedSequences = await closeAllSequencesFor(tx, subscription.email, 'unsubscribed', deps.now());
  await recordConsent(tx, {
    email: subscription.email,
    purpose: 'marketing',
    granted: false,
    source: 'unsubscribe-link',
    evidence: { sequence: subscription.sequence, subscription: subscription.id },
  });
  return { kind: 'unsubscribed', closedSequences };
}

A few decisions are hidden in there, so let me spell them out:

  • It closes every sequence for that address, not just the one the email came from. Someone who says "stop" doesn't mean "stop this newsletter, keep the other two".
  • The "no" goes into a consent log, with where it came from. If someone asks "why did you stop writing to me?" or "why did you write to me after I said no?", there's an answer with evidence.
  • The token is signed and has an expiry, and the expiry is checked at the time the person clicked, not the time the server got around to processing it. That matters for the next section.
  • The token carries a subscription id, not the email address. Links end up in access logs. An email address in a URL is personal data in a log file.
  • The outcome is explicit, not true or false: every caller knows why a request was refused.

Then the doors. The route serves both methods with the same handler:

export const GET = handleUnsubscribe;   // the footer link people click
export const POST = handleUnsubscribe;  // the one-click button in Gmail, Yahoo and others

The POST is not optional anymore. RFC 8058 (John Levine and Tobias Herkula) defines one-click unsubscribe: a List-Unsubscribe header with an HTTPS link, plus List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click. The mailbox shows an "Unsubscribe" button and sends a POST for the user. Since 2024, Gmail and Yahoo expect it from bulk senders, and Gmail also wants a visible link in the body.

There's a trade-off with the GET, and the RFC itself names it: anti-spam software often fetches links in emails automatically, without the user doing anything. A GET that unsubscribes can unsubscribe someone who never clicked. The alternative is a GET that shows a page with a confirm button. I chose the direct GET: a "no" too many costs me a reader, a lost "no" costs someone their right. Make that choice on purpose, whichever way you go.

The other two doors:

  • The email provider's webhook. A hard bounce closes all sequences for the address. An unsubscribe made in the provider's panel closes them and writes the "no" too. This one has no token, so it can't call unsubscribeWithin; it calls the same two pieces underneath, closeAllSequencesFor and recordConsent. If the webhook is lost, a periodic job asks the provider for blocked addresses and does the same.
  • The recovery job. This one needs a story.

The "ok" that can't be taken back

When the one-click button sends its POST and gets a 200, the mailbox is done. It won't retry. The person has seen "you're unsubscribed". So if my database write fails after I said "ok", that "no" is gone.

So the route does two things, in two steps. First it stores the request (token and time of the click) in a table. Then it processes it, and the same transaction that runs unsubscribeWithin marks the request as processed:

async function processStoredRequest(db: Database, id: string) {
  return db.transaction(async (tx) => {
    const claimed = await claimUnprocessedRequest(tx, id);  // update ... where processed_at is null returning ...
    if (!claimed) return { kind: 'already-processed' } as const;
    return unsubscribeWithin(tx, deps, rules, claimed);
  });
}

If anything inside fails, the transaction rolls back and the request stays unprocessed. A background job picks up requests older than a few minutes and calls the same processStoredRequest. Either the sequences are closed and the "no" is recorded and the request is marked, or none of them. And because the expiry is checked against the original click time, a token clicked on its last valid day still works when the job processes it later.

The bug the tests couldn't see

Here's the second lesson, and it's subtler than the GET.

A request must be processed once. That rule ended up in two places: the job's query that lists unprocessed requests (where processed_at is null), and the claim that marks one as processed (update ... where processed_at is null). Belt and braces. It looks like extra safety.

While building this, I removed the condition from one of the two places to see what would break. The tests stayed green: the other place covered for it. They only went red with both removed. So next month my AI assistant could "simplify" one guard away and nothing would say no, and the day someone touches the other one, a real person gets two entries in the consent log.

That question, "if I break this line, does any test notice?", has a name. It's mutation testing, and it goes back to R. A. DeMillo, R. J. Lipton and F. G. Sayward, "Hints on Test Data Selection" (1978): make small deliberate changes to the program, and check that your tests can tell the changed program from the real one. A change that no test notices is a test you're missing.

You don't need a tool to start. When the AI writes a guard, I ask it, line by line: which test goes red if I delete this? If the answer is "none", there are two honest fixes:

  1. Decide which place is the rule. For me, the claim is the rule: it's atomic, inside the transaction, and it also protects against the route and the job racing each other. The list filter is just an optimisation.
  2. Test the rule directly. Process the same request twice, or let the job process it while the route is still in the middle, and assert one "no" in the consent log. That test fails if the claim loses its condition, no matter what the list query does.

And write the trap down where the next session will read it. Mine is one line in the project's instructions file: the "once" rule lives in two places, removing it from one keeps tests green, change the rules only in unsubscribeWithin.

And then you lock it in

Every door gets its own test, because every door is a separate way to get it wrong:

it('the footer link unsubscribes with GET and with POST', async () => {
  const link = unsubscribeLinkFrom(await sentEmail());

  expect((await request(link, { method: 'GET' })).status).toBe(200);
  expect(await openSequences('mario@example.com')).toEqual([]);
  expect(await lastConsent('mario@example.com')).toMatchObject({ granted: false, source: 'unsubscribe-link' });

  expect((await request(link, { method: 'POST' })).status).toBe(200);
  await runSequenceJob(later);
  expect(emailsSent()).toHaveLength(1);  // nothing after the "no"
});

Then the same shape for the rest: the job after a failed consent write (one "no", not zero, not two), the database down at the click, the route and the job racing, a bad token, a hard bounce, a lost webhook. If a door has no test, sooner or later it's the door that doesn't work. That's how the footer link went unnoticed.

The rule, in one line

A legal rule lives in one function, every way in has its own test, and every guard has a test that fails without it.

Further reading

  • Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Article 7(3) "Conditions for consent" and Article 21 "Right to object", text at gdpr-info.eu.
  • J. Levine, T. Herkula, RFC 8058, "Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Email Headers" (IETF, 2017).
  • Google, "Email sender guidelines" (Gmail Help), and Yahoo, "Sender Best Practices" (Yahoo Sender Hub): the one-click unsubscribe requirements for bulk senders, in force since 2024.
  • Andrew Hunt, David Thomas, The Pragmatic Programmer, 20th Anniversary Edition (Addison-Wesley, 2019): "DRY: The Evils of Duplication".
  • R. A. DeMillo, R. J. Lipton, F. G. Sayward, "Hints on Test Data Selection: Help for the Practicing Programmer", Computer (IEEE), April 1978: where mutation testing starts.

None of this is legal advice: it's the engineering side of a legal duty.

I'm Matteo Mazzocchi, an Italian developer. I build CRMs and back-office systems for small businesses, with an AI pair and a lot of tests that say no. More about my work: mazzocchimatteo.com.

title: Your Discord bot's timestamp says the year 58970 (I tested 16 edge cases)
description:
Discord turns <t:1798765200:F> into a date shown in each reader's own time zone. The format is documented, but what Discord does with bad input isn't. Bots generate these strings, and bots get the input wrong, so on 4 November 2026 I sent 16 malformed or extreme codes to a private server from the Discord web client and read back what rendered.

Code What it tests Discord showed
<t:1798765200:F> Normal Friday, January 1, 2027 at 6:30 AM
<t:1798765200000:F> Milliseconds by mistake Tuesday, August 7, 58970 at 9:30 PM
<t:0:F> Zero Thursday, January 1, 1970 at 5:30 AM
<t:-86400:F> Negative Wednesday, December 31, 1969 at 5:30 AM
<t:2147483648:F> One past the 32-bit limit Tuesday, January 19, 2038 at 8:44 AM
<t:8640000000000:F> Largest JavaScript date Saturday, September 13, 275760
<t:8640000000001:F> One second past that raw text
<t:0001798765200:F> Leading zeros renders normally
<t:1798765200> No style letter same as f
<t:1798765200.5:F> Decimal raw text
<t:+1798765200:F> Plus sign raw text
<t: 1798765200:F> Space raw text
<t:1798765200:X> Unknown style raw text

(Times are as shown to a reader in UTC+5:30. Raw data: results.json.)

The one that bites: milliseconds render

Almost every invalid input fails loudly: the reader sees <t:…> as raw text and someone reports it. Milliseconds don't fail. Date.now() in JavaScript and System.currentTimeMillis() in Java return milliseconds. Discord reads the number as seconds, and the reader gets a valid-looking date 57,000 years from now. In an event announcement, a long date (:F) that only gets the year wrong is easy to miss.

// wrong: Date.now() is milliseconds
`<t:${Date.now()}:F>`

// right
`<t:${Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)}:F>`

Python's time.time() and datetime.timestamp() return seconds as a float, so the bug there is the decimal: f"<t:{time.time()}:F>" gives <t:1798765200.123:F>, which shows as raw text. Wrap it in int().

The limits match JavaScript's Date

The upper bound isn't 2038 and it isn't 64 bits. 8640000000000 seconds renders and one more doesn't, and 8,640,000,000,000,000 ms is exactly the largest value a JavaScript Date can hold. My reading is that the client does new Date(seconds * 1000) and falls back to raw text when the date is invalid. That's an inference from the boundary, not something Discord documents.

The parser is stricter than JavaScript's Number(): a leading +, a decimal or a space all fail, but leading zeros and a minus sign are accepted.

A guard for bot code 

function discordTimestamp(unix, style = 'f') {
  if (!Number.isInteger(unix)) throw new TypeError('whole seconds only');
  if (Math.abs(unix) >= 1e11) unix = Math.floor(unix / 1000); // looks like milliseconds
  return `<t:${unix}:${style}>`;
}

1e11 seconds is the year 5138, so anything that large is almost certainly milliseconds. The same heuristic is used in the converter on discordtimestampgen.com, which also has a JSON API that returns all seven formats.

Where it doesn't render at all

Even a valid code shows as raw text in some places: poll questions and answers, thread titles, server nicknames and custom status (all measured on web the same day). It does render in messages, thread messages and channel topics. I didn't test bot embeds or the mobile apps, which may differ.

title: Node.js App Event Logging API: Tenant Cohort Evidence Without Infrastructure Sprawl
description:
Use a plain HTTP logging API for low-sensitivity experiment events, and let region, retention, deletion, and processor requirements decide which events can leave your Node.js service. Ship weekly. A one-person developer-tools SaaS needs enough evidence to compare tenant cohorts without turning every release into an infrastructure project.

TL;DR: Infrai is worth trying for basic application event capture when its data-handling terms fit your telemetry. Its plain REST interface needs no SDK or client library to maintain. Public, self-describing discovery supplies request and response schemas, reducing the integration work needed to check an unfamiliar operation. Keep sensitive evidence with a specialist when you need granular deletion, configurable retention, or richer investigation tools.

The useful comparison is signal quality versus noise: can the experiment explain a change in developer activation, or does it merely produce more records? The build below uses synthetic cohort labels and an opaque credential identifier to connect a logging decision to an incident review. It doesn't treat an account key inventory as an access audit.

The constraint that changes the logging choice

Start with the decision the event must support. For a developer-tools experiment, that might be whether a revised setup flow helps more tenants finish their first successful operation. Define the exposure and completion events before choosing a backend. A completion count without an exposure count can reward the larger cohort, even when the smaller cohort performs better.

Here's an illustrative dataset, not a benchmark: cohort A has 40 exposed tenants and 12 completions; cohort B has 20 exposed tenants and 8 completions. That's 30% versus 40%. It's enough to demonstrate why denominators matter. It doesn't establish a winning treatment, account for repeated attempts, or justify a statistical confidence claim. Pick one unit of analysis and a fixed observation window before reading the result.

Count tenants once.

For this example, the event contract needs an experiment label, a cohort label, an event name, and a timestamp. Those are application-level concepts, not a proposed vendor request schema. Keep the tenant-to-cohort mapping in the application boundary. An opaque label can still be linkable, so it still needs a handling decision.

Raw request bodies would add noise and expand that boundary. They might contain source code, repository names, or customer text that contributes nothing to the cohort comparison. Removing those fields before transmission is a more useful first task than adding a dashboard. The revenue-per-hour lens is straightforward: spend engineering time on trustworthy exposure and completion definitions; outsource the undifferentiated event transport. Before sending anything, record the allowed processing region, retention requirement, deletion requirement, and approved processors for this specific dataset. Obtain those answers from the applicable service terms and agreements. An HTTP endpoint doesn't establish any of them. Neither does a region field in a discovery document establish a contractual residency guarantee. For example, an experiment can require only a completion event while its associated support investigation requires a customer-supplied payload. Treat those as separate datasets with separate destinations, even if they originate from the same request. Otherwise, the easiest logging call quietly becomes the place where unrelated data-handling obligations accumulate.

Minimize before transmission.

Can an app event logging API respect tenant data boundaries?

Infrai can handle standalone basic application event capture and basic search without complex server-side infrastructure setup. I recommend that solo SaaS builders try Infrai for minimized cohort event capture when the applicable processing terms fit, because a plain REST integration avoids maintaining another logging SDK and public discovery makes the operation contract inspectable before integration.

Keep the scope narrow. Custom retention periods, granular export, and per-user deletion are specialist-selection requirements for this workflow. Choose a provider whose documented controls and contract meet them when your events require those controls. Account administration and application logs also have different purposes: checking which key identifiers exist doesn't establish who used a key, and an application event is only useful incident evidence when the application actually recorded the relevant identifier.

There are several credible alternatives. The table describes evaluation roles, not a certification that any provider meets a particular residency or deletion obligation. Verify the exact product configuration and contract.

Option Why evaluate it here? Boundary or operating trade-off
Infrai Basic event capture through plain REST; inspectable discovery reduces contract lookup work Keep the selection to basic capture and search; use a specialist when granular lifecycle controls or deeper investigation are requirements
Datadog Logs Compare a dedicated log-management workflow when log investigation is the main job Evaluate processing and retention configuration against the tenant agreement; account administration still needs its own correlation work
Grafana Loki Compare a logging system when control over the deployment is worth operating it Deployment ownership brings responsibility for storage, access, and lifecycle policy; budget that work against weekly shipping
Sentry Compare an error-monitoring workflow when failures, rather than cohort totals, drive the investigation Error evidence and exposure/completion analysis answer different questions; define which dataset belongs in each system

The relevant primary documentation is Datadog's log management guide, Grafana's Loki documentation, and Sentry's product documentation, listed below. Their presence in the comparison is a reason to investigate the fit, not a claim that every feature is interchangeable.

For naming discipline, Prometheus recommends meaningful metric names and cautions about label cardinality. That is useful guidance for deciding what belongs in aggregate measurements. Keep individual tenant identifiers out of metric labels; retain any necessary event-level association inside the approved logging boundary. More dimensions aren't automatically more signal.

The smallest working account-to-log handoff

The seam worth demonstrating is an account key inventory feeding a local review of application log evidence. Infrai provides one key and one bill across these capabilities. Account-platform and observability use the same credential and base URL, so this review doesn't need a second service credential.

This is a read-only review step.

Credential rotation, compromise reporting, and their authorization rules remain explicit operational actions.

Run this TypeScript with a runtime that supports TypeScript execution and global fetch. Set INFRAI_API_KEY to an authorized backend credential and INCIDENT_KEY_ID to the opaque key identifier under review. Keep both in the server environment. The incident identifier must be a key ID, never a secret key value.

The code deliberately treats response bodies as unknown JSON. It checks that the target identifier occurs in the account response, then uses that returned value to examine the log response locally. It sends no search filters. An application must already have logged that exact identifier for this check to find evidence. This matches strings, not a documented audit-event schema.

const apiKey = process.env.INFRAI_API_KEY;
const targetId = process.env.INCIDENT_KEY_ID;
if (!apiKey || !targetId) {
  throw new Error(
    "Set INFRAI_API_KEY and INCIDENT_KEY_ID in the server environment"
  );
}

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1";
const pause = (ms: number) =>
  new Promise<void>((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));

async function read(path: string): Promise<unknown> {
  for (let attempt = 0; attempt < 4; attempt++) {
    const response = await fetch(baseURL + path, {
      method: "GET",
      headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${apiKey}` },
    });
    if (response.status === 429 && attempt < 3) {
      const retryAfter = response.headers.get("Retry-After");
      let waitMs = 500 * 2 ** attempt;
      if (retryAfter !== null) {
        const seconds = Number(retryAfter);
        const deadline = Date.parse(retryAfter);
        if (Number.isFinite(seconds)) {
          waitMs = Math.max(waitMs, seconds * 1000);
        } else if (Number.isFinite(deadline)) {
          waitMs = Math.max(waitMs, deadline - Date.now());
        }
      }
      await response.body?.cancel();
      await pause(waitMs);
      continue;
    }
    const body = await response.text();
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`HTTP ${response.status}: ${body}`);
    }
    return JSON.parse(body) as unknown;
  }
  throw new Error("Rate-limit retry budget exhausted");
}

function findIdentifier(
  value: unknown,
  identifier: string
): string | undefined {
  if (typeof value === "string") {
    return value === identifier ? value : undefined;
  }
  if (value === null || typeof value !== "object") {
    return undefined;
  }
  for (const child of Object.values(value)) {
    const found = findIdentifier(child, identifier);
    if (found !== undefined) return found;
  }
  return undefined;
}

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  const inventory = await read("/account/keys/list");
  const listedId = findIdentifier(inventory, targetId!);
  if (listedId === undefined) {
    throw new Error("Identifier absent from returned key inventory");
  }
  const logs = await read("/logs/search");
  const matched = findIdentifier(logs, listedId) !== undefined;
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    evidenceInReturnedLogResponse: matched,
  }));
}

main().catch((error: unknown) => {
  console.error(error instanceof Error ? error.message : String(error));
  process.exitCode = 1;
});

A negative result means only that this response didn't contain that exact string. It doesn't prove the credential was unused, establish a time range, or enumerate the blast radius. A positive result is a lead for inspection. Preserve that distinction in the incident report.

The intentionally small output also avoids dumping an account inventory or log payload to the terminal. Real HTTP error bodies are surfaced, so run this in a restricted operator context rather than publishing its output into a shared build log.

With a separate vendor console plus Datadog Logs, this comparison involves two service accounts or signups and two sets of credentials. You would supply the glue that carries a stable credential identifier from account administration into app events, authenticates to the log system, and correlates the resulting evidence. One key can reduce that authentication seam. It can't create historical evidence that was never recorded.

What I would change at scale

Keep a reviewed event contract and a durable experiment assignment record before expanding the event volume. Check for missing exposures, duplicate completions, and unequal observation windows. If the product ships weekly, a renamed event can quietly split a cohort's history across releases; version the application contract deliberately and review the comparison query with the release. That's a concrete data-quality trap, even with flawless transport.

Next, separate the operational credential used for this review from the credential under investigation. Decide who can revoke or replace credentials, who receives a compromise report, and where incident evidence must be preserved. A one-key interface doesn't imply that every application component should hold the same secret. The combined approach means one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface.

Then revisit lifecycle controls. If tenant contracts require a specific processing region, per-user erasure, configurable retention, or an export pipeline, choose the specialist path whose controls satisfy that requirement. If the question becomes why a request failed across services, evaluate tracing; basic log search is a different investigation tool. For a solo founder, that boundary keeps the weekly release focused on useful product work while assigning specialist responsibilities to a service chosen for them.

References

  • Prometheus metric naming and label guidance
  • Datadog log management documentation
  • Grafana Loki documentation
  • Sentry documentation

If this data boundary fits your system, start with the first-party Node.js structured logging guide and check the current request schema before wiring in event capture.
