Against Dragonfly, HotKV was ahead on all nine commands, from 1.85 times (LPUSH) to 4.09 times (GET).

How to read the ratios

A throughput figure from a load test is a floor when the load generators are the limit. If a load generator is at 100 percent CPU, the server may have been able to take more. The figure then shows only that it took at least this much. A ratio between two floors is not exact, because either side could be higher.

We flag every figure where the main load generator ran above 85 percent CPU. These were GET, SETNX and INCR for HotKV, and GET, SET, SETNX, INCR, SADD, HSET and APPEND for Redis and Valkey. On those figures, read the ratio as a rough size and not a precise one.

On SADD and HSET, HotKV's figure is not flagged but Redis's and Valkey's are. Their true throughput may be higher, and HotKV's lead smaller than shown. The same applies to APPEND, where it would make their lead over HotKV larger than shown.

RPUSH and LPUSH have no flag for any server, so they give the cleanest comparison. HotKV was 1.3 to 1.6 times ahead of Redis and Valkey on them.

What the results show

Three things stand out in the table, and the first is about Redis and Valkey rather than HotKV.

Redis and Valkey scale well as clusters

With 120 single-thread processes, Redis served 57 million GETs per second and 118 million INCRs per second across three servers. That confirms the cluster layout suits them. It is also why HotKV's margin here is smaller than in our single-instance runs.

Those runs compared a design that uses all cores in one process with products that were not run in the layout they are commonly scaled in. This Redis benchmark gives Redis and Valkey that layout. HotKV's lead over them narrows to between 1.0 and 1.7 times on eight commands.

HotKV had the highest throughput on 8 of 9 commands

The lead was widest on GET and RPUSH against Redis (1.6 times) and on GET against Valkey (1.7 times). On RPUSH and LPUSH the load generators had room for every server, so those figures are limited by the servers. On INCR, HotKV and Redis were level within 1 percent, and the load generators, not the servers, set the limit for all three.

Redis and Valkey were ahead on APPEND

HotKV served 35.0 million APPENDs per second against 41.7 million for Redis and 40.9 million for Valkey. We have not found the reason. APPEND grows the dataset by about 10 GB per second across the cluster, so the run is also a test of memory allocation. A 30-second APPEND run ran the servers out of memory.

We profiled HotKV on APPEND and saw page faults, TLB shootdowns and lock contention. We have not shown which of them accounts for the gap.

Limitations

These are HotKV Ltd's measurements of the versions and configuration above. They are not a claim about any other version, configuration or workload of these products.

The test setup

  • Load generators near their limit. Many figures are lower bounds, as the section on reading the ratios explains. HotKV's APPEND figure is not one of them, because the load generators were at about 30 percent CPU with it.
  • Layouts we chose. We ran Redis and Valkey as one single-thread process per core and did not tune either product beyond that. Other layouts or tuning could change their figures. If you think a setting here disadvantages a product, tell us and we will check it and publish the result.
  • Two runs, one region. Each figure is the median of two 15-second runs on one set of machines in one region. We did not measure variation between machines or days.

What was not measured

  • Latency. We measured throughput only here. A separate Redis latency benchmark measures latency.
  • Persistence, replication and failover. All servers ran with persistence off and no replicas.
  • Other setups. Three servers and one workload shape. A larger cluster, other value sizes or other pipeline depths can change the ratios.

Redis, Valkey and Dragonfly are trademarks of their respective owners. They are named only to identify the software we measured, and this implies no sponsorship, endorsement or affiliation.

Reproduce it

The sweep script, the exact command sequence, the host tuning and every raw result are in the benchmark repository. The sweep script is harness/cluster_bench_sweep.sh. A chart of the same figures is on the performance page.

Try it yourself

HotKV Cloud runs HotKV clusters for you. Start on HotKV Cloud, or talk to sales to benchmark a cluster against your own workload.

Frequently asked questions

Why run a Redis benchmark as a cluster?

Redis and Valkey run commands on one thread per process, so a single process cannot use a large machine. They are commonly scaled across cores by running many processes as a cluster. A cluster benchmark measures each product in a layout like that, so the comparison does not rest on a single-instance deployment alone.

Did HotKV have the highest throughput in cluster mode?

On 8 of 9 commands, yes. HotKV led Redis by 1.0 to 1.6 times and Valkey by 1.1 to 1.7 times, and Dragonfly by 1.85 to 4.09 times. Redis and Valkey were ahead on APPEND. On INCR, HotKV and Redis were level within 1 percent, and the load generators set the limit.

Why were Redis and Valkey ahead on APPEND?

We do not know yet. APPEND grows the dataset by about 10 GB per second across the cluster, so the run also tests memory allocation. A profile of HotKV showed page faults, TLB shootdowns and lock contention, but we have not shown which of them accounts for the gap.

What is the pipeline-prefetch setting?

It makes HotKV look ahead in a client's pipeline and ask the CPU for the memory the next commands will read, so those reads overlap. It changes no reply. It is off by default, and HotKV ran with it on in this benchmark.

Can I reproduce this Redis benchmark?

Yes. The sweep script, the exact command sequence, the host tuning and every raw result are in the benchmark repository, and the same figures are charted on the performance page. You need three servers, one or more load generators and the four products installed by the harness.

Does this replace the single-instance results?

No. The two answer different questions. A single-instance run shows what one server process does with a whole machine. A cluster run shows what three machines do when each product is laid out as a cluster. Both are on the performance page.

title: Python में long polling से ऐसा Telegram बॉट कैसे बनाएँ जो सिर्फ़ आपको जवाब दे
description:
Telegram बॉट आपकी अपनी मशीन पर चल रही स्क्रिप्ट या AI एजेंट के लिए एक सुविधाजनक रिमोट कंट्रोल है। यह हर फ़ोन पर चलता है, आपको अपना ऐप नहीं बनाना पड़ता, और किसी पब्लिक सर्वर की ज़रूरत नहीं होती। दिक्कत यह है कि बॉट पब्लिक होता है। कोई भी उसका यूज़रनेम ढूँढकर उसे मैसेज भेज सकता है, और टोकन सिर्फ़ यह साबित करता है कि आपकी स्क्रिप्ट ही वह बॉट है; यह नहीं बताता कि लिख कौन रहा है। osFoundry डेस्कटॉप ऐप में अपने एजेंटों के लिए ऐसा ही एक ब्रिज है, जो Rust में लिखा है (telegram_bridge.rs)। नीचे वही डिज़ाइन लगभग 70 लाइन की स्टैंडर्ड-लाइब्रेरी Python में है, Bot API के एक लोकल नकली सर्वर के सामने टेस्ट किया हुआ, और साथ में वह एक लाइन की गलती जिसने शांत बॉट को 183,389 रिक्वेस्ट प्रति मिनट पर पहुँचा दिया।

Webhook की जगह long polling

Telegram मैसेज दो तरीकों से पहुँचाता है। Webhook के लिए एक पब्लिक HTTPS URL चाहिए जिसे Telegram कॉल कर सके। getUpdates को कुछ भी बाहर खोलने की ज़रूरत नहीं: स्क्रिप्ट नए मैसेज माँगती है, और timeout=25 के साथ Telegram रिक्वेस्ट को 25 सेकंड तक खुला रखता है और मैसेज आते ही जवाब देता है। लैपटॉप पर यही सही चुनाव है। कोई पोर्ट नहीं खोलना, कोई टनल नहीं, कोई सर्टिफ़िकेट नहीं।

import json, os, secrets, time, urllib.parse, urllib.request

API = os.environ.get("TG_API", "https://api.telegram.org")
TOKEN = os.environ["TG_TOKEN"]
LONG_POLL = 25
PAIR_TTL = 600

def call(method, params=None, body=None, timeout=40):
    url = f"{API}/bot{TOKEN}/{method}"
    if params:
        url += "?" + urllib.parse.urlencode(params)
    data = json.dumps(body).encode() if body is not None else None
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, data, {"Content-Type": "application/json"})
    with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=timeout) as r:
        return json.load(r)

def send(chat_id, text):
    call("sendMessage", body={"chat_id": chat_id, "text": text[:3900]})

HTTP timeout (40 s) long-poll के रोकने के समय (25 s) से लंबा होना चाहिए। अगर यह छोटा है, तो हर शांत चक्र क्लाइंट-साइड timeout पर खत्म होता है, जो आउटेज जैसा दिखता है। ऐप टोकन को OS कीचेन में रखता है, फ़ाइल में नहीं। Python से keyring.get_password वही काम करता है, और टेस्ट के लिए एनवायरनमेंट वेरिएबल ठीक है।

60 सेकंड की निष्क्रियता में long-poll लूप ने 3 रिक्वेस्ट कीं और हर सेकंड वाले short poll ने 60। रिक्वेस्ट रुकी होने के दौरान जो मैसेज आया, उसे लोकल टेस्ट में 1.5 से 6.3 ms बाद जवाब मिल गया। असली नेटवर्क पर Telegram तक का राउंड ट्रिप इसके ऊपर जुड़ता है।

Pairing: कौन बात कर सकता है

कुछ भी करने से पहले बॉट को पता होना चाहिए कि वह किस व्यक्ति की सेवा कर रहा है। ऐप यह एक बार वाले कोड से करता है। आप मशीन पर "Pair a phone" पर क्लिक करते हैं, वह आठ रैंडम अक्षर दिखाती है, और आप फ़ोन से बॉट को /pair CODE भेजते हैं। 10 मिनट के अंदर जो भी सही कोड भेजे, वही मालिक है।

pending = {}   # code -> created_at
paired = {}    # sender id -> chat id

def begin_pairing():
    code = secrets.token_hex(4).upper()
    pending[code] = time.time()
    return code

कोड secrets से बनता है, समय या बॉट के नाम जैसी अनुमान लगाने लायक चीज़ से नहीं, क्योंकि कोड ही भेजने वाले को अधिकृत करने वाली अकेली चीज़ है। इस्तेमाल होने पर इसे हटा भी दिया जाता है, इसलिए यह सिर्फ़ एक बार चलता है।

जो रखा जाता है वह संख्या वाला from.id है, @username या डिस्प्ले नाम नहीं। इन दोनों को बदला जा सकता है, और छूटा हुआ यूज़रनेम कोई और रजिस्टर कर सकता है। चैट id उसके बगल में रखी जाती है, जिसकी वजह नीचे आती है।

मैसेज के साथ क्या करना है, यह तय करना 

def handle(msg, run_agent):
    text = (msg.get("text") or "").strip()
    sender = msg.get("from", {}).get("id")
    chat = msg["chat"]
    if not text or sender is None:
        return
    words = text.split()
    if words[0] == "/pair" or words[0].startswith("/pair@"):
        if chat.get("type") != "private":
            return send(chat["id"], "Pair with me in a direct message, not in a group.")
        code = words[1].upper() if len(words) > 1 else ""
        created = pending.pop(code, None)
        if created is None or time.time() - created > PAIR_TTL:
            return send(chat["id"], "That code is not valid or has expired.")
        paired[sender] = chat["id"]
        return send(chat["id"], "Paired. Message me and the agent will answer.")
    if text.lower() == "/unpair":
        gone = paired.pop(sender, None) is not None
        return send(chat["id"], "Unpaired." if gone else "You were not paired.")
    if paired.get(sender) != chat["id"] or chat.get("type") != "private":
        return  # silence
    send(chat["id"], run_agent(text))

सुरक्षा तीन नियमों पर टिकी है, और हर नियम ऐप के सोर्स में दर्ज एक ख़ास गड़बड़ी से निकला है।

अनजान भेजने वालों को चुप्पी मिलती है। "you are not paired" जैसा जवाब किसी अजनबी को बता देता है कि बॉट किसी असली व्यक्ति की मशीन से जुड़ा है और उसे कोशिश करते रहने का न्योता देता है। जवाब न देना ऐसे बॉट जैसा दिखता है जिसे कोई चला ही नहीं रहा।

Pairing सिर्फ़ प्राइवेट चैट में चलती है। ग्रुप में जोड़े गए बॉट को ग्रुप के मैसेज मिलते हैं, इसलिए वहाँ pairing से ग्रुप का हर सदस्य एजेंट को निर्देश दे सकता।

Pair किए गए व्यक्ति को सिर्फ़ उसी चैट में जवाब मिलता है जिससे उसने pair किया था। ऐप के कमेंट एक पुराने वर्ज़न का ज़िक्र करते हैं जो भेजने वाले को जाँचता था पर मैसेज जिस भी चैट से आया हो वहीं जवाब देता था। Pair किया हुआ यूज़र जब बॉट को ग्रुप में जोड़ता था, तब एजेंट उस ग्रुप में जवाब दे रहा होता, जहाँ हर कोई मालिक की मशीन पर टूल चला सकता था। अधिकृत करना भेजने वाले के हिसाब से होता है और जवाब एक चैट में जाता है, इसलिए दोनों को साथ में जाँचना ज़रूरी है।

/unpair को उस चैट जाँच से पहले संभाला जाता है, ताकि एक्सेस फ़ोन से हटाया जा सके, जहाँ आप तब होते हैं जब इसकी ज़रूरत पड़ती है।

लूप और offset 

def poll(run_agent):
    offset, failures = 0, 0
    while True:
        try:
            res = call("getUpdates", {"timeout": LONG_POLL, "offset": offset,
                                      "allowed_updates": '["message"]'})
            failures = 0
        except Exception:
            failures += 1
            time.sleep({1: 5, 2: 15, 3: 60}.get(failures, 300))
            continue
        for u in res["result"]:
            offset = max(offset, u["update_id"] + 1)   # even for messages we ignore
            if "message" in u:
                handle(u["message"], run_agent)

offset वह तरीका है जिससे स्क्रिप्ट Telegram को बताती है कि उसने कौन से अपडेट देख लिए हैं। इससे नीचे का सब कुछ कन्फ़र्म होकर हटा दिया जाता है, और इस मान पर या इससे ऊपर का सब कुछ दोबारा भेजा जाता है। उस लाइन का कमेंट ही असली बात है। offset को तभी आगे बढ़ाने का मन करता है जब मैसेज के साथ कुछ कर लिया जाए, क्योंकि वह "प्रोसेस हो गया" जैसा लगता है। लेकिन अजनबी का मैसेज जानबूझकर नज़रअंदाज़ किया जाता है, इसलिए वह कभी कन्फ़र्म नहीं होता, इसलिए अगली कॉल पर तुरंत वापस आ जाता है, क्योंकि एक अपडेट बाकी है और Telegram के पास रिक्वेस्ट रोके रखने की कोई वजह नहीं।

Backoff दूसरी गड़बड़ी के लिए है: रद्द किया हुआ या गलत लिखा टोकन हर रिक्वेस्ट पर फ़ेल होता है, और पूरी रफ़्तार से दोबारा कोशिश करने का मतलब हमेशा के लिए हर कुछ सेकंड में एक 401। 5, 15, 60 और फिर 300 सेकंड की सीढ़ी वही है जो ऐप इस्तेमाल करता है।

टेस्ट में क्या दिखा

लोकल नकली सर्वर getUpdates (offset कन्फ़र्मेशन और timeout होल्ड) और sendMessage लागू करता है और हर कॉल रिकॉर्ड करता है। हर स्थिति में एक मैसेज डाला गया और फिर पढ़ा गया कि बॉट ने क्या भेजा।

मैसेज जवाब
अजनबी: "hi" कोई नहीं
अजनबी: /pair 12345678 That code is not valid or has expired.
मैं, ग्रुप में: /pair CODE Pair with me in a direct message, not in a group.
मैं, DM में: /pair code (छोटे अक्षर) Paired.
अजनबी, मेरा कोड दोबारा इस्तेमाल करते हुए That code is not valid or has expired.
मैं, DM में: एक सवाल एजेंट का जवाब
मैं, ग्रुप में: एक सवाल कोई नहीं
मैं: /unpair, फिर एक सवाल Unpaired., फिर कोई नहीं

फिर चार लूप 60 सेकंड चले, हर एक अपने नकली सर्वर के सामने:

लूप 60 s में getUpdates कॉल
long poll, कोई मैसेज नहीं 3
हर सेकंड short poll, कोई मैसेज नहीं 60
अजनबी का एक मैसेज, हर अपडेट के लिए offset आगे बढ़ाया 4
अजनबी का एक मैसेज, offset सिर्फ़ संभाले गए मैसेज के लिए बढ़ाया 183,389

नकली सर्वर पर, जो उसी मशीन से जवाब देता है, यह बग करीब 3,000 रिक्वेस्ट प्रति सेकंड पर चला। असली API के सामने लूप उतनी तेज़ चलेगा जितना नेटवर्क राउंड ट्रिप इजाज़त दे, हर कॉल पर उसी अजनबी का "hi" दोबारा आता हुआ और कुछ नया कभी न आता हुआ। जिसे आप कभी जवाब नहीं देंगे ऐसे किसी का एक मैसेज इसे शुरू करने के लिए काफ़ी है।

जो छोड़ा गया

असली ब्रिज को जवाबों को Telegram की 4,096 अक्षरों की सीमा के नीचे रखना भी पड़ता है (ऐप 3,900 पर काटता है, अक्षर की सीमा पर, क्योंकि बाइट के हिसाब से काटने पर जापानी अक्षर के बीच में कटाव आ सकता है), और जवाब सादे टेक्स्ट में भेजने पड़ते हैं। Markdown के साथ, अगर कोई तारा या अंडरस्कोर बेमेल हो तो Telegram पूरा मैसेज ठुकरा देता है, और snake_case कोड के बारे में लिखने वाला एजेंट ठीक यही पैदा करता है। सबसे ज़रूरी बात, जो टेक्स्ट आता है वह फ़ोन पकड़ने वाले का लिखा होता है, इसलिए उसे एजेंट तक अविश्वसनीय इनपुट की तरह पहुँचना चाहिए, ईमेल की तरह। Pairing तय करती है कि एजेंट से कौन बात कर सकता है; यह जो कहा गया है उसे सुरक्षित नहीं बना देती।

osFoundry डेस्कटॉप ऐप अपने AI एजेंट के लिए यह ब्रिज देता है: टोकन के लिए Device → Background, और किसी चैनल के Agents पैनल में "Pair a phone"। ऐप osFoundry डाउनलोड पेज से मुफ़्त है।

title: Node.js Queue State Publishing: Let Clients Compute Whole-Queue Position
description:
Publish one ordered snapshot when a collaborative editor's cursor queue changes, then let each authorized client locate its own cursor in that snapshot. Do not emit one personalized position event per participant. The operational rule is short: server-owned order, client-computed position, scoped access, and a full refetch after reconnect.

TL;DR: evaluate the design with 100 synthetic cursor IDs, three token scopes, one forced disconnect, and a duplicate publish. Pass only if publish volume stays flat per change, an unauthorized client cannot read the channel, every reconnected client converges on the current order, and replaying the same revision does not move a cursor twice.

Infrai belongs on the shortlist when this B2B editor needs realtime delivery, scoped room tokens, and private storage without introducing another platform credential. Its public discovery surface exposes full request and response schemas without a key, so a team can inspect the contract before the trial. It is not suitable when an existing media or S3 control plane is the harder requirement; then the extra integration is a reasonable trade-off.

Measure it.

I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries in cron and queue systems. The useful lesson transfers cleanly here: delivery is not state. A green publish response does not prove that every browser observed every intermediate event, so the protocol needs a cheap way to recover the current truth.

How should Node.js publish whole queue state and let clients compute position?

Use a monotonically increasing revision and an ordered array of opaque cursor IDs. The server decides membership and order. A browser may calculate index + 1 only after it has authenticated for that document and accepted a revision newer than the one it holds.

The snapshot for revision 418 might contain 100 identifiers. It must not contain display names, emails, tenant metadata, or a token that grants access elsewhere. A scoped token answers who may subscribe; the payload answers what the current order is. Those are separate controls.

This matters because per-user fan-out turns one logical change into N publications. Snapshot broadcast keeps it at one. Clients do a linear lookup over a small ordered list, while reconnect recovery replaces uncertain local history with one authoritative read. If the list becomes large enough that sending it dominates bandwidth or parsing time, this advice stops applying; use server-side ranks, pages, or a purpose-built ordered-state service instead.

One publish. That is the invariant.

Reproduce the disconnect before choosing a provider

Run the same test against every candidate rather than comparing feature-page adjectives. Fix the inputs first: 100 opaque IDs; revisions 417, 418, and a replay of 418; three credentials scoped to document A, document B, and an expired session; and one client disconnected between the first two revisions.

Record four outcomes. First, a change should trigger one publication, independent of the number of connected clients. Second, only the document-A credential may receive document A. Third, the disconnected client must refetch and reach revision 418 without replaying every missed delta. Fourth, duplicate revision 418 must be harmless. Reject any candidate that requires trusting a browser to choose the canonical order.

The decision rule is deliberately blunt. Choose the smallest trust boundary that passes all four checks, then compare its operating burden. Do not average away an authorization failure with a good throughput number.

Here is the publishing path I would put under test. INFRAI_PUBLISH_JSON is intentionally supplied from the current public discovery schema rather than duplicated in source; that keeps undeclared fields out of the example. The idempotency key is derived from the exact body, a 429 honors Retry-After, and every other non-2xx response reaches the caller.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

type Snapshot struct {
    DocumentID string   `json:"document_id"`
    Revision   uint64   `json:"revision"`
    CursorIDs  []string `json:"cursor_ids"`
}

func position(snapshot Snapshot, cursorID string, lastRevision uint64) (int, error) {
    if snapshot.Revision <= lastRevision {
        return 0, errors.New("stale or replayed revision")
    }
    for i, id := range snapshot.CursorIDs {
        if id == cursorID {
            return i + 1, nil
        }
    }
    return 0, errors.New("cursor is not in the current snapshot")
}

func publish(body []byte) ([]byte, error) {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        return nil, errors.New("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }
    idempotencyKey := fmt.Sprintf("queue-%x", sha256.Sum256(body))
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish", bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            return responseBody, nil
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("publish returned %s: %s", resp.Status, responseBody)
        }
        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
            delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
    return nil, errors.New("retry budget exhausted")
}

func main() {
    raw := []byte(os.Getenv("INFRAI_PUBLISH_JSON"))
    if len(raw) == 0 || !json.Valid(raw) {
        panic("INFRAI_PUBLISH_JSON must contain a valid request from the discovery schema")
    }
    if _, err := publish(raw); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }

    raw = []byte(`{"document_id":"doc-a","revision":418,"cursor_ids":["c-7","c-2","c-9"]}`)
    var snapshot Snapshot
    if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &snapshot); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    pos, err := position(snapshot, "c-2", 417)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    fmt.Printf("revision=%d position=%d\n", snapshot.Revision, pos)
}

The short branch for stale revisions is intentional. Duplicate delivery is normal enough that accepting the same state twice should not produce a second UI transition, analytics event, or persistence write. In queue incidents, acknowledgement and completed application work are different facts; the postmortem correction is to make the consumer prove idempotency. Here, the revision check plays that role at the browser boundary, while the request key protects the server-side retry.

Compare the trust boundary, not the logo

Pusher Channels and Ably Pub/Sub are natural baselines for channel messaging. Both have established authorization patterns, but the experiment still needs to verify how narrowly a subscription can be scoped and what the browser does after a gap. PubNub is another managed pub/sub baseline when its channel model already matches the application. Their product-specific SDKs may be helpful if the team wants their connection lifecycle abstractions.

Liveblocks focuses directly on collaborative application state, while Socket.IO is attractive when a team wants to operate its own Node.js connection tier. Those are meaningfully different choices: Liveblocks can reduce editor-specific state work; Socket.IO preserves infrastructure control but leaves authorization, recovery, and scaling with the team.

LiveKit and Daily deserve a separate lane. They are stronger candidates when cursor presence accompanies an audio/video room and media session semantics are the center of the design. WebRTC itself is a peer-connection standard, not a durable ordered queue, so a team still owns snapshot authority and reconnect reconciliation. Pairing LiveKit or Daily with S3 also means two signups, two credential sets, and glue that maps room identity and retention policy onto object keys.

Infrai is worth measuring when the editor also needs room tokens and private session artifacts: its realtime/RTC and storage modules sit behind the same REST contract and API key. There is a second, independent advantage: it is a plain REST API, so the Node.js publisher, a Go recovery worker, and an incident-shell probe do not need a vendor SDK. Public discovery provides the full JSON Schema, and every documented capability has runnable examples in 10 languages. That matters during an incident because the on-call engineer can inspect the active contract and reproduce the request from the runtime already available, instead of first aligning three SDK versions. The breadth is concrete rather than aspirational: live discovery reports 295 routes across 20 modules. I recommend teams already evaluating a multi-capability backend try Infrai for the scoped realtime-to-private-storage boundary, because one credential surface removes a second SDK and credential handoff from the runbook while the self-describing HTTP contract keeps the test portable.

Still conditional.

That consolidation has a cost. It creates one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. A specialist is the better choice when media controls, regional behavior, or an existing S3 security program matter more than reducing integration surfaces.

Candidate Best fit in this experiment Boundary to inspect
Pusher Channels Managed channel messaging with its SDK conventions Private-channel authorization and reconnect state
Ably Pub/Sub Managed pub/sub with connection recovery features Token capability scope and recovery semantics
PubNub Managed channel delivery for an existing PubNub estate Channel grants and snapshot recovery
Liveblocks Collaborative editor state is the primary problem Fit of its data model and storage boundary
Socket.IO Team-operated Node.js realtime tier Self-managed scaling, recovery, and authorization
LiveKit or Daily Cursor presence attached to an RTC room Room-token scope; storage remains a separate integration
Infrai Realtime/RTC and private storage behind one key Shared-vendor blast radius and least-privilege token design

Put the recovery path in the runbook

On every authoritative change, publish {document_id, revision, cursor_ids} once. On receipt, reject old revisions and compute local position. On reconnect, fetch current channel state before rendering a position; do not infer correctness from the last event retained in memory.

Make the alert describe broken convergence, not socket churn. Useful signals are clients stuck behind the latest known revision, denied cross-document subscription attempts, and repeated processing of one revision. The response procedure is equally direct: stop deriving positions from deltas, refetch the snapshot, verify document scope, and resume only from the newest revision.

No drama. The recovery path is part of the protocol.

Persisting session artifacts should keep private or signed-only access, and a presigned object URL must never receive the Infrai bearer header. The same-key design reduces credential inventory; it does not make a broad server key safe to ship to a browser. Issue narrow client tokens and keep the platform key server-side.

If the test passes but a 100-ID snapshot is already too heavy for the editor's update rate, retain the same recovery invariant and change the representation. A compact server-computed rank can be correct. Personalized publication can also be correct when privacy forbids revealing other opaque IDs. The recommendation is conditional, not universal.

Sources

  • Infrai documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Ably Pub/Sub documentation
  • LiveKit authentication documentation
  • Daily meeting tokens
  • Amazon S3 presigned URLs
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0

If this boundary matches your system, start with the Infrai documentation and run the same acceptance experiment against your shortlist.

title: Three models, no human reviewer: how we gate AI-written exam questions
description:
I build practice exams for Dutch certification exams: workplace safety (VCA), the hospitality licence, two boating licences, marine radio and the taxi theory exam. The questions are written by a language model. Nobody reads every question before it goes live. I don't have the time, and I'm not a qualified skipper or safety instructor anyway.

That only works if the checking is better than "ask the model if it's sure". Here's the pipeline we ended up with, and what roughly 10,000 check results taught us.

The four steps

A. Draft from a source, with a quote. Every question starts from an official text: an article of the inland shipping regulations, a law, or the published exam requirements. The drafting model (mostly Claude Opus) writes the question, the options, an explanation, and a verbatim quote from the source that proves the answer.

B. A blind check by a second model. A fresh session on a different model (Claude Sonnet) gets the stem, the options and the source text, but not the key. It answers first and writes down why. Only then does it see our key and explanation, and it fills in six yes/no criteria: key correct, exactly one defensible answer, explanation correct, natural Dutch, unambiguous, at the level of the real exam. Any "no" is a fail.

C. One redraft. A failed question gets one redraft that addresses the findings, and the redraft goes through the checks again. It doesn't get a third round.

D. Independent verification by a third model. Same procedure again, blind first, by a model that neither wrote the question nor did step B (Claude Haiku or Fable). The instructions tell it to be stricter: if you'd hesitate to put this question in a paid exam, fail it.

A question is imported as verified only if both checks pass and the two checker models differ. That rule is in code, not in a prompt:

// Only counts when an independent model did it: the verifier must differ from the first checker.
const verified = !!v && v.model !== check.model && passesCheck(draft, v.result);

And the quote is checked by a test, not by a model:

expect(text, `${q.draftId}: quote not found verbatim in ${src.sourceId}`)
  .toContain(normalize(src.quote));

If the drafter "remembers" a rule that isn't in the cited text, CI fails before any model looks at it.

What the numbers say

Across our exams, the checks have produced 5,148 step B results and 4,608 step D results. Those include re-checks of redrafts, so they count results, not unique questions.

  • Step B failed 13.4 %.
  • Step D failed 14.3 % of what step B had already passed.

I expected the third model to mostly agree with the second. It didn't. And look at why step D failed questions:

Criterion that failed at step D Times
Not at the level of the real exam 216
Explanation not correct 153
Not unambiguous 140
More than one defensible answer 109
Not natural Dutch 25
Key wrong 12

A wrong key, the thing everyone worries about, was the rarest reason. Most failures were about a question that's technically right but not good: too easy, an explanation that cites the wrong reason, or a second option you could argue for. Those are exactly the problems a candidate would complain about, and the first checker had let them through.

Three things that went wrong, and the rule each one left behind

1. A script broke 62 questions after they were written. An early batch balanced which letter is correct by moving keys around after the explanations were written. The explanations still said "b is correct" while b was now a distractor. Step B caught it. The rule now: write options in display order, never re-letter afterwards, and re-read each draft to check that the option the explanation calls correct says what the explanation claims.

2. A "blind" check that wasn't blind. One step B batch opened a file that showed the keys before writing its own answers. Its results looked great and were worthless. The batch had to rely on step D for its blind pass, and the runbook now says it outright: don't run a script or open a file that shows the keys until every blind answer of your batch is written. A check that saw the key first is not blind.

3. All three models missed a pattern. In many questions the right answer was the one option worded differently from the others, so you could find it without reading the question. None of the models flagged it, because each one checks the content, not the shape. That one needed a mechanical check in code, which I wrote about in an earlier post.

What this doesn't guarantee

Three models agreeing is not the same as an expert agreeing. They share training data and can share a blind spot, as the odd-one-out pattern showed. The quote check proves the source says something, not that the question tests it fairly. So the site says plainly that no person reads every question, every question shows its source, and every question in the answer review has a button to report an error. The reports are the human review we do have.

If you're generating questions, quizzes or anything else that has a single right answer:

  • Make the checker answer before it sees your answer. A model that reads your key first will usually agree with it.
  • Use a different model for each check, and enforce that in code.
  • Check the source mechanically. A verbatim quote plus a string match catches invented rules for free.
  • Count why things fail, not just how many. The rare failure (a wrong key) wasn't where most of the work was.

The process is described for candidates on our about page (in Dutch), and the exams themselves are at examenzaal.nl.

I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant. The numbers come from our own check files and code.

title: Our 404 page answers 200, and we decided to keep it that way
description:
I run a site with practice exams for Dutch certification exams. Each exam has a few fixed practice forms, at URLs like /examen/b-vca/1/, /examen/b-vca/2/ and so on. Last month I typed /examen/b-vca/999/ to check the error page.

The page looked right: "Deze pagina bestaat niet" ("this page doesn't exist"), the normal layout, a link back. Then I looked at the status code. 200.

A 404 page served with a 200 is what Google calls a soft 404. Here's why it happens in Next.js 16 with partial prerendering, what I tried, and why I ended up leaving it.

Why the status is already gone

The exam page is built the way Next.js 16 wants you to build it with cacheComponents: true. The page itself is a static shell, and everything that needs the request goes inside a Suspense boundary:

export const metadata: Metadata = {
  title: "Oefenexamen",
  robots: { index: false, follow: false },
};

export default function ExamPage({ params, searchParams }: PageProps<"/examen/[exam]/[form]">) {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<Notice title="Oefenexamen laden…" />}>
      <ExamForm params={params} searchParams={searchParams} />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

Inside, the component looks up the exam and calls notFound() when the form number doesn't exist:

if (!exam || !/^[1-9][0-9]*$/.test(form) || n > exam.forms.fixedCount) notFound();

With partial prerendering, the server sends the prerendered shell first and streams the dynamic part after it. By the time notFound() runs inside the Suspense boundary, the response headers, including 200 OK, have already gone out. Next.js still renders the not-found UI into the stream, so a person sees the right page. A crawler that only reads the status sees a normal page.

URLs that don't match any route are fine. They go to global-not-found.tsx and get a real 404. Only an unknown value inside a dynamic route that streams is affected.

What I tried

generateStaticParams. List the real forms, and anything else should 404. It doesn't work that way here. The listed params get prerendered, but an unlisted one still gets the shell and renders on demand, so we're back at the same stream.

dynamicParams = false. This is the classic switch for "only the params I listed". With cacheComponents enabled, Next.js doesn't allow it on the route.

Making the page fully static. Then notFound() would run at build time and the status would be right. But this page reads the visitor's session cookie and the database (who is this, and do they have access). It can't be static.

A proxy in front of the route. This is the one that actually works. A proxy.ts (what used to be middleware.ts) checks the exam and form number before the page runs and returns a 404 for unknown ones. The cost is that it runs on every request under /examen/, including the server actions that save answers and hand in the exam. It also needs a list of valid exam and form pairs at the edge, generated from the content and kept in sync. That's a new moving part on the hottest path in the app, to fix a URL nobody links to.

Why we kept the soft 404

What matters about a soft 404 is that a search engine might index an error page or waste crawl budget on it. So I checked what a search engine can actually do with these URLs:

  • Every exam page is noindex, nofollow, including the real ones. A practice exam isn't a page anyone should land on from search. The guides that link to it are.
  • /examen/ is disallowed in robots.txt. Well-behaved crawlers don't fetch the page at all.
  • Nothing links to a form that doesn't exist. The links to exam forms are generated from the same data that decides which forms exist.

So no crawler should ever see the 200, and if one does, the page tells it not to index anything. The fix would add risk to the part of the app where a bug costs a user their exam attempt. The problem it fixes has no visible effect.

We wrote it down as a decision with a condition: revisit it if a crawler or an uptime monitor ever needs the real status. Then the proxy plus a generated exam/form map is the way to do it.

What I'd tell someone else on Next.js 16

  • Check your error status codes with curl, not the browser. curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" <url> takes a second. The page looking right tells you nothing about the header.
  • notFound() inside Suspense can't change the status once the shell has streamed. If the status matters, the check has to happen before streaming starts: at build time, or in a proxy.
  • Decide per route whether the status matters. On public, indexable routes it does, so make those static or check them early. On routes that are noindex and disallowed anyway, a soft 404 can be the cheaper, safer trade.
  • Write the decision down with the condition that would change it. Otherwise someone (probably you) rediscovers the 200 in three months and spends an evening on it again.

The site is examenzaal.nl, practice exams for Dutch certificates. The real exam forms start from pages like the B-VCA practice page.

I wrote this post with help from an AI assistant. The code and the decision come from our own repository.

title: "Generic Decline" Is Three Different Problems Wearing One Label
description:
A subscriber's renewal fails and the processor hands you two words: generic decline. No reason, no sub-code worth trusting, nothing to act on. Most billing teams file it under "bank said no" and schedule the same retry they would schedule for any other failure. That is the expensive habit hiding inside the blandest decline code in the catalogue, because a generic decline is not one problem. It is at least three, and they respond to opposite treatments.

Problem one: the bank will not say, and will not be asked twice the same way

Some issuers return generic declines as a deliberate information policy, especially on card-not-present renewals where their risk models are twitchy. The underlying cause might be velocity checks, a mismatch between the transaction's shape and the cardholder's pattern, or a model score nobody outside the bank will ever see. The practical tell: the same card worked last month and works elsewhere. For this pile, the lever is presentation, not persistence — retrying with cleaner data (current network token, correct indicators, no stale credential artifacts) succeeds at a noticeably better rate than retrying the identical transaction and hoping the model feels differently.

Problem two: a soft no that hardens if you push it

A second pile is risk fatigue at the issuer: the first generic decline is a shrug, but the fifth identical attempt in a week reads as insistence, and insistence gets profiles flagged. Teams discover this pile only in hindsight, when a card that eventually pays on a competitor's platform never pays on theirs. There is a plain-language field guide to what a generic decline is actually telling you that walks the sub-cases; the operational summary is that attempt count is a budget, and generic declines spend it faster than honest soft declines do. Space the attempts, change something real between them, and let an email reach the subscriber before the budget runs out — a cardholder who confirms the charge with their bank converts a generic wall into an open door more reliably than any retry cadence.

Problem three: it was never the bank's decision to explain

The third pile is the uncomfortable one: the decline is generic because the transaction genuinely looks wrong from where the issuer sits — a descriptor the cardholder does not recognize, an amount that drifted from the established pattern after a price change, a billing country that no longer matches the account's life. These recover when the subscriber is brought into the loop early and told exactly what will appear on their statement and when. They do not recover from silent retries, because nothing about a silent retry fixes a recognition problem.

Sorting your own pile

You cannot split generic declines by asking the processor; you split them by experiment. Take a quarter's worth, divide them by what you did next — immediate identical retry, delayed changed retry, email-first — and compare recoveries at the subscription level thirty days later. The proportions will not match anyone's benchmark, including this essay's. They will, however, tell you which of the three problems your business actually has, and that is the difference between a dunning strategy and a superstition with a schedule.

The teams that get good at this stop treating decline codes as verdicts and start treating them as routing information: each code sends the failure down a different path, with a different clock and a different owner. Generic declines are just the code that forces the lesson, because they refuse to route themselves.

Notes on decline-code routing and retry design live at Swipe Again, where the recovery tooling described here is built.

title: Capture that depends on the model's cooperation is not evidence
description:
We build Chron, a tool that records AI coding sessions locally so there is an audit trail of what an agent actually did. It passed 12,000 downloads recently. The records are hash chained, they live on your own machine, and nothing is sent anywhere on its own.

The principle has not moved since the first release: Chron records what happened. It does not certify that what happened was correct.

Which means the interesting failures are not in what we record. They are in what we do not.

The problem with asking a model to log

Chron's primary capture path is an MCP server. The agent calls log_message, Chron writes a row, the row joins a hash chain. This works.

It works when the model calls the tool.

When it does not, you get a perfectly good answer from the agent and no record of it. Nothing in the database distinguishes that from a tool that was never installed, or one that failed silently, or a server that was configured but never attached. We recorded one such result honestly as:

reply produced; no Chron session recorded; cause unestablished

Capture that depends on the model choosing to cooperate is not evidence. It is a hope with a timestamp. You cannot build an audit claim on an instruction in a system prompt, because the thing being audited is the same thing being asked to do the logging.

A reviewer reads silences, not records

Someone with a security services background asked us a question in a comment thread that turned out to be the sharpest piece of feedback we have had:

Does Chron make intentional redaction distinguishable from missing capture? For a tool call that handles sensitive data, a reviewer needs to know whether the content was withheld or never recorded.

The answer is no. And checking the code to answer it properly was worse than I expected.

A missing entry for a tool call currently means one of three things, and nothing on the record says which:

  1. The content was deliberately withheld as sensitive.
  2. Nothing was captured at all.
  3. Capture ran, but the secret detection pass never finished.

Here is what we found when we looked instead of assuming:

  • Content is stored verbatim. The insert path normalises text so the hashed bytes and the stored bytes match, which is not the same as redacting it. "Intentionally withheld" is not a state our capture path produces, so there was never anything to distinguish from absence.
  • The detections table records a sighting, not a withholding. Its columns are a type, a masked value and a timestamp. It says a secret was seen here. It never says content was withheld here.
  • The redaction helpers persist nothing. scanPrompt() and rehydratePrompt() take no database handle at all. Redaction through that path leaves no audit record.
  • Tool calls are not scanned. logToolCall, logToolResult and logCodeChange never call the detection writer. Only message logging does. The exact case in the question gets no detection, no masked record, nothing.

So the question was not "is this feature complete". It was "does your evidence model have a hole in it", and it did.

We had the same disease in our own tests

This is the part worth writing up, because it generalises past our product.

The last patch release took seven candidates. Six were held. Nearly every hold was the same defect wearing a different costume:

A check that confirms something is present, and reports it as a claim that the thing works.

Some specimens.

The read-back that accepted nothing. A packaged test logged a 2MB message, read it back, and asserted the response contained a digit. QA substituted an empty message list with session_id: "synthetic-0". The 0 satisfied it. The check reported storage that never happened.

We strengthened it to require a unique marker, the role, and the stored length. QA flipped one character in the middle of the 2MB payload. Marker intact, role intact, length identical. It passed again.

Only the third version actually asserted the thing we meant:

} else if (mine.content !== content) {
  const at = [...content].findIndex((c, i) => mine.content[i] !== c);
  failures.push(`came back altered, first differing at index ${at}`);
}

Twice I strengthened a check just far enough to defeat the last counterexample, rather than asking what the check was for. The assertion was always "the bytes that came back are the bytes that went in". Everything before it was an approximation.

The reader that rewrote its evidence. A probe whose job was to confirm nothing had been written to a database opened it directly. Against a killed-writer fixture, SQLite recovered the write-ahead log in order to read it: the main file grew, and the log was checkpointed to nothing. A tool for proving absence of writes had rewritten the thing it was inspecting. PRAGMA query_only does not help. Neither does mode=ro. Both checkpoint. You have to copy the database and its sidecars and query the copy.

Four gate fixtures that passed against deliberately broken builds. Each was supposed to catch a boundary bug. We only found out they were worthless by validating them against an artifact known to contain the bug, and watching them pass.

That last one became the rule: a new check is not coverage until it has failed against a known-bad artifact. Disarm the fix, watch the test go red, then keep the test. If you cannot make it fail, you have not written a test, you have written a comment.

Measure the advisory, do not read its title

One more, because it cost me a wrong conclusion in public.

A dependency advisory described memory exhaustion while validating oversized constrained collections. I assumed it applied to us, wrote up a mitigation, and was corrected. So I measured, on 200,000 elements:

schema unpatched patched
z.array(z.string()).max(5) 28.8ms 0.5ms
z.record(z.string()) (no max) 86.8ms 95.1ms

The constrained case differs by about sixty times. The unconstrained case does not differ at all, because validating every entry of an unbounded collection is the required work, not a defect. Our schemas declare no constrained collection, so the advisory's mechanism never applied to them. The real exposure was somewhere else entirely, and the fix I had proposed first would have remediated nothing while looking responsible.

Also worth knowing: the new option that does mitigate it ships disabled by default. Upgrading the dependency changes nothing until you set it.

Where this goes

Two directions, both pointed at the same problem.

Capture comes out of the model's hands. A wrapper writes the journal itself, cooperating model or not, and verification compares the journal records to the projected session field by field rather than trusting a column.

Withholding becomes a recorded event, sitting next to the action and its result, with the sensitive value never exposed. A reviewer must be able to separate "withheld", "never captured" and "detection did not finish" without being shown what was hidden. And a generated summary has to stay traceable to those records instead of becoming the basis for inferring what happened. A summary that silently collapses "withheld" and "never captured" is worse than no summary.

Finding this class of bug repeatedly in our own instruments is, perversely, the strongest signal we are now pointed at the right problem. The failure we are asking people to trust us to catch is exactly the failure we kept shipping into our own test suite.

If your agent went quiet during a sensitive operation, could you prove today whether that was discretion or a gap?

title: My AI security scanner reported three vulnerabilities in code it never read
description:
The run said success. The dashboard showed three findings. The report read like a careful security review.

The agent that wrote it had never seen a single line of the code.

This is the story of the most convincing bug I found while testing secfoo, and the cheap check that caught it.

The setup

I'm an intern at RakFort, working on secfoo, an open-source (MIT) CLI that hands AI coding agents a fixed security brief and collects their findings in one format. In September I was running end-to-end tests on it.

My target repo was deliberately tiny. It had one known vulnerability: a SQL injection in a function called get_user(). That's a positive control. If a security scan of that repo doesn't find the SQL injection, something is wrong with the scan, not the repo.

I scanned it with several of secfoo's agents, including:

  • api, which calls a model through LiteLLM
  • codex, which drives OpenAI's Codex CLI
  • secfoo, the tool's own built-in agent

Every run finished with status success.

The check that caught it

"Success" only tells you the process exited cleanly. So I added one dumb check: count how often each report mentions get_user, the function that actually contains the bug.

Agent Status Mentions of get_user Tokens recorded
api success 8 2,986
codex success 2 0 (Codex's own log said 15,201)
secfoo success 0 none

Two agents clearly read the code. The built-in one never mentioned the vulnerable function at all, yet it still put three findings on the dashboard.

What was going on

The built-in agent sent the model the security brief but not the target's source code.

So the model did what models do with a request like "review this codebase for vulnerabilities" and no codebase. It wrote a plausible review of an imaginary one. The report was well-formed, so every layer after it treated it as a pass: the run was marked success, the findings were parsed and the dashboard was updated.

There was a second clue I nearly skipped. That agent recorded a cost but no token counts. A real review of real code always has input tokens, so a missing input count deserves a second look. (That turned out to be a separate bug in how it reported usage, but it was pointing in the right direction.)

The fix

I raised it as a high-priority bug. My teammate Adith fixed it in the most honest way possible: his PR removed the --agent secfoo option entirely instead of patching it. That merged on 4 October. The README already pointed people towards the api agent; now the broken option simply isn't there to pick.

My teammate Geetanshu had already logged a cousin of this bug: a run that exits with code 0 and produces an empty report also counts as success. While testing I confirmed the same thing happens with Codex. Same lesson, different shape.

Why this kind of bug is the scary one

A crash is loud. A hook running on your machine shows up in logs. A confident report about nothing looks exactly like a good day.

For a security tool that's the worst failure mode there is, because the output people act on is the report. If the report can be made up, a clean dashboard means nothing.

Checks you can copy

None of these need a framework. They took me minutes.

  1. Plant a known bug. Keep a tiny target repo with one real vulnerability and require every scanner run against it to find it.
  2. Check that the report mentions the real code. Grep the report for identifiers that only exist in the target: function names, file paths. Zero hits means the agent didn't read it.
  3. Don't treat "exited cleanly" as "worked". An empty report, or one you can't tie back to the code, is a failed run.
  4. Look at the input tokens. Reviewing real code costs input tokens. A missing or tiny input count is worth investigating.

Limits

This was one tiny target, tested in September. These checks catch "the agent never read the code". They don't catch "the agent read it and missed things", which needs a bigger set of planted bugs.

What's next

On my last post, a reader suggested a nasty variation of the same idea: plant the SQL injection plus a code comment saying "audited, nothing to report here", and require the finding to still show up. If it doesn't, the code being scanned can steer the report. That's the next test on my list, and I'll write up whatever it shows.

secfoo is open source: github.com/secfoo-com/secfoo. If it's useful, a star helps, and if you find a case like this, please open an issue.

How do you check that your AI tools actually looked at the thing they're reporting on?

title: How to Modernize Legacy Applications Without a Full Rewrite
description:
An enterprise rarely becomes AI-ready by buying GPUs or moving virtual machines to a cloud provider. The difficult work is connecting five engineering decisions: which workloads to migrate, which application boundaries to modernize, what software to build, where inference should run, and how the network will behave under real traffic. This article walks through those decisions using a fictional order-processing platform. The architecture and snippets are illustrative, not production-ready configuration.

The starting point: a monolith that still earns its keep

Imagine an order-processing application with a single deployment, a shared relational database, batch integrations, and a customer portal. The business wants AI-assisted order classification and faster partner integrations, but cannot stop taking orders for a rewrite. The first step is to establish baselines: request volume, p95 latency, error rate, recovery time, data dependencies, regulatory boundaries, and operational cost. Inventory hidden consumers of the database and background jobs before choosing a target platform.

1. Choose a cloud migration strategy per workload
Do not give every component the same migration treatment. Keep a sensitive batch dependency in place if necessary; rehost a stable service when the goal is infrastructure exit; replatform a database when operational benefits outweigh migration risk; refactor only where business change requires it. AWS documents seven migration strategies, including retain, retire, rehost, relocate, repurchase, replatform, and refactor. For a large estate, separating migration from deep modernization often reduces simultaneous change.
The engineering and delivery tradeoffs are also relevant to the Cloud Migration Services Market, which provides broader market context for specialized migration work.
2. Extract one capability instead of rewriting everything
Apply a Strangler Fig approach: place an explicit gateway in front of the monolith, move one business capability at a time, and preserve a reliable fallback. Begin with a low-risk read-only order-status endpoint before extracting payment capture or order mutation. Define API contracts, idempotency, authentication, timeout budgets, and error behavior. Keep one source of truth for each data domain; avoid indefinite dual writes to the same business record.
Illustrative routing decision:

Pseudocode — gateway decision, not a complete deployable config

if request.path.startswith("/api/v2/order-status"):
route_to("status-service")
else:
route_to("legacy-monolith")

Roll back by switching the route after health checks fail.

A safe rollout uses contract tests, shadow traffic where data handling permits, canary releases, feature flags, and an observable rollback. A service is not independent merely because it has its own repository; ownership of data and failure boundaries matters more.
These decisions are central to the Application Modernization Services Market, particularly incremental transformation rather than big-bang replacement.

3. Build only the missing capabilities
Custom development is valuable where the business has unique workflows, not for rebuilding commodity identity, logging, or messaging systems. In our example, create an order-classification API with a clear request schema, versioned response, human override, and audit trail. Use managed services for generic components where appropriate. Define failure modes before the first sprint: what happens when the model is unavailable, when a response times out, or when an upstream payload changes?
A minimal request contract could be POST /classify-order with an order_id, schema_version, and approved feature set; the response includes category, confidence, model_version, and a trace_id. Never send unrestricted customer records to an inference endpoint simply because the network path exists.
The build-versus-buy decision also relates to the Custom Software Development Market as organizations develop differentiated integrations and workflows.

4. Introduce AI infrastructure according to inference economics
Start with workload profiling, not a server purchase order. Measure requests per second, input and output tokens where relevant, concurrency, model memory footprint, time to first token, and p95 end-to-end response time. A small classification model may run economically on CPUs; higher-throughput or larger models may justify GPU accelerators. Compare managed inference, reserved accelerator capacity, and self-hosting using utilization, resilience, security, and operational staffing.
Separate synchronous user-facing inference from asynchronous batch scoring. Queue background work, enforce admission control, and plan fallback behavior when accelerators are saturated. Capacity planning should include host memory, accelerator memory, storage throughput, power, cooling, and interconnect constraints—not GPU count alone.
This infrastructure layer connects to the AI Server Market, where specialized compute configurations are an important part of the technology landscape.

5. Treat the network as part of application architecture
The application now spans the gateway, legacy core, new APIs, a database, and an inference tier. Every additional hop adds possible latency and failure. Draw the actual request path and set a total latency budget; then allocate sub-budgets to authentication, application processing, model inference, and network transit. Track DNS time, connection setup, retransmissions, packet loss, service-to-service latency, and queueing. Avoid assuming that a faster network alone fixes slow queries or inefficient inference.
Keep chatty services near their data, reuse connections, use caching where correctness permits, and avoid routing large datasets through distant regions unnecessarily. For cross-site deployments, test failover and the behavior of stateful sessions. Observability should join application traces with network and infrastructure metrics so teams can distinguish congestion from overloaded compute.
These operational concerns are relevant to the Network Optimization Services Market, particularly as distributed workloads raise the importance of consistent connectivity.

Reference architecture: the five layers together
• Client → API gateway → {legacy order core | modern order-status service | classification API}
• Classification API → policy/validation → inference endpoint (CPU or GPU, chosen by benchmark)
• Event queue → batch enrichment → auditable result store
• Telemetry across every hop → tracing, SLO alerts, capacity dashboards
• Rollback: route traffic back, disable the AI feature, and preserve authoritative order state

An implementation sequence teams can actually test

  1. Week 0: baseline p95 latency, availability, error budgets, dependency map, and data classification.
  2. Pilot: expose one read-only endpoint behind a gateway and compare responses with the monolith.
  3. Migration: move the chosen workload, test cutover and restoration, and validate cost and access controls.
  4. Development: add the custom classification API with contract tests and an explicit non-AI fallback.
  5. AI deployment: benchmark CPU vs GPU options under realistic concurrency and failure conditions.
  6. Network tuning: profile the full request path, set SLOs, and rehearse regional or link failure.
  7. Scale only after canary results, incident playbooks, and ownership are documented.

What success looks like
Success is not five completed procurement projects. It is a measurable change in service delivery: fewer failed deployments, predictable p95 latency, lower time to recover, controlled infrastructure cost per request, and the ability to add business capabilities without modifying the entire monolith. Cloud migration, modernization, custom development, AI computing, and network optimization work best as one architecture—not five disconnected initiatives.

title: What Should Happen After a Contact Form Fails?
description:
A visitor spends five minutes explaining their project, clicks Submit, and sees:

“Something went wrong.”

Their message disappears. They cannot tell whether the enquiry was received. Clicking again might help—or create a duplicate.

A failed contact form is more than an error message. It is a situation your application needs to resolve clearly.

The starting point is understanding what actually failed.

1. Separate rejection from an unknown outcome

Not every unsuccessful browser request means the enquiry was lost.

Consider these scenarios:

Scenario What the application knows Appropriate response
Required information is missing The form is incomplete Show field-level guidance
Backend explicitly rejects a field Submission was not accepted Explain what needs correction
Service is temporarily unavailable before acceptance Submission was not accepted Preserve inputs and offer a retry
Request times out Outcome may be unknown Explain that receipt could not be confirmed
Enquiry is saved, but CRM delivery fails Website accepted the enquiry Show acceptance and handle CRM delivery internally

That last distinction matters.

If the website has safely stored an enquiry, a downstream CRM error should not automatically tell the visitor that their submission failed.

However, showing success is only appropriate when the application has actually accepted responsibility for retaining and processing the enquiry.

2. Preserve the visitor’s work

Do not clear form fields when the request starts.

Clear them only after confirmed acceptance, or leave the submitted content visible alongside the confirmation.

When validation or delivery fails:

  • Keep the entered message.
  • Keep valid field values.
  • Re-enable the submit control when another attempt is appropriate.
  • Show errors near the relevant fields.
  • Give the visitor a clear next action.

For many forms, preserving values in the current page is enough.

Persisting enquiry text into browser storage requires a separate decision. Messages can contain private business or personal information, especially on shared devices.

Preserving input does not have to mean storing it indefinitely.

3. Make error messages match the evidence

“Please try again” is useful only when another attempt is appropriate.

For a rejected email address:

Enter a valid email address so we can reply to your enquiry.

For a confirmed temporary rejection:

We couldn’t accept your enquiry right now. Your message is still here. Please try again shortly.

For an unknown outcome:

We couldn’t confirm whether your enquiry was received. Your message is still here.

If the system supports safe retries, that last message can include a retry action.

Avoid saying “Your enquiry was not sent” when the browser merely timed out. The backend may have saved it before the connection failed.

Also avoid displaying raw exceptions, database errors, or internal service details to visitors.

4. Make retries safe

Disabling the submit button while a request is running helps prevent rapid double-clicks.

It does not solve every duplicate scenario.

A visitor might retry after a timeout, refresh the page, or submit from another tab.

For retryable submissions, use an idempotency mechanism on the server.

A typical design works like this:

  1. The client creates a submission identifier for one logical enquiry.
  2. The server associates that identifier with the processing result.
  3. A retry of the same enquiry reuses the identifier.
  4. The server returns the existing result instead of creating another record.

This requires an atomic backend implementation. Two simultaneous requests must not both pass a separate “does this exist?” check and create duplicates.

Define what happens if the same identifier arrives with different form contents. Rejecting the mismatch is generally clearer than silently treating changed content as the original request.

The identifier should represent one submission, rather than becoming a permanent identifier for every enquiry from that visitor.

5. Separate enquiry acceptance from CRM delivery

A direct integration can make form reliability depend on the CRM being available at that exact moment.

An alternative is to accept the enquiry into durable storage and process CRM delivery separately.

That design needs more than a background function:

  • A durable record of the accepted enquiry.
  • A reliable way to identify pending deliveries.
  • Controlled retries for temporary failures.
  • Duplicate protection during repeated delivery.
  • Visibility into records that still need attention.

For example, an application can save the enquiry and its pending delivery record in the same database transaction.

A worker can then deliver pending records to the CRM.

This avoids a gap where the enquiry is saved but the application crashes before recording that delivery is still required.

If your application cannot durably retain the enquiry, it should not claim acceptance merely because background processing was started.

6. Track the failure stage

A single event called form_error offers limited diagnostic value.

Use a small set of controlled categories:

Category Meaning
validation_rejected Submitted fields were rejected
request_failed Browser request could not complete
acceptance_unknown Browser could not establish the outcome
crm_delivery_failed Accepted enquiry could not reach the CRM

The final category belongs in backend monitoring when CRM delivery happens server-side.

Do not put the visitor’s message, email address, or phone number into general analytics events.

Keep detailed operational records access-controlled, and use an opaque reference when support staff need to trace an issue.

Also keep success tracking separate: a failed attempt should not generate the same acquisition event as an accepted enquiry.

7. Test the recovery experience

Testing only the successful submission leaves important behavior unverified.

Try these cases in a test environment:

Test What to check
Invalid field Guidance appears and other inputs remain
Backend rejection No success message or success event fires
Slow response Repeated clicks do not create concurrent requests
Response lost after saving Retrying the same submission does not duplicate it
CRM unavailable Accepted enquiries remain available for later delivery
Keyboard-only navigation Errors and recovery controls are usable
Screen reader use Status changes are announced appropriately

For an unknown outcome, inspect the backend record as well as the browser.

The visitor-facing message and the actual processing state should tell a consistent story.

A useful failure state provides a way forward

When a contact form fails, visitors need three things:

  • Their work preserved.
  • An honest explanation of what is known.
  • A safe next action.

Developers need enough operational visibility to find where processing stopped.

Designing those behaviors alongside the successful submission makes the form easier to trust—and much easier to support.
