title: Pentaho Reporting 11 PDFs: Maven Access, Flexbox, Passwords
description:
A Maven build that pulls classic-core, an invoice header written as a flex row, and a statement guarded by an open password look like routine jobs for Pentaho Reporting's classic engine. Each of them has a catch in the 11.0 line, and this post walks through all three plus the CVEs in its dependency tree. Our test build came from 11.0.0.4-325, committed on 30 October 2026. GitHub's newest service-pack tag on 4 November 2026 is 11.0.0.4-328, three commits later, with the dependency versions below unchanged. Every snippet below ran on JDK 17, and we opened each resulting PDF to check it. The same snippets gave matching output on a build from 11.0.0.0-237, the top 11.0.0.0 tag, committed on 30 December 2025.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

What Does Maven Need Before classic-core Will Resolve?

Repository credentials, or a source build. Neither classic-core nor the eleven org.pentaho.reporting.library modules it depends on is on Maven Central, where every lookup returned 404 on 4 November 2026. Following the README leads to Pentaho's Artifactory at repo.pentaho.com/artifactory/pnt-mvn/, configured through a settings.xml in Pentaho's maven-parent-poms repository, and it refused the 11.0 POMs with HTTP 401 when Maven and curl sent no credentials. Build servers limited to Maven Central stop here, which is why the classes for this post came from the GitHub tag. Our source build skipped 46 core files, the database connection, SQL data factory and query editor code, because parts of it need commons-database-model and rsyntaxtextarea 1.3.2, which are missing from Central too, and no snippet below touches them.

Check the JDK as well. The README still names Java 11 as the minimum, yet release.jdk.version is 17 in the 11.0 parent POM, and Java 11 cannot load classes compiled for release 17. The overview of Maven and the POM explains the repository lookup a build makes.

What Happens to a Flexbox Invoice Header in an HTML Text Field?

The flex layout disappears, and so does the script's output. Pentaho Reporting reads no HTML pages. Markup is only allowed inside a text element flagged as text/html through AttributeNames.Core.RICH_TEXT_TYPE, and HtmlRichTextConverter then hands it to HTMLEditorKit from Java Swing, a kit whose Oracle javadoc says it covers HTML version 3.2 with some extensions.

import org.pentaho.reporting.engine.classic.core.AttributeNames;
import org.pentaho.reporting.engine.classic.core.ClassicEngineBoot;
import org.pentaho.reporting.engine.classic.core.Element;
import org.pentaho.reporting.engine.classic.core.MasterReport;
import org.pentaho.reporting.engine.classic.core.elementfactory.LabelElementFactory;
import org.pentaho.reporting.engine.classic.core.modules.output.pageable.pdf.PdfReportUtil;

public class HtmlInvoiceHeader {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ClassicEngineBoot.getInstance().start();

        // An invoice header as a web template would write it, with a flex row and a script-filled date.
        String header = "<html><head><style>"
                + ".bar { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; }"
                + "</style></head><body>"
                + "<div class='bar'><span>ACME Supplies</span><span>Invoice INV-2041</span></div>"
                + "<p>Issued <span id='issued'>DATE</span></p>"
                + "<script>document.getElementById('issued').textContent = '26 October 2026';</script>"
                + "</body></html>";

        LabelElementFactory factory = new LabelElementFactory();
        factory.setText(header);
        factory.setMinimumWidth(500f);
        factory.setMinimumHeight(80f);
        Element label = factory.createElement();

        // Marking the label as text/html sends it through the engine's rich-text converter.
        label.setAttribute(AttributeNames.Core.NAMESPACE, AttributeNames.Core.RICH_TEXT_TYPE, "text/html");

        MasterReport report = new MasterReport();
        report.getReportHeader().addElement(label);
        PdfReportUtil.createPDF(report, "invoice-header.pdf");
    }
}

Look at invoice-header.pdf and the company name and invoice number share one line, glued together as ACME SuppliesInvoice INV-2041 from the left margin, so justify-content: space-between did nothing. Below it, Issued DATE still shows the placeholder the script was meant to overwrite. Front-end teams that already keep invoices as web templates are the ones affected. Pentaho's answer is one report element per value, laid out in Report Designer or from Java, while the HTML template tutorial keeps the markup as it is.

Does an Open Password Alone Protect a Pentaho PDF?

Not in the test below. Encryption comes in two strengths, 40bit and 128bit, and both produced RC4 here (revision 2 and revision 3 of the standard handler), an algorithm qpdf's encryption notes list as deprecated in PDF 2.0. If the configuration has no OwnerPassword, PdfDocumentWriter writes the PDF padding constant in its place, and a comment in that class says this amounts to an empty password, which Adobe accepts.

import java.io.File;

import org.pentaho.reporting.engine.classic.core.ClassicEngineBoot;
import org.pentaho.reporting.engine.classic.core.MasterReport;
import org.pentaho.reporting.engine.classic.core.elementfactory.LabelElementFactory;
import org.pentaho.reporting.engine.classic.core.modules.output.pageable.pdf.PdfReportUtil;
import org.pentaho.reporting.libraries.base.config.ModifiableConfiguration;

public class OpenPasswordOnly {
    private static final String PDF = "org.pentaho.reporting.engine.classic.core.modules.output.pageable.pdf.";

    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        ClassicEngineBoot.getInstance().start();

        LabelElementFactory line = new LabelElementFactory();
        line.setText("Payroll summary, October 2026");
        line.setMinimumWidth(300f);
        line.setMinimumHeight(20f);
        MasterReport report = new MasterReport();
        report.getReportHeader().addElement(line.createElement());

        // An open password and a copy ban, but no OwnerPassword key.
        ModifiableConfiguration config = report.getReportConfiguration();
        config.setConfigProperty(PDF + "Encryption", "128bit");
        config.setConfigProperty(PDF + "UserPassword", "payroll-2026");
        config.setConfigProperty(PDF + "AllowCopy", "false");

        PdfReportUtil.createPDF(report, new File("payroll-open-password.pdf"));
    }
}

With payroll-2026 the file opens as expected. An empty string opened it too, with every owner permission, in both pypdf and the OpenPDF reader, and pypdf then saved a decrypted copy reading Payroll summary, October 2026. MuPDF was the exception and prompted for the password. This matters to anyone who sets UserPassword by itself on HR or finance output, and supplying an OwnerPassword alongside it closes the gap. Signing and PDF/A have no configuration key in the PDF module, so an export cannot request either. The security and metadata example sets an open password and a permissions password side by side.

Which CVEs Ship With the 11.0 Dependency Tree?

These entries come from OSV and NVD, queried on 4 November 2026 and matched to the compile-scope dependencies of classic-core and its library modules. They are a selection, and CVE.org holds 47 records across the Bouncy Castle Java modules on 1.78.1, none of them on 1.86. Scores follow NVD and name who assigned them, all under CVSS 3.1 apart from Guava's CVSS 4.0, and NVD flags none of the entries as disputed. Each bullet gives the component at 11.0.0.0-237, the release that fixes it and its state in 11.0.0.4-325.

  • CVE-2026-8763, 9.1 Critical (NIST): Affects bcprov-jdk15to18 1.78.1, fixed in 1.85, and cleared by 1.86 in 11.0.0.4-325.
  • CVE-2026-13506, 7.5 High (NIST): Affects the same bcprov-jdk15to18, also fixed in 1.85 and cleared by 1.86.
  • CVE-2025-31672, 5.3 Medium (CISA-ADP): Affects poi-ooxml 5.2.5, fixed in 5.4.0, and cleared by 5.5.1.
  • CVE-2025-66453, 7.5 High (NIST): Affects rhino 1.7.13, fixed in 1.7.14.1, and cleared by 1.7.15.1.
  • CVE-2026-102554, 8.2 High (Google): Affects guava 32.1.2-jre, fixed in 33.7.2, and still open because 11.0.0.4-325 keeps that version.
  • CVE-2026-34478 and CVE-2026-34480, 7.5 High (NIST): Affects log4j-core 2.23.1, fixed in 2.25.4, and still open at 2.25.3.
  • CVE-2026-34477, 5.9 Medium (NIST): Also log4j-core 2.23.1 and fixed in 2.25.4, with 2.25.3 still inside the range.
  • CVE-2026-49844, 5.9 Medium (NIST): Affects log4j-api 2.23.1, fixed in 2.25.5, and 2.25.3 has not reached that fix.
  • CVE-2025-48924, 5.3 Medium (CISA-ADP): Affects commons-lang3 3.14.0, fixed in 3.18.0, and still open because 11.0.0.4-325 keeps 3.14.0.

classic-core declares bcmail-jdk15to18 directly, which is how Bouncy Castle gets in, and Rhino is declared by classic-core and by libloader. In Rhino's case, a crafted number passed to toFixed() can pin the CPU. classic-core declares Guava directly too, and that entry concerns memory allocation while deserializing its CompactHashMap, CompactHashSet and MapMakerInternalMap types, with NVD still listing it as awaiting analysis. The three Log4j Core entries need a particular setup to matter, Rfc5424Layout for log injection, XmlLayout for unsanitized characters and a TLS socket whose verifyHostName setting is silently ignored. OSV lists nothing against OpenPDF 1.3.32. GitHub's newer 11.1.0.0 build tags, from 11.1.0.0-343 onward, already carry Log4j 2.25.5, outside the Log4j ranges above, though 11.1.0.0-461, the newest on 4 November 2026, still pins Guava 32.1.2-jre. A dependencyManagement pin can override these versions as a stopgap, with regression testing on a set Pentaho never released.

Replacing the Pentaho PDF Path for HTML Reports

The engine drops flexbox and script from HTML text, writes RC4 files that pypdf and the OpenPDF reader reopen with an empty password when no OwnerPassword is set, carries Log4j advisories into the 11.0.0.4 service pack, and comes from a repository that answered 401 to Maven and curl requests without credentials.

Where the invoice already exists as an HTML page, IronPDF for Java renders it in full Chromium, and in our 2026.11.3 run the header above put ACME Supplies and Invoice INV-2041 at opposite edges and showed Issued 26 October 2026, with setEnableJavaScript(true) set on ChromePdfRenderOptions. Maven Central carries it as com.ironsoftware:ironpdf, version 2026.11.3 from 3 November. Its setPassword alone also wrote RC4, at 128 bits, and pypdf and MuPDF both refused the empty password. In another run, SecurityOptions with PdfEncryptionType.AES_256 and distinct user and owner passwords wrote an AES-256 file.

IronPDF for Java has a free trial for running these documents against your own templates, and the signing guide covers the digital signatures the Pentaho PDF module has no key for.

Pentaho, OpenPDF, Apache POI, Apache Commons Lang, Log4j, Bouncy Castle, Guava and Rhino are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with any of them, and the details here come from the Pentaho Reporting repository, NVD, OSV, CVE.org, qpdf's documentation, Oracle's Java documentation and Maven Central.

Drafted with AI. Pentaho Reporting code run on the 11.0.0.4-325 engine and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team on 4 November 2026, with com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3 as the IronPDF reference.

title: Trocar de provedor não deveria ser uma dor de cabeça
description:
Se você já trabalhou ou trabalha em startups, em um fluxo rápido de desenvolvimento de produto ou até mesmo criando o seu produto, deve saber que um produto pode e vai mudar em algum momento, devido à necessidade de novos investidores ou clientes, ou à decisão de algum stakeholder. Caso você não tenha experiência ou esteja começando agora nesse mundo de entregas rápidas, neste artigo eu pretendo te passar uma breve dica que provavelmente vai te economizar tempo de trabalho e reduzir as suas chances de ter dor de cabeça.

Sumário

  • Por que trocar de provedor
  • O provedor dentro do domínio
    • A modelagem acoplada
    • O código acoplado
  • E se o provedor mudar?
  • A solução
    • O domínio fala a própria língua
    • Um tradutor para cada provedor
    • Juntando tudo

Por que trocar de provedor

Acredito que o cenário mais comum e prático que eu possa dar para ilustrar o que eu quero te mostrar seja o caso em que você precise lidar com a mudança de um provedor de pagamento. Muitas coisas podem fazer com que uma empresa ou um produto cogite mudar o provedor, como: melhores taxas entre provedores, qualidade no suporte, maturidade do provedor e confiabilidade. Até mesmo o cenário em que o dono do provedor de pagamento é conhecido ou amigo da startup ou empresa em que você trabalha pode motivar essa mudança.

O provedor dentro do domínio

Imagine que chega a task para você fazer a implementação de um provedor de pagamento X dentro de um novo produto da empresa. Com prazo apertado e um único provedor, modelar tudo em cima dele parece o caminho mais rápido. Você faz a modelagem, faz a integração, tudo certinho: testado e funcionando. Mas aí, depois de alguns meses, chega a task para implementar um novo provedor de pagamento, e você percebe que vai ser uma dor de cabeça, porque tanto a modelagem quanto o código do domínio foram feitos com o vocabulário do antigo provedor, tornando tudo acoplado. Essa é uma situação que não é nada interessante de se resolver, mas é bem previsível de se combater.

A modelagem acoplada

O código acoplado

Aqui foi exemplificado o impacto na modelagem, mas, além dele, o código também teria outros problemas, como a repetição de código e inúmeras verificações.

final class ReleaseProduct
{
    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        $isPaid = match ($order->provider) {
            'stripe' => $order->stripe_status === 'succeeded',
            'mercadopago' => $order->mercadopago_status === 'approved',
        };

        if (! $isPaid) {
            return;
        }

        $order->product->release();
    }
}

final class RefundOrder
{
    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        match ($order->provider) {
            'stripe' => $this->stripe->refund($order->stripe_payment_intent_id),
            'mercadopago' => $this->mercadoPago->refund($order->mercadopago_payment_id),
        };
    }
}

E se o provedor mudar?

Eu tive o prazer de ter uma ótima liderança técnica e experiente que, antes mesmo de me deixar colocar a mão na modelagem, me mostrou as seguintes questões: "E se o provedor mudar, o que fazer? Qual a consequência de mudar do provedor X para o Y?" Sinceramente, no começo eu não fazia ideia do que fazer. Foi aí que me foi apresentada a ideia de fazer uma modelagem e um código agnóstico de provedor (provider-agnostic).

Na computação, um dispositivo ou programa de software é considerado agnóstico ou agnóstico de dados se o método ou formato de transmissão de dados for irrelevante para a função do dispositivo ou programa. Isso significa que o dispositivo ou programa pode receber dados em múltiplos formatos ou de múltiplas fontes e ainda assim processá-los de forma eficaz. — Wikipédia, tradução livre

Uma maneira prática de absorver essa ideia, e que me ajudou bastante, foi pensar: caso determinada informação possa ter um caminho diferente, tanto a modelagem quanto o código devem se comportar da mesma maneira, independentemente do caminho. No nosso exemplo, a informação é "o pagamento foi concluído", e os caminhos são o Stripe e o Mercado Pago.

Pagamento é só o exemplo que escolhi, mas a mesma ideia aparece em vários outros lugares: provedor de autenticação (Auth0, Cognito, Firebase Auth), envio de e-mail (SES, SendGrid, Mailgun), armazenamento de arquivos (S3, Google Cloud Storage) e envio de SMS (Twilio, Zenvia). Se você usa Laravel, já usa isso no dia a dia: o Mail e o Storage funcionam do mesmo jeito, seja qual for o driver configurado por trás.

A solução

O domínio fala a própria língua

Para tornar o código e a modelagem agnósticos de provedor, você vai precisar entender o que é domínio. Talvez você já tenha ouvido falar sobre DDD; é dele que vem esse termo. Não vou entrar no tema por completo (recomendo que você leia sobre o assunto depois), mas vou explicar brevemente o que seria esse tal domínio.

Entenda o domínio como a área de conhecimento e as regras do problema que o seu produto resolve. No código, ele vira a parte central, que reúne essas regras e entende como resolver o problema. No exemplo que estou utilizando, a nossa área de conhecimento e as regras são de pedido, então o nosso domínio tem tudo o que é necessário para resolver isso.

Agora que sabemos disso, você já deve ter notado que cada provedor tem uma nomenclatura para as informações de que ele precisa ou que retorna. Um pagamento concluído, por exemplo, é succeeded no Stripe e approved no Mercado Pago. Já o nosso domínio usa os próprios nomes, paid ou canceled, escolhidos por você ou pelo seu time, e os nomes dos provedores nunca chegam até ele.

Olhando para a modelagem: a tabela orders guarda só o vocabulário do domínio. O provedor vira apenas um dado (provider), e o id dele fica em uma coluna genérica (provider_reference).

Schema::create('orders', function (Blueprint $table) {
    $table->id();
    $table->integer('amount_cents');
    $table->string('status');
    $table->string('provider');
    $table->string('provider_reference')->nullable();
    $table->timestamps();
});

enum PaymentStatus: string
{
    case Pending = 'pending';
    case Paid = 'paid';
    case Canceled = 'canceled';
}

enum PaymentProvider: string
{
    case Stripe = 'stripe';
    case MercadoPago = 'mercadopago';
}

final class Order extends Model
{
    protected function casts(): array
    {
        return [
            'status' => PaymentStatus::class,
            'provider' => PaymentProvider::class,
        ];
    }
}

Um tradutor para cada provedor

O próximo passo é lidar com essa diferença de nomenclatura entre os provedores. Para isso, vamos criar uma classe que faz a tradução da nomenclatura da API para o que temos no nosso domínio. Esse tradutor é um adaptador (adapter), e todos os adaptadores seguem o mesmo contrato, a porta (port) que o domínio define. Essa camada de tradução, como um todo, é o que o DDD chama de camada anticorrupção (Anti-Corruption Layer).

                   DOMÍNIO  (fala "paid", "canceled")
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  ReleaseProduct      RefundOrder      HandleWebhook │
  └──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────┘
                             │ depende só do contrato
                 ┌───────────▼────────────┐
                 │ PaymentGatewayContract │  ← porta
                 └───────────┬────────────┘
             ┌───────────────┴────────────────┐
  ┌──────────▼───────────┐       ┌────────────▼───────────┐
  │ StripeGateway        │       │ MercadoPagoGateway     │  ← adaptadores
  │ "succeeded" → paid   │       │ "approved"  → paid     │    (traduzem)
  └──────────┬───────────┘       └────────────┬───────────┘
             ▼                                ▼
         API Stripe                   API Mercado Pago

Depois vem a porta, o contrato que todo provedor precisa seguir:

interface PaymentGatewayContract
{
    public function charge(Order $order): string;

    public function status(string $reference): PaymentStatus;

    public function refund(string $reference): void;
}

E um adaptador para cada provedor. É aqui, e só aqui, que o vocabulário de cada um aparece:

final class StripeGateway implements PaymentGatewayContract
{
    public function __construct(private StripeApi $api) {}

    public function charge(Order $order): string
    {
        return $this->api->createPaymentIntent($order->amount_cents)->id;
    }

    public function status(string $reference): PaymentStatus
    {
        return match ($this->api->getPaymentIntent($reference)->status) {
            'succeeded' => PaymentStatus::Paid,
            'canceled' => PaymentStatus::Canceled,
            default => PaymentStatus::Pending,
        };
    }

    public function refund(string $reference): void
    {
        $this->api->refundPaymentIntent($reference);
    }
}

final class MercadoPagoGateway implements PaymentGatewayContract
{
    public function __construct(private MercadoPagoApi $api) {}

    public function charge(Order $order): string
    {
        return $this->api->createPixPayment($order->amount_cents)->id;
    }

    public function status(string $reference): PaymentStatus
    {
        return match ($this->api->getPayment($reference)->status) {
            'approved' => PaymentStatus::Paid,
            'cancelled', 'rejected' => PaymentStatus::Canceled,
            default => PaymentStatus::Pending,
        };
    }

    public function refund(string $reference): void
    {
        $this->api->refundPayment($reference);
    }
}

Juntando tudo

A configuração diz qual provedor está ativo:

// config/payments.php
return [
    'default' => env('PAYMENT_PROVIDER', 'stripe'),
];

Um resolver sabe qual adaptador corresponde a cada provedor:

final class PaymentGatewayResolver
{
    public function for(PaymentProvider $provider): PaymentGatewayContract
    {
        return match ($provider) {
            PaymentProvider::Stripe => app(StripeGateway::class),
            PaymentProvider::MercadoPago => app(MercadoPagoGateway::class),
        };
    }
}

E o container do Laravel junta os dois: entrega o adaptador do provedor ativo para qualquer classe que peça o contrato.

final class AppServiceProvider extends ServiceProvider
{
    public function register(): void
    {
        $this->app->bind(
            PaymentGatewayContract::class,
            fn () => app(PaymentGatewayResolver::class)
                ->for(PaymentProvider::from(config('payments.default'))),
        );
    }
}

Com isso, aquelas classes do começo do artigo deixam de saber qual provedor está por trás:

final class ReleaseProduct
{
    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        if ($order->status !== PaymentStatus::Paid) {
            return;
        }

        $order->product->release();
    }
}

final class RefundOrder
{
    public function __construct(private PaymentGatewayContract $gateway) {}

    public function __invoke(Order $order): void
    {
        $this->gateway->refund($order->provider_reference);
    }
}

Se amanhã chegar a task de um terceiro provedor, o trabalho é criar um adaptador novo, adicionar um caso no enum PaymentProvider e uma linha no PaymentGatewayResolver. A tabela orders, o ReleaseProduct e o RefundOrder continuam iguais.

title: Streamlining Full-Stack Development: A Monorepo Approach with Next.js and Node.js
description:
Streamlining Full-Stack Development: A Monorepo Approach with Next.js and Node.js

Modern full-stack web applications demand tight cohesion between frontend interfaces and backend microservices. In traditional multi-repository setups, frontend and backend teams face continuous friction: duplicated TypeScript interfaces, out-of-sync API contracts, disparate linting rules, and disjointed deployment cycles. A simple database schema change often requires three separate pull requests, coordinated npm package publishing, and fragile version pinning.

Adopting a unified Monorepo architecture powered by Turborepo and pnpm fundamentally eliminates this overhead. In a monorepo, your Next.js frontend, Node.js API services, and shared libraries (Zod schemas, UI components, utility logic) live together in a single repository. You gain atomic cross-stack commits, instantaneous type inference across network boundaries, and lightning-fast incremental builds powered by computation caching.

In this comprehensive guide, we build a production-grade full-stack monorepo from scratch. We will set up Next.js 15 (App Router), an Express/Node.js API, shared TypeScript validation contracts, and optimize Docker container builds using turbo prune.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                       Enterprise Monorepo Architecture                        |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| apps/                                                                         |
|   ├── web/                     --> Next.js 15 App Router (Frontend)           |
|   └── api/                     --> Node.js / Express Service (Backend API)    |
| packages/                                                                     |
|   ├── shared-types/            --> Zod schemas & TypeScript DTO contracts     |
|   ├── ui/                      --> Shared React design system components      |
|   └── tsconfig/                --> Shared root TypeScript configurations      |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

graph TD
    Root[Monorepo Root: pnpm + Turborepo] --> Apps[apps/]
    Root --> Packages[packages/]

    Apps --> Web[apps/web: Next.js 15]
    Apps --> API[apps/api: Node.js Express]

    Packages --> Types[packages/shared-types: Zod & DTOs]
    Packages --> UI[packages/ui: React Design System]
    Packages --> Config[packages/tsconfig: Strict Configs]

    Web -->|Imports Type Contracts| Types
    API -->|Imports Type Contracts| Types
    Web -->|Consumes Components| UI
    Web -.->|Extends| Config
    API -.->|Extends| Config

1. Setting Up the Workspace

Initialize the repository root using pnpm workspaces:

mkdir fullstack-monorepo && cd fullstack-monorepo
pnpm init

Create pnpm-workspace.yaml:

packages:
  - "apps/*"
  - "packages/*"

2. Shared Base TypeScript Configuration

Create packages/tsconfig/base.json to enforce strict type checking across the entire monorepo:

{
  "$schema": "https://json.schemastore.org/tsconfig",
  "display": "Default",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "es2022",
    "lib": ["es2022", "dom"],
    "module": "esnext",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "strict": true,
    "esModuleInterop": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "forceConsistentCasingInFileNames": true,
    "resolveJsonModule": true
  }
}

3. Shared Domain Contracts: packages/shared-types

This package is consumed by both the Node.js API and the Next.js frontend, ensuring zero contract drift.

// packages/shared-types/package.json
{
  "name": "@repo/shared-types",
  "version": "0.0.1",
  "private": true,
  "main": "./src/index.ts",
  "types": "./src/index.ts",
  "dependencies": {
    "zod": "^3.23.8"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "@repo/tsconfig": "workspace:*",
    "typescript": "^5.5.0"
  }
}

// packages/shared-types/src/index.ts
import { z } from 'zod';

export const UserSchema = z.object({
  id: z.string().uuid(),
  email: z.string().email(),
  name: z.string().min(2),
  role: z.enum(['admin', 'member', 'guest']),
  createdAt: z.string().datetime(),
});

export type User = z.infer<typeof UserSchema>;

export const CreateUserRequestSchema = z.object({
  email: z.string().email(),
  name: z.string().min(2),
  role: z.enum(['admin', 'member', 'guest']).default('member'),
});

export type CreateUserRequest = z.infer<typeof CreateUserRequestSchema>;

export interface ApiResponse<T> {
  success: boolean;
  data: T;
  timestamp: string;
}

4. Node.js Backend: apps/api

apps/api/tsconfig.json 

{
  "extends": "@repo/tsconfig/base.json",
  "compilerOptions": {
    "outDir": "./dist",
    "rootDir": "./src"
  },
  "include": ["src/**/*"]
}

Express Application Server (apps/api/src/index.ts) 

import express, { Request, Response } from 'express';
import cors from 'cors';
import crypto from 'node:crypto';
import { CreateUserRequestSchema, User, ApiResponse } from '@repo/shared-types';

const app = express();
const port = process.env.PORT || 4000;

app.use(cors());
app.use(express.json());

// In-memory store
const users: User[] = [
  {
    id: 'a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7a8b-9c0d-1e2f3a4b5c6d',
    email: 'admin@company.com',
    name: 'Platform Lead',
    role: 'admin',
    createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  },
];

app.get('/api/users', (_req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const response: ApiResponse<User[]> = {
    success: true,
    data: users,
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
  };
  res.json(response);
});

app.post('/api/users', (req: Request, res: Response) => {
  const result = CreateUserRequestSchema.safeParse(req.body);
  if (!result.success) {
    return res.status(400).json({
      success: false,
      error: result.error.flatten().fieldErrors,
    });
  }

  const newUser: User = {
    id: crypto.randomUUID(),
    email: result.data.email,
    name: result.data.name,
    role: result.data.role,
    createdAt: new Date().toISOString(),
  };

  users.push(newUser);

  const response: ApiResponse<User> = {
    success: true,
    data: newUser,
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
  };

  return res.status(201).json(response);
});

app.listen(port, () => {
  console.log(`[Backend API] Service running on http://localhost:${port}`);
});

5. Next.js 15 Frontend: apps/web

Our Next.js application consumes @repo/shared-types directly inside Server Components:

// apps/web/src/app/users/page.tsx
import { User, ApiResponse } from '@repo/shared-types';

async function getUsers(): Promise<User[]> {
  const apiUrl = process.env.INTERNAL_API_URL || 'http://localhost:4000';
  const res = await fetch(`${apiUrl}/api/users`, {
    cache: 'no-store', // Always fetch fresh data
  });

  if (!res.ok) {
    throw new Error('Failed to fetch user list from backend API');
  }

  const json: ApiResponse<User[]> = await res.json();
  return json.data;
}

export default async function UsersPage() {
  const users = await getUsers();

  return (
    <main className="max-w-2xl mx-auto py-12 px-4">
      <h1 className="text-3xl font-bold tracking-tight text-slate-900 mb-6">
        Enterprise Team Directory
      </h1>

      <ul className="divide-y divide-slate-200 border border-slate-200 rounded-xl overflow-hidden bg-white shadow-xs">
        {users.map((user) => (
          <li key={user.id} className="p-4 flex justify-between items-center">
            <div>
              <p className="font-semibold text-slate-800">{user.name}</p>
              <p className="text-sm text-slate-500">{user.email}</p>
            </div>
            <span className="px-2.5 py-1 text-xs font-medium rounded-full bg-slate-100 text-slate-700 capitalize">
              {user.role}
            </span>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </main>
  );
}

6. Turborepo Orchestration: turbo.json

Configure task caching, pipeline dependencies, and output directories:

{
  "$schema": "https://turbo.build/schema.json",
  "tasks": {
    "build": {
      "dependsOn": ["^build"],
      "outputs": [".next/**", "!.next/cache/**", "dist/**"]
    },
    "lint": {
      "dependsOn": []
    },
    "check-types": {
      "dependsOn": ["^build"]
    },
    "dev": {
      "cache": false,
      "persistent": true
    }
  }
}

7. Optimizing Production Docker Builds with turbo prune

A common issue in monorepos is sending the entire repository context to Docker, creating multi-gigabyte image sizes. Turborepo solves this via turbo prune:

# Extract only the files needed for apps/web and its internal dependencies
npx turbo prune --scope=web --docker

This creates an isolated out/ folder containing only apps/web and @repo/shared-types, omitting apps/api and unrelated packages. The resulting production Dockerfile is lightweight and benefits from optimal layer caching.

Production Verification Checklist

  • [ ] Lockfile Single Source of Truth: Confirm all projects share the root pnpm-lock.yaml.
  • [ ] Workspace Protocol: Internal package references use "workspace:*" in package.json.
  • [ ] Topological Builds: Verify turbo.json specifies "dependsOn": ["^build"] so libraries compile before consuming applications.
  • [ ] TypeScript Path Resolution: Confirm TypeScript compiler resolves workspace packages without circular import errors.
  • [ ] Pruned Docker Builds: Validate turbo prune generates lean, isolated Docker deployment contexts.

title: Cómo construir un explorador OLAP de ventas con DuckDB y GitHub Pages
description:
Mariela Estefany Ramos Loza

Este proyecto permite comparar las ventas de distintas regiones y categorías sin descargar los pedidos individuales. DuckDB transforma 120 000 pedidos sintéticos de 2025 en 144 celdas que se pueden consultar desde un explorador web.

Diseñar el cubo

La unidad de análisis es un pedido de una sola categoría. Las dimensiones son mes, región y categoría. Cada celda guarda tres medidas aditivas: cantidad de pedidos, unidades vendidas e ingresos en centavos de dólar. Con 12 meses, 4 regiones y 3 categorías, se generan 144 combinaciones.

select month, region, category, count(*) as orders,
       sum(revenue_cents) as revenue_cents, sum(units) as units
from sales
group by month, region, category;

El script valida que los totales del cubo coincidan con los pedidos originales, tanto para el total general como para cada grupo de mes, región y categoría. Guardar ingresos en centavos permite sumar números enteros y aplicar el formato monetario al mostrar el resultado.

Consultar el cubo en el navegador

El HTML recibe solo las celdas agregadas. Al seleccionar enero se hace un slice. Al combinar enero con la región Norte se hace un dice. Al agrupar esa selección por categoría, el explorador muestra su desglose. Quitar los filtros y agrupar por región suma varios meses y categorías para obtener un total regional, una operación de roll-up. El gráfico puede mostrar pedidos, ingresos o unidades.

Automatizar la publicación

GitHub Actions instala DuckDB, ejecuta python build.py y prepara el HTML para GitHub Pages. El trabajo de despliegue depende del de compilación, de modo que una comprobación fallida detiene la publicación. El workflow se puede ejecutar manualmente y también se activa al actualizar la rama principal.

Para reproducirlo con Python 3.12, instala las dependencias con python -m pip install -r requirements.txt, ejecuta python build.py y abre site/index.html.

Repositorio público · Explorador OLAP

Este artículo fue redactado con IA.

title: ffmpeg और फ्रेम डिफरेंस से वीडियो को अपने आप 9:16 में रीफ्रेम कैसे करें
description:
वीडियो एडिटरों में ऑटो रीफ्रेम को आमतौर पर AI सब्जेक्ट ट्रैकिंग बताकर बेचा जाता है। सबसे आम मामले के लिए, यानी जब कोई व्यक्ति स्थिर बैकग्राउंड के सामने चल रहा हो, एक बहुत सरल तरीका वही फ्रेमिंग निकाल देता है: हर फ्रेम की पिछले फ्रेम से तुलना करो और देखो कि तस्वीर कहाँ बदली। डेस्कटॉप ऐप osFoundry का reframe टूल इसी तरह काम करता है, Rust और ffmpeg में। नीचे वही तरीका करीब 60 लाइन के Python में है, जिसे तीन शॉट वाली 7.5 सेकंड की 1920×1080 क्लिप पर चलाया गया है। यह ऐप जैसे ही crop देता है, पिक्सल तक बराबर।

1. वीडियो को 64×36 के ग्रे फ्रेम में छोटा करें

यह पता लगाने के लिए कि कुछ कहाँ हिला, फुल साइज़ फ्रेम देखने की ज़रूरत नहीं है। ffmpeg वीडियो को raw bytes के रूप में दे सकता है, प्रति सेकंड चार फ्रेम, 64×36 में स्केल करके और हर पिक्सल के लिए एक ग्रे बाइट में बदलकर:

import math, re, subprocess, sys

FFMPEG, SRC = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
W, H, FPS = 64, 36, 4

raw = subprocess.run(
    [FFMPEG, "-loglevel", "error", "-i", SRC,
     "-vf", f"fps={FPS},scale={W}:{H}", "-pix_fmt", "gray", "-f", "rawvideo", "-"],
    capture_output=True, check=True).stdout
frames = [raw[i:i + W * H] for i in range(0, len(raw) - W * H + 1, W * H)]

हर फ्रेम 2,304 बाइट का है। 7.5 सेकंड की क्लिप से 30 फ्रेम मिलते हैं, यानी तुलना के लिए 29 जोड़े। छोटा करने से ज़्यादातर ग्रेन भी औसत होकर खत्म हो जाता है, जो अगले स्टेप में मायने रखता है।

2. बदली हुई जगह का केंद्र निकालें

फ्रेम के हर जोड़े के लिए हर सेल का अंतर निकालें, छोटे अंतर को नज़रअंदाज़ करें, और बाकी का centre of mass निकालें, जिसमें हर सेल का वज़न इस पर निर्भर है कि वह कितना बदला:

def centroid(prev, curr, floor=12):
    total = sx = sy = 0
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(zip(prev, curr)):
        d = abs(b - a)
        if d < floor:
            continue
        total += d
        sx += d * (i % W)
        sy += d * (i // W)
    if total < W * H * 0.5:
        return None
    return sx / total / W, sy / total / H

samples = [centroid(a, b) for a, b in zip(frames, frames[1:])]

ये दो constants ही इसे इस्तेमाल लायक बनाते हैं। 255 में से 12 का noise floor उन बदलावों को हटा देता है जो सेंसर और compression से आते हैं। इस क्लिप में floor 12 रखने पर औसतन 2,304 में से 381 सेल बदले हुए गिने जाते हैं। floor 1 रखने पर 1,855 गिने जाते हैं, यानी लगभग पूरा फ्रेम, और केंद्र तस्वीर के बीच की ओर खिंच जाता है: पहला सैंपल चौड़ाई के 0.40 की जगह 0.44 पर आता है।

दूसरी जाँच तब None लौटाती है जब कुल बदलाव बहुत कम हो। जब कुछ नहीं हिला, तो "बदलाव का केंद्र" असल में noise का केंद्र होता है, और उसके पीछे चलने से फ्रेम बिना वजह खिसकता है। None का मतलब है "पिछली पोज़िशन रखो"।

3. फ्रेम कितनी तेज़ी से हिल सकता है, इसकी सीमा रखें

जब भी शॉट में दूसरा व्यक्ति आता है, कच्चा centroid कूद जाता है। हर सैंपल पर कदम को फ्रेम के 5% तक सीमित कर देने से वह एक झटके में इधर-उधर नहीं भागता:

def smooth(samples, step=0.05):
    cur = next((s for s in samples if s), (0.5, 0.5))
    out = []
    for s in samples:
        if s:
            cur = tuple(min(1, max(0, c + max(-step, min(step, t - c))))
                        for c, t in zip(cur, s))
        out.append(cur)
    return out

track = smooth(samples)

यह पहले असली observation से शुरू होता है, इसलिए जो क्लिप स्थिर फ्रेम से खुलती है वह बीच से pan करती हुई नहीं आती।

4. ffmpeg के scene score से कट खोजें

ffmpeg का select फ़िल्टर हर फ्रेम को 0 से 1 के बीच का scene score देता है, और showinfo उन फ्रेमों को प्रिंट करता है जो पास होते हैं। टाइमस्टैम्प stdout पर नहीं, stderr पर आते हैं:

log = subprocess.run(
    [FFMPEG, "-hide_banner", "-i", SRC,
     "-filter_complex", "select='gt(scene,0.35)',showinfo", "-f", "null", "-"],
    capture_output=True, text=True).stderr
cuts = [round(float(t) * 1000) for t in re.findall(r"pts_time:([\d.]+)", log)]

इस क्लिप में यह 1,767 ms और 4,733 ms पर कट ढूँढता है। हर फ्रेम का score प्रिंट करने (select='gte(scene,0)',metadata=print) पर पता चलता है कि फ़ासला कितना बड़ा है: दोनों कटों का score 0.616 और 0.432 है, और 225 फ्रेमों में से कोई दूसरा 0.068 से ऊपर नहीं जाता।

5. हर शॉट के लिए एक crop

आखिर में, हर शॉट के अंदर track का औसत लें और उस बिंदु के चारों ओर 9:16 की विंडो रखें। 1080 × 9/16 यानी 607.5 होता है; चौड़ाई को घटाकर सम संख्या 606 कर दिया गया है क्योंकि H.264 को सम dimensions चाहिए।

duration = len(frames) * 1000 // FPS
per = duration / len(track)
bounds = [0] + [c for c in cuts if 0 < c < duration] + [duration]
cw = int(1080 * 9 / 16) // 2 * 2
for start, end in zip(bounds, bounds[1:]):
    a = int(start // per)
    part = track[a:max(a + 1, math.ceil(end / per))]
    bx = sum(p[0] for p in part) / len(part)
    x = min(max(round(1920 * bx - cw / 2), 0), 1920 - cw)
    print(f"{start / 1000:.2f}-{end / 1000:.2f}s  crop={cw}:1080:{x}:0")

0.00-1.77s  crop=606:1080:369:0
1.77-4.73s  crop=606:1080:668:0
4.73-7.50s  crop=606:1080:932:0

ये वही तीन crop हैं जो ऐप ने इस क्लिप के लिए निकाले थे। पूरी स्क्रिप्ट इस Mac पर 3.5 सेकंड में चली, ज़्यादातर समय pure-Python लूप में गया।

कट दिखने से ज़्यादा मायने रखते हैं। पूरी क्लिप पर औसत लें तो सब्जेक्ट x = 707 पर बैठता है, सीधे सेंटर crop (657) से सिर्फ 50 पिक्सल दूर, क्योंकि महिला एक शॉट में बाईं ओर और दूसरे में दाईं ओर चलती है। औसत का मतलब तभी बनता है जब वह हर शॉट के हिसाब से निकाला जाए।

शॉट को वापस जोड़ना

इन crop से एक filter_complex बनता है: हर शॉट को trim करें, crop करें और टुकड़ों को जोड़ दें। ऐप यही रूप बनाता है:

[0:v]trim=start=0.000:end=1.767,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:369:0[v0];
[0:v]trim=start=1.767:end=4.733,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:668:0[v1];
[0:v]trim=start=4.733:end=7.500,setpts=PTS-STARTPTS,crop=606:1080:932:0[v2];
[v0][v1][v2]concat=n=3:v=1:a=0[out]

(इसे -filter_complex में देते समय लाइन ब्रेक हटा दें।) आउटपुट 606×1080 है और इनपुट के बराबर लंबा है।

ऐप का Rust बताता है कि वह शॉट के अंदर crop को animate क्यों नहीं करता, जबकि ffmpeg ऐसा कर सकता है:

/// 🔴 Per scene, not per frame. ffmpeg can animate a crop, but a crop that moves continuously is
/// a pan the editor never asked for; cutting between fixed framings is what an editor would
/// actually do, and it is also what stays honest when the tracking is wrong — a bad framing
/// lasts one scene rather than smearing across the whole clip.
pub fn reframe_segments(
    cuts: &[i64],
    duration_ms: i64,
    track: &[(f64, f64)],
    width: u32,
    height: u32,
    target: f64,
) -> Vec<ReframeSegment> {

जहाँ फ्रेम डिफरेंस फेल हो जाता है

यह तरीका यह खोजता है कि क्या हिल रहा है, यह नहीं कि कौन ज़रूरी है। यह तब काम करता है जब सब्जेक्ट ही मुख्य रूप से हिलने वाली चीज़ हो और कैमरा स्थिर हो। यह तब गड़बड़ करता है जब:

  • कैमरा pan करे, तो हर सेल बदलती है और केंद्र बीच के पास आ जाता है;
  • बैकग्राउंड व्यस्त हो, जैसे ट्रैफिक या भीड़;
  • दो लोग विपरीत किनारों पर हिलें, और औसत उन दोनों के बीच आ जाए।

रिफ्लेक्शन एक हल्का मामला है। इस क्लिप के पहले शॉट में खिड़की में महिला का प्रतिबिंब भी हिलता है, लेकिन वह उसके पास ही रहता है, इसलिए फ्रेम फिर भी उसे ढूँढ लेता है। मुश्किल मामलों को चेहरे या व्यक्ति का detector बेहतर संभालता है, लेकिन उसकी कीमत एक model है। ऐसे मामलों के लिए ऐप का जवाब मैन्युअल override है: यूज़र सब्जेक्ट पर एक बिंदु खींचकर रख देता है, और analysis छोड़ दिया जाता है।

यहाँ इस्तेमाल हुआ डेस्कटॉप ऐप osFoundry के डाउनलोड पेज से मुफ़्त है।

title: PD4ML for Java: Scripts, File Access and Layout Width
description:
A one-line script that writes a total into a <span> is enough to show the first issue. PD4ML 4.1.2 printed the label and left the number out. PD4ML is a pure-Java HTML to PDF engine, and 4.1.2, uploaded to PD4ML's own Maven repository on 2 November 2026, is still its newest release on 4 November 2026. This post collects the issues we found running it on Java 17, with the run output and a workaround wherever we found one.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

Every run was unlicensed, which puts PD4ML in evaluation mode. The sections below cover every row of the table.

Issue Affected version Evidence
Script never executed, <canvas> left blank PD4ML 4.1.2 Run and HTML5 support matrix
Local files embedded from user markup PD4ML 4.1.2, null base URL Run and javadoc
CVE-2026-8763, CVE-2026-13506 and 26 more records bcprov-jdk18on and bcpkix-jdk18on 1.84 OSV, GHSA and CVE.org
Grid columns and var() colours ignored PD4ML 4.1.2 Run and features page
Elements wider than 727 px clipped PD4ML 4.1.2 default htmlWidth Run and manual
PDF/A request returns a license error PD4ML 4.1.2 without a license Run and veraPDF

Does PD4ML Run the Page's JavaScript?

No. PD4ML's published HTML5 compatibility table rates <script> N/A by design and explains that the code contains no script engine at all. Whatever a page's own scripts would have added stays invisible to the converter.

import com.pd4ml.PD4ML;

import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class ScriptFilledTotal {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // The span is empty in the markup and a script writes the sum into it after load.
        String html = "<html><body><p>Open invoices: <span id='n'></span></p>"
                + "<script>document.getElementById('n').textContent = [12, 7, 23].reduce(function (a, b) { return a + b; });</script>"
                + "</body></html>";

        PD4ML pd4ml = new PD4ML();
        pd4ml.readHTML(new ByteArrayInputStream(html.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)), null, "UTF-8");
        try (FileOutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("open-invoices.pdf")) {
            pd4ml.writePDF(out);
        }
    }
}

open-invoices.pdf is a single A4 page whose only line reads Open invoices:. The 42 the script would have written is not there, and nothing in the run's output mentions the skipped script. A <canvas> painted by script behaves the same way, and in a separate run the canvas area came out blank, with no image or drawing on the page.

Any template that builds content in the browser runs into this, from chart libraries to totals computed client-side. The workaround is to compute values in Java and put them into the HTML, for example through setDynamicData placeholders, and to switch charts to inline <svg>, drawn as true vector graphics in STD and every higher edition according to PD4ML's products page.

Can User-Supplied HTML Read Files From the Server?

It can. When readHTML gets a null base URL, the javadoc says relative references resolve against the current working directory, and the manual warns that unrestricted HTML can make a server read local files or call internal services.

import com.pd4ml.PD4ML;

import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class UserHtmlReadsDisk {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // Stands in for HTML a user submitted, which points an image at a file on the server.
        String userHtml = "<html><body><p>My profile</p>"
                + "<img src='internal/hr-badge.png'></body></html>";

        // With a null base URL, relative paths resolve against the working directory.
        PD4ML pd4ml = new PD4ML();
        pd4ml.readHTML(new ByteArrayInputStream(userHtml.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)), null, "UTF-8");
        try (FileOutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("profile.pdf")) {
            pd4ml.writePDF(out);
        }
    }
}

The working directory held internal/hr-badge.png, a 240 by 60 pixel image, and profile.pdf came out with that image embedded under My profile. A conversion service that accepts HTML from users can therefore be pointed at images on its own disk, and in two more probes a ../ path and an absolute file: URL each embedded an image from outside that directory. PD4ML has a setting for this. Passing Constants.PD4ML_ALLOWED_RESOURCE_LOCATION to setParam with a URL prefix makes it reject images, stylesheets and attachments from anywhere else, and a rerun with the prefix set to a different folder produced the page without the badge.

Which Advisories Ride Along With the Bouncy Castle Pin?

A search of OSV and GitHub's advisory database for com.pd4ml:pd4ml on 4 November 2026 returned nothing. What does show up is in Bouncy Castle. The manual's Maven snippet, still written for 4.1.1 on that date, sets both Bouncy Castle artifacts to 1.84, and OSV attaches two advisories to that bcprov version, both dated 3 August 2026 and both resolved in 1.85. CVE.org holds far more, with 28 records naming bcprov or bcpkix on 1.84, 21 from August and 7 from October, and none on 1.86.

  • CVE-2026-8763, CVSS 4.0 score 9.3 Critical (Bouncy Castle, the CNA), CVSS 3.1 score 9.1 (GitHub): A certificate whose rfc822Name or URI ends in a trailing dot can slip past Name Constraints
  • CVE-2026-13506, CVSS 4.0 score 8.7 High (the CNA), CVSS 3.1 score 7.5 (GitHub): Forcing a lazily parsed ASN.1 sequence resets the nesting-depth guard

The manual names the encryption and signing packages as depending on Bouncy Castle, so teams protecting or signing PDFs through PD4ML carry these until they move, and 1.86, the current release, is the one clear of them all, since records such as CVE-2026-18036 run from 1.73 to before 1.86. A separate test had PD4ML's PdfSigner sign a PDF with the 1.85 Bouncy Castle jars on the classpath.

The pin is easy to inherit without noticing. According to the manual, Maven resolves Bouncy Castle through PD4ML automatically, but the POM published for 4.1.2 lists none, so whatever versions end up in the build are the ones someone typed, and the manual's snippet offers 1.84. Maven Central doesn't carry PD4ML either, which means a Maven build first registers PD4ML's repository, pd4ml.com/maven2 in the manual.

Layout Gaps Between the Feature List and a 4.1.2 Run

PD4ML's features page says its engine lays out Flexbox and CSS Grid. In a 4.1.2 run, a display: grid container with grid-template-columns: 150px 150px 150px printed its three cards stacked down the left edge, and text coloured through var(--brand) came out black. Flexbox held up in the same session, with a space-between row spread correctly across the page.

The second layout check is width. The manual gives 727 px as the default htmlWidth, the width of the imaginary browser PD4ML lays the page out in, and a wider element is clipped at the right margin rather than scaled down.

import com.pd4ml.PD4ML;

import java.io.ByteArrayInputStream;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;

public class WideTableAt727 {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // A 1000 px wide table, as a desktop page would lay it out, with htmlWidth left at its default.
        String html = "<html><body><table border='1' style='width:1000px'><tr>"
                + "<td>Region</td><td>Q1</td><td>Q2</td><td>Q3</td><td style='text-align:right'>Year total</td>"
                + "</tr></table></body></html>";

        PD4ML pd4ml = new PD4ML();
        pd4ml.readHTML(new ByteArrayInputStream(html.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)), null, "UTF-8");
        try (FileOutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("wide-table.pdf")) {
            pd4ml.writePDF(out);
        }
    }
}

Four of the five cells show on the page. Year total is clipped at the right margin, though its text is still in the content stream and pypdf extracts it. A rerun with pd4ml.setHtmlWidth(1000) ahead of readHTML put it back, and adjustHtmlWidth(true) from the manual sizes the window to the document instead. For grid layouts and shared design tokens, the fallback is a table or flexbox plus plain colour values in the stylesheet the PDF reads.

What Evaluation Output Looks Like

Every page of unlicensed PDF output has two blue watermark bands running vertically along its left and right margins. The manual calls evaluation mode watermarked with no restriction on functionality, yet a run asking writePDF for PdfSpec.PDFA_2B came back with an error status from getLastRenderInfo stating that the license didn't permit PDF/A. Its metadata claimed PDF/A-2B, and veraPDF 1.30.3 passed the file as PDF/A-2B, where the 4.1.1 file failed on a broken header, so a build reading that status stops on output the validator accepts. The message points at licensing, and an evaluation license, a pd4ml.lic file, can be requested from the PD4ML downloads page.

Features are also split across PD4ML's four editions. The javadoc marks TrueType embedding through useTTF and form generation as PRO features, and the products page starts DOCX at DMS and keeps PDF/UA in UA.

How IronPDF Handles Script, Grid and Wide Pages

The script, grid and width results trace back to laying out HTML without a browser, and IronPDF for Java takes the other route. Every PdfDocument render goes through a Chromium instance, so scripts on the page execute before the PDF is produced. Our 2026.11.3 run of a page with the same summing script, three grid columns and a var() colour printed 42, laid the columns out side by side and applied the colour.

When a layout is wider than the paper, the render option UseFitToPageRendering takes its pixel width and scales it to the width of one sheet, which brought a 1,000 px table inside the page next to a canvas bar in our run, and the C3.js chart example waits a second before capture.

It resolves from Maven Central as com.ironsoftware:ironpdf. Eleven versions shipped in 2026, ending with 2026.11.3 on 3 November, and nothing from Bouncy Castle turns up when Maven resolves it. IronPDF has a free trial for running your own script-heavy templates through it.

Weighing PD4ML's Issues Before Production

Missing script output, local files pulled in by untrusted markup, a Bouncy Castle 1.84 pin inside 28 CVE.org records, grid columns, custom properties and anything past 727 px lost in our runs, and a license error on a PDF/A request make up the PD4ML 4.1.2 list. For templates that depend on browser behavior, IronPDF for Java renders the same HTML in Chromium on a paper size you choose.

PD4ML is a trademark of its respective owner, we have no affiliation with its vendor, and the versions, advisories and behavior described above are taken from the vendor's public documentation, its Maven repository, public advisory databases and our own runs.

title: Checking Open HTML to PDF 1.1.108: CVEs, Flex Rows, Fonts
description:
A dependency scan on a build with Open HTML to PDF can report Batik, PDFBox or Commons IO advisories, even though NVD, OSV and GitHub's database list no CVE for the renderer's own jars. That scan result leads this post on 1.1.108, the 1 November 2026 release of the community fork under the io.github.openhtmltopdf group ID. Flex rows, fonts, base URIs and XHTML parsing follow, tested on Java 17 or traced to the README and wiki on 4 November 2026.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

Which CVEs Reach a Build Through Its Dependencies

A search of the three main advisory sources (NVD, OSV and GitHub's database) on 4 November 2026 found no CVE for the renderer's own jars, under the old or the new group ID. The records a scanner reports come in with the modules' dependencies. CVSS 3.1 base scores below are from NVD, with the scorer named.

  • CVE-2022-38398 and CVE-2022-38648, score 5.3 Medium (NIST): Server-side request forgery in Batik 1.14, fixed in Batik 1.15.
  • CVE-2022-40146, score 7.5 High (NIST): Request forgery in Batik 1.14 that reaches files through a Jar URL, fixed in 1.15.
  • CVE-2022-42890, score 7.5 High (NIST): Untrusted SVG runs Java code through JavaScript in Batik before 1.16.
  • CVE-2022-41704, score 7.5 High (NIST): Untrusted Java code runs from an SVG in Batik before 1.16.
  • CVE-2022-44729 and CVE-2022-44730, scores 7.1 High and 4.4 Medium (NIST): Request forgery in Batik up to 1.16, fixed in 1.17.
  • CVE-2022-34169, score 7.5 High (NIST): Integer truncation in Xalan through 2.7.2 when it processes a malicious XSLT stylesheet.
  • CVE-2026-33929, score 4.3 Medium (CISA-ADP): Path traversal through the ExtractEmbeddedFiles example shipped with PDFBox 2.0.24 to 2.0.36 and 3.0.0 to 3.0.7, fixed in 2.0.37 and 3.0.8.
  • CVE-2024-47554, score 4.3 Medium (CISA-ADP): CPU exhaustion in XmlStreamReader in Commons IO before 2.14.0.
  • CVE-2021-29425, score 4.8 Medium (NIST): Limited path traversal in FilenameUtils.normalize in Commons IO before 2.7.

The seven Batik records apply to the com.openhtmltopdf 1.0.10 SVG module, which depends on Batik 1.14, and that group ID has had no newer release. The Xalan record reaches the same module, through Xalan 2.7.2 from batik-dom 1.14. The PDFBox record applies to 1.0.10, which uses PDFBox 2.0.24, and to every fork build on Maven Central before 1.1.100, which used PDFBox 3.0.2 to 3.0.7. GitHub's advisory files that example under the separate pdfbox-examples artifact, but scanners that read NVD match on the PDFBox version even though the renderer never calls that example. CVE-2024-47554 applies to 1.1.108 as well, since its SVG module resolves commons-io 2.11.0 through xmlgraphics-commons 2.9, while OSV's range for CVE-2021-29425 takes in the commons-io 1.3.1 that the 1.0.10 SVG module gets from xmlgraphics-commons 2.6. Seven newer Batik CVEs sit outside those databases. Apache's security page rates them medium, ties them to the 1.20 release of 20 October 2026 and scopes them to 1.19 and older, so the Batik 1.17 that the 1.1.108 module uses falls in that range, with no NVD or OSV entry as of 4 November 2026. The library's own mitigations are Batik 1.17 and PDFBox 3.0.8 in 1.1.108 and a default BatikSVGDrawer that blocks scripts and external requests inside SVG, and a dependencyManagement entry in the Maven build can lift Commons IO to a fixed 2.14.0 or newer.

A Flex Row Stacks Instead of Sitting Side by Side

Two panels in a flex row are the usual shape of a dashboard card.

import com.openhtmltopdf.pdfboxout.PdfRendererBuilder;

import java.io.File;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;

public class FlexPanelsRow {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // Two flex:1 panels meant to sit side by side, the shape of a dashboard card row.
        String panel = "flex: 1; height: 600px; border: 1px solid #999;";
        String html = "<html><body><div style=\"display: flex; gap: 12px;\">"
                + "<div style=\"" + panel + "\">Renewals due in Q1</div>"
                + "<div style=\"" + panel + "\">Renewals due in Q2</div>"
                + "</div></body></html>";

        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("renewal-panels.pdf")) {
            PdfRendererBuilder builder = new PdfRendererBuilder();
            builder.withHtmlContent(html, new File(".").toURI().toString());
            builder.toStream(out);
            builder.run();
        }
    }
}

In 1.1.108 the log reported that flex is not a recognized identifier, ignored gap and both flex declarations, and laid the panels out in block flow. Each panel took the full body width, the Q2 panel started partway down page one, and its border ran onto a second A4 page. According to the README's DISCLAIMER section, flex and grid layouts are unsupported, JavaScript is ignored everywhere in the code, and the suggested substitutes are HTML tables or floated inline blocks. A template built on a flex row or a grid needs that rewrite before it prints, and anything a page script draws or fills in, from a total to a JavaScript chart, has to be produced in Java first.

Text Outside Western European Scripts Needs a Font File

With no font registered, text falls back to the PDF built-in fonts.

import com.openhtmltopdf.pdfboxout.PdfRendererBuilder;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;

public class GreekWithoutFont {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // No font is registered, so the text falls back to the built-in PDF fonts.
        String html = "<html><body><p>Invoice / Τιμολόγιο 2048</p></body></html>";

        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("greek.pdf")) {
            PdfRendererBuilder builder = new PdfRendererBuilder();
            builder.withHtmlContent(html, null);
            builder.toStream(out);
            builder.run();
        }
    }
}

Nothing in the log mentioned the missing glyphs, and the PDF's text layer read Invoice / ######### 2048, with each of the nine Greek letters replaced by the # character. The project's Fonts wiki explains that the built-in fonts cover only a basic Western European character set and that a character with no glyph becomes the replacement character. Any document with Greek, Cyrillic, Arabic or Asian text needs a font file registered through useFont or @font-face, and the README rules out OpenType, so the file has to be TrueType. PDF/A and PDF/UA output bar the built-in fonts entirely, and PDF/A also needs an ICC profile that the project does not ship.

Relative Images Need a Base URI, and Markup Needs to Be XHTML

withHtmlContent takes the markup and a base URI. Passing null is legal, and nothing stops the render.

import com.openhtmltopdf.pdfboxout.PdfRendererBuilder;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;

public class MissingBaseUri {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String html = "<html><body>"
                + "<img src=\"images/logo.png\" alt=\"Company logo\" />"
                + "<p>Statement for October 2026</p></body></html>";

        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("no-base.pdf")) {
            PdfRendererBuilder builder = new PdfRendererBuilder();

            // No base URI, so the relative image path has nothing to resolve against.
            builder.withHtmlContent(html, null);
            builder.toStream(out);
            builder.run();
        }
    }
}

The log printed Couldn't resolve relative URI(images/logo.png) because no base URI was provided three times, and the PDF came out with the text and no image. The program exits normally, so the missing logo shows up only when someone opens the file. The fix is a base URI such as the working folder's file: URI, or withFile, which uses the file's own location.

Markup has its own entry condition. The renderer's parser is an XML parser, and a test HTML5 letter with an unclosed <meta> tag stopped withFile with an XRRuntimeException at line 7, column 3, leaving a zero-byte PDF. The README recommends parsing such files with Jsoup first and passing the renderer a Document, which adds Jsoup to the build, and Jsoup's result has to be converted to the org.w3c.dom.Document that withW3cDocument takes.

Release History of the Two Coordinates

The last com.openhtmltopdf release is 1.0.10, dated 13 September 2021, and danfickle's original repository, unarchived, has had no commit on its default branch since 1 April 2022. Because the fork's pipeline releases each push to main that changes more than Markdown files, its 103 versions count pushes and say little about the size of any one change. It went from 1.1.37 on 21 January 2026 to 1.1.38 on 3 July 2026 with nothing in between, then published 70 more by 1 November 2026. The wiki the README links is still hosted on the old repository and marked as not yet migrated, and the online sandbox carries a 1.0.10 label in the README. The project is distributed under LGPL-2.1-or-later.

Summing Up the Checks

Open HTML to PDF needs flex and grid layouts rewritten, page scripts replaced, TrueType fonts registered for non-Latin text and for PDF/A, a base URI for relative images and well-formed XHTML input, and its dependency tree carries Batik, Xalan, PDFBox or Commons IO advisories depending on the build. For templates that come from a web front end, IronPDF for Java is a commercial alternative from Iron Software that renders that markup through Chromium.

In our runs on 2026.11.3, two renewal panels stayed side by side in a flex row, a grid row took its reference from a page script with a WaitFor delay, and a string with   and unclosed tags rendered with no Jsoup step. An @font-face rule embedded its TrueType file in another run, the Google Fonts example shows the web-font route, and the PDF/A guide converts after rendering, with PDF/A-1, 2 and 3 output passing veraPDF in our run.

The library is declared as com.ironsoftware:ironpdf, and Maven Central carries eleven 2026 builds of it, from 2026.1.3 to 2026.11.3 on 3 November 2026. A free trial covers running your own templates before any purchase.

Open HTML to PDF, Apache PDFBox, Apache Batik, Apache Xalan, Apache Commons IO and Jsoup remain the property of their owners, we have no affiliation with those projects, and what we say about them is based on their READMEs, wiki pages, Apache's security page, Maven Central metadata and the NVD, OSV and GitHub records.

Drafted with AI. Code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team against Open HTML to PDF 1.1.108, with IronPDF APIs checked against com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3, on 4 November 2026.

title: IAM Roles Anywhere now supports automatic certificate revocation checking
description:
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) Roles Anywhere now supports automatic revocation checking using certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution points (CDPs). This helps keep revocation checks in sync with your certificate authority (CA) and can help improve your security posture. When you enable this capability on a trust anchor, IAM Roles Anywhere reads the CDP URLs embedded in authenticating certificates, downloads the corresponding CRLs, and denies credential requests that use revoked certificates.

Previously, to check revocation status, you had to import CRLs into IAM Roles Anywhere and re-import them each time your CA published an update, which added operational overhead. With this launch, IAM Roles Anywhere downloads CRLs from your CDPs and refreshes them periodically, so you no longer need to re-import them. You can use this capability with AWS Private Certificate Authority or your own public key infrastructure (PKI), provided your certificates include publicly accessible CDP URLs that meet the distribution point requirements. To enable it on a trust anchor, use the IAM Roles Anywhere console, AWS SDKs, or AWS CLI.

This feature is available at no additional cost in all commercial AWS Regions. To learn more, see Automatic revocation checking with CRL distribution points in the IAM Roles Anywhere User Guide.

title: Scheduled Scripts in 2026: Backend Cron Alternatives for HTTP Calls and Visual Tools
description:
For scheduled scripts, the most practical backend cron alternatives are usually the timer and infrastructure you already operate, especially when the HTTP call starts a weekly healthtech digest. The expensive term is the work per active customer: rendering the digest, delivering it, and repeating it after an ambiguous failure. An external tool becomes attractive when non-developers must connect many applications without writing code.

Short answer: use basic cron or a small cron API when one HTTP-triggered job is enough and developers can own failure handling. Choose Zapier for visual connections across many SaaS applications, n8n when self-hosting and editable workflows matter, and Kubernetes CronJob when the digest already belongs inside a Kubernetes platform. Infrai is a reasonable middle path when one REST contract needs to cover both the weekly trigger and a queue handoff, provided the application owns customer-level idempotency.

What is the bill actually buying?

For this healthtech case, the unit to count is not “one cron.” It is one digest attempt per active customer, plus any repeated attempt that can produce duplicate email or duplicate downstream work. A retry that re-renders and sends without a stable delivery key can turn one weekly obligation into several operational actions. The retention cost is keeping enough run state to prove what happened, while not retaining sensitive payloads longer than necessary.

I start with three quantities: the customer cohort at the cutoff, the number of delivery attempts, and the amount of state retained for reconciliation. The first two drive compute and provider actions; the third drives the investigation burden when a customer says a digest is missing. A scheduler with a free starting tier can still be expensive in engineering time if every failed HTTP call requires a hand-built replay path.

The deliberate trade-off is to keep a small idempotency record such as (customer_id, digest_week) and a delivery status, while avoiding a copy of the full health record in the scheduler. That makes a retry safe, but it means a later investigation may need to retrieve the source data again. This is a good boundary for a digest: retain the decision and result, not a second clinical dataset. When the delivery provider returns a timeout after accepting a request, the record also gives the worker a place to represent uncertainty instead of guessing that the send failed. That choice is less tidy than a boolean, but it prevents a support ticket from turning into a duplicate customer message.

That is the expensive part.

How should teams choose backend cron alternatives for scheduled HTTP scripts?

Option Integration shape Retry and idempotency responsibility Best boundary
Basic cron on existing infrastructure A timer invokes your script or HTTP endpoint Your application owns backoff, deduplication, and failure records Simple jobs where developers own the service
Infrai scheduling and queues One REST surface for a cron trigger and queue handoff The consumer still must be idempotent; standard queues are at-least-once Teams that want scheduling plus queueing under one contract
Zapier Visual app connections and action-based steps The workflow owner configures retries and guards against repeated actions Non-developers joining several SaaS systems
n8n Visual workflows with a self-hosting option Your team owns workflow operation and application-level deduplication Teams wanting an editable workflow with more infrastructure control
Kubernetes CronJob A scheduled Kubernetes workload Cluster and application operators own restart, overlap, and job history policy A digest already deployed and observed in Kubernetes

Zapier and n8n reduce the time to connect a broader set of applications. That convenience is real, but each action and connection adds another place to inspect when a digest is late. Their operational charges can also grow with frequent execution or larger usage. Basic cron keeps the control plane small and is often the right answer for cost-sensitive digest work when the team can implement failure handling.

How should the retry boundary be drawn?

A weekly trigger should claim work once, then hand off customer-level work to a worker if rendering or delivery can exceed a short request. Infrai cron executions have a 900-second limit, so a long digest must use “cron triggers enqueue, worker consumes.” Queue messages are limited to 256 KB, delayed delivery to 7 days, and retention to 30 days. Those limits are enough for a customer identifier and a digest period; they are a poor place for a full export.

The standard queue is at-least-once. That sentence deserves more attention than a dashboard screenshot. The worker should derive a stable key from the customer and digest period, write or claim that key atomically, and make the send operation safe to repeat. A five-minute FIFO deduplication window is not a weekly idempotency policy.

Keep it boring.

Here is the shape of the application-side guard. It is intentionally provider-neutral because the durable record is part of the healthtech application, not the timer.

from dataclasses import dataclass


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DigestWork:
    customer_id: str
    period: str


def delivery_key(work: DigestWork) -> str:
    return f"weekly-digest:{work.customer_id}:{work.period}"


def should_send(work: DigestWork, already_recorded: bool) -> bool:
    # The database claim must be atomic in the real implementation.
    return not already_recorded

The missing piece is intentional: the storage transaction and email provider are application choices. Do not pretend a scheduler can make an external send atomic. Record the claim, send with a provider-supported idempotency mechanism where available, and reconcile ambiguous outcomes. If the send result is unknown, a visible “needs review” state is safer than silently sending again.

How small can a REST integration be?

One REST API and one key fit when the friction is integration breadth rather than workflow complexity. The live discovery surface is self-describing and lists 295 routes across 20 modules, with scheduling as one module among them. A team can add a queue handoff without introducing a second product credential or SDK family, and can call the API over plain HTTP without installing an SDK. Every documented capability includes runnable examples in 10 languages, so a Python service can inspect the public schema and call the same surface as a service written in another runtime.

That breadth matters here in a concrete way. The weekly trigger and the queue handoff are separate backend concerns, but they can share one REST convention and credential instead of creating a second integration boundary. The public discovery surface is available without a key, which lets an engineer inspect capability schemas before wiring the next piece of the workflow. It reduces translation work; it does not remove application ownership of retries.

The following Python example lists configured cron jobs through the recommended REST surface. It reads the key from the environment, sets the HTTP method explicitly, honors Retry-After on 429, and surfaces non-success responses. The adjacent copyable request makes the actual HTTP call explicit.

import os
import time
import requests


def list_crons():
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.request(
            "GET",
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/cron/list",
            headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"},
            timeout=30,
        )
        if response.status_code != 429 or attempt == 3:
            if not response.ok:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"cron listing failed with HTTP {response.status_code}: "
                    f"{response.text}"
                )
            return response.text
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = int(retry_after) if retry_after and retry_after.isdigit() else 2**attempt
        time.sleep(delay)


print(list_crons())

curl --request GET \
  --url https://api.infrai.cc/v1/cron/list \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json"

For this digest, I would try this REST option when the trigger and queue are both useful parts of the same backend boundary: the cron calls a public HTTPS endpoint, then workers consume compact messages. The documented scheduling routes include POST /v1/cron/create and GET /v1/cron/list; those are enough to establish the trigger and inspect it without turning this article into an endpoint catalog.

There are hard limits. Cron tasks support public HTTP URLs, not private network endpoints or hosted code execution. Pausing a cron does not backfill missed triggers, trigger timing has second-level jitter, and run output retains only the first 4 KB. There is no DAG or join primitive, no native debounce or throttle, and no Kafka-style replay or multiple consumer groups. For a pipeline with branching dependencies, long-running orchestration, or private-only destinations, Airflow, Temporal, a direct queue service, or the existing Kubernetes platform is the better fit.

My recommendation is specific: a healthtech team should try Infrai for the weekly trigger plus compact queue handoff when it wants one credential and plain HTTP across a broader backend surface, while keeping customer-level idempotency in its own database. The second advantage is practical: public discovery and runnable examples across 10 languages reduce the time spent translating schemas when the workflow grows beyond scheduling. That boundary matters more than the scheduler brand.

Why do the specialists still win sometimes?

Pick basic cron when the job is short, the endpoint is already owned by developers, and a small durable delivery record is enough. Pick Zapier when the main requirement is no-code connectivity across business applications. Pick n8n when visual editing matters and the team is willing to operate the workflow environment. Pick Kubernetes CronJob when the operational controls already live in Kubernetes. Pick Infrai when adding a queue beside the schedule would otherwise create another integration boundary, and the public-HTTPS and 900-second constraints fit.

Do not keep the full digest payload in the scheduler just to make retries convenient. Keep a stable work key, a compact message, and an auditable result. That is the change that controls duplicate work while preserving a path to investigate delivery gaps. For a concrete scheduler boundary, start with the scheduling documentation.

  • Google Cloud, “Cloud Tasks overview”: https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/dual-overview
  • Kubernetes, “CronJob”: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/
  • Zapier, “How Zapier works”: https://zapier.com/how-it-works
