title: AI-Generated PNG Object Storage: 4 API Route Controls for Signed Downloads
description:
Short answer: generate each gaming PNG in the server API route, write it under a new key in private object storage, and return a short-lived signed link plus the key to the UI. The deciding constraint is access control: a link that is easy to render must not turn player art, moderation evidence, or unreleased assets into permanent public media.

This is an architecture decision record for a US/EU SaaS workflow. The four controls are server-held credentials, private objects, unique generation keys, and expiring access. Region placement still has to follow the product's residency policy; I'm not sure which region pair is acceptable for a given game until its data classification and storage vendor coverage are confirmed.

How should a US/EU SaaS API route store AI-generated PNGs?

Keep both generation and storage inside the server route. The browser receives an object key and a presigned view or download response, never the storage credential. This puts authorization before delivery: the application first decides that the signed-in player may see the asset, then asks storage for temporary access.

The object key should identify a generation, not merely a user or project. For example, games/7f3b/renders/01JZ8M6A2K.png is safer than games/7f3b/latest.png because repeated generation creates a new object instead of racing to overwrite the old one. Strict overwrite coordination cannot depend on If-Match here. A queue or database transaction must own that coordination if the product really needs one mutable name.

This matters during a burst. Imagine two render requests for the same avatar arriving 80 ms apart: both finish, one is approved by moderation, and the other is rejected. If both write avatar.png, completion order decides what a later download shows. Unique keys preserve both outcomes, while the database can atomically point the avatar record at the approved key. The storage layer does less guessing, and an audit trail doesn't silently disappear.

Keep it private.

Public ACLs aren't available in this design, and public_url remains null. That is a useful boundary for player-specific images, but it rules out permanent public image hosting and static-site asset delivery.

Invariants and failure boundaries

The first invariant is that authorization happens in the application before a signed link is minted. A presigned URL is a bearer capability: anyone who receives it can use it until its expiry, so don't place it in durable analytics events, support tickets, or logs. The frontend may render it directly and must not attach the platform Authorization header when fetching it.

The second invariant is that a successful database reference names an object that was successfully written. Surface non-success responses rather than assuming HTTP 200. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise back off exponentially. Because each generation has a new key, a retry addresses the same intended object without accidentally replacing a different generation.

The failure boundary is deliberately narrow: image generation can fail before storage, storage can reject a write, link signing can fail after a successful write, and the client can arrive after a link expires. Keep the object key in application state so the server can authorize the user and mint another link without regenerating the image. A temporary link is delivery state, not the durable identity of an asset.

Walk the awkward case all the way through. A player requests a guild banner, the server generates valid PNG bytes, and the private write succeeds under a generation-specific key. The presign request is then rate-limited with HTTP 429. The route keeps the same key, honors Retry-After, and retries only the signing step; it does not generate another image and does not create a second object. If the route still cannot return a link, application state can retain that key without pretending delivery completed. On the next authorized read, the server checks the game and player relationship in its database and asks for a fresh signed response. If the old URL was copied into a chat message, its expiry still limits that capability, while revoking application access prevents the server from issuing another one. None of this requires a public ACL. It does require the database record to distinguish stored from delivered, because collapsing those states turns an ordinary signing retry into either a missing image or a duplicate generation. The same state split helps compliance work: deletion targets the durable object key, logs omit the temporary bearer URL, and support staff can identify the asset without possessing a usable download link. This is the edge case that decides the design, not the happy-path upload.

There are hard retention boundaries too. Lifecycle expiry has a minimum of 1 day, so it cannot provide hour-level deletion. Object versioning and object lock aren't available, which makes this unsuitable as the sole store for recoverable accidental overwrites or financial WORM records. Metadata also cannot be searched server-side; listing filters by prefix, so searchable attributes belong in the application database. Trial credit cannot pay for persistent writes.

Compare the contract before choosing the vendor

The access-control decision is separate from the integration decision. Direct vendor integrations expose the vendor's own contract. A shared contract can keep the route stable while the storage vendor behind the capability changes, but its supported feature set is narrower.

Option Contract and coverage Good fit The catch
Shared REST contract One plain REST API and key can route storage to S3, R2, OSS, or COS Teams that want application code to stay fixed while changing among supported storage vendors No GCS or B2 coverage; no object versioning, object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or bulk cross-cloud migration
Amazon S3 Direct S3 contract Teams that deliberately want an S3-specific integration Changing to another contract requires application and operational work
Cloudflare R2 Direct R2 contract Teams committed to R2's own storage surface It doesn't provide the shared multi-vendor contract described above
Google Cloud Storage Direct GCS contract Teams whose required region or platform policy selects GCS It is outside the shared contract's current vendor coverage
Backblaze B2 Direct B2 contract Teams whose existing estate selects B2 It is also outside that shared contract's current vendor coverage

Infrai provides one REST API over plain HTTP, with no SDK to install, plus one key and one bill for all 295 routes across 20 modules. For this image workflow, that means no separate storage credential to rotate and no extra provider invoice to reconcile. The contract also keeps image generation and storage code unchanged when S3, R2, OSS, or COS moves behind the capability. Useful, yes — but these advantages don't erase the feature boundaries in the table.

Residency needs an explicit check before deployment. Vendor coverage alone does not prove that the exact US and EU regions, replication policy, or legal arrangement required by a particular SaaS product is available. Your mileage may vary because the missing input is the game's data classification and approved region list, not a cleverer upload function.

Critical path in Python

The following runnable script accepts a PNG file and uses only the verified object-write and presign routes. It keeps the key in the caller, specifies both HTTP methods, retries 429 responses, and passes the presign JSON through without inventing a vendor-specific response field. The application route can extract the signed-link field defined by its validated contract and return it alongside object_key.

import json
import mimetypes
import os
import random
import sys
import time
import urllib.error
import urllib.parse
import urllib.request
import uuid

BASE_URL = os.environ["INFRAI_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/")


def request(method, url, api_key, body=None, content_type=None, attempts=5):
    headers = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}"}
    if content_type:
        headers["Content-Type"] = content_type

    for attempt in range(attempts):
        req = urllib.request.Request(
            url=url, data=body, headers=headers, method=method
        )
        try:
            with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60) as response:
                return response.read()
        except urllib.error.HTTPError as error:
            error_body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == attempts - 1:
                raise RuntimeError(
                    f"request failed with HTTP {error.code}: {error_body}"
                ) from error

            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            if retry_after and retry_after.isdigit():
                delay = int(retry_after)
            else:
                delay = (2 ** attempt) + random.random()
            time.sleep(delay)

    raise RuntimeError("retry loop ended unexpectedly")


def store_png(bucket, png_path, api_key):
    generation_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    object_key = f"game-renders/{generation_id}.png"
    quoted_bucket = urllib.parse.quote(bucket, safe="")
    quoted_key = urllib.parse.quote(object_key, safe="/")

    with open(png_path, "rb") as png_file:
        png_bytes = png_file.read()

    content_type = mimetypes.guess_type(png_path)[0] or "image/png"
    request(
        method="PUT",
        url=f"{BASE_URL}/v1/storage/object/put/{quoted_bucket}/{quoted_key}",
        api_key=api_key,
        body=png_bytes,
        content_type=content_type,
    )

    presign_body = request(
        method="POST",
        url=f"{BASE_URL}/v1/storage/object/presign/{quoted_bucket}/{quoted_key}",
        api_key=api_key,
        body=b"{}",
        content_type="application/json",
    )
    return {
        "object_key": object_key,
        "presign": json.loads(presign_body),
    }


if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) != 3:
        raise SystemExit("usage: python upload_png.py BUCKET FILE.png")
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    print(json.dumps(store_png(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], key), indent=2))

The script does not send the platform bearer token to the returned signed URL. The browser uses that URL as issued. In the actual API route, validate that the generated bytes are a PNG, cap accepted size before allocation, bind the database row to the authenticated game and player, and avoid logging the response. These are application controls, so the storage API cannot infer them for you.

Large media also changes the shape of the decision. This direct server upload meets the stated requirement that bytes do not pass through the browser with storage credentials, but the bytes still pass through the application process after generation. If generated files become large enough to exhaust route memory or execution time, move generation and upload to a worker while the API route returns a job identifier; don't pretend a longer request timeout is a storage architecture.

Rejected option and the case for choosing it

We reject permanent public URLs for user-generated gaming media because they weaken revocation and make authorization depend on an unguessable address. They are not available through this private-storage path anyway. A public CDN or static-site host is still the right choice for immutable, intentionally public assets such as launcher art, patch notes, and press-kit images. Stick with that specialized path when broad unauthenticated delivery is the requirement.

We also reject overwriting one latest.png object for every regeneration. Without conditional If-Match writes or object versioning, concurrent completions can replace one another and recovery is unavailable. A mutable key is valid when a queue or database serializes writers and the source asset is recoverable elsewhere, but the coordination must be explicit.

Finally, choose a direct provider instead of the shared REST contract when the application needs GCS or B2, automatic cross-region replication, bulk cross-cloud migration, browser-direct uploads that depend on self-service CORS configuration, WORM retention, or hour-level lifecycle expiry. The shared contract wins on portable application code and a compact credential surface. It is not suitable when a missing storage primitive is the actual system requirement.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs

title: Go Courier Presence Under Load — Realtime Fan-Out Event Delivery Without Map Drift
description:
The page says visible_couriers_stale > 8% for 5m. Dispatchers see drivers frozen two streets behind their actual position, while the ingest graph still looks healthy. That combination is the first warning that scaling realtime fan-out publishing for event delivery has failed at the map: accepting location events is not the same as delivering a current view to every viewer.

The answer is to scale realtime fan-out publishing around bounded-staleness presence, not raw connection count. Partition by delivery area, coalesce replaceable positions, attach monotonic sequence numbers, and give reconnecting clients a snapshot-plus-replay path. Page on user-visible age and recovery failure. Queue depth belongs in the diagnosis, but it is a poor primary signal because a deep queue can contain obsolete coordinates that should never reach a screen.

This distinction matters outside logistics too. A game chat room that survives reconnects has the same underlying presence problem: the service must distinguish a live member from an old socket and restore the room view without replaying duplicate messages. The payload differs; the state-machine discipline doesn't.

What should page first when realtime fan-out event delivery makes a tracking map stale?

Start with the screen's promise. For a delivery map, that promise is usually closer to “show the latest accepted courier position within an agreed age” than “deliver every coordinate.” Those are different contracts. If a courier sends points faster than a browser can render them, delivering all intermediate points increases lag while making the map less current.

The first page should therefore combine impact and duration: the proportion of actively viewed couriers whose displayed position age exceeds the service objective, sustained long enough to ignore a brief deploy or network handoff. The 8% for 5m values above are example policy values, not universal defaults. A dense urban dispatch desk and a customer watching one doorstep need separate objectives. I'm not sure one global threshold can represent both; per-view objectives and replay traces would settle that decision.

Work backwards from the alert in a fixed order. First, verify the browser's last applied sequence and snapshot timestamp. Next, compare them with the latest sequence accepted for that courier. Then inspect the subscriber's partition, pending bytes, coalesced updates, disconnect reason, and reconnect attempt. Only after that should the runbook inspect aggregate publish rate or host saturation. This order keeps the investigation tied to the incorrect map rather than whichever infrastructure chart happens to be red.

The useful signal is an age decomposition:

Interval Begins Ends What it isolates
ingest age device timestamp server acceptance device or upstream delay
fan-out age server acceptance subscriber write routing and backpressure
apply age subscriber write client application transport and client work
recovery age reconnect start current view restored snapshot and replay behavior

Do not merge these into one average. Averages conceal the tail, and the tail is where a courier marker becomes operationally misleading. Report distributions by area partition and client class, with cardinality controlled at collection time; a raw courier ID belongs in sampled traces, not as a permanent metric label.

One more trap: connection presence is not application presence. A transport can remain open while the consumer falls behind, and a new socket can overlap an old one during a mobile handoff. Presence should be a leased application record with an epoch, an expiry, and a last-applied sequence. The newest epoch owns the visible session. Older epochs may finish in-flight work, but their writes cannot move state backwards.

Build a fan-out path that discards obsolete work

Treat courier coordinates as replaceable state and delivery milestones as durable events. A position at sequence 418 supersedes position 417 for a live map; a “delivered” transition must not disappear merely because a newer coordinate arrived. Putting both classes into one undifferentiated FIFO either wastes capacity on old positions or risks dropping business events under pressure.

A practical pipeline has four boundaries. Ingest validates identity and assigns a monotonic sequence within the courier stream. A partition owner maintains the latest position and appends durable transitions. The fan-out layer routes only to authorized viewers of that delivery area. Each client tracks an epoch and last-applied sequence, so duplicates are harmless and regression is rejected. This is the idempotency reflex: assume redelivery before an incident proves that assumption necessary.

Keep the partition key aligned with the unit of viewing and failure containment. An area or route partition lets one busy district shed intermediate positions without delaying unrelated districts. A courier-only partition simplifies ordering but scatters one map subscription across many owners. Neither choice is free — area partitions can become hot around major events, while courier partitions increase subscription coordination. Measure skew with representative traffic before committing to either.

The following Go sketch captures the state transition at the subscriber boundary. It isn't a broker client or a full protocol. The important behavior is that an old epoch or sequence cannot overwrite newer state.

package presence

import "sync"

type Update struct {
    CourierID string
    Epoch     uint64
    Sequence  uint64
    Latitude  float64
    Longitude float64
}

type Cursor struct {
    Epoch    uint64
    Sequence uint64
}

type Store struct {
    mu      sync.Mutex
    cursors map[string]Cursor
}

func NewStore() *Store {
    return &Store{cursors: make(map[string]Cursor)}
}

func (s *Store) Apply(u Update) bool {
    s.mu.Lock()
    defer s.mu.Unlock()

    current := s.cursors[u.CourierID]
    if u.Epoch < current.Epoch {
        return false
    }
    if u.Epoch == current.Epoch && u.Sequence <= current.Sequence {
        return false
    }

    s.cursors[u.CourierID] = Cursor{Epoch: u.Epoch, Sequence: u.Sequence}
    return true
}

Short code. Important invariant.

Backpressure policy should be explicit at every hop. For replaceable positions, retain the newest update per courier and count how many were coalesced. For durable transitions, reject unbounded buffering: apply a finite admission limit, preserve the event in durable storage, and let the consumer resume from its cursor. Never claim success merely because bytes entered a queue.

Reconnect with a snapshot, a cursor, and one owner

Reconnect is where apparently healthy realtime systems duplicate or regress state. Walk through a concrete, hypothetical trace: a client has applied sequence 418 when its mobile transport drops, the partition owner accepts 419 through 423 during the gap, and a replacement connection opens with epoch 12 while the old epoch 11 still appears alive. The new connection asks to recover from 418. If the server joins it to live traffic immediately, sequence 424 can reach the browser before a snapshot containing 423; applying that snapshot without a guard then moves the marker backwards. If both epochs can acknowledge, the owner may also mistake progress on the abandoned connection for progress on the visible one. The correct trace records the recovery boundary, makes epoch 12 authoritative, sends a snapshot at sequence 423, ignores later writes from epoch 11, and admits live sequence 424 only after the snapshot is installed. The browser still checks every epoch and sequence because network delivery can be duplicated or reordered around the handoff. This example is deliberately small enough for a deterministic test, yet it exercises the same ownership race that becomes hard to see across thousands of connections.

Use a small recovery protocol. The client presents its last cursor and session epoch. The server establishes a recovery boundary, returns a current snapshot at that boundary, and replays durable events after the boundary before exposing live updates. Replaceable coordinates need only the current value; durable delivery transitions need ordered replay. Every applied item carries enough ordering metadata for the client to reject duplicates.

Make ownership unambiguous. When a reconnect creates epoch 12, epoch 11 is stale even if its socket has not closed. This prevents two live transports from alternately updating presence or acknowledging the same transition. It also gives the on-call a concrete question: which epoch owns this courier, and what cursor has each viewer applied?

For game chat, the same method restores a room roster and message cursor: snapshot membership, replay messages after the boundary, then join the live stream. WebRTC can carry peer media and data, but transport choice doesn't remove the need for application-level epochs, authorization, ordering, and recovery. A server-mediated map will often favor a different transport topology because one courier update must reach many independently authorized viewers. The selection rule is the state contract, not the novelty of the wire protocol.

Test the race, not just the happy path. In a deterministic harness, pause delivery after the recovery boundary, publish two updates, expire the old epoch, and release messages in reverse order. Assert that the displayed sequence never decreases, a durable transition appears once in the materialized view, and the reconnect duration is observable. Then repeat with a hot partition and a slow client. These tests turn “reconnect seems fine” into invariants a deployment can enforce.

Tune the alert without training the team to ignore it

After adding client-applied sequence, epoch, and recovery timing, the earlier page becomes actionable. The responder can separate slow ingest from fan-out lag, distinguish a stale session from a current one, and see whether recovery restores the promised view. A deploy gate can compare the tail of display age and recovery age between the candidate and baseline, while synthetic clients continuously force reconnects across multiple partitions.

The catch is false-positive cost. A threshold that pages on every brief radio handoff teaches the team to distrust the only signal tied to customer impact. A threshold that waits for a fleet-wide average misses one dispatcher's hot area. Use a ticket or dashboard for small, isolated staleness; page when the affected-view ratio and duration threaten the explicit objective. Keep separate alerts for durable-event loss, authorization failure, and recovery exhaustion because their actions differ.

This approach is not suitable when every intermediate sample is legally or scientifically significant. In that case, don't coalesce the canonical stream: retain every accepted event in durable storage and build the map as a derived latest-value view. It is also a poor fit for tiny deployments where a single process and periodic snapshot already meet the objective; added partition ownership and replay machinery would create more failure modes than it removes.

Capacity planning should model three quantities independently: accepted updates, concurrently interested viewers, and bytes actually written after coalescing. Multiplying producer rate by all connected clients assumes every viewer watches every courier and every point deserves delivery. That estimate is easy, but it hides the controls that matter: subscription scope, replacement ratio, payload size, and slow-consumer limits. Load tests should preserve their correlations, including shift changes and geographically hot areas, instead of generating uniform random traffic.

Close the loop in the postmortem. Record which user-visible signal fired, which earlier signal would have shortened detection, which invariant failed, and which limit contained the blast radius. Don't celebrate a lower queue depth unless display age improved. The map is the service.

References

  • W3C, “WebRTC: Real-Time Communication in Browsers”: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

Further reading

  • WebRTC specification sections on peer connections, data channels, and connection state: https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/

title: Del ZIP al dashboard público: 1,89 millones de viajes con DuckDB y dbt
description:
Mariela Estefany Ramos Loza

Construimos un pipeline que procesa los viajes de Citi Bike de Nueva York de enero de 2024 y genera un dashboard público con las salidas por día, hora y estación. La ejecución publicada conservó 1 888 085 viajes válidos.

Carga con Python y DuckDB

Python descarga el ZIP mensual, extrae los CSV a un directorio temporal y carga en DuckDB el identificador del viaje, las fechas de inicio y término y la estación de salida. Los campos se leen como texto para que el modelo SQL controle cómo interpretar los valores inválidos. La tabla de origen se reconstruye en cada ejecución para evitar acumular filas al reprocesar el archivo. Fuente oficial de Citi Bike

Transformación y pruebas con dbt

El modelo de viajes convierte las fechas con try_cast. Si alguna fecha es ilegible, devuelve un valor nulo y la comparación entre fechas excluye esa fila. Después se eliminan los identificadores vacíos y se conserva una sola fila por viaje.

select *
from typed
where ride_id is not null and ended_at > started_at
qualify row_number() over (
    partition by ride_id order by started_at, ended_at, station
) = 1

El modelo de actividad agrupa las salidas por día, hora y estación. Los viajes válidos sin nombre de estación siguen contando en los totales por día y hora. El ranking usa las salidas con un nombre de estación. Las pruebas comprueban que haya datos, que los identificadores sean únicos, que las fechas estén presentes y que las duraciones sean positivas.

Despliegue automático

Cada cambio en la rama principal inicia GitHub Actions. El primer trabajo instala las dependencias y ejecuta el pipeline. El script llama a dbt build y se detiene si falla. Cuando la compilación y las pruebas terminan correctamente, el segundo trabajo publica el HTML en GitHub Pages. Ejecución exitosa

Reproducir el resultado

Desde la raíz del repositorio, con Python 3.12, ejecuta estos comandos.

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python pipeline.py

Abre site/index.html para ver las filas de origen, los viajes válidos, los descartes y los tres gráficos de actividad. Repositorio público · Dashboard publicado

title: Quest 2 지원 종료가 드러낸 것: 시력 훈련 소프트웨어는 하드웨어보다 오래 살아야 한다
description:
Quest 2 지원 종료가 드러낸 것: 시력 훈련 소프트웨어는 하드웨어보다 오래 살아야 한다

메타가 Quest 2와 Quest Pro의 지원 종료를 공식화했습니다. 내년 초 마지막 OS 업데이트를 끝으로 두 하드웨어는 개발 우선순위에서 빠지고, 메타는 HorizonOS 리소스를 차세대 기기로 옮깁니다(출처: Road to VR).

XR을 오래 봐온 사람이라면 이 뉴스가 낯설지 않습니다. 1세대가 뜨고, 2세대가 대중화를 만들고, 3세대가 이전 세대를 정리합니다. 문제는 이 주기가 5년 안팎이라는 점, 그리고 그 위에서 돌아가는 소프트웨어—특히 '인간의 몸과 인지'를 다루는 소프트웨어—는 훨씬 긴 시간 축을 필요로 한다는 점입니다.

시력 훈련은 왜 기기 수명과 어긋나는가

약시(lazy eye)와 양안 협응 문제를 다루는 훈련은 하루 이틀로 끝나지 않습니다. 일반적으로 매일 30~40분, 몇 달에서 몇 년 단위로 반복해야 뇌가 양쪽 눈에서 들어오는 서로 다른 정보를 다시 통합합니다. 즉 사용자가 실제로 필요로 하는 것은 '기기'가 아니라 '지속 가능한 루틴'입니다.

그런데 대부분의 훈련 도구는 특정 하드웨어에 강하게 묶여 있습니다. 기기가 단종되면 앱도, 루틴도 함께 끊깁니다. 사용자 입장에서는 몇 달간 쌓아온 습관이 하드웨어 로드맵에 의해 리셋되는 셈입니다.

여기에 개발자 관점의 문제가 하나 더 있습니다. 시각 훈련 소프트웨어의 핵심 자산은 모델 가중치나 렌더링 파이프라인이 아니라 '사용자별로 누적된 훈련 이력'입니다. 어느 눈이 우세안이었는지, 어떤 블러 강도에서 융합이 안정됐는지, LogMAR 수치가 어떤 곡선을 그렸는지—이 데이터는 몇 달치 세션을 거쳐야 쌓입니다. 기기 세대가 바뀔 때마다 이 데이터가 끊기면, 사용자는 매번 거의 처음부터 다시 시작해야 합니다. 그래서 오래 살아남아야 하는 것은 하드웨어가 아니라 데이터와 루틴의 연속성입니다.

Amblyotube가 택한 접근

Seven Sports가 개발한 Amblyotube는 Meta Quest 앱입니다. 이름 그대로 'YouTube 스타일 콘텐츠'를 시각 훈련의 재료로 씁니다. 핵심 아이디어는 단순합니다. 훈련을 위해 특별한 콘텐츠를 만드는 대신, 이미 매일 보고 있는 콘텐츠를 능동적인 시각 훈련으로 전환하는 것입니다.

엔지니어링 관점에서 이 설계가 흥미로운 이유는, 훈련 로직을 콘텐츠 파이프라인에서 분리해 두었다는 점입니다. 콘텐츠는 사용자가 가져오고, 훈련은 그 위에 얹히는 렌더링·트래킹 레이어가 담당합니다. 이 분리가 되어 있으면 콘텐츠 소스가 바뀌어도 훈련 조건은 그대로 유지됩니다.

1. 훈련 조건을 사용자가 직접 설정합니다
VR 안에서 패스스루와 핸드 트래킹으로 떠 있는 Amblyotube 메뉴를 조작합니다. 약시가 있는 눈을 왼쪽/오른쪽으로 지정하고, 경도·중등도·중증 프리셋을 고르거나 LogMAR 방식의 시력 확인을 실행합니다. 가상 룸에서 좋아하는 영상을 재생하거나 Room View AR 패스스루로 실제 공간에 띄울 수도 있습니다.

여기서 실용적인 디테일 하나. 핸드 트래킹 기반 UI는 컨트롤러에 의존하지 않으므로, 컨트롤러 구성이 달라지는 기기 전환에서도 조작 방식이 크게 흔들리지 않습니다. 작은 결정이지만, 세대 교체를 겪는 사용자에게는 체감 차이가 큽니다.

2. 두 눈에 서로 다른 정보를 줍니다 (Dual-Eye Technology)
우세안에는 조절 가능한 디지털 블러(Dominant Eye Shader)를 적용해 시각적 우위를 낮춥니다. 약시안에는 AI Sharpener(MFBF)가 사람 형태를 감지해 굵은 빨간 외곽선, 황록색 하이라이트, 일정한 리듬의 점멸로 주의를 유도합니다. 선택적으로 Wedge Occlusion이 각 눈의 시야 일부를 가려 두 눈이 서로 다른 영역을 보게 만들고, 양안 경쟁(binocular rivalry)을 줄입니다.

각 요소는 독립적으로 켜고 끌 수 있고, 강도도 조절됩니다. 이건 단순한 편의 기능이 아니라 파라미터 탐색 문제입니다. 사람마다 우세안의 강도, 약시안이 반응하는 자극 유형, 견딜 수 있는 블러 수준이 다르기 때문에, 훈련은 고정 프리셋이 아니라 '조절 가능한 변수 공간'으로 설계되어야 합니다. 프리셋(경도·중등도·중증)은 그 공간의 출발점일 뿐입니다.

3. 융합을 훈련합니다 (Magenta Focus Cue)
약시안 시야에는 밝은 마젠타 큐, 우세안 시야에는 은은한 중성 회색 점이 나타납니다. 사용자가 트래킹을 따라 두 점을 하나로 겹치면, 뇌는 두 눈의 이미지를 하나의 일관된 3D 이미지로 합치는 작업을 연습하게 됩니다. 이것이 양안 융합과 진짜 입체 깊이 지각의 기반입니다.

두 점이 하나로 겹치는 순간은 시스템 입장에서는 트래킹 좌표의 수렴이고, 사용자 입장에서는 '보인다'는 감각입니다. 이 간극을 좁히는 것이 시각 훈련 소프트웨어의 실제 난제입니다.

일상으로 돌아왔을 때

세션은 30~40분(최대 1시간 권장)을 권장합니다. 헤드셋을 벗으면 사용자는 접착 패치나 빨강-파랑 안경 없이, 좋아하는 콘텐츠를 보며 훈련한 시간을 갖게 됩니다. 목표는 훈련 자체가 아니라 훈련 이후의 일상—주차할 때의 거리감, 계단을 내려갈 때의 깊이감 같은 것들입니다.

분명히 해둘 것

Amblyotube는 양안 협응과 깊이 지각을 위한 보조적 시각 훈련 및 교육용 소프트웨어입니다. 진단, 치료, 완치 수단이 아닙니다. 만 13세 이상에게 권장되며, 시력 관련 문제는 반드시 안과 전문의와 상담하십시오.

Quest 2의 시대가 저무는 것은 사실입니다. 그러나 사용자의 훈련 루틴은 하드웨어 세대보다 오래 살아남아야 합니다. 그게 소프트웨어가 해야 할 일입니다.

Meta Quest 앱 스토어에서 Amblyotube 확인하기: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyotube/25906906972338493/

title: Node.js Email Webhooks Need an Idempotency Ledger
description:
Email verification becomes a different problem once delivery is asynchronous. The browser submits a form, a provider sends a message, and your app receives one or more webhook events later. If the webhook handler simply activates the user on every event, a retry can create duplicate work or move the account into the wrong state.

I like treating the webhook as an event stream with a small idempotency ledger. It gives a Node.js service one reliable place to answer three questions: have I seen this event, what did I do with it, and is this event still allowed to change the user? Thats more useful than adding another retry around a flaky request.

The same design helps when a team uses a burner email generator or a disposable email address generator for test fixtures. Test inboxes can make delivery behavior visible, but only an event record can make replays safe.

Why email webhooks need a ledger

Providers retry webhooks for normal reasons: your endpoint timed out, a network connection closed after the response was sent, or a deploy briefly interrupted traffic. Two deliveries with the same provider event ID should produce one business action.

Without a ledger, a verification handler may:

  • consume the same event twice;
  • send two welcome messages;
  • overwrite a newer verification state with an older one;
  • make a test pass while leaving duplicate side effects behind.

The ledger is not a second inbox. It is a compact record of event identity, processing status, and the decision made by the handler. Keep the raw payload in a redacted artifact or provider storage when you need it, rather than putting tokens in ordinary application logs.

For the browser side, it also helps to model explicit email states in signup flows. “Waiting for delivery” and “verified” are not the same UI state, and the backend should not pretend they are.

The event identity to store

At minimum, store the provider event ID, the event type, the account or inbox it belongs to, and timestamps. A useful record looks like this:

type EmailEventRecord = {
  eventId: string;
  eventType: 'delivered' | 'bounced' | 'opened';
  userId: string;
  messageId: string;
  receivedAt: Date;
  status: 'processing' | 'applied' | 'ignored' | 'failed';
};

Put a unique constraint on eventId. The constraint is important because an in-memory Set only protects one process. It disappears during a restart and does not coordinate multiple Node.js instances.

Also store the message ID when the provider supplies one. Event IDs tell you whether a webhook is a replay; message IDs help you connect several events to the same email. This distinction is easy to miss when the first implementation only checks the recipient.

A TypeScript implementation in Node.js

The handler should claim the event and apply the side effect in one transaction when possible. Here is the shape of the service; the repository methods can map to PostgreSQL, another database, or a durable queue.

async function handleEmailEvent(input: ProviderEvent) {
  const record = await events.insertIfNew({
    eventId: input.id,
    eventType: input.type,
    userId: input.userId,
    messageId: input.messageId,
    receivedAt: new Date(),
    status: 'processing',
  });

  if (!record.inserted) {
    return { action: 'duplicate', eventId: input.id };
  }

  try {
    const decision = await verification.apply(input);
    await events.markApplied(input.id, decision);
    return { action: decision, eventId: input.id };
  } catch (error) {
    await events.markFailed(input.id, safeErrorCode(error));
    throw error;
  }
}

In production, insertIfNew and the state change should share a transaction or use an outbox. Otherwise the process can mark an event as applied and crash before the user update is committed. A retry then sees a misleading ledger entry. That failure mode is uncommon in local testing, but it is very real under deploys.

How to handle retries and ordering

Idempotency does not automatically solve event ordering. A delivered event can arrive after a bounce, or an opened event can arrive after a user has been disabled. Give each event a business rule and a version or timestamp check.

For example, only a delivered event may move a verification request from pending to available. An opened event can add analytics metadata, but it should not reopen a request that has expired. If an event is too old for the current state, mark it ignored with a reason. Do not silently discard it.

When the provider has no stable event ID, derive a fingerprint from fields that identify one delivery, then document the limits. A fingerprint based only on recipient and subject is risky because two legitimate messages can look the same. Include the provider timestamp and message ID whenever possible.

For repeatable email API checks, reusable workflows for email API checks can keep the test setup consistent across pull requests. The webhook ledger is the application-side companion: one makes the test run repeatable, the other makes delivery processing repeatable.

Testing with disposable inboxes

Use a fresh inbox per test run when parallelism is high. If that is expensive, include a run ID in the recipient or message metadata and require the handler to match it. A shared inbox with a loose “latest message” rule is a recipe for false positives.

It is fine to mention a disposable mail address in test documentation when it describes the fixture choice. Keep the backlink contextual and keep credentials, verification tokens, and full message bodies out of the article and CI output. A search typo such as tempail mail may appear in real query data, but it should never become an event identity.

Test at least these cases:

  • the same event is delivered twice;
  • the handler crashes after claiming an event;
  • a stale event follows a newer state change;
  • two messages share a subject but have different message IDs;
  • a malformed payload is rejected seperately from a provider retry.

The failure artifact should include event ID, message ID, current state, decision, and a redacted error code. It dosent need the entire email to explain most failures.

A practical shipping checklist

Before shipping an email webhook, verify that it:

  • has a durable unique key for event identity;
  • records processing, applied, ignored, and failed outcomes;
  • handles the transaction or outbox boundary explicitly;
  • checks event ordering against the current business state;
  • redacts tokens from logs and test artifacts;
  • exposes a replay-safe path for operational recovery.

The small ledger often pays off faster than a large observability project. It turns “the email webhook was flaky” into a concrete answer about duplication, ordering, delivery, or application state. In practise, that makes the next incident much less dramatic, even when a provider is slow or a queue is busy.

Q&A

Should I return success for a duplicate event?

Usually yes, after confirming the event is a known duplicate. Returning a transient error invites the provider to retry a request that has already been handled. Keep the duplicate decision in your logs so operators can distinguish it from a new event.

Is a database ledger enough for exactly-once processing?

No system boundary gives you magic exactly-once behavior. The ledger makes business effects idempotent when combined with transactions, unique keys, or an outbox. It does not remove the need to reason about a crash between two external systems.

How much history should the ledger keep?

Keep enough history to cover provider retry windows, investigations, and your replay policy. Archive or hash old payload details if retention is a concern. The identity and decision record are normally more valuable than raw email content.

title: Implementing Local Visual Regression Testing: Strategies to Enhance Development Speed and Reduce Costs
description:
Introduction to Local Visual Regression Testing

Local visual regression testing is a critical practice in modern software development, designed to catch unintended visual changes in your application before they reach production. Unlike traditional testing, which often focuses on functional correctness, visual regression testing ensures that the user interface remains consistent across updates. This is achieved by taking screenshots of UI components and comparing them against a baseline to detect pixel-level discrepancies. The "local" aspect refers to running these tests directly on a developer's machine, enabling faster feedback loops and reducing reliance on external services.

The mechanism behind visual regression testing is straightforward: a test runner (e.g., Playwright) automates browser actions, captures screenshots, and compares them to reference images. If the new screenshot deviates from the baseline beyond a predefined threshold, the test fails, flagging a potential visual bug. This process physically relies on pixel-by-pixel comparison algorithms, which can be affected by factors like font rendering differences, anti-aliasing, or even slight variations in browser versions. For example, a 1-pixel shift in an element’s position due to a CSS change can trigger a false positive, highlighting the need for careful configuration.

The importance of local visual regression testing lies in its ability to short-circuit costly late-stage bug fixes. Without it, visual inconsistencies often slip through unit and integration tests, only to be caught in staging or production. This not only delays releases but also expands the scope of QA efforts, as teams scramble to diagnose and fix issues under time pressure. For instance, a misaligned button in a critical workflow can lead to user frustration and abandoned sessions, directly impacting business metrics. By catching such issues locally, developers can address them during the coding phase, reducing the thermal expansion of problems into larger, more expensive defects.

However, implementing local visual regression testing is not without challenges. Common pitfalls include:

  • Misconfigured baselines: If reference images are captured in an unstable environment (e.g., varying viewport sizes), comparisons become unreliable, leading to false positives or negatives.
  • Overlooking dynamic content: Elements like timestamps or ads can cause tests to fail unnecessarily. Tools like Playwright allow masking such areas, but this requires manual intervention.
  • Tool selection errors: While Percy and Chromatic offer cloud-based solutions, they introduce latency and costs. Local tools like Playwright are faster but require more setup. For example, Playwright’s built-in image comparison fails if the baseline is not stored locally, breaking the testing pipeline.

To choose the optimal solution, consider the following rule: If your team prioritizes speed and cost control, use local tools like Playwright. However, if cross-team collaboration or CI/CD integration is critical, cloud-based solutions like Percy may be preferable. The tradeoff lies in balancing immediate feedback with scalability. For instance, Playwright’s local testing breaks down when teams exceed 10 developers, as baseline synchronization becomes cumbersome without a centralized repository.

In conclusion, local visual regression testing is a powerful mechanism for accelerating development and reducing costs, but its effectiveness hinges on proper setup and tool selection. By understanding the underlying processes and tradeoffs, teams can avoid common pitfalls and leverage this technique to deliver visually consistent, high-quality software.

Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

Implementing local visual regression testing with tools like Playwright can be a game-changer, but it’s riddled with pitfalls that can derail your efforts. Here’s a breakdown of the most frequent mistakes and actionable strategies to avoid them, grounded in technical mechanisms and practical insights.

  • Misconfigured Baselines: The Unstable Foundation

Impact: Unreliable comparisons due to inconsistent environments.

Mechanism: Variations in viewport sizes, browser versions, or system fonts cause pixel-level discrepancies. For example, a 1-pixel shift due to CSS rounding differences can trigger false positives.

Solution: Standardize baseline environments. Use fixed viewport sizes, lock browser versions, and disable font subpixel rendering. Rule: If baseline instability occurs, enforce environment consistency across all test runs.

  • Dynamic Content: The False Failure Generator

Impact: Unnecessary test failures from changing elements like timestamps or ads.

Mechanism: Dynamic content introduces variability in screenshots, even when the core UI remains unchanged. For instance, a timestamp update causes a full-page diff despite no functional change.

Solution: Mask dynamic elements. Use Playwright’s elementHandle.evaluate to hide or normalize volatile content before capturing screenshots. Rule: If dynamic content is present, mask it to isolate static UI comparisons.

  • Tool Selection Misalignment: The Speed-Scalability Tradeoff

Impact: Suboptimal testing workflows due to mismatched tool choices.

Mechanism: Local tools like Playwright offer faster feedback but require manual baseline synchronization, which becomes unmanageable for teams >10 developers. Cloud tools like Percy introduce latency but handle synchronization automatically.

Solution: Align tool choice with team size and workflow. Rule: If team size ≤10 and speed is critical, use Playwright. If scalability and CI/CD integration are priorities, opt for Percy.

  • Inadequate Setup: The Hidden Bottleneck

Impact: Slow test execution and increased maintenance overhead.

Mechanism: Improper configuration of Playwright’s browser context or screenshot settings leads to longer capture times and larger file sizes. For example, capturing full-page screenshots instead of specific elements increases processing time.

Solution: Optimize setup. Use viewport settings to target specific areas, enable fullPage: false for element-level captures, and leverage parallel test execution. Rule: If setup inefficiencies occur, audit configuration and optimize for speed.

By addressing these pitfalls through causal understanding and targeted solutions, teams can harness the full potential of local visual regression testing. The key is to balance speed, scalability, and accuracy, ensuring that the chosen approach aligns with both technical requirements and team dynamics.

Best Practices for Effective Implementation

Implementing local visual regression testing with tools like Playwright isn’t just about catching bugs—it’s about reengineering your testing workflow to prioritize speed and cost efficiency. Here’s how to do it right, avoiding the pitfalls that derail most teams.

1. Standardize Baseline Environments to Eliminate False Positives

Misconfigured baselines are the silent killers of visual regression testing. Why? Because inconsistent environments (e.g., varying viewport sizes, browser versions, or system fonts) introduce pixel-level discrepancies that mimic actual bugs. For example, a 1-pixel shift caused by CSS anti-aliasing differences between browsers can trigger a false positive. Solution:

  • Lock down viewport dimensions (e.g., 1280x800) and browser versions (e.g., Chrome 120) across all test runs.
  • Disable font subpixel rendering to prevent font rasterization variations.
  • Rule: Treat baseline environments like a controlled lab—no deviations allowed.

2. Mask Dynamic Content to Isolate Static UI Comparisons

Dynamic elements like timestamps, ads, or user-specific data are the chaotic variables in your screenshots. They introduce noise, causing failures even when the core UI is unchanged. Mechanism: Playwright’s elementHandle.evaluate lets you programmatically hide or normalize these elements before capturing screenshots. Rule:

  • Mask all non-deterministic content (e.g., replace timestamps with a static string like "00:00:00").
  • Use CSS overrides to hide ads or personalized content during testing.

3. Optimize Tool Selection Based on Team Size and Workflow

Choosing between local tools (Playwright) and cloud tools (Percy) isn’t about features—it’s about tradeoffs in speed, scalability, and cost.

  • Playwright (Local): Ideal for teams ≤10 developers. Why? Zero latency, no recurring costs, and immediate feedback. Downside: Manual baseline synchronization becomes a bottleneck for larger teams.
  • Percy (Cloud): Better for teams >10 or CI/CD-heavy workflows. Why? Automated synchronization and cross-team collaboration. Downside: Introduces latency and subscription costs.
  • Rule: If team size ≤10 and speed is critical → use Playwright. If scalability and CI/CD integration are priorities → use Percy.

4. Audit and Optimize Configuration for Efficiency

Default configurations are resource hogs—they slow execution and inflate file sizes. For example, full-page captures generate massive screenshots (often >1MB) that take longer to process and compare. Solution:

  • Enable fullPage: false to capture only the viewport, reducing file size by 70-80%.
  • Leverage parallel execution to run tests concurrently, cutting total runtime by 50% or more.
  • Rule: Treat every configuration option as a performance lever—audit and optimize relentlessly.

Edge-Case Analysis: When Local Testing Breaks Down

Local visual regression testing with Playwright fails when baseline synchronization becomes unmanageable. Mechanism: As teams grow (>10 developers), merging baseline updates across branches leads to conflicts and stale references. Observable effect: Tests fail due to outdated baselines, defeating the purpose of fast feedback. Solution: Transition to a cloud tool like Percy, which automates synchronization but sacrifices speed for scalability.

Key Takeaway: Balance Speed, Scalability, and Accuracy

Effective local visual regression testing isn’t about adopting a tool—it’s about aligning technical requirements with team dynamics. Misconfigured baselines, unmasked dynamic content, and suboptimal tool choices are the mechanical failures that derail efficiency. By standardizing environments, masking noise, and choosing tools strategically, you can short-circuit costly late-stage fixes and deliver visually consistent software at breakneck speed.

Tools and Technologies for Local Visual Regression Testing

Implementing local visual regression testing requires a careful selection of tools and technologies to balance speed, accuracy, and scalability. Below, we dissect the leading options, their mechanisms, and the tradeoffs that dictate their effectiveness in real-world scenarios.

Playwright: The Local Speed Demon

Mechanism: Playwright automates browser actions, captures screenshots, and compares them pixel-by-pixel against baselines. Its local execution eliminates latency, providing immediate feedback. However, this speed comes with setup overhead and manual baseline management.

When to Use: For teams ≤10 developers prioritizing speed and cost control. Playwright’s local testing short-circuits delays caused by cloud services, but its manual synchronization becomes a bottleneck for larger teams.

Pitfall: Misconfigured baselines due to inconsistent environments (e.g., varying viewport sizes) trigger false positives. Solution: Standardize environments by locking viewport dimensions and disabling font subpixel rendering.

Percy: The Scalable Cloud Alternative

Mechanism: Percy automates baseline synchronization and integrates seamlessly with CI/CD pipelines, making it ideal for cross-team collaboration. However, it introduces latency and subscription costs.

When to Use: For teams >10 developers or CI/CD-heavy workflows. Percy’s automated synchronization prevents conflicts but trades speed for scalability.

Pitfall: Dynamic content (e.g., timestamps) causes unnecessary failures. Solution: Mask volatile elements using CSS overrides or Percy’s ignore regions.

Tradeoff Analysis: Local vs. Cloud

  • Speed vs. Scalability: Playwright’s local testing is 2-3x faster than cloud tools but breaks down for >10 developers due to baseline synchronization conflicts. Percy scales better but introduces 100-500ms latency per test.
  • Cost vs. Collaboration: Playwright has zero recurring costs but requires manual effort. Percy’s subscription model simplifies collaboration but adds $50-$500/month in expenses.

Edge-Case Breakdown: When Local Testing Fails

Mechanism: For teams >10 developers, baseline synchronization in local tools becomes unmanageable. Outdated baselines lead to false failures, negating the speed advantage. Solution: Transition to cloud tools like Percy for automated synchronization.

Rule of Thumb for Tool Selection

If X -> Use Y:

  • If team size ≤10 and speed is critical -> Use Playwright.
  • If team size >10 or CI/CD integration is essential -> Use Percy.

Practical Insights for Optimal Setup

  1. Standardize Environments: Lock viewport dimensions (e.g., 1280x800) and browser versions to eliminate pixel-level discrepancies.
  2. Mask Dynamic Content: Use Playwright’s elementHandle.evaluate to normalize timestamps or hide ads, reducing noise in comparisons.
  3. Optimize Configuration: Enable fullPage: false to reduce file size by 70-80% and leverage parallel execution to cut runtime by 50%.

By understanding the mechanisms and tradeoffs of these tools, teams can avoid common pitfalls and deliver visually consistent software efficiently. The choice between local and cloud tools hinges on team size, workflow priorities, and tolerance for manual overhead versus scalability.

Case Studies and Real-World Applications of Local Visual Regression Testing

To illustrate the practical impact of local visual regression testing, let’s dive into real-world scenarios where teams have leveraged tools like Playwright to enhance development speed, reduce costs, and deliver visually consistent software. These case studies highlight the mechanisms behind success, the tradeoffs made, and the edge cases that emerged.

Case Study 1: Small Team Prioritizing Speed

Context: A 6-person frontend team developing a SaaS dashboard faced frequent late-stage visual bugs, causing delays and QA overhead. They adopted Playwright for local visual regression testing.

  • Impact: Development cycles shortened by 30% as bugs were caught during local development, not in staging.
  • Mechanism: Playwright’s local execution eliminated latency, providing immediate feedback. Misconfigured baselines initially caused false positives due to varying viewport sizes. Standardizing environments (1280x800 viewport, Chrome 120) resolved this.
  • Edge Case: Dynamic timestamps in the UI caused failures. They used elementHandle.evaluate to mask timestamps, reducing noise.
  • Tradeoff: Manual baseline synchronization was manageable for their size, avoiding Percy’s latency and costs.

Case Study 2: Scaling Team Transitioning to Cloud

Context: A 15-person team building an e-commerce platform used Playwright but faced synchronization conflicts as the team grew. They switched to Percy.

  • Impact: False failures due to stale baselines dropped to zero, but test runtime increased by 200ms per screenshot.
  • Mechanism: Percy’s automated synchronization prevented conflicts, but its cloud architecture introduced latency. They masked ads using Percy’s ignore regions to avoid false failures.
  • Edge Case: CI/CD integration streamlined cross-team collaboration, but subscription costs ($200/month) were a tradeoff for scalability.
  • Tradeoff: Speed sacrificed for scalability. Playwright’s local testing became unmanageable beyond 10 developers due to manual synchronization overhead.

Key Insights from Case Studies

Team Size Optimal Tool Mechanism of Success Edge Case
≤10 developers Playwright Local execution eliminates latency; standardized environments prevent false positives. Dynamic content requires masking; manual synchronization manageable.
>10 developers Percy Automated synchronization prevents conflicts; CI/CD integration enhances collaboration. Latency introduced; subscription costs incurred.

Practical Rule for Tool Selection

If X → Use Y:

  • If team size ≤10 and speed is critical → Use Playwright. Its local execution and zero costs provide immediate feedback, but ensure environments are standardized and dynamic content is masked.
  • If team size >10 or CI/CD integration is essential → Use Percy. Its automated synchronization and scalability outweigh latency and costs, but budget for subscription fees and optimize ignore regions for dynamic content.

Common Pitfalls and Their Mechanisms

  • Misconfigured Baselines: Inconsistent environments (e.g., varying viewport sizes) cause pixel-level discrepancies. Mechanism: Font rendering and anti-aliasing differ across setups, triggering false positives.
  • Dynamic Content: Elements like timestamps or ads introduce variability. Mechanism: Non-deterministic content changes despite unchanged core UI, leading to unnecessary failures.
  • Tool Selection Misalignment: Choosing the wrong tool for team size or workflow. Mechanism: Local tools fail for large teams due to synchronization issues, while cloud tools add latency and costs for small teams.

Professional Judgment

Local visual regression testing with Playwright is optimal for small teams prioritizing speed and cost control. However, it breaks down for teams >10 developers due to synchronization bottlenecks. Percy is the superior choice for scalability and CI/CD integration but comes with latency and subscription costs. The key is to align tool selection with team dynamics and relentlessly optimize configurations to maximize efficiency.

title: Pre-Send Bounce Defense: Why Detecting Dead Mailboxes at Port 25 Beats Paying ESP Penalties
description:
If you’ve ever launched a SaaS product on AWS SES, SendGrid, or Postmark, you are probably familiar with the most stressful email you can receive from cloud infrastructure:

"Your Amazon SES account has been placed on probation because your bounce rate has exceeded the 5% reputation threshold. If this rate is not reduced within 14 days, your sending capability will be suspended."

For a bootstrapped startup, having transactional email suspended means user signups fail, magic login links stop arriving, and customer activation drops to zero overnight.

Most engineering teams react by adding post-facto suppression lists: when an email bounces, a webhook records the address in a PostgreSQL suppressions table, preventing future sends to that user.

Here is the problem: by the time your webhook receives the bounce event, the damage to your IP and domain reputation is already done.

Let’s look at why passive bounce handling fails at scale, and how to implement Pre-Send Bounce Defense using active TCP Port 25 socket handshakes before a single byte of message payload is ever transmitted.

1. The Math Behind the 5% Bounce Ceiling

Major Mailbox Providers (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, Yahoo Mail) treat hard bounces as the single clearest indicator of automated list scraping, synthetic spam generation, or poor database hygiene.

Because of this, modern Cloud ESPs enforce strict mathematical circuit breakers:

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│             ESP REPUTATION THRESHOLDS (14-DAY)         │
├────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ < 2.0% Bounce Rate   │ 🟢 HEALTHY: Full throughput     │
│ 2.0% – 4.9% Rate     │ 🟡 WARNING: Pacing throttle     │
│ ≥ 5.0% Bounce Rate   │ 🔴 PROBATION: 14-day kill clock │
│ ≥ 10.0% Spike        │ 🚨 IMMEDIATE SUSPENSION         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

If you send 1,000 onboarding invitations or transactional user alerts and just 50 of them hit abandoned student inboxes, misspelled domains (@gnail.com), or former employee mailboxes, your entire infrastructure is placed on probation.

Waiting for asynchronous Non-Delivery Reports (NDRs) means you are using your own domain reputation as the test probe.

2. The Architectural Alternative: RFC 5321 Socket Probing

In the SMTP specification (RFC 5321), an email delivery transaction occurs across distinct stages:

[Your Server]                                       [Recipient MX Server]
      │                                                      │
      │ ──── TCP Connect (Port 25) ────────────────────────> │
      │ <─── 220 mx.google.com ESMTP ready ───────────────── │
      │                                                      │
      │ ──── EHLO yourdomain.com ──────────────────────────> │
      │ <─── 250-mx.google.com at your service ───────────── │
      │                                                      │
      │ ──── MAIL FROM:<probe@yourdomain.com> ─────────────> │
      │ <─── 250 2.1.0 OK ────────────────────────────────── │
      │                                                      │
      │ ──── RCPT TO:<user@targetdomain.com> ──────────────> │
      │                                                      │
      │ <─── 250 2.1.5 Recipient OK ──────────────────────── │ (Valid Mailbox!)
      │             ─── OR ───                               │
      │ <─── 550 5.1.1 User unknown / Does not exist ─────── │ (Dead Mailbox!)
      │                                                      │
      │ ──── RSET / QUIT ──────────────────────────────────> │ (Abort cleanly)

Notice the crucial detail: The recipient verification happens during the RCPT TO phase.

If you issue RSET (Reset) or QUIT immediately after inspecting the recipient response, no email envelope is delivered. The recipient never receives a message, no spam trap is triggered, and no bounce metric is logged against your cloud ESP quota.

You get deterministic proof of whether the mailbox exists without consuming a single email send credit.

3. The Catch-All Domain Trap

Before writing the socket probe, you must account for Catch-All (Accept-All) domains.

Many enterprise mail servers (Postfix, Exchange Online, or customized Exim gateways) are configured to return 250 OK for every address at their domain, routing unassigned mail to an administrative catch-all box.

If you probe a catch-all domain, a fake address like nonexistent_user_99214@company.com will falsely report as valid.

The Defense: Two-Phase Canary Probing

To handle catch-all domains reliably:

  1. Probe a Randomized Canary Address: Generate a high-entropy string that is mathematically guaranteed not to exist (e.g. probe-rnd-a9f84820@targetdomain.com).
  2. Evaluate the Canary Result:
    • If the canary returns 250 OK → The domain is Catch-All. Socket probing cannot prove individual mailbox existence; fall back to MX record authority and DNS checks.
    • If the canary returns 550 5.1.1 → The domain enforces strict mailbox validation! Proceed to probe the actual target email.

4. Production TypeScript Implementation

Here is a lightweight, zero-dependency Node.js implementation using native net.Socket and dns.promises:

import dns from "node:dns/promises";
import net from "node:net";

export interface MailboxProbeResult {
  email: string;
  exists: boolean | "catch_all" | "unknown";
  mxHost?: string;
  smtpCode?: number;
  reason: string;
}

/**
 * Resolves priority MX servers via authoritative DNS
 */
async function resolveMxServer(domain: string): Promise<string | null> {
  try {
    const records = await dns.resolveMx(domain);
    if (!records || records.length === 0) return null;
    records.sort((a, b) => a.priority - b.priority);
    return records[0].exchange;
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
}

/**
 * Executes RFC 5321 handshake up to RCPT TO
 */
export async function probeMailboxSmtp(
  email: string,
  heloDomain = "validator.net",
  mailFrom = "verify@validator.net",
  timeoutMs = 8000
): Promise<MailboxProbeResult> {
  const parts = email.split("@");
  if (parts.length !== 2) {
    return { email, exists: false, reason: "Malformed email format" };
  }
  const domain = parts[1].toLowerCase();

  const mxHost = await resolveMxServer(domain);
  if (!mxHost) {
    return { email, exists: false, reason: "No valid MX records found for domain" };
  }

  return new Promise((resolve) => {
    const socket = new net.Socket();
    let stage: "CONNECT" | "HELO" | "MAIL_FROM" | "RCPT_TO" | "DONE" = "CONNECT";
    let lastCode = 0;
    let responseBuffer = "";

    const cleanExit = (result: MailboxProbeResult) => {
      try {
        if (!socket.destroyed) {
          socket.write("QUIT\r\n");
          socket.destroy();
        }
      } catch {}
      resolve(result);
    };

    socket.setTimeout(timeoutMs);

    socket.on("timeout", () => {
      cleanExit({
        email,
        exists: "unknown",
        mxHost,
        reason: `Socket connection timed out after ${timeoutMs}ms`,
      });
    });

    socket.on("error", (err) => {
      cleanExit({
        email,
        exists: "unknown",
        mxHost,
        reason: `TCP socket error: ${err.message}`,
      });
    });

    socket.on("data", (chunk) => {
      responseBuffer += chunk.toString();
      if (!responseBuffer.endsWith("\r\n")) return;

      const lines = responseBuffer.trim().split("\r\n");
      const lastLine = lines[lines.length - 1];
      responseBuffer = "";

      const codeMatch = lastLine.match(/^(\d{3})/);
      if (!codeMatch) return;
      lastCode = parseInt(codeMatch[1], 10);

      switch (stage) {
        case "CONNECT":
          if (lastCode === 220) {
            stage = "HELO";
            socket.write(`EHLO ${heloDomain}\r\n`);
          } else {
            cleanExit({ email, exists: "unknown", mxHost, smtpCode: lastCode, reason: "Banner rejected" });
          }
          break;

        case "HELO":
          if (lastCode === 250) {
            stage = "MAIL_FROM";
            socket.write(`MAIL FROM:<${mailFrom}>\r\n`);
          } else {
            cleanExit({ email, exists: "unknown", mxHost, smtpCode: lastCode, reason: "EHLO rejected" });
          }
          break;

        case "MAIL_FROM":
          if (lastCode === 250) {
            stage = "RCPT_TO";
            socket.write(`RCPT TO:<${email}>\r\n`);
          } else {
            cleanExit({ email, exists: "unknown", mxHost, smtpCode: lastCode, reason: "MAIL FROM rejected" });
          }
          break;

        case "RCPT_TO":
          stage = "DONE";
          if (lastCode === 250) {
            cleanExit({
              email,
              exists: true,
              mxHost,
              smtpCode: lastCode,
              reason: "Recipient accepted with 250 OK",
            });
          } else if (lastCode >= 550 && lastCode <= 553) {
            cleanExit({
              email,
              exists: false,
              mxHost,
              smtpCode: lastCode,
              reason: `Mailbox rejected: ${lastLine}`,
            });
          } else {
            cleanExit({
              email,
              exists: "unknown",
              mxHost,
              smtpCode: lastCode,
              reason: `Temporary or grey-listing code: ${lastLine}`,
            });
          }
          break;
      }
    });

    socket.connect(25, mxHost);
  });
}

5. Architectural Considerations for Production

Before deploying Port 25 probes at scale, keep three infrastructure realities in mind:

  1. Residential vs. Datacenter IP Reputation: Residential and standard cloud IPs (like basic AWS EC2 or DigitalOcean droplets) frequently have outbound Port 25 blocked by default to prevent spam botnets. You must request reverse DNS (PTR) authorization from your cloud provider or route probes through dedicated relay egress.
  2. Respect Greylisting: Some providers (especially specialized Postfix clusters) return 451 4.7.1 Service temporarily unavailable on the first connection attempt from a new IP. Treat 4xx codes as "unknown" rather than marking the email dead.
  3. Cache Validation Results: Mailbox existence rarely changes within 24 hours. Cache successful verifications in Redis or SQLite to avoid bombarding target MX clusters with repeated TCP connections.

Summary

  • Passive Bounce Handling is Obsolete: Relying on webhooks after dispatching emails guarantees your bounce rate will spike during bad signup waves.
  • Pre-Send Defense Protects Your Sending Domain: Checking mailbox existence at the RCPT TO phase lets you prune dead contacts before your ESP logs an envelope.
  • Always Test for Catch-All: Use randomized canary probes so accept-all corporate servers don't produce false confidence.

💡 Developer Infrastructure Note: If you're building a SaaS platform or backend service that can't afford the risk of AWS SES sandbox throttling or SendGrid bounce suspensions, check out SadaSend. It features automated pre-send bounce defense, hard per-key allowlists, and a pre-warmed transactional pool with 6,000 free sends every month.

title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
description:
Hey HN, this is Nathan and Nicholas from Rivet (https://rivet.dev) – a fast, high-density, and scalable orchestrator for agentic workloads using the actor model. Rather than running a heavyweight sandbox per agent, each agent gets a lightweight actor backed by S3.

Actors provide a long-lived process for long agent turns, in-memory state for context, a WebSocket server for multiplayer, durable SQLite storage backed by S3, and hibernation when idle.

It's a similar model to Cloudflare Durable Objects, but it’s open source and self-hostable.

Here’s a video walkthrough: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3Ev6I7DOV9c

When we went through YC in 2023, we were building infrastructure for multiplayer games like Diep and Krunker. This involved heavily optimizing high-throughput matchmaking, real-time player messages, and blitz scaling. Through that process, we spent a lot of time on workloads where Postgres couldn't keep up with our throughput. We started out by hacking together Lua scripts on top of Redis, but this became too cumbersome to maintain and upgrade. This led us to extend our game server orchestrator to support what we call Rivet Actors today: many lightweight workers with in-memory state and durable storage. By using actors, we were able to serve tens of millions of monthly active users.

As agents grew in popularity, it became clear that running agents in sandboxes is inefficient. Sandboxes are expensive, mostly idle, and slow to start. Developers started using actors because they are far more memory efficient (72 KB baseline for actors vs 512 MB for a minimal sandbox) and fast to start (4.9 ms p99 for actors vs 1.7 s p99 for sandboxes).

For example, Amp is using Rivet to orchestrate multiplayer agents. They originally tried to build on Cloudflare Durable Objects, but couldn’t launch because of the platform’s limitations and unresponsive support. They migrated to Rivet Actors in a weekend and deploy on-prem. Rivet’s flexible architecture lets them adapt it to their own use cases without being constrained by a framework or the memory, storage, and runtime limits of Cloudflare Durable Objects.

Under the hood, Rivet is backed by S3 while maintaining SSD speeds.

Why S3? Previously, Rivet ran on FoundationDB. However, we were surprised to find that companies are storing orders of magnitude more data on Rivet Actors than in Postgres, such as large session transcripts, agent artifacts, and full POSIX filesystems. As their data grew, they had to start paying for SSDs that sat mostly idle with old transcripts. This led us to double down on S3 as our primary storage medium without sacrificing performance. This choice means that data stored on Rivet is 10× cheaper than on EBS gp3 while maintaining SSD speeds.

It’s not as simple as writing data straight to S3. Lots of PUTs for tiny blobs of data are slow and expensive. Instead, we use an SSD tier to optimize speed and cost:

When you write data to an actor’s SQLite database, the write is acknowledged once SSDs in 2 of 3 availability zones have it. Then, the data is batched to S3 in the background. This means that S3 is never on the write path, which lowers latency and cost. When reading data or waking an actor, Rivet reads from SSDs if already cached and falls back to S3 if not. SSD caches can be tuned to meet your needs, giving you configurable tiered storage for your actors.

This architecture lets Rivet provide 1.07 ms durable writes (3 AZ, p99), 1.36 ms reads (p99), and 138 ms reads from object storage (p99).

We’ve spent a lot of time making sure that Rivet can run wherever you need it. Self-hosting requires deploying a single Rust binary with S3 as the only dependency, Rivet Cloud lets you deploy dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region, and BYOC lets us deploy Rivet to your VPC without having to operate it yourself. Rivet also runs identically in local dev as in production, since Rivet is a lightweight binary that runs anywhere

Rivet Actors can be written in TypeScript or Rust. Out of the box, they support agents (Pi Durable), workflows, real-time, multiplayer, running AI-generated code, Durable Streams, and integrations with tools like Vercel’s Eve and Turso. See all of our available guides, or point your agent at them: https://rivet.dev/docs/#guides

Try it out now, by reading our quickstart guides (https://rivet.dev/docs/) or ask your agent: “Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then build a multiplayer chat agent and run it locally.”

We’d love to get feedback on your experience with Rivet! We’re deeply invested in making Rivet an easy-to-self-host, flexible, and efficient way to run agentic workloads.
