title: How I'd Build a Full Stack App on a $0–$20 Monthly Budget
description:
How much does it actually cost to host a full stack application in 2026?

With so many services offering free tiers, you can get surprisingly far without spending much. But choosing the right combination can get confusing.

Should you use Vercel or Cloudflare? Supabase or Neon? Do you even need a separate authentication provider?

I have worked on several full stack projects and would like to share what I learned to keep infrastructure costs down while choosing the right and reliable services.

So here's my breakdown of the best free and low cost services I'd consider for building a full stack application, and how I'd use them together within a $0–$20 monthly budget.

Pricing and free tier limits are based on November 2026 information and may change.

What Does a Full Stack App Actually Need?

Most applications need a frontend, backend, and database. Depending on the features, you might also need authentication, file storage, and email delivery.

Thankfully, some providers cover several of these needs under one free plan.

Let's compare the options.

Frontend: Which Framework?

Frameworks are generally free. The bigger consideration is how they affect hosting.

Framework Best for Why choose it?
React + Vite SPAs, dashboards Simple setup, static builds, cheap hosting
Next.js Full stack React apps Server rendering, routing, server side logic
Astro Blogs, documentation, content websites Static first architecture, minimal client side JavaScript

My choice would be React + Vite for simple interactive applications. Next.js when I actually need server side features.

Frontend Hosting

1. Cloudflare Pages

Cloudflare Pages is one of my favorites for static websites.

Static asset requests are free and unlimited, making it suitable for React + Vite and other static builds.

Dynamic backend operations still have separate usage limits.

2. Vercel

Vercel offers a convenient Next.js deployment experience, including Git integration and preview deployments.

  • Hobby: $0, restricted to personal, non commercial use.
  • Pro: Starts at $20/month, with included usage credits.

I'd consider it for commercial Next.js applications where the deployment workflow justifies the cost.

3. Netlify

Netlify supports static hosting, serverless functions, and Git based deployments.

Its free plan includes 300 monthly credits, consumed by resources such as bandwidth and compute.

Personally I use Cloudflare Pages for static applications and Vercel for Next.js projects that need its platform features.

Backend: Where Should the API Run?

1. Cloudflare Workers

Cloudflare Workers runs server side JavaScript without requiring you to manage servers.

Free plan:

  • 100,000 requests/day
  • 10 ms CPU time per invocation

The paid plan starts at $5/month, including 10 million requests and 30 million CPU milliseconds monthly, with additional usage billed separately.

Great for lightweight APIs. CPU intensive operations may require a different setup.

2. Vercel Functions

Vercel Functions is convenient when your application already runs on Vercel.

You can keep your frontend and API endpoints in one Next.js project without deploying a separate backend.

Costs depend on your hosting plan and compute usage.

3. Supabase

Supabase combines PostgreSQL, authentication, file storage, and Edge Functions.

Its free plan includes:

  • 500 MB database storage
  • 50,000 monthly active users for authentication
  • Limited storage and function usage

Catch: Inactive free projects can pause after a week, and automatic backups aren't included as they are on paid plans.

My go to pick is usually Cloudflare Workers for lightweight APIs, Supabase when I want several backend features together.

Databases: My Top Three

Service Free allowance Best use
Neon 1 GB storage/project, 100 CU-hours/month Managed PostgreSQL with scale-to-zero compute
Supabase 500 MB PostgreSQL database Apps using Supabase Auth and Storage
Cloudflare D1 5M rows read/day, 100K rows written/day Lightweight SQL apps integrated with Workers

I'd personally consider Neon when I only need PostgreSQL, Supabase for an integrated backend, and D1 for small Cloudflare based applications.

Authentication: Avoid Building It From Scratch

Provider Free allowance / advantage
Clerk Up to 50,000 monthly retained users, ready made auth UI
Supabase Auth 50,000 monthly active users, integrated with Supabase
Firebase Auth Generous free usage for supported methods; limits vary

One detail: monthly retained users and monthly active users are different metrics, so don't directly compare Clerk's and Supabase's allowances.

I'd choose Supabase Auth if I'm already using Supabase. Otherwise, Clerk is worth considering for its ready made authentication components.

File Storage: Don't Forget Bandwidth

Cloudflare R2

Cloudflare R2 provides:

  • 10 GB month Standard storage free
  • 1 million Class A operations/month
  • 10 million Class B operations/month
  • No internet egress bandwidth charges

Operations and storage beyond the free allowance can still cost money.

Supabase Storage

Supabase Storage includes 1 GB of file storage on its free plan, with separate bandwidth limits.

A convenient choice if you're already using Supabase.

Neon Object Storage

Neon also offers object storage, with 5 GB included per free project under its October 2026 offering.

My pick would be Cloudflare R2 for image heavy applications, especially when download bandwidth matters.

Transactional Emails

For verification emails, password resets, and order confirmations:

Service Free / starting price
Resend 3,000 emails/month, 100/day
Brevo 300 emails/day free
Amazon SES Usage based, with sending options starting around $0.16 per 1,000 emails

I'd start with Resend for most small projects because of its simple API.

Brevo is worth considering when a higher daily allowance matters. Amazon SES can be better at higher volumes, although its setup and account requirements are more steep.

Putting It Together: Three Budget Friendly Stacks

We obviously don't need every service mentioned above. Here are three combinations I'd actually think about.

Stack 1: $0/month

For portfolios, experiments, and small applications:

Component Service
Frontend React + Vite
Hosting Cloudflare Pages
Backend Cloudflare Workers Free
Database Cloudflare D1
Storage Cloudflare R2, if needed
Email Resend Free

Estimated base cost: $0/month, provided usage stays within all free allowances.

This would be my first choice for a simple application without demanding backend requirements.

Stack 2: $5/month

Use the same Cloudflare based setup, but upgrade to Workers Paid.

For $5/month, you receive larger included request and CPU allowances.

This makes sense when the application needs more backend capacity, although database and storage limits remain separate.

Estimated base cost: $5/month, excluding overages.

Stack 3: $20/month

For a commercial Next.js application:

Component Service
Frontend / Backend Next.js
Hosting Vercel Pro
Database Neon Free
Authentication Clerk Free
Email Resend Free

Estimated base cost: $20/month.

Vercel Pro starts at $20/month and includes usage credits. However, extra usage, paid addons, team seats, and applicable taxes can push the total higher.

This setup prioritizes Next.js deployment convenience. If $20 is a strict spending ceiling, I'd lean toward the Cloudflare stack.

The Hidden Costs of Free Services

Free tiers are useful, but their limitations are really important to understand before real customers depend on your application.

Here's what I'd check:

Potential issue Why it matters
Usage limits Extra requests, storage, or compute can trigger charges or service restrictions
Inactive projects Some free databases pause when unused
Backups Free plans may lack automatic backups or recovery features
Commercial restrictions Some free hosting plans prohibit commercial use
Bandwidth File downloads and traffic can become expensive
Domains Custom domains typically require an annual registration fee

Another thing people overlook is the cost of maintaining multiple services. Sometimes even if every provider is free, you're still responsible for configuration, credentials, updates, and troubleshooting.

So sometimes paying a little more for one integrated platform is worth it.

What Would I Actually Choose?

For a small project, I'd start with Cloudflare Workers + D1 or Supabase, depending on whether I need a lightweight API or a more complete backend.

If I'm building with Next.js, I'd consider Vercel + Neon, keeping hosting costs and commercial use restrictions in mind.

I wouldn't introduce a separate service unless it solves an actual requirement or bottleneck.

And I certainly wouldn't pay for additional infrastructure just because a project someday might have thousands of users.

Start with a stack that fits your current needs, understand the free tier limitations, and upgrade when there's a clear reason.

title: Node.js Streaming AI-Generated Images to S3-Compatible Storage: Retry-Safe Uploads
description:
Short answer: use a Node.js readable stream with a private S3-compatible upload, a deterministic image key, and an existence check before retrying; use an expiring signed URL for the download.

A fintech service storing private AI-generated images should stream the image into S3-compatible object storage, keep the object private, and issue an expiring signed download URL only after the upload is confirmed. The important design choice is the retry boundary: the image key must be deterministic, the existence check must happen before a write, and every retry must be observable rather than treated as proof that the first attempt failed.

This is a throughput decision with a failure model attached. If the object store cannot provide versioning, object lock, or an If-Match conditional write, the application owns the remaining concurrency and recovery policy.

How can Node.js stream AI-generated images to S3-compatible storage safely?

The critical path has four invariants:

  1. A generated image gets one application-owned object key, rather than a new random key on every retry.
  2. The upload uses a readable stream and private access; public-read is not a fallback.
  3. A timeout or dropped response triggers a check for the existing key before another write.
  4. A download URL is signed and expires; the storage authorization header is never forwarded to that URL.

The third rule is easy to skip. It is also where duplicate work and accidental overwrite begin. A client can lose the response after the storage service has accepted a large body, so “the request failed” does not establish “the object is absent.”

That ambiguity is expensive.

In a fintech workflow, the damage is larger than an untidy bucket. A retry that chooses a new key can leave one image available to the user while another image is recorded against the generation job, and a retry that blindly overwrites can replace evidence without a storage-level version to recover. The worker therefore needs a durable state transition around the object key: pending before the first request, confirmed after a successful response or a positive existence check, and failed only after the retry budget is exhausted. This is an application invariant because the storage limits do not provide the missing conditional write.

For a Node.js implementation, the AWS SDK's S3.upload() accepts a readable stream and is the natural high-throughput primitive for an S3-compatible target. For a service using Infrai, the same boundary is a small REST call: discovery supplies the request schema and examples, while the application still owns the key and recovery record. The example below keeps the object private and uses the verified object-put route; the stream can be the output of an image-generation response.

import os
import time

import requests


def store_image(image_stream, bucket: str, key: str, content_type: str) -> dict:
    api_key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    base_url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
    headers = {
        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
        "Idempotency-Key": f"image:{bucket}:{key}",
        "Content-Type": content_type,
        "x-amz-acl": "private",
    }

    for attempt in range(4):
        check = requests.request(
            method="HEAD",
            url=f"{base_url}/storage/object/head/{bucket}/{key}",
            headers=headers,
            timeout=30,
        )
        if check.status_code == 200:
            return {"status": "already_exists", "key": key}
        if check.status_code not in {404, 400}:
            raise RuntimeError(f"head failed: {check.status_code} {check.text}")

        response = requests.request(
            method="PUT",
            url=f"{base_url}/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key}",
            headers=headers,
            data=store_image_stream,
            timeout=900,
        )
        if response.ok:
            return {"status": "uploaded", "key": key}
        if response.status_code == 429:
            retry_after = int(response.headers.get("Retry-After", "0"))
            time.sleep(max(retry_after, 2**attempt))
            continue
        if 400 <= response.status_code < 500:
            raise RuntimeError(f"upload rejected: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
        if attempt == 3:
            raise RuntimeError(f"upload failed: {response.status_code} {response.text}")
        time.sleep(2**attempt)

    raise RuntimeError("upload retry budget exhausted")

The sample deliberately has no public URL. It also does not pretend that object metadata is a query index; metadata can describe an object, but list operations remain prefix-oriented here. In production, use a stable key derived from the generation job and persist its state in the job database. The retry key is derived from that stable identity, so the same logical upload is not turned into four independent objects.

Which storage boundary fits the throughput target?

“Compatible with S3” describes an interface family, not identical recovery semantics. For large generated images, the first comparison should be the upload path and the second should be what happens after a partial failure.

Option Large-file path Operational strength Boundary to accept
Amazon S3 AWS SDK multipart-capable upload path Mature conditional and lifecycle tooling around the object layer More platform configuration and IAM surface
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API and multipart-oriented workflows Useful when an application already lives at Cloudflare's edge R2-specific behavior and account controls still need testing
MinIO S3-compatible API, self-managed deployment Local control over placement and recovery policy The team owns disks, replication, upgrades, and incident response
Infrai storage Plain REST storage surface, including object put and presign capabilities Discovery is public and self-describing, with runnable examples for the documented capabilities No versioning or object lock, no If-Match write, no cross-region automatic replication, and no self-service CORS route

Amazon S3 is the conservative choice when the organization already operates its IAM, lifecycle, and recovery controls there. R2 is a reasonable fit when its surrounding edge and account model are already part of the design. MinIO makes sense when placement and ownership matter more than outsourcing the storage layer, but its operational burden is not a footnote.

Infrai is the option I would try for the storage leg of a small service that wants a plain REST surface and self-describing discovery: GET /v1/discovery exposes the capability catalog, and the capability documentation includes request schemas and runnable examples. Its consistent API can remove some SDK and integration glue while a team wires storage into an existing backend. The recommendation is narrow: try it for private object writes and signed downloads when the application can enforce its own key coordination and recovery policy.

The limitation is decisive for some fintech workloads. There is no object versioning or WORM-style object lock, so an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through the storage layer. There is no If-Match conditional write either. If an audit requirement demands immutable evidence, or two writers must be excluded by storage-level preconditions, Amazon S3 with the appropriate controls or a separately coordinated MinIO deployment is the better boundary.

How should retries and expiring downloads be separated?

Retries belong to the upload worker. Expiration belongs to the download authorization. Mixing them creates an awkward failure mode: a caller keeps retrying a download URL that was meant to be short-lived, while the worker has no reliable record of whether the object was committed.

For an Infrai-backed path, the verified object write is PUT /v1/storage/object/put/{bucket}/{key} and the signed-read operation is the storage presign capability documented by discovery. Keep the write private, store the resulting key and state in the application database, and generate a fresh signed URL for a user-facing download. Do not attach the Infrai Authorization: Bearer header to the returned presigned URL; that URL is the browser's download credential.

Rate limits deserve the same discipline as ambiguous timeouts. A retry loop should honor Retry-After when the service sends it, use exponential backoff, and stop after a bounded number of attempts. A 4xx response should be surfaced with its body rather than converted into a generic “upload failed” message. For standard queues, assume at-least-once delivery and make the consumer idempotent; a queue retry is not evidence that the previous consumer invocation did nothing.

A useful record has job_id, object_key, state, attempt_count, last_request_id, and timestamps for start, confirmation, and URL issuance. The request identifier is for tracing. It is not a substitute for a deterministic object key or a database uniqueness constraint.

Why the tempting alternatives fail

The first rejected design is “generate a fresh key for every attempt.” It improves neither throughput nor correctness. A lost response then leaves orphaned objects, and a later retry can publish a second image under a different name. That pattern is valid for content-addressed archival where duplicate blobs are intentionally acceptable, but it is a poor default for a user-visible generation job.

The second rejected design is browser-direct upload with a self-configured CORS rule. This storage surface does not expose an independent set_cors route for application-managed configuration, so a browser workflow cannot assume that it can establish the required cross-origin policy itself. Server-side streaming is the safer fit for this stated path; if browser-direct upload is a hard requirement, choose a storage provider whose CORS controls are available and test them before committing to the flow.

The third rejected design is a permanent public URL. It violates the private-upload requirement and creates a revocation problem that expiration cannot solve after the URL is copied. A signed URL is still a bearer credential, so its lifetime should match the download job and its issuance should be logged.

Decision

Choose S3 when storage-native immutability, conditional writes, and established recovery tooling are the primary constraints. Choose R2 when the surrounding Cloudflare architecture is the real reason to use it. Choose MinIO when the team is willing to operate the data plane. Try Infrai for a private, server-mediated upload path when self-describing REST discovery and a consistent interface reduce integration work, provided the application supplies the missing coordination and immutability guarantees.

That is the boundary I would put in the architecture record: the object store moves bytes efficiently, while the application owns identity, retries, concurrency, and evidence of completion. The larger the image, the less acceptable it is to infer success from a missing response.

If this boundary fits your system, start with the storage discovery and object APIs.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • Amazon S3 multipart upload overview
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility
  • MinIO S3 API compatibility
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS)

title: Node.js Presigned URL Audit for Backup Downloads (Object Storage Retention)
description:
A selected backup snapshot should remain private until an authorized tenant asks to restore it. The least complex way to deliver its archive is a short-lived presigned download URL for one object, issued after a tenant-scoped lookup. The deletion timer belongs to the snapshot record, not to the link.

TL;DR: treat a presigned URL as a bearer credential, not delivery proof. Keep the backup object private, authorize the snapshot before signing, record issuance without recording the URL, and alert only when a restore is stalled past evidence you can trust.

For an e-commerce system, this matters after the order database or a tenant configuration has to be rolled back to one selected snapshot. A predictable object key is convenient during an incident. It is also the wrong authorization boundary. The download service needs to resolve an opaque snapshot ID, verify that it belongs to the requesting tenant, and then sign exactly that stored object.

The two clocks are easy to conflate. A signed link might last 10 minutes while a snapshot is retained for 30 days; expiration of the first must not delete the second. The values are policy examples, not universal defaults. Link lifetime is shaped by archive size and retry behavior. Retention is shaped by recovery obligations, legal holds, and the cost of keeping data that should have been deleted.

What should a Node.js service do with a presigned download URL for object storage?

Have its handler authenticate the caller, load the selected snapshot through a tenant-scoped query, and send the resulting object key to a narrow signing interface. A browser must never provide an object key that the signer treats as authorization.

The implementation detail may live in a Node.js service; the boundary is the important part. This Go example makes the boundary testable without coupling the restore workflow to one storage SDK.

package restore

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "net/url"
    "time"
)

type Snapshot struct {
    ID       string
    TenantID string
    ObjectKey string
    DeleteAt time.Time
}

type Presigner interface {
    PresignGet(ctx context.Context, objectKey string, expiresAt time.Time) (string, error)
}

func DownloadURL(ctx context.Context, callerTenantID string, snapshot Snapshot, signer Presigner, now time.Time) (string, error) {
    if callerTenantID != snapshot.TenantID {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("snapshot does not belong to caller")
    }
    if snapshot.ObjectKey == "" || !now.Before(snapshot.DeleteAt) {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("snapshot is unavailable")
    }

    expiresAt := now.Add(10 * time.Minute)
    signedURL, err := signer.PresignGet(ctx, snapshot.ObjectKey, expiresAt)
    if err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("presign snapshot %s: %w", snapshot.ID, err)
    }
    if _, err := url.ParseRequestURI(signedURL); err != nil {
        return "", fmt.Errorf("signer returned an invalid URL: %w", err)
    }
    return signedURL, nil
}

Presigned URLs can be used more than once until they expire, so retrying a click is not evidence of a duplicate restore. Keep backup creation idempotent on a restore-operation ID, and trace link issuance as a separate action. That distinction prevents a queue retry from creating a second snapshot while still allowing a user to obtain a replacement credential after a tab closes.

Start with the page, then trace backward

The page should say that a restore delivery is stalled, and the on-call view should expose the snapshot ID, tenant ID, issuance time, expiry time, deletion deadline, and last trustworthy delivery state. It should not show the signed URL, query string, or an authorization header. Those fields can be credentials.

Work backward from that page. A download_url_issued event means the service authorized a request and created access. It does not mean that a browser reached storage. download_started means a request reached a boundary that can observe it. A completion event is useful only when the transfer mechanism can truthfully emit one; an application redirect is not completion evidence.

Event What it proves What it cannot prove
download_url_issued Authorization and signing occurred. The archive was reachable or received.
download_started An observable transfer request began. The complete archive arrived.
download_completed A trusted transfer boundary observed completion. The data was restored successfully.

This is where a telemetry change pays for itself. Emit an issuance event after authorization and signing, with one stable event ID for that issuance attempt. Store a derived object identifier rather than the raw key when object names can reveal tenant information. The snapshot ID is usually the better correlation key across export, delivery, and restore stages.

package restore

import (
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
)

func ObjectKeyID(objectKey string) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(objectKey))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:8])
}

Small signal, big difference. A missed job and a duplicate delivery can otherwise collapse into the same count, leaving the responder to guess which action is safe.

Retention and deletion are a state machine, not a storage setting

Keep the deletion decision in application state with an auditable DeleteAt value, then make the object lifecycle follow that decision. A restore can be allowed only while the snapshot is still retained. Once it crosses the deletion boundary, the service should reject new links even if an old object reference still exists in an asynchronous cleanup path.

There is a real trade-off here. Immediate deletion after a requested restore reduces residual-data exposure, but it can strand a slow or interrupted download. A longer retention window gives operations room to reissue authorization, yet increases the set of snapshots that must be tracked for policy and deletion. The useful decision rule is explicit: choose the retention window from the recovery obligation, and choose the much shorter URL lifetime from transfer conditions.

This pattern is a poor fit for a client that needs live, per-request transformation or a transfer that must be revoked immediately after the first byte. A short-lived presigned credential may be reusable before expiry, and the storage service usually cannot report business-level restore success. In those cases, a server-mediated delivery boundary or a purpose-built transfer workflow gives more control, at the cost of operating that path and carrying its bandwidth and failure modes.

Deletion needs its own failure handling. Mark a snapshot as pending deletion before removing its object, make the delete worker idempotent, and retain only the audit fields required to show what was removed. If a worker retries, the desired result is still one deleted object and one terminal record. Do not turn an already-deleted object into an incident by treating a repeated delete as a new failure.

Browser behavior is another boundary

CORS controls what a browser may expose to JavaScript across origins; it does not authorize access to a private object. When a web application downloads from a different origin, allow only the required origins and methods, and test the preflight behavior where the browser needs it. A permissive CORS response cannot repair an overly broad signed URL.

The test matrix should be short but deliberate:

  • A correct-tenant request for a retained snapshot receives a link for that snapshot only.
  • A cross-tenant request, malformed snapshot ID, expired link, and deleted snapshot are rejected.
  • Repeating a restore request does not create another snapshot; repeating a link request is traceable as another issuance.
  • A cross-origin browser path is tested with its actual allowed origin and method.

This is operational work, not ceremony. The rejection cases show whether the ownership boundary still holds when a support request, queue retry, or browser retry takes an unexpected route.

Tune the alert for the cost of a false positive

An alert on every issued-but-uncompleted link turns ordinary behavior into a page: a user may close a laptop, switch networks, or decide not to download. Repeated noise teaches responders that a genuine unavailable backup looks routine.

Page only for sustained tenant impact or for a stage that is clearly failed. For weaker evidence, use a ticket or dashboard tied to the promised restore window, then compare the issued, started, and completed populations before changing a threshold. This preserves the signal that matters: an authorized tenant cannot obtain the selected retained snapshot when the recovery workflow says it should be available.

The design stays intentionally plain: private objects, tenant-scoped selection, a narrow expiring credential, redacted telemetry, and an explicit deletion state. It has limits, but it makes each limit visible to the runbook before the next restore page arrives.

Further reading

References:

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

title: # Things I Wish I Knew 5 Years Ago as a Frontend Engineer
description:
When I started my journey as a frontend engineer, I believed becoming better at my craft meant learning more frameworks, writing cleaner code, and building interfaces faster.

If I could take a Figma design, turn it into a responsive interface, integrate the APIs, and get everything working as expected, I considered that a job well done.

And to be fair, it was.

But over six years of building production applications across different industries, particularly fintech and edtech, I've come to understand that there's much more to frontend engineering than writing code that works.

I've worked on applications that started small and became increasingly complex. I've dealt with difficult bugs, changing product requirements, technical decisions that didn't age well, and features that required more thought than I initially expected.

Some lessons came from making mistakes. Others came from working with different teams, learning from more experienced engineers, and seeing how software behaves in production.

Looking back, there are a few things I wish I'd understood earlier.

Here are ten of them.

1. Understanding JavaScript Will Take You Further Than Chasing Frameworks

Early in my career, I was always interested in learning the next framework or library.

There was always something new to explore, and it sometimes felt like keeping up with the ecosystem was the only way to stay relevant.

But the more I worked with Vue, Nuxt, and other frontend technologies, the more I realised that a solid understanding of JavaScript was far more valuable than knowing the syntax of several frameworks.

Understanding closures, promises, asynchronous operations, the event loop, and how JavaScript handles objects and references has helped me solve problems that framework knowledge alone couldn't explain.

For example, knowing how asynchronous operations behave makes it easier to understand race conditions, unexpected state updates, and why a component might display outdated data.

Frameworks provide convenient ways to build applications, but the fundamentals explain what's happening underneath.

What I'd tell myself five years ago: Learn your framework, but invest just as much effort in understanding JavaScript and how the browser works.

2. Getting a Feature to Work Doesn't Mean It's Finished

Earlier in my career, I was mostly concerned with getting features to work.

If the API returned the expected response, the form submitted successfully, and the UI matched the design, I felt the task was complete.

Production experience changed that perspective.

Today, I find myself asking questions like:

  • What happens when the API fails?
  • What if the user submits the form twice?
  • What happens when the response is delayed?
  • What if the data is incomplete?
  • How easy will it be for another engineer to modify this feature?

These are the situations that often separate a feature that works during development from one that works reliably in production.

I've learned to think beyond the happy path and consider how the application should behave when things don't go as planned.

The lesson: A feature isn't truly complete simply because it works under ideal conditions. It should also handle unexpected situations gracefully.

3. Understanding the Product Makes You a Better Engineer

This is probably one of the biggest changes in how I approach my work.

When I was starting out, I focused heavily on implementation.

I'd receive a ticket, review the design, integrate the API, and move on to the next task.

Over time, I started paying more attention to the problem behind the ticket.

Why are we building this feature?

What problem does it solve?

How does it improve the user's experience?

And how does it contribute to the business?

Working on fintech products has made this particularly important.

For example, building a transfer flow isn't simply about collecting an amount, selecting a beneficiary, and calling an API.

You also need to think about how users understand transaction statuses, what happens when a transfer is delayed, and how the interface communicates errors without creating unnecessary confusion.

The technical implementation matters, but understanding the product helps you make better decisions about that implementation.

The lesson: Don't just focus on delivering features. Understand the problem you're solving and why it matters.

4. Simple Code Is Often Better Than Clever Code

There was a time when I thought writing sophisticated code was a sign of being a better engineer.

More abstractions, reusable utilities, design patterns, and layers of separation seemed like good architecture.

But working on larger applications has taught me that complexity comes with a cost.

I've encountered situations where a relatively simple feature became difficult to understand because the implementation had too many moving parts.

Sometimes, a straightforward function is all you need.

Sometimes, local component state is better than introducing another Pinia store.

And sometimes, having two focused components is more maintainable than creating one highly configurable component that tries to handle every possible use case.

This doesn't mean abstraction or reusability is bad.

It means we should introduce them when they solve a real problem.

The lesson: Good engineering isn't about how complicated your solution looks. It's about how clearly it solves the problem and how easy it is to maintain.

5. Debugging Is a Skill You Have to Develop Deliberately

I can remember times when my first response to a bug was to start changing code.

I'd try a different condition, move some logic around, add a console log, and hope the issue disappeared.

Sometimes it worked, but it wasn't an effective way to solve problems consistently.

Over the years, I've become more deliberate about debugging.

Before making changes, I try to understand what is happening.

What should the application be doing?

What is it actually doing?

Can I reproduce the issue?

Where does the behaviour begin to differ from what I expect?

Is the problem coming from the frontend, the API response, or an incorrect assumption?

This approach has been particularly useful when dealing with Vue reactivity, asynchronous operations, complex forms, and API integrations.

I've also learned to make better use of browser DevTools, Vue Devtools, network inspection, and automated tests.

The lesson: Understanding why something is broken is often more valuable than quickly finding a way to make the error disappear.

6. Performance Should Be Considered From the Beginning

Performance used to feel like something you worked on after completing a feature.

Build it first, then optimise it later.

While I still believe premature optimisation can create unnecessary complexity, I've learned that performance problems often come from decisions made much earlier.

Unnecessary API requests, large JavaScript bundles, poorly managed reactive state, and unoptimized assets can gradually affect the user experience.

In Vue and Nuxt applications, I've become more conscious of things like component rendering, lazy loading, API request patterns, and how data is fetched and shared across pages.

The goal isn't to optimise everything.

It's to understand the potential cost of technical decisions and measure performance where it matters.

The lesson: Performance isn't something you simply add at the end. It should influence how you design and build features.

7. Communication Is Just as Important as Technical Ability

One thing I've learned from working with different teams is that being technically good doesn't automatically make you effective.

You also need to communicate clearly.

That means knowing when to ask questions, explain technical decisions, raise concerns, and communicate blockers before they become bigger problems.

It also means being able to discuss technical trade-offs with product managers, designers, and other stakeholders who may not have the same technical background.

I've come to appreciate that good communication reduces misunderstandings and helps teams make better decisions.

And sometimes, asking the right question early can save hours of unnecessary implementation.

The lesson: Your ability to communicate your thinking is part of your value as an engineer.

8. Document Your Work and the Impact It Creates

This is something I genuinely wish I'd started doing much earlier.

As engineers, we often move from one task to another without taking time to reflect on what we've accomplished.

You build a dashboard, improve a user flow, fix a difficult bug, or introduce a reusable component.

Then you move on.

Months later, when you're updating your CV or preparing for an interview, you struggle to remember the details.

I've learned that it's important to document not just what you built, but why you built it and what changed as a result.

For example, instead of simply writing:

"Built a new onboarding flow."

It's more useful to explain the problem with the previous experience, the changes you introduced, and any improvements you were able to measure.

Not every contribution will have a percentage attached to it, and that's fine.

But being able to explain the reasoning and impact behind your work makes your experience much easier to communicate.

The lesson: Don't wait until you're applying for a job before trying to remember everything you've accomplished.

9. AI Can Make You Faster, but You Still Need to Think

AI-assisted development has become a significant part of modern software engineering.

Today, we can use AI tools to explore implementation approaches, generate tests, review code, understand unfamiliar systems, and speed up repetitive tasks.

I've found these tools useful, particularly when exploring unfamiliar technologies or working through complex problems.

But I've also learned that generating code quickly isn't the same as solving a problem correctly.

AI can suggest an implementation that looks reasonable but doesn't account for your application's architecture, business requirements, or edge cases.

That's why understanding what you're building remains important.

You still need to review the output, question assumptions, test the implementation, and take responsibility for what eventually reaches production.

I see AI as something that should improve my productivity and engineering judgment, not replace them.

The lesson: Use AI to work more effectively, but don't outsource your understanding of the problem.

10. Be Intentional About Your Career Growth

For a long time, I believed that if I continued improving technically and delivering good work, career growth would naturally follow.

I've since realised that becoming a better engineer and building a meaningful career require different kinds of effort.

Technical ability matters, but so does how you position yourself, the problems you choose to work on, and the relationships you build along the way.

You also need to think about what you want to be known for.

For me, that has meant becoming more intentional about sharing what I've learned from building production applications, writing technical articles, participating in developer communities, and developing a deeper understanding of software architecture.

It's also one of the reasons I started sharing my Vue Nuggets series.

I wanted to do more than simply consume knowledge. I wanted to document what I've learned, contribute to conversations within the developer community, and hopefully help someone avoid mistakes I've made.

I'm still learning how to do that consistently.

But I wish I'd started earlier.

The lesson: Don't leave your career growth entirely to chance. Be deliberate about the skills you develop, the work you do, and how you communicate your value.

Final Thoughts

Looking back over the past six years, I can confidently say that my understanding of frontend engineering has changed.

I still enjoy building interfaces, solving technical problems, and exploring new technologies.

But I now spend more time thinking about the bigger picture.

How does this feature affect the user?

Will this implementation be easy to maintain?

What happens when something goes wrong?

Are we solving the right problem?

And how can I make the work easier for the next engineer who touches this code?

I don't have all the answers, and I don't expect to.

There are still things I'm learning, decisions I would approach differently, and areas where I want to improve.

But if there's one thing these years have taught me, it's that growth in software engineering goes beyond becoming better at writing code.

It's about developing better judgment, understanding the impact of your work, and learning to approach problems with more clarity and intention.

If I could go back five years, I'd tell myself this:

Don't focus only on becoming an engineer who can build anything. Work towards becoming an engineer who understands what is worth building, why it matters, and how to build it well.

And if you've been in frontend engineering for a while, I'd love to know:

What's one thing you wish you'd understood earlier in your career?

title: Why Your Azure Storage Account Is Leaking Publicly (And How to Fix It)
description:
One of the most common mistakes in cloud administration is assuming that creating a private container inside an Azure Storage Account makes your data secure by default.

When preparing for the Microsoft Azure Administrator (AZ-104) certification or managing production environments, engineers quickly discover that Azure Blob Storage has layered access controls. A single misconfiguration in account-level overrides, SAS token policies, or network endpoints can silently expose sensitive blobs to the public internet.

Here is a breakdown of why these leaks happen, how access mechanisms differ, and how to permanently lock down your storage accounts.

The Root Cause: Why Anonymous Access Gets Exposed

When an Azure Storage account is created, the setting Allow Blob Public Access is often left enabled at the account level.

Even if you intend to keep everything confidential:

  • If public access is enabled at the root account level, any contributor or deployment script can spin up a container with anonymous read access enabled.
  • Once that container is active, any file uploaded inside it generates a direct URL that anyone on the web can view without authentication.
  • Monitoring tools will not raise an immediate alert because the read requests appear as valid anonymous traffic.

To secure this architecture, enforce controls at the storage account level rather than relying on individual container permissions.

Step 1: Disabling Anonymous Read Access Permanently

The safest security posture is to disable anonymous access across the storage resource. When this master switch is disabled, Azure rejects all anonymous requests regardless of individual container settings.

Using the Azure CLI, you can audit and lock this down instantly:

az storage account update --name <YourStorageAccountName> --resource-group rg-evolveskill-prod --allow-blob-public-access false

Once updated, any external request attempting to reach a blob directly will receive an HTTP 401 Unauthorized or HTTP 403 Forbidden error.

Step 2: Replacing Shared Access Keys with Microsoft Entra ID (RBAC)

A major risk factor in Azure environments is the reliance on permanent Storage Account Access Keys. These keys act as root administrator passwords—they never expire on their own, cannot be scoped to specific containers, and allow total data control.

Under secure governance models, shared keys should be retired in favor of Microsoft Entra ID Role-Based Access Control (RBAC):

1. Disable Shared Key Access:

Enforce token-based authentication so requests must be authenticated via Entra ID credentials.

az storage account update --name <YourStorageAccountName> --resource-group rg-evolveskill-prod --allow-shared-key-access false

2. Assign Scoped RBAC Roles:

Instead of handing out connection strings, assign identity-based roles such as Storage Blob Data Reader or Storage Blob Data Contributor to specific developers or Managed Identities. Every read and write request is then tied directly to an identity log inside Azure Monitor.

Step 3: Enforcing Network Boundaries and Firewall Ingress

Defense-in-depth requires that storage accounts do not accept traffic from arbitrary public IP addresses. Even with authenticated identities, traffic should be restricted to known corporate subnets or Virtual Networks (VNets).

  • Change the default network action to Deny.
  • Whitelist only your application's virtual network subnets via Virtual Network Service Endpoints or Private Endpoints.
  • Require a minimum transport security layer of TLS 1.2 for all incoming connections.

Key Takeaways for Cloud Administrators

Securing cloud storage is not just about clicking buttons in the portal; it requires building predictable architectural boundaries:

  • Account-level lockouts prevent human error at the container level.
  • Role-based identity tokens eliminate permanent root secrets.
  • Firewall boundary controls ensure that even authenticated users must connect from trusted infrastructure.

Building hands-on familiarity with command-line auditing and architectural runbooks is essential for passing the AZ-104 exam and managing resilient cloud platforms. For comprehensive exam roadmaps, domain notes, and certification study blueprints, check out the resources at EvolveSkill and join our technical discussions on Substack.

How do you handle storage access control in your cloud environments? Let us know in the comments below!

title: SMS Verification UX Best Practices: 10 Tips for Better OTP Screens
description:
Most people who drop out of a phone sign-up don't mean to. They mistype the number, wait for a code that went somewhere else, or fight a six-box input that won't accept paste. SMS verification UX best practices come down to three things: collect the number cleanly, get the code into the field with as little typing as possible, and say clearly what to do when something goes wrong. Here are ten tips, with code.

1. Use the right input for the phone number

Phone numbers aren't numbers in the maths sense. Use type="tel" so mobile keyboards show a dial pad, and let the browser offer the user's saved number.

<label for="phone">Mobile number</label>
<input id="phone" name="phone" type="tel"
       autocomplete="tel" inputmode="tel">

Pair it with a country selector that defaults to the user's likely country, and normalise to E.164 on the server instead of forcing a format in the field.

2. Accept whatever people type

Spaces, dashes, brackets, a leading 00 or a national 0: people paste numbers from contacts and email signatures. Strip formatting characters before validating, and only show an error for numbers that are actually impossible, never for punctuation.

3. Show where the code went, and make it easy to fix

After sending, echo the number back: "We sent a code to +1 416 555 0199. Wrong number?" The link should return to the previous step with the number pre-filled. Many "code never arrived" tickets are really typos the user never noticed.

4. Let the OS fill in the code

The autocomplete="one-time-code" attribute does more for completion than any custom widget. Safari on iOS and macOS suggests the code from an incoming SMS, and many Android keyboards offer it as a suggestion too.

<label for="otp">6-digit code</label>
<input id="otp" name="otp" type="text"
       autocomplete="one-time-code"
       inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]*"
       maxlength="6" required>

Use type="text" with inputmode="numeric", not type="number": number inputs can drop leading zeros, show spinner arrows and accept values like 1e5.

5. Bind the code to your domain

Ending the SMS with an origin-bound line tells browsers which site the code belongs to, so it's only offered there, which also makes phishing pages less effective:

Your Example code is 482913. It expires in 10 minutes.

@example.com #482913

In Chromium browsers on Android you can go further with the WebOTP API and fill the field after the user consents:

if ('OTPCredential' in window) {
  const input = document.querySelector('#otp');
  const ac = new AbortController();
  input.form.addEventListener('submit', () => ac.abort());

  navigator.credentials
    .get({ otp: { transport: ['sms'] }, signal: ac.signal })
    .then((otp) => {
      input.value = otp.code;
      input.form.requestSubmit();
    })
    .catch(() => { /* dismissed or timed out: manual entry still works */ });
}

Treat this as progressive enhancement. The plain input must always work on its own.

6. One field beats six boxes

Split digit boxes look neat but break paste, autofill and screen readers unless you handle every edge case. A single input with wide letter spacing gives a similar look:

#otp { font-size: 1.5rem; letter-spacing: 0.5em; font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums; }

If you must use boxes, support pasting the full code into the first one and moving back on Backspace.

7. Add a resend cooldown with a visible countdown

Users press "Resend" after five seconds if nothing tells them to wait. Disable it briefly, show the remaining time, and lengthen the delay after each resend, which also limits abuse.

function startCooldown(button, seconds) {
  const label = button.textContent;
  button.disabled = true;
  const tick = () => {
    if (seconds <= 0) {
      button.disabled = false;
      button.textContent = label;
      return;
    }
    button.textContent = `Resend in ${seconds--}s`;
    setTimeout(tick, 1000);
  };
  tick();
}

8. Write error messages that say what to do next

"Invalid OTP" tells the user nothing. Compare:

  • Wrong code: "That code doesn't match. Use the latest message; older codes stop working when you request a new one."
  • Expired: "This code has expired. We can send you a new one."
  • Too many attempts: "Too many tries. You can request a new code in 10 minutes."

Keep the typed value in the field after an error so people can spot a swapped digit.

9. Make it accessible

  • Use a visible <label>; a placeholder vanishes as soon as someone types.
  • Announce "Code sent", the end of the countdown and errors through a polite live region, e.g. <p id="otp-status" aria-live="polite"></p>, and connect errors to the field with aria-describedby.
  • Don't expire codes so fast that slower users can't finish. State how long the code is valid and make a fresh one easy to get (WCAG's "Timing Adjustable" criterion covers this).

10. Test real delivery, not just staging

Mocks and provider test numbers prove you call the API correctly, not that a real handset receives a readable message. Before launch, send to real numbers in each country you support and check timing, sender name and rendering. For quick manual checks, the free public numbers on Temp SMS show incoming texts on a web page with no account. Use them only for disposable test accounts, because anyone can read those messages.

SMS verification UX best practices in short

A clean number input, one autofill-friendly code field, the number echoed back, a visible cooldown, specific errors and real-device tests per country.

FAQ

What does autocomplete="one-time-code" do?
It tells the browser and OS that the field expects a one-time code, so they can suggest the code from a recent SMS instead of making the user switch apps.

How long should an SMS code stay valid?
A few minutes up to around ten is common. Show the expiry in the message and on screen.

Should the OTP field be type="number"?
No. Use type="text" with inputmode="numeric" to get a numeric keyboard without losing leading zeros.

More in this series on SMS verification:

  • How to test SMS OTP verification without a real phone number
  • E.164 phone number format: a developer cheat sheet
  • SMS pumping fraud prevention: a practical guide for developers

title: Sandboxing Untrusted AI Agents at Scale: Google Donates Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF
description:
by Mofi Rahman, Developer Relations Engineer, and Brandon Royal, Product Manager, Google Cloud

When Google introduced Kubernetes twelve years ago, the Pod became the default unit of compute for the cloud. The design assumed a straightforward lifecycle: a program boots, binds to a port, serves traffic, and runs until you stop it.

AI agents work fundamentally differently.

An AI agent that’s running on a machine executes untrusted code, commands, and tool calls, and must be isolated from its host and its network resources. At the same time, these agents, whether they’re an interactive coding assistant, an SRE troubleshooter, or a multi-turn evaluation loop, do not run continuously. They execute a step, call a language model, and wait. Most of the time, the agent does nothing at all while it waits for a model to stream tokens or a human to review a pull request. In the same way that Kubernetes was created to address the needs of containerized applications, we introduced Agent Substrate as a new orchestrator for the emerging agentic applications. Secure by default, highly efficient and built for multi-million agent scale.

Agent Substrate was designed from the ground up for AI agent security and density and brings the best parts of Kubernetes together with a new control and data plane for fully-isolated, ultra-low-latency sandboxed compute and storage. The growing Agent Substrate community has been rapidly building core capabilities and stabilizing APIs, culminating in the latest 1.0 release.

This week at KubeCon North America in Salt Lake City, Google Cloud is donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) in Sandbox status, alongside OpenRL.

This post explains why traditional approaches struggle with stateful agents, how Agent Substrate solves the problem, how it connects to enterprise governance on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), and where to see it in action at KubeCon NA 2026.

Challenges of running AI agents at scale

AI agents introduce two infrastructure bottlenecks that standard Kubernetes was never built to handle: idle resource waste and control plane overload.

1. The idle resource problem

During a typical interactive session, an agent can spend 90% to 95% of its time waiting for model inference, external APIs, or human reviews.

During that wait, the agent consumes zero CPU. However, you cannot simply kill the container. The agent holds critical state in memory and on disk: active language runtimes, local Git repositories, uncommitted file edits, and tool sessions.

With standard Kubernetes, platform engineers face two poor options:

  1. Keep a dedicated Pod running all day: The agent responds quickly because it is already warm, but you pay for idle compute around the clock. At ten thousand active users, cluster costs become unsustainable.
  2. Scale to zero with serverless containers: You save compute costs while the agent sits idle, but resuming from cold storage forces the container to clone repositories, reinstall packages, and rebuild memory. Wakeup latency climbs past 20 seconds, breaking the interactive experience.

Platform teams need agents that wake up in under 500 milliseconds with full memory and disk state intact—without paying for running Pods while the agent sits idle.

2. Control plane overload

The opposite issue occurs when training or evaluating agents. Reinforcement learning loops and benchmark suites need to run untrusted agent code across thousands of tasks at the exact same time.

If every sandbox requires a full Kubernetes Pod, the control plane quickly grinds to a halt. Scheduling, creating, and destroying thousands of short-lived Pods every minute overwhelms etcd, saturates kube-apiserver, and exhausts subnet IP addresses. Kubernetes was built to manage stable application topologies, not to act as a microsecond sandbox allocator.

How Agent Substrate solves the problem

Agent Substrate adds an actor-based control and data plane built on top of Kubernetes. It solves the idle resource problem by decoupling Actors from Workers:

  • Actors hold the state: An Actor represents an individual agent session, complete with its own filesystem, environment variables, memory state, and network rules.
  • Workers provide the compute: A Worker is a pre-warmed Kubernetes Pod running in a shared pool (WorkerPool), equipped with container runtimes and sandbox boundaries.

The lifecycle of an agent turn

  1. Request parking: An incoming call hits the atenet-router L7 proxy. If the target Actor is suspended, the proxy holds the request in memory and alerts the Substrate controller.
  2. Fast placement: The controller assigns the Actor to an available slot in the warm Worker pool.
  3. Sub-second restore: The Actor’s memory and disk state restore from tiered storage, the process wakes up, and the proxy delivers the request. The agent resumes in under 500 milliseconds right where it paused.
  4. Suspension on idle: When the turn finishes, Substrate snapshots the Actor’s state to tiered storage and frees the Worker slot for other workloads.

Because Substrate manages Actor state directly, thousands of agents can activate, suspend, and resume every second without creating new Pod objects or stressing etcd.

Safe execution with gVisor and microVMs

Agents frequently execute model-generated, untrusted code. Standard Linux containers share the host kernel, which presents an unacceptable security risk on multi-tenant nodes.

Agent Substrate pairs with gVisor (runsc), Google's open source application kernel written in Go. gVisor intercepts system calls in user space, isolating untrusted code from the host kernel. Because gVisor virtualizes its own memory and process tables, Substrate can freeze a running environment, write memory pages to storage, and restore them on another node in under 500 milliseconds.

For workloads requiring hardware virtualization or custom kernel modules, Substrate also supports Cloud Hypervisor microVMs under the same unified API.

Why Google donated Agent Substrate to the CNCF

Over the past two years, engineering teams across the industry have run into the same agent scaling boundaries. Without a shared open standard, every organization ends up building custom schedulers on top of VMs or working around Kubernetes.

Donating Agent Substrate and gVisor to the CNCF gives the cloud-native community a neutral, vendor-independent foundation that works across any conformant Kubernetes cluster.

Together with community projects, they form an open stack for agentic infrastructure:

  • Layer 1: Secure Isolation (gVisor): Sandboxes untrusted code execution with user-space kernel isolation and fast memory checkpointing.
  • Layer 2: Agent Runtime (Agent Substrate): Multiplexes stateful actors onto warm worker pools with sub-second wakeups.
  • Layer 3: Training Orchestration (OpenRL): Coordinates Kubernetes-native reinforcement learning loops and evaluation sandboxes.
