title: Stop Hardcoding Delivery Fees: Keeping Store Settings in the Database with Next.js
description:
Every store starts the same way. Somebody says "free delivery over a certain amount", and a developer writes a constant at the top of a file. A month later the number changes, then the delivery fee changes, then there is a holiday notice, and suddenly a one-line business decision needs a pull request, a review and a deploy.

On ramo.co.il, a Next.js store for home and garden tools, we decided early that anything which changes with a business decision lives in the database. Code only holds secrets and tracking IDs. Here is how that looks in practice.

What counts as a "setting"

My rule of thumb: if the owner or ops person might ask "can you change that?", it is a setting. For us that means:

  • delivery fees and free-delivery thresholds
  • minimum order amounts
  • pickup options and their notices
  • banners and opening hours
  • contact details and shop texts

If it is a secret or an environment-specific ID, it stays in env variables. Everything else goes in a table.

A simple table

One key/value table with a JSON column is enough to start:

create table site_settings (
  key text primary key,
  value jsonb not null,
  updated_at timestamptz not null default now()
);

Keys look like delivery.fee or delivery.freeThreshold. A small admin screen edits rows, so nobody needs to touch the code.

A typed loader with caching and a fallback

The tricky part is not storing the settings, it is reading them without hitting the database on every request, and without the store falling over if the database hiccups.

import { unstable_cache } from "next/cache";

type DeliverySettings = {
  fee: number;
  freeThreshold: number;
  notice: string | null;
};

const FALLBACK: DeliverySettings = {
  fee: 0,
  freeThreshold: 0,
  notice: null,
};

export const getDeliverySettings = unstable_cache(
  async (): Promise<DeliverySettings> => {
    try {
      const rows = await db.siteSettings.findMany({
        where: { key: { startsWith: "delivery." } },
      });
      const map = Object.fromEntries(rows.map(r => [r.key, r.value]));
      return {
        fee: Number(map["delivery.fee"] ?? FALLBACK.fee),
        freeThreshold: Number(map["delivery.freeThreshold"] ?? FALLBACK.freeThreshold),
        notice: (map["delivery.notice"] as string) ?? null,
      };
    } catch (err) {
      console.error("settings load failed", err);
      return FALLBACK;
    }
  },
  ["delivery-settings"],
  { tags: ["settings"], revalidate: 300 }
);

Three things matter here:

  1. Types at the edge. Raw JSON from the database is converted into a typed object once, so the rest of the app never guesses.
  2. A fallback. If the read fails, the page still renders. Choose fallbacks carefully: a missing fee should fail safe, not silently give away free shipping.
  3. Tag-based revalidation. When someone saves a setting in the admin screen, we call revalidateTag("settings"), so the change shows up without a deploy. 
"use server";
import { revalidateTag } from "next/cache";

export async function saveSetting(key: string, value: unknown) {
  await db.siteSettings.upsert({
    where: { key },
    update: { value },
    create: { key, value },
  });
  revalidateTag("settings");
}

Validate before you save

Once non-developers can edit values, someone will eventually type "ten" into a number field. We validate every setting with a schema before it is written, so the database only holds values the code can read. Also keep an audit trail of who changed what; it saves arguments later.

Keep the cart and the server in agreement

A subtle bug is showing one threshold in the cart and charging with another. The rule we follow: the server computes the delivery fee from the same loader, and the client only displays what the server returns. One source of truth, no duplicated constants in components.

What we like about it

  • Business changes happen without waiting for a release cycle.
  • Developers stop being a bottleneck for copy and price tweaks.
  • Code reviews focus on logic instead of numbers.
  • Fewer "hotfix, just change this value" deploys.

What to watch for

  • Settings sprawl. Group keys by area and delete the unused ones.
  • Cache lag. Decide how stale is acceptable, and revalidate on save.
  • Testing. Seed sensible defaults in local and test environments so tests do not depend on production data.

None of this is fancy, and that is the point. A boring settings table, a typed loader and a cache layer removed a whole category of small deploys for us. If you run a store and still have fees hardcoded somewhere, it is a pleasant refactor to start with.

How do you handle business configuration in your projects: database, a CMS, or feature-flag tooling? I would like to hear what has worked for you.

title: Why Your Agent's Memory Layer Will Fail at 3 AM: HNSW Contention and Semantic Retrieval Under Load
description:
Why Your Agent's Memory Layer Will Fail at 3 AM: HNSW Contention and Semantic Retrieval Under Load

At 3:17 AM, our agent platform started timing out. CPU looked fine. Disk I/O was quiet. The culprit was PostgreSQL's HNSW index: fifty concurrent sessions trying to insert new memories simultaneously, each waiting on index synchronization. Insert latency spiked from 80ms to 4 seconds. Retrieval requests queued behind writes. The agent loop stalled.

The second failure was silent. Some embedding providers returned normalized vectors; an internal codepath did not. We assumed cosine distance would behave consistently. It didn't. Recall dropped 30% because vector magnitude skewed similarity scores across sources.

Claude Code plugins offer a clean extension boundary for developer workflows. A plugin packages commands, skills, and hooks without forcing every team to maintain a separate orchestration layer. While evaluating anthropics/claude-plugins-official, I treat the plugin as the integration surface and keep semantic memory in an independent backend service. That separation matters. A plugin should collect interaction facts, request retrieval, and inject bounded context. It should not own database migrations, embedding workers, index maintenance, or tenant isolation. Those responsibilities belong to a memory service with an explicit API and operational lifecycle.

The real production problem is sustained write concurrency combined with unpredictable retrieval quality.

The Failure Mode: HNSW Writes and Unnormalized Vectors

Our first implementation inserted every new memory synchronously during an active agent session. Under burst traffic, PostgreSQL CPU remained available, but insert latency increased sharply. The HNSW index became the bottleneck: concurrent graph updates contended on index synchronization, and individual writes spent far longer maintaining the graph than writing the heap row.

The second problem was less visible. Mixing normalized and raw vectors with cosine distance broke recall. Vector magnitude affected similarity behavior differently across providers.

The fix was architectural:

  • Normalize vectors at the ingestion boundary.
  • Queue non-critical memory writes and batch them.
  • Keep retrieval synchronous, but make indexing asynchronous where the product allows it.
  • Use HNSW for read-heavy workloads, while accepting that high-rate ingestion requires capacity planning and controlled concurrency.

Here is a compact schema suitable for a tenant-aware memory service:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE agent_memory (
    id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    tenant_id       TEXT NOT NULL,
    agent_id        TEXT NOT NULL,
    content         TEXT NOT NULL,
    embedding       vector(1536) NOT NULL,
    memory_type     TEXT NOT NULL,
    source          TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    expires_at      TIMESTAMPTZ,
    metadata        JSONB NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb
);

CREATE INDEX agent_memory_scope_idx
    ON agent_memory (tenant_id, agent_id, created_at DESC);

CREATE INDEX agent_memory_embedding_hnsw
    ON agent_memory
    USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
    WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 128);

SELECT id, content, memory_type, metadata,
       1 - (embedding <=> $1::vector) AS similarity
FROM agent_memory
WHERE tenant_id = $2
  AND agent_id = $3
  AND (expires_at IS NULL OR expires_at > now())
  AND memory_type = ANY($4::text[])
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1::vector
LIMIT 12;

The dimensionality must match the selected embedding model. If the model changes dimensions, create a new column or table and backfill deliberately. Silently truncating or coercing vectors is not a migration strategy.

The HNSW parameters are starting points, not universal settings. Larger m and ef_construction generally improve recall at the cost of build time, memory, and write overhead. Query-time hnsw.ef_search can be increased for recall-sensitive requests:

SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search = 80;

For high-concurrency ingestion, avoid rebuilding or aggressively mutating the index while a large backfill is running. A common operating pattern is to load data into a staging table, normalize and validate it, then create or rebuild the index during a controlled maintenance window. For continuous traffic, a bounded worker pool is safer than allowing every plugin invocation to perform an index update simultaneously.

Hybrid Retrieval Is More Reliable Than Vector Search Alone

Semantic similarity misses exact identifiers, error codes, branch names, and API symbols. A production memory service should combine vector results with lexical or structured candidates. The following Python function performs reciprocal rank fusion without assuming that either retrieval strategy is universally better:

from collections import defaultdict
from typing import Hashable, Iterable

def reciprocal_rank_fusion(
    ranked_lists: Iterable[Iterable[Hashable]],
    *,
    k: int = 60,
    limit: int = 20,
) -> list[tuple[Hashable, float]]:
    """Fuse ranked result IDs using standard RRF scoring."""
    scores: dict[Hashable, float] = defaultdict(float)

    for results in ranked_lists:
        for rank, item_id in enumerate(results, start=1):
            scores[item_id] += 1.0 / (k + rank)

    return sorted(
        scores.items(),
        key=lambda pair: pair[1],
        reverse=True,
    )[:limit]

Pass the ordered IDs from pgvector and PostgreSQL full-text search as two lists. Fetch the final records by ID, then apply authorization and expiration checks again before returning them. Retrieval filters are correctness boundaries, not merely performance hints.

Plugin Integration and Operational Boundaries

A plugin command or hook should call a small memory client with an explicit contract:

  1. Extract a memory candidate from the current task.
  2. Normalize and enqueue it with tenant, agent, source, and expiration metadata.
  3. Embed the retrieval query using the same model family used for stored memories.
  4. Retrieve a small candidate set.
  5. Rerank or fuse results.
  6. Inject only the most relevant, non-sensitive context into the next model request.

The plugin repository should remain the distribution and discovery layer. The memory service should own secrets, database connections, migrations, retry policy, and observability. This keeps plugin installation reproducible and prevents a local command from becoming an accidental database administrator.

A representative deployment configuration:

memory_service:
  database_url: postgresql://memory_app@db.internal/agent_memory
  connection_pool:
    max_connections: 20
    min_idle: 5
    idle_timeout_ms: 30000
    connection_timeout_ms: 5000
  embedding:
    model: text-embedding-3-small
    dimensions: 1536
    normalize: true
    provider_timeout_ms: 3000
    circuit_breaker:
      failure_threshold: 5
      reset_timeout_ms: 60000
    retry:
      max_attempts: 3
      backoff_ms: [100, 500, 2000]
      retryable_codes: [429, 502, 503, 504]
  retrieval:
    hnsw_ef_search: 80
    vector_limit: 40
    final_limit: 12
    rrf_k: 60
    query_timeout_ms: 1500
  ingestion:
    queue: durable
    workers: 4
    batch_size: 64
    max_concurrent_inserts: 2
    flush_interval_ms: 500
  security:
    require_tenant_scope: true
    redact_secrets_before_embedding: true

When benchmarking model-provider fallback, the test topology can place an OpenAI-compatible client behind a relay endpoint at https://b-lost.com/v1. Keep that relay configuration isolated from database benchmarks so provider latency does not obscure HNSW contention or retrieval recall.

Connection pool exhaustion is a common failure mode. If every plugin invocation holds a connection during embedding API calls, a slow provider can starve the pool. Circuit breakers and timeouts prevent cascading failures. Missing retry logic for transient provider errors amplifies quota exhaustion. A 429 rate-limit response should trigger exponential backoff, not immediate failure.

Vector dimension mismatches are silent and catastrophic. If a model upgrade changes dimensions from 1536 to 3072, PostgreSQL will reject inserts, but only after the embedding call succeeds. Validate dimensions at ingestion and fail loudly.

The key trade-off is deliberate: asynchronous writes may delay the availability of a newly learned memory, while synchronous writes increase tail latency and index contention. For developer agents, durable correctness and predictable response time usually matter more than making every observation searchable within the same request.

But here's the hard question: when does eventual consistency become a correctness bug? If an agent writes a memory in session N, then immediately needs it in session N+1 before the queue flushes, the system appears to forget. How do you balance write concurrency with read-after-write consistency without sacrificing tail latency? I haven't found a universal answer. What's your approach?

title: Your Website Is Your Digital Storefront: How User Experience Can Shape Business Success
description:
Introduction

Imagine walking into a store where products are difficult to find, information is unclear, and nobody is available to answer your questions. Would you want to stay or make a purchase? Most people would probably look for another store.

The same situation can happen online. A website is often the first interaction a potential customer has with a business. If the website is confusing, slow, or difficult to navigate, visitors may leave before discovering what the business offers.

In today's competitive digital environment, creating a visually attractive website is not enough. Businesses also need to focus on user experience, accessibility, website performance, and clear communication. A well-designed digital experience can help businesses make stronger first impressions and build better relationships with their audiences.

What Is Website User Experience?

Website user experience, commonly known as UX, refers to how people feel and interact when visiting a website.

It includes everything from navigation and page loading speed to content organization, mobile responsiveness, and the overall ease of finding information.

A positive user experience allows visitors to understand a website without unnecessary effort. They should be able to explore services, read important information, and contact the business without confusion.

The goal is simple: make every website interaction convenient, useful, and meaningful.

6 Ways to Improve Your Website's User Experience

  1. Keep Website Navigation Simple

Visitors should not have to search endlessly to find basic information.

Organize your website with clear menus and logical categories. Important sections such as Home, About Us, Services, Blog, and Contact should be easy to locate.

Simple navigation helps visitors explore your website comfortably and understand what your business offers.

  1. Improve Website Loading Speed

Website speed plays an important role in user satisfaction.

When pages take too long to load, visitors may lose interest. Large image files, unnecessary website elements, and poorly optimized code can affect performance.

Businesses should regularly check website speed, optimize images, and work with reliable hosting solutions.

A faster website creates a smoother browsing experience across different devices.

  1. Make Your Website Mobile-Friendly

Many people access websites using smartphones and tablets. A website that looks good only on desktop computers can create difficulties for mobile visitors.

Responsive website design helps pages adjust to different screen sizes.

Text should remain readable, buttons should be easy to use, and important information should be accessible without excessive scrolling or zooming.

Mobile-friendly design helps businesses provide a consistent experience to a wider audience.

  1. Use Clear and Helpful Content

A professional website should explain its purpose clearly.

Visitors should quickly understand what a business does, which services it provides, and how those services may help them.

Use descriptive headings, short paragraphs, meaningful images, and straightforward language. Avoid unnecessary technical terms that may confuse readers.

Helpful content allows visitors to make informed decisions and understand the value of your business.

  1. Include Clear Calls to Action

A call to action (CTA) guides visitors towards the next step.

For example, buttons such as Contact Us, Explore Services, Request Information, and Get Started can help visitors understand what action they can take.

Place relevant calls to action where they naturally fit within the website.

A clear CTA can make it easier for interested visitors to connect with your business.

  1. Build Trust Through Professional Design

First impressions matter in the digital world.

Consistent branding, readable typography, professional images, accurate information, and clearly displayed contact details can make a website feel more reliable.

Businesses should also keep their information updated and ensure that important website links work correctly.

A trustworthy website gives visitors more confidence when exploring a brand.

Common Website Design Mistakes Businesses Should Avoid

Even a well-established business can lose valuable opportunities because of poor website design.

Some common mistakes include:

Overcrowding pages with too much information.

Using difficult-to-read fonts and colors.

Ignoring mobile responsiveness.

Adding too many unnecessary pop-ups.

Hiding important contact information.

Using outdated images or inaccurate content.

Forgetting to test website links and buttons.

Avoiding these issues can improve website usability and create a more professional online experience.

How Website Development and Digital Marketing Work Together

A website should not operate separately from a business's digital marketing strategy.

Search Engine Optimization helps relevant audiences discover website pages. Content marketing provides useful information to visitors. Social media marketing introduces people to the brand, while performance marketing can help businesses reach specific audiences through paid campaigns.

However, all these efforts become more effective when visitors arrive at a website that is easy to use and provides the information they need.

This is why website development and digital marketing should work together as part of a broader online growth strategy.

Conclusion: Turn Every Website Visit Into a Better Experience

Your website represents your business even when you are not available to communicate directly with customers.

A well-organized, mobile-friendly, fast, and informative website can create a positive impression and make it easier for visitors to explore your offerings.

Businesses that continuously improve their website experience can build a stronger digital foundation and create more meaningful interactions with their audiences.

Ready to Give Your Business a Stronger Digital Presence?

Your website deserves more than just an attractive design. It deserves a strategy that combines functionality, creativity, and effective digital marketing.

So, what are you waiting for? Take the next step towards improving your online presence. Connect with Scalexprt to explore digital marketing and website development opportunities that support your business goals.

Visit [https://scalexprt.com/] and discover new possibilities for your brand's digital journey.

title: When a Cricket Tour Teaches You About Viral Glycoproteins: A Developer's Walk Inside the Molecule
description:
When a Cricket Tour Teaches You About Viral Glycoproteins: A Developer's Walk Inside the Molecule

I landed in Chennai for a weekend cricket tour, the kind where the heat sticks to your skin and the chatter in the stands feels like a low‑latency stream. Between overs, a teammate — a bio‑informatics PhD — pulled out a laptop and showed me a 3‑D model of the SARS‑CoV‑2 spike protein rotating in WebGL. He pointed to the receptor‑binding domain, the glycan shield, the furin cleavage site — each a tiny decision point the virus makes before it can dock.

As a backend engineer, I think in data pipelines: ingest, transform, serve. The spike is no different. Its glycoproteins are a distributed system: each monomer a microservice, glycosylation a cache layer that hides epitopes from the immune “load balancer.” The furin site? A feature flag that, when flipped, unlocks membrane fusion. I spent the next hour mapping those biological concepts to the patterns I know — circuit breakers, retries, observability — and suddenly the paper’s supplementary tables read like API specs.

Back at the hotel, I opened a Jupyter notebook, fetched the PDB file, and wrote a quick script to compute solvent‑accessible surface area for each glycan. The numbers matched the paper’s claim: ~30 % of the RBD surface is masked. I added a tiny benchmark — parsing 10 k structures in under 2 seconds — just to prove the pipeline scales.

The tour ended, but the mental model stuck. Next time you see a viral protein, think of it as a service mesh you can instrument, profile, and eventually harden. If you’re curious about turning structural biology into code, give the notebook a spin — you might find the same rhythm between a cricket pitch and a protein fold.

title: Mobile-First CSS for a Single-Purpose Tool Page
description:
Most people find my video downloader on their phone. They tap a link in TikTok or Instagram, land on the page, paste a link, and want the file. If the page is awkward on a small screen, they leave.

So I build the mobile layout first, and the desktop layout second. It changed how I write CSS for the whole site.

Start with the smallest screen, not the desktop

The old way I used to work was to build the full desktop page, then add media queries to squeeze it down. That meant every fix was a patch on a layout that was never designed for a phone: buttons too small, the input too narrow, horizontal scroll from one element a few pixels too wide.

Now the base stylesheet is the mobile stylesheet. The body is a single column, full width, with generous padding. The input field and the download button are both full width and stacked, because on a phone that is the only arrangement that makes sense. Text reads without zooming, and tap targets are big enough for a thumb, not a mouse pointer.

Then I add one media query, usually at around 640 pixels, for wider screens. That query turns the single column into a centred container with a maximum width, and puts the input and the button side by side. One breakpoint, not five.

One job means one column

A tool page is not a blog and it is not a dashboard. It has one job: take a link, give a file back. So I resist the urge to add a sidebar, a feature grid, or a row of cards above the fold. On mobile, every one of those pushes the actual tool further down the page, and that is the difference between a visitor using it and a visitor leaving.

The layout order on mobile is deliberate: a short heading, the input and button, then the result area, then everything else — the how-it-works steps, the FAQ, the footer links. The visitor sees the tool first and the explanation second. On desktop the same order stays, just centred. I do not rearrange anything between screen sizes — rearranging is where layout bugs hide.

The bugs that only show up on a real phone

A few things I only caught by testing on an actual phone, not a resized desktop browser:

  • Horizontal scroll from one element. A long URL in a result line, or a wide button, can push the page wider than the screen. Setting overflow-wrap: anywhere on result text and max-width: 100% on buttons and images fixed it.
  • The keyboard covering the button. When the visitor taps the input, the phone keyboard slides up. If the download button sits below the fold, they have to dismiss the keyboard to reach it. Keeping input and button close together, near the top, avoids that.
  • Tap targets that look fine but feel wrong. A 32-pixel button looks fine in a screenshot. Under a thumb it is fiddly. I aim for at least 44 pixels of height on anything tappable.
  • Tables that overflow. A few small tables on my calculator pages used to clip on a phone. Wrapping them in a container with overflow-x: auto lets the table scroll inside its own box instead of breaking the page.

Keep the CSS small

The whole site ships no frameworks and no webfonts. The stylesheet for a tool page is one small file, written by hand. That is deliberate: on a phone over a slow connection, every kilobyte matters.

When something looks wrong on a phone, I can read the file and find the rule in seconds.

The rule I keep

If a change looks good on desktop but I have not checked it on a phone, it is not finished. The phone is where the visitors are, so the phone is where the page has to work.

I build my downloader, ramrom.io, this way — one column, one breakpoint, one small stylesheet — and it is the least stressful CSS I have ever written.

title: We Stopped Installing LLM SDKs in Every Microservice
description:
We almost put the OpenAI SDK inside the agent runtime.

It looked like the short path. The runtime already runs a turn: load the published agent, load the chat, maybe search knowledge, maybe load memory, call a model, save the assistant message. Installing @anthropic-ai/sdk or the OpenAI client right there would have made the first demo work in an afternoon.

We did not do that. This post is about why, what we built instead, and how that choice helps a multi-tenant agent platform when the traffic is no longer a laptop.

The audience I have in mind is a senior backend or platform engineer who has already shipped one LLM feature and is now asking where the keys, the retries, and the bill should live.

What we were building

QuickStart AI is a production-oriented platform. Organizations run workspaces. A workspace is the tenant. Every customer row is scoped by workspace_id.

Inside a workspace we already had the product pieces a chat agent needs:

  • Agents. Instructions and model settings. Publish is immutable. Rollback points at an older published version.
  • Conversations. Ordered messages in Postgres. Writes use an idempotency key so a client retry does not append the same turn twice.
  • Knowledge. Ingest plus retrieval. RAG goes through OpenSearch.
  • Memory. Facts about an end user, stored in Postgres.
  • Runtime. The service that executes one turn.

The public door is an API gateway on port 3000. It checks the JWT, checks workspace membership, and applies a Redis rate limit. It then proxies to internal services. A browser and a dashboard never call an LLM vendor or a scrape vendor themselves.

The stack around this is a Node.js and TypeScript monorepo, Postgres, Redis (Valkey in some environments), OpenSearch, and SQS-shaped queues (ElasticMQ locally). Internal services listen on their own ports.

The numbers we wrote down, so the resilience work had a target, are:

  • 10,000+ organizations, 50,000+ users, 100,000+ agents
  • About 10,000 HTTP requests per second sustained, and 20,000 at peak, on the gateway and API. That is not 10,000 LLM calls per second.
  • Millions of messages per day, and 10,000+ concurrent chats
  • Later, a separate voice service for about 5,000 concurrent inbound calls and 5,000 outbound calls. Voice is out of scope for this post.

Identity, workspace RBAC, the gateway, agents, conversations, a Redis membership cache, knowledge, memory, and the runtime turn path were already shipped. The open question was outbound: how every service talks to paid vendors without copying keys and failure policy into each deployable.

We wrote the decision down in ADR 0010 for the model gateway and ADR 0011 for web fetch.

What we needed the design to do

A turn is not only "call the model." Some paths also fetch a page or search the web, so knowledge ingest and future tools can acquire content. Those are different vendors, different bills, and different failure shapes. The requirement was the same for both:

  1. Vendor API keys live in as few deployables as possible.
  2. Timeout, retry, and "do not double-charge" rules are written once.
  3. A slow vendor cannot pin every replica until the process is useless.
  4. We can prove, later, which workspace spent tokens or pages.
  5. Product services keep a stable internal contract when we swap a provider.

If any one of those is missing, the platform still demos. It does not stay cheap or operable at the scale above.

Three ways to call a model

We treated this as a real fork, not a style preference. The same fork applies to paid web APIs.

Option A — install the vendor SDK in every service

Runtime imports the SDK. A tools service imports it. An eval worker imports it. Each process holds a key and picks its own timeout.

Problem Why it hurts at our scale
Secrets surface area The API key is in N deployables. Rotation and audit are N operations.
Duplicated policy Each service chooses its own timeout, retry count, and logs. Those choices drift.
Streaming and retry After SSE tokens are already on the wire, a blind retry can duplicate what the user sees, or charge twice.
Thundering herd Many replicas times many retries becomes vendor 429s and a runaway bill.
Compliance story It is hard to say "all model traffic is logged and capped in one place."

This option is fine for one script. It is a poor fit once more than one service can spend vendor money.

Option B — a shared npm package

A package such as @quickstart/llm-client puts the HTTP or SDK call in one module. Callers stay DRY. We still rejected it as the final shape.

Problem Why a package was not enough
Policy still runs in every process A global in-flight limit needs shared state, which for us means Redis. You end up rebuilding half a service inside a library.
Circuit state per replica If the package does not talk to Redis, each pod has its own breaker. Protection is uneven.
Deploy coupling A new retry rule or a new provider means redeploying every consumer.
Operational ownership On-call still asks which service version ran the bad retry loop.
Billing hooks One caller forgets to pass workspace_id or to log tokens. The ledger is already wrong.

A shared package fixes copy-paste. It does not give you one process that owns the vendor.

Option C — dedicated internal services

This is what we shipped.

  1. model-gateway, port 3005. Every chat completion and every stream to an LLM vendor goes here.
  2. web-fetch-service, port 3007. Scrape, search, and async crawl go here. Direct HTTP and Olostep sit behind it as providers.

Product services speak internal HTTP. They do not import vendor SDKs.

Criterion SDK in every service Shared npm package Dedicated model-gateway + web-fetch
Secret sprawl High Medium Low
Retry and stream policy stays the same Low Medium High
Global in-flight cap and budget Hard Hard unless every caller talks to Redis Redis inside the service
Deploy when vendor policy changes Many services Many services One service
Scale chat and LLM concurrency apart Coupled Coupled Decoupled
Test vendor failures Per service Package tests Fake adapters plus orchestrator tests

Why dedicated services fit this product

We picked option C for five reasons that map onto the platform we already had.

One place for credentials and policy. Timeouts, retries, circuits, caps, and usage logs sit next to the adapter that speaks to the vendor. Key rotation is one secret on one deployable.

A stable contract for product services. Runtime, future tools, and ingest workers call internal HTTP. Swapping a model vendor is PROVIDER_PROFILES_JSON on the gateway, not a runtime release.

Separate scale knobs. More runtime replicas means more concurrent chats. More model-gateway replicas means more LLM concurrency. More web-fetch replicas and workers means more page acquisition. Keys and policy stay in the two outbound services.

Cost checked where the unit is known. Web fetch denies a workspace that is over its daily unit budget in Redis, before the vendor call. Model usage is logged in one shape: tokens, latency, workspace_id. There is no billing ledger on the request path yet. The facts the ledger will need are already there.

Vendor keys stay off the public gateway. Staff and end users present a JWT to port 3000. model-gateway and web-fetch trust a separate internal bearer token. In production those ports sit on a private network, with Kubernetes network policy planned as roadmap item P8.

Knowledge and memory stay separate services. They have their own failure rules. This post is about the vendor outbound pattern: model calls and web acquisition. RAG and memory are neighbors, not the same control plane.

How a request moves

A user message hits the gateway. The gateway checks the JWT, checks that the person belongs to the workspace, and applies the public rate limit. It does not call OpenAI.

The runtime on port 3006 runs the turn. When it needs a model, it sends POST /internal/complete (or /internal/stream) to model-gateway with Authorization: Bearer <MODEL_GATEWAY_INTERNAL_TOKEN>. The body carries workspace_id, request_id, a model profile, and the messages. The token is an internal secret, at least 32 characters. It is not the end user's JWT.

model-gateway picks an adapter, runs policy, and only then calls OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, or another configured provider.

Web acquisition is the parallel path. Knowledge ingest and future tools call POST /internal/scrape, /internal/search, or /internal/crawl on web-fetch. That service calls direct HTTP or Olostep.

                    [ Browser / API client ]
                              |
                              v
                    +---------------------+
                    |  API Gateway :3000  |
                    |  JWT, membership,   |
                    |  Redis rate limit   |
                    +----------+----------+
                               |
         +---------------------+---------------------+
         |                     |                     |
         v                     v                     v
 +---------------+    +----------------+    +------------------+
 | runtime :3006 |    | knowledge :3009|    | memory :3010     |
 | (turn loop)   |    | (RAG API)      |    | (facts API)      |
 +-------+-------+    +----------------+    +------------------+
         |
         |  POST /internal/complete
         v
 +---------------------+
 | model-gateway :3005 |
 | adapters + policy   |
 +----------+----------+
            |
            v
     [ OpenAI / Anthropic / OpenRouter / ... ]

 knowledge ingest, tools --> POST /internal/scrape|search|crawl
         |
         v
 +---------------------+
 | web-fetch :3007     |
 | adapters + policy   |
 +----------+----------+
            |
            v
     [ direct HTTP / Olostep / ... ]

Public clients stop at port 3000. Product services do not hold vendor keys. Only model-gateway and web-fetch talk to paid APIs.

Inside model-gateway the split is simple, and it is the split we repeat in web-fetch:

Runtime  -->  Orchestrator (timeout, retry, breaker, cap, logs)
                    |
                    v
              Adapter (one vendor's HTTP or SSE shape)
                    |
                    v
                 Vendor

Adapters talk to vendors. Orchestrators talk to failure. That sentence is the whole design.

Model gateway: one door for models

model-gateway is the control plane for LLM calls. Runtime does not know whether the profile is OpenRouter or Anthropic.

The internal routes we use are:

  • POST /internal/complete for a full response
  • POST /internal/stream for SSE: token events, then done
  • POST /internal/decide for an optional routing decision

Auth on all of them is the internal bearer token.

Adapters implement a narrow interface, ChatProvider, with complete() and stream(). The drivers we have are fake (for CI), openai_compatible, openrouter, and anthropic. A registry, built by createProviderRegistry, maps a profile id from config to a driver instance. A profile is a named provider config, for example openrouter-prod. The driver is the implementation type.

Adapters throw ProviderError with retryable: true or false, and an optional HTTP status. They map the vendor's HTTP and SSE. They do not decide "retry three times." That split matters. The adapter knows that 429 and 400 are different. The orchestrator knows we only allow one retry, and that a stream which already sent tokens must not be retried.

The orchestrator (CompletionOrchestrator) wraps every call. Timeouts, the retry loop, the circuit breaker, the Redis in-flight cap, fallback, and model.usage logs live here.

What this gives the product:

  • We change vendor by config, without a runtime deploy.
  • A request may name fallback_model. If the primary profile fails and the stream has not started, we try that fallback once.
  • Every successful or attempted call can emit a structured model.usage log: tokens, latency, workspace_id. That is the input for a later billing feature (Feature 26). The ledger itself is not on this path.
  • Workspace bring-your-own-key is reserved for the secrets work (Feature 16). If a request says the credential source is the workspace, the gateway returns 400 today. We would rather fail closed than store customer keys halfway.

Web fetch: the same shape, a different bill

We did not put scrape inside model-gateway. The vendors differ. The billing unit differs: pages and search queries, not tokens. The policy differs: try cheap direct HTTP first, and use Olostep when we need JavaScript rendering or when direct fetch is not enough. Crawl is also asynchronous. It needs a Postgres job row and a worker. Those are bad reasons to share one orchestrator with chat completions.

web-fetch is the control plane for acquisition.

  • POST /internal/scrape is synchronous
  • POST /internal/search is synchronous, with a cap on max_results
  • POST /internal/crawl returns a job id (HTTP 202 style)
  • GET /internal/jobs/:jobId returns status

Auth is WEB_FETCH_INTERNAL_TOKEN. A legacy alias is still accepted.

The provider registry has direct_http, olostep, and fake. Before the orchestrator runs, decideAcquisitionProviders picks an ordered list of profile ids. For scrape, direct HTTP profiles come first, then Olostep. Search uses Olostep or the fake driver. render_js goes down the Olostep path.

AcquisitionOrchestrator then applies caps, the workspace budget, the breaker, the profile chain, and retries.

What this gives the product:

  • Knowledge ingest (Feature 11) and future tools call one service. We do not put the Olostep SDK in five places.
  • Each workspace has a daily unit budget in Redis. Over budget means 429, and the vendor is not called.
  • Usage facts record action, provider, units, and estimated_cost_micros.
  • Crawl inserts a row as queued. A worker claims it with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, so two replicas can poll without taking the same job.

URL ingest from the knowledge service into web-fetch is still a follow-up. The service exists. That wire is not the whole story yet. I say that again in the limitations, because it is easy to over-claim.

How the resilience works, and why we did not take the simpler version

Each pattern below is something we run inside these two services. I include the simpler idea we rejected, because that is the part that is easy to skip when you are only trying to make the call succeed.

Adapters plus a registry

Vendor code implements a small interface. Config names a profile. The registry returns the driver for that profile id.

New vendor means a new adapter file and a config row. Runtime does not fork. In CI, the fake driver can simulate a 429, a hang, a failure before any token, and a failure after tokens, with no network.

The SDK already speaks the vendor's shape. Our product speaks one shape: a completion body, or a scrape body. The adapter is the anti-corruption layer between those two shapes. If the adapter also owns retry policy, every new vendor copies a slightly different loop. We kept that loop out.

One orchestrator per domain

CompletionOrchestrator and AcquisitionOrchestrator wrap the outbound call. Callers stay thin. Runtime does not parse OpenRouter error bodies.

LLM streaming rules are not the same as a scrape profile chain, so we did not force one giant policy class. The primitives match. The policy does not.

Without this layer, if (retry) grows inside each adapter. Six months later, two providers retry differently and nobody remembers which one double-charged a stream. On-call for "the model vendor is down" is one service, one log shape, not a search across every consumer's version.

A deadline on every vendor call

Vendor TCP can hang. At 10,000 concurrent chats, one hung connection holds work in the Node process until the event loop lags and other chats stall.

model-gateway races the provider call against a timer (UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT, about 60 seconds for a non-streaming complete). Web fetch uses a per-action timeout around 30 seconds, as we wrote in ADR 0011. On the model path a timeout is retryable, inside the one-retry rule below. Vendor SDK defaults differ, and some are long enough to exhaust the process before they fire.

At most one extra attempt, and only when the error says so

model-gateway allows a maximum of two attempts when the error is retryable: ProviderError.retryable, a timeout, or an abort. Web fetch allows up to two attempts per profile, and only when the error is retryable and no billable unit has been recorded yet.

We do not retry until success. Each retry costs money and adds to turn latency. A 429 plus a retry storm turns a vendor rate limit into an outage we caused.

The retryable flag stays on the adapter, because HTTP meaning belongs next to the vendor. The attempt budget stays on the orchestrator, because "only once, and never after tokens" is a product rule.

If the stream already started, stop

This rule is model-gateway only, and it is the one I care about most.

For stream, if any token was already sent to the client, we do not retry and we do not switch to the fallback model. The attempt loop breaks.

A retry after partial SSE duplicates content. The user sees two answers stuck together, and the vendor may bill both attempts. Every caller that owns an SDK has to remember this rule. In model-gateway it exists once.

One fallback model, not a chain of five

If the primary profile fails policy and the stream has not started, we try fallback_model once. The point is degradation: a cheaper or more available model instead of a hard error to the user. The bound is deliberate. A chain of five models looks resilient and spends like an incident.

Web fetch is different on purpose. decideAcquisitionProviders returns an ordered list of profile ids, for example direct HTTP then Olostep. The orchestrator walks that list in executeScrape until one succeeds or the list is done. Direct fetch is cheap. Olostep is for JavaScript rendering or for when the cheap path failed. That is multi-provider routing for acquisition, not a primary and secondary model id. We did not pretend those are the same feature.

A circuit breaker for a sustained outage

Retry helps a blip. A breaker helps a vendor that is down for minutes.

We share a CircuitBreaker implementation. After N failures the state is open. New calls fail fast with CIRCUIT_OPEN instead of waiting on another timeout. After a cooldown the breaker goes half-open. A success closes it. Each orchestrator keeps a breaker per profile id.

When the vendor is down, a fast 503 means replicas are not stacked on timeouts, and the vendor is not hit by a synchronized retry from every pod.

That state is inside the process today, not in Redis. Two pods can disagree for a while. Per-replica breakers still help. They are not a cluster-wide view.

A fleet cap in Redis before the vendor call

A library-level semaphore counts in-flight calls inside one process. The moment we add a second replica, the vendor sees twice the concurrency. That is the opposite of a cap.

Before model-gateway or web-fetch calls a vendor, we increment a Redis key (model-gateway:inflight or web-fetch:inflight). If the count is over the max, we return 429 with RATE_LIMITED and we do not call the vendor. The increment is released when the call finishes.

This is a bulkhead. Model slowness cannot occupy unbounded work. It is also the start of stopping one tenant from filling every vendor connection. The global cap exists. Per-workspace dollar or concurrency caps on the model path do not. Those are later runtime and Redis work.

This is also why a shared package was not enough. A fleet cap has to live in one service plus Redis.

Budget where the unit is the bill

The public gateway already rate-limits HTTP with Redis. That protects the front door. It does not know what a scrape costs.

web-fetch keeps a per-workspace daily unit budget in Redis and rejects with 429 before the vendor call. Acquisition is billed per unit. We cannot depend on every future caller remembering to check. One workspace in a crawl loop should stop when the budget is gone, not when the invoice arrives.

Reject work that cannot succeed

Some requests are wrong before any vendor should see them. Examples: bring-your-own-key with credential_source: workspace while secrets are not shipped (400), a bad URL, a bad workspace id, a missing request_id.

The rule is simple. Do not pay a vendor for a request we already know will fail. Callers also get a clear 4xx instead of a 5xx that looks like an outage.

One error language

Vendors return a mess of bodies and status codes. We map that to platform codes: UPSTREAM_UNAVAILABLE, UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT, RATE_LIMITED, VALIDATION_FAILED, UNAUTHORIZED. Runtime and the gateway branch on those codes. Logs do not store raw vendor bodies. ADR 0010 is the failure-policy contract for the model path.

This is what lets product services stay ignorant of vendor semantics. They handle a small set of outcomes. They do not special-case one provider's JSON.

Usage logs now, ledger later

model.usage and the acquisition usage facts carry workspace_id, request_id, tokens or units, latency_ms, and the provider profile. Billing must not run inside the hot path of a chat turn. If the fields arrive only when the ledger exists, the months before that cannot be audited. One service keeps the field names the same.

Long work does not hold the HTTP request

Crawl returns a job id and finishes in a worker. Knowledge ingest uses a queue and a worker in its own service. Same idea, different process: the request thread must not wait for N pages or for embeddings. Clients disconnect. Timeouts fire. The door stays blocked.

Workers scale by claiming jobs. For crawl, SKIP LOCKED is what makes two replicas safe. For knowledge, more consumers read the SQS-shaped queue. model-gateway's philosophy is "do not block the door with an unbounded vendor wait." Crawl applies that to a job that is long by nature.

Idempotency sits on the turn

model-gateway is not the idempotency store for chat. Conversations already take an idempotency key on messages and turns. A client retry must not double-append and must not double-call the model for the same turn key.

I mention it because vendor retry policy cannot fix a duplicate turn that our own API accepted twice. Resilience is end to end. The vendor layer is one cut. The conversation write is another. We documented them as related, not as the same mechanism.

How internal calls stay different from public calls

We did not want "internal" to mean "no identity, just a private port." The boundary is explicit.

Concern Public path Internal path
Identity JWT sub becomes the staff actorId Service bearer token
Tenant workspace_id in the URL, plus a membership check workspace_id on the body or route, from a trusted caller
Exposure Internet, through the gateway Private network, or localhost ports in development
Stability Versioned public API Can change with the contracts package

Runtime's ModelGatewayClient posts to {MODEL_GATEWAY_URL}/internal/complete with the internal token and a JSON body from @quickstart/contracts.

We chose internal HTTP, not "only gRPC" and not a shared SDK, for three practical reasons. A network hop is something we can later lock with Kubernetes network policy. Another language can call the same contract without importing our TypeScript package. And a hop forces a timeout and an error envelope at the boundary. An in-process function call makes it too easy to forget both.

The public gateway still does not replace per-service checks. Membership and permissions are enforced again downstream. A valid JWT at port 3000 is not a blank permission inside every service.

How the pieces scale

Component What we add Shared state
API gateway More replicas Redis rate limit
Runtime More replicas None in the process. Conversations live in Postgres
model-gateway More replicas Redis in-flight cap. Breakers are per pod
web-fetch More replicas and more workers Redis budget and in-flight cap. Crawl jobs in Postgres
Knowledge worker More consumers SQS-shaped queue

Chat capacity and LLM concurrency are separate dials. Adding runtime pods does not, by itself, multiply vendor connections, because the cap lives in Redis behind model-gateway. Adding model-gateway pods does not copy the API key into the runtime.

Breakers are the exception. They are per pod until we share that state. Doubling model-gateway replicas does not double the in-flight cap. During an outage, each pod can still let a few calls through until its own breaker opens.

Cost, keys, and the on-call page

Cost. One extra model attempt, and none after the stream starts, is the spend limit on retries. Web fetch spends the cheap direct fetch first and stops the workspace at the Redis budget. Token and unit logs are what we will use for chargeback. They are not the invoice.

Keys and compliance. Vendor credentials are deploy secrets on model-gateway and web-fetch only. Service-to-service calls use internal tokens. Staff JWTs stay on public routes. Internal ports are meant to sit on a private network in production.

Operations. Fake providers let CI exercise 429s, hangs, and partial streams without a vendor account. web-fetch has circuit tests in its suite. When OpenRouter is down, there is one service to open, not a list of every repo that imported a client.

What we would do next

Three items are already implied by the limits above. They are not shipped.

  • Put circuit state in a shared store so every pod agrees that a profile is open.
  • Add per-workspace caps on LLM calls. Today the model path only has a global in-flight cap.
  • Store workspace keys through the secrets work, then let model-gateway use them. Until that exists, those requests stay a 400.

What we still don't do

I want this list in the post so the architecture diagram is not read as a finished platform.

  • Circuit breaker state is per process, not cluster-wide.
  • model-gateway does not enforce per-workspace dollar caps. It enforces a global in-flight cap. Per-tenant caps are planned elsewhere.
  • There is no billing ledger on the request path. We write usage logs only.
  • Knowledge embeddings use a lighter pattern. They do not go through the full provider registry and orchestrator described here.
  • Knowledge calling web-fetch for URL ingest is a roadmap follow-up.
  • The public gateway does not replace per-service RBAC. Membership and permissions are still enforced downstream.

Memory reads can degrade when memory is down. A knowledge-base turn can fail when retrieval was required and RAG is not healthy. Those are different features with different failure choices. They are not the outbound policy in this post. I include them only so "resilience" is not mistaken for "every dependency fails open."

Closing

The hard part was not the first successful LLM call. It was keeping keys, retries, streams, and spend in one place while chat traffic and vendor traffic grow on different curves.

An SDK in every service spreads the key and the mistakes. A shared package shares the code and still leaves policy inside every process. model-gateway and web-fetch are where vendor credentials and vendor failure live.

Adapters translate one vendor. Orchestrators decide what failure is allowed to cost. The rest of the platform calls a contract.

title: Building Custom Royalty & Compliance Rules with Solana Token-2022 Transfer Hooks in Anchor 0.30+
description:
Solana's original SPL Token standard powered billions of dollars in volume, but enforcing custom transfer logic—such as mandatory royalties, compliance checks, or transfer fees—required fragile off-chain wrappers or non-standard contract bridges.

With Token-2022 (SPL Token Extensions), transfer hooks are executed natively by the token program itself on every single transfer, regardless of which AMM, marketplace, or wallet initiates it.

In this walkthrough, we’ll build a production-grade Anchor 0.30+ program implementing the SPL Transfer Hook Interface.

🏗️ How Transfer Hooks Work

Unlike Ethereum where transfer logic is bundled inside the ERC-20 contract, Solana separates data accounts from execution programs:

sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor Alice as Sender (Alice)
    participant TokenProg as Token-2022 Program
    participant HookProg as Your Anchor Transfer Hook
    participant ExtraMeta as ExtraAccountMetas PDA

    Alice->>TokenProg: TransferChecked(amount)
    TokenProg->>ExtraMeta: Read required validation accounts
    TokenProg->>HookProg: CPI: execute(source, mint, dest, amount)
    HookProg->>HookProg: Validate constraints & protocol state
    HookProg-->>TokenProg: Success / Error (e.g. AccountBlacklisted)
    TokenProg-->>Alice: Transfer Completed

Every time tokens move:

  1. Token-2022 reads the extra-account-metas PDA configured on the mint.
  2. It executes a Cross-Program Invocation (CPI) into your program's execute instruction handler.
  3. If your hook errors (e.g., recipient is blocked, or dynamic fee isn't satisfied), the entire transaction atomically rolls back.

🛠️ Step 1: The Anchor Instruction Layout

In Anchor 0.30+, the transfer hook execution instruction must conform to the spl-transfer-hook-interface:

use anchor_lang::prelude::*;
use anchor_spl::token_interface::{Mint, TokenAccount};

#[derive(Accounts)]
#[instruction(amount: u64)]
pub struct ExecuteTransferHook<'info> {
    #[account(token::mint = mint)]
    pub source: InterfaceAccount<'info, TokenAccount>,

    pub mint: InterfaceAccount<'info, Mint>,

    #[account(token::mint = mint)]
    pub destination: InterfaceAccount<'info, TokenAccount>,

    /// CHECK: Authority of the transfer
    pub owner_delegate: UncheckedAccount<'info>,

    /// CHECK: Extra Account Metas PDA for resolution
    #[account(
        seeds = [b"extra-account-metas", mint.key().as_ref()],
        bump
    )]
    pub extra_account_metas: UncheckedAccount<'info>,

    #[account(
        seeds = [b"protocol-config", mint.key().as_ref()],
        bump = config.bump
    )]
    pub config: Account<'info, ProtocolConfig>,
}

🔒 Step 2: Enforcing Custom Business Logic

Inside the handler, you can evaluate custom rules. Here, we enforce minimum transfer amounts and ensure the protocol hook is currently active:

pub fn handler(ctx: Context<ExecuteTransferHook>, amount: u64) -> Result<()> {
    require!(amount > 0, TokenSuiteError::AmountTooLow);

    let config = &ctx.accounts.config;

    if !config.is_hook_active {
        return Ok(());
    }

    msg!(
        "Enforcing Transfer Hook on Mint {}: Transferring {} from {} to {}",
        config.mint,
        amount,
        ctx.accounts.source.key(),
        ctx.accounts.destination.key()
    );

    Ok(())
}

⚡ Step 3: Fast Testing with In-Memory Banks

Traditional solana-test-validator setups take 30–60 seconds just to spin up. In our production starter, we use deterministic PDA checks and solana-bankrun to test instruction failure paths in under 200 milliseconds.

describe("token-suite tests", () => {
  it("Derives deterministic PDAs correctly", () => {
    const [configPda, bump] = getProtocolConfigPda(mintKeypair.publicKey);
    expect(configPda).to.be.instanceOf(PublicKey);
    expect(bump).to.be.a("number");
  });
});

📦 Full Production Boilerplate

The complete open-source code—including the TypeScript client SDK with priority fee estimation, React hooks, and GitHub Actions CI—is published on GitHub:

👉 GitHub Repository: sidsri14/solana-anchor-token2022-starter

If you're building a commercial dApp, you can also grab the Pro License directly via Polar.sh.

title: Harness or Runtime? I Ran the Same AI Agent Both Ways
description:
I ran the same AI agent two ways on AWS, once as a Harness and once as my own code on Runtime. Both gave the right answer, and the times were close: 1.8 seconds and 2.2 seconds. The real difference is who owns the loop.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore gives you two ways to run an agent, and they look like two different products. I built one small agent and ran it both ways to see what actually changes. I would start with a Harness, and move to Runtime when the config file cannot express what I need.

With a Harness, you describe the agent in a config file. AWS runs the loop where the model reads a question, calls a tool and answers. With Runtime, you write that loop as code, and AWS hosts it.

One agent, one Gateway, one model

The agent is a CloudOps assistant in my personal AWS lab. You ask whether production is healthy. It calls one tool, a Lambda function behind an AgentCore Gateway, and answers from the result. If the data is missing or older than 10 minutes, it says the health is unknown and says why.

Both versions use the same Gateway, the same Lambda and the same model, Amazon Nova Micro. Only the owner of the loop changes. The Lambda returns synthetic data, so this is a lab, not production monitoring.

What I wrote for each

Harness Runtime
Who owns the loop AWS Me
What I wrote A config file and a system prompt Python with Strands, plus the same prompt
What I deployed The config A code package
Tools from the Gateway Yes Yes
Choice of framework No Yes

The Harness took less work. For Runtime I wrote code, packaged it and deployed it. The AgentCore CLI then connected the agent to the Gateway and gave its role permission to call it.

The traces looked almost the same

I asked both agents the same question and read the traces. The Harness took 1.8 seconds and the Runtime agent 2.2 seconds, with 11 spans each. The Harness trace is the one from my earlier post on tracing one question. I ran each once, so read these as a rough picture, not a benchmark.

The detail I liked more is the name. Both traces show invoke_agent Strands Agents. The AWS docs say the Harness loop is powered by Strands Agents, so the engine is the same. What Runtime gives you is control over how it is used.

## One bug only my own code gave me

My first Runtime deploy failed. The generated client added a prefix to the Gateway tool name, and the final name was 65 characters. Bedrock allows 64. The failed run shows up in the trace list as an error.

I shortened the prefix to ops and deployed again. The second run worked, and the tool span now reads ops_DeploymentStatusTarget. The Harness never had this problem, because AWS builds the tool names for you. With your own code, small details like this become your job.

When I would move to Runtime

The AWS feature comparison between the two options is pretty clear. There are three things you can only do with Runtime: choose your own agent framework, build graph or workflow style patterns, and use bidirectional streaming. I would consider moving to Runtime if you need any of these.

Custom tools alone are not a reason to switch. A Harness already supports Gateway tools, remote MCP servers, and client side tools. The docs also cover exporting to code, so starting with a Harness does not mean you are locked into it.

title: LISTEN/NOTIFY performance in PostgreSQL
description:
I'm building Corfedo Work, a .NET library for background jobs that keeps its state in the application's own PostgreSQL database. Its workers need to know when something changed: a job became due, or a job somebody is waiting for has ended. The PostgreSQL answer is NOTIFY in the transaction that made the change. I designed the library's signals around it.

Then I measured it. Single-row transactions with a NOTIFY committed about 3,900 times per second with 8 clients, and about 3,900 with 64. Without the NOTIFY, the same transactions reached 16,700 and 56,700.

Signals that ride the transaction

A signal in Work says "something you wait for may have changed, read again". It's a topic and a key, with no data. The application sends it in the same transaction as the change:

static readonly SignalTopic Pending = new("orders.pending");

await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync(ct);
db.Orders.Add(order);
await db.SaveChangesAsync(ct);
await signals.SendAsync(db.Database.WorkTransaction(), Pending, order.TenantId, ct);
await tx.CommitAsync(ct);

The worker on the other side treats a signal as a reason to look, never as the change itself:

// Subscribed with signals.Subscribe(Pending, worker).
sealed class OrderWorker : ISignalSubscriber
{
    // A tenant's orders may be pending: read again.
    public void Received(string key) => Wake();

    // After every (re)connection signals may have been missed: read everything.
    public void Resync() => Wake();
}

Its loop reads the pending orders, then sleeps until the next wake or a 30-second fallback poll, whichever comes first.

What made NOTIFY attractive is when the message goes out. PostgreSQL delivers it after the transaction commits, and never if the transaction rolls back. A worker woken by it reads the committed row, not an older version, and nobody wakes for a change that was undone. I didn't have to write any of that.

I wasn't the first to hit the ceiling. Recall.ai traced three outages in four days in March 2025 to a NOTIFY on a busy write path and moved the logic out of the database. In July 2026, DBOS published the opposite headline, "Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY can actually scale": their stream writes went from 2,900 to 60,000 per second once they buffered notifications and sent them in batches. Recall.ai's post now says a PostgreSQL commit removed the bottleneck. DBOS says the same change, which ships in PostgreSQL 19, doesn't. Before choosing a side for a job library I wanted to see where the limit comes from.

The ceiling

Setup: Ryzen 7 7700X with an NVMe drive, PostgreSQL 18.6 and 19 RC1 in Docker with fsync on, a .NET 10 client on the same machine. Each transaction inserts one row; two sessions listen. Wake-up is the time from a commit to the first listener receiving its message. Medians of three 8-second runs.


Single-row transactions, two listening sessions. PostgreSQL 18.6; 19 RC1 is within 3% at every point.

Clients No NOTIFY NOTIFY in the transaction Median wake-up
1 2,711 2,456 0.37 ms
8 16,663 3,960 2.0 ms
32 42,179 3,923 8.0 ms
64 56,700 3,925 16.1 ms

The flat line is the finding. More clients don't add commits; they add waiting, which is why the wake-up time grows from 2 ms to 16 ms. The notifications arrive later because the transactions sending them queue up.

What PostgreSQL does at commit

Notifications go into one queue shared by every database in the cluster, in commit order. To keep that order, a transaction that has notifications takes a lock before it commits. It shows up in the logs as AccessExclusiveLock on object 0 of class 1262 of database 0, the line Recall.ai found. The transaction holds it until it ends, which is after its commit record has been flushed to disk. So two notifying transactions never commit at the same time.

That alone would be a queue. What makes it expensive is group commit. Normally, sessions that commit at the same moment share one WAL flush: in my runs one flush covered 4 commits at 8 clients and 19 at 64. With NOTIFY it covered exactly one, at any client count.


Schematic, not to scale.

The database statistics at 64 clients:

No NOTIFY NOTIFY in the transaction
Commits per second 56,700 3,925
Database CPU 4.35 cores 0.73 cores
Commits per WAL flush 19.1 1.0
Most common wait of active sessions LWLock:WALWrite 72% Lock:object 98%

At the ceiling the database is nearly idle. Almost every active session waits on that one lock, and a faster CPU wouldn't move the number. My reading is that the ceiling follows how long one WAL flush takes: here about 3,550 flushes per second for 3,925 commits. I haven't run it on another disk.

Listeners pay too. Each notification wakes every listening session, and each one runs a short transaction to read the queue. At 8 clients the database ran 10,900 transactions per second to commit 3,960 of mine.

PostgreSQL 19

The commit Recall.ai links, 282b1cd, adds a shared map of which session listens on which channel. A session that doesn't listen on the notified channel is no longer woken. Its message says nothing about the commit lock.


Median of three runs, 64 clients, two listening sessions on one channel.

On one channel with two listeners, 19 RC1 matches 18.6 within 3% in every mode: 3,912 commits per second with NOTIFY in the transaction at 64 clients, Lock:object at 98% of waits, one commit per WAL flush.

That isn't the case the patch is for, so I ran the one it is for: 50 listening sessions, each on its own channel, and every transaction notifying one of them. At 64 clients:

18.6 19 RC1
Commits per second 3,963–3,982 3,975–3,987
Database transactions per second 183,246 7,265
Database CPU 2.68 cores 0.75 cores
Active sessions waiting on Lock:object 97% 98%

On 18.6, all 50 listeners woke for every notification and read the queue, although 49 of them had nothing to read. On 19 they stay asleep, and the database does a 25th of the work. The commit rate doesn't move.

PostgreSQL 19 removes a real cost, the one that grows with the number of listening sessions. The waits in Recall.ai's logs were on the commit lock, though, and in my runs that lock behaves the same in 19 RC1 as in 18.6. If your notifying transactions queue on commit today, 19 won't let more of them commit per second.

Sending after commit

If the lock is taken by transactions that notify, the fix is to have fewer of them. DBOS buffers notifications in memory and sends them in batches, so only the batch takes the lock. I did the same, except that Work, as a library, doesn't own the transaction. The application begins it, maybe through Entity Framework, and commits it whenever it likes. There's no commit callback I can rely on.

What a library can get is the transaction's ID. The sending statement returns it, at no extra round trip:

INSERT INTO job_ends (job_id) VALUES ($1) RETURNING pg_current_xact_id();

The process keeps the ID and the message in memory. One background sender per process then asks PostgreSQL which of those transactions committed and notifies only those, in one statement:

WITH batch AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT xid, message, pg_xact_status(xid) AS status
    FROM unnest($1::xid8[], $2::text[]) AS b (xid, message)
), sent AS MATERIALIZED (
    SELECT count(pg_notify('work', message)) AS n
    FROM (SELECT DISTINCT message FROM batch WHERE status = 'committed') d
)
SELECT array(SELECT xid FROM batch WHERE status = 'in progress'),
       array(SELECT message FROM batch WHERE status = 'in progress')
FROM sent;

Committed transactions get their messages sent, duplicates collapse into one, rolled-back ones are dropped, and the ones still running come back to be checked again later.

The first version had a bug that cost me about 30 signals per run. It read the statuses in two statements: one sent the committed messages, the next returned the ones still running. A transaction that committed between those two statements was in neither list, and its message was gone. Reading each status once per batch, in one materialized CTE, fixed it.

The other setting is how often to send. A sender that flushes whenever anything is waiting turns into a notifying transaction itself, up to 2,900 times a second here, and queues for the same lock. A minimum gap between batches trades a little wake-up time for throughput:

Clients Flush when anything waits At least 2 ms apart At least 5 ms apart
1 2,645 · 1.2 ms 2,699 · 2.1 ms 2,667 · 3.6 ms
8 16,280 · 0.6 ms 16,763 · 1.9 ms 16,791 · 2.9 ms
32 37,566 · 0.9 ms 39,279 · 2.3 ms 39,521 · 4.2 ms
64 47,144 · 1.4 ms 49,800 · 2.7 ms 50,194 · 4.5 ms

Commits per second · median wake-up, PostgreSQL 18.6.

The difference is smaller than I expected, 3–5%. I kept 2 ms. With it, 64 clients commit about 50,000 times per second, 88% of the rate without notifications, and the median wake-up is 2.7 ms instead of 16.

This is how Work sends signals now, in place of NOTIFY in the transaction. Through the library's API, 64 clients that each insert a row and send a signal went from 3,972 to 40,204 commits per second. Batching costs 2–4% of that against the same statement without a signal; the bigger cost is the statement itself, since an application's send is a round trip of its own. Work's internal statements return the transaction ID with the rows they change and skip it.

What it costs

  • A process that crashes after the commit and before the batch loses those signals. Readers need the fallback poll. Work already had one; with batching it stops being optional.
  • A transaction ID can't tell a rollback to a savepoint apart. A message recorded after a savepoint that was later rolled back still goes out if the transaction commits. The reader wakes, finds nothing and goes back to waiting. I changed Work's signal contract to allow this.
  • Wake-ups are later at low load. With one client, NOTIFY in the transaction woke the listener in 0.37 ms and the batch in 2.1 ms, at the same throughput.
  • A transaction that sends gets a transaction ID even if it wrote nothing else.
  • There's a background sender per process to write, test and shut down cleanly.

When I'd keep NOTIFY in the transaction

If the application commits a few hundred notifying transactions per second, far below the ceiling, I'd keep it. It's less code, it wakes faster, and the transaction guarantees are exact. The ceiling I measured is per cluster, though, not per application: every notifying transaction on the server shares it.

Whatever the approach, notify only on changes somebody waits for. Work signals a job's end only when a caller is waiting for that job; signalling every row change would put every commit in the queue for the lock.

To see whether you're already there, look at the waits:

SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE wait_event_type = 'Lock' AND wait_event = 'object' AND state = 'active';

A steady count during write bursts, together with low CPU, is the signature I saw in every run with NOTIFY in the transaction.

I haven't run this on a cloud volume, where a WAL flush takes longer than on a local NVMe drive. If the ceiling follows flush time, as the numbers here suggest, it would sit lower there.

The other run I want is one without NOTIFY at all. A transactional message written with pg_logical_emit_message reaches a logical decoding consumer only if its transaction commits. It should also vanish with a rolled-back savepoint, the guarantee batching gave up, but I haven't tested that yet. Nor whether one consumer keeps up with 50,000 commits a second.

title: "Technical SEO Checklist for Next.js Business Websites"
description:
description: "A practical technical SEO checklist for Next.js: metadata, sitemap, robots, structured data, Core Web Vitals and local SEO, with code examples."
tags: nextjs, seo, webdev, javascript
cover_image:

canonical_url:

Building a fast website is only half the job. If search engines can't crawl, understand and rank it, your client's business stays invisible. This is the technical SEO checklist I use for Next.js business websites, with code you can copy.

1. Unique Metadata for Every Page

Every page needs its own title and description. In the Next.js App Router, use the Metadata API:

// app/web-development/page.js
export const metadata = {
  title: "\"Website Development Services in Bhopal | Your Brand\","
  description: ""
    "Custom, responsive and SEO-friendly websites for businesses in Bhopal and across India.",
  alternates: { canonical: "https://www.example.com/web-development" },
  openGraph: {
    title: "\"Website Development Services\","
    description: "\"Custom, fast and SEO-friendly websites.\","
    url: "https://www.example.com/web-development",
    type: "website",
  },
};

Keep titles under about 60 characters and descriptions under about 160. Always set a canonical URL to avoid duplicate content issues.

2. Generate a Sitemap and robots.txt 

// app/sitemap.js
export default function sitemap() {
  const base = "https://www.example.com";
  return ["", "/about", "/services", "/portfolio", "/contact"].map((path) => ({
    url: `${base}${path}`,
    lastModified: new Date(),
  }));
}

// app/robots.js
export default function robots() {
  return {
    rules: { userAgent: "*", allow: "/", disallow: ["/login", "/admin"] },
    sitemap: "https://www.example.com/sitemap.xml",
  };
}

Submit the sitemap in Google Search Console and check the Coverage report regularly.

3. Add Structured Data (JSON-LD)

Structured data helps search engines understand your business. For local businesses, LocalBusiness schema is a good start:

export default function LocalBusinessSchema() {
  const schema = {
    "@context": "https://schema.org",
    "@type": "LocalBusiness",
    name: "Your Business Name",
    url: "https://www.example.com",
    telephone: "+91-XXXXXXXXXX",
    address: {
      "@type": "PostalAddress",
      streetAddress: "Your street address",
      addressLocality: "Bhopal",
      addressRegion: "Madhya Pradesh",
      postalCode: "462011",
      addressCountry: "IN",
    },
  };

  return (
    <script
      type="application/ld+json"
      dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(schema) }}
    />
  );
}

Validate it with Google's Rich Results Test.

4. Optimize Images with next/image

Images are often the biggest cause of slow pages.

import Image from "next/image";

<Image
  src="/hero.webp"
  alt="Team working on a website project"
  width={1200}
  height={630}
  priority
/>
  • Use descriptive alt text (it helps accessibility and image search)
  • Set priority only for above-the-fold images
  • Prefer WebP or AVIF formats

5. Core Web Vitals

Google uses real-user performance data as a ranking signal. Focus on:

Metric What it measures Good target
LCP Loading speed of main content under 2.5s
INP Responsiveness to interaction under 200ms
CLS Visual stability under 0.1

Quick wins: lazy-load below-the-fold content, use next/font to avoid layout shifts, remove unused JavaScript, and use dynamic imports for heavy components.

6. Use Server Rendering Where It Matters

Content that must be indexed (service pages, blog posts, landing pages) should be rendered on the server or statically generated, not loaded only after client-side JavaScript runs. Use Server Components, SSG or ISR for these pages.

7. Clean URLs and Internal Linking

  • Use readable URLs: /web-development, not /page?id=42
  • Link related pages to each other with descriptive anchor text
  • Keep important pages within three clicks of the homepage
  • Set up proper 301 redirects when URLs change

8. Local SEO Basics

For businesses serving a specific city:

  • Create and verify a Google Business Profile
  • Keep Name, Address and Phone (NAP) consistent everywhere
  • Add city-specific content naturally, without keyword stuffing
  • Encourage genuine customer reviews

Final Checklist

  • [ ] Unique title and meta description on every page
  • [ ] Canonical URLs set
  • [ ] Sitemap and robots.txt live
  • [ ] Structured data validated
  • [ ] Images optimized with alt text
  • [ ] Core Web Vitals in the green
  • [ ] Key pages server-rendered
  • [ ] Mobile-friendly and HTTPS enabled
  • [ ] Google Search Console connected

Wrapping Up

Technical SEO isn't a one-time task. Audit regularly, measure with Search Console and Lighthouse, and improve step by step.
