const NATURES = ['natif', 'declare'];
const CARDINALITY = /^[01n],[01n]$/;

/** POST /ajax/sdm/links — déclare un lien entre deux entités. */
/**
 * Le cycle qu'ajouterait le lien natif source → cible, ou null (TH.13). Un
 * lien natif impose d'importer la cible avant la source : un cycle rend
 * l'ordre impossible. Le lien d'une entité vers elle-même (hiérarchie
 * interne) n'en est pas un.
 */
function nativeCycle(links, source, target) {
  if (source === target) return null;
  const following = new Map();
  for (const l of links) {
    if (l.SDM_LN_SourceEntity === l.SDM_LN_TargetEntity) continue;
    if (!following.has(l.SDM_LN_SourceEntity)) following.set(l.SDM_LN_SourceEntity, []);
    following.get(l.SDM_LN_SourceEntity).push(l.SDM_LN_TargetEntity);
  }
  // Un chemin cible → … → source ferme la boucle.
  const stack = [[target, [source, target]]];
  const seen = new Set();
  while (stack.length) {
    const [node, filePath] = stack.pop();
    if (node === source) return filePath;
    if (seen.has(node)) continue;
    seen.add(node);
    for (const s of following.get(node) || []) stack.push([s, [...filePath, s]]);
  }
  return null;
}

const createLink = reply(async (req) => {
  const { source, attribute, target, targetAttribute, nature, cardinality } = req.body || {};
  if (!NATURES.includes(nature)) throw error(`nature : ${NATURES.join(' ou ')}`);
  if (cardinality && !CARDINALITY.test(cardinality)) throw error('cardinalité : de la forme 1,n');
  const registry = await S.loadRegistry();
  for (const code of [source, target]) if (!registry.entities.has(code)) throw error(`entité inconnue : ${code}`);
  let name = null;
  if (nature === 'natif' && attribute) {
    const declared = registry.entities.get(source).attributes.get(attribute);
    if (!declared) throw error(`${source} ne déclare pas l'attribut ${attribute}`);
    name = declared.Nom;
    G.linkTableName({ SDM_LN_SourceEntity: source, SDM_LN_SourceAttribute: name });   // valide le nom de table
  }
  if (nature === 'declare' && attribute) throw error('un lien non natif n\'a pas d\'attribut : il n\'est dans aucun fichier');
  // L'attribut cible, dont la source reprend les valeurs (le « champ cible » de Standards) : pour les deux natures.
  let targetName = null;
  if (targetAttribute) {
    const declared = registry.entities.get(target).attributes.get(targetAttribute);
    if (!declared) throw error(`${target} ne déclare pas l'attribut ${targetAttribute}`);
    targetName = declared.Nom;
  }
  const existing = await S.listLinks();
  const duplicate = existing.find((l) => l.SDM_LN_SourceEntity === source && l.SDM_LN_TargetEntity === target
    && (l.SDM_LN_SourceAttribute || null) === name && (l.SDM_LN_TargetAttribute || null) === targetName
    && l.SDM_LN_Nature === nature);
  if (duplicate) throw error('ce lien est déjà déclaré');
  if (nature === 'natif') {
    const cycle = nativeCycle(existing.filter((l) => l.SDM_LN_Active && l.SDM_LN_Nature === 'natif'), source, target);
    if (cycle) throw error(`cycle de liens natifs : ${cycle.join(' → ')} — aucun ordre d'import possible`);
  }
  const id = await S.createLink({ source, attribute: name, target, targetAttribute: targetName, nature, cardinality });
  return { id };
});

/**
 * Le cycle que fermerait la réactivation du lien `id`, ou null. Réactiver un
 * lien natif revient à le déclarer de nouveau : même contrôle (TH.13).
 */
function reactivationCycle(links, id) {
  const link = links.find((l) => String(l.SDM_LN_Id) === String(id));
  if (!link || link.SDM_LN_Active || link.SDM_LN_Nature !== 'natif') return null;
  const native = links.filter((l) => l.SDM_LN_Active && l.SDM_LN_Nature === 'natif');
  return nativeCycle(native, link.SDM_LN_SourceEntity, link.SDM_LN_TargetEntity);
}

/** PUT /ajax/sdm/links/:id — active ou désactive un lien. */
const updateLink = reply(async (req) => {
  if (typeof req.body?.active !== 'boolean') throw error('actif : vrai ou faux');
  if (req.body.active) {
    const cycle = reactivationCycle(await S.listLinks(), req.params.id);
    if (cycle) throw error(`cycle de liens natifs : ${cycle.join(' → ')} — aucun ordre d'import possible`);
  }
  const n = await S.enableLink(req.params.id, req.body.active);
  if (!n) throw error('lien introuvable', 404);
  return { id: req.params.id, active: req.body.active };
});

/** L'entité racine d'un référentiel : sans parent (ou parente d'elle-même), la première. */
function root(registry, referential) {
  return R.referentialEntities(registry, referential)
    .filter((e) => e.Actif && (!e.ParenteCode || e.ParenteCode === e.Code))
    .sort((a, b) => a.Ordre - b.Ordre)[0] || null;
}

/**
 * POST /ajax/sdm/links/backfill — reprend les liens de l'existant :
 *   la hiérarchie (le parent de chaque entité) ;
 *   DEPENDS_ON (standards-integrations), au niveau du référentiel, sans
 *   attribut : pas de table tant que la colonne n'est pas précisée ;
 *   les liaisons du modèle hiérarchique publié (`STD_HL`, TH.13).
 */
const linkBackfill = reply(async (req) => {
  const [registry, existing, stdLinks, { cards, unpublished }] = await Promise.all([
    S.loadRegistry(), S.listLinks(), S.standardsLinks(), S.standardsCards(),
  ]);
  const { toCreate, ignored } = linksToBackfill(registry, existing, stdLinks);
  const matches = await S.transaction(async (transaction) => {
    for (const l of toCreate) await S.createLink(l, transaction);
    // T3.2.1 : puis les correspondances des cartes publiées, sur les liens non natifs (anciens et nouveaux).
    if (!cards.length) return { backfills: 0, already: 0, ignored: [] };
    const declared = (await S.listLinks(transaction)).filter((l) => l.SDM_LN_Active && l.SDM_LN_Nature === 'declare');
    const presence = await cardsPresence(registry, cards, transaction);
    const decisions = await S.listDecisions({ linkIds: declared.map((l) => l.SDM_LN_Id) }, transaction);
    const already = new Set(decisions.map((d) => `${d.SDM_DC_LinkId}|${d.SDM_DC_SourceId}|${d.SDM_DC_TargetId}|${d.SDM_DC_VersionNum}`));
    const r = matchesToBackfill(cards, { registry, declared, presence, already });
    await S.writeDecisions(r.toWrite, { by: user(req) }, transaction);
    return { backfills: r.toWrite.length, already: r.already, ignored: r.ignored };
  });
  return {
    created: toCreate.map((l) => `${l.source}${l.attribute ? `.${l.attribute}` : ''} → ${l.target} (${l.nature}, ${l.origin})`),
    ignored,
    matches: { ...matches, cards: cards.length, unpublishedCards: unpublished },
  };
});

/**
 * Les codes présents, par entité et par version, des deux côtés des cartes :
 * Map<'entite|version', Map<code, objetId> | null> — null si l'entité n'a pas
 * de tables ou pas cette version dans SDM.
 */
async function cardsPresence(registry, cards, transaction) {
  const tables = await S.presentTrio(transaction);
  const presence = new Map();
  const load = async (referential, version) => {
    for (const e of R.referentialEntities(registry, referential)) {
      const key = `${e.Code}|${version}`;
      if (presence.has(key)) continue;
      if (!tables.has(e.Code)) { presence.set(key, null); continue; }
      const members = await S.memberships(e.Code, version, Boolean(e.ParenteCode), transaction);
      presence.set(key, members.size ? new Map([...members].map(([id, m]) => [m.code, id])) : null);
    }
  };
  for (const c of cards) {
    await load(c.fromRef, c.fromVersion);
    await load(c.toRef, c.toVersion);
  }
  return presence;
}

/**
 * Les correspondances des cartes publiées de Standards à écrire en décisions
 * « confirmé » (T3.2.1). Pour chaque paire de codes, le lien non natif dont la
 * source porte le code de départ (à la version de départ) et la cible le code
 * d'arrivée ; un lien déclaré dans l'autre sens prend la paire retournée.
 * La décision est datée de la version du côté source du lien, comme
 * l'établissement à la main. Ce qui est déjà décidé (même refusé) n'est pas
 * touché. Rien d'écrit pour une paire sans lien, sans code ou sans version :
 * motif regroupé dans `ignorees`.
 */
function matchesToBackfill(cards, { registry, declared, presence, already = new Set() }) {
  const toWrite = [];
  const views = new Set(already);
  const reasons = new Map();
  const ignore = (reason, example) => {
    const m = reasons.get(reason) || { nb: 0, examples: [] };
    m.nb += 1;
    if (m.examples.length < 3) m.examples.push(example);
    reasons.set(reason, m);
  };
  let alreadyBackfilled = 0;

  for (const c of cards) {
    const card = `${c.fromRef} ${c.fromVersion} → ${c.toRef} ${c.toVersion}`;
    const initial = R.referentialEntities(registry, c.fromRef).map((e) => e.Code);
    const arrival = R.referentialEntities(registry, c.toRef).map((e) => e.Code);
    if (!initial.length || !arrival.length) {
      for (const p of c.pairs) ignore(`${card} : ${initial.length ? c.toRef : c.fromRef} n'est pas déclaré`, `${p.from} → ${p.to}`);
      continue;
    }
    const missing = (codes, version) => codes.every((e) => !presence.get(`${e}|${version}`));
    if (missing(initial, c.fromVersion) || missing(arrival, c.toVersion)) {
      const [ref, v] = missing(initial, c.fromVersion) ? [c.fromRef, c.fromVersion] : [c.toRef, c.toVersion];
      for (const p of c.pairs) ignore(`${card} : version ${v} de ${ref} absente de SDM — reprenez d'abord ses données`, `${p.from} → ${p.to}`);
      continue;
    }
    // Les liens non natifs entre les deux référentiels, dans un sens ou dans l'autre.
    const candidates = declared.flatMap((l) => {
      if (initial.includes(l.SDM_LN_SourceEntity) && arrival.includes(l.SDM_LN_TargetEntity)) return [{ link: l, direction: 1 }];
      if (arrival.includes(l.SDM_LN_SourceEntity) && initial.includes(l.SDM_LN_TargetEntity)) return [{ link: l, direction: -1 }];
      return [];
    });
    if (!candidates.length) {
      for (const p of c.pairs) ignore(`${card} : aucun lien non natif déclaré entre ${c.fromRef} et ${c.toRef}`, `${p.from} → ${p.to}`);
      continue;
    }
    const idOf = (entity, version, code) => presence.get(`${entity}|${version}`)?.get(code) || null;

    for (const p of c.pairs) {
      let found = null;
      for (const { link, direction } of candidates) {
        const [entOf, entTo] = direction === 1
          ? [link.SDM_LN_SourceEntity, link.SDM_LN_TargetEntity] : [link.SDM_LN_TargetEntity, link.SDM_LN_SourceEntity];
        const from = idOf(entOf, c.fromVersion, p.from);
        const to = idOf(entTo, c.toVersion, p.to);
        if (!from || !to) continue;
        found = direction === 1
          ? { linkId: link.SDM_LN_Id, sourceId: from, targetId: to, versionNum: c.fromVersion }
          : { linkId: link.SDM_LN_Id, sourceId: to, targetId: from, versionNum: c.toVersion };
        break;
      }
      if (!found) {
        const knownFrom = initial.some((e) => idOf(e, c.fromVersion, p.from));
        const knownTo = arrival.some((e) => idOf(e, c.toVersion, p.to));
        const reason = !knownFrom ? `code absent de ${c.fromRef} ${c.fromVersion}`
          : !knownTo ? `code absent de ${c.toRef} ${c.toVersion}`
            : 'aucun lien non natif déclaré entre les entités de ces deux codes';
        ignore(`${card} : ${reason}`, `${p.from} → ${p.to}`);
        continue;
      }
      const key = `${found.linkId}|${found.sourceId}|${found.targetId}|${found.versionNum}`;
      if (views.has(key)) { alreadyBackfilled += 1; continue; }
      views.add(key);
      toWrite.push({ ...found, state: 'confirme', human: true, reason: `repris de Standards (carte ${card})` });
    }
  }
  const ignored = [...reasons].map(([reason, m]) => `${reason} — ${m.nb} paire(s), ex. ${m.examples.join(', ')}`);
  return { toWrite, already: alreadyBackfilled, ignored };
}

const sameName = (a, b) => String(a || '').toUpperCase() === String(b || '').toUpperCase();

/**
 * L'entité d'un côté d'une liaison `STD_HL`. Référentiel découpé : la
 * couverture (`champ = valeur` sur le discriminant) désigne l'entité ; sinon,
 * l'entité qui déclare le champ (côté source) ; sinon, la racine.
 * Rend { entite } ou { motif }.
 */
function sideEntity(registry, referential, decl, field) {
  const entities = R.referentialEntities(registry, referential).filter((e) => e.Actif);
  if (!entities.length) return { reason: `${referential} n'est pas déclaré` };
  const rule = SPLIT_RULES[referential];
  if (rule && decl?.field && sameName(decl.field, rule.column)) {
    const code = Object.entries(rule.values).find(([v]) => sameName(v, decl.value))?.[1];
    const e = code && entities.find((x) => x.Code === code);
    if (e) return { entity: e };
    return { reason: `${referential} : aucune entité pour ${decl.field} = ${decl.value}` };
  }
  if (field) {
    const carriers = entities.filter((e) => [...e.attributes.values()].some((a) => sameName(a.Nom, field)));
    if (carriers.length === 1) return { entity: carriers[0] };
    if (carriers.length > 1) return { reason: `${referential}.${field} porté par plusieurs entités, sans couverture pour choisir` };
    return { reason: `${referential} ne déclare pas la colonne ${field}` };
  }
  const e = root(registry, referential);
  return e ? { entity: e } : { reason: `${referential} sans entité racine` };
}

/** Les liens de l'existant pas encore déclarés. */
function linksToBackfill(registry, existing, stdLinks = []) {
  // Un lien désactivé à la main compte comme déjà repris : on ne le recrée pas.
  const already = new Set(existing.map((l) => `${l.SDM_LN_SourceEntity}|${l.SDM_LN_SourceAttribute || ''}|${l.SDM_LN_TargetEntity}`));
  // Les liens natifs, existants puis repris : pour refuser un cycle (aucun ordre d'import possible).
  const native = existing.filter((l) => l.SDM_LN_Active !== false && l.SDM_LN_Nature === 'natif')
    .map((l) => ({ SDM_LN_SourceEntity: l.SDM_LN_SourceEntity, SDM_LN_TargetEntity: l.SDM_LN_TargetEntity }));
  const toCreate = [];
  const ignored = [];
  const added = (l) => {
    const key = `${l.source}|${l.attribute || ''}|${l.target}`;
    if (already.has(key)) return;
    const nature = l.nature || 'natif';
    if (nature === 'natif') {
      const cycle = nativeCycle(native, l.source, l.target);
      if (cycle) { ignored.push(`${l.origin} : cycle de liens natifs ${cycle.join(' → ')}`); return; }
      native.push({ SDM_LN_SourceEntity: l.source, SDM_LN_TargetEntity: l.target });
    }
    already.add(key);
    toCreate.push({ ...l, nature });
  };

  for (const e of registry.entities.values()) {
    if (!e.Actif || !e.ParenteCode) continue;
    const parent = [...e.attributes.values()].find((a) => a.Role === 'parent');
    added({ source: e.Code, attribute: parent?.Nom || null, target: e.ParenteCode, cardinality: 'n,1', origin: 'hiérarchie' });
  }
  for (const [referential, deps] of Object.entries(DEPENDS_ON)) {
    for (const dep of [].concat(deps)) {
      const source = root(registry, referential);
      const target = root(registry, dep);
      if (!source || !target) { ignored.push(`DEPENDS_ON ${referential} → ${dep} : référentiel non déclaré`); continue; }
      added({ source: source.Code, attribute: null, target: target.Code, cardinality: 'n,1', origin: `DEPENDS_ON ${referential} → ${dep}` });
    }
  }
  // STD_HL : `fwd` couvre le côté source (FromRef), `rev` le côté cible (ToRef).
  for (const h of stdLinks) {
    const origin = `Hiérarchie ${h.fromRef}.${h.fromField} → ${h.toRef}.${h.toField}`;
    const source = sideEntity(registry, h.fromRef, h.coverage?.fwd, h.fromField);
    const target = sideEntity(registry, h.toRef, h.coverage?.rev, null);
    if (!source.entity || !target.entity) { ignored.push(`${origin} : ${source.reason || target.reason}`); continue; }
    const attribute = [...source.entity.attributes.values()].find((a) => sameName(a.Nom, h.fromField))?.Nom || null;
    added({
      source: source.entity.Code, attribute, target: target.entity.Code, cardinality: 'n,1',
      nature: h.isNative ? 'natif' : 'declare', origin,
    });
  }
  return { toCreate, ignored };
}

const asDecision = (d) => ({
  id: d.SDM_DC_Id,
  linkId: d.SDM_DC_LinkId,
  sourceId: d.SDM_DC_SourceId,
  targetId: d.SDM_DC_TargetId,
  versionNum: d.SDM_DC_VersionNum,
  state: d.SDM_DC_State,
  decidedAt: d.SDM_DC_DecidedAt,
  decidedBy: d.SDM_DC_DecidedBy,
  reason: d.SDM_DC_Reason,
});

/** GET /ajax/sdm/links/:id/decisions — les instances d'un lien non natif. */
const linkDecisions = reply(async (req) => {
  const links = await S.listLinks();
  const linksById = new Map(links.map((l) => [l.SDM_LN_Id, l]));
  if (!linksById.has(req.params.id)) throw error('lien introuvable', 404);
  const decisions = (await S.listDecisions({ linkIds: [req.params.id] })).map(asDecision);
  return withCodes(decisions, linksById);
});

/**
 * POST /ajax/sdm/links/:id/decisions — établit une instance d'un lien non
 * natif : { sourceCode, cibleCode, versionNum? }. C'est une décision humaine :
 * elle est enregistrée confirmée, pour la version donnée (par défaut, la
 * dernière de la source).
 */
const establishLink = reply(async (req) => {
  const { sourceCode, targetCode } = req.body || {};
  const link = (await S.listLinks()).find((l) => l.SDM_LN_Id === req.params.id);
  if (!link) throw error('lien introuvable', 404);
  if (link.SDM_LN_Nature !== 'declare') throw error('seul un lien non natif s\'établit à la main : un lien natif vient du fichier');
  const present = await S.presentTrio();
  for (const e of [link.SDM_LN_SourceEntity, link.SDM_LN_TargetEntity]) if (!present.has(e)) throw error(`${e} n'a pas encore de tables`);

  const sourceId = (await S.identities(link.SDM_LN_SourceEntity)).get(String(sourceCode || '').trim());
  const targetId = (await S.identities(link.SDM_LN_TargetEntity)).get(String(targetCode || '').trim());
  if (!sourceId) throw error(`code source inconnu dans ${link.SDM_LN_SourceEntity} : ${sourceCode}`);
  if (!targetId) throw error(`code cible inconnu dans ${link.SDM_LN_TargetEntity} : ${targetCode}`);
  const versionNum = String(req.body?.versionNum || '').trim()
    || read.lastVersion(await S.versionsOf(link.SDM_LN_SourceEntity));
  if (!versionNum || !VERSION_NUM.test(versionNum)) throw error('numéro de version invalide');

  await S.writeDecisions([{
    linkId: link.SDM_LN_Id, sourceId, targetId, versionNum, state: 'confirme', human: true, reason: 'établi à la main',
  }], { by: user(req) });
  return { linkId: link.SDM_LN_Id, sourceCode, targetCode, versionNum, state: 'confirme' };
});

/** GET /ajax/sdm/links/to-confirm — la file d'attente, avec le motif du doute. */
const confirmationQueue = reply(async () => {
  const links = await S.listLinks();
  const decisions = (await S.listDecisions({ state: 'propose' })).map(asDecision);
  return withCodes(decisions, new Map(links.map((l) => [l.SDM_LN_Id, l])));
});

/**
 * PUT /ajax/sdm/links/decisions/:id — { etat: confirme | rejete, motif? }.
 * Une décision à la fois : il n'y a pas de « tout confirmer » (décision B).
 */
const decideLink = reply(async (req) => {
  const { state, reason } = req.body || {};
  if (!['confirme', 'rejete'].includes(state)) throw error('etat : confirme ou rejete');
  return S.transaction(async (transaction) => {
    const d = await S.readDecision(req.params.id, transaction);
    if (!d) throw error('décision introuvable', 404);
    if (d.SDM_DC_State !== 'propose') throw error(`décision déjà ${d.SDM_DC_State}`);
    await S.settleDecision(d.SDM_DC_Id, { state, by: user(req), reason }, transaction);
    return { id: d.SDM_DC_Id, state };
  });
});

/** GET /ajax/sdm/data/:entity?version=&langue=&limite=&decalage= */
const readData = reply(async (req) => {
  const registry = await S.loadRegistry();
  const entity = registry.entities.get(req.params.entity);
  if (!entity) throw error(`entité inconnue : ${req.params.entity}`, 404);
  if (!(await S.presentTrio()).has(entity.Code)) throw error(`${entity.Code} n'a pas encore de tables`, 409);
  const { version, lang, limit, offset } = req.query;
  if (version && !VERSION_NUM.test(version)) throw error('numéro de version invalide');
  if (lang && !['fr', 'en'].includes(lang)) throw error('langue : fr ou en');
  return read.read(entity, { versionNum: version, lang, limit, offset });
});

/**
 * GET /ajax/sdm/explore/:entity?version=&q=&parent=&limite=&decalage=
 * L'onglet Données : une page de lignes toutes langues, le total, et pour
 * chaque objet le nombre de ses enfants dans les entités filles.
 */
const explore = reply(async (req) => {
  const registry = await S.loadRegistry();
  const entity = registry.entities.get(req.params.entity);
  if (!entity) throw error(`entité inconnue : ${req.params.entity}`, 404);
  const present = await S.presentTrio();
  if (!present.has(entity.Code)) throw error(`${entity.Code} n'a pas encore de tables`, 409);
  const { version, q, parent } = req.query;
  if (version && !VERSION_NUM.test(version)) throw error('numéro de version invalide');

  const versions = (await S.versionsOf(entity.Code)).sort(compareVersions);
  const versionNum = version || read.lastVersion(versions);
  const empty = { entity: entity.Code, versionNum, versions, total: 0, rows: [], children: [] };
  if (!versionNum) return empty;

  const limit = Math.min(Math.max(Number(req.query.limit) || 50, 1), 500);
  const offset = Math.max(Number(req.query.offset) || 0, 0);
  const { total, rows } = await S.exploreData(entity.Code, {
    versionNum,
    search: q ? String(q).slice(0, 200) : null,
    withParentRow: entity.ParenteCode || null,
    parentCode: parent || null,
    limit,
    offset,
  });

  // Les entités filles créées (elle-même si elle est sa propre parente) :
  // une hiérarchie dépliable objet par objet.
  const children = [...registry.entities.values()]
    .filter((e) => e.ParenteCode === entity.Code && e.Actif && present.has(e.Code));
  const ids = rows.map((l) => l.objet_id);
  const counts = await Promise.all(children.map((f) => S.countChildren(f.Code, versionNum, ids)));
  return {
    ...empty,
    total,
    children: children.map((f) => f.Code),
    rows: rows.map(({ objet_id: id, ...l }) => ({
      ...l,
      children: Object.fromEntries(children.map((f, i) => [f.Code, counts[i].get(id) || 0])),
    })),
  };
});

/**
 * GET /ajax/sdm/data?entite=&langue=&version=current|all&q=&parent=&limite=&decalage=
 * L'onglet Données aux filtres de Standards (E32) : sans entité, toutes les
 * entités de tête (les filles se déplient dessous) ; sans langue, une ligne
 * par langue ; `all`, une ligne par version. Chaque ligne porte son entité,
 * sa version, sa langue et le nombre de ses enfants dans cette version.
 */
const records = reply(async (req) => {
  const registry = await S.loadRegistry();
  const present = await S.presentTrio();
  const { entity: code, lang, version = 'current', q, parent } = req.query;
  if (lang && !['fr', 'en'].includes(lang)) throw error('langue invalide');
  if (!['current', 'all'].includes(version)) throw error('version invalide : current ou all');
  const created = [...registry.entities.values()].filter((e) => e.Actif && present.has(e.Code));
  let chosen;
  if (code) {
    const e = registry.entities.get(code);
    if (!e || !created.includes(e)) throw error(`entité inconnue ou sans tables : ${code}`, 404);
    chosen = [e];
  } else {
    chosen = created.filter((e) => !e.ParenteCode || e.ParenteCode === e.Code);
  }

  const sources = [];
  for (const e of chosen) {
    const versions = (await S.versionsOf(e.Code)).sort(compareVersions);
    if (!versions.length) continue;
    sources.push({
      code: e.Code,
      withParentRow: e.ParenteCode || null,
      rootsOnly: !code && e.ParenteCode === e.Code,
      versions,
      current: versions[versions.length - 1],
      allOf: version === 'all',
    });
  }
  const { total, rows } = await S.browseData(sources, {
    langs: lang ? [lang] : ['fr', 'en'],
    search: q ? String(q).slice(0, 200) : null,
    parentCode: code && parent ? String(parent) : null,
    limit: Math.min(Math.max(Number(req.query.limit) || 20, 1), 500),
    offset: Math.max(Number(req.query.offset) || 0, 0),
  });

  // Les enfants, comptés par entité fille et par version de la ligne.
  const childrenOf = (c) => created.filter((f) => f.ParenteCode === c);
  const counts = new Map();
  const groups = new Map();
  for (const l of rows) {
    const key = `${l.entity}|${l.version_num}`;
    if (!groups.has(key)) groups.set(key, { entity: l.entity, versionNum: l.version_num, ids: new Set() });
    groups.get(key).ids.add(l.objet_id);
  }
  for (const [key, g] of groups) {
    for (const f of childrenOf(g.entity)) {
      counts.set(`${key}|${f.Code}`, await S.countChildren(f.Code, g.versionNum, [...g.ids]));
    }
  }
  return {
    total,
    referentialsWithoutData: chosen.length - sources.length,
    rows: rows.map(({ objet_id: id, ...l }) => ({
      ...l,
      children: Object.fromEntries(childrenOf(l.entity).map((f) => [f.Code,
        counts.get(`${l.entity}|${l.version_num}|${f.Code}`).get(id) || 0])),
    })),
  };
});

/**
 * GET /ajax/sdm/api/:func?… — une fonction de l'API compat Standards
 * (sdm-api.utils), ses arguments pris dans la requête. Sert l'onglet Test API.
 */
const callApi = reply(async (req) => {
  const args = api.argsOf(req.params.func, req.query);
  if (!args) throw error(`fonction inconnue : ${req.params.func}`, 404);
  const start = Date.now();
  const result = await api[req.params.func](...args);
  return { func: req.params.func, arguments: args, durationMs: Date.now() - start, result };
});

title: 16,000 databases, and the four ways row-level security silently fails
description:
In late September 2026, UpGuard researchers reported finding more than 16,000 Supabase databases exposing readable tables containing personal data, passwords, or authentication tokens. They had analysed roughly 300,000 domains for the signature of a Supabase project, then checked whether a users table — or something with another name — answered.

The attribution matters more than the number. In the reporting, the researchers point at "poor application security configurations, including missing or ineffective row-level security policies and misuse of public keys", and add: "The common thread is that these sites are created by AI coding agents and the humans are unaware of the configuration." (BleepingComputer)

That last sentence is not an accusation about AI. It is a statement about a specific property of Postgres: row-level security fails silently. A missing WHERE clause returns an error you can see. A missing policy returns data, and a 200.

Here are the four ways it happens, in the order I find them, with the query that detects each one.

1. RLS was never enabled on the table

Row-level security is opt-in, per table. CREATE TABLE does not enable it. A table created through a dashboard editor may arrive with RLS on; a table created by a SQL migration — which is how a real project creates tables — arrives with relrowsecurity = false. A policy cannot exist on a table that has RLS disabled, and nothing warns you.

select c.relname
from pg_class c
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
where n.nspname = 'public'
  and c.relkind = 'r'
  and not c.relrowsecurity;

Every row this returns is a table where anon and authenticated can read whatever the API exposes, policy or no policy.

2. The policy exists, but not for the role that is asking

A policy can be scoped to authenticated, to anon, to a custom role — or to PUBLIC, which is the default and is the one people forget.

select tablename, policyname, roles, cmd
from pg_policies
where schemaname = 'public'
order by tablename, policyname;

Read roles first. A policy granted {public} applies to every role that has table privileges — including the two the Data API speaks for. Policies and grants are two separate layers, and a table can be protected by one and open at the other. Supabase's 2026-10-30 change to automatic grants exists because those two layers were being confused in production.

3. A security definer function runs as its owner and steps around RLS

This is the one that survives a clean-looking schema. A function declared security definer executes with the privileges of the role that created it. If that role owns the table — usually postgres — the function reads across every tenant, and any caller who can execute it inherits that ability. Your policies are still in place; they are simply not in the path.

select p.proname, r.rolname as owner
from pg_proc p
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = p.pronamespace
join pg_roles r on r.oid = p.proowner
where n.nspname = 'public' and p.prosecdef
order by 1;

Each row needs reading line by line: does it take the tenant from an argument or from the authenticated claim, and does it verify membership before returning anything?

4. The view on top of the correct policy is not correct

A view runs with the privileges of its owner by default. So a view that joins two tenant tables can hand back rows the caller's policies would have blocked: the tables are protected, the view is a hole in the same database.

select c.relname, c.reloptions
from pg_class c
join pg_namespace n on n.oid = c.relnamespace
where n.nspname = 'public'
  and c.relkind = 'v'
  and not coalesce(array_to_string(c.reloptions, ',') like '%security_invoker=true%', false)
order by 1;

security_invoker = true makes the view run as the caller. A view without it deserves a test, not a glance.

The test that settles it

Reading the schema tells you what was declared. It does not tell you what your application does. The only way to know whether tenant A can reach tenant B is to be tenant A and try — as the role your application actually uses, with the same session variable it actually sets.

In a Postgres app that pins the tenant with SET LOCAL, that is one transaction and one assertion:

begin;
set local role app_rw;
set local app.current_tenant = '<tenant-A-uuid>';

-- returns rows belonging to anyone other than A? then it leaks.
select count(*) from notes
where tenant_id is distinct from current_setting('app.current_tenant', true)::uuid;
rollback;

Run it against a seeded database. On an empty table both a correct policy and a broken one return zero, which is why "0 rows" on its own is not evidence of anything — that is the mistake a scanner makes and a probe must not.

Then put the probe in CI, and the next policy regression fails a build instead of leaking quietly.

What "done" looks like

Not a grade, and not a PDF. Four artefacts:

  1. every policy listed with a verdict — enforced, bypassable, or absent;
  2. the cross-tenant probes committed to the repository, so they run on every pull request;
  3. the missing or wrong policies as a reviewable migration diff;
  4. before/after output of the same probes, which is the only thing that answers a security questionnaire.

I wrote the pattern up, with the probe and the four queries above as a runnable kit: verdantstack.dev/services/rls-audit. If you would rather do it yourself, the queries in this post are the ones to start with, and they cost nothing.

title: Clean Code Best Practices: 10 Rules with Java Examples
description:
Clean code is code that a developer other than its author can read, change and extend without fear. The idea was made popular by Robert C. Martin in his book Clean Code.

This post shows ten clean code rules with real Java examples, each one a before taken from production code and an after you can copy. You will learn how to:

  • choose names that make comments unnecessary;
  • split functions so each one does one thing;
  • replace hard-coded values without waiting for a big project;
  • cut long argument lists down to one object;
  • make a block of code read like a story.

At the end there is a code review checklist with one line per rule.

1. Use intention-revealing names

A name should tell the reader why a variable, function or class exists, what it does and how it is used. If a name needs a comment, the name is wrong.

Real code from a project:

int sId; // supplier id
int artDelPrice;

Refactored:

int supplierId;
int articleDeliveredPrice;

The same applies to types from external libraries, whose names you can't change:

private Z_E2F_RS_Result e2fResult; // ingredients record set

You can't rename Z_E2F_RS_Result, but you can name your variable after what it holds:

private Z_E2F_RS_Result ingredients;

Now imagine the original code without the // ingredients record set comment. Further down, in a loop, you find this line:

e2f = e2fResult[i];

What is e2f? Someone suggests asking the developer who wrote the code. They're not in the office. You send them an email, and the auto-reply says they're on holiday for three weeks.

With an intention-revealing name, nobody has to ask:

ingredient = ingredients[i];

Robert C. Martin spends a whole chapter of Clean Code on naming, with dozens of before-and-after examples like this one. If this rule saves you a single "what does e2f mean?" conversation, the book has paid for itself.

2. Make functions do one thing

We retrieve images from an external web service. For each image we first receive metadata: two flags that tell us whether the image is valid, and up to three image IDs from different systems. We need the first ID that isn't null.

private String retrieveImageId(String[] values) {
  if (!values[2].equals("Y") || !values[3].equals("Y"))
    return null;

  String imageId = null;
  // get the first not null value as the imageId
  if (values[4] != null) {
    imageId = values[4]; // imageAIXId
  } else if (values[5] != null) {
    imageId = values[5]; // imageLIXId
  } else if (values[6] != null) {
    imageId = values[6]; // imageOIXId
  }
  return imageId;
}

This function does two things: it validates the image and it picks the ID. Its name only mentions the second one, so a caller can't tell that null might mean "invalid image" or "no ID". Split it into two functions, each with one job and a name that says it:

private static final int AIX_IMAGE_ID = 4;
private static final int LIX_IMAGE_ID = 5;
private static final int OIX_IMAGE_ID = 6;

private boolean isValidImage(String[] values) {
  return "Y".equals(values[2]) && "Y".equals(values[3]);
}

private Optional<String> findImageId(String[] values) {
  return Stream.of(values[AIX_IMAGE_ID], values[LIX_IMAGE_ID], values[OIX_IMAGE_ID])
      .filter(Objects::nonNull)
      .findFirst();
}

A few details changed on the way:

  • Named constants replace the // imageAIXId comments.
  • "Y".equals(...) doesn't throw a NullPointerException when a flag is missing.
  • Optional tells the caller that there might be no ID, so they can't forget to handle it.

The caller now reads like the requirement:

public void synchronizeImages() {
  Response response = api.getImages();
  for (Row row : response.getRows()) {
    String[] values = row.getValues();
    if (isValidImage(values)) {
      findImageId(values).ifPresent(this::downloadImage);
    }
  }
}

I tested the new functions against the original one with every combination of flags and IDs, and they return the same image ID in all 32 cases.

3. Don't comment bad code, rewrite it

We request metadata for a list of articles, but the external API also returns articles we didn't ask for. Before processing a row, we check that the article is in our map of requested articles, and we add a comment so our colleagues understand why:

public void synchronizeImages() {
  Response response = api.getImages(mapOfArticles);
  for (Row row : response.getRows()) {
    String[] values = row.getValues();
    String articleId = values[1];

    // only requested articles
    if (!mapOfArticles.containsKey(articleId))
      continue;

    // code omitted for brevity
  }
}

The comment exists only because the variable name is vague. Rename the map and the comment becomes unnecessary:

public void synchronizeImages() {
  Response response = api.getImages(requestedArticles);
  for (Row row : response.getRows()) {
    String[] values = row.getValues();
    String articleId = values[1];

    if (!requestedArticles.containsKey(articleId))
      continue;

    // code omitted for brevity
  }
}

The name also drops mapOf: the type already says it's a map. Comments go out of date because nobody runs them. Names are read every time the code is read.

4. Choose simplicity over cleverness

To build an article's image URL, the image ID must be valid, and if the image is restricted, the partner must be allowed to see it. Someone wrote it as one line:

String articleImageUrl = (imageId <= 0 || (imageIsRestricted && !partnerCanSeeImage)) ? null : IMAGE_URL + imageId;

It's short, but to understand it you have to evaluate the negations in your head. Nesting if statements spells it out, but three levels deep is hard to read too. Instead, give the rule a name and write it with early returns:

private boolean canShowImage(int imageId, boolean imageIsRestricted, boolean partnerCanSeeImage) {
  if (imageId <= 0) return false;
  if (!imageIsRestricted) return true;
  return partnerCanSeeImage;
}

String articleImageUrl = canShowImage(imageId, imageIsRestricted, partnerCanSeeImage)
    ? IMAGE_URL + imageId
    : null;

Each line of canShowImage is one business rule, and you can unit test the rule on its own. I checked all 12 combinations of inputs: it gives the same result as the one-line version.

This is the KISS principle (Keep It Simple, Stupid): the simplest code is the one the next developer understands fastest, not the one with the fewest characters.

Any software design is generally a matter of opinion. There is no definitive guide. -- codersite.dev

KISS is one of the principles my book Software Design Principles covers with worked Java examples, together with DRY, YAGNI and SOLID, and twelve clean code habits like the ones in this post.

5. Avoid hard-coded values

Hard coding means writing data, such as IDs, URLs or limits, directly into the source code instead of reading it from configuration, a file or a database.

Here is how it usually happens. A company has image copyright problems with two providers and must block their images for some customers immediately. The standard process is slow: a DBA writes a database function, developers add parameter classes, and the change goes through development, test and production. There's no time for that, so a developer writes this:

boolean pictureIsRestricted = result.getProviderId() == "530636" || result.getProviderId() == "36507";

This line has two problems.

It's a bug. In Java, == compares String references, not their text. A provider ID read from a database or a web service is a new String object, so == returns false even when the text is "530636". The restricted images are shown anyway. Always compare strings with equals.

It doesn't stay in one place. Other modules need the same check, then a third provider is added, and soon the same IDs are copied into many classes. Every new provider means a code change and a deployment.

You don't need the full database project to fix this. Put the IDs in a text file, one per line, and read them behind an interface:

public interface ProviderRepository {

  Set<String> findRestrictedProviders();
}

public class FileProviderRepository implements ProviderRepository {

  private final Path file;

  public FileProviderRepository(Path file) {
    this.file = file;
  }

  @Override
  public Set<String> findRestrictedProviders() {
    try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(file)) {
      return lines.map(String::strip)
          .filter(line -> !line.isEmpty())
          .collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableSet());
    } catch (IOException e) {
      throw new UncheckedIOException("Cannot read restricted providers from " + file, e);
    }
  }
}

If the file is missing, the method throws an exception instead of returning an empty list. An empty list would silently mean "no provider is restricted", and every image would be shown again.

Every class that needs the check uses the same repository:

Set<String> restrictedProviders = providerRepository.findRestrictedProviders();
boolean pictureIsRestricted = restrictedProviders.contains(result.getProviderId());

contains on a Set uses equals, so the comparison bug is gone too. The day the database function is ready, you write a DatabaseProviderRepository that implements the same interface, and no other code changes.

Small, safe steps like this one, where you change the structure without changing the behavior, are what Martin Fowler calls refactoring. His book Refactoring is a catalog of more than 60 of them, each with the motivation, the mechanics and a before-and-after example.

6. Name variables by their context

A Buyer and a Supplier both have an email address:

public class Buyer {

  private int buyerId;
  private String lastName;
  private String email;

  // code omitted for brevity
}

public class Supplier {

  private int supplierId;
  private String contact;
  private String email;

  // code omitted for brevity
}

Inside each class, email is clear: the class is the context. Don't rename the fields to buyerEmail and supplierEmail. That repeats the class name in every call, as in supplier.getSupplierEmail(), and Clean Code warns against adding this kind of redundant context.

The context gets lost in local variables, far from the object they came from:

String email = supplier.getEmail();
// 40 lines later: whose email is this?

Put the context in the variable name instead:

String supplierEmail = supplier.getEmail();
String buyerEmail = buyer.getEmail();

The rule of thumb: the further a name is used from where its context is visible, the more context the name needs.

7. Use method overloading to keep existing callers working

A method subscribes a new buyer to an external service, and it is called from many places:

public int subscribe(String email, Buyer buyer) {
  // code omitted for brevity
}

subscriberId = wsClient.subscribe(email, buyer);

Now some callers must also send a tag that tells the service what to do with the subscriber. If you add a third parameter to the method, you must change every existing caller, and most of them would pass null:

subscriberId = wsClient.subscribe(email, buyer, null);

Instead, overload the method. The new version does the work, and the old version calls it, so the logic exists only once:

public int subscribe(String email, Buyer buyer) {
  return subscribe(email, buyer, null);
}

public int subscribe(String email, Buyer buyer, Integer tagId) {
  // code omitted for brevity
}

Existing callers don't change. Only the new code that needs a tag uses the new version:

subscriberId = wsClient.subscribe(email, buyer, 102911);

8. Avoid long argument lists

A function with more than three arguments is hard to call correctly. When two arguments have the same type, nothing stops a caller from swapping them:

public boolean validateAddress(String street, int number, String postalCode, String city, String country) {
  // code omitted for brevity
}

All these arguments describe one concept, an address, so pass one object:

public record Address(String street, int number, String postalCode, String city, String country) {}

public boolean validateAddress(Address address) {
  // code omitted for brevity
}

The same idea fixes a common pattern: a method that receives a String[] and decodes each position itself:

public ListOrdersResponse listOrders(String[] values) {
  Integer buyerId = Integer.valueOf(values[0]);
  Integer supplierId = Integer.valueOf(values[1]);
  LocalDate orderDateFrom = LocalDate.parse(values[2]);
  LocalDate orderDateTo = LocalDate.parse(values[3]);
  String sortBy = values[4];
  String sortOrder = values[5];
  Integer offset = Integer.valueOf(values[6]);
  Integer limit = Integer.valueOf(values[7]);

  // code omitted for brevity
}

Replacing the array with eight separate parameters would only trade one problem for another. Instead, parse the array once into a record, and let the method receive the record:

public record ListOrdersRequest(int buyerId, int supplierId,
                                LocalDate orderDateFrom, LocalDate orderDateTo,
                                String sortBy, String sortOrder,
                                int offset, int limit) {

  public ListOrdersRequest {
    if (orderDateFrom.isAfter(orderDateTo)) {
      throw new IllegalArgumentException("orderDateFrom must not be after orderDateTo");
    }
  }

  public static ListOrdersRequest from(String[] values) {
    return new ListOrdersRequest(
        Integer.parseInt(values[0]),
        Integer.parseInt(values[1]),
        LocalDate.parse(values[2]),
        LocalDate.parse(values[3]),
        values[4],
        values[5],
        Integer.parseInt(values[6]),
        Integer.parseInt(values[7]));
  }
}

public ListOrdersResponse listOrders(ListOrdersRequest request) {
  // code omitted for brevity
}

Now the array positions are decoded in one place, the date range is checked when the request is created, and listOrders works with named values: request.buyerId(), request.limit().

9. Make code tell a story

When you fix a bug, you read the sequence of calls to understand what the program does. Requirements change over time, so code that was clear on day one slowly stops telling a clear story. Refactoring it back is part of the job.

This job sends buyer data to a partner called ACME:

ACMEWebServiceClient.login();
if (process.equals("core")) {
    ACMEWebServiceClient.transfer_buyersCoreData_to_ACME();
}
if (process.equals("status")) {
    ACMEWebServiceClient.transfer_buyersStatusChanges_to_ACME();
}
if (process.equals("events")) {
    ACMEWebServiceClient.transfer_events_to_ACME();
}
ACMEWebServiceClient.logout();

The story is hidden by three problems:

  • Typos fail silently. If process is "statsu", no branch runs and the job logs in and out without doing anything.
  • An exception skips the logout. The session stays open on ACME's side.
  • The names repeat themselves. Every method says ACME on a class that is already the ACME client.

Here is the same job as a story:

public enum TransferProcess { CORE, STATUS, EVENTS }

public void transferToAcme(TransferProcess process) {
  acmeClient.login();
  try {
    switch (process) {
      case CORE -> acmeClient.transferBuyersCoreData();
      case STATUS -> acmeClient.transferBuyerStatusChanges();
      case EVENTS -> acmeClient.transferEvents();
    }
  } finally {
    acmeClient.logout();
  }
}

Read it aloud: log in, transfer the chosen data, always log out. Converting the input with TransferProcess.valueOf(process.toUpperCase()) throws an exception for an unknown value like "statsu", so a typo fails at once instead of doing nothing. The finally block logs out even when a transfer throws an exception.

10. Copy one constant instead of keeping a dead library

We migrate an application to a new application server and find out that a library it uses is no longer supported there:

import org.apache.axis.transport.http.HTTPConstants;

HttpServletRequest httpServletRequest =
    (HttpServletRequest) context.get(HTTPConstants.MC_HTTP_SERVLETREQUEST);

We spend a lot of time looking for a compatible version of Apache Axis. Then we notice that the whole application uses only one thing from that library: the MC_HTTP_SERVLETREQUEST constant, whose value is the string "transport.http.servletRequest".

The simple solution is to declare that constant in our own code:

public final class AxisContextKeys {

  // Same value as org.apache.axis.transport.http.HTTPConstants.MC_HTTP_SERVLETREQUEST
  public static final String SERVLET_REQUEST = "transport.http.servletRequest";

  private AxisContextKeys() {}
}

HttpServletRequest httpServletRequest =
    (HttpServletRequest) context.get(AxisContextKeys.SERVLET_REQUEST);

Before you remove the library, search the whole code base for other org.apache.axis imports. If this was the only one, the dependency can go, and the migration is no longer blocked by a library nobody maintains.

Clean code review checklist

Copy this list into your next code review. Each line is one of the rules above.

  1. Names: can you understand every name without a comment?
  2. One thing: does each function do what its name says, and nothing else?
  3. Comments: does any comment explain something a better name could say?
  4. Simplicity: can you read each condition aloud as a business rule?
  5. Hard coding: are IDs, URLs and limits read from configuration, compared with equals, and kept in one place?
  6. Context: do local variables far from their object say where they came from?
  7. Callers: does a new parameter force changes on callers that don't need it?
  8. Arguments: does any function take more than three arguments, or decode array positions?
  9. Story: can you read the main flow aloud, and is cleanup in a finally block?
  10. Dependencies: does a large library stay in the project for one constant or one small helper?

Clean code is one habit of a professional developer. The Pragmatic Programmer covers the rest: taking responsibility for your code, avoiding duplication, testing and automating, and knowing when code is good enough to ship. It's the book I recommend after Clean Code.

FAQ

What is clean code?

Clean code is code that another developer can read, understand and change safely. It has intention-revealing names, small functions that do one thing, no duplication, and tests. The term comes from Robert C. Martin's book Clean Code: A Handbook of Agile Software Craftsmanship (2008).

Does clean code mean no comments?

No. Clean code avoids comments that explain what the code does, because a better name or a smaller function can say that. Comments that explain why, such as a business rule, a legal requirement or a workaround for a bug in a library, are still useful. The // Same value as ... comment in rule 10 is an example.

Is clean code slower?

Almost never in a way you can measure. Small functions and named variables are optimized by the JIT compiler. Performance problems usually come from algorithms, database queries and network calls, which are easier to find and fix in clean code. See how to optimize Java application performance.

How do I start cleaning an existing code base?

Don't rewrite it. Follow the Boy Scout Rule: leave every file you touch a little cleaner than you found it. Rename one variable, extract one function, add one test. Small refactorings in the code you're already changing add up, and they're easy to review.

How does clean code relate to SOLID?

Clean code works at the level of names, functions and classes. SOLID works at the level of classes and their dependencies. Rule 5 above, with its ProviderRepository interface, is the dependency inversion principle in practice. See SOLID principles: the definitive guide.

Originally published at codersite.dev.

title: VPS vs VDS vs Colocation: which one does your workload actually need?
description:
"Should I get a VPS, a dedicated server or just colocate my own box?"

I work at a hosting company that sells all three, and this is the question we hear most. The honest answer is that none of them is better. They solve different problems. Here's how to tell which one is yours

The one-line version

  • VPS: a virtual server with shared CPU time. Cheapest. Good when your load comes in bursts.
  • VDS (virtual dedicated server): a virtual server with physical cores reserved for you. Steady performance under constant load.
  • Colocation: your own hardware in someone else's data center. You bring the server; they provide space, power, network and physical security.

VPS: shared vCPU

A VPS splits a physical host into virtual machines. Your RAM and disk are yours, but the processor time is shared with the other VMs on the same host. When your traffic spikes, you can borrow idle CPU. When your neighbours spike at the same time, you wait (that waiting shows up as st, "steal", in top).

Good for:

  • websites, blogs, small APIs
  • staging and dev environments
  • bots, cron jobs, internal tools
  • Docker or Coolify hosts for small projects

Watch out for:

  • performance that varies with time of day
  • confusing "more vCPUs" with "more guaranteed CPU": a bigger shared plan still has neighbours

Cost shape: lowest monthly price, no hardware to buy, online in minutes.

VDS: dedicated cores

Same idea as a VPS (virtual machine, root access, images, snapshots), but the physical cores behind your vCPUs are reserved for you. No other customer runs on them, so a request that takes 40 ms at 3 a.m. still takes about 40 ms at peak hours.

Good for:

  • databases under steady load
  • CI runners, builds, video encoding
  • game servers (players notice latency spikes before anything else)
  • ERP, CRM and business apps where "slow today" is a support ticket

Watch out for:

  • paying for dedicated cores your workload never uses. If your CPU graph is flat at 5% all day, a VPS is fine.

Cost shape: several times the per-core price of a VPS, still no hardware to buy, still online in minutes.

Colocation: your hardware, their building

With colocation you own the server. You ship it (or drive it) to the data center. They rack it, connect power and network, and keep the building secure and cooled. You manage everything from the OS up.

Good for:

  • workloads that run 24/7 for years, where owning the hardware is cheaper than renting it
  • specific hardware: lots of disks, GPUs, special NICs, or a server you already own
  • compliance or data-residency reasons for knowing exactly where the hardware sits
  • moving a server out of an office closet that keeps losing power or overheating

Watch out for:

  • Power. Plans come with a fixed amperage (1–2 A for a single server is common). Check your server's real draw, especially with GPUs.
  • Rails. Rack plans usually require a rails kit. Order it with the server.
  • Remote access. If a bad network change locks you out, you need a way back in that doesn't involve a truck. Look for an out-of-band console option (IPMI, iDRAC or iLO over a separate network).
  • Spare parts. Your hardware, your failed disk. Keep a spare drive and PSU in mind.

Cost shape: you buy the hardware once, then pay a monthly fee for space, power and network.

Side by side

VPS VDS Colocation
Who owns the hardware Provider Provider You
CPU Shared vCPU Dedicated cores Whatever you install
Performance under load Varies with neighbours Steady Steady (it's your box)
Time to get online Minutes Minutes Days (shipping and racking)
Upfront cost None None The hardware
Scaling Resize the plan Resize the plan Add servers or rack space
You manage OS and up OS and up Hardware, OS and up
Best when Load comes in bursts Load is constant Load is constant for years, or the hardware is special

Five questions that decide it

  1. Is your CPU busy most of the day, or in short bursts? Bursts → VPS. Busy → VDS or colocation.
  2. Does a slowdown cost you money or users? Yes → dedicated cores (VDS) or your own hardware.
  3. Do you already own the server, or need specific hardware? Yes → colocation.
  4. Will this workload exist, unchanged, in two years? Yes → do the rent-vs-own maths below.
  5. Who fixes it at 2 a.m.? If nobody on your team wants to handle hardware, stay virtual (VPS or VDS), or use colocation with a provider that offers out-of-band access and hands-on support.

Rent vs own: the maths

The break-even point is simple:

months to break even = hardware cost / (monthly rental price − monthly colocation fee)

Hypothetical example: you rent a dedicated-core server for $160/month. A comparable server you buy costs $1,500, and a 1U colocation slot costs $69/month.

1500 / (160 − 69) = 1500 / 91 ≈ 16.5 months

After about a year and a half, owning is cheaper, provided the workload stays the same and you're fine handling hardware. If the workload might change or disappear in a year, renting wins. Put your own numbers in. That's the whole point.

Where Avant fits

Disclosure first: this is the company I work for. The prices below are what's on our site today.

VPS: shared vCPU (Flint, MI in USD, or Sofia, Bulgaria in EUR excl. VAT)

Plan vCPU RAM SSD Monthly 12 months upfront
VPS-1 1 2 GB 40 GB $5 $36
VPS-2 2 4 GB 80 GB $8 $57.60
VPS-4 4 8 GB 160 GB $16 $115.20
VPS-8 8 16 GB 320 GB $32 $230.40

Larger tiers go up to VPS-32 (32 vCPU, 64 GB, $128/mo).

VDS: dedicated cores (Flint or Sofia)

Plan Cores RAM SSD Monthly 12 months upfront
VDS-2 2 8 GB 100 GB $40 $288
VDS-4 4 16 GB 200 GB $80 $576
VDS-8 8 32 GB 400 GB $160 $1,152

Larger tiers go up to VDS-32 (32 cores, 128 GB, $640/mo)

Both include full root access, one public IPv4, and free Linux images (Ubuntu, Debian, AlmaLinux, Rocky), with Docker, Coolify and CloudPanel ready to go. Windows Server is $5 per vCPU or core per month.

How you pay (same on VPS and VDS, discounts don't stack):

  • Monthly: every 4th month is free while the subscription stays active
  • 6 months upfront: 30% off, and it renews at that rate
  • 12 months upfront: 40% off, and it renews at that rate

  • Mini PC $35/mo, Tower $65/mo, Full Tower $75/mo in Flint (Sofia: €34, €64, €74)
  • 1U $69/mo, 2U $79/mo, 4U $99/mo (all US sites)
  • Private racks: quarter, half and full. In Flint these are $330, $530 and $930/mo; Phoenix and Ashburn are priced higher.
