title: Por qué du y el Finder muestran tamaños distintos para la misma carpeta
description:
Ejecuta du -sh sobre una carpeta y compáralo con el tamaño del Finder: a menudo no coinciden, a veces por varios gigabytes. Ninguno se equivoca. Responden a preguntas distintas: cuánto miden los archivos y cuánto espacio del disco ocupan. Cuando el disco está lleno solo importa la segunda, y calcularla bien exige algo más que sumar st_size.

Las reglas de abajo son las que sigue la pantalla Disk de la aplicación de escritorio osFoundry. Su escáner es una función corta de Rust sobre std::fs, y la misma lógica cabe en unas 40 líneas de Python. Todos los números salen de una carpeta de prueba en un volumen APFS con bloques de asignación de 4 KB.

Cuenta bloques, no bytes

st_size es la longitud del archivo. st_blocks es el número de unidades de 512 bytes que el sistema de archivos ha asignado, sea cual sea el tamaño de bloque real del volumen. El escáner de la aplicación usa por defecto la segunda:

fn allocated_bytes(meta: &fs::Metadata, apparent: bool) -> u64 {
    if apparent {
        return meta.len();
    }
    #[cfg(unix)]
    {
        use std::os::unix::fs::MetadataExt;
        meta.blocks().saturating_mul(512)
    }
    #[cfg(not(unix))]
    {
        meta.len()
    }
}

Tres archivos de la carpeta de prueba muestran por qué:

Archivo st_size st_blocks × 512
small.txt (2 bytes de texto) 2 4,096
sparse.img (truncado a 1 GiB, nunca escrito) 1,073,741,824 0
big.bin (200 MiB de datos) 209,715,200 209,715,200

Un archivo diminuto ocupa igualmente un bloque entero, así que una carpeta con 100.000 archivos pequeños ocupa en disco varios cientos de megabytes más de lo que indica su recuento de bytes. Un archivo disperso (sparse) es lo contrario: los discos de máquinas virtuales, los archivos de bases de datos y algunas descargas reservan una longitud grande y solo usan bloques en las partes escritas. El du de macOS cuenta bloques; du -A muestra el tamaño aparente. La casilla Apparent size de la aplicación hace ese mismo cambio.

No sigas enlaces ni salgas del volumen

Un escáner que sigue enlaces simbólicos puede contar dos veces la misma carpeta, o entrar en un bucle infinito con un enlace que apunta a su propio directorio padre. Uno que entra en una unidad montada suma los archivos de otro disco al total de este. La aplicación lee cada entrada con symlink_metadata, que describe el enlace y no su destino, y compara los ID de dispositivo con los de la carpeta donde empezó el escaneo:

if child_meta.file_type().is_symlink() || !same_device(root_meta, &child_meta) {
    continue;
}

same_device compara st_dev, que es la misma comprobación que hacen du -x o find -xdev.

Enlaces duros y clones

Los enlaces duros son un único archivo con varios nombres. En la carpeta de prueba, ln big.bin hard.bin hace que ls -l muestre dos archivos de 200 MiB, pero du cuenta los datos una sola vez porque recuerda cada par (st_dev, st_ino) que ya ha visto siempre que st_nlink sea mayor que 1. Cualquier escáner que sume bloques debería hacer lo mismo. Las copias de Time Machine en discos HFS+ y algunos gestores de paquetes dependen mucho de los enlaces duros.

Los clones de APFS son más difíciles. cp -c big.bin clone.bin (o Duplicar en el Finder) crea un segundo archivo que comparte los bloques del original hasta que uno de los dos cambia. Cada archivo tiene su propio inodo, su propio st_blocks y un recuento de enlaces de 1, de modo que du cuenta 400 MiB para el par. Medido con df antes y después, el clon ocupó 0 KB de espacio libre, mientras que un cp normal del mismo archivo ocupó 204.984 KB. Ningún campo POSIX muestra que se comparten bloques, así que un total basado en bloques exagera lo que se recupera al borrar un clon. Para carpetas llenas de proyectos duplicados o bibliotecas de fotos, comparar df antes y después es la única comprobación fiable.

Una versión en Python

Las mismas reglas, solo con la biblioteca estándar:

import os
import stat
import sys

def usage(root):
    root_dev = os.lstat(root).st_dev
    seen = set()
    allocated = apparent = 0
    skipped = 0
    stack = [root]
    while stack:
        path = stack.pop()
        try:
            entries = list(os.scandir(path))
        except OSError:
            skipped += 1
            continue
        for e in entries:
            try:
                st = e.stat(follow_symlinks=False)
            except OSError:
                skipped += 1
                continue
            if stat.S_ISLNK(st.st_mode) or st.st_dev != root_dev:
                continue
            if stat.S_ISDIR(st.st_mode):
                stack.append(e.path)
                continue
            if st.st_nlink > 1:
                key = (st.st_dev, st.st_ino)
                if key in seen:
                    continue
                seen.add(key)
            allocated += st.st_blocks * 512
            apparent += st.st_size
    return allocated, apparent, skipped

if __name__ == "__main__":
    alloc, appar, skipped = usage(sys.argv[1])
    print(f"on disk  {alloc / 2**30:8.2f} GiB")
    print(f"apparent {appar / 2**30:8.2f} GiB")
    if skipped:
        print(f"skipped  {skipped} unreadable entries")

En la carpeta de prueba imprime 0,39 GiB en disco y 1,39 GiB aparentes, lo que coincide con du -sk (409.604 KB) y du -sAk. En un árbol de código fuente de 14 GiB coincide con du -sk hasta dos decimales. Conserva el recuento de entradas omitidas: en macOS, las carpetas protegidas por permisos de privacidad (Mail, Mensajes, Safari) no se pueden leer sin Acceso total al disco, y un total que las deja fuera sin avisar parece más completo de lo que es.

La aplicación mantiene el resultado lo bastante pequeño como para dibujarlo. Cada carpeta conserva sus 36 hijos más grandes y el resto se suma en un único nodo "Other items"; así, al abrir una carpeta node_modules con mil paquetes se ven 36 cajas y una más para todo lo demás, no mil rendijas.

Borrar con seguridad

El verdadero riesgo de una herramienta de disco está en el paso de borrar. La aplicación mueve los elementos a la Papelera del sistema con el crate trash en lugar de eliminarlos con unlink, y comprueba cada ruta antes de mover nada:

if !target.starts_with(&root) || target == root || home.as_ref() == Some(&target) {
    return Err("Cannot move a scan root or home folder to Trash".into());
}
if mount_points
    .iter()
    .any(|mount| target == *mount || target.parent() == Some(mount.as_path()))
{
    return Err("Cannot move a volume or its top-level items to Trash".into());
}

Las rutas se canonicalizan primero, de modo que .. o un enlace simbólico no pueden colar un destino fuera de la carpeta escaneada. También se rechaza una selección en la que una carpeta marcada contiene a otra, porque en cuanto la carpeta padre está en la Papelera la ruta del hijo deja de existir y el lote fallaría a medias.

La aplicación de escritorio es gratuita en la página de descarga de osFoundry.

title: Designing a workout screen that nobody is supposed to look at
description:
I work on FightNome, so this post is about our own app.

FightNome is a pad-work trainer for boxing, Muay Thai, kickboxing and MMA. A recorded voice calls strikes on the beat of the music and you throw them. The whole idea only works if your eyes stay on the bag or the pads, so the phone is meant to sit in a pocket or a waistband for the entire round. That puts the app in an odd spot as a design problem. Most of the time the main screen has no audience at all.

I've written before about timing the voice files and about the combo editor. This one is about everything around the round itself.

Before the bell: show the whole plan

If you can't glance at the phone mid-round, you need to know what's coming before you start. So the workout screen lays out the full plan before you press play: every
section, every round, every rest, in order. A workout is sections (striking or conditioning) made of rounds, and the conditioning parts are rope, shadow work and bodyweight between the striking rounds.

That screen gets the attention the in-round screen doesn't. People read it once with gloves still off, and after that they listen.

During the round: the screen still exists

There is an active-session screen. It shows the round counter, time left, the called combination as strike tiles and a timeline of the tempo. It's there for the moment when someone does pull the phone out, between rounds or to check how long is left. I don't treat it as the main interface, though. If a session only feels right while you're watching the tiles light up, the audio side has failed.

Controls you can reach without the screen

The controls that matter during a round have to work with the phone out of sight:

  • play and pause from the headphone remote,
  • a lock-screen card, so a quick look doesn't mean unlocking,
  • workout alarms, where the phone rings at the set time with a short recorded coach line and one tap starts that workout.

The alarm uses AlarmKit on iOS 26. Its permission text says the alarm appears on screen even if a Focus is active, which is the reason we picked it over a regular notification for this.

The voice carries the information

Because the screen is out of the loop, everything you need mid-round has to be in the audio. Every strike is a recorded word, and the words are chosen per strike in the editor, so a gym that says "two" and a gym that says "cross" can both get what they're used to. The session ends with a spoken line too ("Breathe. You've earned this."), so you know you're done without checking.

The stats come after, when you're back to looking at the phone: streak, rank, volume over time, personal records and how many calls you answered in that session. History syncs privately through iCloud. There's no account and no server of ours in between.

What I'm still unsure about

The hardest part is deciding what to say out loud and what to leave on screen. Time left in a round is a good example. Saying it often gets annoying fast, and never saying it makes people pull the phone out, which defeats the point. If you've built anything that's used eyes-free, like a running app, a cooking timer or something for cyclists, I'd like to know how you decided what the voice says and what it leaves out.

If you want to try it

FightNome is on the App Store (iOS 26 and up) and Google Play. It's a paid subscription, and only the yearly plan has a 3-day trial. More at https://fightnome.app.

title: Get Expert Answers to Your StackOverflow Questions
description:
Stack Overflow is one of the most popular online platforms where developers can ask technical questions, share knowledge, and find solutions to programming challenges. Whether you are a beginner learning web development or an experienced software engineer, getting expert answers to your Stack Overflow questions can help you solve complex coding problems efficiently.
**web development **services at dot simplify.

  1. Ask Clear and Specific Questions

The first step towards getting expert answers is to frame your questions clearly. Instead of asking broad questions, describe the exact problem you are facing. Mention the programming language, framework, tools, and expected outcome. A well-defined question makes it easier for experienced developers to understand your issue.

  1. Include Relevant Code Examples

Always provide a minimal, reproducible example of your code. Include only the sections necessary to demonstrate the problem. This helps other developers identify errors without going through unnecessary code.

  1. Explain the Error Message

If you encounter an error, share the complete error message and explain when it occurs. Providing details about your operating system, programming environment, and software versions can also help experts identify the root cause.

  1. Use Proper Tags

Stack Overflow allows users to add tags to their questions. Using relevant tags such as JavaScript, Python, ReactJS, HTML, or CSS helps your question reach developers who have expertise in those technologies.

  1. Research Before Posting

Before submitting a question, search Stack Overflow to check whether someone has already discussed a similar problem. Reviewing existing answers can save time and help you understand different approaches to solving the issue.

  1. Engage with the Community

Getting expert answers is not just about posting questions. Respond to comments, provide additional information when requested, and acknowledge helpful answers. Accepting the most appropriate answer also helps other developers facing similar challenges.

title: I built an MCP tool and the agent never called it. Here's what worked instead.
description:
Every codebase has rules nobody wrote down. One package always checks rows.Err() after iterating. Another logs through slog and never log.Printf. Every method on Store names its receiver s. Tests in this directory use testify; tests over there use the standard library.

AI coding agents break these rules constantly, not because they're careless but because they cannot see them. The rules live in the statistics of the code, not in any file. The standard fix is to write them down in a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. Someone has to write it, keep it current, and hope it covers what matters. A typical hand-written file has 20 or 30 rules for an entire repository. The repository has thousands.

I spent the summer trying to close that gap automatically. The first two attempts failed, and the way they failed is the useful part.

Attempt 1: give the agent a tool

The obvious design in 2026 is an MCP server. Index the repo, mine its conventions, and expose one tool, get_style_context, that takes a file path and returns the rules, tendencies and example functions for that file's directory. The agent calls it before editing, reads the rules, writes conforming code.

I ran a controlled experiment: 15 runs, same tasks, the tool available every time. The agent called it zero times.

I assumed the tool description was the problem and rewrote it. More imperative. More specific about when to use it. Still zero. The agents did what they always do: read the file, read a neighbour or two, write code. They had no signal that they were missing anything, so they never went looking.

That's the general lesson, and it's bigger than my tool. An agent will not voluntarily look up knowledge it doesn't know it lacks. A knowledge-lookup tool that depends on the agent's initiative is a tool that doesn't get used.

Attempt 2: push the rules at it

If the agent won't pull, push. Claude Code has a PreToolUse hook that runs before an Edit or Write. I used it to inject the relevant conventions right before each edit landed.

Six blind-scored runs on Kubernetes with Claude Opus. The agent wrote the same code with or without the injected rules.

In hindsight the reason is obvious. By the time PreToolUse fires, the agent has already authored the edit. The content is in the tool call. Rules that arrive at that moment are advice about a decision that's already been made.

Attempt 3: stop telling, start checking

The thing that works is boring. Don't try to inform the agent at all. Let it write the code, then check the code, and if it breaks a rule hand the violation back as an error.

OpenTuple does this with a PostToolUse hook on Edit|Write. After every edit it re-parses the file with tree-sitter, works out which directory each function belongs to, and compares the function with the conventions mined from that directory. If something breaks a rule, the hook exits with status 2, which is the code Claude Code uses to show a hook's stderr to the agent. The agent sees this:

internal/cli/summary.go:9: PrintIndexSummary calls fmt.Fprintf but never Render
  Rule: In internal/cli, functions that call fmt.Fprintf also call Render. [helper_pairing]
  Evidence: 12 of 12 functions in internal/cli that call fmt.Fprintf also call Render (100%); 4% of the functions that do not call fmt.Fprintf call Render.
  Example: reportWrittenFiles (internal/cli/generate.go:218) follows this rule.

That's from a real run with Claude Haiku. It was asked to add a summary printer to a CLI package and its first version printed with a bare fmt.Fprintf. Every other printer in the package styles its output through the theme. The hook said so. The agent's next edit wrapped the text in StyleDim.Render(...), the check passed, the session ended. Four turns, nine seconds. Nobody told it about the theme. The repository did.

Why does this work when the first two didn't? Because an agent treats a hook error the way it treats a failing test. It's not advice it can weigh and discard. It's a blocker it has to clear. The timing that made attempt 2 fail (the hook fires after the content exists) is exactly the timing a check needs.

The hard part was silence

Detection turned out to be the easy half. The hard half was not flagging things that aren't wrong.

A convention checker lives or dies on false positives. The first time it complains about something that was fine, the developer learns the check is noise, and the second time they turn it off. So OpenTuple's rules are deliberately strict:

  • A rule exists only where at least 98% of a directory's functions follow it, with at least 10 of them.
  • A helper pairing (functions that call Lock also call Unlock) has to beat the paired helper's base rate by 30 points. Otherwise, in a package where everything calls Errorf, everything that calls Close "pairs" with Errorf too.
  • An absence rule ("nothing here calls panic") needs enough functions that you'd expect some to call it at the repo-wide rate. Ten functions that never needed Close is a small sample, not a policy.
  • Test files are their own scope, so a convention of your tests is never imposed on your library code.

The measure of this is how quiet it is on code that already follows its own conventions. Running the check across whole repositories:

Repository Files Flags
fzf 79 0
GitHub CLI 860 3
Kubernetes v1.29 7,845 49
10 JS/TS repos 3,191 0

The 49 in Kubernetes are real minority deviations: 31 test functions using a different assertion library from the rest of their package, 11 doc comments, 3 receiver names, 2 pairings, 1 logging call outside klog, 1 error-handling site.

What it looks like to use 

go install github.com/CtrlAltDelete-Ops/opentuple/cmd/opentuple@latest
cd your-repo
opentuple init .

init indexes the repo (Kubernetes, 9,711 files, takes 27 seconds on an M3), writes a short CLAUDE.md per directory and one AGENTS.md for tools that read a single file, and installs the hook in .claude/settings.local.json. Then you start a Claude Code session and forget about it. Not on Claude Code? --git-hook runs the same check on staged files as a pre-commit hook.

One Go binary. Runs locally. No network requests. Apache-2.0. Go, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Rust and C.

What I don't know yet

I'll be upfront about the gaps. .tsx files go through the TypeScript grammar, which has no JSX, so React components are only partly seen. There are no prebuilt binaries yet, so you need Go installed. And my behavioural numbers come from small runs. I know the mechanism works; I don't yet have a large, independently graded measurement of how often it fires on real agent-written code, and I'd like help designing one.

The repo is at https://github.com/CtrlAltDelete-Ops/opentuple. If you run it on your codebase, the thing I most want to hear is what it flagged and whether it was right.

title: I ran the same three programs in six languages. Rust did not win all of them.
description:
"Rust is fast" is true often enough that people stop checking. While building Ruststudio (an IDE for Rust, written in Rust) I wanted a page that tells newcomers when Rust is worth the learning curve, so I measured instead of repeating slogans.

The setup: three small programs, written the same way in Rust, Go, C#, Java, Node and Python. Each prints a checksum, and all six languages print the same one, so they did the same work. Each ran three times at below-normal priority; I report the median. Machine: i7-10750H, 12 logical cores, Windows 11. Rust 1.93, Go 1.26.5, .NET 10, OpenJDK 17, Node 22, Python 3.13. Start-up time is included, so Java and C# pay for starting their runtime.

Speed (seconds, lower is better)

Rust Go C# Java Node Python
Mandelbrot 800x800 0.09 0.09 0.17 0.18 0.15 2.74
Primes below 20 million 0.16 0.18 0.23 0.24 0.26 1.15
Word count, 3 million words 0.81 0.43 0.47 0.55 0.60 1.71

On the two number-crunching programs Rust and Go lead. Python is 30 times slower on the Mandelbrot set.

Now look at the last row. Go and C# beat Rust on the word count, nearly twice as fast. The program creates millions of small strings and looks each one up in a hash map. Rust's default hash map uses an attack-resistant hash, and the program used the system allocator, which loses to the allocators built into Go and .NET for many tiny objects. A fast hasher helped only a little (0.75 s), so most of the cost is allocation. Rust gives you the control to fix that (reuse buffers, avoid the allocation, choose another allocator). It does not do it for you.

Memory (peak MB)

Rust Go C# Java Node Python
Mandelbrot 3.9 5.6 21.0 38.0 30.7 10.7
Primes 23.0 25.5 39.6 55.8 47.9 48.8
Word count 8.0 13.0 35.3 99.1 49.5 16.2

Rust used the least in all three. There is no garbage collector, so memory comes back when a value goes out of scope.

What you ship

The Rust benchmark became one 146 KB executable that needs nothing installed. Go: 2.4 MB, also standalone. C# and Java need their runtimes; Node and Python need the interpreter and their packages.

The bugs that never run

I wrote the same small bug in each language. A missing value used as if present, use after move, a reference that outlives its target: in Rust all three are compile errors. In every other language the first one crashes at run time.

The one that surprised me: eight threads adding to one counter with no lock. Rust refuses to compile it. Go printed 244,043, C# 207,098 and Java 117,040, where the right answer is 800,000. No error, and a different wrong total each time. (Node is single threaded, and Python's global lock happened to hide it in my run. That is luck, not a guarantee.)

What Rust costs

It is wordier: 83 lines against Python's 41. Release builds compile slower. Ownership takes weeks to feel natural. Some ecosystems (mature GUI toolkits, enterprise libraries) are thinner than Java's or .NET's. And integer overflow is not stopped: a release build wraps like everyone else's.

So when?

Choose Rust when a crash or a security hole is expensive, when you need predictable latency without GC pauses, when you want one small executable, or when the code will live for years. Choose something else for throw-away scripts, or when your team already ships fast Java or .NET and the hot path is not critical.

Everything here is regenerated by scripts. The full write-up, with the bug table and the method, is at https://ruststudio.org/why-rust. These are small programs on one PC: an illustration of trade-offs, not a verdict. If you think a program is unfair to your favourite language, send a fix.

title: How we built a RabbitMQ desktop client with Electron, tRPC and SQLite
description:
Introduction

RabbitGUI is a desktop client for RabbitMQ that runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. It is built with Electron, and this article explains how the pieces fit together. The main process talks to RabbitMQ, exposes everything to the UI through a typed tRPC API, and stores messages in a local SQLite database. The renderer is a plain React app that never touches the network or the disk itself.

If you are building a developer tool on Electron, most of this applies to you too. None of it is specific to RabbitMQ.

Why a desktop app at all?

RabbitMQ already ships a web UI, the management plugin. We could have built another web app on top of the same HTTP API. We didn't, for three reasons:

  1. A browser can't speak AMQP. The management HTTP API is fine for listing queues and reading stats, but the interesting features need a real AMQP 0-9-1 connection over a raw TCP socket: consuming a whole queue, spying on live traffic, republishing thousands of messages with throttling. Browsers only get TCP through WebSockets, which would need an extra plugin on the broker. A Node.js process gets TCP sockets out of the box.
  2. No server in the middle. A hosted web app would need a backend that holds your broker credentials and can reach your private network. A desktop app connects from your machine directly to your broker, the same way your own services do. Credentials never leave your computer (more on that in how security is built into RabbitGUI).
  3. Local storage that can handle real volumes. Debugging a dead-letter queue often means looking at tens of thousands of messages. We wanted to copy them once and then search, filter and group them as often as needed without loading the broker again. That calls for a real database on disk, not localStorage.

Electron gives us all three while keeping a single language, TypeScript, from the AMQP socket down to the React components.

The architecture in one picture 

┌──────────────────────────── Electron app ────────────────────────────┐
│                                                                      │
│  Renderer process (Chromium)          Main process (Node.js)         │
│  ─────────────────────────            ──────────────────────         │
│  React 19                             tRPC router                    │
│  TanStack Router + Query   ── IPC ──▶ ├─ fetch  ──▶ Management API   │
│  tRPC client (ipcLink)     ◀───────── ├─ amqplib ─▶ AMQP 0-9-1       │
│  Monaco, React Flow,                  └─ Kysely + better-sqlite3     │
│  Recharts, Tailwind                        │                         │
│                                            ▼                         │
│                                    user-data.db (SQLite, WAL)        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼
                         Your RabbitMQ broker(s)

The rule is simple: the renderer only renders. Anything that touches the network, the file system or a secret lives in the main process, and the renderer reaches it only through typed tRPC procedures.

The main process speaks two protocols

The management HTTP API

Most of what you see in RabbitGUI comes from the RabbitMQ management API: queues, exchanges, bindings, policies, users, vhosts and the message rate time series. In the main process it is just fetch with basic auth:

export const api = async <T>(path: string, { method = 'get', credentials, body }) => {
  const response = await fetch(credentials.baseUrl + path, {
    method,
    headers: {
      Authorization:
        'Basic ' +
        Buffer.from(`${credentials.username}:${credentials.password}`).toString('base64'),
      'Content-Type': 'application/json',
    },
    body: JSON.stringify(body),
  })

  if (!response.ok) {
    // Map RabbitMQ errors to typed tRPC errors (404 => NOT_FOUND, etc.)
  }

  return (await response.json()) as T
}

Since the request comes from Node.js and not from a web page, there is no CORS to configure on the broker. You point RabbitGUI at the same URL you would open in your browser, and it works.

The API is paginated, so the main process walks every page before returning. The renderer always receives the full list and can sort and filter it instantly:

const data = await queues(credentials, { page: 1, pageSize: 100 })

while (data.page_count > data.page) {
  const next = await queues(credentials, { page: data.page + 1, pageSize: 100 })
  data.items.push(...next.items)
  data.page = next.page
}

AMQP 0-9-1 with amqplib

The management API has a "get messages" endpoint, but the RabbitMQ docs describe it as a diagnostics tool for sysadmins: it does not implement reliable delivery and pulls messages one HTTP request at a time. For anything involving many messages we open a real AMQP connection with amqplib, still from the main process.

The live queue spy is a good example. To watch a queue without stealing messages from your consumers, RabbitGUI declares a temporary, exclusive queue and copies the bindings of the queue you are watching onto it. RabbitMQ then delivers a copy of each matching message to both queues:

const connection = await amqp.connect(amqpUrl)
const channel = await connection.createChannel()

// Server-named, exclusive, deleted when the connection closes
const { queue: tempQueue } = await channel.assertQueue('', {
  exclusive: true,
  autoDelete: true,
})

// Same bindings as the queue we are spying on
for (const binding of await queueBindings(credentials, { vhost, queue })) {
  if (binding.source) {
    await channel.bindQueue(tempQueue, binding.source, binding.routing_key, binding.arguments)
  }
}

await channel.consume(tempQueue, async (msg) => {
  if (!msg) return
  channel.ack(msg)
  await db.insertInto('consumed_messages').values(toRow(msg)).execute()
})

Because the spy queue is exclusive and auto-delete, closing the app or the connection removes it. Nothing is left behind on your broker.

The same idea powers browsing a queue without consuming it. RabbitGUI consumes the queue, writes every message to SQLite, and either requeues them or removes them, depending on the mode you pick. Requeued messages come back with the redelivered flag set, and on quorum queues with an incremented x-delivery-count. So we strip those headers and hash the body plus the remaining headers. If you extract the same queue twice, you don't get duplicates in the local database.

tRPC over Electron IPC

Electron's IPC is untyped. You ipcRenderer.invoke('some-channel', args) and hope the main process handles that string. With a few dozen features, that gets fragile fast. So we put tRPC on top of it with trpc-electron.

The main process defines ordinary tRPC routers, validated with zod:

export const queuesRouter = router({
  list: publicProcedure.input(z.string()).query(async ({ input: connexionId }) => {
    // management API + local SQLite counts
  }),
  purge: publicProcedure
    .input(z.object({ connexionId: z.string(), vhost: z.string(), queue: z.string() }))
    .mutation(async ({ input }) => {
      await purgeQueue(getCredentials(input.connexionId), { name: input.queue, vhost: input.vhost })
    }),
})

export const appRouter = router({
  connexions: connexionsRouter,
  queues: queuesRouter,
  exchanges: exchangesRouter,
  localMessages: localMessagesRouter,
  spy: spyRouter,
  // ...
})
export type AppRouter = typeof appRouter

It is wired to the window with a single call:

createIPCHandler({ router: appRouter, windows: [mainWindow] })

The preload script exposes the bridge (exposeElectronTRPC()), and the renderer creates a client with an IPC link instead of an HTTP one:

export const trpcClient = createTRPCClient<AppRouter>({
  links: [ipcLink()],
})

export const trpc = createTRPCOptionsProxy<AppRouter>({
  client: trpcClient,
  queryClient,
})

What we get out of this:

  • End-to-end types. The renderer imports only the AppRouter type. Renaming a procedure or changing an input breaks the renderer build, not the app at runtime.
  • TanStack Query for free. Every procedure becomes useQuery(trpc.queues.list.queryOptions(connexionId)), with caching, refetch intervals, loading states and invalidation after mutations. Live dashboards are just a refetchInterval.
  • Typed errors. The main process maps RabbitMQ failures to TRPCErrors. The renderer can, for example, skip retries on a NOT_FOUND when a queue was deleted under your feet.
  • No channel names to maintain. There is not a single hand-written ipcMain.handle for app features.

Long-running jobs, like extracting 50,000 messages, don't block a request. The mutation starts the job in the main process and returns. The renderer polls a status query that reports progress until the job is done.

SQLite as the local source of truth

Messages you extract, spy on or publish go into a SQLite database in Electron's userData folder. We use better-sqlite3 with Kysely as a type-safe query builder:

const sqlite = new SQLite(path.join(app.getPath('userData'), 'user-data.db'))
sqlite.pragma('journal_mode = WAL')

export const db = new Kysely<DB>({
  dialect: new SqliteDialect({ database: sqlite }),
})

Schema changes ship as Kysely migrations defined in code and run at startup with migrator.migrateToLatest(), so a user who skips a few versions still ends up with the right schema. In development, kysely-codegen regenerates the DB type from the real database after each migration. Queries stay typed without maintaining types by hand.

The main table, consumed_messages, stores the payload, the AMQP properties, and a few columns lifted out of the headers for fast filtering: delivery count, and the first and last death exchange, queue and reason from x-death. Composite indexes on (connexionId, vhost, queue, …) keep filters and facet counts fast on large extractions.

Having the messages in SQL is what makes the dead-letter workflow possible:

  • Filters, full-text search and facets ("how many messages per routing key or death reason?") are SQL queries, not something RabbitMQ can answer.
  • You can republish a hand-picked subset, to its original queue or anywhere else, with throttling.
  • The queue list joins live stats from the management API with local counts, so you can see which queues have messages saved on your machine.

The spy view keeps the newest 1,000 messages per queue and deletes older rows, so a busy queue can't fill your disk.

Small settings, like connections, saved table views and appearance, live in a JSON config file managed by electron-conf and not in SQLite.

The renderer: just a React app

Because everything heavy happens in the main process, the renderer is a regular single-page React app:

  • React 19 with TanStack Router for file-based routes, and TanStack Query through the tRPC proxy.
  • Tailwind CSS and Radix UI primitives for the interface.
  • Monaco, the editor behind VS Code, for the JSON message editor.
  • React Flow with elkjs for automatic layout of the routing graph of exchanges, bindings, queues and dead-letter paths.
  • Recharts for the message rate charts and the drain-time forecast.

There is no API base URL to configure, no auth token to refresh, no CORS. The renderer could run in a browser tab against a different link without code changes, which also makes it easy to iterate on with hot reload through electron-vite.

Building and shipping

  • electron-vite builds the main, preload and renderer bundles with Vite.
  • electron-builder packages the app for macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel, signed and notarized), Windows and Linux. Linux builds run in the electronuserland/builder Docker image.
  • better-sqlite3 is a native module, so it has to be compiled against Electron's Node ABI and not your system Node. electron-builder install-app-deps runs on postinstall to take care of that. It is the one part of the stack that occasionally needs attention after an Electron upgrade.
  • electron-updater checks for a new version a few seconds after launch and installs updates in the background.

Trade-offs we accepted

Electron isn't free. The download is bigger than a native app's, and an idle window uses more memory than a terminal tool would. For a tool you open to debug a broker, we think it's the right trade:

  • One language and one type system from the AMQP consumer to the button that triggers it.
  • Mature Node.js libraries for exactly what we need (amqplib, better-sqlite3), running in-process with no sidecar.
  • The same codebase and UI on macOS, Windows and Linux.

Start your own app from a boilerplate

Wiring all of this by hand takes days: the IPC bridge, native module rebuilds, migrations, code signing, notarization and auto updates. If you want the same architecture for your own desktop app, start from a boilerplate instead.

We extracted the stack behind RabbitGUI into Electron AppStack, a free, production-ready Electron + TypeScript starter. It ships with React, tRPC over IPC, SQLite, auto updates and signed releases, plus documentation for each piece:

npx degit nick-keller/electron-appstack/template my-app
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev

You get the main process / renderer split described in this article on day one, and can spend your time on the features that make your app different.

If you are curious what this architecture adds up to in practice, RabbitGUI is available for macOS, Windows and Linux, or have a look at what it does compared to the management UI.

Originally published on the RabbitGUI blog.

title: The Psychology of Digital Habits: How Developers Can Build Healthier User Experiences
description:
Modern applications are designed to keep users engaged. Notifications, personalized recommendations, infinite scrolling, and gamification make digital products convenient and entertaining.

But there is an important question every developer should consider:

Are we building products that genuinely help people, or simply products that keep them coming back?

Understanding the psychology behind digital habits can help development teams create better user experiences without encouraging compulsive behavior.

  1. Variable Rewards and User Engagement

One common mechanism in digital products is the variable reward system.

Users open an application without knowing exactly what they will find. There might be a new message, an interesting recommendation, or a notification.

This uncertainty can encourage repeated checking.

You can find similar mechanisms in:

Social media feeds

Short-video platforms

Online games

Recommendation systems

Notification-driven applications

From a product analytics perspective, these interactions may increase session frequency and daily active users.

However, engagement metrics do not always reflect user satisfaction.

A person opening an application twenty times a day is not necessarily getting more value from it than someone who opens it twice.

  1. Infinite Scrolling and the Lack of Stopping Points

Infinite scrolling removes the natural boundaries between content sections.

Traditional pagination gives users a moment to decide whether they want to continue. Infinite scrolling automatically presents another piece of content.

This design can be useful when browsing large collections, but it can also make sessions longer than users originally intended.

Developers can make this experience more responsible by:

Providing clear content boundaries.

Offering a way to save interesting materials.

Avoiding unnecessary automatic content loading.

Making navigation and stopping points visible.

Giving users control over recommendations.

Good UX should make it easy to accomplish a task, not difficult to leave the application.

  1. Notifications Should Have a Purpose

Notifications are valuable when they communicate something important.

A message about a security issue, a completed deployment, or an incoming work request may require immediate attention.

But not every event deserves a push notification.

Consider separating notifications into three categories:

Critical notifications: Security alerts, production incidents, and urgent system events.

Useful notifications: Messages, task updates, and relevant reminders.

Optional notifications: Recommendations, promotional content, and general engagement reminders.

This approach helps users distinguish important information from background noise.

It also gives developers a practical framework for designing notification preferences.

  1. Measure Value, Not Just Time Spent

Product teams often focus on metrics such as:

Daily Active Users (DAU)

Monthly Active Users (MAU)

Session duration

Retention rate

Number of interactions

These metrics are useful, but they should not be considered in isolation.

For example, a productivity application might become more effective when users spend less time inside it because they can complete tasks faster.

Other useful indicators include:

Metric

What it measures

Task completion rate

Whether users achieve their goals

Time to completion

How efficiently tasks are completed

User satisfaction

How users evaluate the experience

Notification opt-out rate

Whether notifications are perceived as excessive

Return rate

Whether users find ongoing value

The best metric depends on the purpose of the product.

  1. When Digital Habits Become a Problem

Frequent technology use is not automatically an addiction.

However, it may be worth paying attention when a person repeatedly tries to reduce certain behaviors but cannot, or when digital activities begin interfering with sleep, work, relationships, and everyday responsibilities.

Developers should remember that products exist within people's real lives.

Design decisions can influence attention, routines, and behavior. This makes responsible UX an important part of product development.

For readers interested in the psychology of addictive behavior, recovery, and professional support, the Panacea center website provides additional educational information:

https://panacea.clinic/

Conclusion

Developers have a unique opportunity to shape how people interact with technology.

Responsible design does not mean removing engaging features or making applications less useful. It means creating experiences that respect users' time, attention, and ability to make decisions.

Instead of asking only how to increase engagement, product teams should also ask:

How can we help users get the value they came for — and leave when they are ready?

That is a better foundation for building sustainable digital products.

title: Support Email API Bounce Suppression With Auditable Error Logs and Retries
description:
Error logging for failed support email deliveries must establish recipient eligibility before a worker can retry a bounced reply. That constraint changes the design: the application needs a durable decision about whether another attempt is justified, even when API submission results and subsequent delivery reports arrive at different times.

Short answer: record each logical support reply separately from its submission attempts, classify delivery evidence before scheduling another attempt, and check recipient suppression again immediately before dispatch. Retry temporary failures within an explicit deadline; suppress an invalid mailbox when the evidence identifies that condition. Keep uncertain submissions pending reconciliation. An API error log alone cannot establish whether a reply reached its destination.

This approach makes integration effort visible. The substantial work is connecting the support case, submission attempt, delivery report, and suppression decision into one auditable history; adding a retry loop is a comparatively small part of that contract.

What error logging evidence should justify a retry for failed email deliveries?

Start with three distinct records: the intended reply, its attempts, and the recipient's current eligibility. For an illustrative case, case-273 can have a logical reply reply-17 and attempts attempt-1 and attempt-2. These identifiers are example data, not a claim about any existing service. A worker restart should preserve the reply identifier while creating a new attempt identifier only when the application actually authorizes another submission.

Identity comes first.

SMTP and an HTTP API expose different boundaries. RFC 5321 defines SMTP reply classes, including transient negative completion replies in the 4yz class and permanent negative completion replies in the 5yz class; an HTTP status must be interpreted according to the submission API's documented contract, rather than treated as an SMTP delivery verdict. If a request times out after transmission, the local observation is uncertainty about submission. Repeating the request might create a second message unless the receiving system provides and honors an applicable idempotency contract.

Acceptance needs context.

Even an SMTP server accepting responsibility for a message does not establish that a human read the support reply. A useful audit trail therefore distinguishes submission accepted, delivery outcome reported, and support workflow completed, with the evidence for each transition retained separately. The support UI should reflect the strongest available evidence rather than silently promoting acceptance into a stronger claim.

For recipient handling, the enhanced status code matters more than an undifferentiated permanent-failure flag. RFC 3463 identifies 5.1.1 as a bad destination mailbox address, whereas 5.7.1 concerns authorization or refusal. Treating both as an invalid customer address would turn a policy or permission problem into an incorrect suppression decision. SPF belongs to this diagnostic boundary too: RFC 7208 specifies authorization of hosts to use a domain in SMTP identities; it does not verify that a particular customer mailbox exists.

Derive the retry policy from the delivery state

A practical design can begin with five internal states: ready, awaiting outcome, retry scheduled, suppressed, and review required. These are proposed application states. Each transition should record its previous state, the triggering evidence identifier, the decision reason, and the policy version that interpreted the evidence, so that a later reconciliation can explain why a support reply was attempted again or withheld.

For a temporary delivery failure, schedule another attempt only if the recipient remains eligible and the reply remains useful. A support conversation may have advanced while the message was waiting. The application therefore needs a business deadline as well as an attempt limit, and should stop scheduling when either is exhausted. A delayed answer to an already resolved case can be worse than an explicit delivery failure shown to the support agent.

Use bounded backoff with jitter as an application policy, with values selected for the support workflow and the upstream contract. Do not present an arbitrary interval as an SMTP requirement or create a second retry scheduler without first establishing which component owns redelivery. If the upstream mail system is already retrying an accepted message, another application submission is a separate message unless that system documents otherwise.

An invalid-mailbox outcome calls for a different transition: suppress the affected recipient within a deliberately defined scope and cancel pending attempts covered by that suppression. Check eligibility during dispatch as well as during enqueueing, because a reply can enter the queue before a bounce changes the recipient's status. A corrected address should create a recorded eligibility change; deleting the old bounce obscures why earlier attempts stopped.

The dangerous shortcut is easy to describe: convert every negative callback into a new queued send. That erases the distinction between a recoverable transport condition and a recipient that should receive no further attempts.

Unknown stays unknown.

For ambiguous submission outcomes, reconcile against whatever receipt or status mechanism the upstream contract actually supplies. If the contract offers neither durable lookup nor a usable idempotency guarantee, automatic resubmission trades unresolved delivery for duplicate-message risk. Make that trade-off explicit in the support workflow, with a review state and an audit reason, instead of declaring exactly-once delivery from a local database constraint.

Make error logging part of the transaction boundary

The following Go example is a small internal decision function, not a provider adapter or a complete delivery system. It assumes that a separate adapter has validated the event source and normalized its evidence. The illustrative policy schedules a retry after 30 seconds and permits at most 3 attempts; those numbers demonstrate bounded behavior and must be chosen again for an actual deployment.

package delivery

import "time"

type Evidence struct {
    ID         string
    MailboxBad bool
    Temporary  bool
    Ambiguous  bool
}

type Decision struct {
    State  string
    Reason string
    NextAt time.Time
}

func Decide(e Evidence, suppressed bool, attempts int,
    now, deadline time.Time) Decision {
    if suppressed || e.MailboxBad {
        return Decision{State: "suppressed", Reason: "recipient_ineligible"}
    }
    if e.Ambiguous {
        return Decision{State: "review_required", Reason: "submission_unknown"}
    }
    if !e.Temporary {
        return Decision{State: "review_required", Reason: "unclassified_failure"}
    }
    next := now.Add(30 * time.Second)
    if attempts >= 3 || !next.Before(deadline) {
        return Decision{State: "review_required", Reason: "retry_budget_exhausted"}
    }
    return Decision{State: "retry_scheduled", Reason: "temporary_failure", NextAt: next}
}

The fixed delay deliberately keeps this function readable; production scheduling would apply the chosen backoff and jitter policy before checking the resulting time against the deadline. Successful outcomes belong in a separate transition path. This function accepts failure evidence only.

Persist the decision together with the attempt update and its audit entry in one local transaction. Use a uniqueness constraint on the normalized evidence identity within its source scope to make repeated event processing idempotent, and condition state changes on the current stored version so that concurrent workers cannot both authorize the same local transition. If queue publication is separate, a transactional outbox can make the dispatch intention durable alongside that transition. These are local correctness guarantees; the remote send still requires its own reconciliation contract.

Log stable reply and attempt identifiers, the upstream receipt identifier when available, the normalized failure category, the original status code, the evidence time, the ingestion time, and the policy decision. Keep the original diagnostic in a restricted evidence store when operationally necessary, with a reference from the routine log. Avoid copying the support message body, authorization headers, or a full callback payload into every error entry.

An audit trail has limits. Retention duration, access permissions, deletion obligations, and the lawful basis for processing customer identifiers require an organization-specific compliance decision. A redacted log schema and an immutable event history do not, by themselves, establish regulatory compliance; preservation of evidence also needs to fit the applicable retention and deletion rules.

Compare integration effort after defining the invariants

The useful comparison is the amount of evidence normalization and state ownership your team must implement. Evaluate a documented integration contract against the same support-reply lifecycle, including the duplicate-event path and the uncertain-submission path, before estimating how many lines the initial send call needs.

Integration shape Work the application must own Boundary to establish first
Submission with delivery callbacks Validate callbacks, correlate receipts, deduplicate events, update suppression Which outcomes arrive, and how repeated or late events are identified
Submission with status lookup Persist receipt identifiers, schedule reconciliation, handle incomplete results Which states can be queried and for how long
Direct SMTP submission Interpret SMTP replies and connect later failure reports to support replies Which component owns queued delivery and how reports reach the application

These are evaluation categories, not promises that a particular service implements them. A callback can reduce polling work while increasing the need for event validation and ordering controls; a status lookup can simplify inbound integration while leaving the application responsible for reconciliation scheduling. Direct submission moves more protocol handling into the team's operating boundary. Choose according to the evidence needed to enforce suppression, and budget engineering time for the unhappy paths.

Operational cost follows from those choices: reconciliation calls, retained evidence, and staff time spent resolving ambiguous deliveries all belong in the estimate. A message submission price does not explain them.

Roll out suppression with replayable decisions

Begin by recording normalized outcomes and proposed decisions without allowing the new policy to authorize additional sends. Compare that history with the existing support workflow, then enable suppression enforcement for a limited scope once the mapping of invalid-mailbox evidence has been reviewed. Introduce automated retries only after that boundary is working, with a recorded policy version for each decision.

Test repeated events, a bounce arriving after enqueue, two workers attempting the same transition, a timeout after request transmission, and a temporary failure whose next retry falls beyond the support deadline. Include an authorization refusal to verify that it does not become an invalid-address classification. Replay should reproduce local decisions without making external sends.

Track pending reconciliation age, suppressed dispatch attempts, retries per logical reply, and cases left without a confirmed delivery outcome. Alert thresholds should reflect the support team's response obligations. Preserve suppression records during rollback, and pause dispatch while resolving any change that would otherwise bypass an eligibility check.

The acceptance criterion is concrete: every additional support-email attempt has an attributable reason, an eligible recipient, and a bounded place in the conversation's lifetime. That is an exactly-once mindset applied to business decisions, with the remote delivery boundary kept explicit.

References

The SMTP specification supports the distinction between reply classes and acceptance responsibility. The enhanced status specification supports mailbox-versus-policy classification; the SPF specification defines the narrower sender-authorization check. The state machine, example identifiers, and retry limits above are proposed application design choices.

Sources

  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5321
  • RFC 3463, Enhanced Mail System Status Codes: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3463
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208

title: Rust Observability in 2026: OTLP Logs and Metrics Are Stable—What About Traces?
description:
Rust has a strong observability ecosystem built around tracing, but getting its events into an observability backend involves a few distinct pieces: spans, log records, metrics, and exporters.

There is a useful milestone in the current OpenTelemetry Rust release that makes this setup more interesting: as of OpenTelemetry Rust 0.33.1, the OTLP exporters for logs and metrics are stable, while the OTLP exporter for traces remains in beta.

That distinction is easy to miss if we just say “OpenTelemetry is stable.” Let’s look at what changed and how it maps to a real Rust service.

What became stable?

The OpenTelemetry Rust 0.33.1 release, published on October 8, 2026, declared the OTLP exporters for Logs and Metrics stable after a release-candidate period. The Traces exporter remains beta.

Signal OTLP exporter status in 0.33.1
Logs Stable
Metrics Stable
Traces Beta

This is specifically about the OTLP exporters in the Rust implementation—not a blanket statement that every OpenTelemetry crate or API has the same stability guarantee. The release notes also describe the Logs and Metrics APIs and SDK as stable, while Distributed Tracing remains pre-stable.

There is another useful reliability improvement: starting in 0.33.0, OTLP retries are enabled by default for HTTP and gRPC exporters. The default policy uses exponential backoff and jitter, with up to three retries after the first attempt. In other words, a temporary collector hiccup no longer necessarily means an export is immediately lost.

tracing events can become either logs or trace data

One source of confusion is that two similarly named integrations do different jobs:

  • tracing-opentelemetry connects Rust tracing spans and events to OpenTelemetry traces.
  • opentelemetry-appender-tracing forwards tracing events to the OpenTelemetry Logs pipeline.

Both can be installed as layers on a tracing_subscriber. A log record and a span event are related, but they are not the same telemetry signal; the bridge you choose determines where the event goes.

In our service setup, the key pieces look like this:

let trace_layer = tracing_opentelemetry::layer().with_tracer(tracer);
let log_layer = OpenTelemetryTracingBridge::new(&logger_provider);

The trace provider and logger provider each receive exporters. The metrics provider is separate again: it creates instruments and collects measurements on its configured interval. All three can share the same OpenTelemetry Resource, so telemetry is attributed to the same service name and version.

A small configuration example

The AICC crate wraps provider and subscriber setup behind a builder-style API. With a local OpenTelemetry Collector listening on gRPC port 4317, initialization is just a few lines:

use aicc::o11y::prelude::*;
use tracing::info;

let options = TracingOptions::default()
    .with_service("orders-api", "1.2.0")
    .with_otlp_exporter(OtlpExporterOptions::new("http://localhost:4317"));

let _guard = init_tracing(&options)?;

info!(order_id = 42, "Order accepted");

The exporter options enable all three signals by default. In the implementation, separate builders create the OTLP span, metric, and log exporters, and the resulting providers are attached to the subscriber or registered as global providers where needed.

The returned guard matters. Keep it alive for the lifetime of the application: when it is dropped, it shuts down the providers and flushes pending telemetry. If you create a provider manually, make sure your shutdown path does the equivalent.

A practical detail: exporters can produce telemetry too

The OTLP exporter and its transport stack can emit tracing events of their own. If those events are sent through the log bridge, exporting a log could produce another log, which could trigger another export, and so on.

The service code avoids that feedback loop by filtering infrastructure targets out of the OpenTelemetry log layer. It still allows warnings and errors from that infrastructure to appear in the console layer, which is useful when the collector is unavailable.

This is a small implementation detail, but it is exactly the sort of thing that turns a “hello, telemetry” demo into a setup you can operate.

Metrics are collected when requested

OpenTelemetry observable instruments use callbacks that run during collection. They are a good fit for values such as current CPU or memory usage: the application registers how to read the value, and the SDK asks for it when a metrics reader collects data.

In this project, the server registers observable system metrics using sysinfo. The callbacks refresh and read the relevant values; there is no separate polling task that wakes up just to update gauges. If you adapt the example for your own service, you can add application counters or histograms alongside those system metrics.

One caveat for a demo: the OTLP example initializes all three pipelines and emits spans and log records, but it does not record a custom metric. To demonstrate all three signals end to end, add a metric instrument or run the server path that registers the system metrics.

What should you take away?

OpenTelemetry Rust 0.33.1 is a meaningful point to revisit your observability setup:

  1. Logs and metrics have stable OTLP exporters. That is useful if you want to standardize your output format and backend integration.
  2. Tracing is still beta. Treat its API stability separately rather than assuming every signal has the same guarantee.
  3. Retries are now on by default for OTLP exporters. That improves resilience to transient failures, but it is still worth monitoring exporter errors and having a clear shutdown path.
  4. tracing can feed more than one signal. Use the trace bridge for spans and the appender for OpenTelemetry log records, and filter exporter-generated events to prevent feedback loops.

The interesting question is no longer just “Can Rust send telemetry to OpenTelemetry?” It can. The more useful question is: which signals are stable in the versions you deploy, and what does your application do when the collector is slow or unavailable?

References

  • OpenTelemetry Rust 0.33 release notes
  • opentelemetry-otlp changelog
  • opentelemetry-otlp 0.33.1 documentation
  • opentelemetry-appender-tracing documentation

title: One path, many spellings: normalizing a robots.txt match
description:
A URL path has more than one legal spelling, and a robots.txt matcher that compares a rule to the path as written gets some of them wrong in both directions. /%7Euser/notes and /~user/notes name the same resource, so a rule written Disallow: /~user/ has to catch both of them. /a%2Fb and /a/b do not name the same resource, so nothing in the matcher may quietly read %2F as a separator. A table of special cases per escape is not the way out. You rewrite both sides into one form before any comparison happens, and then you live with the fact that this moves the number which decides precedence.

Two failure modes, opposite directions

The first is a rule that slips. A site owner writes Disallow: /~user/, because that is what the URLs look like in a browser. A crawler sends GET /%7euser/notes: lowercase hex, encoded tilde, entirely within its rights, since a tilde is unreserved and a client may encode it anyway. Byte comparison says no rule applies. The path comes back allowed, and if you are auditing access logs to decide whether a verified crawler respected the policy, you have just recorded a compliant fetch of something the site refused.

The second is a rule that over-reaches. Decode everything before comparing and /a%2Fb becomes /a/b, which Disallow: /a/ now matches. But an encoded slash is one octet inside a single path segment, not a segment boundary. The rule was about a directory; the path was never in it.

Both failures come from one place: the two inputs arrive at the comparison in different alphabets. In the robots package of crawlwarrant (https://github.com/polycratia/crawlwarrant) the only comparison that happens is between two strings that have already been through the same function.

One form, applied to both sides

RFC 9309, Section 2.2.2, asks for exactly one transformation before matching: escapes of unreserved characters are decoded, every other escape is uppercased. Reserved octets stay escaped, and that is what keeps %2F from turning into a slash. The matcher does this to the path once, and to each pattern as it considers it:

func (g Group) Match(path string) (rule Rule, ok bool) {
    p := normalize(path)
    if p == "/robots.txt" {
        return Rule{}, false
    }
    best := -1
    for _, r := range g.Rules {
        pattern := normalize(r.Pattern)
        if pattern == "" || !matches(pattern, p) {
            continue
        }
        if n := len(pattern); n > best || (n == best && r.Kind == Allow && rule.Kind == Disallow) {
            rule, best = r, n
        }
    }
    return rule, best >= 0
}

Three things in those lines are worth naming.

The path is normalized before the /robots.txt exemption is checked, so /%72obots.txt gets the exemption too. The exemption belongs to the resource, not to one spelling of it.

A pattern that normalizes to the empty string is skipped. That is how an empty Disallow: value matches nothing: without the skip it would reach the prefix test as an empty prefix and match every path on the site, which is the opposite of what the line means.

And best holds the length of the normalized pattern, not of the pattern in the file. That is the whole cost of this design, and I come back to it below.

normalize 

const hexDigits = "0123456789ABCDEF"

func normalize(s string) string {
    var b strings.Builder
    b.Grow(len(s))
    for i := 0; i < len(s); {
        c := s[i]
        switch {
        case c == '%':
            if v, ok := unescape(s[i:]); ok {
                if unreserved(v) {
                    b.WriteByte(v)
                } else {
                    writeEscape(&b, v)
                }
                i += 3
                continue
            }
            writeEscape(&b, '%')
            i++
        case c <= ' ' || c >= 0x7f:
            writeEscape(&b, c)
            i++
        default:
            b.WriteByte(c)
            i++
        }
    }
    return b.String()
}

func unreserved(c byte) bool {
    switch {
    case c >= 'a' && c <= 'z', c >= 'A' && c <= 'Z', c >= '0' && c <= '9':
        return true
    }
    return c == '-' || c == '.' || c == '_' || c == '~'
}

func writeEscape(b *strings.Builder, c byte) {
    b.WriteByte('%')
    b.WriteByte(hexDigits[c>>4])
    b.WriteByte(hexDigits[c&0xf])
}

unescape reads the two hex digits in either case, so %7e and %7E arrive at the same byte. From there the rule is short: if the byte is a letter, a digit, a hyphen, a period, an underscore or a tilde, it is written plainly, and anything else is re-emitted as a percent sign plus two uppercase digits. A percent sign that does not begin a valid escape is itself escaped, to %25. Any byte at or below the space character, or at or above 0x7f, gets the same treatment.

Two properties matter more than the details here.

It is idempotent. Run it twice and nothing moves: %7E becomes a tilde and stays a tilde, a stray percent sign becomes %25, and %25 decodes to a percent sign, which is not unreserved, so it is written straight back as %25. That matters because patterns and paths go through the same function, and because a caller may hand the matcher a path that some earlier layer has already canonicalized.

It leaves * and $ untouched. They are printable ASCII and not percent signs, so they fall through to the default branch unchanged. %2A does not: an asterisk is a reserved character, unreserved rejects it, and writeEscape puts the escape back. So an encoded asterisk stays a literal octet instead of becoming a wildcard, and an encoded dollar sign does not become an anchor.

Wildcards are read on the normalized text 

func matches(pattern, path string) bool {
    anchored := strings.HasSuffix(pattern, "$")
    if anchored {
        pattern = pattern[:len(pattern)-1]
    }
    parts := strings.Split(pattern, "*")
    if len(parts) == 1 {
        if anchored {
            return path == pattern
        }
        return strings.HasPrefix(path, pattern)
    }
    if !strings.HasPrefix(path, parts[0]) {
        return false
    }
    pos := len(parts[0])
    for _, part := range parts[1 : len(parts)-1] {
        i := strings.Index(path[pos:], part)
        if i < 0 {
            return false
        }
        pos += i + len(part)
    }
    last := parts[len(parts)-1]
    if anchored {
        return len(path)-pos >= len(last) && strings.HasSuffix(path, last)
    }
    return strings.Contains(path[pos:], last)
}

The pattern is split on the asterisk. The first part must be a prefix of the path, each middle part is found leftmost after the previous one, and the last part must occur in what remains, or, when the pattern ended in $, be a suffix of the path beginning past the bytes already consumed. That last condition is what the length check enforces: without it an anchored suffix could overlap bytes a middle part already matched, and a pattern would match a path shorter than itself.

Because the split happens after normalization, the alphabet the splitter sees is fixed. No spelling of a path introduces a wildcard, and there is no spelling of a pattern where a literal asterisk hides inside an escape and then springs open during matching.

The cost: precedence is measured on the normalized form

RFC 9309 breaks ties by octet count: the longest matching rule wins, and an allow beats a disallow of equal length. The count is taken after normalization, which means it is not the count in the file. Consider:

User-agent: ExampleBot
Disallow: /%7Euser/
Allow: /~user/

As written, the disallow is eight bytes and the allow is seven, so the disallow is longer and would win. Normalized, both patterns are the same seven bytes, and the tie goes to the allow. /~user/notes is allowed, and the rule that decided it sits on line 3.

Normalization moves lengths the other way too. /a b/ is five bytes in the file and seven once the space is escaped, so it can take precedence over a competing rule it would have lost to on raw bytes. A rule can gain or lose precedence purely because of how its author spelled it.

I do not think a better answer is available. Ranking by the bytes in the file makes the outcome depend on exactly the authoring choice that normalization exists to erase, and it puts the first failure mode back at the tie-break instead of at the match. The specification already made this trade when it defined the comparison on normalized text, and measuring length anywhere else would be inconsistent with the comparison that produced the candidates.

What it does cost is explainability. The verdict chain in the identity package quotes the rule as the file wrote it (the kind, the pattern and the line), which is the right thing to show a site owner reading an audit. But when a rule loses on normalized length, a line naming /%7Euser/ and line 2 does not carry the reason it lost...

What I would change

Normalize patterns at parse time rather than inside Match. Today every call re-normalizes every rule of the group, and an audit replaying an access log calls it once per request. The reason it is not done yet: Rule.Pattern is public and reports what the file said, so the normalized form has to arrive as a second field rather than a rewrite of the first.

And once that field exists, put it in the explanation: report the pattern as written, then add the normalized form when it differs. A site owner who wrote two spellings of the same prefix should be able to read that off the output instead of reconstructing it.

One thing I would not change is the handling of query strings. The path handed to Match includes the query as the request carried it, and normalize treats those bytes like any other, so ? and & pass through as printable ASCII. Query strings have their own encoding conventions, and a matcher that started applying them would be deciding things RFC 9309 never asked it to decide.

Close

The discipline here is narrow and worth keeping narrow: a matcher should have exactly one place where its two inputs become comparable, and nothing downstream of that place should know anything about spellings. Once normalize is the only door, %2F cannot become a slash by accident, because nothing past the door is looking at escapes at all.

Originally published on polycratia.com — where I write about payment systems, crypto rails and marketplace backends.

title: Convert OneNote .one File to an Excel File in Java
description:
OneNote notebooks are used to create digital notes to keep things organized. They can be useful to increase the productivity of teachers, students, or other professional people. In certain use cases, you may intend to convert a OneNote .one notebook to an Excel worksheet. This article explains how to convert a Microsoft OneNote .one file to XLSX or XLS format in Java.

OneNote .one Notebook to Excel Converter – Java API Installation

You can convert a OneNote file to an Excel file in two steps. Firstly, export the .one file to a PDF document using Aspose.Note for Java API. Secondly, convert the output PDF file to a Excel file using Aspose.PDF for Java API. You can get the JAR files from the Downloads, or use the following Maven configurations in pom.xml file of your project:

Repository:

 <repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>AsposeJavaAPI</id>
        <name>Aspose Java API</name>
        <url>https://repository.aspose.com/repo/</url>
    </repository>
</repositories>

Dependency:

 <dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.aspose</groupId>
        <artifactId>aspose-note</artifactId>
        <version>22.7</version>
        <classifier>jdk17</classifier>        
    </dependency>

    <dependency>
        <groupId>com.aspose</groupId>
        <artifactId>aspose-pdf</artifactId>
        <version>22.7</version>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>

Convert OneNote .one Notebook to Excel XLSX or XLS File in Java

You can convert a OneNote Notebook with .one file extension to an Excel file with the following steps:

  1. Create an object of ByteArrayOutputStream class.
  2. Initialize an instance of the Document class to load the OneNote Notebook.
  3. Write the intermediary file in PDF format using the save method.
  4. Load the intermediate file with the Document class.
  5. Export the OneNote .one Notebook as an Excel file.

The following sample code demonstrates how to convert a OneNote .one file to an Excel file in Java:

// Initialize an instance of ByteArrayOutputStream class.
final ByteArrayOutputStream stream = new ByteArrayOutputStream();

// Load the OneNote .one file using Document class.
com.aspose.note.Document oneFile = new com.aspose.note.Document("Aspose.one");

// Export the .one file as PDF
oneFile.save(stream, com.aspose.note.SaveFormat.Pdf);

// Load the file using Aspose.PDF Document class.
com.aspose.pdf.Document file = new com.aspose.pdf.Document(stream.toByteArray());

// Convert the OneNote .one file as Excel file.
file.save("SaveOutput.xlsx" , com.aspose.pdf.SaveFormat.Excel);

Conclusion

In conclusion, you have learned how to convert a OneNote .one Notebook file to an Excel file programmatically in Java. This can be useful when you need to perform some numeric calculations on the data present in the Notebook. Furthermore, you may take a look at the documentation space to explore other features of the API. In case you need to discuss any queries or concerns, please write to us at forum.

title: Split AI-generated Storybook stories into one interaction each
description:
I used to ask the agent for “Storybook coverage for this component.” It came back with one mega-story: default, hover, focus, error, loading, disabled, and a knobs panel that looked impressive and tested almost nothing.

Reviewers clicked the Control panel once, shrugged, and merged. Then Playwright started failing on the empty state we never actually rendered as its own story.

Now I force a boring rule: one interaction (or one meaningful state) per story. The agent can still generate many stories — just not one blob that pretends to be coverage.

What “one interaction” means

Not “one prop.” One thing a human would verify in isolation:

  • Default — happy path, no extras
  • Empty — zero items / blank slate
  • Loading — skeleton or spinner only
  • Error — recoverable failure message
  • Disabled — cannot activate
  • KeyboardFocus — focus ring visible without hover
  • WithLongLabel — truncation / wrap edge

Hover-only variants are fine as separate stories when hover changes layout or reveals controls. Don’t bury them behind a state select in Controls.

Why agents invent mega-stories

Models optimize for “looks complete.” One file with every arg mapped to a Control feels thorough. It’s also:

  • hard to screenshot for visual regression (which state is the baseline?)
  • easy to miss in review (you never open every Control combination)
  • useless as a failing repro — “open the story and toggle Error” is not a stable handoff

A failing Storybook story should be a URL + a story name, not a checklist of knobs.

Prompt I paste now 

Add Storybook stories for `ShippingForm` in `ShippingForm.stories.tsx` only.

Rules:
- One story export per meaningful state/interaction (Default, Empty, Error, Loading, Disabled, KeyboardFocus).
- No mega-story with a `state` enum Control that switches everything.
- Prefer `args` / `render` per story over nested conditionals in one template.
- Each story must render without touching Controls.
- Max ~120 lines for the stories file. No new addons.
- Do not invent props the component doesn’t have — grep the component first.

If the component truly needs a Control (theme, locale), I allow one shared Control at the meta level — not a state machine per story.

What I reject in review

Reject / ask to split

  • Single Playground story that covers empty + error + loading via Controls
  • render with a giant switch (args.variant) that duplicates the component’s own branches
  • Stories that only work after the reviewer toggles three knobs
  • “AllStates” grids that pack six UIs into one canvas (fine as a docs appendix, not as the only coverage)

Accept

  • Small, boring named stories
  • play functions that assert one interaction (tab to submit, see error text) on that story alone
  • Reused decorators for providers — shared setup is fine; shared “all states” is not

Visual regression loves this

Chromatic / Playwright story shots become obvious:

  • ShippingForm--Empty.png
  • ShippingForm--Error.png

When the agent “fixes” empty-state copy, the Empty shot moves. When it only tweaked the happy path, Default moves. Mega-stories hide which branch changed.

Tiny habit

Next time an agent ships a Playground story with twelve Controls, don’t argue taste in the PR thread. Leave a comment: split into named stories, one interaction each, same args — then paste the prompt above into the follow-up.

You’re not asking for more Storybook. You’re asking for stories that can fail out loud.
