title: How a Spring Boot Request Travels: A Quick Walkthrough
description:
You type a URL, hit enter, and JSON comes back. Between those two moments, your Spring Boot app runs a small relay race: the request passes through an embedded web server, a front controller, and a few helpers before your code ever runs. Once you can picture that path, debugging gets much easier - a 404, a missing parameter, and a broken interceptor all fail at different stops on the same road.

Let's follow one GET request end to end, with a real app you can run yourself.

The five stops

Here is the whole journey, animated. Watch the request packet travel from the client to the controller and the response come back:

In plain words:

  1. The client sends the request. A browser, curl, or another service sends GET /api/greet?name=Vishnu.
  2. The embedded server accepts it. Spring Boot runs its own web server inside the app. Per the Spring Boot reference, "Spring Boot includes support for embedded Tomcat and Jetty servers", and by default it "listens for HTTP requests on port 8080". No separate server install - main() starts everything.
  3. The DispatcherServlet takes over. Spring MVC is "designed around the front controller pattern where a central Servlet, the DispatcherServlet, provides a shared algorithm for request processing, while actual work is performed by configurable delegate components" (Spring Framework docs). In practice: one servlet receives everything, then looks up which @GetMapping matches the path.
  4. Interceptors get a look. Before and after your controller, interceptors can inspect or reject the request - good for logging, auth checks, and timing.
  5. Your controller runs. The method returns data, Spring converts it to JSON, and the response travels back out the way it came.

A real app that shows its own journey

This is a complete Spring Boot app. The interceptor and controller print a line at each stop, so the server's own log narrates the relay:

package com.example.reqdemo;

import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.HandlerInterceptor;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.InterceptorRegistry;
import org.springframework.web.servlet.config.annotation.WebMvcConfigurer;

import java.util.Map;

@SpringBootApplication
public class ReqDemoApplication {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(ReqDemoApplication.class, args);
    }

    @RestController
    static class GreetController {
        @GetMapping("/api/greet")
        public Map<String, String> greet(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "world") String name) {
            System.out.println("[controller] DispatcherServlet handed me GET /api/greet, name=" + name);
            return Map.of("message", "Hello, " + name + "!");
        }
    }

    @Component
    static class FlowInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
        @Override
        public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, Object handler) {
            System.out.println("[interceptor] request passed the servlet and filters: "
                    + req.getMethod() + " " + req.getRequestURI());
            return true;
        }

        @Override
        public void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res,
                                    Object handler, Exception ex) {
            System.out.println("[interceptor] response written, status=" + res.getStatus()
                    + " - request journey complete");
        }
    }

    @Component
    static class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
        private final FlowInterceptor interceptor;
        WebConfig(FlowInterceptor interceptor) { this.interceptor = interceptor; }
        @Override
        public void addInterceptors(InterceptorRegistry registry) {
            registry.addInterceptor(interceptor);
        }
    }
}

I compiled and ran this on JDK 21 (Temurin 21.0.13) with Spring Boot 3.5.7 before publishing. Here is the real, unedited output.

Startup - the embedded Tomcat coming up inside the app (port 8090 here, because 8080 was already in use in the run environment):

Tomcat initialized with port 8090 (http)
Tomcat started on port 8090 (http) with context path '/'
Started ReqDemoApplication in 1.054 seconds

Then curl http://localhost:8090/api/greet?name=Vishnu returned:

{"message":"Hello, Vishnu!"}

And the app's own log narrated the journey, exactly in the order of the animation:

[interceptor] request passed the servlet and filters: GET /api/greet
[controller] DispatcherServlet handed me GET /api/greet, name=Vishnu
[interceptor] response written, status=200 - request journey complete

Three things worth noticing:

  • The interceptor's preHandle runs before the controller, and afterCompletion runs after the response is written. Your controller is the middle of the sandwich, not the start.
  • Returning a Map was enough to get JSON. Spring Boot auto-configures an HTTP message converter that serializes the return value - you never wrote JSON yourself.
  • The journey back through the server is mostly invisible to your code, which is why the interceptor's completion callback is a handy place to log it.

A 404 travels the same road

One detail that surprises people: an unknown path goes through the same pipeline. Calling curl http://localhost:8090/api/nope produced this log:

[interceptor] request passed the servlet and filters: GET /api/nope
[interceptor] response written, status=404 - request journey complete
[interceptor] request passed the servlet and filters: GET /error
[interceptor] response written, status=404 - request journey complete

Two journeys for one request. The DispatcherServlet found no mapping for /api/nope, so it raised an error, and the servlet container then dispatched the request again, this time to Spring Boot's built-in /error endpoint - which is what generated the JSON error body:

{"timestamp":"2026-11-05T10:56:56.906+00:00","status":404,"error":"Not Found","path":"/api/nope"}

So when you debug a 404, the first question is: did the request reach the DispatcherServlet at all? If your interceptor logged it, the server side is fine and the path or mapping is wrong. If it did not, the problem is earlier - wrong port, wrong context path, or something in front of the app.

When this mental model pays off

  • Debugging 404s and 405s: find out which stop rejected the request instead of guessing.
  • Placing cross-cutting logic: auth checks, request IDs, and timing belong in interceptors or filters, not copied into every controller.
  • Reading startup logs: Tomcat started on port ... tells you the embedded server is the entry point, and it is part of your app's process.

If dependency injection is how your beans find each other, the DispatcherServlet is how the outside world finds your beans. Both are quiet machinery that runs before your code does.

Sources

  • Spring Boot reference: Embedded web servers

title: Supercharging XLA-based inference: Announcing the launch of XLA Serving Engine
description:
by Oleg Shaldybin and Monica Song, Google TPU Software

Today we are excited to announce the launch of XLA Serving Engine (XSE), a general-purpose model export and inference runtime for the OpenXLA ecosystem, open-sourced under the Apache 2.0 license.

We created XLA Serving Engine to enable a “Train in Python, Serve in C++” workflow. Most ML engineers develop models using Python (with frameworks like JAX and PyTorch); however, some production serving environments do not allow Python due to operational and deployment complexity. XLA Serving Engine offers a solution by providing an API for engineers to export their ML models to an “XLA SavedModel” containing the StableHLO representation of their model’s function, which can then be loaded and executed by the XLA Serving Runtime.

This approach allows users to serve models (typically non-LLMs) directly in a C++ runtime, which enables high throughput at any scale and optimizes for low latency by removing the overhead of the Python interpreter. In our studies, we found that for short requests, XSE delivers 2–5x the throughput of the best Python server we could build, and 8–36x that of a straightforward one, while using 30–70% less CPU time per prediction and a quarter of the memory.

Last year, we began deploying core components of XLA Serving Engine as part of Google’s internal load-bearing, production serving infrastructure. Today, XSE serves over 6 million queries per second and powers some of Google's highest-volume online inference pipelines, including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, Search, and parts of Gemini Omni, with plans to onboard more customers internally.

Having successfully scaled XSE to support the high-throughput workloads of our internal teams, we are now ready to bring this core piece of infrastructure to the wider ecosystem of hardware partners and Cloud TPU users. We designed XLA Serving Engine to be self-contained and modular, so users can deploy it as a standalone inference engine or plug it into their more complex serving solutions.

Core production-ready features

  • Python-Free Serving: XSE enables a “Train in Python, Serve in C++” workflow via the intermediary compiled XLA SavedModel serialization format. In our studies, we found that XSE delivers 2–5x the throughput of a pure Python server.
  • Low-latency execution: The XLA Serving Runtime wraps PJRT directly and optimizes the model using the XLA compiler. This eliminates Python runtime overhead and the global interpreter lock. XSE is C++ native, which means one process is capable of using all eight cores.
  • Orbax Checkpointing Integration: XLA SavedModel stores JAX model computations as StableHLO and uses Orbax checkpoint to store the weights.
  • Flexible Scale: Supports both single-host and multi-host serving by leveraging PJRT.
  • Performance Parity: XSE preserves the performance of the model’s forward function (including kernel optimizations). Hand off your model to XLA Serving Engine with confidence that performance will be identical to its training environment.
  • Docker Packages: We provide a suite of Docker images that are tested on CPU, GPU, and TPU and expose simple gRPC APIs for calling your model.

Customer testimonials and partner use cases

Our Private Preview partners have been actively leveraging XLA Serving Engine to bring their deep learning stacks to production. Here is a selection of private preview customers (alphabetized) to showcase the diversity of uses:

Arm: Performance Parity on Arm Neoverse platforms

Our work with Arm has proven the production capabilities of JAX and XLA for training and serving on Arm-based CPUs:

“As AI inference scales, software optimization is critical to delivering performance and efficiency across diverse workloads. Through our collaboration with Google and contributions to OpenXLA, we’ve optimized the XLA CPU backend and serving runtime for vision, embedding and recommendation workloads on Arm Neoverse-based platforms, including Google Cloud Axion.”

— Ian Bratt, Vice President of ML Technology and Fellow, Arm

Intel: Native JAX on Xeon server CPUs

We have also been partnering with Intel to showcase the power of Intel’s optimized compute:

“Our partnership with Google showcases the XLA Serving Engine (XSE) on Intel® Xeon® processors, delivering native, high-performance JAX inference accelerated by Intel® AMX. With XSE, enterprises get out-of-the-box performance across Vision, Recommendation, and LLM workloads — and the flexibility to serve them efficiently wherever their business runs, from cloud to edge to on-prem.”

— Bill Pearson, Vice President of Data Center and AI software, Intel

Moloco: Scaling advertising and recommenders

“To support our demand-side platform (DSP) processing over 650 billion daily inferences and peaking at 10.5 million QPS, we needed an inference runtime that could match our massive scale. XLA Serving Engine is the high-performance, C++-based JAX serving solution we’ve been waiting for that keeps us framework agnostic and complements our Cloud TPU Trillium investments.”

— Kunal Kukreja, Staff Machine Learning Engineer, Moloco

What’s next

  • Torch Support: We plan to integrate with TorchTPU, allowing PyTorch users to export to an XLA SavedModel to serve their models on TPUs in C++.
  • Ahead-of-Time (AOT) Compilation: We are working on rolling out AOT compilation to our internal users before bringing this feature to external users. AOT compilation will reduce cold-start time by offering users the ability to compile their models offline (on CPU) for their target serving hardware.
  • C++ Data Preprocessing: We are offering a C++ based preprocessor for users who want to combine their data processing with their model’s graph in C++.

Limitations

XSE is a lightweight, one-shot inference engine. For large autoregressive language models with long context lengths, we recommend popular projects such as vLLM or SGLang, which benefit from LLM-specific memory management techniques.

Get started today

Ready to streamline your JAX production pipeline?

  • Check out the XLA Serving Engine quick-start instructions at github.com/openxla/xla-serving. You can find the list of available Docker images here.
  • File an issue or contribute pull requests at github.com/openxla/xla-serving.

Acknowledgements

Thank you to everyone who contributed to XLA Serving Engine, including but not limited to the following individuals:

Ashish Agarwal, MD Faijul Amin, Carlos Araya, Renato Arantes, Isha Arkatkar, Sagun B, Ashok Bhat, Xevi Miró Bruix, Chris Chan, Ray Chen, Chen Cheng, Hyun Min Choi, Andrea Covre, Gauri Deshpande, Tiffany Dong, Sayce Falk, Happy Gao, Vaibhav Gurunathan, Michael Hudgins, Kritanjali Jain, He Jiang, Leon Kennedy, Young Seok (Tony) Kim, Penporn Koanantakool, Kunal Kukreja, Younghee Kwon, Shawn Lee, Shawn Lu, Siddhartha Menon, Marek Michałowski, Sachin Muradi, César Naranjo, Pat Notz, Adam O’Brien, Olivia Qin, AG Ramesh, Shubha Rao, Mayank Raunak, Crefeda Rodrigues, Gassan Salama, Oleg Shaldybin, Brian Seung, Juanli Shen, Alex Shires, Jeyeon Si, Prairie Sims, Monica Song, Anne Stern, Quoc Truong, Armando Ugalde Velasco, Jess Wiser, Siqiao (James) Wu, Qinglan Xiang, Yunjie Xu, Jeffrey Yoo, Hyungsuk Yoon, and Wangyuan Zhang.

title: Is Your Exposure Management Platform Leaving You Exposed? Five Tests to Find Out
Decoupling React Components with Hexagonal Architecture and Events
description:
As a React application grows, a single component can easily take on too many responsibilities: collecting input, running a search, handling errors, and rendering results. That may be quick to build initially, but it couples concerns that should be able to change independently.

This small product-search example uses three techniques to keep those dependencies under control:

  1. Give React components focused responsibilities.
  2. Organize application logic around hexagonal architecture boundaries.
  3. Use events to communicate outcomes without wiring components directly to one another.

You do not need a large framework to establish these boundaries. Explicit interfaces and injected dependencies are enough.

Project structure

The search feature is organized like this:

src/
├── main.tsx
├── search/
│   ├── domain/
│   │   └── productSearchRepository.ts
│   ├── service/
│   │   └── search.ts
│   ├── infrastructure/
│   │   ├── repository/
│   │   │   └── inMemoryProductSearchRepository.ts
│   │   └── ui/
│   │       ├── searchInput.tsx
│   │       └── searchResults.tsx
│   └── factory.tsx
└── shared/
    ├── eventBus.ts
    └── useSubscription.ts

The folder structure is not the goal. Its value is that it makes each module's role easier to see: the domain defines the core concepts and repository contract; the service coordinates the use case; and infrastructure supplies concrete implementations, including the UI.

React components with clear responsibilities

The page has two main components:

  • SearchInput owns the input value and loading state. Once the trimmed query reaches four characters, it calls the search service.
  • SearchResults subscribes to search events and renders the corresponding state: results, an empty state, or an error.

Separating these components does not mean they never collaborate. It means they do not need direct knowledge of each other. SearchInput neither imports nor updates SearchResults' internal state, and the component that starts the search does not need to call the results component.

They share one dependency: the Search service, passed in as a prop. The input asks the service to run the operation; the results component listens for what happens.

The hexagonal boundary: depend on a contract

The domain defines the contract the application expects from a product search repository:

export interface ProductSearchRepository {
  search(query: string): Promise<Products>;
}

The application service, Search, receives an implementation of that contract through its constructor:

export class Search {
  constructor(
    private readonly searchRepository: ProductSearchRepository,
    private readonly eventBus: EventBus<AppEvents>,
  ) {}

  async execute(query: string): Promise<Products> {
    // runs the search and publishes its outcome
  }
}

The service does not know how data is stored or retrieved. Today, the factory creates an InMemoryProductSearchRepository. That adapter could later call an API or query a database without requiring the React components to know about the change.

That is the core idea behind hexagonal architecture: application logic depends on ports (contracts), while concrete implementation details live in adapters connected at the application boundary. In this example:

  • ProductSearchRepository is the outbound port for product data.
  • InMemoryProductSearchRepository is an in-memory adapter for that port.
  • The React components form the presentation adapter: they invoke the use case and render its outcomes.
  • createSearch wires the concrete implementations together and injects them into the service.

The direction of dependencies matters more than the folder names: the service depends on the interface, not on the in-memory class.

Events decouple the components

After the repository responds, the service publishes an event for either outcome:

async execute(query: string): Promise<Products> {
  return this.searchRepository.search(query)
    .then((results) => {
      this.eventBus.emit("searchExecuted", { query, results });
      return results;
    })
    .catch((error) => {
      this.eventBus.emit("searchFailed", { query, error });
      throw error;
    });
}

SearchResults subscribes to the events it cares about:

useSubscription(() => {
  return search.subscribe("searchExecuted", (event) => {
    setState(
      event.results.isEmpty()
        ? { status: "empty" }
        : { status: "success", results: event.results },
    );
  });
}, [search]);

The flow looks like this:

the user types
  → SearchInput updates the query
  → SearchInput calls Search.execute(query)
  → Search calls ProductSearchRepository
  → Search publishes searchExecuted or searchFailed
  → SearchResults receives the event and updates its UI

Search does not need to know about SearchResults, and the results component does not need to know about the repository. They communicate through the service and an event contract. That makes it easier to replace the UI, add another subscriber, or test each part independently.

A typed event bus

The event bus maps each event name to its payload type:

export interface AppEvents {
  messageSent: { message: string };
  searchExecuted: { query: string; results: any };
  searchFailed: { query: string; error: Error };
}

The generic EventBus ties the types of on and emit to this map. The on method also returns an unsubscribe function. The useSubscription hook calls it from the useEffect cleanup, removing the subscription when the component unmounts or its dependency changes.

That cleanup matters in React: without it, callbacks can remain registered after the component's lifecycle has ended.

Why not pass a callback between components?

Passing a callback from SearchInput to SearchResults would work in an example this small. But it would directly connect the two components: the component starting the operation would need to know who handles the result.

An event describes something that has happened (searchExecuted or searchFailed). Any interested consumer can subscribe without the producer knowing who those consumers are. This is especially useful when several parts of the interface react to the same operation—for example, results, a result count, analytics, or a notification.

Events are not automatically the right choice for every piece of state. For a direct, local parent-to-child relationship, props and callbacks are simpler. An event bus is useful when producers and consumers should not depend directly on one another.

Testing: verify contracts, not coupling

Hexagonal architecture improves testability by making dependencies explicit. If a use case needs a repository and an event bus, tests can replace them with controlled implementations. There is no need to start a server, connect to a database, or render the UI to test the application logic.

For Search, a hand-written repository mock can record the query and return a known result—or reject with a predetermined error. A hand-written event bus mock can record the events that were published. The tests can then verify the observable contract: the query is forwarded, the result is returned, and searchExecuted is emitted; if the repository fails, searchFailed is emitted and the error still propagates.

The same boundary makes it straightforward to test each component in isolation:

  • For SearchInput, a service mock that records queries is enough to verify that a short query does not start a search and a valid query invokes the use case.
  • For SearchResults, a mock that exposes subscribe and lets the test emit events is enough to verify the results, empty, and error states without running a real search.

These tests verify both the input crossing a boundary and the component's reaction to an event. They do not need to mount all the components together or inspect one another's internal state. A lightweight DOM environment is still useful for checking React rendering, while the application dependencies remain deterministic, hand-written mocks.

Test public contracts and visible behavior, not implementation details such as how many times setState is called or the components' internal structure. When a contract changes, updating the relevant tests makes the impact on producers and consumers explicit. And, as with any mocking strategy, keep some integration tests: a mock can confirm that a component follows a contract, but it cannot prove that all the real modules are wired together correctly.

Limitations to keep in mind

This project demonstrates architectural boundaries; it is not a complete search engine:

  • The in-memory repository waits two seconds and returns the full product collection; it does not currently filter by query.
  • results is typed as any in the searchExecuted event. Using Products instead would make the contract safer and catch invalid consumer assumptions at compile time.
  • The event bus is a shared singleton. That is convenient in a small app, but a global bus can make feature and test isolation harder. As the application grows, consider a bus with an explicit scope that is injected through the factory.
  • The input starts a search on every change once the query is long enough. A real remote integration should consider debouncing, request cancellation, and out-of-order responses.

These limitations do not undermine the approach. They show how clear boundaries let you improve an adapter or a contract without rewriting the entire interface.

Takeaways

Separating React components keeps each part of the UI focused. Hexagonal architecture protects application logic from concrete implementation details. Events let independent components react to the same use case without holding direct references to one another.

The result is more than a tidy folder structure. It is a set of explicit contracts that lets you change the repository implementation, add consumers, and test behavior with less coupling.

When building a feature, ask:

  1. What is the use case, and what contract does it need?
  2. Which component is responsible for starting the operation?
  3. Who needs to react to the outcome, and do they really need to know about one another directly?

The answers help you decide where props are enough, where to define a port, and where an event makes collaboration simpler.

title: Your UV Lamp Is On. Why Doesn’t That Prove Disinfection?
description:
A controller reports that a UV lamp is running. Your application receives the signal and displays a green badge:

Disinfection: OK

It is a small interface decision with a large assumption behind it.

The controller reported a component state. The application turned it into a claim about treatment performance.

For developers working with physical equipment, UV water treatment offers a useful example of why those two things must remain separate.

A Running Lamp Is Only One Part of the Process

Effective UV treatment depends on sufficient ultraviolet exposure under the conditions the reactor was designed and validated to handle.

Lamp output, water flow, and water’s UV transmittance all influence that exposure. Sleeve fouling and lamp ageing also matter. Public-water guidance therefore calls for monitoring several operating parameters, including flow, lamp status, and UV intensity.

A lamp-running signal cannot answer all those questions.

Even visible light is misleading: ASHRAE notes that UV lamps can continue emitting blue visible light after their useful germicidal life has passed.

Name the Signal Before Naming the Badge

Before implementing a status indicator, ask what the source actually reports.

Is it a command to switch the lamp on? Electrical operating feedback? A sensor measurement? A controller assessment based on multiple inputs?

These represent different levels of information.

Received information Appropriate display
Start command accepted Start requested
Lamp-running feedback Lamp reported running
Current UV sensor reading UV measurement, with units and timestamp
Controller-reported process alarm Process alarm, with its specific cause
Required telemetry unavailable Status unavailable

This mapping is an illustrative interface design. The actual labels must follow the equipment’s documented signal definitions.

The important step is preserving meaning as data moves from hardware to API to screen.

Keep Measurements and Assessments Separate

A useful data model distinguishes observations from conclusions.

An observation might be a flow measurement with a timestamp and quality flag. An assessment might be the controller reporting operation outside its configured limits.

Store both when available. Include the source of the assessment so that users can distinguish an equipment-generated alarm from an application-generated communication warning.

Do not invent a universal “safe UV intensity” threshold in the frontend. Relevant operating limits depend on the reactor and its validated conditions.

Handle Missing Data Explicitly

Suppose the lamp status updates normally, but flow measurements stop arriving.

Keeping the previous overall green badge would hide the uncertainty. Replacing missing flow with zero would introduce a different error.

Instead, show which information is unavailable and when it last updated. The appropriate response belongs in the system’s agreed monitoring requirements.

A browser dashboard also should not become the accidental implementation of a protective shutdown function. Equipment controls and protective functions need their own engineered requirements.

Test the Meaning, Not Just the Colour

Test combinations that challenge the interface:

  • Lamp running, but a process alarm is active.
  • Lamp running, but required measurements are stale.
  • Start command accepted, but running feedback never arrives.
  • Alarm acknowledged, but its triggering condition remains.

For each case, check whether the display says more than the evidence supports.

A good industrial interface makes a precise promise. “Lamp reported running” is useful information. Turning it into “disinfection confirmed” requires evidence that a single status bit cannot provide.

*Disclosure: This article was generated with AI assistance. The software examples are illustrative and do not describe a deployed system.*

title: Go JSON v2 Is Here: A Safe Migration Path for encoding/json
description:
A JSON decoder can accept a payload that another service interprets differently. Duplicate object names, unexpected capitalization, and invalid UTF-8 are not merely formatting quirks when the data controls an authorization decision or updates a record. A parser that quietly tolerates them can leave two components disagreeing about what the request meant.

That is one of the problems the Go team is addressing with encoding/json/v2, now available in Go 1.27. The new package is not just a faster spelling of the old one. It has stricter defaults, options for configuring behavior, and a lower-level package for JSON syntax. The original encoding/json remains supported, so upgrading does not require an all-at-once rewrite.[1][2]

This is a practical, test-first migration guide, not a benchmark or a report from a production migration. The code examples follow the current Go package documentation, but I have not run them in a local Go toolchain for this article. Start with the tests in your own module before changing imports.

First, understand what changed

Go 1.27 introduces two related packages:

  • encoding/json/v2 handles the semantic mapping between JSON values and Go values. Its familiar Marshal and Unmarshal functions accept options.
  • encoding/json/jsontext works at the syntax level, with token and value APIs for applications that need to process JSON structure directly.[1][3]

For ordinary calls, migration can look deceptively small. The migration guide says many simple uses continue to compile after switching the import path.[2] But the defaults differ in ways that can change what inputs your service accepts and what output it emits. That behavior, not the import edit, is the real migration.

The important differences include:

  • Object names are case-sensitive by default. The old package used a loose case-insensitive match when decoding object names into struct fields. V2 defaults to strict matching.[3]
  • Duplicate object names are rejected by default. V1 accepted them, leaving interpretation to its processing behavior. V2 rejects them unless configured otherwise.[1][3]
  • Invalid UTF-8 is rejected by default. V1 replaced invalid bytes with the Unicode replacement character. V2 takes the stricter path unless the corresponding syntax option is enabled.[3]
  • Nil slices and maps encode as empty JSON arrays and objects by default. If an existing API depends on null, v2 provides options to preserve that output.[3]
  • Unknown members are still ignored by default. You can opt into rejecting them when that is the contract you want.[3]

These are not all “breaking changes” in the Go compatibility sense. They are differences to evaluate when you deliberately adopt the new package. The Go team says the old encoding/json API will continue to be supported, and existing behavior is preserved there, although exact error text can differ under Go 1.27 because its implementation is backed by v2.[1]

Step 1: Record the current contract

Before changing a package import, write tests for the behavior your API currently promises. Avoid treating current output as accidental until you have checked clients, snapshots, generated SDKs, and stored JSON.

A small request type makes the examples concrete:

type CreateAccountRequest struct {
    DisplayName string   `json:"displayName"`
    Roles       []string `json:"roles"`
}

The fields are illustrative. Replace them with a type from your own service and add tests for the actual boundary that receives JSON. At minimum, test:

  • The exact field spelling clients send, including capitalization variants.
  • Whether unknown fields are ignored or rejected.
  • Whether duplicate names are possible in requests you receive and how they should be handled.
  • Whether a nil slice or map is serialized as null or an empty collection.
  • Custom MarshalJSON or UnmarshalJSON methods used by nested types.
  • Invalid UTF-8 and malformed input, if your application has a policy for them.

This test inventory gives you a compatibility map. It also prevents an import diff from being mistaken for a complete migration review.

Step 2: Add a v2 decode path deliberately

The basic shape remains familiar. V2's options let a call choose behavior explicitly:

package api

import (
    "encoding/json/v2"
)

type CreateAccountRequest struct {
    DisplayName string   `json:"displayName"`
    Roles       []string `json:"roles"`
}

func decodeCreateAccount(data []byte) (CreateAccountRequest, error) {
    var req CreateAccountRequest
    err := json.Unmarshal(data, &req, json.RejectUnknownMembers(true))
    return req, err
}

The example opts into rejecting unknown members. That can catch misspelled fields and outdated clients, but it can also reject payloads that older versions intentionally tolerated. Apply it only where strict schema behavior is appropriate, and test older clients before enabling it on a public endpoint.[3]

V2 uses case-sensitive field matching by default. If compatibility requires case-insensitive matching, the package exposes an explicit option:

err := json.Unmarshal(data, &req, json.MatchCaseInsensitiveNames(true))

Treat this as a compatibility choice, not a universal fix. A service that accepts both displayName and DisplayName may be more forgiving, but broader matching can create ambiguity across systems that do not share the same rules.[2][3]

One useful migration strategy is to keep the existing decode function in place and introduce a second path behind a small boundary. Run the same fixture corpus through both implementations. Compare successful values and errors, then decide which differences are intended. Avoid silently falling back from v2 to v1 for every error: that can erase the stricter behavior you adopted and make malformed inputs hard to reason about.

Step 3: Make output shape explicit

Nil collections deserve particular attention because clients often distinguish null from [] or {}. In v2, a nil slice is encoded as an empty array by default. If a particular contract needs null, use the explicit formatting option:

out, err := json.Marshal(req, json.FormatNilSliceAsNull(true))

There is a corresponding option for nil maps, json.FormatNilMapAsNull(true).[3] Prefer defining the intended API shape in tests rather than adding options everywhere preemptively. A service may have one endpoint where empty means “no roles” and another where null means “not provided.” Those semantics should be visible in the type or handler design, not left to an undocumented global assumption.

V2 also provides omitzero behavior for struct fields. It is based on the Go value's zero-ness, including an IsZero method when available. That differs from omitempty, which is defined in terms of the JSON representation. For example, a non-nil empty slice can be omitted by omitempty, while omitzero focuses on whether the Go value itself is zero.[3] Changing tags can therefore alter which fields appear in a response. Add exact JSON output tests before changing a tag on a shared response type.

Step 4: Check the security-sensitive inputs

Duplicate names are a particularly important test case. Consider an object that includes the same key twice with different values. If a gateway, logger, and application parser do not resolve that object identically, they may act on different values. The Go announcement explains why v2 rejects duplicate names by default: the JSON specification does not assign them a single universal meaning, and inconsistent interpretation can be security-relevant.[1]

The safe default is usually to reject ambiguous input at the boundary. If a legacy partner sends duplicates, investigate the source and document an explicit temporary compatibility rule rather than assuming every downstream parser will make the same choice. V2's syntax package has options that can permit duplicate names, but allowing them should be a deliberate exception.[3]

Case sensitivity is another boundary issue. If one service treats userId and UserID as equivalent while another does not, a request can have different meanings at different hops. V2's default strict matching makes the accepted contract clearer. If your API has historically accepted variations, use tests to enumerate them and decide whether to preserve them intentionally.[2][3]

Step 5: Test custom types and error handling

An import replacement can expose assumptions inside custom JSON methods. The v2 package defines newer interfaces, including MarshalerTo and UnmarshalerFrom, and also supports the familiar Marshaler and Unmarshaler methods.[3] Review custom implementations that depend on encoder state, nested values, or options before assuming they behave identically.

Do not make tests depend on exact error strings unless that text is part of a deliberate user-facing contract. Go 1.27's release notes say the original encoding/json is backed by the v2 implementation, preserving its marshaling and unmarshaling behavior while allowing exact error messages to differ.[1] Prefer asserting that an error occurs and checking structured details only when the API provides a stable way to do so.

For stream processing, evaluate the new APIs separately from a simple Unmarshal replacement. V2 includes reader and writer functions, while jsontext provides lower-level syntax processing.[3] Choose the simplest API that meets the boundary requirements. A token API is useful when the application needs to inspect or transform JSON structure without first mapping the whole document to a Go struct; it is unnecessary complexity for a small request DTO.

Step 6: Roll out with a small compatibility matrix

A safe rollout can be staged:

  1. Capture fixtures. Use representative valid requests and responses from tests, logs that are safe to retain, and client examples. Remove secrets and personal data first.
  2. Run both decoders in tests. Compare values, accepted inputs, and rejection behavior for each fixture.
  3. Classify every difference. Mark it as intentional tightening, required compatibility, or an unexpected regression. Do not paper over the third category with a broad permissive option.
  4. Check serialized output. Compare exact JSON where clients or snapshots depend on field presence, null handling, or formatting.
  5. Migrate one boundary. Start with a low-risk endpoint or internal message type rather than changing every package at once.
  6. Observe rejection changes. During rollout, monitor error categories and client versions without logging sensitive payload contents.
  7. Keep rollback simple. A small wrapper around the decode operation makes it easier to revert a boundary if real clients depend on behavior your fixtures missed.

The Go migration guide notes that encoding/json and encoding/json/v2 can interoperate, including when types implement v2 custom marshal behavior.[2] That gives teams room to migrate incrementally. It does not remove the need to check each type's tags, custom methods, and external contract.

When should you migrate?

Use v2 for new code when your module targets Go 1.27 or later and the stricter defaults fit the contract. The option-based API makes decisions such as rejecting unknown fields explicit at the call site.

Consider a gradual migration when an existing service needs stricter input handling, the JSON boundary is security-sensitive, or you want the new streaming and customization APIs. Start with tests and one boundary at a time.

Stay on the old import for now when you cannot validate client compatibility, your module supports toolchains before Go 1.27, or your custom JSON behavior has not been inventoried. The old package is not being removed, so there is no need to rush a mechanical migration.[1][2]

The key change is not that every Go service must replace encoding/json this week. It is that Go now offers a standard-library path where stricter JSON semantics and compatibility exceptions can be expressed directly. Use the defaults to make ambiguous input less ambiguous, and use options only where a real contract requires them.

Migration checklist to save

  • Pin the Go toolchain version your module supports.
  • Add tests for case variations, duplicate names, unknown fields, and nil collections.
  • Inventory custom JSON methods and struct tags before switching imports.
  • Decide whether each endpoint should reject unknown fields.
  • Compare exact serialized output for public response types.
  • Treat compatibility options as documented exceptions.
  • Roll out at one request or message boundary before migrating broadly.

I write about developer tools, backend engineering, and AI systems. Subscribe for more practical guides. Have you started evaluating encoding/json/v2? Which behavior would be most likely to surprise your existing clients?

Sources

[1] Go 1.27 Release Notes: JSON packages

[2] Go encoding/json/v2 Migration Guide

[3] Go encoding/json/v2 package documentation

[4] Go: A new API for JSON

title: 10 Essential Website Design Principles for Better User Experience
description:
A website may look attractive, but does it make things easy for visitors? If users struggle to find information, understand your services, or navigate between pages, the design needs improvement.

Effective website design principles help businesses create websites that are visually appealing, easy to navigate, accessible, and user-friendly.

Whether you are building a new website or improving an existing one, these 10 principles will help you understand what makes a better user experience.

10 Essential Website Design Principles

1. Understand Your Target Audience

Good website design starts with understanding your visitors. Identify their needs, expectations, and goals before deciding on layouts and features.

How to apply it:

Understand what information visitors are looking for.
Organize content around their needs.
Use simple, audience-friendly language.
Make important services and information easy to find.

Example: A business website should clearly present its services, relevant work, and contact options instead of focusing only on company information.

2. Create a Clear Visual Hierarchy

Visual hierarchy helps visitors identify the most important information first. Use headings, font sizes, spacing, and colors to guide their attention.

How to apply it:

Make primary headings prominent.
Highlight important information.
Use consistent spacing.
Give primary CTAs clear visual emphasis.

Example: A clear headline, short description, and visible CTA are easier to understand than a page where every element competes for attention.

3. Keep Navigation Simple

Visitors should be able to find important information without unnecessary effort.

How to apply it:

Use familiar menu labels.
Group related pages logically.
Avoid overcrowded menus.
Maintain consistent navigation across pages.
Make mobile menus easy to use.

Example:

Weak navigation Better navigation
Explore, Discover, More Services, About, Contact
Click Here Explore Website Design Services
Explore Amron’s website design services to understand how UX design and information architecture contribute to a website experience.

4. Maintain Design Consistency

Consistent design makes a website easier to understand and navigate.

Keep these elements uniform:

Brand colors and typography.
Button styles and shapes.
Heading formats.
Navigation patterns.
Spacing and page layouts.

Example: If your primary CTA uses a particular color and style on the homepage, maintain the same visual treatment across relevant pages.

5. Use White Space Effectively

White space separates content and prevents pages from feeling overcrowded. It improves readability and helps visitors focus on important information.

How to apply it:

Add spacing between sections.
Keep paragraphs readable.
Separate unrelated content.
Give buttons and images enough room.
Avoid unnecessary visual elements.

Example: A service page with clear sections and balanced spacing is easier to scan than one filled with tightly packed text and images.

6. Choose Readable Typography and Colors

Typography and color choices directly influence how visitors read and understand website content.

Best practices:

Use readable fonts and appropriate text sizes.
Maintain consistent heading styles.
Choose text and background colors with sufficient contrast.
Avoid excessive font styles.
Ensure text remains readable on mobile devices.

Example: Dark text on a light background is generally easier to read than light-gray text on white.

For accessibility guidance, refer to WCAG 2.2.

7. Make Your Website Responsive

Your website should provide a usable experience across desktops, tablets, and smartphones.

How to apply it:

Use flexible layouts.
Optimize images for different screens.
Adjust text sizes appropriately.
Make buttons easy to tap.
Test menus and forms on mobile devices.

Example: Three service cards displayed in one desktop row should rearrange into a readable layout on smaller screens.

8. Make Buttons and Forms Clear

Visitors should understand what happens when they click a button or submit a form.

Best practices:

Use descriptive CTA labels.
Keep forms simple.
Clearly identify required fields.
Display helpful error messages.
Show confirmation after successful submissions.

Example:

Vague wording Clear wording
Click Here Request a Free Quote
Submit Send Your Enquiry
Download Download the UX Design Checklist
Clear instructions help visitors understand the next step.

9. Prioritize Website Accessibility

An accessible website helps people with different abilities use its content and features.

Important practices:

Add meaningful alternative text to informative images.
Use proper heading structures.
Support keyboard navigation.
Maintain sufficient color contrast.
Use descriptive form labels.
Make keyboard focus visible.

Example: Visible keyboard focus helps visitors identify which button or menu item is currently selected.

Refer to the W3C Web Accessibility Initiative for accessibility guidance.

10. Improve Website Speed and Performance

Slow-loading pages and delayed interactions can make websites frustrating to use.

How to improve performance:

Compress and optimize images.
Reduce unnecessary scripts.
Use efficient hosting and caching.
Minimize unused CSS and JavaScript.
Test important pages regularly.

Example: Replacing oversized images with appropriately optimized versions can reduce unnecessary page weight.

Use Google PageSpeed Insights to identify performance improvement opportunities.

Common Website Design Mistakes to Avoid

Mistake Recommended improvement
Cluttered layouts Use better spacing and content grouping.
Confusing navigation Choose clear menu labels.
Inconsistent design Follow a consistent design system.
Difficult-to-read text Improve typography and contrast.
Poor mobile experience Test responsive layouts.
Unclear CTAs Use specific action-oriented labels.
Inaccessible elements Include accessibility checks.
Slow-loading pages Optimize website performance.
Website UX Checklist
Before launching or updating your website, review these important elements:

Is the website designed around its target audience?
Is the visual hierarchy clear?
Can visitors find important pages easily?
Are colors, fonts, and buttons consistent?
Is there enough white space?
Is the website responsive across devices?
Are forms and CTAs easy to understand?
Does the website support accessible navigation?
Are images and other resources optimized?

Use this checklist to identify usability gaps and prioritize improvements.

How Amron Softech Can Help
Creating a better website experience requires more than attractive visuals. It involves thoughtful layouts, intuitive navigation, accessible design, and functionality that supports visitors’ needs.

Amron Softech provides website design services covering UI/UX design, web animation, and information architecture. You can also explore its broader design and digital solutions and client projects.

Frequently Asked Questions

  1. What are the most important website design principles?
    The key principles include audience-focused design, visual hierarchy, simple navigation, consistency, white space, readable typography, responsive design, clear interactions, accessibility, and performance.

  2. Why are website design principles important?
    They help businesses create websites that are easier to navigate, understand, and use, improving the overall visitor experience.

  3. How does visual hierarchy improve UX?
    It guides visitors toward important information through headings, spacing, contrast, and element positioning.

  4. Why is responsive design important?
    Responsive design helps website layouts adapt to different screen sizes, making content and functionality more usable across devices.

  5. How can I improve my website’s user experience?
    Review your navigation, content structure, mobile layout, forms, accessibility, and performance. Identify usability problems and prioritize improvements.

title: Dark Mode in Firefox: How It Works, What It Covers, and How to Force It Everywhere
description:
Dark mode has become a standard browser feature, but how it actually works, what sites support it, and how to get consistent dark experience across the whole web isn't well understood. Here's a practical guide.

How Dark Mode Propagates from Browser to Websites

The browser doesn't just "dark mode" websites. What it does is set the CSS media query prefers-color-scheme to dark. Sites that check this media query and have a dark color scheme defined will switch to it automatically. Sites that don't support the media query remain their default (usually light) appearance.

To set it in Firefox: Settings → General → Language and Appearance → Website Appearance → Dark. This sets the preference; the browser applies it to all sites that support it.

What doesn't switch: Any site that hasn't implemented prefers-color-scheme support. This is the majority of sites on the web. Major platforms (Twitter, GitHub, Reddit, Gmail, most Google products) support it. Smaller sites, older sites, and many corporate web apps don't.

Firefox UI Dark Mode

The browser UI itself (tabs, address bar, settings panels) has its own theme separate from website dark mode. To darken the Firefox UI:

  • Settings → General → Language and Appearance → Firefox's themes panel
  • Or install a dark theme from addons.mozilla.org/themes (many options, most free)

Firefox's built-in "Dark" theme darkens the browser chrome. Pairing the dark theme with the Website Appearance → Dark setting gives you dark browser UI + dark websites where supported.

Forcing Dark Mode on All Websites

For sites that don't support prefers-color-scheme, there are two approaches:

Browser-level force dark (experimental): In about:config, search for layout.css.prefers-color-scheme.content-override. Setting this to 0 forces dark on all sites. This is a blunt instrument — it inverts colors rather than applying a designed dark theme, so images and carefully designed UI can look wrong.

Dark mode extension: Extensions like "Dark Reader" apply intelligent dark mode transformations to any website. Dark Reader analyzes the page and generates a dark version, handling colors, images, and contrast appropriately. It's significantly more polished than the browser-level force dark. Dark Reader is the standard solution for comprehensive dark mode coverage.

Dark Reader vs Native Dark Mode

Native dark mode (via prefers-color-scheme):

  • Site's intended dark design — proper contrast ratios, intended color palette
  • No extension overhead
  • Only works where the site has implemented it

Dark Reader forced dark:

  • Works everywhere
  • Slight performance overhead (transforms every page)
  • Some pages look wrong despite the smart algorithm — particularly sites with complex layouts, PDFs, media-heavy pages

Best setup for most users: Enable native dark mode in Firefox settings, and also use Dark Reader for the remaining light sites. Dark Reader can be set to only apply to sites that don't have native dark mode (turn off for sites that handle it themselves).

OLED and Energy Considerations

For users on OLED displays (many modern laptops, all phones), true black (#000000) backgrounds turn off those pixels entirely, reducing power consumption and improving perceived contrast. Dark mode generally uses near-black backgrounds, not pure black, but on OLED displays there's still a meaningful energy benefit from dark interfaces compared to bright white backgrounds.

This is a reason to use dark mode on a laptop for battery reasons, not just comfort.

Eye Strain: What the Research Says

The research on dark mode and eye strain is more nuanced than the marketing suggests:

  • In low-light environments, dark mode reduces glare and is generally easier on the eyes
  • In bright environments (daytime office, outdoor), dark text on light background has better contrast and is easier to read
  • For users with certain types of astigmatism, light mode can be easier to read in some conditions

The practical takeaway: dark mode is better for evening use and comfortable for many users all day. If you find you're straining to read in dark mode, switching to a medium-contrast gray theme (not full white, not full black) may be more comfortable.

New Tab Dark Mode

The new tab page has its own styling. With a dark Firefox theme, the default new tab may still have a light background depending on your configuration.

Weather & Clock Dashboard for Firefox has a dark interface by default — dark background with light text for the time, weather, and world clocks. This matches a dark browser theme and dark website setting, giving a visually consistent experience when opening a new tab.

Firefox for Android Dark Mode

On Android, Firefox respects the system dark mode setting. Set your Android system to dark mode → Firefox UI and supported websites both switch to dark. The behavior is the same as desktop Firefox following the OS setting.

Per-Site Dark Mode Exceptions

If a specific site looks bad in dark mode (via Dark Reader or force dark), you can whitelist it. Dark Reader has a per-site disable button. For native dark mode, you can't override a specific site's dark implementation without developer tools.

Sites that have known dark mode issues and may warrant whitelisting: Google Maps (dark map themes can reduce readability), some banking sites with strict security styling, medical imaging tools, and anything where accurate color rendering matters (photo editing apps, color pickers).

Summary

The simplest setup: Settings → Website Appearance → Dark + a dark Firefox theme + Dark Reader extension. This gives you dark UI, dark sites where native support exists, and intelligent forced dark on everything else. Toggle Dark Reader off for specific sites where it looks wrong.

title: Fonts in headless Chromium: what your PDF really carries
description:
A template looks right in the editor, the PDF comes back, and the text is a little wider, a little rounder, and the line that used to fit now wraps. Nothing failed. There was no error, no warning and no log line. The PDF simply carries a different font from the one the template asked for.

It can happen with any HTML-to-PDF service that runs Chromium on a Linux server, ours included. We rendered four one-line templates with our render worker (Chromium 153, the image we run in production) and read back which fonts each PDF embedded.

The template says The PDF carries
font-family: "Segoe UI", Helvetica, sans-serif Liberation Sans
font-family: Inter, sans-serif, nothing loaded Liberation Sans
font-family: Inter, sans-serif, Google Fonts <link> Inter
the same, text with ✓, ✗ and → Inter, DejaVu Sans for ✓ and ✗, Liberation Sans for →

A family name is a wish

font-family is a list of names, and the browser takes the first one it has. On a Windows laptop that is Segoe UI. A Linux server has no Segoe UI and no Helvetica, so Chromium goes down the list, arrives at sans-serif, and the system hands it Liberation Sans. That is not a bad font: it was made with Arial's widths, so a line set for Arial keeps its length. It is just not the font the template names.

The second row is the one that catches people. Inter looks like a font the template has. On a designer's machine it is installed, so the editor preview shows Inter and everybody is happy. The server does not have it, and nothing in the template tells Chromium where to get it. The PDF comes out in Liberation Sans, and the first two lines of the picture are the same line.

The fix is to load every font you name. Either a <link> to Google Fonts or another web font service in the template's head, or an @font-face rule with the file. For fonts that are yours — a licensed corporate typeface — the same holds: serve the files from somewhere the server can fetch, and give the header and footer the @font-face rule too, because Chromium prints them from a separate document that never sees the template's stylesheet.

Check the PDF, not the preview

The preview in your browser uses the fonts on your computer, so it cannot tell you what a server lacks. The PDF can. It lists every font it embeds:

  • pdffonts invoice.pdf from poppler-utils prints one line per font.
  • In Acrobat or Acrobat Reader: File → Properties → Fonts.
  • In Chrome's PDF viewer there is no list; open the file in one of the above.

Names come with a six-letter prefix like ABCDEF+Inter-Regular. That means the PDF carries a subset: only the characters the document uses, which keeps it small. When the list says LiberationSans, DejaVuSans or NotoSans and your template named something else, either a font was never loaded or some characters were not in it (more on that below).

What a Google font costs

The worker has to fetch a web font before it can print, and it waits for document.fonts.ready, so a font that has not arrived is never skipped. That fetch takes time. We started a fresh worker three times, each with an empty cache, printed a plain page once to warm Chromium up and three more times to measure it, then printed the Inter template once and three more times. The worker reports its own render time.

Render time (median)
Page without web fonts 58 ms
Inter, first render, empty cache 318 ms
Inter, every render after 72 ms

The first render fetched Google's stylesheet and the font files; the ones after found both in the worker's disk cache and cost 14 ms more than a page with no web font at all. In production that cache lives on a disk that outlasts restarts and deployments and keeps a file for a week, so the fetch happens once per server and week, not once per document. Organisation fonts come from our own storage and go through the same cache.

Those are the numbers of a laptop in Germany talking to Google, with nothing heavy running beside it; next to three busy builds the same runs took four to five times as long, in the same proportions. The point is the shape, not the milliseconds. A service without such a cache pays the first line on every render.

A checkmark from a third font

The last row is the subtle one. Inter was loaded, the words are Inter, and still the PDF embeds three fonts. The Inter files Google served for this request do not contain ✓ and ✗, so Chromium looked for each character in the fonts installed on the server and found them in DejaVu Sans; the arrow came from Liberation Sans. Look at the picture: the check mark is heavier than the letters next to it, the arrow sits lower.

Chromium decides this per character, silently, and the result depends on what the server has installed — our image ships DejaVu, Liberation and the Noto families, so nothing falls out as an empty box, but it may well be a different design. Three ways out:

  • Pick a font that has the symbols you use, and load it.
  • Load a second font just for them (Noto Sans Symbols 2, say) and name it after your text font: font-family: Inter, "Noto Sans Symbols 2", sans-serif.
  • Draw status marks as inline SVG, which no font decides.

In short

  • Name only fonts you load, and load every font you name.
  • Read the font list of the PDF, not the look of the preview.
  • The first render with a web font is slower; after that a cache should make it free.
  • Symbols fall back one character at a time. If they matter, bring a font that has them.

The four PDFs are here to check for yourself: Segoe UI, Inter not loaded, Inter from Google Fonts, with symbols.

title: Maintain a banned CSS patterns list the agent must respect
description:
I used to paste “follow our design system” into every agent prompt. The PR still arrived with !important, magic z-index: 9999, and a one-off hex that matched nothing in the theme.

The agent wasn’t being rebellious. It just didn’t know which habits we had already decided were off-limits.

So I keep a short banned CSS patterns list next to the tokens file, and I paste it into UI prompts the same way I paste the ownership map.

What goes on the list

Not “write good CSS.” Specific patterns that keep showing up in agent diffs and keep failing review:

# banned-css.md (keep under ~30 lines)

Banned — do not introduce:
- `!important` (except existing legacy files listed below)
- hardcoded hex / rgb outside `tokens.css` / theme modules
- `z-index` above 20 without a comment pointing at the stacking doc
- `position: absolute` for layout that flex/grid already solves
- `font-size` / `line-height` / spacing as raw px when a token exists
- `outline: none` without a visible `:focus-visible` replacement
- `overflow: hidden` on interactive parents (clips focus rings / menus)
- vendor-prefixed properties we no longer need in supported browsers

Allowed escapes (name the file if you must use one):
- `src/legacy/datepicker.css` — still has `!important` until rewrite

If a rule needs a paragraph of nuance, it doesn’t belong here. Put the nuance in the design-system doc and keep this file scannable.

Why a ban list beats “use tokens”

Token constraints tell the agent what to prefer. A ban list tells it what to refuse even when the model is “sure” a quick hack is fine.

Agents love:

  • patching specificity wars with !important
  • inventing a new gray because the closest token is “almost”
  • burying a modal under z-index: 99999 so it “just works”
  • killing the outline to make the mock look clean

Each of those is a one-line “fix” that becomes a week of cleanup. Naming them up front cuts the argument out of review.

How I wire it into prompts

I don’t dump the whole design system. I attach the ban list + the relevant token slice:

Edit only `src/checkout/ShippingForm.module.css` (+ colocated component).

Respect `docs/banned-css.md` literally. If a banned pattern seems required,
stop and propose an alternative instead of writing it.

Prefer tokens from `src/styles/tokens.css` for color, space, type.
Do not invent new color literals.
Max ~80 lines of CSS change.

When the agent hits a wall (“I need higher z-index for the sticky bar”), I want a short note in the PR description — not a silent 9999.

What I reject in review

Reject on sight

  • New !important outside the legacy allowlist
  • Hex/rgb not imported from tokens
  • outline: none with no :focus-visible style in the same diff
  • z-index cliff without a stacking-context comment

Ask to split / redo

  • “Temporary” hacks with no ticket link
  • Copy-pasted utility classes that reintroduce banned patterns under a new name
  • Global selectors (div, button) to dodge a specificity problem the ban list was meant to prevent

If the ban list itself is wrong, we edit the list in a separate PR. We don’t “except this once” in the feature branch — that’s how the list dies.

Keeping the list alive

A dead ban list is worse than none. Once a month I:

  1. Grep the repo for each banned pattern and see what’s still real
  2. Drop rules nobody hits anymore
  3. Add the last two patterns that burned us in review
  4. Cap the file at roughly a screen of markdown

Agents follow short, concrete rules. They skim novels.

Prompt snippet I reuse 

Follow docs/banned-css.md. No !important, no raw colors, no outline:none
without :focus-visible, no z-index > 20 without a stacking comment.
If blocked by a ban, propose an alternative and stop — do not “just make it work.”

Tiny habit

Next time an agent sneaks !important into a “quick UI polish” PR, don’t only revert the line. Add that pattern to the ban list and paste the file into the next prompt.

You’re not teaching taste in chat. You’re giving the model a deny-list it can actually obey.

title: Which font is this? Chrome DevTools knows, in a section most people never scroll to
description:
Every front-end developer has done it: right-click, Inspect, read font-family, and announce the answer. Half the time that answer is wrong, because font-family is a wish list. The browser may have drawn something else entirely.

Chrome already knows which font it used. It tells you at the very bottom of the Computed tab, in a section called Rendered Fonts. Here is the whole route, plus the places where it goes wrong.

1. Select the element that holds the words

Right-click the text and choose Inspect, or press Ctrl + Shift + C (Cmd + Shift + C on a Mac) to open DevTools with the element picker already on.

The picker tooltip shows a font line. Treat it as a preview, not a verdict: it reports the declared family.

Make sure you land on the element that directly contains the text, not a wrapper div around it. font-family is inherited, so a wrapper reports a perfectly plausible stack while the real text node two levels down is styled differently.

2. Computed, not Styles

The side pane opens on Styles, which lists every rule that touches the element, including the ones that lost the cascade. Switch to Computed and type font in the filter. You get one final value per property:

Property What you see Watch out
font-family The full declared stack A list of preferences, not the result
font-size Final size in px 1.125rem shows as 18px
font-weight A number bold is resolved to 700
line-height px, or normal Divide by font size for the ratio: 28 / 18 is about 1.56

3. Scroll to Rendered Fonts

Below the last property there is a small section called Rendered Fonts. It does not come from CSS. It is a report from Chrome's text layer about what it actually painted for the selected element:

  • Font name: the name stored inside the font file. It can differ from the alias in the CSS.
  • Network resource: a web font the page downloaded through @font-face.
  • Local file: a font installed on your machine. Either a system fallback or a font the site expects you to have.
  • Glyph count: how many characters of the element's text were drawn with that font.

When the first name in font-family and the rendered font do not match, you are looking at a fallback.

Several fonts can be listed for one element because browsers pick a font per character, not per element. Most glyphs from the brand font and two from an emoji font is normal. Every glyph from Arial while the stack starts with a web font means the web font never loaded.

One trap: if you happen to have the site's font installed, Chrome may use your copy and report a local file. Visitors without it see the next font in the stack. Check on a clean machine when it matters.

4. Where the files come from

Rendered Fonts names the font. For the files and the weights, two more places:

Network panel, Font filter. Reload with DevTools open, because it only records what it sees. Each row is a font file. The domain is the fastest clue: fonts.gstatic.com is Google Fonts, use.typekit.net is Adobe Fonts, the site's own domain means self-hosted.

Search for @font-face. Press Ctrl + Shift + F (Cmd + Option + F) with DevTools focused to search every loaded file. The rules show which weights really exist, so you can tell a true bold from one the browser faked:

@font-face {
  font-family: "Site Serif";
  src: url("/fonts/literata-400.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 400;
}
@font-face {
  font-family: "Site Serif";
  src: url("/fonts/literata-700.woff2") format("woff2");
  font-weight: 700;
}

If you prefer the Console, $0 is the selected element:

getComputedStyle($0).fontFamily;

[...document.fonts]
  .filter((f) => f.status === "loaded")
  .map((f) => `${f.family} ${f.weight} ${f.style}`);

The second snippet lists web fonts only. System fonts never appear in document.fonts.

5. Four ways to get the wrong answer

  1. You selected a wrapper. Rendered Fonts describes the selected node's own text. No text, no section.
  2. The text is in an iframe. Inspect still works, but the Console runs in the top document by default. Switch the JavaScript context selector to the frame before running the snippets.
  3. The text is in Shadow DOM. Expand #shadow-root in the tree to reach the real element. Inherited properties such as font-family pass through from the host.
  4. The text is a pseudo-element. ::before and ::after show up as their own nodes; select them directly. ::first-line has no node at all, so read its rules in the parent's Styles tab.

The one-click version

We check fonts on other people's sites every day, and the route above is a lot of clicks. So we built Font Inspector, a free Chrome extension that puts the same facts in one panel next to the text: the declared family and the rendered font side by side with a fallback flag, size in px, em and rem, line height as a ratio, where each family comes from, every font on the page ranked by share of text, and copy as CSS, Tailwind or SCSS. No account, nothing uploaded.

DevTools is still the right tool for editing CSS live or debugging why a font file failed to load. For "what font is this", Rendered Fonts is the honest answer, and now you know where it hides.

The long version of this guide, with the Edge and Brave notes and more on fallbacks, is on font-inspector.com.
