title: Presentation: Zero Trust Agent Systems that Pass Audits and Still Ship
description:
Advait Patel shares a playbook for securing AI agent systems in production. He discusses moving defense boundaries from the prompt to the tool layer, enforcing scoped workload identities, and mitigating prompt injection via tool outputs. He explains how to structure audit-ready observability and implement kill switches to protect critical data while keeping deployment fast and compliant.

By Advait Patel

title: Design by numbers: is AI ruining UX or just pouring gasoline on the fire?
description:
Everyone seems to be asking whether AI will replace UX designers. I think that’s the wrong question.

In March 2025, the Computer History Museum and IEEE Spectrum staged a debate on a single question: when a large language model answers you, does it even understand what it’s saying? Does it comprehend what the words mean, or is it only predicting which word comes next?

Emily Bender, a linguist at the University of Washington, argued it’s only predicting. In fact, she has a name for these systems: stochastic parrots, machines that string words together by probability, the way a parrot repeats sounds, with no idea what any of it really means. Sébastien Bubeck, a researcher at OpenAI, took the opposite stance. Understanding, he argued, is in the eye of the beholder, and you judge it by what a system does.

“Let’s say I want to build an app, and I ask one of those models to build the app for me… I just specify in natural language what I want, I come back the next day and, boom, the app is there. Did the model understand on the way of creating this? In a way, I don’t really care. It did something for me.”

Let’s unpack this statement, because I think it’s a fairly common argument and also one that is dangerously misleading. Not only does this misrepresent how designers actually work, but the real danger is in the shrug. It lacks accountability. Once you stop caring whether AI understands what it’s doing, then you shift your measure of success away from outcomes and toward output.

UX design exists to make things work for the people who use them. Can the user complete a task easily and intuitively? That’s the outcome. The things designers produce along the way (journey maps, wireframes, prototypes, etc.) are outputs. They’re evidence of a process; they aren’t proof that anyone’s life got easier.

AI is a bit like a microwave — it will cook your food faster but not as well. Successful products are not ones that get made as quickly as possible but ones that resonate with users. A TV dinner is not fine dining. When we remove empathy and understanding from the deliverable, we risk delivering bad experiences that may not actually solve user pain points. Ignoring that is a treacherous path.

For the past year, I’ve spent eight or more hours a day designing with a range of AI tools. I’ve built everything from Chrome extensions to websites to enterprise-level multi-agent orchestration workflows. What I’ve learned is that, even for an experienced UX designer, this is no small feat. It requires tireless attention to detail over weeks or months to get a usable product from AI. It does not happen overnight, and it takes a hell of a lot of natural language cursing to get there.

What Bubeck is describing is a proof of concept, and a proof of concept is very different from a well-designed product. It shows that something can exist; it doesn’t show that it works for the people who will use it. By Bubeck’s own assertion that we should judge a system by what it does, the overnight app doesn’t pass muster.

Once that first, overnight build is in, what follows is actual UX design: noticing that the flow is wrong, that an error state is missing, that users get hung up in closed-loop modals. When we rush the first iteration, it can take a great deal of time and effort on the back end to repair these issues, especially if we’re trying to explain them to a tool that doesn’t understand what it’s doing.

But, if we’re being honest, this is not a problem that started with AI. Bubeck’s assertion comes from a misunderstanding of design that’s decades old: that the job is about outputs, rather than outcomes. So is AI really what we should be worried about here, or is it just pouring gasoline on a fire that was already burning?

But first: Is AI taking UX jobs?

Every few weeks, someone asks me whether I’m worried about losing my job to AI. All the headlines, the LinkedIn posts, and the steady stream of clickbait declaring that “designers are finished” make this an obvious question to ask, and I think I’m in a decent position to address it. As a design lead, I use AI tools every day — everything from Codex to Claude, IDEs, Mistral, Copilots, n8n, and GitHub Actions. I even developed my own VS Code extension to orchestrate cross-model prompt chaining. When I get spare time, I lecture about the history and impact of human-computer interaction at the university level.

I won’t pretend nothing has changed. Layoffs are real, and I’ve seen them firsthand, but the numbers are anecdotal. The only hard counts are tech-wide, not design-specific.

The best public data I could find for open design jobs comes from two sources: Indeed’s postings index for design and UX, and the job tracker TrueUp, which covers tech companies and startups. Indeed shows postings more than doubling from early 2021 to a peak in early 2022, then dropping roughly 70% by mid-2023. Most of this happened before anyone had ever heard of ChatGPT. TrueUp shows the same drop and what came after. Since autumn of 2023, it has kept mostly stable around 2,200, with a brief spike in spring 2026 before settling back down again.

That’s what a correction after a hiring surge looks like, and it doesn’t necessarily correlate with the spread of AI. If AI were driving these numbers, I’d expect the line to keep falling as the tools spread. Yet, Figma’s 2026 State of the Designer report found that 72% of the designers it surveyed are using generative AI. That doesn’t disprove AI is playing a role in the job market; it just means the data doesn’t show AI as a negative catalyst.

But still we feel the squeeze, and part of it may simply be supply and demand: too many new designers chasing the same amount of openings. Nobody publishes how many people are newly entering the UX field, or how many unemployed designers there are at each level, but a quick LinkedIn search for “UX designer” showed that the first 25 postings had already passed LinkedIn’s display cap of “Over 100” applicants. That’s just one search (and these applicants aren’t necessarily all out of work) but it does give you an idea of what looking for a job right now is like.

Put together, these numbers don’t really describe a sea change of job loss. AI doesn’t seem to be changing whether the jobs exist so much as what the jobs are. I’m less afraid of losing my job to AI than I am of the job itself becoming unrecognizable. Design has been misunderstood for decades, and if we’re not careful, AI agents will let that misunderstanding become the job description, leaving the user experience to chance.

Design (without) thinking

I believe true UX designers are a rare breed. The work is a combination of critical thinking, empathy, and taste. These are things you can’t really teach, and they’re also things that AI fundamentally lacks.

I say that as someone who teaches and has seen the limits of what teaching can accomplish. A course can show you how to run a usability test or build a journey map, but it can’t make you care whether the person on the other side struggled. It can’t give you the instinct that something is off before you can say exactly what. What a course can teach is process, and that’s where AI and human designers both get tripped up: it’s hard to empathize when you’re following a prescribed process. Thoughtlessly following processes can imitate outputs, but not outcomes.

The trouble is that process is visible and ability is not, so the two are often conflated. You can see a workshop, journey maps, or wireframes, but you can’t see the judgment that decided what question to ask during a user interview, or when to challenge the obvious solution. When design is reduced to a checklist of methods and deliverables, it’s easier to report what has been delivered, but a team can run a flawless process and still deliver an unusable product.

This is what I mean by “design by numbers”: the fallacy that if you follow the steps and produce the artifacts, good design is guaranteed at the end.

But where did this misunderstanding come from? In the 1960s, the design methods movement set out to “scientise” design into a linear process that anyone could follow and repeat. Some of its own pioneers later turned against this idea, describing the attempt to make design scientific as a misguided effort to turn dynamic problem solving into a linear, repeatable process. They argued that the problems designers face don’t sit still long enough to be universal. Horst Rittel called these “wicked” problems: ill-formulated, with confusing information, many decision makers with conflicting values, and consequences that ripple through the whole system.

Design is not a linear, repeatable process, and it never was. There is no single path to a solution waiting to be found.

I liken it to IKEA assembly instructions: you can follow the steps and build a perfectly fine shelf, but what if now you need to build a table or paint a wall? Would you use the same instructions? Or even the same tools?

Design thinking, the most widely used methodology in the field, is a genuinely good way to get a team collaborating. In practice, though, it can devolve into a clutter of sticky notes that no one will ever look at again, with designers speculating about what stakeholders actually need, think, and feel. Graphic designer Natasha Jen made this point in her talk Design Thinking Is Bullsh*t. She regretted that design practice had been reduced to a defined sequence of steps, and argued that “real designers surround themselves with evidence.” When we limit ourselves to preconceived processes, we may be the ones preventing ourselves from solving what looks impossible. Writer and designer John Thackara offers a better frame, which he calls sense-and-respond design, where you describe the desired outcomes but not the detailed means of reaching them.

That can be a bitter pill to swallow for stakeholders who need to report quarterly deliverables, but here’s the thing: users don’t care about deliverables — they care whether a product works for them. And that outcome depends on whether designers have the time and ability to understand what they are doing.

Slop is as slop does

If you believe process and output is the job of design, then AI might look like a handy replacement. It produces outputs quickly and confidently: personas, flows, copy — even working prototypes. And designers aren’t resisting that. In the Figma survey, 89% of designers using generative AI said it makes them faster, and I’d say the same about my own work. AI is a genuinely useful tool, but it’s a tool like any other. Generating these artifacts is only part of a designer’s job, and it’s the part that doesn’t require critical thinking, empathy, or taste.

When I talk to my students about how to work with AI, I like to separate tasks into two different categories: thinking and doing.

AI is good at doing. In my experience, that typically includes three things in UX design:

  • Synthesizing user research. It can take a pile of interview notes or survey responses and group, summarize and surface patterns far faster than I can by hand. That’s the legwork. What the patterns mean for the product is still mine to decide.
  • Meta-work. Slide decks, readouts, summaries and the other work about the work. It’s necessary and it takes time, but none of it is the design itself.
  • Translating mockups into prototypes. Once I’ve decided what the experience should be, AI can turn the mockups into something clickable much faster than I could build it myself. But the design work I do at the whiteboard is still the source of truth.

Designers can let AI do things for them. But it should never think for them. There’s a name for this: automation bias, the tendency to trust what an automated system hands us over our own judgment. A hammer is an incredibly useful tool, but would you let a hammer think for you? Deciding what the problem is, what the research means, what to build, and what’s good enough requires critical thinking skills, and that’s where AI stops and the designer’s judgment takes over. When we outsource our thinking to AI, what comes back might look like a solid answer but is really just stochastic parroting from something that doesn’t understand the problem.

AI is a translation tool. It can turn natural language into code very quickly, but it doesn’t understand how to ask the right questions. It can’t properly architect a product, and it frequently misses visual bugs that are glaringly obvious to a real designer.

When anyone can generate a prototype in an afternoon, a prototype stops being evidence of anything important. In a world where AI slop is cheap and fast, the designer’s ability to discern good design from bad and to ask whether we’re solving the right problem becomes more important, not less.

When the enshittification hits the fan

The more I work with AI, the more I see a need to change the way we think about design.

The pressure starts with expectations. If the story is that you can “come back the next day and, boom, the app is there,” then someone down the hall will ask why designing the first MVP has taken two weeks. A proof of concept gets mistaken for the product, timelines compress, and the output gets treated as the outcome.

Figma’s survey lists unrealistic timelines among the things that stand in the way of designers doing their best work. AI puts that into a pressure cooker because the artifacts can be built faster than we can understand them. With an expedited delivery timeline, the first things to go are the parts that are hard to report: talking to the people who will use the product, testing, critiquing, discovering you are wrong and then iterating as you learn. These things look like delays when AI can just cut straight to the end result.

But there’s a problem with jumping straight to the end: it’s reckless. Letting AI build products for you creates a kind of house of mirrors that only the AI knows how to navigate. Because of context limits, it builds piecemeal, one function at a time, supplanting holistic architecture for a labyrinth of myopic patches. The result is a product that might work but that nobody really understands. I can’t tell you the number of times I’ve had to prompt AI to refactor an entire codebase because it lacked any architectural spine. Say goodbye to your tokens.

Building products this way also shifts the means of production out of your business and into the hands of a few AI companies (OpenAI and Anthropic, to name a few). Your business ends up relying on agent subscriptions and usage limits to stay in operation, while your own employees become less skilled. That should be a very dubious prospect for any business owner.

We’re already starting to see what this shift looks like day to day. A product manager I worked with recently surprised me one day with designs he’d made using AI. He was visibly excited about what he’d created, but to me they were a jumbled mess: no hierarchy, no clear calls to action, useless icons on every surface… To someone who isn’t a designer, they probably looked fine. That’s the trick with these tools. They sound like they know what they’re talking about, but only to people who don’t know what they’re talking about.

And this is not just a design problem. It’s becoming more and more pervasive across disciplines. Designers using AI can see the flaws in its designs just like developers can see the flaws in its code. So the next time you vibe-code something, understand that what you’re creating is not a finished product that any god-fearing developer would bless.

The key here is to maintain accountability by learning to spot the warning signs. Is a PM asking AI instead of doing market research? Red flag. Is a designer using AI as a beta tester instead of talking to actual users? Red flag. Did a stakeholder say everything looks good on a call, then immediately dump five paragraphs of feedback into Slack? Maybe start to question how much thought actually went into that.

We need to get into the habit of not limiting our focus to artifacts and output and instead ask deeper questions about how we are creating better experiences. If you can answer that, you’ll be fine with or without AI. And if you can’t — or don’t really care — you’re going to have bigger problems than any tool can fix.

AI is a powerful tool, and in the hands of someone who understands its limitations, it can make the work easier. The open question is who gets to decide how it’s used, and whether they understand the difference between producing an output and enabling an outcome.

What businesses need to understand is that design is qualitative, not quantitative. It can’t be reduced to steps and artifacts, and it can’t be measured by how much gets produced. Design is a conversation between the business and its users that says “we’ve thought about this more than you’ll ever have to.” The companies that stand apart will be the ones that invest in that level of thinking. The companies that outsource their thinking to AI will get the same slop as everyone else.

Further reading

  • Bender, E. M., Gebru, T., McMillan-Major, A. & Shmitchell, S. (2021). On the dangers of stochastic parrots: Can language models be too big? Proceedings of the 2021 ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT ‘21), 610–623. https://doi.org/10.1145/3442188.3445922
  • Buchanan, R. (1992). Wicked problems in design thinking. Design Issues, 8(2), 5–21.
  • Carr, N. (2014). The Glass Cage: Automation and Us. W. W. Norton.
  • Challenger, Gray & Christmas. (2026, August). Challenger Report, July 2026. https://www.challengergray.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Challenger-Report-July-2026.pdf
  • Computer History Museum & IEEE Spectrum. (2025, March 25). The Great Chatbot Debate. https://computerhistory.org/events/great-chatbot-debate/
  • Cross, N. (2001). Designerly ways of knowing: Design discipline versus design science. Design Issues, 17(3), 49–55.
  • Doctorow, C. (2023, January 21). TikTok’s enshittification. Pluralistic. https://pluralistic.net/2023/01/21/potemkin-ai/
  • Figma. (2026). State of the Designer 2026. https://www.figma.com/reports/state-of-the-designer-2026/
  • Indeed Design. (2023). UX job listings plunged in 2023. https://indeed.design/article/ux-job-listings-plunged-in-2023
  • Jen, N. (2017). Design Thinking Is Bullsh*t. Talk presented at the 99U Conference, New York. https://youtu.be/_raleGrTdUg
  • Layoffs.fyi. Tech layoffs tracker. https://layoffs.fyi
  • Rittel, H. W. J. & Webber, M. M. (1973). Dilemmas in a general theory of planning. Policy Sciences, 4(2), 155–169.
  • Thackara, J. (2005). In the Bubble: Designing in a Complex World. MIT Press.
  • TrueUp. Design jobs tracker. https://www.trueup.io/design/reports
  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. (2026). Current Population Survey, 2025 annual averages: Unemployed web and digital interface designers. https://www.bls.gov/cps/

title: Everyone’s got a quick question
description:
And you shouldn’t have to answer them all.

There’s an interactive version of this story. Explore it →

I became the team’s search engine

Every team has a person everyone reaches out to. They know where things live, why a decision went the way it did, and who to ask when you’re stuck. If you’re on a team, you’ve probably messaged yours today. 😏

In Radical Candor, Kim Scott calls the steady, dependable people a team is built on its rock stars. Our team has a few too many sports fans, so we call ours the GOAT: the greatest of all time.

I lead a remote design team of fifteen, and a lot of the team’s questions find their way to me. Each seems small enough on its own, but the constant interruptions were starting to wear on me. 🫣

And apparently, there’s research behind that frustration: a 2008 CHI paper found that people often work faster to make up for interruptions, but feel more stressed and frustrated as a result.

I wondered how many of these interruptions were actually necessary. So I reviewed two and a half years of requests — 2,413 in total — and sorted them by what it took to answer. That led Bryan, my intern, and me to build a Slack agent to take some of them off my plate.

What was in my inbox

At my busiest, about nine housekeeping requests reached me every workday, close to fifty a week. Spread across a calendar, they filled almost every workday.

Some questions kept coming back

Plenty felt like déjà vu. 203 had been asked before, some more than a dozen times. The most repeated — how to access user study recordings — came up 32 times. My guess is that most repeats happened in DMs, where nobody else could see the answer. And even in public channels, how often does anyone dig through old Slack threads?

The wait by hour

Most of my designers are part-timers who work their own hours, often in the evening, while I keep a nine to five. During the day, I tried to get back to people as soon as I could, usually within about 15 minutes (allow me to feel proud of myself for a second 😎). Outside working hours, however, a question could wait 12 to 13 hours, until I was back the next morning.

Did these all need me?

Not really. After going through the cases carefully, I found that 53% didn’t need me at all. The answer already existed somewhere, in a doc, a Figma file or an old thread; people just couldn’t find it, or didn’t know it was there. Another 35% were mostly legwork, like digging up which spec was current or what a handoff thread had settled, before I signed off. The last 12% were the calls only I could make: someone’s role, their hours, who should help with what.

Most questions didn’t need my judgment. They just needed an answer

Could an agent answer them?

I’ll admit, I’d been quietly “cheating” on the easy questions: paste them into my own agent, check the answer, and pass it along in my own words. It worked often enough that I wondered, why not let the team ask directly? So Bryan and I built a quick Slack prototype. We called it le goat 🐐 (my fellow LeBron fans, iykyk).

Here’s what happened when I tried an easy one. A small server on Cloudflare picked up the mention and reacted with 👀, so whoever asked knew le goat was on it. It kept track of the thread and handed the question to Gemini, which looked things up in Notion, GitHub and the web, then wrote back in the same thread.

It worked, but a simple question could get a 639-word essay in return. I’d feel really guilty dropping that on someone in Slack. le goat needed work.

Making it a bot with manners

Before anyone else saw it, I taught it how to reply. Much of the interaction design was inspired by principles in Google’s People + AI Guidebook, especially around communicating uncertainty, handling errors, and keeping people in control. The challenge was making those principles feel natural in a Slack conversation.

  • Show it’s working. A question used to meet four silent minutes, then the bot’s inner monologue. Now “Thinking” appears right away, with the steps folded under it and a Stop button.
  • Get to the point. The answer used to hide in paragraph two. Now it comes first, in one line. A comparison becomes a small table, and counts become bars.
  • Know what you don’t know. One of our developers loves quoting Socrates: real wisdom is knowing what you don’t know. Instead of a confident claim with nothing behind it, le goat now says what it couldn’t find and who would know, and its sources fold away under one tap.
  • Leave the calls to people. Instead of editing our guidelines without asking, le goat drafts the change, like an update to a doc or a new card, and never makes it itself. The draft arrives on a card in Slack, and nothing changes until the right person approves it.

The MVP for everyday questions

With its manners in place, I scoped the MVP to the five kinds of questions people asked me most often: finding something (314 asks), catching up on what they missed (565), knowing who to ask (448), asking for design-system guidance (731), and turning a discussion into a card.

A tryout with the team

For the pilot, I invited the whole team to try le goat and ask it anything in Slack. And they kept asking: 228 questions in two weeks, averaging 31 a day in week two. That’s more than three times my busiest week.

They wanted it in the flow

The funny thing about giving people an agent they can ask anything: they start wanting it everywhere. Designers wanted le goat in Figma, where they spend their day, so we built that. Now they can @le goat in a Figma comment and get a reply right there.

From answering to asking

People were clearly using le goat. But I also wanted to know if I could trust its answers.

Competent, but not confident

So I checked 56 of its answers for hallucinations. Luckily, none were confidently wrong. But only 37 were confident and right. The other 19, about one in three, came back unsure. That’s a lot of uncertainty for an agent meant to unblock the team.

What puzzled me was that the answers seemed well grounded. The tools were connected, and the sources were cited correctly. So why was le goat so unsure?

Here’s one of those 19 cases, recreated. Someone asked how big the field labels on our forms should be. le goat found three answers: the Forms PRD in Notion said TBD, Figma said 13px, and the code said 14px. It couldn’t tell which was current.

Finding the answers wasn’t the problem. Knowing which one to trust was.

Why the docs disagreed

To see how they drifted apart, I lined up the sources chronologically. A PM asked about the field-label size, and the PRD recorded TBD. Design later settled on 13px, and the code followed. But the PRD never caught up, and an unrelated refactor eventually changed the code to 14px. No wonder le goat was unsure.

This is partly a team coordination problem. Practices like Atlassian’s working agreements help clarify how teams work together and where decisions live. But decisions change, and documentation doesn’t always keep up.

A proactive teammate

And this wasn’t the only time our sources disagreed. Of the 2,413 asks, 204 (8.5%) were people checking which version of something was right. Those were some of the best questions I got. They helped catch discrepancies and kept the team aligned.

A real GOAT doesn’t just answer questions. They know which questions need asking.

So I wondered if le goat could do that too. That became the idea behind the next iteration: making it a proactive teammate that could speak up on its own, in three ways.

Shares the FYI. Decisions don’t always reach everyone who needs to know. So le goat sends a short morning update every day with what’s changed and where it was decided.

Flags the discrepancy. Every Monday, le goat checks for sources that don’t agree. Instead of just raising questions, it brings the right people the evidence and a proposed fix to review.

Follows through. Fixes can slip through the cracks. When one goes unreviewed, le goat checks whether it’s already been handled before sending the owner a reminder.

Every accepted fix leaves a cleaner source. And with each owner only reviewing their part, nobody has to maintain everything alone. A little divide & conquer.

A few tweaks under the hood

For anyone curious about the tech, here are a few nerdy improvements I made since the first prototype.

Classification. Not every message needs the same amount of thinking (or spending 🤑). Jev, a small, fast model, classifies messages first: simple ones get a prescribed reply, while real questions go to the LLM with an appropriate thinking level.

Connector expansion. We added Figma and our service knowledge base through Supabase, alongside Notion, GitHub and the web. That’s how we got le goat answering directly in Figma comments: a webhook picks up the mention, and the reply goes back into the same thread.

Permissions. We made le goat aware of where it’s speaking — public channels, private channels or DMs — to avoid oversharing sensitive information. People can opt in by linking their Slack account, letting le goat search their private conversations while keeping the answers visible only to them.

Triple-double for the team

I tracked three things to see if le goat helped: how many questions still reached me, how long people waited, and how often it was confident and right. All three improved. And the answers now live in shared threads, where the next person can find them.

Setting the GOAT free

Every team needs someone who knows where things live, why decisions were made, and who owns what. But their days shouldn’t go to answering the same questions.

le goat takes care of the everyday asks, freeing those people for the work that needs them: hard design calls, riffing on ideas, pushing boundaries, and raising the ceiling.

There’s a bigger benefit, too. As agents become part of everyday work, a reliable knowledge base matters even more. Fewer discrepancies mean fewer made-up answers and better information for people and agents alike.

Let le goat handle the busywork, so the real GOATs have time for the hard work.

What’s next: the agent farm

Now that le goat is out of the barn, I’ve been thinking about recruiting a few teammates. A sassy owl for critiques, a diligent mule for the dirty work, a quick horse for urgent requests. Every GOAT needs a team, right?

Further reading

A few resources that informed this work or offer useful perspectives on the challenges discussed:

  • Radical Candor — Kim Scott. On building effective teams and recognizing the contributions of rock stars and superstars.
  • The Cost of Interrupted Work: More Speed and Stress — Gloria Mark, Daniela Gudith & Ulrich Klocke (CHI 2008). On the hidden costs of workplace interruptions.
  • People + AI Guidebook — Google PAIR. On designing AI interactions around uncertainty, trust, and human control.
  • Working Agreements — Atlassian Team Playbook. On establishing shared expectations for how teams communicate and make decisions.

title: There is not one pixel size on our big screen: 128 container-query values, and the same component is a card on our homepage
description:
PubTrivia has a screen that goes on a pub television. The host runs the quiz from a laptop, mirrors or screen-shares it to whatever is on the wall, and the room reads the question off it from twenty feet away. The same component also appears, scaled down to about 300 pixels wide, inside the homepage: the demo there is not a screenshot or a video, it is the real host view with a made-up round in it.

One component, two sizes two orders of magnitude apart, and no media queries. The trick is that the component contains no pixel sizes at all.

cqmin, against a size container

The frame declares itself a container, and every size inside it is a fraction of that container rather than of the viewport or of the root font size:

export function StageFrame({ children, className = 'h-[100dvh]' }) {
  return (
    <div className={`relative flex w-full flex-col overflow-hidden [container-type:size] ${className}`}>
      {children}
    </div>
  )
}

container-type: size is the strict one: it establishes containment on both axes, so cqw, cqh and cqmin all resolve against this box. That is why the frame carries a height (h-[100dvh] in the app, whatever the demo's frame is on the homepage) rather than letting content decide it. container-type: inline-size would only give you the width, which is not enough when the constraint you are actually fighting is vertical: a question that wraps onto a third line must not push the leaderboard off the bottom of a television.

Inside, everything is cqmin, which is the smaller of the two container dimensions:

<div className="grid grid-cols-[minmax(0,1fr)_auto_minmax(0,1fr)] items-center gap-[2cqmin] px-[3cqmin] pt-[2.4cqmin] pb-[1.6cqmin]">

Padding, gaps, border radii, badge diameters, the height of the row the question sits in, and every font size as text-[length:4.4cqmin]. Five files, 128 such values at the commit currently deployed. Icons inside text are sized h-[1em] w-[1em] so they ride the font size they are next to, which means they scale too without being counted.

Choosing cqmin rather than cqw is the part worth arguing about. On a 16:9 television cqmin is the height, so the layout is driven by the dimension that actually runs out. A 4:3 projector, which plenty of pubs still have, gets proportionally larger text rather than a layout that overflows the bottom. The cost is that an unusually wide, short window makes everything small, which a laptop in full screen never is.

What it buys

Three things that would otherwise each be their own piece of code:

  1. The demo is the product. The marketing page passes a different className to the same frame and gets a faithful miniature. There is no second set of styles to drift, and when the real screen changes, the homepage changes with it.
  2. No breakpoints for screen size. A 13-inch laptop, a 55-inch TV and a 4K display are the same layout at the same proportions. There is nothing to test at 1080p that differs from 4K except the pixel density.
  3. Alignment survives. One exported constant, STAGE_TOP_ROW = 'h-[8cqmin]', fixes the height of the top row across the question screen and the final screen, so the leaderboard beside them does not jump by a few pixels when the quiz ends. In pixels that constant would have to be a different number per screen size.

The rule that breaks it

Container units resolve against the nearest ancestor container, not the one you had in mind. So the frame's own doc comment carries a warning that is really an architectural constraint:

Put nothing in between that is a container itself, or the units inside it measure the wrong box.

Tailwind's @container utility, which is handy for component-level responsive design, is exactly the thing you must not use inside this subtree. One well-meaning @container on an intermediate wrapper and every cqmin below it silently starts measuring a card instead of the stage: nothing errors, the text just comes out wrong on the television and right on the laptop.

There is a second, quieter trap. container-type: size applies containment, which means the box no longer sizes itself from its contents. Give the frame no height and it collapses, and the error message for that is "the screen is blank", which is a long way from "you forgot a height".

Then I replaced all 128 of them with one letter

The version in my working tree now does the same thing through a single custom property, because the stage had to work on a phone-shaped window as well (a host running the quiz from their own phone, with no TV involved):

<div className="... [container-type:size] [&>*]:[--u:1cqmin] @max-3xl:[&>*]:[--u:1.8cqw]">

Every size then reads calc(N * var(--u)):

className="px-[calc(3*var(--u))] pt-[calc(2.4*var(--u))] text-[length:calc(2.6*var(--u))]"

The numbers are identical. What changes is that the unit is now a variable: 1cqmin on a wide stage, and 1.8cqw below 48rem, where the window is tall and narrow and the height is no longer the dimension that runs out. 128 cqmin literals became 143 references to var(--u) across the same five files, and the entire phone adaptation is two declarations on one element.

Two details made that work. The custom property is set on [&>*], the frame's children, rather than on the frame itself, because a property whose value is a container unit resolves against the element's own nearest container, and on the frame that is the frame's parent. And the code is noticeably uglier: py-[calc(1*var(--u))] is not as nice to read as py-[1cqmin]. The uglier version is the one that works on both shapes, so it wins.

Check it yourself

Open pub-trivia.app, find the big-screen demo, and drag the window narrower and wider. Every bit of that panel, text included, scales continuously rather than snapping at breakpoints, because nothing in it is expressed in pixels. The feature page for the screen itself is here.

You can also count the technique from outside. The deployed homepage carries 38 cqmin classes in its HTML, 34 of them distinct:

$ curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/ | grep -oE '[a-z-]+-\[[^]]*cqmin[^]]*\]' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5
   3 gap-[2cqmin]
   2 text-[length:1.9cqmin]
   2 gap-[0.8cqmin]
   1 text-[length:4.4cqmin]
   1 w-[26cqmin]

And the stylesheet it loads contains 160 of them, with exactly one container-type: size rule in it:

$ curl -s https://pub-trivia.app/ | grep -o '/_next/static/chunks/[^"?]*\.css' | sort -u \
    | while read f; do curl -s "https://pub-trivia.app$f" | grep -o cqmin | wc -l; done
0
160

One rule, because there is one stage.

title: Blind RSA in circl ignored the reader you passed it
description:
Cloudflare's circl has a partially blind RSA signer. Its Blind method takes an io.Reader. The blinding factor used that reader. The salt did not. It read from crypto/rand directly.

That breaks the contract. Two calls with the same deterministic reader should give the same blinded message. They did not, because half the randomness came from somewhere else. The sibling code in brsa.go did it right and used the supplied reader throughout.

The fix is one line in blindsign/blindrsa/partiallyblindrsa/pbrsa.go:

_, err := io.ReadFull(random, salt)

It used to read from rand.Reader. Now it reads from random, the reader the caller passed in.

The test pins it down. TestBlindUsesSuppliedReader calls Blind twice with fresh deterministic readers that emit the same byte sequence. Both blinded messages must be identical. It fails before the fix and passes after. Callers passing crypto/rand see no behavior change.

Merged as cloudflare/circl#711: https://github.com/cloudflare/circl/pull/711

title: Your brand has one color. The color wheel knows the other four.
description:
Every designer has been here. You have one good brand color, maybe a blue you love, and now you need four more that go with it. So you open a color picker, guess a lighter blue, guess a pink that might work, and twenty minutes later your palette looks like five strangers at a bus stop.

That guessing is the problem. Color harmony is not taste, it is math, and the color wheel has done the work for you for about three hundred years.

The wheel is a calculator

A color is really three numbers: hue (where it sits on the wheel, 0 to 360), saturation (how vivid it is) and lightness (how bright). Harmony rules are just recipes for picking hues at fixed distances from your base color.

Complementary: your color plus the one exactly opposite it on the wheel, 180 degrees away. Blue and orange, purple and yellow. High contrast, high energy, and the reason every "50 percent off" banner you have ever seen is orange on blue. Use it for accents and calls to action, never for two big areas side by side, or the page starts vibrating.

Analogous: your color plus its two neighbors, 30 degrees on either side. Blue, blue-green and green. Calm, natural, almost impossible to get wrong. This is the palette of dashboards and documentation sites, the ones that feel quiet and professional without trying.

Triadic: three colors evenly spaced, 120 degrees apart. Bold and balanced at the same time, which is why it shows up in branding for kids products, games and anything that needs to feel fun without feeling random. The trick is letting one color dominate and using the other two sparingly.

Split-complementary: your color plus the two colors next to its opposite. You get almost the punch of complementary without the vibration. It is the safe version of the loudest rule, and it is the one I reach for most.

Tetradic: two complementary pairs, a rectangle on the wheel. Four colors is a lot, so this one needs discipline: one dominant color, the rest as support. Get it right and a site feels rich; get it wrong and it feels like a carnival.

Monochromatic: one hue, different lightnesses. The easiest palette that always works. A dark navy, a mid blue, a pale sky blue, and you have a complete UI with zero risk. Boring is a feature when the content needs to do the talking.

The mistake everyone makes with tints

Pick a palette from a generator and the first thing people do is lighten a color by mixing it with white in RGB. That is how you get washed out pastels that look tired. Lighten in HSL space instead: keep the hue and saturation, raise the lightness. The color stays itself, just brighter. The same applies to darkening, which is how you get deep, rich shades instead of muddy ones.

The second mistake is contrast. A beautiful palette is useless if nobody can read the text on it. The rule is simple and checkable: body text needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 against its background, large text 3 to 1. You can compute this exactly from the two colors, so there is no reason to guess. If your light grey text fails on your light blue background, darken the text or darken the background until the number passes.

The workflow that saves the twenty minutes

You do not need to memorize the wheel. Pick your base color, pick a rule, and let the math build the palette: https://www.theutilityhub.online/tools/color-palette-generator

The generator I built gives you all six harmony rules from one base color, lets you lock the swatches you like and regenerate the rest, checks the WCAG contrast ratio for any text and background pair, and exports the finished palette as CSS variables, a Tailwind config or JSON. Copy the variables into your stylesheet and the palette is live in your project.

One habit worth stealing: export the palette as CSS variables on day one, before you write a single component. --color-primary, --color-accent, --color-surface, --color-text. When the brand color changes later, and it will, you change one line instead of hunting hex codes through fifty files.

Your brand color was never the hard part. The wheel already knew the other four. Let it tell you.

title: How CSS Controls the Visual Appearance of Text: A Beginner’s Guide to CSS Typography
description:
When you visit a website, you probably don't consciously think about every detail of the text you're reading.

You simply read it.

But what if the text were extremely small? What if the lines were packed tightly together? What if the font was difficult to recognize? What if the colour had poor contrast with the background?

You might struggle to read the content—or leave the website altogether.

This is one reason CSS typography is so important in web development.

CSS doesn't just make a webpage look attractive. It gives developers control over how text is presented, helping users read, scan, understand, and navigate information.

In this beginner-friendly guide, we'll look at some of the most important CSS properties used to control text appearance, including:

  • color
  • background-color
  • font-family
  • font-size
  • font-weight
  • line-height
  • letter-spacing
  • text-align
  • text-decoration

Let's get started.

What Is CSS Typography?

Typography refers to the way written text is arranged and presented.

In web development, CSS typography involves using CSS properties to control things such as:

  • Font type
  • Font size
  • Font thickness
  • Text colour
  • Line spacing
  • Character spacing
  • Text alignment
  • Text decoration

HTML provides the structure of your content.

For example:

Welcome to My Website

This is my first paragraph.

HTML tells the browser:

This is a heading.

and:

This is a paragraph.

CSS then allows you to decide how those elements should appear.

For example:

h1 {
font-size: 36px;
font-weight: 700;
color: navy;
}

p {
font-size: 18px;
line-height: 1.6;
}

Now the content has a visual hierarchy and is easier to read.

  1. The color Property

The color property controls the colour of text.

For example:

p {
color: #333;
}

This makes the paragraph text a dark grey.

You can use named colours:

h1 {
color: blue;
}

Hexadecimal colours:

h1 {
color: #800020;
}

Or other CSS colour formats such as RGB and HSL.

Why does text colour matter?

Because readability depends partly on the relationship between your text colour and its background.

For example, light grey text on a white background may look subtle, but it can be difficult to read.

Good typography considers both appearance and accessibility.

Instead of asking:

Does this colour look attractive?

also ask:

Can people comfortably read this text?

  1. The background-color Property

background-color controls the background colour of an element.

For example:

p {
background-color: #f5f5f5;
}

The paragraph's box will have a light background behind the text.

You might also use it for headings:

h1 {
background-color: lightyellow;
}

Or for an entire section:

section {
background-color: #f5f5f5;
}

Remember that background-color applies to the element's box. It isn't a separate colour applied only to the individual characters.

Background and text colours should work together.

A beautiful background is not useful if the text placed on top of it becomes difficult to read.

  1. The font-family Property

Have you ever noticed that different websites seem to have completely different personalities?

Some look formal.

Others look playful.

Some look modern and minimal.

Typography plays a major role in creating that feeling.

The font-family property determines which typeface the browser should use.

For example:

body {
font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
}

You can also provide multiple fonts as fallbacks:

body {
font-family: "Helvetica Neue", Arial, sans-serif;
}

The browser will try to use the first available font and move through the list if necessary.

Why does font choice matter?

Font choice affects:

  • Readability
  • Visual hierarchy
  • Brand personality
  • Professional appearance
  • Overall consistency

However, choosing a font shouldn't become a competition to find the most unusual typeface.

A font can look beautiful and still be uncomfortable to read.

For body text especially, readability should be a major consideration.

  1. The font-size Property

As the name suggests, font-size controls how large or small text appears.

For example:

p {
font-size: 18px;
}

You can also use other CSS units such as rem , em , % , or responsive units depending on the situation.

For example:

h1 {
font-size: 2rem;
}

Different types of content may require different sizes.

A main heading should normally stand out more than a paragraph.

For example:

h1 {
font-size: 2.5rem;
}

h2 {
font-size: 2rem;
}

p {
font-size: 1rem;
}

This creates a visual hierarchy.

The visitor can quickly recognize:

Main heading → Subheading → Body text

That's useful because people don't always read webpages word for word.

They often scan them first.

  1. The font-weight Property

font-weight controls the weight or thickness of text.

For example:

h1 {
font-weight: 700;
}

A higher value generally produces a heavier weight when the chosen font provides that weight.

You can also use keywords such as:

font-weight: normal;

or:

font-weight: bold;

Weight can help establish hierarchy.

For example, you might use a heavier weight for headings and a regular weight for paragraphs.

h1 {
font-weight: 700;
}

p {
font-weight: 400;
}

The result is a clearer distinction between important headings and supporting information.

But heavier doesn't always mean better.

If everything on a webpage is bold, nothing feels particularly important.

  1. The line-height Property

This is one of the most useful properties for readable paragraphs.

line-height controls the height of the line boxes, affecting the vertical space between lines of text.

Consider this:

p {
line-height: 1.6;
}

Compared with tightly packed text, the paragraph will generally feel more open and comfortable to read.

For example:

p {
font-size: 16px;
line-height: 1.6;
}

This is particularly useful for:

  • Blog articles
  • Documentation
  • News websites
  • Long-form content
  • Educational websites

If the line height is too small, paragraphs can feel cramped.

If it is excessively large, the relationship between lines can become harder to follow.

The goal is balance.

  1. The letter-spacing Property

letter-spacing controls the space between characters.

For example:

h1 {
letter-spacing: 1px;
}

This slightly increases the spacing between characters.

You can also reduce spacing:

h1 {
letter-spacing: -0.5px;
}

Letter spacing can be useful for headings, labels, navigation items, and other short pieces of text.

For example, uppercase headings sometimes use a little additional letter spacing:

.logo {
letter-spacing: 2px;
}

However, excessive letter spacing can make words difficult to recognize as a unit.

Use it intentionally rather than simply because you can.

  1. The text-align Property

text-align controls the horizontal alignment of inline content within its containing block.

Common values include:

text-align: left;

text-align: center;

text-align: right;

and:

text-align: justify;

For example:

h1 {
text-align: center;
}

This centres the heading.

A common mistake beginners make is assuming that centred text automatically looks better.

It doesn't.

Center alignment can work well for:

  • Short headings
  • Hero sections
  • Promotional messages
  • Certain landing-page designs

But large blocks of centred body text can become harder to scan.

The correct choice depends on the content and layout.

  1. The text-decoration Property

text-decoration controls decorative lines associated with text.

For example:

a {
text-decoration: underline;
}

You can also remove an underline:

a {
text-decoration: none;
}

Other decoration types include:

  • Underline
  • Overline
  • Line-through

For example:

del {
text-decoration: line-through;
}

Links often use underlines because they provide a visual clue that the text is clickable.

If you remove underlines from links, make sure there is another clear way for users to identify interactive elements.

Putting Everything Together

Now let's combine several properties into a simple example.

HTML:

Learn Web Development


Web development allows you to build websites and web applications
that people can interact with online.

CSS:

article {
background-color: #f5f5f5;
}

h1 {
color: #800020;
font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
font-size: 2rem;
font-weight: 700;
text-align: center;
}

p {
color: #333;
font-family: Arial, sans-serif;
font-size: 1rem;
line-height: 1.6;
letter-spacing: 0.2px;
}

Notice how each property has a specific job.

color controls the colour.

font-family controls the typeface.

font-size controls the size.

font-weight controls the thickness.

line-height controls the vertical rhythm of the text.

letter-spacing controls character spacing.

text-align controls alignment.

background-color controls the background of the article.

Together, these properties create a more organized reading experience.

CSS Typography Is About More Than Beauty

This is one of the biggest lessons beginners should understand.

CSS isn't simply about making a webpage pretty.

Good typography helps users:

Read.

Scan.

Understand.

Navigate.

Focus on important information.

Imagine an article with one font size, one weight, no spacing, poor colour contrast, and extremely tight paragraphs.

Even if the information is excellent, many visitors may not want to read it.

Now imagine the same information with:

  • Clear headings
  • Comfortable body text
  • Appropriate line spacing
  • Good contrast
  • Consistent font choices
  • Useful visual hierarchy

The information becomes much easier to consume.

That's the real value of CSS typography.

Common Typography Mistakes Beginners Make

  1. Making everything large

If every piece of text is huge, your page loses hierarchy.

Different text elements should have different levels of importance.

  1. Using too many fonts

Five different fonts on one webpage can quickly make the design feel inconsistent.

A small, intentional type system is often easier to manage.

  1. Making paragraphs too bold

Bold text should communicate emphasis.

If every paragraph is bold, emphasis disappears.

  1. Ignoring line height

Beginners often focus on font size while forgetting the space between lines.

A readable font with poor line spacing can still produce an uncomfortable reading experience.

  1. Choosing colours based only on appearance

A colour combination might look stylish but still have poor readability.

Always consider contrast.

  1. Centre-aligning everything

Centred text can work beautifully in the right context.

But using it for every paragraph can make long-form content harder to scan.

  1. Removing link underlines without another visual cue

If users can't easily recognize clickable text, navigation becomes less obvious.

Design should communicate interaction clearly.

A Simple Typography Checklist for Beginners

Before publishing a webpage, ask yourself:

Is the text easy to read?

Check the font size, font choice, colour, and line height.

Is there a clear hierarchy?

Can users quickly distinguish headings from supporting text?

Is the contrast sufficient?

Can the text be comfortably distinguished from its background?

Is the typography consistent?

Are similar elements styled in similar ways?

Does it work on smaller screens?

A design that looks good on a desktop-sized screen may not feel comfortable on a phone.

Are important elements easy to find?

Headings, links, buttons, and important information should have enough visual distinction.

These questions can prevent many common typography problems.

The Bigger Picture: CSS Helps People Understand Information

When beginners learn CSS, they sometimes think about properties individually:

font-size changes size.

color changes colour.

font-weight makes text thicker.

That's technically correct, but there's a bigger picture.

These properties work together to create visual communication.

A heading tells you:

This is important.

A larger font tells you:

Pay attention to this.

Spacing tells you:

These pieces of information are related—or separate.

A bold word tells you:

This deserves emphasis.

A link tells you:

You can interact with this.

Good typography therefore isn't just decoration.

It's part of how a website communicates with its users.

Final Thoughts

CSS gives web developers remarkable control over the appearance and readability of text.

With properties such as:

  • color
  • background-color
  • font-family
  • font-size
  • font-weight
  • line-height
  • letter-spacing
  • text-align
  • text-decoration

you can create text that is clearer, more organized, more readable, and more visually consistent.

But don't fall into the trap of thinking that good typography means adding more styles.

Sometimes the best typography is surprisingly simple.

Choose a readable font.

Use appropriate sizes.

Create clear hierarchy.

Give paragraphs enough breathing room.

Use colour carefully.

And always think about the person who will actually read the page.

Because the goal of CSS typography isn't simply:

“Make the text look good.”

The goal is:

“Make the information easy to understand.”

And that's a much more important skill for any web developer to learn.

What CSS Typography Property Would You Learn First?

If you're just starting with CSS, which property do you find most interesting?

font-size ? font-family ? line-height ? font-weight ?

Share your answer in the comments.

title: Amazon SageMaker AI Studio Now Supports IAM Identity Center Multi-Region Replication
description:
Amazon SageMaker AI now supports IAM Identity Center (IdC) multi-region replication, enabling you to deploy SageMaker AI Studio domains in different regions from your IdC instance's primary region. Previously, the primary IdC instance had to reside in the same region as the SageMaker AI Studio domain; now customers can replicate their primary IdC instance into the region where they wish to use SageMaker AI Studio domains. This capability helps customers maintain compliance while utilizing centralized workforce identity management.

As an Amazon SageMaker AI Studio administrator, you can deploy SageMaker AI domains that align with your workforce's location and data residency requirements, independent of where your primary IdC instance is set up. Organizations can retain their primary IdC instance in one region while operating SageMaker AI Studio workloads in compliance-mandated regions, support global operations through centralized identity management, and satisfy data sovereignty requirements without compromising single sign-on (SSO) capabilities.

To get started see the SageMaker AI documentation and to learn about setting up IAM Identity Center multi-region support see the IAM Identity Center User Guide.

Multi-region IdC replication is available in all standard AWS Regions where Amazon SageMaker AI Studio is supported, including: Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Ireland), US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), South America (São Paulo), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Canada (Central), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Europe (Paris), Europe (Stockholm).

Google Kubernetes Engine

Issue

Starting with GKE version 1.36, the default engine for kube-dns is CoreDNS. For Pod IP DNS queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format, CoreDNS returns NXDOMAIN if the specified <namespace> does not exist. The legacy kubernetes/dns implementation skipped checking the existence of the namespace provided in the <namespace> segment in these queries.

Queries in the <a-b-c-d>.<namespace>.pod.cluster.local format are not part of the Kubernetes DNS specification. We can't guarantee that uses outside of those specified in the DNS spec will remain consistent across releases.

Mitigation:

  • Recommended: Migrate to supported headless Service DNS records (<hostname>.<subdomain>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local).
  • Workaround: Ensure the <namespace> specified in the DNS query exists in the cluster.

App Optimize API

Feature

The App Optimize API remote MCP server is in Preview. For more information see Use the App Optimize API remote MCP server.

BigQuery

Feature

BigQuery offers TimesFM 3.0, a built-in time series forecasting model that implements Google Research's open source TimesFM model. You can use TimesFM 3.0 with the following functions:

  • Use AI.FORECAST to perform time series forecasting. In addition to univariate forecasting, you can now perform multivariate forecasting that predicts values for multiple time series based on historical values and additional covariates.
  • Use AI.EVALUATE to perform univariate time series evaluation.
  • Use AI.DETECT_ANOMALIES to perform univariate time series anomaly detection.

Conversational analytics in BigQuery also supports using TimesFM 3.0 with these functions.

To try using the TimesFM 3.0 model for multivariate forecasting with the AI.FORECAST function, see Forecast a single time series with a TimesFM multivariate model and Forecast multiple time series with a TimesFM multivariate model.

The TimesFM 3.0 model is in Preview.

When you enable Pay-as-you-go usage on an invoiced Cloud Billing account with an active subscription, users can continue using features at pay-as-you-go rates after reaching their pooled quota limits.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for VMware 1.36.100-gke.144 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade a cluster. Google Distributed Cloud 1.36.100-gke.144 runs on Kubernetes v1.36.4-gke.100.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for use with GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.36.100-gke.144:

  • Link to Vulnerability fixes for the list of security vulnerabilities addressed in this release.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster had a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.
  • Updated etcd to v3.5.33-0-gke.3 to address security vulnerabilities CVE-2026-46595 and CVE-2026-39821.
  • Fixed an issue where cluster diagnostics (gkectl diagnose) and pre-upgrade validations failed with false-positive datastore '<name>' not found errors. After the fix, validation correctly resolves datastores across all configured vSphere data centers in split-data center architectures where control plane nodes reside in the admin datacenter.
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a cluster could stall indefinitely in the terminating state due to orphaned machine resources.

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal

Announcement

Google Distributed Cloud (software only) for bare metal 1.36.100-gke.144 is now available for download. To upgrade, see Upgrade clusters. Google Distributed Cloud for bare metal 1.36.100-gke.144 runs on Kubernetes v1.36.4-gke.100.

After a release, it takes approximately 7 to 14 days for the version to become available for installations or upgrades with the GKE On-Prem API clients: the Google Cloud console, the gcloud CLI, and Terraform.

If you use a third-party storage vendor, check the listing of our previously-qualified storage partners.

Feature

The following changes were added in 1.36.100-gke.144:

  • Extended the validity period for new certificates generated for GKE Identity Service from 5 years to 10 years.
  • Fixed an issue in clusters using bundled BGP load balancing where control plane upgrades or configuration updates could cause up to 20 seconds of API server connection failures while a control plane node restarted. After the fix, failover to a healthy control plane node completes in approximately 4 seconds.
  • Fixed an issue where node drain in maintenance mode did not wait for attached storage volumes to detach.
  • Added support in bgpadvertiser for advertising IPv6 addresses in addition to IPv4 addresses for bundled BGP control plane load balancing.

Fixed

The following issues were fixed in 1.36.100-gke.144:

  • Link to Vulnerability fixes for the list of security vulnerabilities addressed in this release.
  • Fixed an issue where user clusters repeatedly alternated between reconciling and running states if the management cluster had a different pod density configuration than the user cluster.
  • Updated etcd to v3.5.33-0-gke.3 to address security vulnerabilities CVE-2026-46595 and CVE-2026-39821.
  • Fixed an issue where updating control plane configurations could cause transient Kubernetes API server downtime. After the fix, the update process strictly verifies that each API server is healthy before restarting subsequent control plane nodes.
  • Fixed an issue where deleting a cluster could stall indefinitely in the terminating state due to orphaned machine resources.
  • Fixed an issue where worker node pool creation could stall during provisioning in environments with strict network firewall policies. The node pool controller no longer waits for all inventory machines to be ready before declaring the node pool, eliminating a provisioning deadlock.
  • Fixed an issue where BareMetalMachine status conditions prematurely reported nodes as ready and available during maintenance mode transitions.

Google Kubernetes Engine

Feature

The microVM sandbox type is now Generally Available (GA) with GKE Sandbox in clusters that run version 1.37.0-gke.4713000 and later. MicroVM sandboxes provide hardware virtualization and isolation for untrusted workloads, AI agent runtimes, and multi-tenant environments. GKE microVM sandboxes use Kata Containers and Cloud Hypervisor to provide this isolation while maintaining a full Linux kernel that includes standard Linux features

For more information, see the GKE Sandbox documentation.

General Availability: VPC Flow Logs supports TCP connection logging for VM instances and serverless endpoints. Connection logging captures outbound TCP connection attempts and acknowledged inbound TCP connections.

You can enable this feature in a VPC Flow Logs configuration for a subnet (through the Network Management API), a VPC network, or an organization.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL now supports the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct database flag.

Managed buffer pool automatically adjusts the InnoDB buffer pool size to reduce out-of-memory events. When instance memory usage remains at or below 70% for 10 minutes or longer after prior reductions, Cloud SQL increases the buffer pool size. You can now use the innodb_cloudsql_managed_buffer_pool_tuneup_pct flag to change this 70% threshold to a different percentage. Increase the threshold to restore the InnoDB buffer pool size when baseline usage exceeds 70%, or decrease it to preserve additional RAM allocation for memory spikes.

This flag requires the Cloud SQL maintenance version MYSQL_VERSION.R20260726.00_05 or later. For more information, see Enable managed buffer pool.

Feature

Cloud SQL for MySQL supports blue-green deployments (Preview).

Blue-green deployments let you update databases—such as performing major version upgrades from MySQL 8.0 to 8.4 and staging hardware or configuration modifications—while minimizing downtime. During a blue-green deployment, Cloud SQL creates a separate staging environment (green) that mirrors your existing production environment (blue) and maintains continuous logical replication from blue to green. You can test application compatibility and performance on the green environment without affecting production traffic, and then trigger a switchover to the green environment with minimal application downtime.

For more information, see About blue-green deployments in Cloud SQL.

Compute Engine

Feature

Generally available: You can sync a Compute Engine VM's clock with its host server's clock by using chrony and ptp_kvm to achieve accuracy designed to be within 1 ms. Accurate time synchronization is supported in all standard public Google Cloud regions and zones. For more information, see Configure accurate time for Compute Engine VMs.

Gemini Enterprise: Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5.5 in AI developer tools

Administrators can enable Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5 (claude-sonnet-5-5) for AI developer tools (Antigravity 2.0, Antigravity CLI, and Antigravity for IDEs). Third-party models are turned off by default:

  • Location availability: Third-party model inference is available in the global, us, and eu locations (in-country regions aren't supported). For a list of countries and regions that can access the model, see Anthropic's Supported countries and regions.

Pay-as-you-go usage above quota must be turned on before you can enable a third-party model. For more information, see Configure pay-as-you-go usage above quota and the Cloud Billing SKUs for Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 and Anthropic Claude Sonnet 5.5.
  • Thinking levels: Developers sign in with their existing Gemini Enterprise license and select Claude Opus 5.5 or Claude Sonnet 5.5 in the model picker at a thinking level of Low, Medium, High, or Max (for example, Claude Opus 5.5 (High)). Medium is the default.

Google Cloud CCaaS 6.19

We've released version 6.19 of Google Cloud CCaaS.

The timing of the update to your instance depends on the deployment schedule that you have chosen. For more information, see Deployment schedules.

Fixed

This release addresses the following issues:

  • Fixed an issue where agents could be assigned more concurrent chats than their configured maximum limit when multiple chat offers arrived almost simultaneously.

  • Fixed an issue where calls were unevenly distributed among available agents on skills-based queues.

  • Fixed an issue where supervisor-initiated sign-outs silently discarded mandatory interaction dispositions during an agent's wrap-up period.

  • Fixed an issue where an agent's corporate email address and internal ID were exposed in the browser's network metadata during a virtual agent to human escalation.

  • Fixed an issue where voice calls were incorrectly routed back to the virtual agent queue instead of the intended destination.

  • Fixed an issue where inbound callers experienced a 2-second delay when connecting to an agent.

Looker

Announcement

Looker 26.20 will roll out to Looker (original) and Looker (Google Cloud core) instances on the following schedule:

  • Expected deployment start: Monday, October 12, 2026
  • Expected final deployment and download available: Sunday, October 25, 2026

Looker 26.20 is expected to include the following changes, features, and fixes.

Breaking

Custom TopoJSON URL validation is updated to improve security. This change is isolated to Google Maps rendering in preview. Existing dashboards and Looks with the Google Maps Enhancements preview feature enabled that use custom TopoJSON files may be impacted.

Feature

The Gemini in Looker admin page has been restructured to allow Looker admins to selectively enable Conversational Analytics features and capabilities. Enablement for generally available Conversational Analytics features is now organized under the follow settings:

  • Conversational Analytics (Conversations page): Enables access to the Conversations page for data agents with Explores and direct chats with an Explore.
  • Dashboard agents: Enables default data agents on user-defined and LookML dashboards.
  • Additional options: Allows Conversational Analytics data agent creators to enable the Advanced Analytics feature for all conversations with their data agent. To use Advanced Analytics, you must also enable whichever Conversational Analytics toggle corresponds to the content that you are querying (Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents). If both the Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents toggles are turned off, then Advanced Analytics cannot be enabled. If either Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) or Dashboard agents is enabled, Advanced Analytics can be enabled, but it is turned off by default.

The Conversational Analytics (Conversations page) and Dashboard agents settings inherit the enablement state of the Conversational Analytics setting in previous versions of Looker.

Conversational Analytics preview features can still be enabled selectively under the Enable Trusted Tester Features setting.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

Conversational Analytics data agents for both user-defined dashboards and LookML dashboards are now generally available.

(Note: This item was added on October 14, 2026.)

Feature

You can now apply themes to Looks in addition to internal dashboards.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where duplicating a scheduled plan could fail to retain the custom message value. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

Table visualizations now proportionally scale left-pinned columns during automatic sizing, which prevents unnecessary horizontal scrollbars. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where enabling subtotals on table visualizations did not automatically disable the Cell Visualizations option. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where previews for Looker charts in Slack integrations could fail to be displayed. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where editing and saving a dashboard could cause the dashboard to reload indefinitely, forcing users to refresh the page. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where table cell visualizations that included both positive and negative values could display unwanted scrollbars and hide value labels. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the BigQuery JDBC driver could fail to properly parse certain data types, such as BYTES, STRUCT/RECORD, and nested ARRAY structures. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where linked filters on a dashboard could fail to display autocomplete suggestions even when a parent filter is selected. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity query_metrics Explore has been updated to ensure that phase timings (such as connection acquisitions, execution runtimes, and optimistic pivot fallback retry loops) are successfully captured for queries that fail or time out. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

The System Activity Dashboard Diagnostics dashboard has been updated to fully support statistics, tile run counts, and performance recommendations for LookML dashboards. This feature now performs as expected.

Fixed

An issue has been fixed where the color palette popover in visualization settings failed to dynamically reposition when it expanded, causing controls to overlap or truncate. This feature now performs as expected.

Breaking

When you set up a connection, self-service modeling will now be available only if a role that grants create_self_service_from_table also selects it through that role's model set.

Fixed

The opacity for the comparison bar in short KPI visualizations has been reduced to increase legibility.

Memorystore for Redis

Feature

To help protect your data and provide a baseline level of persistence, RDB snapshots are enabled by default when you create an instance using the Google Cloud console. This feature is generally available.

VPC Service Controls

Feature

General availability support for the following integration:

  • Cloud Storage for Firebase

Feature

VPC Service Controls feature (Status: Preview): Support for automated remediation suggestions is available in the VPC Service Controls violation analyzer.

Remediation suggestions analyze access denial events and generate actionable, narrowly scoped configuration changes to resolve perimeter denials and adhere to the principle of least privilege. The remediation engine can automatically propose ingress rules, egress rules, VPC accessible services updates, and existing or new context-aware access levels.

For more information, see Resolve access denials with remediation suggestions.

Note: Near real-time sync upon Knowledge Catalog (KC) enablement isn't available for existing instances created before April 18, 2026. For more information, see the release note from October 14, 2026.

When you enable Knowledge Catalog (formerly Dataplex Universal Catalog) integration on an eligible Cloud SQL for MySQL instance created before April 18, 2026 where the integration is currently turned off, the instance now syncs schema and metadata updates to Knowledge Catalog in near real-time instead of once a day (instances created on or after April 18, 2026 have near real-time sync enabled by default).
