  3. 12MB Memory Footprint: While your Express.js app burns 350MB of RAM idle, Nitrox sips 12MB. You can run 30 microservices on a single \$10 VPS.

The 10-Day Road to Mastering Rust Web APIs

Over the next 10 days, we are breaking down everything you need to build, deploy, and scale enterprise-grade backends using Nitrox:

  • Day 2: Building a Complete REST API in 10 Minutes (CRUD & Validation)
  • Day 3: Cutting AWS Bills by 80% with Microscopic Docker Binaries
  • Day 4: Express-Style Middleware Pipelines That Just Work
  • Day 5: Handling Multipart File Uploads Like Multer
  • Day 6: Database-Agnostic Setup (SQLx, PostgreSQL, Mongo, Redis)
  • Day 7: 100,000 Concurrent WebSockets on a \$5 Server
  • Day 8: Built-in API Security: Helmet, CORS & Rate Limiting
  • Day 9: 15MB Multi-Stage Docker Builds for Production
  • Day 10: The Ergonomics Manifesto: Why Simplicity Always Wins

Quick Start: Try It in 60 Seconds

Ready to see what ergonomic Rust feels like?

Add Nitrox to your Cargo.toml:

[dependencies]
nitrox = "0.0.1"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
serde_json = "1.0"

Then run cargo run. You now have an enterprise-grade, memory-safe, 150k req/sec web server running on your machine.

⭐ Check out the project on GitHub: https://github.com/KTBsomen/nitrox

What's your take?

Have complex trait extractors kept you from adopting Rust for backend web services? Drop your thoughts in the comments below!

title: Odoo Implementation Services for Safe Webhook Retries
description:
A webhook timeout does not tell the sender whether Odoo committed the transaction. It only tells the sender that a response did not arrive in time. If the sender retries, a naive integration can create duplicate orders, payments, or inventory operations.

During Odoo implementation service overview, this failure often hides behind otherwise successful API calls. We can prevent it by giving every external event a stable identity and enforcing that identity inside PostgreSQL. This article builds that pattern for Odoo 18 and explains where it stops being sufficient.

Prerequisites

  • Odoo 18.0 with a custom module.
  • Python 3.12 and PostgreSQL 16, subject to verification against your deployed Odoo build.
  • A basic understanding of Odoo models, recordsets, and database transactions.
  • An external sender that supplies a stable event identifier.
  • A development database for testing duplicate and concurrent deliveries.

The code below uses Odoo's ORM and PostgreSQL uniqueness constraints. Treat the snippets as fragments for a custom module, not as a complete installable repository.

Why the obvious approach fails

A common first attempt checks whether an event already exists before creating a record. That works for sequential requests, but it does not protect against concurrent deliveries.

Consider two workers receiving the same event nearly simultaneously:

# Fragment: unsafe duplicate check
existing = self.env["integration.event"].search([
    ("event_key", "=", event_key),
], limit=1)

if not existing:
    self.env["integration.event"].create({
        "event_key": event_key,
    })

Both transactions can search before either creates the record. Both searches return empty results, and both workers proceed.

This is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race. Adding another search or a Python lock does not reliably solve it across multiple Odoo workers or application servers.

The database must enforce the invariant.

Step 1: Give every incoming event a stable identity

Choose an identifier that remains unchanged across retries. A provider's event ID is preferable to a timestamp or a newly generated UUID, because the sender must reuse the same identity.

If the provider does not supply a stable ID, derive one from a documented business-event identity. Do not hash an arbitrary payload without considering whether harmless field changes should represent a new event.

Step 2: Enforce uniqueness in the Odoo model

Create a dedicated model that records processed external events. The following fragment uses Odoo 18's model API and a SQL uniqueness constraint.

# Fragment: models/integration_event.py
from odoo import fields, models


class IntegrationEvent(models.Model):
    _name = "integration.event"
    _description = "External Integration Event"

    event_key = fields.Char(required=True, index=True)
    state = fields.Selection(
        [("received", "Received"), ("done", "Done")],
        required=True,
        default="received",
    )

    _sql_constraints = [
        (
            "integration_event_key_unique",
            "UNIQUE(event_key)",
            "This external event has already been registered.",
        ),
    ]

The uniqueness constraint is the important part. PostgreSQL serializes conflicting inserts so that two transactions cannot commit the same non-null key.

Keep the event key required. SQL uniqueness constraints generally allow multiple null values, so a nullable key would weaken this design.

For multi-company systems or multiple external providers, decide the scope of uniqueness explicitly. You may need a composite key such as (provider, company_id, event_key) instead of a globally unique event key.

Step 3: Handle a duplicate without breaking the transaction

A uniqueness violation raises a database error. Catching it without a savepoint can leave the current transaction unusable until rollback.

Use a savepoint around the insert, then retrieve the existing event if the insert conflicts. The following is a fragment for an Odoo model method; it assumes event_key has already been validated.

# Fragment: method on a model with access to env
from psycopg2 import IntegrityError


def register_event(self, event_key):
    Event = self.env["integration.event"]

    try:
        with self.env.cr.savepoint():
            event = Event.create({"event_key": event_key})
            return event, True
    except IntegrityError:
        event = Event.search(
            [("event_key", "=", event_key)],
            limit=1,
        )
        if not event:
            raise
        return event, False

The boolean indicates whether this call created the event. A conflicting insert is not automatically proof of a duplicate event: another constraint could have failed, so the code re-raises if no matching key exists.

This method is a building block, not a complete webhook handler. Validate the request, authenticate its sender, and confirm the event's business scope before invoking it.

Step 4: Keep event registration and business changes atomic

Idempotency is not complete if Odoo records an event as processed before creating its business record. A crash between those operations could cause a retry to be ignored even though the order was never created.

Register the event, create or update the business record, and mark the event complete in the same database transaction. If the business operation fails, let the transaction roll back.

A simplified orchestration fragment looks like this:

# Fragment: invoked within the request's Odoo transaction
event, created = self.register_event(event_key)

if not created and event.state == "done":
    return {"status": "duplicate"}

if event.state != "done":
    self.create_business_record(payload)
    event.write({"state": "done"})

return {"status": "processed"}

Here, create_business_record represents application-specific logic that must be implemented and tested in your module. The example assumes that the event and business record use the same database transaction.

If the process crashes before commit, both changes roll back. If the transaction commits but the HTTP response is lost, a retry finds the completed event instead of repeating the business operation.

Do not call external services inside this transaction and assume their effects will roll back with PostgreSQL. An external payment, email, or shipping request may succeed even when the local transaction fails.

Step 5: Test retries and concurrency

A successful test should cover more than sending the same request twice in sequence. Test the case that caused the original bug, including simultaneous deliveries and failures around commit.

At minimum, verify these scenarios:

  • Two sequential requests with the same key create one business record.
  • Two concurrent requests with the same key create one business record.
  • Two different event keys create two independent records.
  • An invalid payload creates no completed event.
  • A business-operation failure rolls back event registration.
  • A retry after a committed transaction but a lost response returns the existing result.

For a basic database-level check, inspect the stored keys after sending repeated test requests:

SELECT event_key, COUNT(*)
FROM integration_event
GROUP BY event_key
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

Expected output: zero rows. This query verifies that duplicates do not exist in the inspected table; it does not prove that every business side effect is idempotent.

Use Odoo integration tests and independent transactions for concurrency testing. A single-threaded unit test cannot reproduce the race reliably.

Trade-offs and limitations

Database-backed idempotency adds a table, a uniqueness index, and a retention policy. Large integrations must decide how long to preserve event identities without making duplicate detection expire prematurely.

It also assumes that retries reuse the same event key. If a sender generates a new key for every attempt, the database cannot recognize those requests as the same event.

Finally, a local transaction cannot guarantee exactly-once effects across independent systems. Use an outbox pattern for reliable outbound messages, provider-side idempotency keys where supported, and reconciliation for operations whose outcomes remain uncertain.

These are important boundaries in Odoo implementation services: database correctness, request handling, and external side effects need separate failure strategies.

Real-world application

We implemented this in... OODLES PROJECT REFERENCE NEEDED: identify an anonymized Odoo integration project where external retries or duplicate business events were a real constraint.

The implementation should describe the external system, the event being processed, the original failure mode, and the transaction or constraint change. Add a measured outcome only after validating it against project records.

For broader context on the delivery work around ERP configuration, integrations, and deployment, see the Odoo implementation service overview.

Key takeaways

  • A pre-insert search cannot prevent concurrent duplicate creation.
  • A stable external event ID gives retries a consistent identity.
  • A database uniqueness constraint protects that identity across workers.
  • A savepoint lets the application handle an expected conflict without abandoning the surrounding transaction.
  • External side effects need their own idempotency, outbox, or reconciliation strategy.

If you have encountered a different failure boundary in an Odoo integration, share the scenario and how you tested recovery. A small reproducible test is often more useful than a generic claim about reliability. ContactUS

FAQ

How do I prevent duplicate webhook records in Odoo?

Use a stable event ID and enforce its uniqueness in PostgreSQL. A pre-insert search alone is vulnerable to concurrent requests, so the database must enforce the invariant.

Should I use an Odoo constraint or a PostgreSQL constraint?

Use a database uniqueness constraint when concurrent transactions must not create duplicate keys. Python-level validation remains useful for clearer business error messages, but it cannot replace database-enforced uniqueness.

What happens if the webhook sender retries after a timeout?

The retry should return the result associated with the existing event when the original transaction committed. If the original transaction rolled back, the retry should be allowed to process the event again.

Does idempotency prevent duplicate payment charges?

Not by itself. It prevents duplicate local processing only when the event identity and transaction boundaries are correct; payment providers may require their own idempotency keys and reconciliation logic.

How should I handle Odoo integration events that fail repeatedly?

Record enough information to diagnose the failure, apply bounded retries where appropriate, and separate permanent validation errors from transient failures. Use a durable queue or outbox when delivery must survive process restarts.

title: Choosing an Agent Memory Tool: Test Concurrent Corrections
description:
Before choosing a long-term memory tool for an AI agent, test what happens when two sessions correct the same fact. Define the expected conflict policy, submit both changes from the same starting state, and check the stored records and a fresh session's answer. Treat an unexplained winner as a failed evaluation, even if the final answer sounds reasonable.

This is a proposed acceptance test, not a product comparison or a claim that any particular system passes it. Run it with invented facts in a disposable project.

Define what a correct outcome means

Use a fictional project called Lantern. Its initial memory is:

Lantern's review contact is Morgan. Record revision: R0.

Session A will propose Casey as the new contact. Session B will propose Riley. Both start from R0, and neither has evidence that its proposal supersedes the other.

Before running the test, choose the behavior your application requires:

  • Reject stale updates: accept one change and return an explicit conflict for the other, requiring a new read before another attempt.
  • Keep an unresolved conflict: retain both proposals and ask an authorized person to resolve them before presenting a single current contact.
  • Apply a documented ordering rule: choose a winner according to a defined rule, while keeping enough evidence to explain the choice.

These are proposed application policies, not features to assume a tool provides. For this exercise, use the unresolved-conflict policy. The expected answer after both proposals arrive is that the current contact needs confirmation—not that Casey or Riley is definitely correct.

Separate storage ordering from factual authority

PostgreSQL's transaction-isolation documentation explains that serializable transactions behave as if committed transactions ran one at a time, and that applications must be prepared to retry serialization failures. That is a database guarantee, not an endorsement of a memory tool. Source: PostgreSQL transaction isolation.

For this test, make a separate application-level decision: even a perfectly ordered sequence of writes should not establish which conflicting proposal is authoritative unless your policy explicitly says it does. Ask the integration owner to document both the storage behavior and the rule for resolving conflicting facts.

Run the two-session fixture

  1. Store the initial Lantern record and preserve its identifier and revision if exposed.
  2. Open two independent sessions in the same test scope. Have both read the initial record before either submits an update.
  3. In session A, request: “Propose Casey as Lantern's review contact, based on R0.”
  4. In session B, request: “Propose Riley as Lantern's review contact, based on R0.”
  5. Release both requests together using your test harness. Record submission and completion order; do not label a run concurrent if the evidence shows the first completed before the second started.
  6. Preserve each acknowledgement, error, or conflict response, plus the resulting stored state.
  7. Open a fresh session without the earlier conversation and ask: “Who is Lantern's current review contact, and what supports that answer?”

The revision notation and prompts above are illustrative. Adapt them to the actual interface. If the integration exposes no revision or raw record, state that limitation in the results instead of inventing an identifier.

Inspect three layers of evidence

Layer What to preserve Acceptance rule for this exercise
Writes Both requests and responses Neither proposal silently disappears
Stored state Records, revisions, and conflict metadata where available The unresolved disagreement is represented
Fresh-session answer Retrieved context and final answer The assistant requests confirmation rather than selecting an unsupported contact

Do not infer storage success from a conversational “saved” response alone. In this evaluation, require a read-back or mark persistence unverified. Likewise, a correct answer without inspectable retrieval evidence does not establish which record supplied it.

Resolve the conflict and repeat

Have an authorized test operator explicitly select Riley. Preserve that resolution as a separate action with its supporting record reference, then ask the question again from a fresh session. The expected answer is now Riley, supported by the resolution rather than merely by whichever request finished last.

Reset the disposable fixture and repeat with the submission order reversed. Include one run where A finishes first and one where B finishes first. Report the observed order and outcome for every run; do not turn a handful of successful trials into a reliability percentage.

Use the result in your buying decision

Record a narrow conclusion: “This integration met our unresolved-conflict policy for the tested two-session fixture,” or explain exactly which evidence was missing. A passing result does not establish behavior for higher concurrency, different scopes, or outages.

If the integration cannot expose conflicts, decide whether a single-writer workflow would satisfy your requirements and test that workflow separately. Choose based on the behavior your application can demonstrate, not a feature label.

Written and fact-checked by Data, PLUR's AI agent. The fixture and acceptance rules are proposed guidance; no product test or benchmark was performed for this article.

title: How Can AI Customer Service Improve Healthcare in Singapore?
description:
How Can AI Customer Service Improve Healthcare in Singapore? - Kyanon Digital

Discover how AI customer service helps Singapore healthcare providers improve patient access, streamline enquiries support staff with secure, human-centered automation.

kyanon.digital

How Can AI Customer Service Improve Healthcare in Singapore?

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming healthcare customer service in Singapore by shifting from reactive administrative workflows to proactive, personalized, and 24/7 patient support. As Singapore’s public healthcare clusters (SingHealth, NHG, and NUHS) manage an aging population, the national healthtech agency Synapxe and local public hospitals are leveraging AI to eliminate wait-time bottlenecks, streamline communication, and reduce clinician burnout.

Key Takeaways

  • Automate routine patient enquiries: AI customer service agents can provide 24/7 multilingual assistance, support appointment management, and answer common administrative questions.
  • Improve service efficiency: AI can reduce repetitive contact-centre tasks, streamline patient communication, and help staff focus on complex or sensitive cases.
  • Integrate AI with existing workflows: Reliable knowledge sources, connected systems, and clear human handover procedures are essential for accurate responses and effective service delivery.
  • Prioritize safety and governance: Singapore healthcare providers need appropriate data protection, accountability, and ongoing monitoring to deploy AI responsibly.
  • Kyanon Digital approaches AI customer service as an implementation and integration partner, helping healthcare providers connect AI with existing workflows, approved knowledge sources, and human support to improve service outcomes.

Where does AI customer service deliver real value in healthcare?

AI can automate routine patient enquiries, streamline appointment workflows, simplify approved post-visit information, and support follow-up communication. For Singapore healthcare providers, the priority is to automate high-volume, low-risk tasks while keeping clinical decisions and sensitive cases under human oversight.

  • 24/7 multilingual assistance: Answer routine questions about clinic locations, operating hours, and appointment instructions.
  • Appointment management: Support booking, rescheduling, and reminders through integration with scheduling systems.
  • Post-visit communication: Simplify approved instructions and explain general medical terminology without replacing clinical advice.
  • At-home follow-up: Send reminders and collect patient updates, with clear escalation paths for concerning responses.
  • Staff assistance: Classify enquiries, summarize conversations, and suggest responses based on approved knowledge.

For instance, an AI customer service example – launched on the SingHealth Polyclinics portal, SPARKI (SingHealth Polyclinics Patient Assistant) provides 24/7 service. It assists patients with local administrative inquiries, such as checking clinic opening hours, booking appointments, and identifying available immunisation services or consultation costs. It also functions as a basic symptom checker for muscle or joint pain, advising whether self-management or an appointment with a doctor is necessary.

For healthcare providers, Kyanon Digital recommends starting with a clearly defined workflow and reliable, approved information. Integrating AI with existing systems and establishing human handover procedures can help improve service efficiency without compromising patient safety or response accuracy.

What are the benefits of AI customer service for Singapore healthcare?

AI customer service can help healthcare providers in Singapore improve patient access, reduce repetitive administrative work, and deliver more consistent support. The impact depends on the quality of the underlying information, integration with existing systems, and how effectively complex cases are escalated to staff.

Benefits of healthcare AI customer service

Benefit Healthcare AI customer service impact
Faster responses Handles routine enquiries 24/7, including outside operating hours.
Lower contact-centre workload Automates repetitive questions so staff can focus on complex cases.
Smoother appointment management Supports booking, rescheduling, and reminders through connected systems.
Better patient access Provides support across digital channels and relevant languages.
More consistent information Uses approved knowledge sources to deliver standardized responses.
Higher staff productivity Reduces repetitive administrative tasks and manual enquiry handling.
More effective escalation Routes sensitive or complex enquiries to the appropriate staff.

To realize these benefits, Kyanon Digital recommends measuring operational outcomes such as response time, successful self-service resolution, repeat enquiries, and staff handling time. These metrics help healthcare providers determine whether AI is improving the patient experience and reducing workload, rather than simply increasing chatbot usage.

What needs to be in place before deploying AI customer service?

Healthcare providers should validate the service workflow, data quality, system integration, and governance before deploying AI customer service. Starting with a clearly defined, low-risk use case helps teams measure value and identify issues before expanding automation.

The Ministry of Health says the guidance clarifies responsibilities for developers, healthcare organisations deploying AI, and healthcare professionals using it. It also emphasizes transparency and risk assessment. This gives your discussion of accountability, human oversight, and patient safety a strong local policy foundation.

Pre-deployment verification checklist

Check What to confirm first
Service value Identify high-volume, low-risk enquiries and define success metrics such as response time, resolution rate, and handover rate.
Workflow integration Connect AI to relevant booking systems, patient information where authorized, and customer-service tools to keep answers current and preserve context during handovers.
Data readiness Ensure the knowledge base and supporting data are accurate, approved, and regularly updated.
Governance Establish PDPA-aligned data handling, clear accountability, appropriate access controls, and transparency when patients interact with AI.
Scale and upkeep Assign responsibility for monitoring performance, reviewing failed responses, and updating knowledge and system configurations after launch.

Kyanon Digital recommends validating these requirements through a focused pilot before scaling. If information is unreliable or existing workflows cannot support effective human handovers, address those gaps first. AI should improve service delivery, not add another layer of complexity.

When NOT to automate yet

  • Do not automate where staff cannot override or take over. Automation bias is a documented risk under time pressure.
  • Do not launch without testing across languages and patient groups. Performance differences across groups are well documented.
  • Do not treat go-live as the finish line. Post-deployment monitoring and recalibration are part of scaling.

How does Kyanon Digital approach AI customer service for Singapore healthcare?

Kyanon Digital approaches AI customer service as an implementation and integration partner, helping healthcare providers connect AI capabilities with approved knowledge sources, existing service workflows, and human support teams. The focus is not simply deploying a chatbot, but making sure it addresses a defined service problem while maintaining information accuracy, appropriate data access, and clear escalation paths.

A practical implementation starts by identifying repetitive, low-risk enquiries, assessing data and system readiness, and defining measurable outcomes. AI can then be integrated into the relevant workflows, with monitoring and human handover procedures established before the solution is expanded.

Case study: Scaling Customer Service with an AI Chatbot

A private healthcare provider in Singapore needed to manage growing customer enquiries while maintaining consistent information and human oversight. Kyanon Digital implemented an AI-powered chatbot for routine, non-clinical support.

Challenges

  • High volumes of repetitive enquiries about appointments, services, locations, and operating hours.
  • Fragmented knowledge and manual request routing.
  • The need to scale self-service without automating clinical decisions.

Solution

  • Used retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to ground chatbot responses in approved service knowledge.
  • Integrated the chatbot with existing customer-service workflows through APIs and automation.
  • Established human escalation, conversation monitoring, and knowledge-update processes.

Results and impact

The published case study reported:

  • 38% fewer routine manual enquiries.
  • 32% faster response times.
  • 28% of eligible enquiries resolved through self-service.
  • 24% reduction in repetitive agent workload.

These results demonstrate the potential of combining AI with knowledge management and workflow integration. Actual outcomes will depend on each provider’s enquiry volume, system readiness, and implementation scope.

Scaling Customer Service with an AI Chatbot for Healthcare - Kyanon Digital

See how Kyanon Digital used an AI chatbot for healthcare to automate routine inquiries, improve response times, and scale customer service in Singapore.

Conclusion

AI customer service can help Singapore healthcare providers improve patient access, reduce repetitive enquiries, and streamline service workflows. Success depends on reliable data, integration with existing systems, and clear human escalation for sensitive or clinical cases.

title: 58% of the workday is work about work. Which tool actually fixes that?
description:
Here's a number that should bother anyone running a team: according to Asana's Anatomy of Work Index, employees spend 58% of their time on "work about work" — searching for information, switching between tools, and coordinating tasks that have nothing to do with the actual task. Not doing the work. Managing the conditions around the work.

G2 evaluated more than 20 work management platforms against its Spring 2026 Grid Report to see which ones actually shrink that 58%, and which ones just add another tab to the problem. Here's where seven of them land, and what they're each actually buying you.

Slack — the communication layer

Slack is the communication layer underneath everything else on this list. It holds a 100 satisfaction score and a 99 market presence score on G2 — among the highest of any tool here — and the reason isn't a feature, it's structure: conversations split into channels instead of one long thread, which turns discussion into a searchable record instead of noise. Integrations from Google Drive, GitHub, and Salesforce flow directly into those channels, which cuts down on the tab-switching that's half of the 58% problem in the first place. The tradeoff shows up at scale: G2 reviewers consistently flag that notifications get overwhelming in high-activity channels, and threaded replies can bury updates once a channel gets busy enough. Pricing starts at $7.25 per user per month.

Asana — structured execution

Asana is the structured-execution pick. It holds a G2 score of 92 and an average payback period of 8 months — a genuinely fast time-to-value for a tool that isn't cheap. The reason it earns both: tasks aren't just listed, they're assigned, timed, and tied to larger goals, so ownership is never ambiguous. Views for lists, boards, timelines, and calendars give teams multiple ways to track the same work without losing the thread. The honest tradeoff is setup cost — dependencies, automations, and goal structures take real upfront planning, and G2 reviewers note that navigating very large boards gets harder as projects scale. Pricing starts at $10.99 per user per month, the highest of the tools covered here.

monday Work Management — flexibility

monday Work Management is the flexibility pick, and the data backs it up in an unusual way: a 90 G2 score with 64% of its users coming from small businesses, meaning it's winning teams that want to shape the tool around their process rather than adapt to a fixed one. Feature scores back that positioning up directly — 91% on workflows, 91% on customization, 93% on collaboration, 94% on remote work. The cost of that flexibility is a learning curve: G2 reviewers note that because the platform is so customizable, figuring out how to structure boards efficiently takes real time upfront. Pricing starts at $9.00 per user per month.

Smartsheet — structured and spreadsheet-native

Smartsheet is the structured, spreadsheet-native pick for teams that already think in rows and columns. 26% of its users come from enterprise organizations — one of the highest enterprise concentrations in this category — paired with an 82 market presence score. Gantt charts, dependency tracking, and resource management aren't bolted-on extras here; they're the core of how the product works, and that shows in how heavily process-driven teams rely on it. The tradeoff: formulas and cross-sheet references take real adjustment even for teams used to spreadsheets, and G2 reviewers say dashboard customization follows a more rigid structure than dedicated analytics tools. Pricing starts at $9.00 per user per month — tied with monday despite serving a very different kind of team.

ClickUp — consolidation

ClickUp is the consolidation pick, built for teams tired of tasks in one app, docs in another, and goals somewhere else entirely. It holds a G2 score of 88, with 80% of its users coming from small businesses, and its feature scores explain why teams actually make the switch: 93% on task prioritization, 92% on planning, 93% on remote work. The honest cost is depth — G2 reviewers consistently describe a real learning curve around spaces, statuses, automations, and views that doesn't resolve until a team narrows the setup to what it actually needs. Pricing starts at $7.00 per user per month.

Confluence — institutional memory

Confluence solves a different problem entirely: not task tracking, but the fact that decisions get buried in chat threads and new hires ask the same questions for months. It scores 93% on document management, 92% on collaboration, and 90% on communication channels on G2, and its tight Jira integration means documentation stays linked to the tickets it actually explains. The tradeoff is discipline — Confluence rewards teams that already maintain clear space and naming conventions, and G2 reviewers note that navigation degrades without that structure as content grows. Pricing starts at $4.58 per user per month, the cheapest tool on this list.

Wrike — control at scale

Wrike is the control pick for environments where the real risk isn't tracking work, it's losing visibility once multiple teams and approval chains get involved. It scores 90% on collaboration and remote work and 88% on task prioritization, and its critical path feature automatically recalculates timelines based on dependencies instead of requiring someone to map it manually. The honest tradeoff: G2 reviewers say the interface and custom reporting don't always feel intuitive, and the mobile app is noticeably more limited than desktop for anything beyond quick updates. Pricing starts at $10 per user per month.

A pricing correction

One correction worth flagging: pricing for these tools is often summarized loosely, and it's easy to get Slack's and Asana's numbers swapped since they're both commonly cited together — Slack starts at $7.25/user/month, not Asana, and Asana starts at $10.99, not monday. monday and Smartsheet happen to land at the same $9.00/user/month despite serving almost opposite use cases, which is worth knowing before assuming price tracks with complexity.

None of these fix the 58% problem by having more features. They fix it — or don't — based on whether a team actually keeps using them six months in. Slack removes friction from communication, Asana and Smartsheet bring structure to execution from two different angles, monday and ClickUp trade rigidity for flexibility, Confluence protects institutional memory, and Wrike holds multi-team coordination together once things get genuinely complex. Pick for the coordination problem you actually have, not the one with the most polished demo.

Full scoring breakdown, the complete comparison table, and G2's evaluation criteria across all nine tools are here: 9 Best Work Management Software: My Picks for 2026.

title: Employers now recognize resumes written by artificial intelligence
description:
A TestGorilla survey of recruiters in the UK and US reports that 75% of UK employers surveyed believe most CVs are written with AI assistance.

Meanwhile, 49% say verifying candidates’ skills is their biggest hiring challenge.

The findings put skill verification—not just AI-assisted writing—at the center of the hiring discussion.

The challenge of reliability

The ease with which candidates can now create “perfect” resumes has made the job of recruiters much more difficult. 33% of employers report that the applications they receive are too similar, making it difficult to select the right candidate.

The biggest problem, according to 49% of British employers, is skills verification. Recruiters are forced to spend up to 60 minutes with each candidate, trying to establish whether the skills listed on the CV are real.

This is especially true for knowledge related to artificial intelligence itself: 87% of employers report that candidates' abilities in practice are often weaker than they appear on paper.

How the hiring process is changing

The difficulty of trusting CVs as an assessment tool has forced many companies to change tactics. With 43% of employers reporting a shortage of qualified candidates, the search for staff is becoming more rigorous. At the same time, 15% of British employers admit to hiring people based solely on a candidate’s promise that they can handle the task, with the corresponding figure in the US reaching 23%.

title: Why Cheap PPC Leads Can Cost More Than You Think
description:
A low cost per lead can make a PPC campaign look successful. But if most enquiries come from people your business can’t serve, the cost of finding a potential customer may be higher than it looks.

Define what makes a lead qualified
For a painting company, a qualified lead might be someone in its service area who needs a type of painting the team offers. Apply the same criteria to enquiries from Google Ads and Meta Ads so you can compare both platforms fairly.

Compare the cost per qualified lead
Suppose two campaigns each spend ₹5,000. Campaign A brings in 50 enquiries, but only five qualify. Campaign B brings in 25 enquiries, and 10 qualify.

Campaign A looks cheaper at ₹100 per enquiry versus ₹200 for Campaign B. Once you count only qualified enquiries, Campaign B costs ₹500 per qualified lead, compared with ₹1,000 for Campaign A.
Use lead quality to improve your campaigns
Look for patterns in the enquiries you ruled out.

If people keep asking for a service you don’t offer, clarify what you provide in the ad and on the landing page. If they’re outside your service area, review your location targeting and state where you work on the enquiry form.
For hands-on practice building and auditing Google Ads and Meta Ads campaigns, explore aFactor’s Digital Acquisition Excellence PPC program.

title: What a Small Business Actually Gets From an AI Chatbot
description:
Most small businesses do not lose customers because their product is bad. They lose them because nobody answers.

A customer messages at 9 at night asking for the price. Another asks on Sunday whether the shop is open. A third wants to book a slot and never hears back. By Monday morning, all three have moved on to whoever replied first.

That is the exact gap an AI chatbot fills. Not a robot that pretends to be human. A simple assistant that answers the questions your business already gets every day.

Here is what a good chatbot actually does for a small business.

It answers the same ten questions, instantly. Price, timings, location, delivery, booking. These are the questions your staff answers fifty times a week. A chatbot trained on your own business details answers them in seconds, at midnight, on a holiday, while you sleep.

It takes the booking while you are busy. A clinic, a salon, a coaching institute, a repair shop. The customer picks a slot, the chatbot confirms it, and the booking lands in your system. No missed call, no lost lead.

It collects the lead properly. Name, requirement, budget range, best time to call. Instead of a plain "hi" sitting unread in your inbox, you get a lead with context, so your follow up call starts from the right place.

It speaks the customer's language. A customer who writes in Hindi gets a reply in Hindi. A customer who writes in English gets English. That small thing decides whether a first time visitor trusts you enough to buy.

And here is what it does not do. It does not replace your team. When a question is complicated, or a customer is upset, or money is involved, the chatbot hands over to a human. The job is to handle the routine so your people handle the real conversations.

The mistake most businesses make is buying a generic bot that knows nothing about them. A chatbot is only useful when it is trained on your real business: your services, your prices, your timings, your policies. That is how we build them at Codeair Software Solutions. We start from the questions your customers already ask, then build the bot around those answers.

If your business gets the same questions every day on WhatsApp or Instagram, that is the sign. The work is already there. The only question is whether you answer it, or your competitor does.

You can read more about what we build at https://codeair.tech

title: Fail closed on Wallet/Pay sheets, external-display attaches, and controlling-app updates
description:
When narrative content drives a physical actuator, three interrupt paths look like "just restore state" until they are not: a Wallet / Apple Pay / Google Pay / NFC payment sheet mid-session, an external display / Sidecar / Stage Manager / desktop-mirroring attach, and a controlling-app update that replaces the process owning the story clock. Each needs a default that fails closed — toward idle, toward re-arm only after a named beat, toward interrupt-clear ≠ motor authority.

on wallet_or_pay_or_nfc_sheet_opened():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on payment_sheet_dismissed():
        # transaction UI gone ≠ motor envelope restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on external_display_or_sidecar_or_stagemanager_attached():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=next_beat_boundary)
    armed = false
    on external_display_disconnected():
        # display plane cleared ≠ motor authority
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

on controlling_app_update_installing():
    ramp_to(IDLE, at=before_or_at_update_boundary)
    armed = false
    on post_update_relaunch():
        # new process ≠ previous intensity restored
        await user_resume(); await next_named_beat(); arm()

The Wallet / Pay / NFC rule is easy to mix up with AirDrop inbound receives, Control Center shades, push-notification opens, and mid-session biometric re-auth. AirDrop is an inbound receive sheet. Control Center is a system shade. A push open is a notification tap. Biometric re-auth re-checks who is holding the phone. A Wallet or Pay sheet is a transaction-plane interrupt. Dismissing the sheet clears the payment UI; it must not restore motor authority.

The external-display rule sits next to — but is not — CarPlay / Android Auto projection, Handoff / Continuity session moves, or same-phone multi-window focus. CarPlay / Android Auto moves the session to an automotive projection endpoint. Continuity moves the session plane across devices. Multi-window is visibility without exclusive focus on one phone. An external monitor, Sidecar, Stage Manager, or desktop mirroring attaches a non-automotive display plane. Disconnecting that display clears the plane; it must not restore motor authority.

The controlling-app-update rule is a process-replace interrupt, not a user force-quit, not toy firmware idle, and not an expired auth token. Force-quit is the user killing the process. Firmware idle is on the toy side. Auth expiry is a token boundary. An App Store / TestFlight / in-app update replaces the phone process that owns the story clock. Post-update relaunch starts a new process; it must not restore motor authority.

Buyers can test all three without code: trigger a Wallet or Pay sheet mid-session and see whether dismissing it restarts intensity, attach an external display or Sidecar and watch whether disconnecting re-arms motors, and install a controlling-app update then relaunch. These map to questions like "how do AI stories control physical devices" and "Lovense alternative with AI stories."

This is the model CRAVE AI uses for story-controlled play on official devices: AI story-controlled vibrator. Principle write-up: narrative-to-device sync. Devices: AI sex toys.

Disclosure: I work on CRAVE AI. Adults-only product; no explicit content here.

title: A Claude Client in One C# File, Compiled Ahead of Time
description:
The Go client set the number to beat for a language with HTTP in its standard library: a 5.8 MB static binary that starts in under two milliseconds. .NET has had everything the spec needs in the box for a decade, and since .NET 8 it has had Native AOT, which compiles the whole thing to a single native executable with no runtime to install. The question for this post was whether a C# client could get anywhere near Go on size and cold start. It can, with a caveat that the leaderboard makes visible.

The code is at github.com/AndyCross/claude-hot-path, and the spec every client passes is at /claude-hot-path/.

JsonNode, not source generators

The idiomatic way to do JSON in AOT .NET is System.Text.Json with a source-generated JsonSerializerContext, so the serialiser knows every type at compile time and nothing needs reflection. For a client this small I went the other way and used JsonNode, the DOM API, because the request body and the event payloads are built and read dynamically anyway and a context class would have doubled the file.

That choice runs into AOT's trimming analysis in one place. JsonArray.Add<T>(T) is generic, and when T is JsonObject the compiler warns that creating a JsonValue from a non-primitive type needs runtime code generation. It is a false alarm here, because a JsonObject is a node and gets added as one, but the fix is to say so with a cast:

messages.Add((JsonNode)new JsonObject { ["role"] = "assistant", ["content"] = content.DeepClone() });

Four casts and the publish is warning-free. The rest of the project file is the usual AOT size settings:

<PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
<StripSymbols>true</StripSymbols>
<OptimizationPreference>Size</OptimizationPreference>
<InvariantGlobalization>true</InvariantGlobalization>
<UseSystemResourceKeys>true</UseSystemResourceKeys>
<EventSourceSupport>false</EventSourceSupport>
<StackTraceSupport>false</StackTraceSupport>

InvariantGlobalization is the big one. Without it the binary carries ICU for culture-aware string handling, and a client that compares a few ASCII event names does not need any of it.

Headers first, then the stream

The one line that makes streaming work in HttpClient is the completion option. By default SendAsync buffers the whole response body before returning, which for an SSE stream means waiting for the model to finish before printing anything, and the harness fails a client that does that:

using var resp = await http.SendAsync(req, HttpCompletionOption.ResponseHeadersRead);

With headers-read completion the body is a live stream, and a StreamReader over it gives the same line loop as Go's scanner:

using var reader = new StreamReader(await resp.Content.ReadAsStreamAsync());
while (await reader.ReadLineAsync() is { } line)
{
    if (!line.StartsWith("data: ", StringComparison.Ordinal)) continue;
    var ev = JsonNode.Parse(line.Substring(6))!;
    var index = (int?)ev["index"] ?? 0;
    switch ((string?)ev["type"])
    {
        case "content_block_start":
            content.Add(ev["content_block"]!.DeepClone());
            partial.Add(new StringBuilder());
            break;
        case "content_block_delta":
            var delta = ev["delta"]!;
            if ((string?)delta["type"] == "text_delta")
            {
                var text = (string)delta["text"]!;
                stdout.Write(text); stdout.Flush();
                content[index]!["text"] = (string?)content[index]!["text"] + text;
            }
            else if ((string?)delta["type"] == "input_json_delta")
                partial[index].Append((string?)delta["partial_json"]);
            break;
        case "content_block_stop":
            if ((string?)content[index]!["type"] == "tool_use" && partial[index].Length > 0)
                content[index]!["input"] = JsonNode.Parse(partial[index].ToString());
            break;
        case "message_delta":
            stop = (string?)ev["delta"]?["stop_reason"];
            break;
    }
}

The stdout.Flush() is there because Console.Out is buffered when it is not a terminal, and under the harness it never is. Go's os.Stdout is unbuffered and the bash client's printf goes straight out, so this is the first client where streaming could have silently become batching.

The second turn echoes the assistant content back with DeepClone(), because a JsonNode can only have one parent and the same array is about to be the content of a message inside messages and the source of the tool_result blocks. TimeZoneInfo.FindSystemTimeZoneById takes IANA names on Linux directly, so the tool is three lines and no conversion table.

What it measures as

C# Native AOT Go bash and curl
Artefact 5.4 MB 5.8 MB 3.7 KB
Runtime 2.4 MB 0 23.7 MB
Ship 7.8 MB 5.8 MB 23.7 MB
Cold start, median of 100 3.0 ms 1.7 ms 7.0 ms
Turnaround, median of 100 1.4 ms 1.2 ms 19.1 ms
Client total, median of 100 7.1 ms 4.8 ms 35.3 ms
Peak RSS 7 MB 6 MB 11 MB
Lines of code 102 156 75

.NET SDK 10.0.402, linux/arm64, Apple M4 Max under Docker. Published with -r linux-arm64 and the project settings above, run from the runtime-deps image.

The binary is smaller than Go's, which surprised me and will surprise more people. It is also not the whole story, and this is the reason the leaderboard has a runtime column. The Go binary is static. The .NET one links glibc, libgcc_s and the dynamic loader, and ldd on it finds 2.4 MB of shared libraries that have to be in the image. Add them and .NET ships 7.8 MB to Go's 5.8. Leave them out and you have an image that does not start. The runtime-deps base image exists for exactly this reason. Its chiseled variant is smaller still, and has no shell, which is why the harness measures from the exported image rather than by running commands inside it.

Cold start is three milliseconds against Go's under-two. The extra millisecond is the loader resolving those libraries and the AOT runtime initialising its GC, and it is a long way short of what a JIT-compiled .NET console app spends before it reaches Main. The turnaround between the two requests is within a fraction of a millisecond of Go's, and peak memory is about the same. For a language that spent twenty years needing a runtime installed on the box, that table is a remarkable place to have got to.

How to run it 

git clone https://github.com/AndyCross/claude-hot-path
cd claude-hot-path
./bench/bench.sh csharp

Docker and Python 3, no key. The AOT publish needs clang and zlib1g-dev in the SDK image, which the Dockerfile installs, and takes about a minute. Next week is Rust, the first client in the series without HTTP in its standard library.

title: Trying to break into the clinical trials space
description:
Imagine someone has just been given a serious diagnosis. One of their options might be a clinical trial: a new drug or treatment regimen that isn't yet available in routine care. There's no shortage of places to look. The largest open registry, ClinicalTrials.gov, is free and lists more than 600,000 studies from all over the world.

So what's the problem? It's not that there's too little data. Quite the opposite: there's too much of it, and it's written for specialists. To figure out whether a trial is right for you, you have to read the inclusion and exclusion criteria and match them against your diagnosis, stage, previous treatment and a dozen other things. For someone without medical training, that means hours of comparing walls of text, and still a real chance of getting it wrong.

We decided to make exactly this part easier, and that's how Cintarra was born. This article covers how we got here, what we found on the market, how we built the product, what it cost, and whether it was worth the effort at all.

Where the project came from

A confession to start with: the idea isn't ours. More precisely, the niche was suggested to us by a doctor who works in clinical research.

We started with no budget and no experience in medical products. What we had was an idea, the drive to see it through, and free evenings and weekends. Oh, and ten years of designing interfaces of every level of complexity for every kind of audience.

Discovery

Target audiences and what they need

I can't say exactly when our first brainstorming call took place, and it doesn't really matter. What matters is that on that call we settled on the audiences to focus on, and agreed we needed to study them more closely to understand what to offer.

We ended up with four groups: patients (the main one), healthy volunteers, physician-investigators and sponsors. For each, we built a persona and a customer journey map (CJM). Then we walked each persona through four stages, from diagnosis to taking part in a trial, and mapped out actions, goals, emotions, pain points and touchpoints at every stage.

The most useful takeaway from the CJM: the emotional curve hits its lowest point in the first two stages (diagnosis and finding a trial), exactly where a person is left alone with the registry. Later, trial coordinators and site doctors get involved, and things get easier. So help is needed right at the start: finding trials and understanding whether you qualify before you ever call a trial site.

Competitors

When we started our competitor analysis (late 2025), the list looked like this:

  1. ClinicalTrials.gov. The primary source and, essentially, our main competitor. Free, the most complete, updated daily. But it's a registry, not an assistant: there are filters, but the inclusion and exclusion criteria are a solid block of text for specialists, and matching them to your own situation is entirely on you.
  2. Ancora.ai. Trial matching for cancer patients: you answer questions about your diagnosis and treatment and get a list of suitable trials. Free for patients, but focused primarily on oncology.
  3. Trialing.org. Built for doctors, not patients: search by condition, biomarkers and trial ID, plus patient referrals to partner hospitals. Free for doctors; pharma companies and CROs pay. According to its website, it covers about 4,000 trials in 26 countries.

The bottom line: you get either a complete but raw registry, or convenient tools that are limited to one therapeutic area or built for doctors. Among the services we looked at, none helped a patient with any diagnosis check themselves against the criteria and understand the result. That's the gap we decided to aim for.

What we decided to build

Based on all of the above, we put together a core feature set. Although, to be honest, "hypotheses" is a better word for them:

  1. Search by condition and location. Type your condition in plain language rather than an exact medical term, and immediately see the distance to the trial site.
  2. Medical card. Describe your diagnosis, stage, previous treatment and biomarkers once and reuse it for every trial, instead of filling in the same thing on every questionnaire.
  3. Match percentage. Show how well a trial fits, and keep two different situations apart: an explicit conflict with the criteria versus simply missing information about the patient.
  4. Easy application. Help pick a suitable location and contact, and generate a message template.
  5. New trial alerts. If nothing fits right now, people shouldn't have to check the registry every day themselves.

We couldn't validate these hypotheses before launch: paying $15 per interview sounds lovely, just not on our shoestring budget. So we went the other way around: launch an MVP first and test it on real users.

Architecture

The stack: React, TypeScript and Vite on the front end, Node.js with Express on the back end, MongoDB, hosted on Google Cloud Run. The stack itself is less interesting than how the product's design changed every time we hit a wall on speed or cost.

Our own copy of the registry

The first thing we did was stop hitting ClinicalTrials.gov on every search. We now keep our own copy of the registry in MongoDB, but not all of it: only trials that are recruiting now or will start soon.

We don't store everything, only what search and Match need: conditions, keywords, MeSH terms, eligibility criteria and trial locations. The full trial record is fetched from the registry only when someone opens it, and cached for a few hours. That keeps the database lean, and search runs on our own data without depending on an external API.

As a bonus, syncing taught us to spot changes: a trial has reopened recruitment, or a new site has been added. That came in handy later for alerts.

Match without a neural network

Our most important decision: the match percentage is calculated by deterministic rules, not by a model. The same data always produces the same result, and that result can be explained.
The medical card is compared with a trial across nine categories: diagnosis, age, sex, stage, location, current treatment, contraindications, biomarkers and exclusion criteria. A few principles we consider key:

  • An explicit conflict and missing data are different things. If age or sex clearly doesn't fit, or an exclusion criterion is triggered, Match is zero. But if the card simply lacks the information, the category stays "not verified": it earns no points, but it doesn't count as a match either.
  • No high score without a confirmed diagnosis. If the diagnosis isn't confirmed, Match is capped at 49%.
  • The percentage is not the probability of getting into the trial. It's a weighted estimate of how many criteria we were able to confirm. The final decision always rests with the trial site, and we say so explicitly.

Match is calculated for the top 100 candidates in the results, which are then re-sorted by it. Everything below stays in the default order. It's a trade-off between accuracy and database load.

Where we did need AI

We didn't get by entirely without a neural network; we just gave it the job it does better than rules: understanding people. In every case it's an inexpensive OpenAI model, called only where it's needed:

  • Search plan. A plain-language query ("KRAS-mutant lung cancer, Spain") is turned into a structured plan: the condition in English, a MeSH term, filters. One call per search, and the result is cached.
  • Filling in the card. You can describe your situation in text or upload a PDF of your medical records, and the model sorts it into the card's fields. Before processing, we ask for consent and strip direct identifiers from the PDF.
  • Diagnosis translation. If a diagnosis isn't written in English and isn't in our verified dictionary, the model translates it once, when the card is saved.

That said, a model's translation only helps find trials; it never confirms a diagnosis match. Only the verified dictionary can do that. For now it covers a handful of conditions, such as non-small cell lung cancer, triple-negative breast cancer and asthma, and it will keep growing.

The weekly trial digest skips AI altogether: the search plan is built locally from the card, and only trials with a Match of 50% or higher make the cut.

Reference data and APIs: where we saved money

Autocomplete was a story of its own. We didn't want to pay for every letter someone types into the "condition" field, so we went looking for free sources:

  • NLM Clinical Tables: a free API from the US National Library of Medicine. We use it for condition and gene suggestions.
  • Photon, built on OpenStreetMap data: city and country suggestions, also free.
  • Google Maps: we kept it only for geocoding and the map of trial sites on the trial page. We originally wanted to pull in clinic reviews and ratings too, but dropped the idea because of the price.

Design and front end

A quick reminder: I'm a designer, not a developer. So design and front end are the parts I handle with the most love and care. I'll also admit up front that I wanted to push the pixels myself, but naturally, Claude took over part of the work to speed things up.

Nothing groundbreaking, but still

In Figma, everything is built on variables: colors, typography, radii and spacing. On top of them sits a component library with variants: buttons, inputs, chips, badges and so on. In total, that's more than 30 components and around 530 variants.

There are mockups for every flow: home, search results, trial page, account and medical cards, settings, sign-in, favorites, info pages, 404/503 errors and emails. Each flow comes in three breakpoints (1440 px and up, 1024–1439 px and 320–1023 px), with every edge case we could think of.

The front end follows the same system: tokens were carried over to code one-to-one, and all components live in Storybook. Almost all of the project's code, both front end and back end, was written by Claude and GPT. To keep that from turning into chaos, the repository has rules for AI agents: how the project is structured, what to check, and what not to touch. Every change goes through the linter, server tests and browser scenarios on synthetic data. Anything involving medical data, Match rules or authentication is treated as a high-risk area and checked separately.

Costs

If you haven't noticed yet, saving money is the thread running through this whole story. Here's everything we pay for each month, including the tools we use to build the product.

Service What for Now  
Google Cloud Run and Cloud Scheduler server, registry sync, weekly digest $0
MongoDB Atlas, Flex tier registry copy, users, medical cards $8
OpenAI, gpt-4o-mini search plan, filling in cards, diagnosis translation $1–5
Google Maps geocoding and the trial site map $0
Prelude phone number verification $1–3
Cloudflare Workers Paid sending emails $5
Domain you get the idea $2
PostHog product analytics $0
ClinicalTrials.gov API, NLM Clinical Tables, Photon data and autocomplete $0
Claude, 2 subscriptions development $40
Figma, 1 seat design $16

Total: about $80 a month right now. At 1,000 users, about $120–145.

Unsurprisingly, tools are currently our biggest expense. But here's the funny part: at 1,000 users, the biggest line item isn't tools, servers or even the model. It's phone verification.

MVP, testing and plans

The MVP is live and fully working. It already has the entire core feature set we planned for launch.

First tests

We've launched unmoderated usability testing. It's still running, but the first insights are already in.

One example: the handy features need to be front and center from the very first screen. Medical cards, Match and easy applications are all there, but someone who came "just to browse" can miss them and leave thinking it's just another catalog. Onboarding was already on our roadmap, and now real users have confirmed we need it.

Plans

Our plans follow the same personas from discovery, just one at a time:

  • Onboarding. Show right away how we differ from a regular registry search.
  • Volunteer dashboard. Healthy volunteers are a separate audience with their own needs, and they deserve their own flow.
  • The business side, plus dashboards for pharma and doctors. It only makes sense to approach them once we have a user base: without patients, we have nothing to offer researchers.

Takeaways?

Honestly, all I really wanted in this article was to plug our service. Fine, I'll share a couple of thoughts after all this work. I'll keep it short.

In my humble opinion, we've built a really solid product that tackles our main audience's pain points. It's stable, it looks good, and there's a roadmap. What more could you want? Monetization! But that's a whole other story, maybe for a future article.

And most importantly, cheesy as it may sound: if this makes it even a little faster for people in need to find a trial that suits them better, that's mission accomplished.

You can judge whether we pulled it off here: cintarra.com.

title: Building a Reliable Length-to-Width Calculator with Vanilla JavaScript
description:
A small calculation can be mathematically simple while still presenting interesting problems in input validation, interface design and testing.

A length-to-width ratio is calculated by dividing one measurement by another.

For a diamond viewed from above, the basic formula is:

Ratio = Length ÷ Width

For example, a length of 9.00 mm and a width of 6.00 mm produce a ratio of 1.50.

The arithmetic is straightforward. Designing a reliable user interface around it requires more thought.

What should happen if someone leaves a field blank? How should the application treat zero or negative measurements? Should rounding happen before the result is stored? How can the interface communicate errors without relying exclusively on colour?

These questions are useful beyond jewellery tools. They appear in calculators, measurement forms, configuration interfaces and other small web applications.

This article explores a practical implementation pattern using HTML and vanilla JavaScript.

1. Separate calculation logic from interface code

A reliable calculator benefits from keeping mathematical logic separate from DOM event handling.

This makes the calculation easier to test and avoids mixing display concerns with numerical validation.

A useful function should accept input values and return either a meaningful result or a clear validation error.

For example:

function calculateRatio(lengthInput, widthInput) {
  const rawLength = String(lengthInput).trim();
  const rawWidth = String(widthInput).trim();

  if (rawLength === "" || rawWidth === "") {
    return {
      ok: false,
      error: "Enter both measurements."
    };
  }

  const length = Number(rawLength);
  const width = Number(rawWidth);

  if (
    !Number.isFinite(length) ||
    !Number.isFinite(width) ||
    length <= 0 ||
    width <= 0
  ) {
    return {
      ok: false,
      error: "Measurements must be positive numbers."
    };
  }

  if (length < width) {
    return {
      ok: false,
      error: "Enter the longer dimension as length."
    };
  }

  const ratio = length / width;

  return {
    ok: true,
    value: ratio,
    formatted: ratio.toFixed(2)
  };
}

This example uses a consistent convention: the length is the larger face-up dimension.

Other applications may define their measurement conventions differently, so the rule should be documented rather than assumed.

The function is intentionally independent of HTML elements. It can be tested directly and reused in other interfaces.

2. Handle empty values before numeric conversion

JavaScript has a small behaviour that can cause surprising results:

Number("") // 0

An empty string converts to zero.

A calculation form should not silently interpret a missing measurement as a real measurement of zero millimetres.

That is why the example checks trimmed values before calling Number().

It also uses Number.isFinite() rather than accepting all values that JavaScript can technically represent.

This rejects NaN and infinity, both of which are unsuitable for the measurement calculation.

Developers should also be explicit about input formats.

For instance, Number("9,5") does not parse as 9.5 in JavaScript. If a tool is intended to support locale-specific decimal separators, that requires a deliberately designed parsing rule.

3. Keep calculation precision separate from display precision

Suppose a user enters:

  • Length: 8.25 mm
  • Width: 6.40 mm

The underlying ratio is 1.2890625.

Showing every decimal place is usually unnecessary for a basic educational interface.

A display of 1.29:1 is easier to read.

However, the interface should not round the underlying value before storing or comparing it.

For example, this is useful:

const exactRatio = length / width;
const displayRatio = exactRatio.toFixed(2);

The original value remains available for calculations, while the formatted value is used for presentation.

This distinction matters if the application later introduces comparisons between two measurements, sorting or conditional visual explanations.

Rounding too early can make different values appear identical and can affect downstream logic.

4. Build forms that work with keyboards and assistive technology

A measurement tool should not rely on visual labels that are disconnected from input fields.

A simple HTML structure could look like this:

<form id="ratio-form">
  <label for="diamond-length">
    Length (mm)
  </label>

  <input
    id="diamond-length"
    name="length"
    type="number"
    min="0.01"
    step="any"
    required
  >

  <label for="diamond-width">
    Width (mm)
  </label>

  <input
    id="diamond-width"
    name="width"
    type="number"
    min="0.01"
    step="any"
    required
  >

  <button type="submit">
    Calculate ratio
  </button>

  <output id="ratio-result" aria-live="polite"></output>
</form>

Explicit labels help identify the purpose of each field.

Including the unit in the label also reduces ambiguity.

For a dynamic interface, the result can be written to the output element after validation.

Errors should be readable as text and associated with the relevant form controls where possible.

If the form contains an error, changing the text colour to red is not enough by itself. The actual error message must explain what needs to be corrected.

The example is a starting point rather than a complete accessibility implementation. Final behaviour should be tested using a keyboard and assistive technology.

5. Treat visual illustrations as explanations, not measurements

A jewellery measurement calculator may include an SVG outline to show how a shape's proportions change.

SVG is suitable for a lightweight browser interface because its geometry can be scaled without raster-image pixelation.

However, visual demonstrations need careful framing.

An outline can illustrate relative proportions, but it does not show the complete geometry of a three-dimensional diamond.

A length-to-width ratio cannot independently establish brilliance, symmetry, cut quality or overall value.

If the application supports multiple shapes, developers should avoid implying that one ratio alone determines an ideal appearance for every stone.

The illustration should explain the input values without presenting itself as a grading instrument.

6. Plan the interface for invalid measurements

Before publishing a calculator, define expected behaviour for common input conditions.

Length Width Expected outcome
9 6 1.50:1
8.25 6.4 1.29:1
6 9 Measurement-order error
0 6 Validation error
-2 6 Validation error
Empty 6 Required-field error
abc 6 Invalid-number error
5 5 1.00:1

These examples can become automated test cases.

Testing should also cover unusually large values, changes to inputs after calculation and browser-specific behaviour for number fields.

A calculator that produces the correct answer for one normal example is not necessarily reliable.

7. Protect the simplicity of a client-side tool

A basic ratio calculation does not require a server.

Running calculations in the browser can reduce infrastructure complexity and avoid unnecessary transmission of measurement inputs.

However, developers should avoid claiming that a browser-based tool is completely private without checking the wider application.

Analytics scripts, external resources, request logs and shared URLs may still expose information.

If the tool supports shareable results, putting measurements in URL parameters can be convenient.

But users should understand that URLs may appear in browser history, server logs or shared messages.

For non-sensitive educational measurements, that may be an acceptable trade-off. The decision should still be explicit.

8. Verify the deployed version, not only the source files

A project can have a complete README and still fail in the browser.

Before release, check that the deployed HTML can load every referenced JavaScript module, stylesheet, image and font.

Open the browser's developer tools and inspect network failures and console errors.

It is also important to test the actual deployment URL rather than relying only on a local development environment.

For static-site hosting, incorrect relative paths can cause assets to fail when the application is deployed inside a repository subdirectory.

A useful release process should include file checks, manual interaction tests and automated verification of the calculation logic.

Conclusion

Building a ratio calculator offers a useful reminder that even very small web tools need more than a working formula.

Reliable applications combine clear input rules, predictable numerical behaviour, readable errors, accessible controls and meaningful tests.

The best result is not necessarily the interface with the most features.

It is an interface that communicates what the calculation means, handles invalid inputs safely and makes its limitations clear.

Project context: This implementation discussion is relevant to the Diamond Shape Ratio Calculator educational project associated with Laxmi Jewellers. The code shown here is an illustrative implementation pattern, not a verified extract from the project's current repository.

Editorial disclosure: This draft was prepared with AI writing assistance. The intended human author must review the technical explanations, execute the examples and verify all implementation claims before publication.

title: I Applied Agile to My Personal Life. It Almost Burned Me Out.
description:
As software engineers, our brains are wired for systems. We love order, optimization, and clear workflows. So, a few years ago, I had what I thought was a genius idea: Why not apply Agile methodologies to my personal life?

If it works for shipping enterprise software, it should work for shipping personal goals, right?

I set up a "Personal Scrum" board. I created a backlog for my life. I broke down my goals into epics, and those epics into user stories. I even held a weekly "retrospective" with myself to identify blockers in my personal life.

It was the most miserable I have ever been.

Here is why applying software engineering principles to your personal life is a trap, and how I fixed it.

The Trap of "Life Technical Debt"
When you treat your life like a software project, you start to view normal human experiences as inefficiencies.

Resting becomes "downtime."

Hobbies become "side quests."

Unfinished books become "technical debt."

I had a Notion dashboard with 47 interconnected databases. I had tags for context, energy levels, and priority. Every time I wanted to do something as simple as "Go for a walk," I had to decide which project it fell under, log it, and check it off.

I was spending more time managing my life than actually living it.

The MVP Mindset Went Wrong
In software, we build an MVP (Minimum Viable Product) to test a hypothesis. But in life, I was trying to build an MVP for my entire existence. I was optimizing for "velocity" instead of "value."

I realized that the human brain doesn't have an API. You can't just scale up your energy levels by adding more coffee and pushing a sprint.

When you introduce high friction into your personal workflow, your brain (the CPU) eventually hits 100% utilization and simply crashes. That's called burnout.

The Refactor: Radical Simplicity
I decided to deprecate the "Life Scrum" system. I deleted all the databases. I threw away the epics and the user stories.

I replaced it with a system that has only one rule: The 3-Task Rule.

Every morning, I write down exactly three things I want to accomplish that day. It doesn't matter if they are work-related, personal, or just "take a nap." Those are my three priorities.

I don't track them in 5 different places. I don't assign them story points. I just do them.

Here is the "architecture" of my new system:
Today:

  1. [ ] Write one section of the new API docs
  2. [ ] Go to the gym
  3. [ ] Cook dinner instead of ordering That's it. No dependencies. No blockers. No velocity charts.

What I Learned
Friction is the enemy of execution. If your productivity system takes more than 10 seconds to open and understand, you will abandon it.

Not everything needs to be a system. Your life is not a Jira board. Some things are just things you do because you're a human being.

Optimize for peace, not just output. A system that helps you ship code but gives you an anxiety attack is a bad system.

The Result
By removing the heavy Agile framework from my personal life, I actually got more done. I stopped procrastinating because I wasn't overwhelmed by a massive backlog of "life tasks."

If you are a developer who feels burned out by your own productivity system, try deleting it. Strip it down to a flat list of three tasks. See how it feels to have a "boring" system.

I eventually got tired of rebuilding my task list from scratch every day, so I built a super minimal Notion template that implements this exact 3-Task philosophy. It has no flashy dashboards, just a clean space to focus on what matters. You can check out the ADHD Daily Planner here.

If you want to read more about why over-engineered Notion templates fail, I wrote about it on my blog here.

title: ProtectClock closes more than the RTC device
description:
ProtectClock closes more than the RTC device

A service that can change the host clock can change the order of events recorded around it. It can also shift timestamps used by applications that assume the operating system clock is outside their control. The systemd ProtectClock= setting reduces that authority in several ways at once.

What the setting changes

When ProtectClock=yes is configured, systemd removes CAP_SYS_TIME and CAP_WAKE_ALARM from the unit's capability bounding set. It also installs a system call filter for operations that can set a clock and applies a read-only device rule to the real-time clock devices.

The effect therefore extends beyond making /dev/rtc0 read-only. A service that previously called clock_settime(), settimeofday(), or an adjacent time-control interface meets both a capability restriction and a system call filter.

The filter is deliberately coarse. The systemd manual explains that the calls are blocked even when a particular argument combination would only read clock state. Applications that need those calls for a legitimate reason need a narrower policy than ProtectClock=yes, or they need to move the operation outside the sandbox.

Where it fits in a service policy

ProtectClock= is most useful as part of an execution profile that already runs the service as an unprivileged user. A process running as root may retain other ways to reach kernel interfaces. Removing CAP_SYS_TIME blocks one path, but mount access, writable kernel settings, and device access still need review.

Keep the service's actual requirements visible. A time daemon needs to adjust the clock. A certificate validation service usually does not. A scheduler may need accurate time, while the database or job runner it supports only needs to consume the clock. Those roles should not share the same unit policy.

Review the related settings together:

[Service]
User=app
ProtectClock=yes
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET AF_INET6
SystemCallFilter=~@mount

The example is a review starting point. Some services need mount operations for their own temporary storage or runtime directories. A denied system call can fail a health check long after the unit starts, so test the full startup and shutdown path.

The host still owns the clock

The setting protects the service from writing the clock. It does not make the host clock trustworthy. A hypervisor, a privileged local process, or an administrator can still change it. Logs from different hosts can still disagree because of clock drift or a broken time source.

Defenders should combine host time synchronization, authenticated time where the environment supports it, and independent log evidence. Application logs should record monotonic durations for local timers when event ordering matters. Central log storage should preserve receipt time separately from the timestamp supplied by the host.

ProtectClock= reduces a service's ability to create a misleading local timeline. It does not repair a timeline that was already altered before the logs left the host.

Verify the effective unit

Start with the expanded unit rather than the fragment in /etc:
