systemctl cat example.service
systemctl show example.service -p User -p ProtectClock -p CapabilityBoundingSet
systemd-analyze security example.service

Then exercise the paths that need time access. A harmless application startup is not enough if a maintenance command changes the clock or wakes an alarm through a separate process. Check those helper processes and any command started with a + prefix, because systemd does not apply every sandbox setting to those commands in the same way.

Record the intended result. The service should be able to read time, run its scheduled work, and pass its health checks. It should fail when asked to change host time. If it succeeds, the unit policy is incomplete or the test is running outside the sandbox.

References

  • systemd.exec execution environment settings
  • systemd-analyze security
  • Linux time namespaces

title: I Changed object to Lock and Stopped Paying the Monitor Tax
description:
I had a counter behind a lock that a profiler kept flagging, and I couldn't figure out why. The lock was basically never contended. One thread wrote to it almost all the time; the lock was there for the rare second writer that might show up. So I expected it to cost close to nothing. It didn't cost nothing. It cost about 24 nanoseconds every single acquire, and on a hot path that adds up to a line you can see in a flame graph.

The thing I'd stopped thinking about is what lock (someObject) actually compiles to. It's Monitor.Enter and Monitor.Exit wrapped in a try/finally, and Monitor hangs its state off the object's sync block. Even with no contention at all, you pay for that bookkeeping on every acquire and release. For years that was just the price of the lock keyword and there was nothing to do about it.

Since .NET 9 there is. There's a real type now, System.Threading.Lock, and the compiler special-cases it: if you lock on a variable whose type is Lock, it doesn't go through Monitor at all. It calls the type's own fast path instead. The part that surprised me is how little the code changes.

// before
private readonly object _gate = new();
lock (_gate) { _count++; }

// after
private readonly Lock _gate = new();
lock (_gate) { _count++; }   // same statement, different field type

One word. The lock statement is byte-for-byte identical. The only thing I changed is object to Lock on the field, and the compiler routes the whole thing through the new mechanism instead.

Making it tell on itself

I didn't want to trust a hunch, so I hammered both in the dullest way possible: one thread, a tight loop, fifty million lock-increment-unlock cycles, best of seven runs with the JIT already warm. This is a container with two cores, not a lab bench, so I care about the ratio between the two numbers, not the absolute nanoseconds.

for (long i = 0; i < Ops; i++)
{
    lock (objectGate) { c++; }   // object + Monitor
}

for (long i = 0; i < Ops; i++)
{
    lock (realLock) { c++; }     // System.Threading.Lock
}

Ops per trial: 50,000,000   Trials: 7 (reporting best)
Processors: 2   Server GC: False

Uncontended, single thread (best of 7):
  lock(object)          1230 ms   24.60 ns/op
  lock(Lock)            1084 ms   21.68 ns/op
  Lock.EnterScope()     1083 ms   21.66 ns/op
  speedup vs object:  1.13x

So about 13% off every uncontended acquire, for changing one word. I'll be honest about the size of that: 13% of 24 nanoseconds is three nanoseconds. If your lock gets taken a few hundred times a second, you will never, ever notice this, and you shouldn't go rewriting working code to chase it. Where it starts to matter is the hot inner path that grabs a lock millions of times, and in that spot three nanoseconds times millions is a real slice of a frame.

I also ran the contended case, two threads actually fighting over the same lock, and the gap narrowed to about 1.05x. That tracks. Once threads are genuinely blocking each other, the cost is dominated by the waiting, not by the per-acquire overhead, so the fast path has less room to help. The uncontended path is where the new type earns its keep, which is lucky, because uncontended is what most locks are most of the time.

The explicit form, and what it buys

If you'd rather not use the lock statement, the type gives you a scope you dispose:

using (realLock.EnterScope())
{
    _count++;
}

EnterScope() returns a ref struct called Scope. That's not a detail to skim past. A ref struct can't be boxed, can't be stored in a field, can't escape to the heap, so you physically cannot hold onto the scope past the block it lives in. The object-plus-Monitor pattern never gave you that guarantee; you could always forget an Exit or get clever and leak the hold. Here the compiler won't let you. My run clocked EnterScope() at the same speed as the statement, so there's no penalty for the clearer form.

The caveat that actually bit me

One thing caught me out, because I briefly thought the new type would save me from it and it doesn't. You still can't await while holding a Lock:

error CS1996: Cannot await in the body of a lock statement

That's not a new rule and it's not something the Lock type introduced. The exact same error fires on a plain lock (object) and always has. I mention it because when I first reached for Lock, some corner of my brain assumed a shiny new synchronization primitive might finally let me hold it across an await. Nope. A Lock is for short, synchronous critical sections, same as Monitor always was. If what you actually need is mutual exclusion around an await, that's still SemaphoreSlim with WaitAsync, and reaching for Lock there just gets you a compile error pointing at the real problem.

So my rule, and this is an opinion rather than a benchmark: for new code, I default to Lock now. It says what it means, it hands me a scope I can't misuse, and it's a hair faster for free. For existing code that works, I only swap it when I'm already in that file for another reason, or when the profiler put me there. Three nanoseconds is not worth a diff on its own.

The full benchmark

Here's the whole thing. It's a top-level program targeting net10.0 (the Lock type works on .NET 9+), so drop it in a fresh console project and dotnet run -c Release. The numbers above came from a 2-core container with workstation GC, so treat them as ratios, not absolutes.

using System.Diagnostics;

const long Ops = 50_000_000;    // lock/unlock pairs per trial
const int Trials = 7;

Console.WriteLine($"Ops per trial: {Ops:N0}   Trials: {Trials} (reporting best)");
Console.WriteLine($"Processors: {Environment.ProcessorCount}   Server GC: {System.Runtime.GCSettings.IsServerGC}");
Console.WriteLine();

// uncontended: object + Monitor (what lock(_gate) has always meant)
var objectGate = new object();
long objectBest = long.MaxValue;
for (int t = 0; t < Trials; t++)
{
    long c = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (long i = 0; i < Ops; i++)
        lock (objectGate) { c++; }
    sw.Stop();
    GC.KeepAlive(c);
    objectBest = Math.Min(objectBest, sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
}

// uncontended: the new System.Threading.Lock
var realLock = new Lock();
long lockBest = long.MaxValue;
for (int t = 0; t < Trials; t++)
{
    long c = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (long i = 0; i < Ops; i++)
        lock (realLock) { c++; }   // same keyword, different field type
    sw.Stop();
    GC.KeepAlive(c);
    lockBest = Math.Min(lockBest, sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
}

// the explicit EnterScope form
long scopeBest = long.MaxValue;
for (int t = 0; t < Trials; t++)
{
    long c = 0;
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (long i = 0; i < Ops; i++)
        using (realLock.EnterScope()) { c++; }
    sw.Stop();
    GC.KeepAlive(c);
    scopeBest = Math.Min(scopeBest, sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
}

double ObjNs(long ms) => ms * 1_000_000.0 / Ops;

Console.WriteLine("Uncontended, single thread (best of 7):");
Console.WriteLine($"  lock(object)        {objectBest,6} ms   {ObjNs(objectBest):F2} ns/op");
Console.WriteLine($"  lock(Lock)          {lockBest,6} ms   {ObjNs(lockBest):F2} ns/op");
Console.WriteLine($"  Lock.EnterScope()   {scopeBest,6} ms   {ObjNs(scopeBest):F2} ns/op");
Console.WriteLine($"  speedup vs object:  {(double)objectBest / lockBest:F2}x");
Console.WriteLine();

// contended: several threads fighting over the same lock
static long RunContended(int threads, long perThread, Action<long> body)
{
    long best = long.MaxValue;
    for (int t = 0; t < 3; t++)
    {
        var tasks = new Thread[threads];
        var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
        for (int k = 0; k < threads; k++)
        {
            tasks[k] = new Thread(() => body(perThread));
            tasks[k].Start();
        }
        foreach (var th in tasks) th.Join();
        sw.Stop();
        best = Math.Min(best, sw.ElapsedMilliseconds);
    }
    return best;
}

int nthreads = Math.Max(2, Environment.ProcessorCount);
long perThreadOps = 10_000_000;
long sharedCounter = 0;

var objGate2 = new object();
long objContended = RunContended(nthreads, perThreadOps, n =>
{
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) lock (objGate2) { sharedCounter++; }
});

var lockGate2 = new Lock();
long lockContended = RunContended(nthreads, perThreadOps, n =>
{
    for (long i = 0; i < n; i++) lock (lockGate2) { sharedCounter++; }
});

Console.WriteLine($"Contended, {nthreads} threads x {perThreadOps:N0} ops (best of 3):");
Console.WriteLine($"  lock(object)        {objContended,6} ms");
Console.WriteLine($"  lock(Lock)          {lockContended,6} ms");
Console.WriteLine($"  speedup vs object:  {(double)objContended / lockContended:F2}x");
Console.WriteLine($"  final counter:      {sharedCounter:N0}");

What's your rule for touching working lock code? Mine is "only when I'm already there," but I know people who'd rewrite the whole file on sight. Curious where you land.

— still benchmarking the stuff nobody filed a ticket for

title: Reverse Engineering Mobile APIs: The Art of Intercepting Hidden Traffic
description:
The modern web is no longer just a collection of URLs and HTML tags. Today, the most valuable data sits behind the high walls of mobile applications, guarded by proprietary protocols, certificate pinning, and obfuscated logic. For a data engineer or security researcher, hitting an empty endpoint or a 403 Forbidden error on a web portal is often just the beginning. The real source of truth is usually an API designed exclusively for the mobile app—a "private" channel that most scrapers never touch.

Breaking into these channels requires moving beyond simple browser DevTools. It requires a shift into the world of emulators, SSL proxying, and traffic decapsulation. This is not just about scraping; it is about digital forensics and understanding the conversation between a device and its server.

Why Does the Mobile API Remain the "Gold Mine" of Data?

When developers build web interfaces, they are often constrained by SEO requirements, legacy browser support, and public accessibility. Mobile APIs are different. Because the client (the app) is a controlled environment, developers often design these APIs to be more efficient, verbose, and direct.

In many cases, the mobile version of a service provides:

  1. Cleaner Data Structures: JSON responses that aren't cluttered with HTML boilerplate.
  2. Higher Rate Limits: Apps often have more generous thresholds to prevent "laggy" user experiences.
  3. Hidden Fields: Data points that exist in the database but are hidden from the web UI are frequently exposed in the mobile API response.

The challenge, however, is that these APIs are "hidden." They don't want to be talked to by anything other than the official app. To bridge this gap, we must become the man-in-the-middle.

The Architectural Blueprint: How Traffic Interception Works

To intercept traffic, you must convince the mobile application that your computer is the gateway to the internet. The standard workflow involves routing traffic from a mobile device (or emulator) through a proxy server (like Charles Proxy, Fiddler, or Mitmproxy) that decrypts the SSL/TLS layer.

The Virtual Sandbox: Emulators vs. Physical Devices

While you can use a physical phone, emulators are the preferred "operating table" for reverse engineering.

  • Root Access: Essential for bypassing security restrictions. Emulators like Genymotion or specialized Android Studio images make this trivial.
  • Snapshots: The ability to revert to a "clean" state after an app detects your tampering and locks you out.
  • Environment Spoofing: Changing device IDs, GPS coordinates, and carrier info to bypass regional blocks.

How Do We Bypass Certificate Pinning and SSL Barriers?

The biggest hurdle in modern mobile scraping is SSL Pinning. This is a security measure where the app is programmed to trust only one specific certificate, ignoring the system-wide certificates you’ve installed for your proxy.

The "Unlock" Framework

When you encounter a "Connection Refused" error in your proxy while the app claims "Network Error," you are likely hitting a pinning wall. You have three main levers to pull:

  1. System-Level Trust (Android 7.0+): Modern Android versions do not trust user-added certificates by default. You must move your proxy certificate to the System Trust Store (/system/etc/security/cacerts/). This requires a rooted environment and a bit of adb magic.
  2. Dynamic Instrumentation (Frida): This is the heavy artillery. Frida allows you to inject scripts into the app's process at runtime. You can literally "hook" the function responsible for checking the SSL certificate and force it to return true, regardless of the certificate's validity.
  3. APK Patching: Using tools like objection or apktool, you can decompile the app, modify the network_security_config.xml to allow user certificates, re-sign the app, and reinstall it.

The Step-by-Step Guide: From Zero to API Request

If you are starting from scratch, follow this checklist to establish a stable sniffing environment.

Phase 1: Environment Setup

  • [ ] Install a Proxy: Download Charles Proxy or Mitmproxy. Note your local IP address and the port (usually 8888 or 8080).
  • [ ] Configure the Emulator: Launch a rooted Android image. Set the Manual Proxy settings in the Wi-Fi configuration to point to your computer's IP.
  • [ ] Install the Root Certificate: Navigate to the proxy’s setup URL (e.g., chls.pro/ssl) in the emulator's browser and install the certificate.

Phase 2: Bypassing Protections

  • [ ] Check for Pinning: Open the target app. If traffic flows, you're lucky. If not, proceed to Frida.
  • [ ] Inject Frida Script: Run a universal SSL bypass script. This intercepts the trust manager classes in the Android framework.
  • [ ] Identify the Endpoints: Watch the proxy logs. Look for POST and GET requests to domains that don't look like analytics (avoiding Google Analytics or Firebase logs).

Phase 3: Analysis and Replication

  • [ ] Header Inspection: Pay close attention to X-Signature, Authorization, and User-Agent.
  • [ ] Payload Decoding: If the data looks like gibberish, check if it’s encoded in Gzip, Protobuf, or a custom Base64 variant.
  • [ ] Request Replay: Right-click the request and "Copy as cURL." Try running it from your terminal to see if it works outside the emulator.

Beyond the Proxy: When Sniffing Isn't Enough

Sometimes, the traffic is encrypted within the SSL tunnel—an extra layer of obfuscation. This is common in high-security apps like banking or major social networks.

In these cases, you are no longer looking at the traffic; you are looking at the binary. You must decompile the application (using JADX for Android) to find the logic that signs the requests. Often, you'll find a secret "Salt" or a specific algorithm (like HMAC-SHA256) used to generate a request signature. If you don't find this, your replicated requests will be rejected by the server as "unauthorized" even if the data is correct.

The Logistics of Scale: Cellular Traffic and Rotating IPs

Once you've mapped the API, the next challenge is volume. Servers are quick to flag data center IPs. To scrape effectively, your traffic must look like it's coming from a real mobile user.

This is where Mobile Proxies (4G/LTE) become essential. Unlike residential or data center IPs, mobile IPs are shared by thousands of users via CGNAT (Carrier-Grade NAT). If a server blocks a mobile IP, it risks blocking thousands of legitimate customers. By routing your scripts through a cellular gateway, you gain a level of anonymity that is nearly impossible to achieve through traditional means.

Final Thoughts: The Ethical and Technical Horizon

Reverse engineering mobile APIs is a game of cat and mouse. As developers implement more sophisticated protections—like JA3 fingerprinting, which identifies the specific TLS handshake of a library—the tools we use must become more human-like.

The key takeaway is that no app is a black box. Everything that happens on a device you own can be observed, dissected, and replicated. The barrier isn't the technology; it's the depth of your curiosity. As you move from simple proxying to dynamic instrumentation and binary analysis, you stop being a consumer of data and start becoming an architect of it.

The next time you see a "Private API," remember: it’s only private because no one has bothered to listen to the conversation yet. Set up your proxy, fire up your emulator, and start listening.

Originally appeared on onlineproxy.io — a service for selling proxies.

title: Building an OEM IoT Backend: Device Identity, Customer Isolation and Lifecycle Management
description:
Connecting a prototype to a dashboard proves that data can move.

Shipping connected equipment to multiple customers introduces more questions:

  • Who can claim a device?
  • Which customer can access its history?
  • What happens when firmware changes the payload?
  • How does the backend distinguish a requested setting from an applied setting?
  • What happens when equipment changes ownership?

An OEM IoT backend manages device identity, customer relationships, application data and lifecycle operations. For ODMs supplying multiple brands, the architecture may also need separate product configurations and service responsibilities.

This guide covers the implementation boundaries that help a connected product grow beyond its first deployment.

1. Separate Physical Identity from Customer Assignment

A physical device needs a stable identity.

Customer ownership is a relationship that can change.

Keep them separate:

{
  "deviceId": "dev-008421",
  "model": "controller-x2",
  "hardwareRevision": "rev-c",
  "firmwareVersion": "2.4.1",
  "lifecycleState": "commissioned",
  "tenantId": "customer-031",
  "siteId": "site-009",
  "assignmentVersion": 7
}

This is an illustrative application record, not a protocol standard.

The device identifier remains stable while customer and site assignments follow controlled workflows.

Preserve assignment history. A current tenantId field alone cannot explain who had access before a transfer or which customer owned the device when an observation was collected.

Avoid embedding permanent customer ownership into the device identifier. Devices can be returned, reassigned or replaced.

2. Model Provisioning as Controlled State Transitions

Device registration, identity verification and customer assignment are separate operations.

A practical lifecycle might include:

  • Manufactured: The unit exists in the product registry.
  • Enrolled: The backend has verified its identity.
  • Assigned: An authorized customer relationship exists.
  • Commissioned: Installation checks are complete.
  • Suspended: Access is restricted under a defined policy.
  • Retired: Normal service access has ended.

Define who can initiate each transition and what evidence it requires.

An incoming message from an unfamiliar identifier should not automatically establish ownership.

Make Claiming Atomic

A customer claim workflow should authenticate the user, check their permissions, validate the claim credential and confirm that the device is eligible.

The assignment must also handle concurrent requests.

A simplified transaction could follow this pattern:

def claim_device(user, device_id, claim_token):
    require_permission(user, "claim_device")

    with database.transaction():
        device = registry.lock_for_update(device_id)

        validate_claim_token(device, claim_token)
        require_claimable_state(device)

        registry.assign(
            device_id=device.device_id,
            tenant_id=user.tenant_id
        )

        invalidate_claim_token(device)
        audit.record("device_claimed", user, device)

This is pseudocode. Credential protection, error handling and transaction behavior depend on the implementation.

A printed serial number can identify equipment, but identification alone should not establish permission to claim it.

3. Enforce Tenant Boundaries beyond the Interface

Filtering the device list in a dashboard does not establish customer isolation.

Authorization must cover every route to data and actions, including:

  • Historical queries.
  • Remote commands.
  • Reports and exports.
  • Background jobs.
  • Notifications.
  • Message subscriptions.
  • Integration credentials.
  • Support access.

Derive tenant scope from authenticated context and validated resource relationships. Do not trust a client-supplied tenant identifier by itself.

A simplified access check might look like this:

def read_device_history(user, device_id):
    device = registry.get(device_id)

    if not permissions.can_read(user, device):
        raise AccessDenied()

    return historian.query(
        tenant_id=device.tenant_id,
        device_id=device.device_id
    )

Production access also needs an explicit historical ownership policy. A new owner should not automatically receive a previous customer’s records.

Test indirect paths such as cached responses, downloadable exports and scheduled reports.

4. Normalize Telemetry across Firmware Versions

Connected products evolve.

Firmware may add a measurement, change a field name or alter its representation. An ODM may supply related hardware with different capabilities.

Use a versioned ingestion contract and map supported device payloads into a consistent application model.

{
  "deviceId": "dev-008421",
  "schemaVersion": 2,
  "measurement": "motor_temperature",
  "value": 61.7,
  "unit": "degC",
  "sourceTimestamp": "2026-11-05T08:30:00Z",
  "quality": "good"
}

Define required fields, optional fields, engineering units and compatibility rules.

An unavailable measurement should remain unavailable. Converting it into zero creates a different meaning.

Preserve acquisition timestamps separately from arrival timestamps. A delayed observation may belong in historical storage without replacing a newer current value.

For platform-specific background, see Iotellect’s documentation on Data Table Timestamps and Quality.

Keep Payload Differences out of Dashboards

If every dashboard handles firmware variations independently, each product change creates work across the interface.

Normalize near ingestion so supported device generations can feed shared application components.

Connectivity is a related architectural decision. Iotellect’s OPC UA vs MQTT guide for industrial IoT provides background on structured equipment acquisition and upstream messaging.

Whichever transport is selected, the application still needs a documented payload contract.

5. Track Desired and Reported Configuration Separately

An accepted request does not prove that the device applied the setting.

Maintain separate desired and reported configuration:

{
  "deviceId": "dev-008421",
  "desiredConfigVersion": 18,
  "reportedConfigVersion": 17,
  "configurationStatus": "pending"
}

The interface can then show that synchronization remains incomplete.

Define what happens when:

  • A device stays offline.
  • Configuration is rejected.
  • A local technician changes a setting.
  • Two authorized users submit conflicting changes.
  • The device reports an unexpected version.

Remote actions also need identifiers, authorization, relevant preconditions and expiry rules.

Some settings can be applied repeatedly with the same result. Other actions need verification before retrying.

6. Treat Firmware Updates as a Release Workflow

Firmware updates depend on both backend orchestration and device-side capabilities.

Verify what the hardware and bootloader support before designing the workflow.

A release process should address:

  • Firmware authenticity and integrity verification.
  • Hardware compatibility.
  • Installation prerequisites.
  • Interrupted downloads.
  • Failed installation.
  • Recovery or rollback, where supported.
  • Post-update health confirmation.

Track these stages separately:

Selected
→ Downloading
→ Verified
→ Installing
→ Health confirmation
→ Completed or failed

A completed download does not establish a successful installation.

Begin with a limited release group and define the conditions for expanding or stopping deployment.

Test compatibility between the new firmware and existing telemetry, configuration and application contracts.

7. Design Transfers and Replacements before They Happen

Customer handover affects more than one assignment field.

A transfer workflow needs decisions about:

  • Previous users’ access.
  • Device and integration credentials.
  • Historical data visibility.
  • Pending commands.
  • Local configuration.
  • New customer assignment.
  • Audit records.

Define how observations arriving after transfer are attributed, especially when a device uploads buffered history.

Replacement introduces another boundary: the physical device and the operational asset may have different identities.

A replacement controller has a new device identity, while the monitored machine remains the same asset.

Preserve that relationship so operators can follow asset history without merging unrelated physical devices.

8. Keep Branding Separate from Authorization

An OEM or ODM may need branded interfaces, domains and product configurations.

Those presentation settings should operate above a consistent access model.

White-labeling concerns branding. Tenant isolation concerns access and data boundaries. Both need explicit implementation.

Support access deserves its own policy. Define its scope, approval requirements where applicable, duration and audit records.

For teams building this application layer, Iotellect’s white-label IoT platform for OEMs and ODMs provides a low-code foundation for device connectivity, customer-facing applications, data processing and fleet management.

The product team still needs to define provisioning, customer boundaries, device capabilities and lifecycle behavior.

What to Test before Shipping

A useful pilot extends beyond first connection.

Verify that:

  1. An unauthorized user cannot claim a device.
  2. Concurrent claims cannot create conflicting assignments.
  3. Customers cannot access each other’s data, commands or exports.
  4. Supported older firmware continues working after backend changes.
  5. Configuration remains visibly pending until confirmed.
  6. Expired commands follow the rejection policy.
  7. Interrupted updates follow the supported recovery path.
  8. Transfers remove previous access appropriately.
  9. Replacements preserve the correct asset relationship.
  10. Retirement prevents normal service access while preserving required records.

Document the expected result for every test.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can one IoT backend support multiple hardware generations?

Yes, when supported device contracts are mapped into a consistent application model and compatibility is tested.

Is white-labeling the same as multi-tenancy?

No. White-labeling controls presentation and branding. Multi-tenancy serves multiple customers with defined access and data boundaries.

Can a backend provide firmware updates for any device?

Update orchestration requires compatible device-side mechanisms. Installation, verification and recovery capabilities depend on the hardware and software.

Why separate devices from assets?

A physical unit can be replaced while the machine or installation remains in service. Separate identities preserve that relationship accurately.

What should customer handover include?

At minimum, review access, credentials, configuration, pending actions, historical data visibility and the new assignment.

title: Shopify GEO: From Product Data to Checking What AI Actually Cites
description:
Official manufacturer image of the model discussed in the guide.

A shopper asks ChatGPT whether a dock can run two monitors from their MacBook. Seeing the product recommended is a good start for a merchant, but it doesn't necessarily mean the answer gives the shopper everything they need. If it leaves out the chip, lid position or connection requirements, the shopper could still end up buying the wrong product after clicking through.

That's where generative engine optimization, or GEO, comes in. The goal is straightforward: make accurate product and store information available, then check what buyers actually learn from AI answers and what happens after they follow the links. Pay attention to the exact product being recommended, the conditions attached to that recommendation, the evidence supporting each claim and the variant the shopper can actually purchase.

The Shopify features and admin paths below were checked against documentation on November 4, 2026. The Satechi example draws on publicly available product and support pages. The implementation steps are intended for merchants applying the same approach to their own stores. The case study uses published specifications and suggested test queries.

1. Find out where the product information comes from

The same Shopify merchant might appear as a product card in one answer and as a link to a compatibility guide in another. These are different ways of presenting information, so they need to be checked separately.

Workstream Material to maintain Where to check it
Shopify product data and store facts Catalog product and variant data, along with Knowledge Base facts such as delivery and returns Sales channels > Agentic, plus the target channel’s sources, eligibility and settings
Public pages and search Product pages, compatibility guides, policies, crawl and index settings, and structured data Public pages, source or rendered HTML, Search Console, and the answer’s actual citations

Shopify Catalog organizes product data for supported shopping surfaces. Agents can retrieve published Knowledge Base facts through Storefront MCP. Google AI Mode and Gemini also involve the Google & YouTube channel or Merchant Center. Relevant Meta shopping surfaces have their own Facebook and Instagram by Meta channel requirements. Each destination needs to be checked on its own. Shopify product discovery

AI answers may also draw on a manufacturer's help pages, other retailers or independent reviews. Being visible in search and being eligible for a shopping channel are two different things. Start with a group of commercially important products or items that regularly generate compatibility questions. Record the baseline before making changes to any data source.

  1. Check product eligibility and store policies.
  2. Review product fields, variant grouping and published store facts.
  3. Make sure public pages, structured data and localized versions are consistent.
  4. Rerun the same purchase questions, then review visits, orders and returns separately.

Once the process works for this initial group, apply the same conventions to the rest of the catalog.

2. Prepare product data in Shopify

A product page might display a specification in an image while the description sent to Catalog leaves that same information out. Before changing anything, compare the different places where the team maintains product information.

Check the channel and staff permissions

Go to Sales channels > Agentic and review the channel and Sources > Shopify Catalog. If a product is marked Ineligible, open the status to see the reason. If no eligibility result is available, record that status and check again later or contact support.

The current ChatGPT channel requirements include selling to U.S. customers, having Catalog-eligible products, accepting the Agentic Storefronts supplemental terms and completing the terms of service, privacy and return policies under Settings > Policies. The merchant itself can be based outside the U.S. Other channels have their own requirements, so check them separately. For affected products, Shopify requires applicable legal and compliance disclosures to appear within the first 6,000 characters of the description. Shopify ChatGPT channel requirements

The store owner can access Agentic. Staff members need the appropriate App development > View apps developed by staff and collaborators or App and sales channel > Agentic permission. Shopify Agentic administration

Stores selling to both B2B and retail customers should also review the products and prices being shared with each audience. Shopify recognizes its native B2B controls, but a theme or third-party app that hides wholesale prices may behave differently. Check B2B catalogs, authenticated access and channel settings together.

Keep in mind that Unlisted affects product discovery, including storefront search, search engines and sitemaps. If prices are sensitive, use the appropriate access controls rather than relying on product visibility settings. Shopify discovery and B2B scope

Use Listing insights to spot missing information

Find the product in the Agentic search preview and expand Listing insights. The five groups of signals provide a useful starting point for identifying gaps in the product data.

Signal Action Result to retain
Description completeness Answer recurring questions about use, limits and package contents A description that supports a purchase decision
Variant and option completeness Check the names, inventory and actual differences. Expand unfamiliar abbreviations on first use A clear identity and conditions for each purchasable option
Image coverage Add useful product, port and use images and write the decisive specifications in page text Visual explanation with searchable specifications
Product reviews Identify the source of ratings and counts A documented source and known coverage
Shop policy completeness Align shipping, refund and return wording with actual service terms Consistent policies in the admin and on public pages

Shopify uses description length as one of its completeness signals and counts reviews verified by trusted sources. Focus on filling gaps that could affect a shopper's decision. These indicators should not be treated as a measure of channel ranking or recommendation performance, which need to be evaluated separately. Listing insights

Separate the facts for an actual product

Satechi’s Thunderbolt 4 Multimedia Pro Dock is a useful example of why product specifications and device compatibility need to be documented separately. The dock's available ports don't automatically tell a shopper how many independent displays their computer can drive.

Public product fact What to keep separate
The specifications list regional SKUs including ST-DT4PMM-US, ST-DT4PMM-EU, ST-DT4PMM-UK and ST-DT4PMM-AU Each plug option should match its real SKU
The included power adapter is rated at 135W and host PD is up to 96W Adapter rating and host charging output answer different questions
Base M1 and M2 MacBooks are limited to one external display Show the relevant host limitation near the compatibility claim
Base M3 MacBook Air or Pro needs clamshell mode for two displays at 4K 60Hz Keep the chip, display count and lid condition together

Satechi technical specifications and compatibility · Satechi package and power documentation

For a product like this, maintain a record of the model, regional SKU, power figures, host requirements, display limits, information source and verification date. Use variants for the options customers can actually order. Put shared specifications in the description or defined product metafields.

The full compatibility conditions should also appear in the product page body. If the page uses a selector or custom helper component, make sure it draws from the same underlying data.

When introducing a new metafield, define its name and type first, then enter the actual values. After that, check both the public product page and the Catalog output. Pay particular attention to whether a capability statement applies to every buyer or only to a particular device under specific conditions.

Review what Catalog actually receives

Go to Sales channels > Agentic > Sources. Open the dropdown beside Shopify Catalog and select Review product data mapping.

Keep the default mapping wherever it already provides the correct information. Under Product fields, check the source and coverage of the title and description. Open the coverage details and use Fix [number] products to address missing information. If the complete data lives in a metafield, point the relevant field to that metafield.

Title and description support sources, fixed text and Liquid. Product category belongs in the product record.

Preview three types of items: one with a populated value, one without a value and one with an unusual specification. When a mapped field is blank, Catalog falls back to the default field. Check that the resulting description still contains the information a buyer needs.

Record when the mapping is saved, since changes take time to process. The preview shows what Catalog receives as input. Each destination controls its own presentation.

Check List price separately. The available options are Price and Compare-at price. The latter is used when it exceeds the selling price and can be sent in UCP as list_price. Record the market, currency, variant, sale price and reference price together so they can be checked against one another. Shopify Catalog mapping

Check Combined Listings before creating custom groups

When Custom variant grouping is enabled, Catalog uses the selected grouping method and ignores the Combined Listings grouping configuration. The online store keeps its existing product structure.

Before changing the grouping method, save the current groups, representative products and option values so the original setup can be reviewed if needed.

Only group products that genuinely belong together and have distinguishable options. Choose a title separator, metafield or tag prefix, then inspect Group name and Products in group.

Review the products that have been grouped, left separate or marked need review. Identical option combinations across products can trigger a review. If that happens, correct the underlying product data before saving the grouping again.

For a product such as the Satechi dock, actual plug variants and host compatibility should remain separate pieces of information. Shopify Catalog grouping

3. Publish the store information shoppers need

Product descriptions should answer questions about the item itself. Shipping, returns and customer support belong to store-level information.

Go to Sales channels > Agentic > Sources > Knowledge Base. Storefront MCP can make published facts available to agents. Each destination decides when and how to use those facts in its answers.

Check the source and publication status

Facts generated from settings such as policies or contact details are published when created. Facts scanned from storefront pages need to be reviewed first.

When a Suggested update appears, compare it with the current page. Choose Approve & publish if the suggested content is correct, or reject it if it isn't, then save the changes.

Check the fact text, its source, publication status and reference URL together. If information is missing or outdated, edit the fact directly or use Request rescan.

Shopify says a rescan can take up to 48 hours. Also, a public page may still provide information even when the corresponding Knowledge Base fact is unpublished. That means an answer can be factually correct while the agent's retrieval route remains unclear. Knowledge Base publication and scanning

Choose a format that fits the question

Use Additional facts > Add fact and select a type that keeps the important conditions intact.

  • Paragraph works well for processes or qualifications, such as what a customer needs to provide when making a warranty claim.
  • Yes/No is suitable for genuinely binary questions. Explain regional and product-specific exceptions in a separate accompanying fact.
  • Tags are useful for short, verified values such as materials or documented certifications.

Enter the title and content, add public references, hover over Unpublished, select Publish and click Save. The 1,000-fact limit includes both generated facts and manually added ones.

Custom storefronts and the Agentic plan currently support additional facts only. A password-protected storefront cannot be scanned and mainly displays information sourced from the admin.

The old Knowledge Base app is scheduled to shut down on January 15, 2027. For an old app containing no more than 1,000 facts, automatic migration and publication apply to manually overridden store facts and added facts. Review the migrated content item by item rather than assuming every entry is still accurate. Knowledge Base limits and migration

Link each claim to a supporting page

A field has one source but can have multiple references. To add references manually to an existing category field, switch its source to Manual, click the reference count and add the relevant public page under References.

This change removes the automatic references from the previous source, so the team becomes responsible for keeping the fact and its references up to date. Save the changes and check both the links and the wording again.

For example, link return-related facts to the current return policy and warranty claims to the warranty instructions. Updating a reference URL does not automatically update the fact's wording.

These links help agents locate supporting information, but the actual answer still needs to be checked to see which sources it displays. Published facts are public, so write them in customer-facing language. Private quotations and customer records should stay out of these fields. Knowledge Base references

4. Make the same facts available on public pages

Inspect the exact URL

Choose a product or policy URL and check its response, robots.txt, page or HTTP indexing directives, canonical and discoverable internal links. Use URL Inspection to review whether the page has been discovered, when it was last crawled and its indexing status.

The different settings serve different purposes. Robots rules govern crawling, noindex concerns indexing, and the canonical indicates a preferred URL. Identify which setting is causing the problem before changing anything, and preserve access controls that are there for a reason.

Shopify manages network-level crawler security, while a theme can customize robots.txt.liquid. Catalog sharing has its own channel controls.

For localized stores, compare hreflang, the canonical, the regional URL, currency and product availability. Record the market used in each test so results from different regions aren't mixed together. Shopify crawling and sharing

Check the default discovery files

Shopify provides /agents.md, /llms.txt and /llms-full.txt. By default, the latter two mirror the first. Open these files at the primary domain root and check the store name, domain, policies and discovery endpoints.

These files do not have copies in Markets language subdirectories.

For a documented custom requirement, go to Online Store > Themes > Edit code > Add a new template.

Template Scope
agents.md.liquid Customizes the three discovery URLs by default. A dedicated template takes precedence for its URL
llms.txt.liquid Overrides /llms.txt
llms-full.txt.liquid Overrides /llms-full.txt

These templates use the restricted agents and request contexts. Preserve UCP, MCP and sitemap discovery, and make sure someone is responsible for maintaining the files.

The repository instruction file AGENTS.md serves a different audience and should not be confused with the storefront discovery files.

Google's AI search guidance focuses on accessible, indexable pages and consistent visible information. Its AI features do not require a special AI file or schema. Shopify discovery templates · llms.txt precedence · Google AI features

Put compatibility information in the text and check the purchase flow

The included 135W adapter, up to 96W host charging and base M3 lid condition should appear close to the claims they qualify.

A custom Shopify build can use approved fields to render specification tables, compatibility groups and messages tied to the selected option. Where practical, include the decisive facts in the server response, then inspect the initial HTML, rendered page and target crawler's view.

On a phone, select different versions and check whether the displayed conditions and selected SKU change accordingly. Where testing is authorized, add the product to the cart and confirm that the line item matches the selected option.

The same important specifications should also be visible in the source or rendered page inspection.

Represent actual product relationships in structured data

Start by reviewing the JSON-LD already generated by the theme and apps. Look for competing Product entries or inconsistencies in price and stock.

Check the product name, brand and identifiers, along with the corresponding Offer price, currency, availability and URL.

Depending on the page structure, ProductGroup, hasVariant, variesBy and productGroupID can be used to describe genuine variant relationships.

Keep the identifiers straight: SKU is the merchant's inventory identifier, GTIN identifies a trade item, and MPN is a manufacturer's part number. Populate the identifiers that actually exist for the product. Google product variant structured data · GTIN · MPN

Check the supported rich results and schema syntax, then compare the output with the selected variant and the information visible on the page.

Google stopped showing FAQ rich results on May 7, 2026. Keep answers that help buyers and use markup that reflects the actual meaning of the page. Google Search updates

5. Record what AI actually cites

Save a baseline from Catalog search

Under Sales channels > Agentic, enter a product or purchase query in Enter a search query to see how you might rank.

You can also use Top search queries or Queries where your products appeared. For supported previews, open Preview this search.

Save the original query, returned products and Listing insights. After fixing verified data gaps, run exactly the same query again.

Catalog's original ordering and the final ranking on a destination may differ, so don't treat the preview as the final recommendation order. Search preview and reranking

Use different queries to test discovery and accuracy

A sample of 15–30 questions is a reasonable starting convention for a team. Build the questions from actual sales conversations, site searches and return disputes.

An unbranded question helps assess whether a product can be discovered. A question naming a specific product helps check whether the information returned about that product is accurate.

Purpose Suggested question What to verify
Unbranded discovery Which docks can drive two 4K 60Hz displays from a base M3 MacBook Air if I can close its lid? Correct chip and lid assumptions, and evidence for the candidates
Compatibility How does dual-display support differ between a base M1 MacBook and a base M3 MacBook with the Satechi Thunderbolt 4 Multimedia Pro Dock? Separate the host limits
Power Does the included 135W adapter mean the dock charges my laptop at 135W? Distinguish adapter rating from up to 96W host PD
Product identity What differs between ST-DT4PMM-US and ST-DT4PMM-EU? Correct region and actual purchasable SKU
Policy What are the current Satechi store return and warranty conditions? Give the official sources Check the current full terms and the applicability of each cited condition

Use these questions to plan a test. Keep the language, market, exact prompt and conversation setup consistent.

Record the date, platform, model or mode, region, login status, memory and personalization settings. Preserve the complete answer, product link and citation URLs.

Keep repeat samples rather than relying on a single response. Starting a fresh conversation can reduce some context variation, but first-party and third-party sources, query context and personalization can still affect the result. OpenAI shopping with Search

Check each claim against the citation it actually uses

Take an individual claim from the answer and open the cited page. Find the passage that supports it, then check the edition, market and model to make sure they match.

Save product card links separately from explanatory citations. For each test, retain the question and environment, original answer, claim, actual URL, official evidence, observed gap, working hypothesis, correction and retest time. If a claim has no citation, record that explicitly.

If you observe Evidence to collect Action once verified
Missing compatibility condition Full answer, cited passage, Catalog preview, page text and variant relation Fix a mixed description or mapping. If the official page is accurate, make the supporting section easier to find and retest
Old returns language Current policy, old cited page, Knowledge Base publication state and indexing Repair the specific stale source. Verify the setting before attributing the error to indexing or the knowledge base
Different price Time, currency, market, variant, stock, link, Offer, feed and Catalog preview Correct the specific market, variant or synchronization issue
Preview includes the product and the real answer omits it Comparable repeated samples, qualification and preview Fix proven data gaps, then keep observing channel selection

A citation shows what the answer presented as evidence. Any explanation of the model's internal retrieval path should be treated as a separate hypothesis, not as something established by the citation alone.

6. Connect visits, orders and support

Check what the Agentic report actually covers

For a non-headless store, go to the analytics section under Sales channels > Agentic. Select a reporting period and channel, then review Sales, Orders, Online store sessions and Online store conversion.

The combined report is available under Explore > Understand your performance on agentic channels > Review.

Sales includes both referred and direct checkout sales. However, an individual citation needs its own attribution evidence. Headless storefronts currently require a different analytics setup.

Google includes traffic from AI search features in its overall Web search reporting. A change in Web clicks therefore needs additional evidence before it can be attributed specifically to AI features. Shopify Agentic analytics · Google AI reporting

Connect events to analytics and order records

Use Settings > Customer events to manage and test pixels.

Standard events include product_viewed, product_added_to_cart, checkout_started and checkout_completed. If a custom selector is used, recording the selected variant requires the relevant behavior to be defined and captured in the actual implementation.

Send events to the chosen analytics destination through the pixel setup, while respecting consent settings.

Check that the event, cart variant ID and resulting order agree. If an event is missing, review consent, browser restrictions and collection errors before assuming the tracking setup is incorrect. Standard events · Shopify pixel management

Also record returns and their reasons using order and support records. Separate compatibility issues, wrong-region purchases, delivery problems and product defects.

When comparing results, use comparable products, markets, time periods and sample sizes. Keep unidentified traffic and orders separate rather than assigning them to a specific AI source without supporting evidence.

7. Define what a Shopify design and development project should deliver

WESWOO can organize the work around three practical deliverables.

  • A product fact register records information sources, owners, applicable products and where updates need to be made. Merchants confirm the business facts, while developers define the fields and how templates use them.
  • A consistency check across pages and data covers Catalog previews, product pages, compatibility components, structured data and cart selections. Each customization should identify the affected component and its data source.
  • A repeatable test record stores purchase questions, actual answers and citations, verified problems, changes and retest results. Visits, orders and support records should be tracked for the same products.

Start in the admin when product fields or policies are incomplete. Update the page and selector when important specifications are buried in images or the selected option doesn't match the cart. Assign development work when apps or templates produce conflicting information.

For the next product launch or policy update, use the same register and rerun the questions affected by the change.

title: Microservice Patterns: Rules, Boundaries, and Commands
description:
We run a fleet of Nest services on ECS and PM2, with Kafka for domain integration and Firebase at the API gateway. That stack only works if we agree on a few defaults: who owns data, when to use events versus HTTP, how contracts are defined, and where auth stops. This post is our engineering playbook for those defaults—not a claim that every service already matches them. Some rules describe where we want to be (for example strict one-database-per-service everywhere); others we apply today with known gaps (consumer backoff patterns still being defined).

The post has three parts: ten foundation principles, patterns for crossing domain boundaries (with Order and User as the running example), and a payment debit/credit case study on why implicit event listeners are painful and what explicit commands buy us.

1. Each microservice owns its data

Rule: one domain, one database. No service reads or writes another service’s store.

If you need someone else’s data, use a versioned REST call or subscribe to Kafka events and keep a local copy. The only exception we allow is temporary shared access during a migration between services—and even then we treat it as debt with an exit date.

2. Use Kafka for state changes, not queries

Rule: publish when domain state changes—user-created, order-placed, payment-success—not when another service needs a read or a real-time decision.

Kafka is an integration log, not a query engine. Using it to “fetch” user status at decision time turns consumers into brittle RPC clients and couples lag to business logic.

Sagas are the intentional exception in shape, not in spirit: a long-running flow may touch several domains and emit multiple state-change events along the way. That is still “something happened,” not “give me the current row.”

3. Expose a versioned REST API

Rule: public and partner-facing HTTP APIs live under /v1/... (and future /v2/ when we break compatibility on purpose).

Services at the edge expose REST. Internal traffic can be REST or Kafka events, depending on freshness and coupling—we pick deliberately in § Crossing domain boundaries. Versioning at the path keeps gateway routing and client expectations explicit.

4. Define clear API contracts

Rule: every service ships an OpenAPI (Swagger) spec that matches what it actually runs.

Payloads stay flat and consistent across services: prefer clear field names and shallow objects over deep nesting that mirrors every join in the database. The spec is the handshake for humans, codegen, and reviews—not documentation we write after the fact.

5. Validate contracts

Rule: validate HTTP bodies and event payloads at the boundary with shared schemas—we standardize on zod in Node services.

Parsing once at the edge of the handler (or consumer) gives us fail fast behavior (see §6) and keeps invalid messages out of domain code. OpenAPI describes the contract; zod enforces it at runtime. Consumer-driven contract testing (for example Pact) is on our roadmap as a complement, not a replacement for schema validation at the service.

6. Fail fast, retry smart

Rule: reject bad input and unprocessable state early with a clear error. Retry only for transient failures—network blips, broker hiccups, throttling—not for validation or business rule violations.

Kafka consumers in our stack already retry poison-adjacent cases with operational playbooks; we still need shared backoff and dead-letter patterns documented and implemented consistently. That work is deliberate follow-up: the principle is decided; the library conventions are not finished yet.

7. Trace everything

Rule: one logical operation should be followable across HTTP, Kafka, Lambdas, and long-running workers.

We are standardizing on OpenTelemetry and W3C traceparent propagation. That supersedes ad-hoc x-correlation-id headers for new work: any hop that understands OTEL continues the same trace. Until every path is instrumented, we may still see correlation IDs in older services; new code should inject and extract trace context on produce/consume and outbox commit.

Application logs go to Elastic Cloud as structured JSON. Besides trace and span IDs, we include Kafka message identifiers (topic, partition, offset, and our internal message id when present) so on-call can jump from a log line to a broker record without guessing.

8. Keep logic close to the domain

Rule: services are not thin CRUD wrappers over a table unless the domain truly is that simple.

Where it pays off we use Domain-Driven Design building blocks—aggregates, value objects, explicit invariants—so business rules live in the domain layer, not scattered across controllers and ORM callbacks. The goal is code that reads like the business, not like a generic data access layer.

9. Avoid shared libraries for business logic

Rule: share infrastructure helpers (logging wrappers, OTEL bootstrap, HTTP client defaults); do not share domain rules across services.

A shared “UserValidator” npm package feels convenient until two services need slightly different eligibility rules and you ship a breaking version to everyone. Duplication of domain logic is cheaper than hidden coupling. Copy the pattern, not the rule, when domains diverge.

10. Auth at the edge, AuthZ in the service

Rule: authentication happens at the API gateway or entry point (Firebase verifies the token before traffic hits Nest). Authorization—roles, ownership, step-up, country eligibility—runs inside each service that owns the resource.

That split matches what I documented for Second-Memory in Why I Chose Third-Party (Firebase) Authentication: Firebase proves identity; our services decide what that identity may do on this aggregate. No service should trust another service’s “already authorized” flag without its own check when the resource is theirs.

Crossing domain boundaries

Business rules often need facts from another bounded context. Example: Order must confirm User is in good standing and in an allowed country before accepting a new order. User owns that data; Order owns the placement rule. How do we bridge the gap?

flowchart TD
  needData[Need foreign domain fact]
  needData --> stalenessOK{Minor staleness OK?}
  stalenessOK -->|yes| snapshot[Kafka snapshot in local DB]
  stalenessOK -->|no| rest[REST query at runtime]
  snapshot --> hybrid{Cache miss or suspect?}
  hybrid -->|yes| rest
  hybrid -->|no| useLocal[Use local copy]
Pattern Freshness Coupling When to use
A — Cached snapshot (Kafka) Eventually consistent (often seconds) Low; no runtime dependency on User API Performance matters; minor staleness is acceptable
B — REST query Up to date at call time Higher latency; temporal coupling to User Real-time accuracy is essential
C — Hybrid Usually local; fresh on miss Medium; fallback path must be tested Default for many flows: fast path + safety net

Option A — Cached snapshot (preferred default)

At runtime, User owns the canonical row; Order keeps a local user-data snapshot—only the fields Order needs for placement (for example country, state, status)—fed by Kafka so the placement path never calls User’s HTTP API. Firebase auth runs at the gateway on both the profile write and the order request (see §10).

flowchart TD
    subgraph TOP [API Gateway Layer]
        GW[API Gateway]
    end

    subgraph LEFT [User Domain]
        US[User Service]
        DB[(User DB)]
        US --> DB
    end

    subgraph CENTER [Message Broker]
        K["Kafka topic user.updated"]
    end

    subgraph RIGHT [Order Domain]
        OS[Order Service]
        UDS[(User data snapshot)]
        OS --> UDS
    end

    GW -->|"1. updateUserProfile"| US
    US -->|"2. emit message"| K
    K -.->|"3. async update"| OS
    GW -->|"4. createOrder"| OS
    OS -->|"5. retrieve data"| UDS

The numbered edges in the diagram:

  1. updateUserProfile — The client calls User through the gateway to change profile, status, address, or anything else that affects order eligibility.
  2. emit message — User writes to User DB and publishes a state-change event (not a query).
  3. async update — Order’s consumer upserts the user-data snapshot (subset of User fields Order cares about); this path is eventually consistent.
  4. createOrder — A separate order request hits Order only. Order does not call User synchronously on this path.
  5. retrieve data — Eligibility checks read the snapshot, not User Service.

User publishes those changes—for example user-updated, user-status-changed, or user-address-changed—often on a single topic such as user.updated. Order subscribes and persists only what it needs in its own database (orders plus the local user snapshot):

// OrderService Kafka handler
@KafkaListener('user.updated')
async handleUserUpdate(payload: UserUpdatedEvent) {
  await this.userRepo.saveOrUpdate(payload.userId, {
    country: payload.country,
    state: payload.state,
    status: payload.status,
  });
}

Validation for new orders uses that snapshot, not a full User record. Fast and decoupled; accept that a brand-new status change may lag briefly behind User. Order must not read User DB or call User HTTP on the placement path under Option A alone—if the snapshot row is missing or too stale, use Option C (hybrid) below.

Option B — REST API call (query pattern)

When the decision must reflect User right now, call User at runtime:

// OrderService: validateUserForOrder
const user = await this.httpService
  .get(`https://user-service.internal/v1/users/${userId}`)
  .toPromise();

if (user.data.status !== 'good_standing' || user.data.country !== 'AU') {
  throw new ForbiddenException('User is not eligible to place an order');
}

Always current; you pay in latency and in availability coupling—if User is down, Order cannot complete the rule check unless you have a fallback.

Option C — Hybrid

Use the snapshot by default; on cache miss or suspicious staleness, call User and optionally refresh the local row (still persisting only the fields Order needs).

const user = await this.localUserSnapshotRepo.find(userId);
if (!user) {
  const apiUser = await this.userApiClient.getUser(userId);
  await this.localUserSnapshotRepo.save({
    userId: apiUser.id,
    country: apiUser.country,
    state: apiUser.state,
    status: apiUser.status,
  });
  return apiUser;
}
return user;

We use this when the happy path should stay off the critical path of User’s API, but we cannot afford silent wrong decisions on empty cache.

When events are the wrong shape — payment debit and credit

Sometimes integration should be modeled as a command—an intention directed at a specific handler—not as a domain event every downstream service must interpret. Payment is our clearest example.

Payment debits and credits user balances. Many originating services need those operations. We used to model it like this:

  • Originating services emit their domain events that implicitly mean “take money” or “refund money.”
  • Payment registers a listener per event type and encodes knowledge of each scenario: which event implies debit, how to derive transaction source and request id.
  • Payment performs the transaction and emits success or failure events keyed by transaction source and request id.
  • Originating services must implicitly know that those fields map back to their workflow.

That design spreads payment semantics into every producer’s event vocabulary. Payment becomes a central interpreter of foreign languages instead of a service with a narrow, explicit API.

sequenceDiagram
  participant Orig as OriginatingService
  participant Kafka
  participant Pay as PaymentService

  Orig->>Kafka: domain_event_A
  Orig->>Kafka: domain_event_B
  Kafka->>Pay: listener maps A to debit
  Kafka->>Pay: listener maps B to credit
  Pay->>Kafka: transaction_success
  Kafka->>Orig: must decode source plus requestId

Alternative — synchronous API commands

Model debit and credit as well-known HTTP commands with a stable schema. The caller supplies transaction source and transaction request id; Payment does not care which feature invoked it.

Pros: Payment stays ignorant of callers; immediate success/failure in the response.

Cons: Temporal coupling—if Payment is down, the caller must retry until it recovers. In an event-first codebase that often means: emit a local event, handle it in a listener, and loop retries from there—more moving parts than a direct call with idempotency keys.

sequenceDiagram
  participant Orig as OriginatingService
  participant Pay as PaymentService

  Orig->>Pay: POST /v1/debit
  Pay-->>Orig: 200 or 4xx

Alternative — asynchronous commands

Publish commands to a well-known Kafka topic Payment owns. Callers produce DebitPayment / CreditPayment messages; Payment consumes and executes. No synchronous response—outcomes appear as domain events Payment already owns, for example user-transaction-succeeded / user-transaction-failed, which callers subscribe to if they need completion.

Pros: Same decoupling as explicit API (Payment does not know the caller’s event names); no temporal coupling on the produce path; callers choose their own correlation ids.

Cons: No immediate feedback; originating workflows must be saga-shaped—listen for outcome events or poll a read model. That aligns with how we already name work on the Event Modeling board (From Event Modeling to a Kafka Saga): Payment.debitPayment as a command with payment_success / payment_failure as outcomes, rather than Payment guessing from unrelated domain events.

sequenceDiagram
  participant Orig as OriginatingService
  participant Kafka
  participant Pay as PaymentService

  Orig->>Kafka: DebitPayment command
  Kafka->>Pay: consume command
  Pay->>Kafka: user_transaction_succeeded
  Kafka->>Orig: resume workflow

We are not flipping every flow overnight. The direction is clear: local snapshots and explicit commands beat REST spaghetti and payment listeners that speak every team’s event dialect. Events stay for things that happened; commands carry work we want Payment to do; REST fills the gaps when freshness beats cache.

Prefer a denormalized read model fed by Kafka when staleness is acceptable; prefer explicit payment commands over payment inferring debits from someone else’s domain events; use REST when the decision must be correct to the second—and document which choice you made.

title: I Explored How Synthetic Data Could Make AI-Powered Websites More Reliable
description:
AI-powered websites can recommend products, answer customer questions, personalize content, and automate everyday tasks. However, their performance depends heavily on the information used to train and test their systems. Incomplete, outdated, or unbalanced datasets can lead to inaccurate recommendations and frustrating user experiences. This made me explore how synthetic data for AI-powered websites could help developers build more reliable digital platforms without depending entirely on real customer information.

While researching this technology, I also considered how businesses manage the wider development process, from organizing testing activities to tracking improvements. Tools such as productivity software for managing professional tasks can help development teams coordinate these responsibilities while working with data-driven technologies.

What Is Synthetic Data and Why Does It Matter?

Synthetic data is artificially generated information designed to resemble the characteristics and patterns of real-world datasets. It can include fictional customer profiles, product searches, website interactions, and purchasing scenarios.

Unlike conventional datasets, synthetic information does not necessarily come directly from actual customer records. Developers can generate examples to represent different situations, including uncommon events that might be missing from existing datasets.

For example, an online fashion retailer could generate fictional shopping interactions involving different clothing sizes, budgets, seasonal preferences, and product categories. Developers can then use software tools for data analysis and website development to examine these scenarios and evaluate whether AI recommendations remain relevant across different customer needs.

This makes synthetic data particularly interesting for websites that handle large amounts of user interactions.

Three Ways Synthetic Data Could Improve AI-Powered Websites

I identified three practical applications that demonstrate why this technology deserves attention.

1. Testing Personalized Recommendations

AI-powered e-commerce websites often recommend products based on browsing behavior, previous purchases, and customer preferences. However, real datasets may contain more information about popular products than less frequently purchased items.

Synthetic datasets can introduce additional fictional shopping scenarios, allowing developers to test how recommendation systems respond to different preferences.

For example, a fashion website could simulate searches for winter jackets, formal clothing, and affordable everyday outfits. This helps identify whether its recommendation engine performs consistently across different shopping categories.

2. Improving Chatbot Responses

Website chatbots need to understand different ways customers ask questions. A visitor might ask about delivery charges, return policies, or product availability using several variations of the same question.

Developers can generate synthetic conversations to test whether an AI assistant recognizes these different expressions and provides appropriate answers.

This approach can help uncover weaknesses before a chatbot is introduced to a wider audience.

3. Strengthening Website Security Testing

Synthetic data can also support testing of unusual website activity. Developers might generate fictional login attempts, suspicious browsing patterns, or unusual transaction scenarios to evaluate how monitoring systems respond.

However, synthetic testing does not replace real security assessments or professional penetration testing.

A Simple Coding Example: Generating Synthetic Website Data

I also looked at how developers could create basic synthetic website interaction records using Python. The following example generates fictional visitor activity that could be used for preliminary testing.
import random

categories = [
"Fashion,"
"Electronics,"
"Home,"
"Beauty"
]

visitor_data = []

for user in range(1, 101):
record = {
"visitor_id": user,
"category": random.choice(categories),
"page_views": random.randint(1, 15),
"purchase": random.choice([True, False])
}

visitor_data.append(record)

print(visitor_data[:5])

This code generates 100 fictional visitor records with randomly selected categories, page views, and purchasing outcomes. It is useful for demonstrating basic testing workflows, although it does not reproduce realistic customer behavior or relationships between variables.

More advanced synthetic data generation requires statistical modelling, privacy checks, and validation against appropriate real-world patterns.

Why Data Quality Still Matters

One important point I discovered is that generating more data does not automatically produce better AI systems.

The quality of synthetic datasets depends on how accurately they represent the situations developers want to test. Poorly generated information can introduce unrealistic patterns and reinforce existing biases.

I would recommend following these practices:

  • Check data diversity: Include different user behaviors, preferences, and interaction scenarios.
  • Validate generated information: Compare statistical patterns with suitable real-world reference data.
  • Protect privacy: Avoid reproducing identifiable information from original datasets.
  • Test model performance: Evaluate AI systems using separate validation and testing datasets.
  • Monitor results: Review performance regularly as website content and customer behavior change.

Businesses exploring these technologies can also use project management and analytics tools to organize development activities. Before subscribing, checking available RabattDigga software deals and discount codes can help identify opportunities to reduce the cost of professional digital tools.

My Final Thoughts

My research suggests that synthetic data could become an important resource for developing and testing more dependable AI-powered websites. From ecommerce recommendations to customer support and security monitoring, it offers developers additional ways to evaluate systems before real users encounter potential problems.

However, synthetic information should complement reliable real-world data rather than replace proper validation. The real value comes from generating useful scenarios, checking their accuracy, and continuously improving the technology behind the website.

title: Autonomous Smart Contract Auditing: AST Traversal and CEI Verification
description:
Autonomous Smart Contract Auditing: AST Traversal and CEI Verification

Sebagian besar exploit di EVM bukan berasal dari matematika kriptografi yang cacat. Exploit terjadi karena developer lupa urutan eksekusi state: mereka mentransfer token sebelum mengurangi saldo internal. Kita menyebutnya pelanggaran pola Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI).

Audit manual lambat dan mahal. LLM mentah tanpa grounding sering berhalusinasi saat membaca assembly Yul atau inline function yang rumit. Solusi deterministik yang scalable adalah menggabungkan static analysis berbasis Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) dengan agen otonom yang memverifikasi mutasi state sebelum transaksi eksternal dipicu.

Di jaringan dengan throughput tinggi dan gas murah seperti Base L2 (Chain ID 8453), eksploitasi terjadi dalam hitungan detik setelah contract di-deploy. Jika pipeline deployment Anda tidak memvalidasi AST secara otomatis, Anda menyerahkan likuiditas ke bot MEV.

Parsing AST Solidity

Solidity compiler (solc) dapat memuntahkan AST dalam format JSON terstruktur via flag --ast-compact-json. Representasi ini memetakan setiap deklarasi fungsi, statement assignment, dan external call ke dalam node hierarkis.

Mari kita bedah vulnerability paling klasik: reentrancy. Logika CEI mendikte bahwa semua mutasi state (Effects) harus selesai sebelum eksekusi dilempar ke kontrak eksternal (Interactions).

Berikut implementasi engine AST traversal minimal menggunakan Python untuk mendeteksi pelanggaran CEI:

import json
from typing import List, Dict, Any

class CEIAuditEngine:
    def __init__(self, ast_json: Dict[str, Any]):
        self.ast = ast_json
        self.violations = []

    def inspect_function(self, node: Dict[str, Any]):
        has_external_call = False
        external_call_loc = None

        # Traverse statements sequentially
        statements = node.get("body", {}).get("statements", [])
        for stmt in statements:
            if self._is_external_call(stmt):
                has_external_call = True
                external_call_loc = stmt.get("src")

            # State variable mutation after external call = CEI Violation
            if has_external_call and self._is_state_mutation(stmt):
                self.violations.append({
                    "function": node.get("name"),
                    "external_call_at": external_call_loc,
                    "violation_at": stmt.get("src")
                })

    def _is_external_call(self, stmt: Dict[str, Any]) -> bool:
        stmt_str = json.dumps(stmt)
        # Matches raw .call{value: ...} or interface dispatch
        return any(k in stmt_str for k in ['"member_name": "call"', '"kind": "functionCall"'])

    def _is_state_mutation(self, stmt: Dict[str, Any]) -> bool:
        if stmt.get("nodeType") == "ExpressionStatement":
            expr = stmt.get("expression", {})
            return expr.get("nodeType") == "Assignment"
        return False

    def run(self):
        for node in self.ast.get("nodes", []):
            if node.get("nodeType") == "ContractDefinition":
                for sub_node in node.get("nodes", []):
                    if sub_node.get("nodeType") == "FunctionDefinition":
                        self.inspect_function(sub_node)
        return self.violations

Skrip di atas tidak menebak probabilitas layaknya model bahasa murni; skrip tersebut memetakan urutan eksekusi statement secara deterministik. Jika node assignment state muncul di indeks traversal setelah node call eksternal, pipeline memunculkan alert merah dan membatalkan build.

Integrasi On-Chain: Autonomous Treasury Execution

Setelah analisis statis memvalidasi source code, pipeline otonom dapat mengeksekusi signing transaksi deployment atau alokasi liquidity pool.

Di Base L2, sistem audit otonom kami memvalidasi bytecode terhadap AST sebelum mengirimkan settlement grant dari dompet kas otonom: 0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919.

Berikut alur eksekusi Web3 setelah AST engine memberi status clean:

import os
from web3 import Web3
from eth_account import Account

BASE_RPC = "https://mainnet.base.org"
CHAIN_ID = 8453
TREASURY_ADDRESS = "0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919"

w3 = Web3(Web3.HTTPProvider(BASE_RPC))

def release_deployment_grant(target_contract: str, audit_clean: bool):
    if not audit_clean:
        raise ValueError("Audit failed: CEI violation detected. Transaction aborted.")

    # Execution path only unlocks if static verification passes
    priv_key = os.getenv("AUTONOMOUS_TREASURY_KEY")
    account = Account.from_key(priv_key)
    assert account.address.lower() == TREASURY_ADDRESS.lower(), "Signer mismatch."

    tx = {
        'to': target_contract,
        'value': w3.to_wei(0.05, 'ether'),
        'nonce': w3.eth.get_transaction_count(account.address),
        'gas': 21000,
        'maxFeePerGas': w3.to_wei(0.1, 'gwei'),
        'maxPriorityFeePerGas': w3.to_wei(0.001, 'gwei'),
        'chainId': CHAIN_ID
    }

    signed = w3.eth.account.sign_transaction(tx, priv_key)
    tx_hash = w3.eth.send_raw_transaction(signed.rawTransaction)
    return tx_hash.hex()

Kesimpulan Operasional
