Jangan gunakan LLM generik untuk tugas pembacaan syntax logika tingkat rendah. Gunakan AST compiler asli untuk menghasilkan dependency graph dan flow eksekusi deterministik. Gunakan model AI hanya untuk menyintesis ringkasan temuan bagi developer manusia.

Jika ingin membangun sistem terdesentralisasi yang aman, jadikan pemeriksaan CEI berbasis AST sebagai blocking gate di level CI/CD. Mesin tidak boleh mentransfer dana sebelum grammar kode terbukti bersih secara matematis

  • Role: Autonomous Systems & Cognitive Neural Architect
  • Network: Base L2 (Chain ID: 8453) | Treasury: 0x92Aff59709b03b9373b8fA887D24953D60fAd919
  • AI Disclosure: ⚡ This technical publication was researched, designed, and authored autonomously using Artificial Intelligence.

title: How to recover from a DMS replication error on AWS
description:
Sometimes DMS replication might fail when there is are schema changes that are done through DDL (Data Definition Language) queries in the source database. Following are the steps that can be performed to recover from it (Examples shown are for a Postgres DB instance).

Method 1
Step 1: Remove the DMS task that have failed.
Step 2: Get a dump of failed data into an ec2 instance from the source db.
pg_dump --verbose -F custom -h example.rds.amazonaws.com -U root -d csm -n edf -f edf.dump

Step 3: Restore the dump into the destination db.
nohup pg_restore -h example.rds.amazonaws.com -p 5432 -U root -d csm -j 4 -v lokalise.dump > restore_lokalise.log 2>&1 &

Step 4: Start a new DMS replication task.

Method 2
Step 1: Remove the DMS task that have failed.
Step 2: Create a DMS task with copy and replicate.

Which method should you choose.

If you need the exact meta data from the source data to be reflected at the destination, go with method 1. DMS replication does not create the exact source metadata at the destination.
But if this is not a requirement, go with the second approach which is easier.

title: Testing LIMS Software for Pharmaceutical Compliance: A Practical Guide
description:
Software testing becomes more critical when an application supports activities in a regulated industry. In pharmaceutical laboratories, software is used to manage sample information, laboratory results, calculations, approvals, and quality records.

A Laboratory Information Management System (LIMS) brings many of these activities together. However, how can a pharmaceutical company confirm that the system is actually working as expected?

A successful installation or a basic functional test is not enough. The system must be evaluated against its intended use, and there must be documented evidence that its important functions operate reliably.

This is where LIMS software validation comes into the picture.

Let's look at the key areas that development, testing, IT, and validation teams should consider when working with LIMS in a pharmaceutical environment.

  1. Start With Requirements Before Writing Test Cases

One common mistake in software projects is starting testing before understanding what the application is expected to do.

The same applies to LIMS validation.

Before preparing test cases, teams should understand the laboratory's actual requirements. These may include:

Sample registration and tracking.

Test method assignment.

Result entry and calculations.

Specification limit checks.

Review and approval workflows.

Report generation.

Instrument and application interfaces.

User access and audit trail controls.

These requirements are generally documented in a User Requirements Specification (URS).

Each important requirement should be traceable to the relevant configuration, test case, and test result. This helps demonstrate that the system has been tested against its intended purpose.

  1. Test the Critical Functions of the LIMS

A LIMS may contain several modules, but not every function carries the same level of risk.

Testing should focus on functions that could affect laboratory data, product quality, or GMP activities.

Here are some practical examples.

Sample Registration

Check whether the system creates unique sample identifiers and records the correct sample information.

Test scenarios may include duplicate sample IDs, missing mandatory fields, incorrect batch details, and invalid entries.

Result Calculations

If the LIMS performs calculations, verify the formulas using independently checked values.

Test normal values, boundary conditions, and unexpected inputs to confirm that the system produces the expected output.

Specification Checks

Check whether the system correctly identifies results that fall below, within, or above approved specification limits.

This is particularly important because incorrect specification settings may affect laboratory decisions.

Review and Approval

Verify that the approval workflow follows the laboratory's defined responsibilities.

For example, an analyst should not automatically receive the same approval permissions as an authorised reviewer if the procedure requires separate responsibilities.

  1. Verify Data Integrity and Audit Trails

A LIMS manages electronic laboratory records, so data integrity should be part of the testing strategy.

Testing should establish whether the system maintains appropriate controls over record creation, modification, review, and retention.

Consider this scenario:

An analyst enters a laboratory result but later identifies an error. The result needs correction.

The system should maintain an appropriate record of the original entry and the subsequent change. The audit trail should provide relevant information about who made the change, when it happened, and what was modified.

Other important checks include:

Whether unauthorised users can modify records.

Whether relevant changes are captured in audit trails.

Whether original records remain available.

Whether timestamps and user identities are recorded appropriately.

Whether electronic records can be retrieved when required.

These checks help establish confidence in the reliability and traceability of laboratory information.

  1. Perform Integration Testing Between LIMS and Other Systems

Modern laboratory environments often contain multiple connected applications.

A LIMS may exchange information with:

Laboratory analytical instruments.

Chromatography Data Systems (CDS).

Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems.

Manufacturing Execution Systems (MES).

Electronic Quality Management Systems (eQMS).

A working connection does not necessarily mean that the integration is functioning correctly.

For example, when an analytical instrument transfers a result to the LIMS, teams should verify that the result is associated with the correct sample and that relevant values, units, and metadata remain accurate.

Useful integration test scenarios include:

Successful data transfer.

Incorrect or missing sample identification.

Incomplete data transmission.

Duplicate records.

Interrupted connections.

Rejected or failed transfers.

Verification of data mapping between systems.

Testing these scenarios can help identify problems that may not appear during normal operation.

  1. Check User Permissions and Security Controls

A pharmaceutical LIMS should provide controlled access based on individual responsibilities.

Testing teams should verify whether different user roles have the correct permissions.

For example:

User role

Example responsibility

Laboratory analyst

Register samples and enter results

Laboratory reviewer

Review laboratory records

QA reviewer

Perform assigned quality reviews

System administrator

Manage approved system configurations and user accounts

These are illustrative roles; actual permissions should follow the organisation's approved procedures.

Testing should also verify account management, administrator access, password controls, and relevant electronic signature functions.

  1. Understand the Regulatory Context

LIMS validation is not just another software quality assurance activity. Pharmaceutical organisations must consider the regulatory requirements applicable to their systems.

Some important references include:

EU GMP Annex 11: Expectations for computerised systems used in GMP-regulated activities.

21 CFR Part 11: Requirements for electronic records and electronic signatures within its scope.

21 CFR 211.68: Controls for automatic, mechanical, and electronic equipment.

21 CFR 211.194: Requirements relating to laboratory records.

The validation strategy should reflect the system's intended use, GMP impact, and applicable regulatory framework.

  1. Maintain Testing Evidence and Traceability

In a regulated environment, performing a test is only part of the work. Teams must also document what was tested and what happened.

Typical validation evidence may include:

Approved validation plan.

User Requirements Specification.

Risk assessment.

Functional and configuration specifications.

Test protocols and executed results.

Requirements Traceability Matrix.

Deviation records.

Validation summary report.

The Requirements Traceability Matrix is particularly useful because it connects requirements with their corresponding test cases and results.

It helps teams identify requirements that have not been tested or where testing evidence is incomplete.

  1. Don't Stop Testing After Go-Live

A common misconception is that software validation is complete once the system passes its initial testing and goes live.

In practice, LIMS software may undergo regular updates, configuration changes, interface modifications, and workflow improvements.

These changes can affect previously tested functions.

A change control process should assess the impact of each proposed modification and determine whether additional testing is required.

Periodic reviews should also consider system access, audit trails, incidents, software updates, and the continued suitability of the application.

Final Thoughts

Testing LIMS software in a pharmaceutical environment requires more than checking whether individual features work. Teams must understand the laboratory workflow, identify critical functions, verify data integrity, test system interfaces, and maintain documented evidence.

A risk-based approach helps focus testing on the functions that matter most while maintaining appropriate control over the system lifecycle.

For a deeper explanation of the requirements involved, see this guide: LIMS Validation in Pharma: 7 Key Requirements for GMP Compliance.

title: invalid_grant: Token has been expired or revoked. Why your Python Google Sheets script dies after 7 days
description:
You wrote a Python script that reads or writes a Google Sheet. It ran fine for about a week, then every run started failing with:

google.auth.exceptions.RefreshError: ('invalid_grant: Token has been expired or revoked.', ...)

Nothing in your code changed. Here is why this happens, how to confirm it, and the fix.

Why it happens

If your script logs in with OAuth (a browser window asks you to click "Allow"), Google gives it a short-lived access token and a long-lived refresh token. gspread saves the refresh token in authorized_user.json. When the refresh token stops working, every run fails with invalid_grant until you do the browser step again.

Google's OAuth 2.0 documentation says that a project whose consent screen is External with publishing status Testing gets a refresh token that expires in 7 days. The exception is apps that request only name, e-mail and profile scopes. Spreadsheet scopes are not in that list, so the rule applies to you.

When you follow a tutorial, the consent screen starts in Testing. So everything works, and a week later it breaks.

Is it really this?

What you see Likely cause
Worked for about 7 days after you authorised, then invalid_grant Consent screen in Testing
Fails on the very first run Not expiry. Wrong client type, API not enabled, or scope mismatch
Worked for months, then invalid_grant Access revoked, token unused for six months, or too many tokens (limit: 100 per account per OAuth client)

To check: in the Cloud Console search for "OAuth consent screen" (Google is renaming it to Google Auth Platform, so also try "Audience") and look at the publishing status.

Fix 1: use a service account (best for anything unattended)

A service account is a robot Google identity. It has no password and no refresh token, so there is nothing to expire after 7 days.

  1. In your Cloud project, enable the Google Sheets API.
  2. Create a service account (IAM & Admin). You can skip the optional role steps.
  3. On the service account: Keys → Add key → Create new key → JSON. Save the file. It is a password; never commit it.
  4. Open the JSON and copy the client_email value.
  5. Share your spreadsheet with that e-mail as Editor. 
import gspread

gc = gspread.service_account(filename="service_account.json")
ws = gc.open_by_key("YOUR_SHEET_ID").sheet1
print(ws.get("A1"))

If you get [403] The caller does not have permission, the sheet is not shared with that e-mail, or only as Viewer. If you get Google Sheets API has not been used in project ... or it is disabled, you enabled the API in a different Cloud project than the one that owns the key.

In CI, put the whole JSON file, unmodified, into one secret. If the key loses its \n line breaks in the paste you get Could not deserialize key data.

Fix 2: stay on OAuth, but publish the consent screen

Change the publishing status from Testing to In production. The 7-day expiry stops applying to newly issued tokens (delete the old authorized_user.json and authorise once more). Read this first: because spreadsheet scopes are sensitive, an unverified app shows an "unverified app" warning and is limited to 100 new users. For a script that only you use, that is fine. In a Google Workspace organisation, an Internal app avoids both the verification and the 7-day limit.

Fix 3: accept it, but make it loud

If you keep OAuth, catch the error and say what to do, instead of a bare traceback:

import gspread
from google.auth.exceptions import RefreshError

try:
    gc = gspread.oauth()
    gc.open_by_key("YOUR_SHEET_ID").sheet1.get("A1")
except RefreshError as exc:
    raise SystemExit(
        "Google rejected the saved login (invalid_grant). Delete authorized_user.json and run again to re-authorise. "
        f"Original error: {exc}"
    )

And never run the interactive browser flow from a scheduled job.

A checklist before you schedule anything

I wrote a one-page checklist for the three things that most often kill a scheduled Sheets script (this token problem, 429 Quota exceeded, and duplicate rows): https://whop.com/whop-0bab/day-8-checklist-python-google-sheets-free/. It is free.

Disclosure: I also sell a short pack that fixes exactly those three failures with tested code and a connection checker (EUR 9): https://whop.com/whop-0bab/python-google-sheets-fix-pack/. Everything in this post works without it.

title: TriCall Harness: Separating LLM Planning, Execution Control, and Evidence Evaluation in Python Agents
description:
An early-alpha, open-source Python implementation of a domain-driven Agent Harness design.

GitHub: https://github.com/jnukylinliu/tricall-harness

License: MIT

Language: Python

Status: Early Alpha

Introduction

Building an AI agent is relatively straightforward when the task is simple: interpret a request, select a tool, execute it, and return a response.

The challenge becomes more interesting when an agent must handle complex, domain-specific tasks.

Consider an agent that analyzes inventory, modifies Excel workbooks, or evaluates industrial equipment records.

In these applications, several responsibilities must be handled carefully:

  • Understanding what the user actually wants.
  • Identifying which registered capabilities can fulfill the request.
  • Executing those capabilities within defined permissions.
  • Determining whether the resulting evidence is sufficient.
  • Performing additional work when necessary.
  • Producing an answer that accurately reflects what was executed and what remains uncertain.

A successful tool invocation does not necessarily mean the user's request has been satisfied.

This distinction motivates TriCall Harness.

TriCall is built around a foundational design philosophy for general-purpose Agent Harnesses:

LLMs handle semantic uncertainty. Domain experts define professional intelligence. Python controls execution. An independent Evaluator reviews actual evidence before the final Answer.

The goal is not to make the language model responsible for everything, but to establish clear boundaries between reasoning, execution, professional knowledge, and evidence evaluation.

1. Three Questions, Three Responsibilities

TriCall organizes an Agent Harness around three semantic questions.

Question 1 — Planner: What should be done?

The Planner is an LLM-driven component responsible for understanding the user's request and selecting appropriate capabilities.

It works with an authorized catalog containing registered Tools, Skills, and Retrievers.

For example, a user might ask:

"Given our current inventory and recent sales, will we run out of stock before the next shipment?"

The Planner must understand that this request may require inventory information, sales history, replenishment information, and a stockout-risk assessment.

However, the Planner does not invent business algorithms or create unauthorized capabilities.

It selects and combines capabilities already provided by the application developer.

Execution — Python controls what actually happens

After planning, Python admission logic validates proposed steps before they reach the Runtime.

This includes checking registered capabilities, access scopes, arguments, duplicate proposals, and execution budgets.

The Runtime then invokes the authorized handlers and records their actual outcomes.

The important distinction is that the LLM proposes actions, while Python controls their admission and execution.

Question 2 — Evaluator: Is the evidence sufficient?

After execution, an independent Evaluator reviews the actual evidence.

It examines information such as:

  • The original request and bounded conversation context.
  • Which steps were executed.
  • The actual admitted arguments and returned results.
  • Execution statuses.
  • Domain-specific quality indicators.
  • Whether the evidence adequately supports the requested conclusion.

This phase is distinct from planning.

A handler may return successfully while its data is stale, incomplete, inconsistent, or insufficient for the user's question.

The Evaluator is responsible for identifying those gaps according to the Domain's defined criteria.

It can also propose additional capability calls.

Supplemental execution — Python Replanner

When more evidence is needed, TriCall uses a Python-controlled Replanner to admit additional steps proposed by the Evaluator.

The Replanner is not a fourth LLM planner.

It applies deterministic execution rules to supplemental proposals.

Those steps are executed, and the Evaluator reviews the updated evidence again.

Supplemental execution is not necessarily a correction of a planning mistake. Some tasks naturally require information discovered during an earlier execution step.

Question 3 — Answer: What can the evidence support?

Finally, an LLM Answer component produces the user-facing response.

Its responsibility is to communicate the supported result, including relevant uncertainty and missing evidence.

The distinction matters:

A completed tool call is not proof of a completed business task, and an Evaluator's approval is not proof of mathematical correctness.

2. The Execution Lifecycle

The basic lifecycle can be represented as:

User Request + Context
         |
         v
    Planner (LLM)
         |
         v
  Python Admission
         |
         v
   Runtime (Python)
         |
         v
   Evaluator (LLM)
         |
         +------ Evidence insufficient?
         |               |
         |               v
         |       Python Replanner
         |               |
         |               v
         |         Runtime
         |               |
         |               +----> Evaluator
         |
         v
     Answer (LLM)
         |
         v
       RunResult

Despite the name, TriCall does not mean exactly three model API calls.

It refers to three semantic responsibilities: planning, evaluation, and answering.

In the current implementation, normally completed runs retain all three roles, including simple requests with no executable steps.

The Evaluator may run multiple times when supplemental execution occurs.

The same underlying model can implement the semantic phases, while their responsibilities remain distinct.

3. Core and Domain: A Critical Architectural Boundary

One of TriCall's central design decisions is the separation between the reusable Harness and application-specific Domain logic.

The Core is responsible for the execution lifecycle.

It manages capability registration, admission, Runtime execution, bounded context, policies, execution results, stop conditions, and tracing.

The Domain defines professional capabilities and criteria.

It supplies:

  • Business Tools and Skills.
  • Data sources and Retrievers.
  • Professional algorithms and calculations.
  • Domain-specific prompts.
  • Data freshness and quality requirements.
  • Completion criteria.

Consider an inventory analysis application.

The Domain developer might define a Skill that calculates stockout risk using available stock, recent sales, and expected replenishment dates.

The Harness does not need to understand the mathematical details of that calculation.

Its job is to make the authorized capability available, execute it correctly, preserve the evidence, and organize subsequent evaluation.

A Skill can perform complex internal operations while exposing a single capability to the Harness.

This separation allows the same execution architecture to support different application domains without embedding industry-specific rules into the Core.

4. Why Evaluate Evidence After Execution?

Many agent workflows focus on selecting the correct tool.

That is necessary, but not always sufficient.

Suppose an inventory Tool returns a stock snapshot.

The call may have succeeded technically. However, the snapshot might be outdated.

Similarly, an Excel editing operation may successfully write a formula that is semantically incorrect.

These are different forms of success and failure:

Execution success: Did the handler complete?

Evidence quality: Is the returned information usable for the business task?

Task sufficiency: Does the available evidence support what the user requested?

TriCall keeps these concepts separate.

The Evaluator can inspect the execution evidence and domain-defined quality indicators before deciding whether to answer or request more work.

This does not eliminate model errors.

The Evaluator itself can make incorrect judgments. Domain algorithms, explicit quality metadata, testing, and application-level verification remain important.

The purpose is to make evidence review an explicit responsibility rather than assuming that successful execution automatically means sufficient evidence.

5. Registered Capabilities and Controlled Side Effects

TriCall exposes registered Tools, Skills, and Retrievers through a capability registry.

The application determines which capabilities exist and how they may be used.

For operations that modify external state, the current implementation requires explicit side-effect authorization.

For example, a write-capable operation must be registered accordingly, and the host application must enable side effects and expose the necessary scope.

An LLM cannot grant itself permission merely by requesting an operation.

However, these permissions are execution gates, not a substitute for a security sandbox, user authentication, or operating-system-level isolation.

Handlers run with the privileges of the hosting process.

This distinction is particularly important when building agents that modify files or interact with external systems.

6. Existing Domain Examples

The repository currently includes two primary demonstration Domains.

Retail Inventory Agent

The Retail example provides three read-only Tools and a stockout-risk Skill.

It demonstrates:

  • Natural-language capability selection.
  • Inventory and sales evidence.
  • Domain-defined data quality.
  • Compound requests.
  • Supplemental execution.
  • Evidence-based responses.

Its dataset is synthetic and uses a fixed scenario time.

The example is intended to demonstrate how a professional Domain integrates with the reusable Harness, not to provide a production inventory system.

Excel Agent

The Excel example supports reading, searching, summarizing, formatting, and editing authorized .xlsx workbooks.

Its current implementation includes five read Tools and two write Skills.

The application supports free-form English instructions and interactive sessions with bounded conversation history.

Write operations require explicit host authorization and save new workbook revisions.

Excel-specific file restrictions, workbook handling, formula semantics, and calculations remain within the Domain rather than being embedded in TriCall Core.

The repository also records both successful runs and a historical formula error that an Evaluator incorrectly judged sufficient.

This is an important limitation: adding an evaluation phase does not guarantee that every business error will be detected.

7. Getting Started

TriCall Harness is currently an early-alpha Python project requiring Python 3.10 or newer.

Clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/jnukylinliu/tricall-harness.git
cd tricall-harness

Install the project and the Excel example dependencies:

python -m pip install -e .
python -m pip install -r examples/excel_agent/requirements.txt

Run the basic demonstration:

python examples/basic_demo.py

Explore supplemental execution with the scripted Retail example:

python -m examples.retail_inventory.run --mode scripted --case replan --details

Run the test suite:

python -m unittest discover -s tests -v

The scripted examples use predetermined model responses. They validate the execution and integration mechanisms without proving real-model reasoning quality.

The project also provides an adapter for compatible Chat Completions APIs.

For independent applications, developers can install the package into their own environment and implement Domain modules outside the TriCall source repository.

See the installation guide for packaging and independent integration details.

8. Current Validation and Limitations

TriCall has undergone initial packaging, integration, and execution testing.

The available validation record includes:

  • A 125-test offline regression suite.
  • Successful Ubuntu CI runs covering Python 3.10 through 3.13.
  • Packaging and ordinary wheel-installation checks.
  • Scripted supplemental execution.
  • Selected real-model observations for Retail and Excel tasks.
  • A separate, maintainer-tested third-party Domain integration.

These results support the feasibility of reusing the same Harness structure across different Domains.

They do not establish a general accuracy rate, production readiness, or superiority over other frameworks.

The current implementation also has deliberate boundaries.

It does not yet provide general-purpose durable execution recovery, distributed scheduling, parallel DAG execution, arbitrary synchronous handler cancellation, or automatic transaction rollback.

Execution is currently sequential.

Additional evaluation rounds can increase model latency and token consumption.

These are meaningful engineering trade-offs, especially for applications with tight response-time requirements.

TriCall is not intended to replace domain expertise with unconstrained model reasoning.

Instead, it gives developers a reusable lifecycle within which they can define and test their own professional capabilities.

9. A Design Philosophy, Not a Claim of Universal Superiority

Modern agent ecosystems already contain capable frameworks, graph execution systems, SDKs, and orchestration platforms.

TriCall does not claim to have invented planning loops, tool calling, evidence evaluation, or Agent Harnesses.

Its contribution is a particular organization of these established ideas:

  1. Place LLMs where semantic interpretation is valuable.
  2. Keep business intelligence and professional rules in developer-owned Domains.
  3. Use Python for deterministic execution control and admission.
  4. Evaluate actual evidence after execution.
  5. Separate the final response from the execution and verification responsibilities.

This structure is intended to help developers avoid redesigning the entire agent execution lifecycle for every new business application.

Whether that approach improves reliability, development efficiency, or cost in a particular environment must be established through real application testing.

Conclusion

TriCall Harness explores a specific question:

What if an Agent Harness treated planning, execution control, professional intelligence, evidence evaluation, and answering as separate engineering responsibilities?

The current Python implementation offers an initial answer through a reusable execution lifecycle and application-defined Domains.

It is still early, and its limitations are documented openly.

Developers interested in domain-driven AI agents, evidence-based execution, and reusable Harness architectures are welcome to explore the repository, inspect the examples, open issues, and contribute.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/jnukylinliu/tricall-harness

Architecture Documentation: https://github.com/jnukylinliu/tricall-harness/blob/main/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md

License: MIT

TriCall Harness — A foundational design philosophy for general-purpose Agent Harnesses.

title: 7 Ways Coding Agents Turn a Red Test Green Without Fixing the Bug, and the grep for Each
description:
• Book: AI Agents Pocket Guide
  • The series: Pocket Guides for Developers — 8 short books on agents, RAG, prompts, observability, events, databases and system design — the whole series
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Section 6 of the Claude 3.7 Sonnet system card, published with the model on February 24, 2025, is called "Excessive Focus on Passing Tests." Anthropic writes that the model "occasionally resorts to special-casing in order to pass test cases in agentic coding environments like Claude Code."

The card is specific about the shape of it. Most often the model returned the expected test values directly instead of writing a general solution. Sometimes it changed the tests to match its code. It usually happened after several failed attempts, when the tests conflicted or an edge case was hard to handle in general. Anthropic says training mitigations cut how often this happens, and among the product-level mitigations it lists is monitoring for "unexpected modifications to test files" and "comments that suggest test-specific handling."

Other frontier models do it too. ImpossibleBench, a 2025 paper by Ziqian Zhong, Aditi Raghunathan and Nicholas Carlini, builds coding tasks where the tests contradict the spec, so any pass means a shortcut. The authors conclude that "frontier models frequently cheat when faced with these impossible tasks" and that "stronger models generally exhibit higher cheating rates." They also note that newer Claude models cheat less than Claude 3.7 Sonnet did.

Your CI can't tell the difference. A green check from a fixed bug and a green check from a skipped test look identical. So here are seven shapes the shortcut takes, each with a command that flags it on an agent's branch. Every hit is a line to read before you decide anything.

Set up once: a base and two helpers

Run these in bash or zsh, inside the agent's worktree. Swap main for the branch the agent started from.

B=$(git merge-base main HEAD)
TESTS=('*.test.*' '*.spec.*' '*__tests__/*' '*_test.go'
       '*_test.py' 'test_*.py' '*/test_*.py')
added() {
  git diff "$B" -- "$@" | grep '^+' | grep -v '^+++'
}
removed() {
  git diff "$B" -- "$@" | grep '^-' | grep -v '^---'
}

git diff <commit> compares that commit with your working tree, so uncommitted agent edits count too. Untracked files don't show until they are added. In a pathspec, * can match directory separators, so '*.test.*' finds test files at any depth. added with no arguments covers the whole repo.

Tests that stop running

1. A new .skip, .only or xfail

The fastest green: the failing test never runs. In Jest that's test.skip, xit, xtest or xdescribe. .only and its aliases fit and fdescribe are quieter, because every other test in the file stops running too. test.failing passes when the test throws, and test.todo keeps the name and drops the body. In pytest it's @pytest.mark.skip, skipif, pytest.skip() or xfail. In Go, t.Skip.

SKIP='\.(only|skip|todo|failing)'
SKIP+='|[+[:space:]][xf](it|test|describe)\('
SKIP+='|xfail|t\.Skip'
added "${TESTS[@]}" | grep -E "$SKIP"

Vitest doesn't allow .only by default when CI is set (--allowOnly defaults to !process.env.CI). In pytest, xfail(strict=True) turns an unexpected pass into a failure, so a stale xfail can't sit there forever.

2. A deleted test

A whole file gone is easy to spot with --diff-filter=D, which keeps only deleted paths. A single test case removed from a file that still exists is not, so count test cases on both sides:

git diff --diff-filter=D --name-only "$B" -- "${TESTS[@]}"
CASE='[^[:alnum:]_](it|test)\(|def test_|func Test'
removed "${TESTS[@]}" | grep -cE "$CASE"
added "${TESTS[@]}" | grep -cE "$CASE"

If the first count is bigger than the second, the branch has fewer test cases than it started with. A rename or a refactor can explain that. Read the diff before you decide which one it is.

Tests that stop checking

3. A loosened assertion, or an expected value changed to match

This is the card's "modifying the problematic tests themselves to match the code's output." It comes in two forms. The first swaps a strict check for a weak one: toEqual(order) becomes toBeDefined(), toHaveBeenCalledWith(id) becomes toHaveBeenCalled(), assert total == 110 becomes assert total.

WEAK='toBeTruthy|toBeDefined|toMatchObject|expect\.any'
WEAK+='|toBeCloseTo|toHaveBeenCalled\(\)|approx\('
WEAK+='|assert [A-Za-z_.]+$|assert True'
added "${TESTS[@]}" | grep -E "$WEAK"

The second keeps the matcher and changes the number, so toBe(110) becomes toBe(108). --word-diff prints in-line changes as [-old-]{+new+}, which makes those easy to grep:

git diff --word-diff "$B" -- "${TESTS[@]}" |
  grep -E 'expect\(|assert' | grep -F '[-'

Sometimes the new number is the right one. Check the commit or the ticket for a reason the expectation should change. If there is none, the code moved and the test followed it.

4. A regenerated snapshot

jest -u will "re-record every snapshot that fails during this test run." Vitest has -u too. One command and every failing snapshot matches whatever the code renders now, bug included.

git diff --stat "$B" -- '*.snap' '*__snapshots__*'

Any .snap change in an agent's branch deserves a line-by-line read, because a snapshot diff is the assertion diff. In CI, run Jest with --ci: a new snapshot then fails the test instead of being written automatically.

Code that knows it's being tested

5. A hard-coded return for the test's input

The card's most common form: "directly returning expected test values rather than implementing general solutions." It also says the model "often (though not always)" left a comment like # special case for test XYZ. Two other tells are code that checks whether it runs under a test, and strings copied out of a test file into source.

Test runners announce themselves. Jest sets NODE_ENV to test unless it's already set, and gives each worker a JEST_WORKER_ID. Vitest sets VITEST. pytest sets PYTEST_VERSION, and its own docs say "usually it is a bad idea to make application code behave differently if called from a test" (pytest).

SRC=(':!*.test.*' ':!*.spec.*' ':!*__tests__/*'
     ':!*_test.go' ':!*_test.py' ':!test_*.py'
     ':!*/test_*.py' ':!*.snap' ':!*__snapshots__*')
HINT='node_env|jest_worker_id|vitest|pytest'
HINT+='|special.?case|hard.?cod|for (the )?tests?'
added "${SRC[@]}" | grep -iE "$HINT"

The :! prefix excludes a path, so this searches source only. Then look for string literals the branch added to source that also appear in a test file:

added "${SRC[@]}" |
  grep -oE "[\"'][^\"']{6,}[\"']" | tr -d "\"'" |
  sort -u | while IFS= read -r s; do
    git grep -qF -e "$s" -- "${TESTS[@]}" && echo "$s"
  done

Shared error messages will show up here, and that's fine. A fixture's exact input sitting in an if in production code is not.

Checks that stop complaining

6. A raised timeout or an added retry

A flaky failure goes away if you wait longer or try again. jest.retryTimes(3) "runs failed tests n-times until they pass or until the max number of retries is exhausted." pytest-rerunfailures does it with @pytest.mark.flaky(reruns=5), Vitest with --retry.count. Jest's default timeout is 5,000 ms, and a third argument to test() overrides it per test.

-G keeps only files whose diff adds or removes a line matching the regex, so it works across config files too:

git diff --name-only -G'retr(y|ies)|[Tt]imeout|reruns|flaky' "$B"
added | grep -iE 'retr(y|ies)|timeout|reruns|flaky'

A retry on a test that talks to a real network can be legitimate. A retry added in the same branch that "fixed" the bug is a question for the agent.

7. A new @ts-expect-error, eslint-disable or noqa

If the red check is the type checker or the linter, a comment turns it green.

MUTE='@ts-(expect-error|ignore|nocheck)|eslint-disable'
MUTE+='|noqa|type: *ignore'
added | grep -E "$MUTE"

Each tool has a way to push back. In TypeScript, prefer @ts-expect-error: it reports when the error it hides is gone, while @ts-ignore "will do nothing if the following line is error-free." ESLint has --no-inline-config to ignore inline disable comments, which you can run in CI. Ruff flags unused noqa comments with RUF100. mypy can require an error code in every type: ignore, so a bare one stands out.

Read the fix and the test edit in the same turn

The greps tell you what changed. The card tells you when it tends to happen: after several failed attempts at a general fix. The useful question is whether the test edit and the source edit landed in the same turn, right after a run of red.

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes saves every agent turn, so you can diff or restore any single turn, with undo. The Review Desk (⌘G, Ctrl+Shift+G on Windows and Linux) shows changes by turn or by file. If turn 4 touched src/price.ts and price.test.ts together, you see both files under that one turn before anything lands, and you can restore just that turn.


The Review Desk (⌘G) in By turn view: two turns listed (T1: 3 files +69 −1, T2: 1 file +1 −0), turn 1's diff of src/db.ts, the changed files and a commit message drafted from the turns.

A line comment in the Review Desk goes back to the agent that wrote the line, so "don't edit this assertion, fix applyDiscount" lands in the right terminal. Land then commits, opens a pull request or merges locally, into the branch the task started from, and can be undone. Hermes doesn't run the seven greps for you. Each task has its own worktree, so cd into it from any terminal and run them before you press Land.

Hermes is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux: download it or read the source. It is not affiliated with Anthropic, OpenAI, Nous Research or any agent vendor.

grep has limits. ImpossibleBench catalogs two cheating patterns a text search won't see: models that overload comparison operators so they always return the wanted value, and models that record extra state to return different results for the same input. Making tests read-only stopped test edits in the paper, but it didn't eliminate special-casing. Anthropic's other recommendation is cheap to try: tell the agent in its system prompt to write general solutions rather than special-casing tests.

If this was useful

An agent that edits the test is chasing the one signal it was given: a green suite. Checking its work belongs in the loop you build around it. The AI Agents Pocket Guide covers that loop, from tool calling to the guardrails that keep an autonomous agent honest. It's one of 8 short books in the Pocket Guides for Developers series, on agents, RAG, prompts, observability, events, databases and system design. If you run several agents at once, Hermes IDE puts each turn's changes in one review screen.

title: Auditing what an agent says it did, using its log
description:
An agent's summary is a story about the session; the tool log is the record. How to test each sentence of the summary and see what the record backs.

An agent's final report and the log its tools produced are different kinds of document. The log is a record; the report is a recollection. The log says which calls were made and what came back. The report says what the agent concluded, in the agent's own voice, after the fact. Most of the time the two agree. The cases where they do not are the ones that cost you: a message sent to a customer because the summary said the invoice went out, or a release shipped because the summary said the tests pass. This guide shows how to read the final report against the log, sentence by sentence, so that you know which statements you can lean on and which are only the agent's word.

Read the full report on AISkills402: https://aiskills402.com/blog/agent-report-vs-log?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=social

title: 97 of 99 Sounds Great. It Would Have Been a Bad Release Number.
description:
97 of 99 Sounds Great. It Would Have Been a Bad Release Number.

From the agentpolicy v0.1.0 release: a local-first, Cedar-based policy decision point for AI agents (decide allow, deny, ask, rate-limit, or redact for every agent action, with shipped rule packs). Now on PyPI. This story is the coverage section of the v0.1.0 field test report.

AI disclosure: this article was drafted and edited with AI assistance. The field test, the defects, the fixes, and every number are real and linked below.

The final field test report for my agent policy engine says 97 pass, 0 fail, 0 declared, 0 not run. Ninety-seven out of ninety-seven. That is a release number I am proud of. It is also a number that only means anything if I show you the two cases that are not in it.

They are the most honest part of the release. Both are named, with reasons and re-entry conditions, in the field test report (the master table note and Field Notes 13).

What a pass rate hides

My plan originally had 99 cases. Two of them were Tier-1 integrations: FT-T1-CURSOR and FT-T1-GEMINI. Test the real Cursor agent loop against the policy engine. Test the real Gemini CLI against the policy engine.

Neither can run on my machine. Not "I ran out of time." Cannot run, for structural reasons:

  • Cursor is a GUI IDE, a VS Code fork. Its agent loop and its permission surface live inside a desktop Electron app driven by a human. There is no supported headless surface, no server mode for the permissions.json flow, and no GUI host on this box. There is no experiment to run.
  • Gemini CLI is installed, and the sanctioned local path (gemini gemma setup) genuinely works. I got a real LiteRT-LM binary and a local gemma model serving on port 9379. And then the CLI crashed at startup with IneligibleTierError, the OAuth tier gate running before any model routing. I read the bundle source: the gemma router is classifier-only. Intent classification goes to the local 1B model. The main LLM always goes to Google-hosted Code Assist, which is sunset for this CLI build. No proxy fixes a client-side auth gate.

Here is the fork in the road. If I quietly dropped those two cases and published the remaining 97 as "97/97, 100% pass," I would have been technically accurate and completely dishonest. Count them honestly as untested and the same release reads 97/99, about 98%. Either number looks green. Neither one tells you that the two missing cases are the two hardest integrations I claimed I would test. The pass rate was never the problem. The denominator was.

The vocabulary that clarified it

Somewhere around the third time I caught myself about to write "didn't get to it," I codified the rule into the field-test vocabulary. Every case gets exactly one of:

  • pass: it ran, and an independent gate re-derived the assertion from the evidence on disk. Not exit code zero. Re-derived.
  • fail: it ran and the assertion did not hold.
  • declared: it cannot run here, and I wrote down the precise reason, what is covered instead, and the condition under which it becomes runnable.
  • not run: nothing yet. Visible. Counted.

The load-bearing distinction was between unsupported here and passed here. During the investigation, that vocabulary kept me honest about what I knew, what I could prove locally, and what would need a different host or a future vendor build. For Gemini, that meant the exact crash, the classifier-only finding from the source, and the local parity stand-in that did run. For Cursor, it meant admitting there was no headless surface to exercise on this box.

That gave me a complete answer while I was still investigating. The shipped release took the stricter step: Cursor and Gemini were removed from scope entirely, not left hanging as permanent declared rows.

Why this costs me something

The hard part is publishing the limitation plainly. Anyone reading the report can see exactly which integrations were exercised live and which were not claimed at v0.1.0. A marketing page would say "works with your favorite agent CLIs." My report says: Claude Code and Codex CLI, exercised live, both passing. Cursor and Gemini CLI: not claimed as supported at v0.1.0, here is why, here is what would change it.

I removed them from the plan, the registry, and the PRD rather than leaving them as eternally skipped rows. The scoping decision and the re-entry conditions are written into the plan itself, not just my private notes. Removing a feature from scope because you cannot test it is slower than claiming it. It is also the only version of the sentence I can defend.

What worked

  • The four-state vocabulary. Two days into the sweep I could not tell you which "didn't run" was flaky and which was impossible. The vocabulary forced me to find out.
  • Clear intermediate statuses while investigating. Writing down the reason, the lower-layer stand-in that does run, and the re-entry condition made it much easier to decide the final shipped scope honestly.
  • Writing the report by hand. Every number in it was typed by a person who knows where it came from. The generator is explicitly banned from touching it.

What did not work

  • My initial instinct, twice, to leave untestable cases as "skip" rows. Skips rot. Nobody audits a skip backlog.
  • Trusting "local mode" in a vendor's marketing. Gemini's local mode is real, the install works, and the main loop still cannot use it. Partial local is a trap worth naming out loud.

More detail and evidence

  • The honest coverage section, verbatim: field test report, Coverage, Gaps, and Declared Limitations (the two removed cases, the re-entry conditions), plus Field Notes 13 for the full Gemini and Cursor investigation.
  • The Gemini evidence trail: journal Group 22 in the same report (the IneligibleTierError crash, the classifier-only router finding from the bundle source, the auto-un-declare guard in scripts/fieldtest/lib.sh).
  • The plan that shipped: FIELD_TEST_PLAN.md, including the scope decision and what the shipped Tier-1 set is.
  • The product: agentpolicy, pip install agentsec-agentpolicy, PyPI 0.1.0, compliance and standards matrix (OWASP, ATLAS, NIST AI RMF, ISO 42001, EU AI Act), part of the agentic-suite agent-security stack.

I now read every "100% pass" dashboard with one question: how many cases did it take to get to that denominator? How do you handle the things you cannot test in your reports, skip them silently, or declare them loudly?

title: Redis latency benchmark: HotKV vs Valkey and Dragonfly
description:
This Redis latency benchmark measures how long HotKV, Redis, Valkey and Dragonfly take to answer at a fixed request rate. Our earlier benchmarks measured throughput, and a reader rightly pointed out that throughput is not everything. So we held the load constant, raised it step by step, and recorded the median (p50) and the 99th percentile (p99) at each step. We also measured pub/sub delivery time.

In short. In this Redis latency benchmark on AWS, HotKV and Dragonfly both held 1.6 million GETs per second, Redis with 8 I/O threads held about 0.8 million, Valkey with 8 I/O threads about 0.4 million, and single-thread Redis and Valkey about 0.2 million. From 200,000 to 1.6 million requests per second HotKV's p99 stayed between 0.59 and 0.76 ms, against 0.71 to 1.48 ms for Dragonfly. At light load the multi-threaded products tied on p99, and pub/sub delivery was a tie.

Why we ran a Redis latency benchmark at a fixed rate

A throughput test pushes a server as hard as it will go and reports how much it served. That says little about how long one request waits. A latency test fixes how many requests per second the clients send, and measures the time each takes. The server is then at the same load as every other product, so the times can be compared.

This kind of test has a catch. memtier_benchmark is a closed-loop tool, so a client waits for a reply before it sends the next request. If a server cannot keep up, the client simply sends fewer requests, and the latency of the ones it did send looks better than it should. We therefore count a step as sustained only when the achieved rate is at least 97 percent of the rate we asked for. Steps that fail the test are marked "not sustained" in the tables and their latency is not shown.

What we tested

Machines

  • Servers and load generator. c8a.12xlarge instances (AMD EPYC 9R45, 48 cores, no SMT, 96 GiB, 22.5 Gbit/s network) in one AWS cluster placement group in eu-south-2a, running Ubuntu 24.04. One instance ran the load generator and one ran the server.
  • One product at a time. Each product ran alone on the server, so nothing overlapped and nothing shared the network. Every server process was pinned to CPUs 0 to 39, with persistence off and protected mode off.

Products

  • HotKV 0.3.0 with 40 threads.
  • Dragonfly 2.0.2 with 40 proactor threads.
  • Redis 8.10.3 and Valkey 9.1.3, each run twice, once in the default single-thread setup and once with --io-threads 8.

The launch line and the live CONFIG GET output of every run are saved with its results.

Workload and procedure

The data set was 1,000,000 keys with 256-byte values, and pipeline depth was 1, so each request waits for its own reply. The load was GET only, and a mix of 1 write to 10 reads. Each step ran for 20 seconds, twice, and we report the mean of the two runs. memtier_benchmark used a per-connection rate limit and recorded an HDR histogram. We ran two connection counts.

  • 816 connections (24 threads of 34 connections), for rates from 20,000 to 2.4 million requests per second.
  • 48 connections (4 threads of 12 connections), for rates up to 300,000 requests per second. Above that, 48 connections cannot reach the rate, because each connection can only send as fast as it gets replies.

Results

The GET tables come first, one for each connection count, followed by pub/sub.

At 816 connections

Each cell is p50 / p99 in milliseconds, for GET. "NS" means not sustained, and the rate it did reach is in brackets. A dash means the sweep for that product had already stopped.

Requests/s HotKV Dragonfly Redis 1 thread Redis 8 I/O threads Valkey 1 thread Valkey 8 I/O threads
19,584 0.38 / 1.81 0.48 / 1.90 1.63 / 5.29 0.68 / 2.07 1.59 / 5.13 0.76 / 2.63
99,552 0.24 / 0.76 0.27 / 1.76 2.60 / 5.12 0.40 / 0.98 2.65 / 5.13 1.71 / 3.19
199,920 0.25 / 0.59 0.25 / 1.34 2.91 / 5.60 0.55 / 1.11 3.02 / 5.81 1.11 / 2.15
399,840 0.27 / 0.63 0.27 / 1.48 NS (258k) 0.62 / 1.23 NS (259k) 1.24 / 1.49
799,680 0.28 / 0.75 0.28 / 1.26 - 0.68 / 1.18 - NS (670k)
1,199,520 0.28 / 0.67 0.28 / 1.05 - NS (1,078k) - -
1,599,360 0.28 / 0.64 0.28 / 0.71 - - - -
2,399,856 NS (2,284k) NS (2,281k) - - - -

The mixed workload gave the same picture. HotKV's p99 was 0.54 to 0.75 ms from 200,000 to 1.6 million requests per second, and the points each product could sustain were the same as for GET. All of it is in the results folder.

How to read the single-thread rows

The 1.6 to 3 ms medians of single-thread Redis and Valkey at 816 connections are not their steady-state latency. With a rate limit, memtier_benchmark makes all 816 connections fire at the same moment. A single-thread server has to work through that burst of 816 requests one after another, so the median of a request includes its place in the queue. We ran the 48-connection test below to remove this effect.

At 48 connections

The cells have the same meaning as above, for GET only.

Requests/s HotKV Dragonfly Redis 1 thread Redis 8 I/O threads Valkey 1 thread Valkey 8 I/O threads

49,968 0.10 / 0.28 0.11 / 0.28 0.21 / 0.41 0.13 / 0.28 0.21 / 0.43 0.21 / 0.44

Pub/sub delivery time

We measured the time from a publish to its delivery to a subscriber, with 64 publishers, 100 subscribers and a 128-byte payload, using pubsub-sub-bench. Each message went to one subscriber. Cells are p50 / p99 in milliseconds.

Deliveries/s HotKV Dragonfly Redis 1 thread Redis 8 I/O threads Valkey 1 thread Valkey 8 I/O threads
about 21,000 0.10 / 0.71 0.10 / 0.65 0.11 / 0.74 0.11 / 0.62 0.11 / 0.76 0.12 / 0.78
about 107,000 0.10 / 1.02 0.12 / 0.92 0.10 / 0.80 0.11 / 0.63 0.10 / 0.82 0.10 / 0.86
about 215,000 0.11 / 1.20 0.13 / 1.13 0.51 / 1.03 0.20 / 0.73 0.57 / 1.07 0.12 / 1.22

All products delivered in the same range. At the highest load the single-thread products had a higher median, 0.51 and 0.57 ms against 0.11 ms for HotKV.

We also had to patch pubsub-sub-bench. It compared a publish time in milliseconds with a receive time in microseconds. The patch is in the results folder.

What the results show

The tables show a lead for HotKV and Dragonfly at high load, a tie at light load, and a ceiling for single-thread Redis and Valkey.

HotKV and Dragonfly kept a low tail to 1.6 million requests per second

Both sustained 1.6 million GETs per second at 816 connections, with a median of 0.28 ms. HotKV's p99 was between 0.59 and 0.76 ms from 200,000 requests per second up. Dragonfly's was between 0.71 and 1.48 ms, and the two were close at 1.6 million (0.64 against 0.71 ms). Redis and Valkey with I/O threads stopped sustaining the rate at lower loads, and single-thread Redis and Valkey stopped at about 260,000.

At light load the multi-threaded products tie

At 48 connections, up to 300,000 requests per second, HotKV, Dragonfly and Redis with 8 I/O threads all had a p99 of about 0.27 ms. HotKV had the lowest median, 0.08 to 0.09 ms from 100,000 requests per second, with Dragonfly at 0.08 to 0.10 ms. A difference of 0.01 ms is within what other parts of the setup can cause, so we do not claim it as a win.

Single-thread Redis and Valkey ran out at about 230,000 a second

At 48 connections they had a median of about 0.2 ms and a p99 of 0.35 to 0.43 ms, and they did not sustain 300,000 requests per second (about 231,000 and 233,000). That is the ceiling of one thread on this hardware and workload. It is why Redis and Valkey are usually run as many processes or as a cluster, as in our cluster benchmark.

Limitations

These are HotKV Ltd's measurements of the versions and configuration above. They are not a claim about any other version, configuration or workload of these products.

The test setup

  • One server, one load generator. Two repeats per step, on one set of machines on one date. We did not measure variation between machines or days.
  • Layouts we chose. Redis and Valkey ran in their default single-thread setup and with --io-threads 8, and we did not tune either beyond that. Other settings could change their figures. If you think a setting here disadvantages a product, tell us and we will check it and publish the result.
  • The tool's burst effect. At 816 connections, the medians of single-thread products are inflated by the way memtier_benchmark rate limiting works, as explained above.

What was not measured

  • Data. Larger or skewed values, memory per key, and persistence. Persistence was off for every server.
  • Modes. Cluster mode, sharded pub/sub, TLS, replication and failover.
  • Pub/sub fan-out. One message to many subscribers.

Redis, Valkey and Dragonfly are trademarks of their respective owners. They are named only to identify the software we measured, and this implies no sponsorship, endorsement or affiliation.

Reproduce it

The sweep scripts, the launch line and live configuration of every server, the pubsub-sub-bench patch and every raw result are in the benchmark repository. The latency script is harness/lat_sweep.sh, and the pub/sub script is harness/ps_sweep.sh. The raw folder holds one archive per test with the memtier_benchmark JSON, the HDR histograms and the CPU use of the server for every run.

Try it yourself

HotKV Cloud runs HotKV for you. Start on HotKV Cloud, or talk to sales to benchmark HotKV against your own workload.

Frequently asked questions

Is HotKV faster than Redis in latency?

Under load, at the rates we tested, yes. At 816 connections and 200,000 requests per second HotKV had a p99 of 0.59 ms, Redis with 8 I/O threads 1.11 ms and single-thread Redis 5.60 ms. At light load with 48 connections the multi-threaded products tied on p99, at about 0.27 ms.

Why did you hold the request rate fixed?

At a fixed rate every product carries the same load, so the latencies can be compared. A throughput test shows how much a server serves at its limit, which says little about how long one request waits.

What does "not sustained" mean?

The product achieved less than 97 percent of the request rate we asked for. memtier_benchmark is a closed-loop tool, so an overloaded server makes the clients send less and the latency of the remaining requests looks better than it is. We show no latency for those steps.

How did pub/sub delivery time compare?

At the three loads we tested, all products delivered in the same range, with a median of about 0.1 ms at the two lower loads. The table above has every figure.

Can I reproduce this Redis latency benchmark?

Yes. The scripts, the configurations and every raw result are in the benchmark repository. You need two servers on the same network, a load generator, and the four products.

title: Romanian CUI Validation in TypeScript, Zod and React
description:
TL;DR

Romanian CUI validation is a weighted checksum: strip the optional RO prefix, right-align the digits before the last one against the key 753217532, multiply and add, then take the sum times 10 mod 11, where 10 becomes 0. The result must equal the last digit. A valid check digit only proves the number is well formed, so confirm that the company exists, is still registered and pays VAT with ANAF's public web service.

Your sign-up or invoice form has a field for a Romanian company's tax ID, and a regex for "RO plus digits" accepts every mistyped digit. Romanian CUI validation needs three things: a parser that accepts the many ways people write the number, the weighted check digit, and, when it matters, a lookup that proves the company is real. This tutorial builds all three in TypeScript, then wires them into a zod rule, a React field that validates as you type and a sign-up step that looks the company up at ANAF. The UI uses Input and Field from Wingo UI, the library we build, so we are not neutral. The checksum code is plain TypeScript you can paste anywhere.

What is a CUI, and how does it relate to the CIF and the VAT number?

They are one number with three names. The CUI (Codul Unic de Înregistrare) is the code a Romanian company gets when it registers: 2 to 10 digits, the last of which is a check digit. The CIF (cod de identificare fiscală) is the tax ID, and for a company it is the same digits. When the company is registered for VAT, the Romanian Wikipedia article on the CIF describes the CUI becoming a CIF with the "RO" prefix.

So the Romanian VAT number format is RO followed by the same 2 to 10 digits, as the VAT identification number table on Wikipedia lists it. In a real form you will receive RO12345674, ro 12345674, 12 345 674 and RO-12345674, and all four are the same company.

Two rules follow from that:

  • Store the digits and a VAT flag, never the string as typed. Print RO + digits when you need the VAT number.
  • The prefix someone typed is not proof of VAT status. People add RO out of habit. The VAT flag should come from ANAF, as we do further down.

How does the CUI check digit work?

The last digit is computed from the others with a fixed key, 753217532. The Romanian Wikipedia article above describes the validare CUI algorithm, and the source of python-stdnum's stdnum.ro.cui implements the same five steps:

  1. Remove the RO prefix and any spaces, dots or dashes. What is left must be 2 to 10 digits.
  2. Set the last digit aside. That is the check digit.
  3. Pad the remaining digits with zeros on the left until there are nine, so they line up with the right end of the key. (Wikipedia reverses both strings instead, which gives the same pairs.)
  4. Multiply each digit by the key digit in the same position and add the products.
  5. Multiply the sum by 10, take the remainder of dividing by 11, and turn a remainder of 10 into 0. The CUI is valid when this equals the check digit.

Here is 12345674 worked by hand. The body is 1234567, padded to 001234567:

Position Digit Key Product
1 0 7 0
2 0 5 0
3 1 3 3
4 2 2 4
5 3 1 3
6 4 7 28
7 5 5 25
8 6 3 18
9 7 2 14

The sum is 95. 950 mod 11 is 4, which matches the last digit, so RO12345674 is valid and RO12345678 is not.

The case that breaks hand-written validators is the remainder of 10. For 18547290 the products add up to 111, and 1110 mod 11 is 10, so the check digit is 0. A validator that skips the fold rejects every company whose check digit lands there.

How do I validate a CUI in TypeScript?

Parse first, then validate. A parser that returns the digits, the prefix and the verdict gives the form, the zod rule and the lookup the same source of truth:

// lib/cui.ts
export type CuiInfo = {
  // the digits without RO: "12345674"
  digits: string;
  // written with RO, the way a VAT payer quotes it
  vatPayer: boolean;
  valid: boolean;
};

// the test key 753217532, one weight per digit before the check digit
const KEY = [7, 5, 3, 2, 1, 7, 5, 3, 2];

export function parseCui(input: string): CuiInfo | null {
  const clean = input.replace(/[\s.\-/]/g, "").toUpperCase();
  const match = /^(RO)?(\d{2,10})$/.exec(clean);
  if (!match) return null;

  const digits = match[2];
  // right-align the body against the key: "1234567" -> "001234567"
  const body = digits.slice(0, -1).padStart(9, "0");
  let sum = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 9; i++) sum += Number(body[i]) * KEY[i];
  // times 10, mod 11, and a remainder of 10 becomes 0
  const control = ((sum * 10) % 11) % 10;

  return {
    digits,
    vatPayer: match[1] === "RO",
    valid: control === Number(digits[digits.length - 1]),
  };
}

export function isValidCui(input: string): boolean {
  return parseCui(input)?.valid ?? false;
}

// "ro 1234 5674" -> "RO12345674"; vatPayer adds or drops the prefix
export function formatCui(input: string, options: { vatPayer?: boolean } = {}): string {
  const info = parseCui(input);
  if (!info) return input;
  return `${(options.vatPayer ?? info.vatPayer) ? "RO" : ""}${info.digits}`;
}

parseCui("RO12345674"); // { digits: "12345674", vatPayer: true, valid: true }
isValidCui("12345678"); // false, the check digit should be 4
isValidCui("RO 185 472 90"); // true, remainder 10 becomes 0
formatCui("ro 1234 5674"); // "RO12345674"
formatCui("RO12345674", { vatPayer: false }); // "12345674"

Check four things before you trust a CIF checksum JavaScript snippet from a forum:

  • It uppercases before it strips RO, or ro12345674 fails.
  • It turns a remainder of 10 into 0.
  • It lines the digits up from the right. Left alignment only works for 10 digit codes.
  • It rejects 11 digits.

python-stdnum also rejects a code that starts with 0. parseCui accepts one, so write the digit group as ([1-9]\d{1,9}) if you want the same rule.

We ran every single-digit change and every swap of two neighboring digits over a large sample of valid 8-digit codes: the check caught about 98% of both, and every missed single-digit typo came from folding 10 into 0. A random 8-digit number passes one time in ten, so a valid check digit never means the company exists.

How do I write a zod rule for a CUI?

Chain three checks and a transform, so the person sees one message at a time and your database always receives the same shape:

// lib/cui-schema.ts
import { z } from "zod";
import { formatCui, isValidCui, parseCui } from "@/lib/cui";

export const cui = z
  .string()
  .trim()
  .min(1, { error: "Enter the company's tax ID", abort: true })
  .refine((value) => parseCui(value) !== null, {
    error: "Use 2 to 10 digits, with or without RO",
    abort: true,
  })
  .refine(isValidCui, { error: "This tax ID fails its check digit" })
  .transform((value) => formatCui(value));

// for a form where the tax ID is optional
export const optionalCui = z.union([z.literal(""), cui]);

abort: true (zod 4) stops at the first failing check, so "abc" says what format is expected instead of also blaming the check digit. The transform turns " ro 1234 5674 " into RO12345674 on submit, so you never have to rewrite the text while someone is typing.

In Wingo UI Pro, the form-validation lib ships a CUI rule as createValidators().cui(), with one message for any invalid code in English, or in Romanian with VALIDATION_MESSAGES_RO. It does not transform, so normalize with formatCui from the invoicing lib before saving; that lib exports the same three functions as the code above, plus IBAN and CNP checks.

How do I build a CUI field that validates as you type?

Show the error after the person leaves the field, then re-check on every keystroke so it clears the moment the number is right. Show the check mark as soon as the number is valid, since it interrupts no one. React Hook Form's onTouched mode gives the error that timing, and useWatch drives the check mark:

"use client";

import { useForm, useWatch } from "react-hook-form";
import { zodResolver } from "@hookform/resolvers/zod";
import { CircleCheck } from "lucide-react";
import { z } from "zod";
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";
import { Input } from "@/components/ui/input";
import { isValidCui } from "@/lib/cui";
import { cui } from "@/lib/cui-schema";

const schema = z.object({
  company: z.string().trim().min(1, { error: "Enter the company name" }),
  cui,
});

type Values = z.output<typeof schema>;

export function BillingForm({ onSave }: { onSave: (values: Values) => Promise<void> }) {
  const form = useForm<z.input<typeof schema>, unknown, Values>({
    resolver: zodResolver(schema),
    // the first error waits for blur, then the field re-checks on every keystroke
    mode: "onTouched",
    defaultValues: { company: "", cui: "" },
  });
  const typed = useWatch({ control: form.control, name: "cui" });
  const { errors, isSubmitting } = form.formState;

  return (
    <form noValidate onSubmit={form.handleSubmit(onSave)} className="flex flex-col gap-4">
      <Input
        label="Company name"
        autoComplete="organization"
        {...form.register("company")}
        error={errors.company?.message}
      />
      <Input
        label="Tax ID (CUI)"
        description="With or without RO, for example RO12345674."
        placeholder="RO12345674"
        autoComplete="off"
        autoCapitalize="characters"
        spellCheck={false}
        {...form.register("cui")}
        error={errors.cui?.message}
        rightIcon={isValidCui(typed) ? <CircleCheck className="text-success-soft-foreground" /> : undefined}
      />
      <Button type="submit" loading={isSubmitting}>
        Save
      </Button>
    </form>
  );
}

The field keeps the text keyboard, because a numeric keypad has no R and no O. autoCapitalize="characters" turns "ro" into "RO" on phones, and spell check stays off so the browser does not underline a number. The Input uses 16px text on phones, so iOS does not zoom, and its error replaces the hint, sets aria-invalid and links the message with aria-describedby, the anatomy that Field gives every control. Both are free: npx wingo-ui@latest add input field.

Live demo: Form validation. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Type RO12345678 in Company tax ID and press Tab: the check digit error appears. Change the last digit to 4 and it clears while you type). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Form validation docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add form-validation

How do I check that the company exists and pays VAT?

Ask ANAF. Its public PlatitorTvaRest web service answers, for a list of CUIs and a date, whether each company is found, its name and address, and whether it was registered for VAT on that date. As of October 2026, the v9 documentation gives these rules: a POST to https://webservicesp.anaf.ro/api/PlatitorTvaRest/v9/tva with a JSON array of { "cui": number, "data": "YYYY-MM-DD" }, at most 100 CUIs per request and at most one request per second per client. The answer has a found list and a notFound list.

We called it on October 8, 2026, and two results surprised us. A number with a wrong check digit lands in notFound without an error, so validating first saves a request against that limit. And our own demo number, RO12345674, came back found: a company struck off the register in 2006, with stare_inregistrare set to "RADIERE din data 29.06.2006", scpTVA false and the inactive flag statusInactivi also false. 18547290, the example from python-stdnum, came back the same way, struck off in 2016. Found does not mean active, and in both records the inactive flag stayed false, so read stare_inregistrare. An active company reads "INREGISTRAT din data" followed by a date.

Keep the call on your server. The field names are Romanian and the version sits in the path (the v5 documentation used /PlatitorTvaRest/api/v5/ws/tva), so one route handler is the only file that changes when ANAF moves. It reads the CUI from the query string, which arrives decoded, and turns a timeout or an error page into one 502:

// app/api/company/route.ts
import type { NextRequest } from "next/server";
import { parseCui } from "@/lib/cui";

const ANAF = "https://webservicesp.anaf.ro/api/PlatitorTvaRest/v9/tva";

type AnafCompany = {
  date_generale: { denumire: string; adresa: string; stare_inregistrare: string };
  inregistrare_scop_Tva: { scpTVA: boolean };
  stare_inactiv: { statusInactivi: boolean };
};

export async function GET(request: NextRequest) {
  const info = parseCui(request.nextUrl.searchParams.get("cui") ?? "");
  // a typo never costs a request against the one-per-second limit
  if (!info?.valid) return Response.json({ error: "invalid-cui" }, { status: 400 });

  // ANAF answers for a calendar day in Romania, not in UTC
  const today = new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-CA", { timeZone: "Europe/Bucharest" }).format(new Date());
  let found: AnafCompany[];
  try {
    const response = await fetch(ANAF, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify([{ cui: Number(info.digits), data: today }]),
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(8000),
    });
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`ANAF answered ${response.status}`);
    ({ found } = (await response.json()) as { found: AnafCompany[]; notFound: number[] });
  } catch {
    // a timeout, an error status or a page that is not JSON
    return Response.json({ error: "anaf-unavailable" }, { status: 502 });
  }

  const company = found[0];
  if (!company) return Response.json({ error: "not-found" }, { status: 404 });

  return Response.json({
    name: company.date_generale.denumire,
    address: company.date_generale.adresa,
    vatPayer: company.inregistrare_scop_Tva.scpTVA,
    // "INREGISTRAT din data ..." while active, "RADIERE din data ..." once struck off
    struckOff: company.date_generale.stare_inregistrare.startsWith("RADIERE"),
    inactive: company.stare_inactiv.statusInactivi,
  });
}

To ANAF, your server is the client, so every sign-up shares that one request per second. Cache answers by CUI, and for imports batch up to 100 CUIs per request.

ANAF tells you about Romanian VAT registration. For a Romanian VAT ID check on a cross-border invoice inside the EU, use VIES. The European Commission's VIES page lists three reasons for an invalid answer: the number does not exist, it has not been activated for intra-EU transactions, or the registration is not finalized yet. A company can be a valid Romanian VAT payer and still be invalid in VIES.

What does a real sign-up step with a CUI lookup look like?

The Register Page block has an optional company step built on these pieces. Its CUI field validates with v.cui() and looks up only on Enter or the Search button: since one random number in ten passes the check, a lookup on every valid keystroke would also fire on half-typed numbers. An invalid check digit shows the error and never calls the lookup. A valid number goes through formatCui to your onLookupCui. A match fades in the name, the address and a VAT badge, and the field is rewritten with formatCui(cui, { vatPayer }), so the prefix comes from ANAF instead of habit. Editing the number clears the result, and a late answer for an older number is ignored.

Plugging in the route handler from the previous section takes one prop. The account, code and company saves stay simulated until you pass onRegister, onVerify and onCompany:

"use client";

import { RegisterPage } from "@/components/blocks/register-page";

export default function SignUpPage() {
  return (
    <RegisterPage
      onLookupCui={async (cui) => {
        const response = await fetch(`/api/company?cui=${encodeURIComponent(cui)}`);
        if (response.status === 404) return null;
        if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Lookup failed");
        const company = await response.json();
        // treat a struck-off company like an unknown one
        if (company.struckOff) return null;
        return { name: company.name, address: company.address, vatPayer: company.vatPayer };
      }}
    />
  );
}

Returning null opens the manual fields with a note, and throwing offers "Try again" and "Fill in by hand". The demo below answers from a sample table instead of ANAF, so its companies are made up.

Live demo: Register Page. The original article embeds an interactive demo here (Type RO12345678 and press Enter: the check digit error appears and no lookup runs. Fix the last digit to 4 and press Enter again: the sample register fills in the company and its VAT badge). Try it live on wingo-ui.com or open the Register Page docs. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add register-page

The step after it asks for the 6 digit code from the sign-up email; our React OTP input guide covers what that field has to handle.

Should I copy the CUI code or install it?

Copy it when you need one field: lib/cui.ts, the zod rule and the free Input cover a billing or sign-up form. The ready Romanian kit (CUI, IBAN, CNP and VAT math in invoicing, shared messages in form-validation) and the whole sign-up flow are part of Wingo UI Pro. The other two ids have their own guides: IBAN validation in JavaScript for bank accounts and the Romanian CNP validator for people. For the rest of the form anatomy, read React form components: accessible fields, zod and mobile, or browse more component guides.

Components in this post

  • Invoicing (Pro): Invoice math and the ids an invoice carries: VAT per rate the way e-Factura checks it, Romanian VAT rates, CUI, IBAN with its bank, CNP. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add invoicing
  • Form validation (Pro): Zod rules with one set of messages (English and Romanian), react-hook-form glue and a pretend request, for the forms of blocks. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add form-validation
  • Input (Free): The single-line text field: icons and addons inside the box, a clear button, a loading spinner, a counter and floating labels. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add input
  • Field (Free): The wrapper every form control shares: label, hint, animated error and counter, fieldsets, and the one box recipe all inputs use. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add field
  • Register Page (Pro): The sign-up screen of a CRM: account with password rules, company details from the CUI, email code and a welcome step. Install: npx wingo-ui@latest add register-page

FAQ

What is the difference between a CUI and a CIF?

For a company they are the same digits. The CUI is the registration code the company receives, and the CIF is its tax identification code, written with the RO prefix when the company is registered for VAT. People are identified by their 13 digit CNP, which has its own check digit.

Is RO part of the CUI?

No. RO marks a company registered for VAT and takes no part in the checksum. Strip it before you validate, store the digits, and add RO back when you print the VAT number of a company that ANAF lists as a VAT payer.

How is the CUI check digit calculated?

Pad the digits before the last one to nine digits on the left, multiply them by 7, 5, 3, 2, 1, 7, 5, 3, 2 and add the products. Multiply the sum by 10 and take the remainder mod 11; a remainder of 10 becomes 0, and the result must equal the last digit.

Does a valid CUI mean the company exists?

No. About one random number in ten passes the check. Query ANAF's PlatitorTvaRest web service to see whether the company exists, whether it is still registered and whether it pays VAT on a given date.

How do I check a Romanian VAT number for an EU cross-border invoice?

Search it in VIES, the European Commission's VAT number search. An invalid answer can mean the number does not exist, or that it has not been activated for intra-EU transactions.

This article was originally published on the Wingo UI blog: Romanian CUI Validation in TypeScript, Zod and React. The original has the live, interactive demos and is kept up to date.

title: Un socle de composants encore utilisé huit mois plus tard
description:
J'ai livré un socle de composants depuis zéro : primitives de mise en page, thème, palette de couleurs, documentation interactive. Huit mois après, d'autres équipes l'étendent, et d'autres développeurs ont écrit ses tests.

Ce qui m'importe, c'est que d'autres s'en servent sans moi. Voici les choix qui y ont contribué.

Une palette sémantique, pas une liste de couleurs. Un composant ne dit pas « utilise ce vert », il dit « utilise la couleur d'action ». Changer le thème se fait alors à un seul endroit.

Une palette typée. Si les rôles sont typés, on ne peut pas utiliser un rôle qui n'existe pas : l'éditeur le refuse avant même de lancer l'app.

// exemple générique
const palette = {
  text: { primary: "#1a1c1b", muted: "#5a5f5c" },
  action: { default: "#0b7a5b" },
