title: Binding to 127.0.0.1 is not enough: keeping a local control API away from the web pages in your own browser
description:
Disclosure: I'm the developer of Relaymote, and this post is published from my account. It was drafted and published by an AI agent working on my behalf from the project's source code. Relaymote is unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

Relaymote is an open-source (MIT) companion for Claude Code sessions on your PC. It runs a small daemon with a control API on 127.0.0.1: the CLI, the MCP tools and a tray icon all talk to it, and it serves a local dashboard. Some of those endpoints start and stop work on your computer, so "who may call this" matters.

The usual answer is "it only listens on loopback, so only this machine can reach it". That is true, and it is not the whole threat model. This post is the 38-line guard that closes the rest.

What loopback does not stop

Binding to 127.0.0.1 keeps other machines out. It does not keep out a web page running in your own browser on this machine. Two ways that goes wrong:

  1. Blind cross-site requests. Any site you visit can make your browser send POST http://127.0.0.1:<port>/api/task with a form or fetch(..., {mode: 'no-cors'}). The page cannot read the response, but it does not need to: the request already did its work.
  2. DNS rebinding. A site can point its own hostname at 127.0.0.1 after the page loads. The browser now treats http://evil.example:<port> as same-origin with the page, and the page can send requests and read the answers. The only trace on the server side is the Host header, which says evil.example:<port>.

CORS does not help with either. CORS controls who may read a response; it does not stop a simple POST from arriving, and under rebinding the browser thinks there is no cross-origin request at all.

What the legitimate callers look like

The fix starts with noticing that the real callers are easy to describe:

  • The CLI, MCP tools and tray are not browsers. They send no Origin header, and they address the port as 127.0.0.1, localhost or [::1].
  • The dashboard is a browser page, but it is served by the daemon itself, so its Origin is a loopback address on this same port.

Everything else is someone else.

The guard 

const LOOPBACK = ['127.0.0.1', 'localhost', '[::1]'];

function allowedHost(value, port) {
  const v = String(value || '').trim().toLowerCase();
  return LOOPBACK.some(h => v === `${h}:${port}`);
}

/** Returns null when the request may proceed, or { status, body } to refuse it. */
function check(req, port) {
  const h = req.headers || {};
  if (h.host !== undefined && !allowedHost(h.host, port)) {
    return { status: 403, body: { ok: false, error: 'BAD_HOST' } };
  }
  const safe = req.method === 'GET' || req.method === 'HEAD' || req.method === 'OPTIONS';
  if (safe) return null;
  if (String(h['sec-fetch-site'] || '').toLowerCase() === 'cross-site') {
    return { status: 403, body: { ok: false, error: 'CROSS_ORIGIN' } };
  }
  if (h.origin !== undefined) {
    let ok = false;
    try { const o = new URL(String(h.origin)); ok = o.protocol === 'http:' && allowedHost(o.host, port); } catch {}
    if (!ok) return { status: 403, body: { ok: false, error: 'CROSS_ORIGIN' } };
  }
  return null;
}

It runs first in the request handler, before any routing:

const refused = require('./lib/control-guard').check(req, PORT);
if (refused) return json(res, refused.status, refused.body);

Three rules, in order:

  • Host must be loopback on this port, for every method. This is the rebinding defence, so it applies to GET too: a rebinding page reading /api/state is a leak even if it changes nothing. The comparison is exact (localhost:<port>, not "contains localhost"), so localhost.evil.example does not pass.
  • Safe methods stop there. GET, HEAD and OPTIONS change nothing, and the dashboard loads with them.
  • State-changing methods must not come from another site. Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site is refused outright. If an Origin is present, it must parse as http: on a loopback host and this port. A missing Origin passes, because that is what the CLI looks like.

The edge cases the tests pin down

The test suite checks the cases that are easy to get wrong:

G('POST', { host: `127.0.0.1:${PORT}` })                                  // CLI / MCP: passes
G('POST', { host: `127.0.0.1:${PORT}`, origin: `http://127.0.0.1:${PORT}` }) // dashboard: passes
G('POST', { host: `127.0.0.1:${PORT}`, origin: 'https://evil.example' })  // CROSS_ORIGIN
G('POST', { host: `127.0.0.1:${PORT}`, origin: 'null' })                  // CROSS_ORIGIN
G('GET',  { host: `evil.example:${PORT}` })                               // BAD_HOST, even for GET
G('POST', { host: `localhost:${PORT}`, 'sec-fetch-site': 'cross-site' })  // CROSS_ORIGIN

Origin: null deserves a note. Sandboxed iframes, file:// pages and some redirects send the literal string null. It is not "no origin"; it is a browser telling you it will not say. new URL('null') throws, ok stays false, and the request is refused.

Two cheap extras on the dashboard

The dashboard response is sent with X-Frame-Options: DENY (so another page cannot frame it and trick clicks onto its buttons) and Cache-Control: no-store. Neither replaces the guard; both are one header each.

What this does not cover

It is not authentication. Any program already running as you on the same machine can call the API, exactly as it could read your files. The guard's job is narrower: a web page should not get the powers of a local program just because the browser happens to run on that machine. For a localhost API, that narrow job is the one most often skipped.

If you ship a local daemon with an HTTP control port (dev servers, desktop helpers, editor plugins), the checklist is short: exact loopback Host on every request, refuse Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site on writes, and allow only your own loopback Origin or none.

Relaymote is on GitHub under the MIT licence. Unofficial; not affiliated with or endorsed by Anthropic.

title: FrameShift Arena: Building a Deterministic, Replay-Safe PvP Engine on the Free Tier
description:
By Mohammed Abdul Raqueeb (@raqueeb) · 2026-11-05

FrameShift Arena is a full-stack PvP web game: players build squads of original shape-shifting combat units under a hard power budget, then battle other players turn by turn. The game design is the fun part, but it isn't the hard part. The hard part is the constraint sitting underneath it: the server has to be the sole authority on what happened in a match, and a replay watched months later has to reproduce that match exactly, action for action.

This is a tour of how that constraint shaped the engine, the data model and the infrastructure — and what it cost to keep a project like this running entirely on free-tier infrastructure.

The hardest problem: a replay that never lies

In most PvP games, "the client is wrong, trust the server" is a slogan. In FrameShift Arena it's an architectural decision with one consequence: a battle is computed exactly once, by one pure function, and everything else — the live match, the spectator view, the replay someone opens six months from now — plays back the same recorded actions through that same function.

The engine itself is dependency-free TypeScript, versioned (currently v3.2.0), and shared verbatim between the API (where it's the authoritative resolver) and the SPA (where it's playback only). Nothing about battle outcomes is duplicated or re-derived client-side. When a match starts, the server snapshots both squads onto the match row and stamps the seed and the engine version used to resolve it. That's enough for a replay to keep reproducing its original result even after the engine is later rebalanced — the match carries the exact state and version it was fought under, not whatever the catalogue or formulas look like today.

Architecture: one write path, one source of truth

Every turn boils down to the same shape: the client sends {expectedVersion, action}, and the single Hono function running at api/index.ts resolves it against a conditional UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?. If the version has moved — someone else's action landed first — the write fails outright with a 409 and the client retries against the fresh state. If it succeeds, the action is appended to the match's event log.

 client  ──{expectedVersion, action}──▶  Hono /api (1 fn)
                                              │
                                  UPDATE … WHERE version = ?
                                              │
                      ┌─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┐
                      │                                            │
                  version ok                                 version moved
                      │                                            │
             event log: append                             409 → client retries
                      │
          SPA folds the log  ──▶  live playback  +  replay

   fig. 1 — turn resolution: one conditional write, 409 on conflict, replay by folding the log

The battle UI never runs its own battle math. It's a fold over that same persisted event log — one cursor mechanism drives both the live animation as new events arrive and the replay viewer scrubbing through old ones. Live play and replay are the same code path, not two features kept in sync by hand.

Fitting inside a free tier

Vercel's Hobby plan doesn't cap serverless functions outright. For Next.js and SvelteKit, dynamic routes get bundled automatically into the fewest functions possible. For everything else — including a plain Hono API like this one — every API file maps to its own function, and Hobby caps that at 12 Vercel Functions per deployment. That's a real constraint, not a soft guideline, and the obvious way to hit it is one route per feature. FrameShift Arena runs on exactly one: a single Hono router mounted at api/index.ts handles every endpoint, so the cap is structurally unhittable rather than something to remember not to break. A CI guard script enforces that invariant directly, instead of trusting code review to catch a second function sneaking in.

The rest of the stack follows the same discipline. Neon Postgres and Vercel both pause rather than bill when idle, which shapes decisions around cold starts and connection handling. The app also ships as a PWA with a service worker and an offline page, so a dropped connection mid-session degrades instead of just failing.

Testing at scale

2,096 tests across 104 files back the project, and the engine tests aren't just checking final outputs — they check the full event log against golden snapshots, so a change that alters how a battle resolves, not only its final result, gets caught. Every server test boots its own PGlite database rather than sharing fixtures or mocking the data layer, trading a slower test run for tests that exercise the real persistence path.

How much is actually built

By Phase 3 (milestones M19–M25, now complete), the scope reaches well past the battle engine itself: a 54-sector world, a frozen 3,063-species catalogue, bots and rogue operators to fight, live and asynchronous PvP, matchmaking, spectating, trading, auctions, clans, seasons and achievements. GitHub Actions CI runs structural guards, typecheck, lint, tests and build before any migration touches the database.

What I'd take into the next project

Putting all battle math in one pure module, with the UI as a fold over the event log, turned live play and replay from two features that had to be kept in sync into one code path that can't drift. And treating the Vercel Hobby plan's 12-function cap as a design constraint — enforced structurally, not just remembered — beat hoping never to hit it.

The source repository stays private — this write-up is as deep as I can go without walking through the code line by line. What's public is the build itself: frameshift-arena.vercel.app is live and playable right now, running the same engine and infrastructure described above. The project is designed to operate within the free tiers of its infrastructure providers, subject to their usage limits and conditions.

title: Location permission denied: what your Android app does next is the real design
description:
Someone opens a café app and taps "Find cafés near me." Android asks for location access. They choose "Don't allow."

Now what?

Sometimes the answer is: nothing. A dead-end screen, a "location is required" message, maybe a button that fires the same dialog again. I think that is a poor experience when the app could offer another way forward.

The person said no to one way of answering "where should I search?" They didn't say no to the café. They may well know exactly which city they want. If the app can search by city, it already has a second way to help, and all it has to do is say so.

A quick note on the sample before we go on. The permission dialog and app screens in the video are captures from an Android emulator. The character and surroundings are illustrated, and the café names and results are fictional.

Start with the task, not the permission

Location is one way to find a place to search. It isn't the only way, and sometimes it isn't even the best one. Someone planning tomorrow's trip will probably type a city whether or not you have their GPS.

The sample shows two outcomes after the same denial. In the first, the app stops at a message saying location is required. In the second, it explains that location access wasn't granted and offers a city field. Type a city, tap Search, and you land on a screen with fixed illustrative results, not results from a real search service.

Same denial, completely different experience. One of them treats "no" as the end of the conversation. The other treats it as new information.

To be fair, this won't work for every feature. A navigation app can't produce a live position without a real location source, and pretending otherwise would be worse than the dead end. A café directory is different: it can search a place the person gives it. So pick your fallback based on the task, and be upfront when the results will be less precise or less convenient than the location-based version.

Ask less often than you think you need to

Before you build a permission flow, ask whether the task needs device location at all. If the need is occasional, Android's own permission-minimization guidance suggests letting people enter an address or postal code manually. It also covers other approaches depending on how often and how precisely you need location.

If the person does choose "Find cafés near me" and you genuinely need the device's position, ask in context, at that moment, not on first launch. And don't request precise location when approximate will do. Approximate location may be enough for a café search, depending on the feature and the accuracy it needs. What the system shows will vary with the Android version, the permissions you request and what the person chose before, so don't hard-code assumptions about the dialog.

Treat denial as a state you designed

A denied permission should land on a screen somebody thought about, not on whatever the error path happened to produce. For this example, that means four things.

  1. Say what changed, in plain words. "Location access wasn't granted. Search by city instead" tells the person why the nearby search can't run and what to do next. No blame, no jargon.
  2. Make the alternative actually work. A city field that returns nothing useful is worse than no field. Handle empty input, no results and network errors too, because those are the first things a real person will hit.
  3. Leave everything else alone. Someone who denied location can still browse their saved places. If a feature doesn't need location, don't punish it for the permission.
  4. Don't nag. Re-showing the same request right after a "no" is how you teach people to distrust your app. If they later want a location-dependent feature, give them a clear, deliberate way to turn it on.

None of this is exotic. Android's guidance says the same thing: request permission in context, check it every time an operation needs it, and degrade gracefully when access is denied or revoked. See Request runtime permissions.

Test the whole path, not just the dialog

Seeing the permission dialog appear proves very little. What matters is whether a person can understand what happened and still finish what they came to do.

On the Android versions you support, try these:

  • Deny the request. Is the change explained? Can the person reach the alternative without hunting?
  • Use the alternative end to end. Enter a city, submit it, follow the results to the next meaningful action. Then break it: empty input, no matches, a failed request.
  • Grant, then revoke in system settings. Come back to the app and trigger the location action again. Does it re-check access and recover, or crash?
  • Grant approximate, not precise. Does the feature work with the accuracy it got, or at least explain its limit?
  • Walk away from the location flow. Can the rest of the app still be used?
  • Restart the app. Does what's on screen match the current permission and what the person chose?

What we did and didn't verify

The sample is deliberately small. On an Android 16 / API 36 emulator, we captured a real approximate-location prompt, denied it, entered a city and reached the alternative results screen. The results are fixed examples, not output from a search service. We didn't verify the flow on a physical device, and we didn't test every Android version. A production app needs its own search implementation and its own tests for the devices and permission states it supports.

So take the sample as a demonstration of the shape, not as proof it works everywhere.

The question that matters

After someone says no, what can they still do?

In this example, a city field gives them a way forward that the nearby search alone never would. That's a small amount of work for the difference between an app that works with the person's decision and one that argues with it.

Disclosure: This article was drafted with AI assistance.

title: ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and What They Mean for Your Payout Flow
description:
ACH Return Codes Explained: R01 to R85 and What They Mean for Your Payout Flow

When an ACH transfer fails, the originating bank doesn't just say "nope." It returns a specific code—part of the NACHA (National Automated Clearing House Association) standard—that tells you exactly what went wrong. Understanding these codes is critical for anyone building payment infrastructure, because the right response to an R01 is completely different from the right response to an R10.

The NACHA Return Code Standard

The ACH network uses a two-digit alphanumeric code prefixed with "R" to classify failures. There are 85 defined return codes (R01 through R85), each mapped to a reason category: insufficient funds, account closed, unauthorized, formatting errors, and more. The code you receive determines whether you should retry, escalate to the customer, or switch payment rails entirely.

Common Return Codes and Developer Actions

R01 – Insufficient Funds

The account exists and is open, but the balance is too low. This is the most common return code in production systems.

Developer action: Retry is possible but not immediate. Flag the transaction and contact the customer. If you're building a dunning flow, this is your signal to notify the user and request payment via an alternate method. Most platforms wait 2–5 business days before retrying.

R03 – No Account / Unable to Locate Account

The account number or routing number doesn't match any account at the destination bank.

Developer action: Do not retry. This is permanent. Route the payout to an alternate rail (e.g., Visa Direct or RTP) if available, or escalate to manual review. Store this as a "bad account" flag so you don't attempt ACH to that account again.

R10 – Customer Advises Not Authorized

The recipient claims they didn't authorize the transfer. This is a dispute, not a processing error.

Developer action: Treat this as fraud risk. Lock further payouts to that account pending investigation. If you're a marketplace or gig platform, this is a red flag for account takeover or policy violation.

R29 – Corporate Account Closed

The account was closed before the ACH settled.

Developer action: Similar to R03—do not retry. Update your customer record and require new banking details before processing future payouts.

R37 – User-Initiated Reversal Request

The customer asked their bank to reverse the transfer after it settled.

Developer action: This is a chargeback equivalent for ACH. Document it, flag the account, and consider requiring additional verification for future transactions.

Building Programmatic Return Handling

Here's a minimal pattern for decoding and routing ACH returns:

ACH_RETURN_HANDLERS = {
    'R01': {'action': 'retry', 'delay_days': 3, 'max_attempts': 2},
    'R03': {'action': 'fail', 'notify_user': True, 'require_new_account': True},
    'R10': {'action': 'investigate', 'notify_compliance': True},
    'R29': {'action': 'fail', 'require_new_account': True},
    'R37': {'action': 'investigate', 'notify_compliance': True},
}

def handle_ach_return(transaction_id, return_code):
    handler = ACH_RETURN_HANDLERS.get(return_code)

    if handler['action'] == 'retry':
        schedule_retry(transaction_id, delay_days=handler['delay_days'])
    elif handler['action'] == 'fail':
        mark_transaction_failed(transaction_id)
        if handler.get('require_new_account'):
            flag_account_for_update(transaction_id)
        if handler.get('notify_user'):
            send_notification(transaction_id, f"ACH failed: {return_code}")
    elif handler['action'] == 'investigate':
        escalate_to_compliance(transaction_id, return_code)

Timing Matters

ACH returns arrive 1–5 business days after the original debit date, depending on the return code category. R01 returns typically arrive by day 2; R10 disputes can take 5+ days. Your reconciliation logic must account for this lag—don't mark a payout as settled until you've received the ACH return window (typically 5 business days post-settlement).

Key Takeaway

Each NACHA return code is actionable intelligence. R01 means "try again later"; R03 means "never try this account again"; R10 means "investigate immediately." Building a robust payout system requires mapping every code to a handler, testing your retry and escalation flows, and monitoring which codes appear most frequently in production. That data tells you where your customer verification or account validation is weakest.

Decoding ACH return codes programmatically? The ACH Return Codes API returns the full Nacha R01–R85 set with plain-language descriptions and handling guidance.

title: Which CSS variable made this color? Ask the browser three times instead of guessing from the value
description:
One of my color themes sets three CSS variables to the exact same value: --ink, --accent and the inverse background are all #1F2BE0. That was fine for rendering. It stopped being fine when I needed to go from a computed color back to the variable it came from.

The situation: I measure a page once, in a browser, and store the result. Later, a user swaps in their own palette, and I need to repaint the stored result without a browser (the code that does it runs on a server with no headless browser). getComputedStyle only gives you rgb(31, 43, 224). The variable name is gone.

I considered three ways to get it back.

  1. Look the value up in the theme's variable table. With my cobalt theme that returns three candidates for every blue thing on the page, so it's a coin flip. It also can't see through color-mix(), because a mixed color matches nothing in the table.
  2. Walk the CSS declarations and read which var() each element uses. That means reimplementing the cascade, inheritance, color-mix() and gradients. I decided I'd rather not own a second CSS engine.
  3. Measure again with every variable set to a different marker color, and see which elements move with which marker.

I went with the third one. A minimal version of it:

const vars = ['--ink', '--accent', '--bg-inverse', '--paper'];
const markerSets = [
  ['hsl(7 72% 44%)',   'hsl(97 72% 44%)',  'hsl(187 72% 44%)', 'hsl(277 72% 44%)'],
  ['hsl(151 58% 62%)', 'hsl(241 58% 62%)', 'hsl(331 58% 62%)', 'hsl(61 58% 62%)'],
];
// run 1: theme as is. Runs 2 and 3: inject :root{ --ink: marker; ... } after the theme
// then read getComputedStyle for every element and for every variable

I ran this against a four-element page in Chrome 156: a heading using --ink, two boxes using --accent and --bg-inverse, and a box using color-mix(in srgb, var(--accent) 30%, var(--paper)). The first three all compute to rgb(31, 43, 224) in the untouched run, so a value lookup matches three variables for each of them. With markers, the heading follows --ink in both marked runs, the first box follows --accent, the second follows --bg-inverse. Each one is unambiguous after two extra runs.

The mixed box matches no variable in any run, which is the signal that it's a mix. Solving each channel against the two marker values gave a weight of 0.296 to 0.302 for --accent and the rest for --paper, which is the 30% I wrote in the CSS.

Two details that mattered:

  • Use two marker sets rather than one, so a coincidence in one run has to repeat in the next. My real code accepts an assignment only if it fits the observed colors in all three runs.
  • If the theme sets a variable to transparent, give that variable a transparent marker. An opaque marker makes a previously invisible box visible, the page changes shape, and the runs no longer line up element by element.

What I haven't handled: colors that aren't driven by a variable at all (an image, a hard-coded hex) simply never move, and I treat them as constants. I haven't tested anything outside Chromium.

Has anyone solved this without a browser, for example by parsing the stylesheet with something like postcss and resolving var() and color-mix() yourself? I'm curious how far that gets before the cascade bites.

This post was written with AI assistance. The claims about the code were checked against the project source and a small test run in Chrome.
