title: Docmosis in Java Setup: License Key, LibreOffice, Security
description:
Before a Java service can turn a Docmosis template into a PDF, it needs a jar that Maven Central does not carry, a license key the core accepts and a LibreOffice converter on a host it can reach. All three apply to Docmosis-Java 4.9.1, the current embedded library from May 2026, so they come first here, ahead of the advisories and the PDF/A ceiling. Where the library would run we show its output, and otherwise we name the public record behind the claim, whether the vendor's documentation and release notes, NVD, LibreOffice's advisories, GitHub or Maven Central.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

Installing the Jar Without Maven Central

The com.docmosis group on Maven Central holds three Docmosis Cloud SDKs and no Docmosis-Java artifact, so the 4.9.1 jar comes out of the vendor's zip and goes into a local repository with mvn install:install-file. This introduction to Maven explains what a POM file declares, and the POM is where this install can go wrong. Run with the usual flags on Maven 3.9.16, which Apache now lists as previous stable, the install succeeded and the first compile of a project that depends on it stopped with these lines, trimmed here.

[ERROR] Failed to read artifact descriptor for com.docmosis:docmosis-java:jar:4.9.1
[ERROR]   Caused by: The following artifacts could not be resolved: com.docmosis:docmosis:pom:4.9.1 (absent)

Several poms are packed inside the jar, and Maven registered one whose parent, com.docmosis:docmosis, does not exist on Central. The workaround is one more flag, which tells Maven to generate a minimal pom without the parent reference.

mvn install:install-file -Dfile=java-4.9.1.jar -DgroupId=com.docmosis \
    -DartifactId=docmosis-java -Dversion=4.9.1 -Dpackaging=jar -DgeneratePom=true

With -DgeneratePom=true the same project compiled. Maven 3.10.0, out since 27 September 2026 and Apache's current version, wrote that minimal pom without the flag, and the project compiled there too. Each Docmosis upgrade repeats the install, as does each machine that does not pull from a shared company repository, and the coordinates are a local choice because the vendor publishes none.

Starting the Core Without a Valid Key

The Configuration class is the start-up route the Developer Reference recommends, and it checks the key before it looks for LibreOffice. The manual's own sample chains setOpenOfficeLocation, which the 4.9.1 jar does not contain, so the code below calls setOfficeLocation instead.

import com.docmosis.SystemManager;
import com.docmosis.util.Configuration;

public class ConfiguredStart {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // The Configuration route keeps the settings out of global system properties.
        Configuration config = Configuration.standard()
                .setKeyAndSite("YOUR-LICENSE-KEY", "YOUR-SITE-NAME")
                .setOfficeLocation("C:/Program Files/LibreOffice");

        // Start-up validates the key before it looks for LibreOffice.
        try {
            SystemManager.initialise(config);
            System.out.println("converters online");
        } catch (Exception e) {
            System.out.println(e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage());
        } finally {
            SystemManager.release();
        }
    }
}

The run printed InvalidLicenseException: Unable to process the license:com.docmosis.util.InvalidLicenseException:No valid license available. and no converter came online. Data preparation, on the other hand, runs without a key, which makes the gap easy to miss in unit tests.

import com.docmosis.document.DocumentProcessor;
import com.docmosis.template.population.DataProvider;
import com.docmosis.template.population.DataProviderBuilder;

import java.io.File;

public class OrderJsonThenRender {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        String json = "{\"orderId\":\"PO-7731\",\"items\":[{\"sku\":\"A-100\",\"qty\":4},{\"sku\":\"B-220\",\"qty\":12}]}";

        // The JSON maps onto template data with no key and no converter involved.
        DataProviderBuilder dpb = new DataProviderBuilder();
        dpb.addJSONString(json);
        DataProvider data = dpb.getDataProvider();
        System.out.println(data.getString("orderId") + " items: " + data.getDataProviderCount("items"));

        // The PDF step is where the started core and its LibreOffice converter come in.
        try {
            DocumentProcessor.renderDoc(new File("purchase-order.docx"), new File("purchase-order.pdf"), data);
        } catch (IllegalStateException e) {
            System.out.println("render: " + e.getMessage());
        }
    }
}

Here the output read PO-7731 items: 2, followed by an IllegalStateException saying the store is unavailable until the factory is initialised, and no purchase-order.pdf appeared. A test suite can pass on the data side, yet with no key this render path produced no document. The vendor offers a 30-day trial key for evaluation, limited to one converter.

Tornado CVEs and the LibreOffice Patch Cycle

NVD returned four CVEs for a Docmosis keyword search on 4 November 2026, every one of them filed against the Tornado server product and none against Docmosis-Java.

  • CVE-2023-25264, CVSS 3.1 score 7.5 (NIST): Crafted relative path segments bypass authentication in Tornado before 2.9.5.
  • CVE-2023-25265, CVSS 3.1 score 7.5 (NIST): A directory traversal in Tornado 2.9.4 and earlier.
  • CVE-2023-25266, CVSS 3.1 score 8.8 (NIST): A signed-in user can redirect Tornado's office path to a network share and have Tornado run the soffice binary found there, in releases before 2.9.5.
  • CVE-2024-42733, CVSS 3.1 score 9.8 (CISA-ADP): Code execution through a crafted script sent to the UNC path input in Tornado 2.9.7 and earlier, its only score, with no fixed version listed by NVD.

NVD gives 2.9.5 as the fixed release for the first three. The GitHub report NVD cites for the fourth says those fixes could be bypassed in 2.9.7, and a Docmosis commit dated 4 November 2024 closed that report by moving its Docker image to Tornado 2.10.0, stating that all items have been addressed.

The Tornado 2.11.4 release notes (August 2026) add a flaw with no CVE, one of several security fixes those notes list without a number. The storeTo=file: option of the render API could write generated content to unintended locations, and 2.11.4 disables it until a path whitelist is configured.

LibreOffice keeps its own advisory list, so a converter host has a second set of records to read, for Docmosis-Java and Tornado alike. On 5 October 2026 it published six, CVE-2026-63266 through CVE-2026-63270 plus CVE-2026-63277, whose records name the 26.2 series below 26.2.5, with the fixes shipped in versions 26.2.5 and 26.8.0. Its page now adds CVE-2026-76181, fixed in 26.2.6 and 26.8.1. Whether any of them applies depends on the version a host runs, and the Docmosis 4.9.1 download page names LibreOffice 7. The Docmosis manual asks for automatic updates to stay off.

LibreOffice on Every Converter Host

Every converter runs on LibreOffice, so each machine hosting one carries that office suite. Version 6 is the minimum in the Developer Reference, while the 4.9.1 download page names version 7. The JVM and LibreOffice have to share a bitness, LibreOffice 7 or newer needs Java 8 or newer, servers should match each other version for version, and Linux machines need a set of X libraries. When converters do not launch, the Developer Reference points first at the LibreOffice setup. Release 4.9.0 from October 2025 lists turning off automatic updates for LibreOffice 24 among its stability fixes.

Where the converters live is a choice between two sets of costs. Run embedded, they share a JVM with the Docmosis core, stay on that one machine, and go down and come up only together with the core. Run remotely, each machine needs its own office install plus a service that starts the converter at boot. Initialisation is slow enough that the manual recommends doing it once per application lifetime.

HTML Snippets, Floating Images and PDF/A Levels

Docmosis templates are Word or Writer documents, so HTML arrives through a <<html:name>> field. The Template Guide cautions that complex HTML can come out differently in the document than in a browser, and it points users to inline styles and simple snippets. Pictures in Word templates must be inline too, since Docmosis locates each one through a bookmark that Word strips from floating pictures.

Archive output follows the installed LibreOffice. setPdfVersion on ConversionInstruction offers PDF/A-1b, PDF/A-2b from LibreOffice 6 and PDF/A-3b from LibreOffice 7, the 4.9.1 PdfVersion enum has no a-level entry, and setPdfArchiveMode has been deprecated since 4.8.0. The PDF/A guide for Java explains what the archive format is for. By default a broken field is printed into the output in red, because the populator's fatal-error property starts as false, and the vendor tells production systems to switch it on.

A Route Without the Converter Pool

IronPDF for Java, sold commercially by Iron Software, replaces the converter with its own engine. Templates are HTML and CSS, rendered by Chromium with page JavaScript on by default. Rendering happens in IronPdfEngine, which is downloaded for the platform the first time the library runs or bundled through a platform-specific Maven artifact, so no LibreOffice goes on the host and engine updates arrive with IronPDF upgrades. com.ironsoftware:ironpdf itself is an ordinary Maven Central coordinate, published eleven times in 2026 up to version 2026.11.3, and the engine can also run on a separate server kept at the matching version, as the IronPdfEngine guide shows.

With IronPDF, the purchase order becomes an HTML string passed to PdfDocument.renderHtmlAsPdf. We ran one on 2026.11.3 and veraPDF passed the converted file as PDF/A-3b, and a version of the page with a title and language set also passed through convertToPdfA as PDF/A-1a, 2a and 3a, the a-levels that Docmosis enum lacks. IronPDF offers a free trial for running it against your own templates, and the HTML file example covers templates kept on disk.

Recap of the Docmosis Checks

Docmosis-Java 4.9.1 needs a manual Maven install, with -DgeneratePom=true on Maven 3.9.16, a valid key at start-up and LibreOffice installed on every converter host, and its PDF/A levels stop at 3b, while Tornado's record holds four CVEs plus fixes with no number, such as the storeTo=file: flaw. IronPDF for Java takes HTML templates in place of Word ones, resolves from Central and renders in Chromium, and its guide to PDFs from templates shows the HTML template setup.

Docmosis is a trademark of Docmosis Pty Ltd, LibreOffice belongs to its owner, we have no affiliation with either, and the details here come from the vendor's public manuals and release notes, NVD, the LibreOffice advisories page, GitHub and Maven Central.

Drafted with AI. Docmosis code run against Docmosis-Java 4.9.1 and Maven 3.9.16 and 3.10.0, and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team on 4 November 2026, with com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3 as the IronPDF reference.

title: Testing DynamicReports 6.20: Grouped Totals and Encryption
description:
Grouped totals that split in two, an encrypted export that needs an extra jar, HTML that loses its tables, and a dependency tree with remote code execution advisories are the issues we hit when we put DynamicReports 6.20.1 through a set of test reports on Java 17. The library builds JasperReports report designs through a fluent API in Java, and 6.20.1, published on 21 November 2023, is its newest release. Each issue below comes with the run or the advisory record behind it.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

Grouped Totals Split When Rows Arrive Unsorted

A DynamicReports group breaks every time the grouping value changes from one row to the next. It does not collect matching rows together, so the order of the data decides the layout. The listing below groups four orders by customer, with one Harbor Supply order arriving last.

import static net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.DynamicReports.col;
import static net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.DynamicReports.grp;
import static net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.DynamicReports.report;
import static net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.DynamicReports.sbt;
import static net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.DynamicReports.type;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;
import java.math.BigDecimal;

import net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.column.TextColumnBuilder;
import net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.group.ColumnGroupBuilder;
import net.sf.dynamicreports.report.datasource.DRDataSource;

public class UnsortedGroupReport {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        TextColumnBuilder<String> customer = col.column("Customer", "customer", type.stringType());
        TextColumnBuilder<String> orderId = col.column("Order", "orderId", type.stringType());
        TextColumnBuilder<BigDecimal> amount = col.column("Amount", "amount", type.bigDecimalType());

        // The last row belongs to Harbor Supply but arrives after the Northwind Tools rows.
        DRDataSource data = new DRDataSource("customer", "orderId", "amount");
        data.add("Harbor Supply", "A-100", new BigDecimal("1250.00"));
        data.add("Northwind Tools", "A-101", new BigDecimal("86.40"));
        data.add("Northwind Tools", "A-103", new BigDecimal("442.10"));
        data.add("Harbor Supply", "A-102", new BigDecimal("310.75"));

        ColumnGroupBuilder byCustomer = grp.group(customer);

        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("orders-unsorted.pdf")) {
            report()
                    .columns(customer, orderId, amount)
                    .groupBy(byCustomer)
                    .subtotalsAtGroupFooter(byCustomer, sbt.count(orderId), sbt.sum(amount))
                    .setDataSource(data)
                    .toPdf(out);
        }
    }
}

The PDF holds three groups instead of two. Harbor Supply appears first with one order and a subtotal of 1,250.00, Northwind Tools follows with two orders and 528.50, and a second Harbor Supply group closes the page with one order and 310.75. Nothing in the run warns about it. Any report fed from a query without a matching ORDER BY can print a customer twice with two partial subtotals. Adding sortBy(customer) to the builder, or sorting the query, merged the two Harbor Supply orders into a single group (2 orders, 1,560.75) in a follow-up run.

The same class of quiet output change shows up in number columns. type.doubleType() formats with the pattern #,##0.#, so a double price of 8.99 printed as 9 in a separate run, while type.bigDecimalType() keeps at least two decimal places.

Encrypted Export Needs Bouncy Castle and a 128-Bit Switch

Encryption is configured on a JasperPdfExporterBuilder. The listing below sets metadata, both passwords, a print permission and the 128-bit key flag, then writes the JasperReports design out as JRXML.

import static net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.DynamicReports.col;
import static net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.DynamicReports.export;
import static net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.DynamicReports.report;
import static net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.DynamicReports.type;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;
import java.math.BigDecimal;

import net.sf.dynamicreports.jasper.builder.JasperReportBuilder;
import net.sf.dynamicreports.jasper.builder.export.JasperPdfExporterBuilder;
import net.sf.dynamicreports.jasper.constant.PdfPermission;
import net.sf.dynamicreports.report.datasource.DRDataSource;

public class ProtectedOrderExport {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        DRDataSource data = new DRDataSource("orderId", "amount");
        data.add("A-100", new BigDecimal("1250.00"));
        data.add("A-101", new BigDecimal("86.40"));

        JasperReportBuilder orders = report()
                .columns(
                        col.column("Order", "orderId", type.stringType()),
                        col.column("Amount", "amount", type.bigDecimalType()))
                .setDataSource(data);

        // An exporter builder carries the metadata and encryption settings that toPdf(OutputStream) leaves at defaults.
        // Encryption needs bcprov-jdk18on on the classpath, and setBitKey128 lifts the 40-bit default key.
        JasperPdfExporterBuilder pdf = export.pdfExporter("orders-protected.pdf")
                .setMetadataTitle("Open orders")
                .setMetadataAuthor("Accounts team")
                .setEncrypted(true)
                .setBitKey128(true)
                .setUserPassword("reader")
                .setOwnerPassword("owner")
                .permissions(PdfPermission.PRINTING);
        orders.toPdf(pdf);

        // The same builder can also write out the JasperReports design it generated.
        try (OutputStream jrxml = new FileOutputStream("orders.jrxml")) {
            orders.toJrXml(jrxml);
        }
    }
}

Two things stand between this listing and a working file. With only dynamicreports-core declared, the first encrypted export threw NoClassDefFoundError for a Bouncy Castle class from inside OpenPDF's PdfEncryption, because OpenPDF 1.3.30.jaspersoft.3, the PDF writer JasperReports 6.20.6 uses, lists Bouncy Castle as an optional dependency. Adding org.bouncycastle:bcprov-jdk18on 1.86 fixed that. The second is the key length. Without setBitKey128(true), a run of the same exporter wrote an encryption dictionary with V 1 and R 2, which is 40-bit RC4. With the flag set as above, the dictionary moves to version 2, revision 3 and a 128-bit RC4 key, and the file opens with the password reader.

Teams that protect payslips or statements this way should check both settings in their build, since the missing class only shows up when an encrypted export runs, and the key length only in the file's encryption dictionary. The walkthrough on password protecting a PDF in Java shows how a password and print and copy restrictions are applied to a file.

What Happens to HTML Passed Through Markup.HTML?

DynamicReports has no HTML or CSS input. A report is a chain of builder calls, and the only place HTML enters is a text field whose markup is set to Markup.HTML.

import static net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.DynamicReports.cmp;
import static net.sf.dynamicreports.report.builder.DynamicReports.report;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;

import net.sf.dynamicreports.report.constant.Markup;

public class HtmlMarkupReport {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        // A text field with HTML markup is the closest the builder gets to HTML input.
        String html = "<b>Invoice 1042</b> <i>due 30 November</i>"
                + "<table><tr><td>Widget</td><td>120</td></tr></table>"
                + "<div style=\"display:flex\"><span>Left</span><span>Right</span></div>";

        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("html-markup.pdf")) {
            report()
                    .title(cmp.text(html).setMarkup(Markup.HTML))
                    .toPdf(out);
        }
    }
}

The bold and italic runs came through in Helvetica-Bold and Helvetica-Oblique. The table did not. Widget and 120 printed on two separate lines at the left margin, and the flex container printed LeftRight, which is also what a browser gives two unspaced spans, so this short test says nothing about flex either way. A team with existing HTML invoice or statement templates would have to rebuild each one as a report design, in Java or through a JRXML file.

Remote Code Execution Advisories Arrive With JasperReports

Declaring dynamicreports-core 6.20.1 alone in an empty Maven project pulls in JasperReports 6.20.6, because the parent POM's jasperreportsVersion property says so. OSV lists nothing against DynamicReports itself on 4 November 2026, but the resolved tree matches a longer list, which starts with these.

  • CVE-2025-10492 (GHSA-7c3f-cg9x-f3gr), CVSS 3.1 score 9.8 (NIST): A Java deserialization flaw in JasperReports 6.20.6 that NVD describes as allowing remote code execution through externally supplied data. The CNA gives 8.7 High under CVSS 4.0, and 7.0.4 clears it.
  • CVE-2026-6009 (GHSA-9wxq-mwqw-8hhg), CVSS 4.0 score 8.7 (CNA): Another deserialization flaw in that JasperReports build, which NVD says can lead to remote code execution. NVD analysis is still pending, and 7.0.7 clears it.
  • CVE-2025-48734, CVSS 3.1 score 8.8 (CISA ADP): An access control issue that commons-beanutils 1.9.4 matches, cleared by 1.11.0.
  • CVE-2025-52999, CVSS 4.0 score 8.7 (CNA): Deeply nested input overflows the stack in jackson-core 2.14.1, cleared by 2.15.0.
  • CVE-2025-48924 and CVE-2024-47554, CVSS 3.1 scores 5.3 and 4.3 (CISA ADP): They match commons-lang3 3.13.0 and commons-io 2.11.0, cleared by 3.18.0 and 2.14.0.

Eleven further GHSA entries from the June to September 2026 window match jackson-databind 2.14.1. CVE.org also holds CVE-2026-110879 for that version, scored 9.8 by HeroDevs and cleared by 2.18.12, which describes command execution where Spring is on the classpath and which an OSV package query misses. The same tree falls inside CVE-2026-89425 for jackson-core (7.5 from HeroDevs, cleared by 2.18.11) and CVE-2026-78254 for ant 1.7.1 (7.4 from CISA ADP, cleared by 1.10.18). NVD marks none of these CVEs as disputed. Both JasperReports fixes exist only on the 7.x line, so the last 6.x build on Maven Central, 6.21.5, sits inside both ranges as well. Maven's dependency management system decides which of these versions a real application ends up with, so the scan of the actual build is the one that counts.

Why Can a Version Pin Not Clear the JasperReports Advisories?

Pinning JasperReports 7.0.7 in dependencyManagement, with its separate jasperreports-pdf and jasperreports-json artifacts added, compiled the grouped report above cleanly against 6.20.1. The export did not run. Each attempt ended in NoClassDefFoundError with a zero-byte PDF, naming SimpleJsonMetadataReportConfiguration or SimplePdfReportConfiguration from net.sf.jasperreports.export depending on the run. JasperReports 7 moved both classes to new packages, so the advisory fix needs a DynamicReports build made for JasperReports 7.

That build has not been released. Maven Central's newest dynamicreports-core is still 6.20.1, and the GitHub releases page ends at the same tag. The default development branch carries 7.0.0-SNAPSHOT pinned to JasperReports 7.0.6, which clears the first advisory but not the second, and nothing has been committed to it since 30 March 2026. A user request for a 7.x build, issue #198, dates from 5 December 2024 and is still open. That leaves the 7.0.0-SNAPSHOT on Sonatype's snapshot repository, last redeployed on 30 October 2026, or a source build, either way with its JasperReports version bumped to 7.0.7 by hand, a route read from the POM and not run for this post. Both 6.20 releases also require Java 17, class file version 61, and teams on Java 8 or 11 stay on 6.12.1 from May 2021. DynamicReports is licensed under the LGPL-3.0.

Where These DynamicReports Issues Leave a Reporting Stack

Unsorted groups, rounded doubles, encryption that needs an extra jar and a flag, markup without tables, and two JasperReports advisories that a version pin cannot clear all come with DynamicReports 6.20.1.

IronPDF for Java takes a different route to a PDF report. It renders HTML with a Chromium engine, and in our 2026.11.3 run the markup test above kept Widget and 120 in one table row. Chart scripts run when setEnableJavaScript is on, with setWaitFor giving them time before the capture. The library resolves from Maven Central as com.ironsoftware:ironpdf, with no JasperReports in its POM and eleven 2026 releases, the latest 2026.11.3 on 3 November 2026.

The grouping and number formatting move into the Java code that writes the rows. The Java PDF report generator tutorial shows a report table written as an HTML string in Java, and getSecurity().setPassword() encrypted the finished file with a 128-bit RC4 key in our run. A free trial is enough to render one of your current reports from HTML and compare the files.

Has a split group or a rounded total turned up in your DynamicReports output, and what fixed it?

DynamicReports and JasperReports are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with either project, and the facts above are based on the project's public repository, Maven Central, NVD, OSV, CVE.org and runs of each listing.

Drafted with AI. Code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team against net.sourceforge.dynamicreports:dynamicreports-core 6.20.1 and com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3 on 4 November 2026.

title: iText pdfHTML in Practice: Invoice Totals, CSS and Signing
description:
An invoice template with three line items and a script that adds them up came out of iText pdfHTML with a total of 0.00. That 4 November 2026 run on Java 17 opens this look at pdfHTML 6.3.4 and iText Core 9.8.0, on Maven Central since 30 September 2026. CSS rules that never reach the page, a signing setup that stops on a missing module, advisories on older releases and lines that only receive security patches follow, with every output taken from that day's runs.

We work at Iron Software, and the end of this article covers our library, IronPDF.

Scripts Never Execute During Conversion

According to iText's knowledge base, JavaScript is not evaluated by pdfHTML, and the HTML feature FAQ lists the <script> tag as unsupported. The invoice below leaves its total row at 0.00 and expects a script to fill it in.

import com.itextpdf.html2pdf.HtmlConverter;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.OutputStream;

public class ScriptedInvoice {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        // The table has three line items, and the script is meant to add them up into the total row.
        String html = "<html><body><h1>Invoice INV-2026-0418</h1><table id='items'>"
                + "<tr><td>Paper</td><td class='amt'>120.50</td></tr>"
                + "<tr><td>Toner</td><td class='amt'>89.99</td></tr>"
                + "<tr><td>Binders</td><td class='amt'>42.00</td></tr>"
                + "<tr><td>Total</td><td id='total'>0.00</td></tr></table>"
                + "<script>var sum = 0;"
                + "document.querySelectorAll('.amt').forEach(function (c) { sum += parseFloat(c.textContent); });"
                + "document.getElementById('total').textContent = sum.toFixed(2);</script>"
                + "</body></html>";

        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("scripted-invoice.pdf")) {
            HtmlConverter.convertToPdf(html, out);
        }
    }
}

scripted-invoice.pdf is a single page of 1,345 bytes, and its total row reads 0.00, where the script would have written 252.49. A canvas chart drawn by a script fares the same way, and in a second run the canvas area held no drawing at all, not even its border. Templates that compute totals, format dates or draw charts with JavaScript are the ones affected. iText's documented workaround is to load the page in headless Chrome through Selenium WebDriver and a chromedriver binary, then hand the evaluated HTML to pdfHTML.

CSS That Chrome Draws and pdfHTML Skips

The FAQ, written against pdfHTML 6.3.3, has a long list of CSS marked unsupported. It includes box-shadow, text-shadow, filter, mix-blend-mode, writing-mode, z-index, text-decoration-style, and pseudo-elements such as ::marker, ::first-line and ::first-letter. Flexbox and grid are marked supported. The snippet below uses three of the unsupported rules.

import com.itextpdf.html2pdf.HtmlConverter;

import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.OutputStream;

public class DecoratedInvoice {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        // A drop cap, a wavy underline and vertical text, three rules the pdfHTML FAQ marks as unsupported.
        String html = "<html><head><style>"
                + "p.note::first-letter { font-size: 32pt; color: #c0392b; }"
                + "h1 { text-decoration: underline; text-decoration-style: wavy; }"
                + ".stamp { writing-mode: vertical-rl; background: #f1c40f; padding: 6px; }"
                + "</style></head><body>"
                + "<h1>Invoice INV-2026-0418</h1>"
                + "<p class='note'>Payment is due within 30 days.</p>"
                + "<div class='stamp'>PAID</div>"
                + "</body></html>";

        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("decorated-invoice.pdf")) {
            HtmlConverter.convertToPdf(html, out);
        }
    }
}

In decorated-invoice.pdf (1,364 bytes) the note's first letter is the same 12-point black as the rest of the line, the heading's underline is a straight line, and PAID runs horizontally across a full-width yellow band. Release 6.3.4, which postdates the FAQ, brought initial vertical-rl and vertical-lr handling that applies only with text-orientation set to upright, and once that property was added, a further run stacked the four letters of PAID one above the other. A related run with text-shadow, box-shadow and filter: grayscale(100%) gave the same result, with no shadow under the text or the card and the card still in its original blue. Teams that reuse stylesheets from a web front end lose these effects with no exception, and the FAQ lists no substitutes.

Signing Stops Without a Bouncy Castle Adapter

html2pdf 6.3.4 brings in kernel, layout, forms, svg, pdfa and pdfua, but not sign, so signing starts with a second dependency. The class below signs the invoice with a PAdES Baseline B signature from a self-signed PKCS#12 key.

import com.itextpdf.kernel.pdf.PdfReader;
import com.itextpdf.signatures.PdfPadesSigner;
import com.itextpdf.signatures.SignerProperties;

import java.io.FileInputStream;
import java.io.FileOutputStream;
import java.io.InputStream;
import java.io.OutputStream;
import java.security.KeyStore;
import java.security.PrivateKey;
import java.security.cert.Certificate;

public class SignInvoice {
    public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception {
        char[] password = "changeit".toCharArray();
        KeyStore keyStore = KeyStore.getInstance("PKCS12");
        try (InputStream in = new FileInputStream("keys/signer.p12")) {
            keyStore.load(in, password);
        }
        PrivateKey key = (PrivateKey) keyStore.getKey("signer", password);
        Certificate[] chain = keyStore.getCertificateChain("signer");

        // PAdES Baseline B, the level that needs no timestamp authority.
        try (OutputStream out = new FileOutputStream("invoice-signed.pdf")) {
            new PdfPadesSigner(new PdfReader("invoice.pdf"), out)
                    .signWithBaselineBProfile(new SignerProperties().setFieldName("Approval"), chain, key);
        }
    }
}

With html2pdf and sign alone on the classpath, the class compiled and then threw an UnsupportedOperationException from signWithBaselineBProfile, whose message asks for one of the two Bouncy Castle adapter artifacts before any cryptographic call can run. The failed run also left an empty invoice-signed.pdf of 0 bytes. iText's installation guide confirms that one of the two adapters is required and that both together are not supported. With bouncy-castle-adapter 9.8.0 added, the run wrote a 48,052-byte file carrying one ETSI.CAdES.detached signature. Every iText 8.x or 9.x project that signs PDFs in Java needs sign plus an adapter, and the block below adds the standard one.

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.itextpdf</groupId>
    <artifactId>sign</artifactId>
    <version>9.8.0</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.itextpdf</groupId>
    <artifactId>bouncy-castle-adapter</artifactId>
    <version>9.8.0</version>
</dependency>

Advisories on iText and the Bouncy Castle It Pins

NVD has eight entries that name iText, the newest published on 26 November 2023, and all of them concern older releases. OSV returns none for html2pdf 6.3.4, kernel 9.8.0 or sign 9.8.0, though its iText records sit on itext7-core, itextpdf, itext-rups and the older com.lowagie:itext, so a query on kernel returns none for 7.1.17 either.

  • CVE-2021-43113, CVSS 3.1 score 9.8 (NIST): Command injection through a CompareTool file name passed to Ghostscript, fixed in 7.1.17 and 5.5.13.3 according to GitHub's advisory.
  • CVE-2017-9096, CVSS 3.0 score 8.8 (NIST): XML external entities in iText's XML parsers, fixed in 5.5.12 and 7.0.3.
  • CVE-2017-20151, CVSS 3.1 score 9.8 (NIST): An XML external entity in iText RUPS, the PDF inspection tool, which VulDB scores at 5.5.
  • CVE-2022-24196 and CVE-2022-24197, CVSS 3.1 score 6.5 each (NIST): Denial of service from crafted PDFs in 7.1.17, addressed in 7.1.18 and 7.2.2 according to iText's CVE page.
  • CVE-2023-6299, CVSS 3.1 score 6.5 (NIST): NVD describes a memory leak in 8.0.1 fixed in 8.0.2, and VulDB scores it at 4.3, but iText's CVE page says that report is wrong and that 7.2.4 and 7.1.16 were the versions affected.
  • CVE-2022-24198 and CVE-2023-6298, CVSS 3.1 score 6.5 each (NIST): Filed against 7.1.17 and 8.0.2, and NVD marks both as disputed.

The Bouncy Castle jars carry more, reaching 7.x builds from 7.1.10 on through kernel and 8.x and 9.x builds through the signing adapter. Each iText release pins a Bouncy Castle version, 1.75 for 7.2.6, 1.78 for 8.0.5, 1.83 for 9.6.0 and 1.84 for 9.7.0 and 9.7.1. CVE-2026-5588, a weak-algorithm issue in bcpkix that the 9.7.0 notes cite for the move to 1.84, covers most Bouncy Castle releases between 1.67 and 1.84, and NVD has not scored it yet. CVE.org holds 28 records on the bcprov and bcpkix 1.84 pair that 9.7.x pins. OSV shows two of them, CVE-2026-8763 (a name-constraints bypass, 9.1 from NIST) and CVE-2026-13506 (lazy ASN.1 parsing that resets a depth guard, 7.5 from NIST), which reach every Bouncy Castle release before 1.85. The 9.8.0 release moves to Bouncy Castle 1.86, which neither OSV nor CVE.org lists a record against, so upgrading is iText's remedy. That tree still carries jackson-databind 2.22.3 through commons, inside CVE-2026-110879 (9.8 from HeroDevs, cleared by 2.22.4), a record the OSV package query misses.

End of Life for iText 7.1, 7.2 and 8.0

Published on 8 July 2026, the iText Core 9.7.0 notes record 7.1 reaching end of life in April 2025, with 7.2 following that October and 8.0 in October 2026. Once a line reaches that point it moves into maintenance and gets security patches and nothing else. Maven Central's last 7.x build is 7.2.6, released 9 January 2024, and its last 8.x build is 8.0.5, released 18 July 2024, while iText 5's 5.5.13.6 arrived on 22 July 2026 as a security release that took the 9.7.0 fix for single-layered decompression bombs. Features such as WebP images and footnotes, added in 9.7.0 alongside a default 100 times growth limit on streams, only ship in 9.x. iText releases Core and pdfHTML under the AGPLv3 and also offers a commercial license. Codebases still on 7.x or 8.x have a migration to plan, and the table below sets the four lines side by side.

iText release lines with the newest build of each on Maven Central, its status in iText's notes and the Bouncy Castle version its POM pins.

Line Newest on Maven Central Status in iText's notes Bouncy Castle pinned
5.x itextpdf 5.5.13.6, 22 Jul 2026 Maintenance, security releases only 1.84, optional
7.x kernel 7.2.6, 9 Jan 2024 End of life, 7.2 since October 2025 1.75
8.x kernel 8.0.5, 18 Jul 2024 End of life from October 2026 1.78
9.x kernel 9.8.0, 30 Sep 2026 Current line 1.86

For invoice templates that rely on scripts or on CSS that Chrome draws, IronPDF for Java is a commercial option that renders HTML on a Chromium engine. We ran an invoice with a script-computed total on 2026.11.3 and it printed Total due 662.24, and a separate statement drew a canvas bar and printed its script's balance. The decorated invoice above came out with its 32-point red first letter, a wavy underline and a vertical PAID, and a related page kept its text and box shadows and turned its blue card grey. A WaitFor render delay on ChromePdfRenderOptions sets how long a page's scripts get before the capture.

It comes from Maven Central as com.ironsoftware:ironpdf, with engine binaries that the docs say download on the first run or arrive through a platform artifact, and Central lists eleven releases published in 2026, up to 2026.11.3 on 3 November. Signing with a .pfx or .p12 certificate goes through getSignature().SignPdfWithSignature on the same PdfDocument, and IronPDF's signing example lists no separate signing module. Our run with the same self-signed key returned true from VerifyPdfSignatures with none added, on a detached PKCS#7 signature (adbe.pkcs7.detached). A free trial runs for 30 days.

What the pdfHTML Runs Showed

pdfHTML 6.3.4 skips page scripts and a long list of CSS effects, signing needs sign plus a Bouncy Castle adapter, the Bouncy Castle records on iText's pinned versions clear only at 9.8.0, and Jackson 2.22.3 in that tree still wants 2.22.4. For HTML that depends on a browser, IronPDF for Java renders it in Chromium instead, with script and CSS media settings on ChromePdfRenderOptions.

iText and pdfHTML are trademarks of their respective owners, we have no affiliation with iText or Apryse, and the details above come from NVD, CVE.org, the GitHub Advisory Database through OSV, iText's knowledge base and release notes, and the Maven Central record.

Drafted with AI. Code run and claims checked by the Iron Software DevRel team against iText Core 9.8.0, pdfHTML 6.3.4 and com.ironsoftware:ironpdf 2026.11.3 on 4 November 2026.

title: Operational Dashboards People Actually Use
description:
Almost every business software project produces a dashboard. Almost every dashboard is opened enthusiastically for two weeks and then not at all.

The usual diagnosis is that people need training, or that the dashboard needs more data. Both are wrong, and adding more data reliably makes it worse.

Dashboards fail because they answer questions nobody was asking. A screen full of accurate, well-presented numbers that do not change what anyone does is a screen with no reason to be opened. The ones that survive share a single property: every element on them is attached to a decision somebody actually makes.

The test each number should pass

Before a metric appears on a dashboard, it should survive three questions.

Who looks at this, and when? Not "management" — a specific person, at a specific point in their day or week. A number without an owner and a moment is decoration.

What would they do differently? If the figure is high, what happens? If it is low, what happens? If the honest answer is "nothing, it's just useful to know", it does not belong on an operational dashboard.

How quickly do they need it? A figure reviewed monthly does not belong on a screen checked daily. Different cadences want different surfaces.

Most metrics fail the second question. That is the filter that does the work.

Awareness and action are different screens

The most common design error is mixing two purposes.

Awareness answers how are we doing — revenue, volume, trend. It is reviewed periodically, it is interesting, and it rarely triggers an immediate act.

Action answers what needs attention now — stock below reorder, invoices past due, variance beyond threshold, an outlet that has not closed its day.

They belong on different screens because they are consumed differently. Awareness is reviewed on a cadence. Action should be checked whenever there might be something to do — and if action items are buried among charts, they are missed.

The practical consequence: an operational dashboard should mostly be a list of exceptions, not a wall of charts. If nothing needs attention, it should say so and be short.

Why more data makes it worse

When a dashboard is not being used, the instinct is to add to it. This is exactly backwards.

Every additional element costs attention and dilutes the signal. A screen with six numbers where two matter is a screen where the two get missed. A screen with thirty is not opened at all.

Our position is focused screens, not dashboards — every screen shows what a decision needs and nothing else. Decorative analytics cost attention and return nothing. It is one of the three principles that decide what we ship, described in how Truffaire builds software.

The discipline is subtraction. A useful review question is not "what else should we show" but "what could we remove without changing any decision".

What belongs on an operational screen

For most operations, a short list:

  • Exceptions requiring action today — with enough context to act, not just a count
  • Yesterday's close — did the day settle, and was there variance
  • Anything below a threshold — stock, cash position, margin
  • Anything overdue — receivables, deliveries, follow-ups
  • A single trend line for the one number the business steers by

Notice what is absent: breakdowns by every dimension, comparisons nobody requested, and charts that exist because the data was available.

Exceptions need context, not just counts

"14 items below reorder level" is a number. It requires the reader to go and find out which, how far below, and whether it matters.

"14 items below reorder — 3 are fast-moving and will stock out this week" is a decision. The work of interpretation has been done by the system rather than deferred to the person.

That difference decides whether a dashboard saves time or creates it.

Where dashboards get abandoned

Stale data. If the numbers are yesterday's and the decision is today's, the screen is worse than useless — it is confidently wrong. This is the strongest argument for a shared record: figures derived from one source are current by construction rather than by a sync schedule. It is the architecture in what a business operating system actually is.

Numbers that disagree with reality. One instance of a dashboard contradicting what someone can see with their own eyes destroys trust in the whole screen, permanently and reasonably.

Requiring interpretation. If reading it needs a mental calculation, it will be skipped when busy.

Built for the buyer, not the user. Dashboards specified by an owner and used by a manager frequently answer the owner's questions. The manager opens it twice.

No mobile reality. Most operational checking happens on a phone, often away from a desk. A dashboard that only works on a large screen is checked far less than one designed for the device it is actually opened on.

What we have seen

Dashboards appear in most of the ten systems we have delivered. The pattern is consistent: what gets used long-term is narrower than what was originally requested.

Clients typically ask for comprehensive visibility. Six months in, the screens still open daily are the exception lists — what needs attention, what did not close, what is below threshold. The comprehensive analytics are reviewed occasionally, if at all, and usually by one person.

The other finding is that the most valuable screen in an operation is frequently the daily close: did yesterday settle, and if not, by how much. It is unglamorous, it is one number with a variance, and it is checked every morning — because it is attached to something the person is accountable for.

That is the whole principle. Attachment to accountability is what makes a number get looked at.

Frequently asked questions

How many metrics should a dashboard have?

Fewer than you think. For a daily operational screen, five to seven elements is generally the ceiling before attention disperses. If more seems necessary, it is usually two screens for two audiences.

Should everyone see the same dashboard?

No. A counter supervisor, an outlet manager and an owner make different decisions and need different screens. One shared dashboard is a compromise that serves nobody particularly well.

Real-time or periodic?

Match the decision. Stock and daily close benefit from being current. Monthly trends do not need real-time and updating them constantly adds noise. Real-time everything is a cost with no corresponding benefit.

What about alerts instead of dashboards?

Often better for the action category — if something needs attention, pushing it is more reliable than hoping someone checks. The risk is volume: alerts that fire too often get muted, and then the important one is muted too.

How do we know if ours is working?

Look at whether it is opened, and by whom. If a screen is not being checked, do not add to it — remove from it, or ask the person what they actually needed to know.

Where to start

Take your existing dashboard and, for each element, name the person who acts on it and what they do differently based on it. Remove anything that fails.

What remains is usually a short list of exceptions and one or two trends. That is the dashboard people will actually open — and it will be more useful than the comprehensive one it replaces.

If nothing survives the filter, the honest conclusion is that the screen was built because dashboards are expected, not because a decision needed support. That is worth knowing before investing further in it.

SPEXA treats dashboards as exception surfaces first. If you want a read on which of your numbers are actually load-bearing, get in touch.

Originally published at truffaire.in.

title: Is your body text too small and too grey? An accessibility pass you can ship this week
description:
A paragraph set at 13px in #999 on a white card looks calm in a mockup and is unreadable on a phone held outdoors. It also fails the contrast rule on its own: #999999 on white is 2.85:1.

None of what follows needs a redesign. It needs a floor — a minimum type size, a contrast rule, alt text written on purpose, and a focus ring nobody deletes.

Body text: pick a floor and keep it

Sixteen pixels is the absolute floor for body copy, and on a marketing page 18px reads better than 16. Secondary text — captions, metadata, form hints — should not go below 14px. Line height of 1.5 to 1.6 for anything longer than a sentence, and a measure of roughly 60 to 75 characters per line.

:root {
  --text: #1a1a1a;
  --text-muted: #5a5a5a;
  --step-0: 1.125rem;   /* 18px body */
  --step--1: 0.875rem;  /* 14px, the floor for secondary text */
}

body {
  font-size: var(--step-0);
  line-height: 1.6;
  color: var(--text);
  background: #ffffff;
}

.prose { max-width: 65ch; }

.meta {
  font-size: var(--step--1);
  color: var(--text-muted); /* ~6.9:1 on white */
}

Set the viewport without blocking zoom. user-scalable=no and maximum-scale=1 are the two values that stop people from enlarging text on a phone, and both still show up in starter templates.

<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

Contrast: the numbers, and where they apply

Normal-size text needs 4.5:1 against its background. Large text — 24px and up, or 18.66px and up when bold — needs 3:1, and so do borders, icons and control outlines that carry meaning.

#767676 is the lightest grey that still clears 4.5:1 on white, at 4.54:1. One step lighter, #999999, is 2.85:1 and fails. That single pair of hex values explains most of the grey text on the web.

Things that get forgotten in the audit:

  • Placeholder text inside inputs is text. It needs to pass, and it also should not be the only label.
  • Text laid over a photo needs a solid or near-solid overlay behind it. A gradient that works on the desktop crop will not work on the mobile crop.
  • Links inside body copy need more than a color difference. Underline them, or the link disappears for anyone who cannot separate the two hues.
  • Required fields marked only in red are invisible to a chunk of your readers. Add the word.
  • Disabled buttons are exempt from the contrast rule, which makes "disable until valid" a bad pattern for a primary action. Let the button work, validate on submit, and show a readable message.

Check every color pair you actually ship, not the ones in the palette file — hover states, footer links on the dark band, and the text inside a filled button included.

Alt text is about purpose, not description

The question is not "what is in this picture" but "what is this picture doing here".

  • Decorative shapes, background flourishes, spacer images: alt="". An empty alt is not laziness; it is the instruction to skip the image.
  • A logo at the top of the page: the company name. Nothing else.
  • A product photo in a grid: the product and the variant a person would use to tell it apart — material, size, color.
  • An icon that is the only content of a link: the destination. Better still, put visible text next to it and drop the image from the accessible name.
  • A chart: a short alt naming what it plots, plus a real sentence or table of the numbers nearby. No alt text can carry a chart.
  • Captions and alt text should not repeat each other. If the caption says it, the alt does not need to.

Skip "image of" and "photo of" — the screen reader already says it is an image.

Keyboard: unplug the mouse and use the page

Tab from the address bar to the last link in the footer. Every stop should show a visible ring, in an order that matches the reading order, with nothing skipped and nothing trapped.

:focus-visible {
  outline: 3px solid #0b5fff; /* ~5.1:1 on white, clears the 3:1 non-text rule */
  outline-offset: 2px;
}

If a stylesheet in the project contains outline: none or outline: 0 on :focus, that is the bug. Replace it with the rule above rather than deleting the line and hoping.

A skip link is four lines and saves a keyboard user from tabbing through the whole nav on every page.

<a class="skip" href="#main">Skip to content</a>
<!-- ... -->
<main id="main">

.skip {
  position: absolute;
  left: 0;
  top: 0;
  transform: translateY(-120%);
  background: #ffffff;
  color: #1a1a1a;
  padding: 0.75rem 1rem;
  z-index: 100;
}

.skip:focus-visible { transform: translateY(0); }

Use <button> for anything that changes something on the page and <a href> for anything that goes somewhere. A clickable <div> is unreachable and unannounced; if you must keep it, add role="button", tabindex="0" and a keydown handler for Enter and Space, then ask why the <button> was not an option.

For dialogs, a native <dialog> opened with showModal() keeps focus inside and closes on Escape, which removes most of the hand-written focus-trap code. For menus and pickers, native <select> and <details> behave correctly with a keyboard by default. Hover-only navigation is unusable on a keyboard and on a touch screen at the same time.

Form errors have to be spoken

An error message that only changes color is an error message half your readers never receive. Tie the message to the field and let it be announced when it appears.

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" name="email" type="email" autocomplete="email"
       aria-describedby="email-error" aria-invalid="true">
<p id="email-error" role="alert">Enter an email address, for example name@company.com.</p>

Render the container empty on page load and fill it on submit. A message that is inserted into an existing live region is announced; one that arrives already populated inside freshly injected markup is less reliable.

Motion is the other thing people turn off. A short media query covers the carousels, the parallax and the smooth scrolling in one go.

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}

The pass to run before you publish

Work through this on the real staging site, not on a component library page.

  • Tab from the browser chrome to the end of the page with the mouse untouched. Visible ring at every stop, order matches the layout, no trap in a modal, no stop on a decorative element.
  • Zoom the browser to 200%. Nothing overlaps, nothing is clipped, no content disappears.
  • Narrow the window to 320px wide. No sideways page scroll — intentional scroll regions like a data table are fine.
  • Run a contrast checker on every text and background pair you ship, including placeholders, captions and hover states. 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text and for borders that carry meaning.
  • Turn on a screen reader for five minutes: NVDA on Windows, or VoiceOver on macOS with Cmd+F5. Listen to the navigation and the contact form. You are checking whether the labels make sense out loud, not whether every element is perfect.
  • Submit the contact form empty. The error is announced, the field is described by it, and focus lands somewhere sensible.
  • Open the accessibility panel in devtools and read the heading outline. One h1, no skipped levels, headings used for structure rather than for size.
  • Look at every image on the page: it either has alt text that says what it is for, or alt="".
  • Check tap targets on a phone. 24×24 CSS pixels is the floor with spacing, and primary actions want more room than that.
  • Finish with an automated scan and clear what it flags. It catches the mechanical failures — missing labels, low contrast, bad ARIA — and it cannot tell you whether your alt text is meaningful. That part is still yours.

title: Cloud Storage CORS Support for Direct Browser Receipt Uploads (A Go Retention Boundary)
description:
TL;DR: For a property-management receipt workflow, the decisive cloud-storage question is not which service has the lowest advertised rate. It is whether the upload, retention, audit, and deletion boundaries are explicit enough to survive an audit. Put a short-lived upload capability in front of object storage, validate the receipt server-side after upload, and make deletion a state transition with an observable record. CORS only lets the browser make the request; it does not enforce retention.

A useful design keeps the original receipt immutable, stores processing results separately, and gives the platform one place to decide when an original may be deleted. That design can sit above S3-compatible storage, including Cloudflare R2, Amazon S3, or Wasabi, but the provider comparison should happen after the lifecycle contract is written. Otherwise an apparently simple upload path becomes an expensive retention problem.

Keep it boring.

What should survive a browser upload?

I model the production event as a small, bounded transaction. A property manager selects a PDF or image, the browser uploads the bytes directly to an object key, and the application records an upload intent before issuing a capability. A worker then checks the object, extracts receipt fields, and records the result without replacing the original.

The original needs a deliberately boring identity: a tenant or property identifier, a receipt identifier, and a server-generated object key. The browser should not choose an arbitrary path. The metadata record should include the expected size, a content-type allowlist, creation time, processing state, retention class, and the audit reference that explains why the file is being held.

The failure mode I care about is a successful HTTP upload followed by an application timeout. If the client retries with a new key, the property system can retain two originals. If it retries with the same key, a partial or overwritten object can become indistinguishable from the accepted receipt. The fix is an idempotency key tied to the upload intent, plus a server-side state machine such as issued, uploaded, verified, retained, and deletion_pending. I initially treat this as a client-retry problem; the harder problem is deciding which copy the audit record is allowed to name after the timeout.

That state machine is an operational control, not decoration. A deletion request should record who or what initiated it, the reason, the object version or checksum where available, and the result. The worker that performs deletion must be safe to retry. A missing object is not automatically a mystery; it can be a successful prior deletion, but the metadata must make that conclusion auditable.

Where does CORS stop helping?

CORS answers a narrow browser question: may JavaScript from this origin make this cross-origin request, and which response headers may it read? It does not authenticate the person, decide which receipt key is legal, or stop a client from retaining a local copy. It also does not turn a public object into a private one.

For direct upload, configure the smallest practical origin set, methods, request headers, and exposed response headers. Keep the upload capability short-lived and scoped to one object key. The API that mints it should check the authenticated property-management action, not trust an object name supplied by the browser.

Here is the control path in Go. The storage interface is intentionally generic, because the important contract is the state transition and cleanup behavior, not a provider-specific SDK.

type ReceiptStore interface {
\tPutUploadIntent(ctx context.Context, intent UploadIntent) error
\tMarkUploaded(ctx context.Context, receiptID string, size int64) error
\tDeleteOriginal(ctx context.Context, objectKey string) error
}

func IssueUpload(ctx context.Context, store ReceiptStore, receiptID string) (string, error) {
\tkey := "receipts/" + receiptID + "/original"
\tintent := UploadIntent{
\t\tReceiptID: receiptID,
\t\tObjectKey: key,
\t\tState:     "issued",
\t\tMaxBytes:  10 * 1024 * 1024,
\t}
\tif err := store.PutUploadIntent(ctx, intent); err != nil {
\t\treturn "", err
\t}
\treturn SignScopedUpload(ctx, key, intent.MaxBytes)
}

The 10 MiB value is an example policy, not a universal limit. Capacity planning starts with the actual receipt distribution, retry rate, quarantine duration, and retention schedule. I would alert on pending uploads, verification age, deletion age, and bytes retained by lifecycle class; aggregate storage size alone hides a stuck state machine.

How should cloud storage support direct browser uploads?

A comparison is a test checklist, not a winner's podium. Each candidate has to be tested against the same browser origin, upload headers, object-key rules, lifecycle semantics, deletion observability, export path, and incident tooling. A CORS example copied from one service can still fail when its allowed headers, endpoint shape, or signed-request rules differ.

Decision boundary What to verify before adoption Why it matters for receipts
Browser upload Preflight behavior, allowed methods and headers, exposed response headers A failed preflight looks like an application outage while leaving no receipt record
Original retention Lifecycle rules, legal hold behavior, versioning, and deletion timing Processing success must not silently authorize deletion
Portability Object export, metadata preservation, checksums, and readable audit records A retention policy is weaker if the evidence cannot be moved or inspected
Operations Metrics, event delivery, retry behavior, and access logs SLOs need signals for missing, duplicated, and late receipts

The table is the easy part.

The build-versus-managed decision is also less binary than it sounds. A managed object store removes much of the durability machinery, while the application still owns identity, authorization, validation, retention classification, and evidence. Self-hosting can expose more control over placement and deletion workflows, but it transfers capacity planning, repair, replication, and on-call work to the platform team. I would reject any design whose cost model counts bytes but omits operator hours and recovery testing. The limitation is material: a managed service cannot decide whether a receipt is under dispute, while a self-hosted system cannot outsource its repair queue merely by exposing an S3-shaped API.

Retention is the primary decision axis here. Start with classes such as quarantine, active_audit, and eligible_for_deletion, then attach an owner and an exit condition to every class. Do not use a bucket-wide expiry as the only policy when a receipt may be under dispute. A lifecycle rule can be a backstop; it should not be the only record of why a file disappeared.

How do I make deletion observable and repeatable?

The deletion worker should consume a durable command or scheduled record, acquire the receipt's current state, and refuse to delete an object that is still required by policy. It should emit a result for both success and a provider-reported absence. Retries need bounded backoff and a dead-letter path with an owner.

func DeleteIfEligible(ctx context.Context, store ReceiptStore, r Receipt) error {
\tif r.State != "deletion_pending" || r.HoldReason != "" {
\t\treturn nil
\t}
\tif err := store.DeleteOriginal(ctx, r.ObjectKey); err != nil {
\t\treturn fmt.Errorf("delete receipt %s: %w", r.ID, err)
\t}
\treturn MarkDeleted(ctx, r.ID, time.Now().UTC())
}

This path has an important boundary: it does not prove that every replica, cache, browser download, or exported backup vanished. The application can prove that its controlled object and audit record reached the intended state. The retention policy must say what that proof covers. GDPR Article 20 also makes portability a real design consideration for data subjects, so an export format and metadata mapping deserve tests rather than a last-minute script.

A practical test matrix includes a denied preflight, an expired upload capability, a duplicate idempotency key, a truncated object, a content-type mismatch, a worker crash after verification, a deletion retry, and a hold placed while deletion is pending. Run the same matrix against each candidate endpoint. The test is more valuable than a feature comparison because it exercises the exact browser and retention boundary this system depends on.

The decision I would put in the design record

Choose the storage boundary whose CORS behavior, retention controls, portability, and operational signals meet the receipt policy with the fewest application-specific exceptions. Do not choose from a price table first. The storage bill is only one input; the harder cost is an incomplete deletion proof, a duplicate original, or an audit trail that cannot explain a missing file. A provider is not suitable when its lifecycle or export behavior forces the application to invent an exception to the retention policy.

For this workflow, the durable invariant is simple: processing may add derived data, but it must never silently rewrite the original or advance it past its retention obligation. CORS gets bytes from a browser to storage. The state machine, policy owner, and deletion record decide what those bytes mean later.

Sources

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • https://gdpr-info.eu/art-20-gdpr/
