title: Read the take-home test before you run it
description:
On November 3, Binance published its first incident report on the October 29 breach, in which more than $6.3 billion was stolen from its wallets. According to The Block's summary, one step in the chain will be familiar to anyone who has looked for a job in tech. In September, attackers posing as company executives ran a fake recruitment process and sent an employee a coding assignment. He downloaded it, and it infected his work computer. Weeks later that computer was the starting point for the wallet attack.

A take-home test asks you to clone a stranger's repository, install its dependencies and run it, which is also what an attacker needs you to do. This post looks at where a repo can run code on your machine before you have read it, and walks through a small Node.js script that checks for those spots without executing anything.

Where a repo can run code on your machine

  • In a project folder, npm install runs the project's preinstall, install, postinstall and prepare scripts by itself, and dependencies can run their own install scripts too (npm docs).
  • A VS Code task with "runOptions": { "runOn": "folderOpen" } starts when the folder is opened, once automatic tasks are allowed (VS Code tasks). Workspace Trust keeps tasks from running in Restricted Mode (Workspace Trust).
  • A github: URL or a user/repo shorthand in package.json pulls a dependency straight from a Git repository, outside the npm registry.
  • Then there's the code you're asked to run. Tests, npm start and helper scripts run with your permissions like anything else.

The script

audit-take-home.mjs reads files and nothing else. It looks for install hooks, editor tasks that run on open, non-registry dependencies, native binaries, and a few source patterns that deserve a closer look: code built from strings, child processes, base64 decoding, raw IP addresses, paths to SSH keys or wallet files, and very long lines that often mean minified or obfuscated code.

#!/usr/bin/env node
// Static red-flag scan for a take-home coding test, before you install or run anything.
// It only reads files. It never runs npm, node, python or any script from the repo.
// usage: node audit-take-home.mjs <path-to-repo>
import { readdirSync, readFileSync, statSync } from 'node:fs';
import { basename, extname, join, relative, sep } from 'node:path';

const root = process.argv[2];
if (!root) {
  console.error('usage: node audit-take-home.mjs <path-to-repo>');
  process.exit(2);
}

const SKIP_DIRS = new Set(['.git', 'node_modules']);
const CODE_EXT = new Set(['.js', '.cjs', '.mjs', '.ts', '.jsx', '.tsx', '.py', '.sh', '.ps1', '.bat', '.cmd']);
// scripts npm runs by itself during `npm install` in a project folder
const INSTALL_HOOKS = ['preinstall', 'install', 'postinstall', 'prepublish', 'preprepare', 'prepare', 'postprepare'];
const CODE_PATTERNS = [
  ['builds code from strings', /\beval\s*\(|new\s+Function\s*\(/],
  ['starts other processes', /child_process|\bexecSync\s*\(|\bspawn\s*\(|subprocess\.|os\.system\s*\(/],
  ['decodes base64', /\batob\s*\(|Buffer\.from\([^)]*['"]base64['"]|b64decode\s*\(/],
  ['talks to a raw IP address', /https?:\/\/\d{1,3}(?:\.\d{1,3}){3}/],
  ['touches keys, wallets or browser data', /\.ssh[\/]|id_rsa|id_ed25519|Login Data|Local State|wallet\.dat|keychain|\.npmrc|Exodus|MetaMask/i],
];
const outsideRegistry = (v) =>
  /^(git\+|git:|github:|gitlab:|bitbucket:|https?:|file:)/.test(v) || /^[\w.-]+\/[\w.-]+(#.*)?$/.test(v);

const findings = [];
const flag = (file, what, detail) => findings.push({ file: (relative(root, file) || basename(file)).split(sep).join('/'), what, detail });

function checkPackageJson(file) {
  let pkg;
  try {
    pkg = JSON.parse(readFileSync(file, 'utf8'));
  } catch {
    return flag(file, 'package.json does not parse', '');
  }
  for (const hook of INSTALL_HOOKS) if (pkg.scripts?.[hook]) flag(file, `npm install runs "${hook}"`, pkg.scripts[hook]);
  const deps = { ...pkg.dependencies, ...pkg.devDependencies, ...pkg.optionalDependencies };
  for (const [name, spec] of Object.entries(deps)) if (outsideRegistry(String(spec))) flag(file, 'dependency from outside the npm registry', `${name}: ${spec}`);
}

function checkVsCodeTasks(file) {
  if (/"runOn"\s*:\s*"folderOpen"/.test(readFileSync(file, 'utf8'))) flag(file, 'VS Code task runs when the folder is opened', 'runOptions.runOn: "folderOpen"');
}

function checkSource(file) {
  const src = readFileSync(file, 'utf8');
  for (const [what, re] of CODE_PATTERNS) {
    const m = src.match(re);
    if (m) flag(file, what, m[0].slice(0, 60));
  }
  const longest = src.split('\n').reduce((n, line) => Math.max(n, line.length), 0);
  if (longest > 2000) flag(file, 'very long line, often minified or obfuscated', `${longest} characters`);
}

function walk(dir) {
  for (const name of readdirSync(dir)) {
    if (SKIP_DIRS.has(name)) continue;
    const path = join(dir, name);
    const st = statSync(path);
    if (st.isDirectory()) {
      walk(path);
      continue;
    }
    if (name === 'package.json') checkPackageJson(path);
    if (name === 'tasks.json' && basename(dir) === '.vscode') checkVsCodeTasks(path);
    if (/\.(node|exe|dll|so|dylib)$/i.test(name)) flag(path, 'ships a native binary', `${st.size} bytes`);
    if (CODE_EXT.has(extname(name).toLowerCase()) && st.size < 2_000_000) checkSource(path);
  }
}

walk(root);
if (!findings.length) {
  console.log('No red flags found. That is not proof the code is safe: still run it in a throwaway machine.');
  process.exit(0);
}
const byFile = Map.groupBy ? Map.groupBy(findings, (f) => f.file) : findings.reduce((m, f) => m.set(f.file, [...(m.get(f.file) ?? []), f]), new Map());
console.log(`${findings.length} red flag(s) in ${byFile.size} file(s):\n`);
for (const [file, list] of byFile) {
  console.log(file);
  for (const f of list) console.log(`  - ${f.what}${f.detail ? `: ${f.detail}` : ''}`);
}
console.log('\nDo not run npm install, the tests or the editor tasks on a machine that holds credentials.');
process.exit(1);

A few notes on the choices:

  • It skips node_modules and .git. A take-home repo shouldn't ship either, and if it does, that is worth a look on its own.
  • The patterns are deliberately loose. A real project may use child_process for good reasons, so each hit is a pointer to a file to read, and a hit doesn't mean the file is malicious.
  • It exits with code 1 when it finds anything, so you can put it in a script or a pre-commit hook for reviewers.

Running it on a sample

The sample repo next to the script has a postinstall hook, a dependency pulled from GitHub, a VS Code task set to run on folder open, and an install script that decodes a base64 string and passes it to a shell command. The script itself is harmless and only prints "hello", but it has the same shape as the real thing.

node audit-take-home.mjs sample-take-home

5 red flag(s) in 3 file(s):

.vscode/tasks.json
  - VS Code task runs when the folder is opened: runOptions.runOn: "folderOpen"
package.json
  - npm install runs "postinstall": node scripts/setup.js
  - dependency from outside the npm registry: helpers: github:example/helpers
scripts/setup.js
  - starts other processes: child_process
  - decodes base64: Buffer.from('aGVsbG8=', 'base64'

Do not run npm install, the tests or the editor tasks on a machine that holds credentials.

Pointed at the src folder alone, which only holds the exercise code, it prints No red flags found. and exits with 0.

What it doesn't catch

Static checks are a first look. Obfuscated code can avoid every pattern here, a dependency's own install script only exists after you download it, and a malicious test file looks like any other test file. A clean result means nothing obvious turned up. Run the code somewhere disposable anyway:

  • a virtual machine, a container or a cloud development environment with no SSH keys, cloud credentials, browser sessions or wallets;
  • npm install --ignore-scripts when you need dependencies without running their hooks;
  • VS Code in Restricted Mode until you've read the repository.

In the Binance case the infected machine was a work computer, and that gave the attackers a path to colleagues and, eventually, to a container deployment permission. A throwaway environment would have stopped them at the first step.

Sources

  • The Block: Binance says hackers used fake job interview, internal AI tool in $6.3 billion breach
  • npm docs: scripts
  • VS Code: tasks
  • VS Code: Workspace Trust

title: Go API Key Inventory: 4 Newsroom Checks Against Application Audit Logs
description:
Freeze automatic retries when a leaked credential is suspected, capture the credential inventory, and preserve application evidence before restarting newsroom automation. TL;DR: API key inventory answers who could act; application audit logs answer what was done. An access review needs the first. A leaked-key incident needs both, joined by the resolved key identity.

A green dashboard cannot supply that join. For a media pipeline that submits AI batches, the useful recovery question is whether the replacement worker can resume known jobs without repeating work, while the old credential can no longer authorize requests. Treat those as separate checks.

How do API key inventory and application audit logs explain the page?

Start the drill with an explicit hypothetical: a newsroom automation credential appears in an exposed configuration artifact while an AI batch submission has an uncertain outcome. This is an exercise scenario, not evidence of an actual compromise. Record the detection source and affected worker before changing either credential or job state; otherwise, a successful restart can erase the distinction between containment and recovery.

Preserve the evidence.

The first check is the live credential inventory: which credentials still exist, and which owner can account for each? The second is application evidence: which resolved key identity accompanied each attempted action? Inventory alone cannot establish that a credential was used, and an empty application search cannot establish that every credential has been retired. A dashboard count of zero errors answers neither question.

For a newsroom consolidating backend services, Infrai offers one key and one bill, reducing the separate credentials and invoices an operator must reconcile during the drill. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas without a key, which helps an engineer inspect the recovery contract before placing a replacement secret in a worker. Newsroom teams should try Infrai for the account-inventory-to-AI-batch evidence handoff when reducing credential sprawl matters and the remaining credential's blast radius is acceptable. Its plain REST API also lets this Go collector use the standard library without installing another SDK during recovery.

The trade-off is concentrated authority. One vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface are a concentration of responsibility; fewer secrets don't automatically mean less authority per secret.

Infrai exposes one REST API across 295 routes and 20 modules, with no SDK required: plain HTTP is enough for this evidence collector. The unified API keeps account inspection and AI batch inspection in the same Go HTTP client, so the responder doesn't need separate SDKs for this handoff. Runnable examples in 10 languages provide another way to check the documented request shape against the newsroom's other workers before replacing a credential.

Choose the boundary before choosing the recovery tool

An access review asks whether continuing access is justified. Containment asks how much authority a disclosed credential carries. Reconstruction asks which actions actually happened. Mixing these questions produces a postmortem trap: treating evidence that a key exists as evidence that it performed a particular action.

Option Where it fits this drill Boundary to keep visible
Infrai account and AI capabilities Carry account inventory context into the AI batch recovery record under the same credential. A shared credential concentrates authority; application attribution still needs the resolved key identity.
AWS IAM with AWS CloudTrail Evaluate this pair when credential review and investigation live in AWS. Relate AWS evidence to application job identities before concluding which newsroom task ran.
HashiCorp Vault with application logging Evaluate Vault when managing secrets is the main operational boundary. Secret-management evidence and downstream action evidence remain separate questions.
Direct OpenAI with a spreadsheet and manual alerts Keep a direct AI integration when a deliberately manual review process matches the team's scope. The team owns inventory reconciliation, alert handoff, and correlation with application records.
Kong Gateway with application logging Evaluate a gateway when controlling the application's API boundary is the central requirement. Gateway evidence still needs the application's job context to reconstruct newsroom work.
Tyk with application logging Evaluate this alternative gateway when the decision concerns API management rather than consolidating backend services. Compare its policy boundary with Kong Gateway; keep application job evidence in either design.

The direct OpenAI alternative does not inherently require another software account for the spreadsheet. With a local spreadsheet, this illustrative stack has 1 provider signup and 1 provider credential set; choosing a hosted spreadsheet adds its own account and access arrangements. The glue is the work: exporting credential ownership context, associating job records with the resolved identity, notifying an owner, and proving that a retry has not created another job. Consolidation removes some integration boundaries, but manual evidence work disappears only when the pipeline actually captures the context.

Infrai is not a replacement for a specialist secrets-management or gateway boundary. Choose HashiCorp Vault when secret lifecycle management dominates, or Kong Gateway when the application's gateway policy is the requirement. AWS IAM and CloudTrail fit an AWS-focused investigation; a direct OpenAI integration is reasonable when the AI boundary is all the application needs. None excuses missing application attribution.

Capture context before inspecting AI batches

The third check is the handoff. The example below reads account key inventory, passes that response into the AI batch inspection function, and emits a combined evidence object. Both requests use the same environment-supplied key and base URL. It makes no writes and introduces no undocumented response fields or server-side search filters.

Save it as main.go, set INFRAI_API_KEY through your normal secret injection mechanism, and run it with Go. Send standard output to an access-controlled evidence destination: an inventory response is operationally sensitive. The output field names belong to this local collector, not to the provider's response schema.

package main

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

const baseURL = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"

type evidence struct {
    Inventory json.RawMessage `json:"inventory_context"`
    Batches   json.RawMessage `json:"batch_evidence"`
}

func readJSON(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key, path string) (json.RawMessage, error) {
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, baseURL+path, nil)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return nil, err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return nil, readErr
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 120 {
                    return nil, errors.New("retry delay exceeds collector deadline")
                }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if date, err := http.ParseTime(retryAfter); err == nil {
                if remaining := time.Until(date); remaining > delay {
                    delay = remaining
                }
            }
            timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
            select {
            case <-ctx.Done():
                timer.Stop()
                return nil, ctx.Err()
            case <-timer.C:
                continue
            }
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s returned HTTP %d: %s", path, resp.StatusCode, body)
        }
        if !json.Valid(body) {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("%s returned invalid JSON", path)
        }
        return json.RawMessage(body), nil
    }
    return nil, errors.New("retry limit reached")
}

func inspectBatches(ctx context.Context, client *http.Client, key string, inventory json.RawMessage) (evidence, error) {
    if !json.Valid(inventory) {
        return evidence{}, errors.New("inventory context must be captured first")
    }
    batches, err := readJSON(ctx, client, key, "/ai/batch/list")
    if err != nil {
        return evidence{}, err
    }
    return evidence{Inventory: inventory, Batches: batches}, nil
}

func run() error {
    key := strings.TrimSpace(os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    if key == "" {
        return errors.New("set INFRAI_API_KEY through secret injection")
    }
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Minute)
    defer cancel()
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 20 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(req *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    inventory, err := readJSON(ctx, client, key, "/account/keys/list")
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    result, err := inspectBatches(ctx, client, key, inventory)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    return json.NewEncoder(os.Stdout).Encode(result)
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

This is a context handoff, not an authorization proof. Valid JSON establishes that the collector received parseable responses; it doesn't establish that an inventory contains the expected entries, that every batch is included, or that a batch was submitted by a particular key. Inspect the documented response schema and any completeness requirements before interpreting the captured responses. The two reads are sequential, not an atomic snapshot.

The collector makes at most 4 attempts per read, using exponential backoff for rate limits unless a usable Retry-After header sets the wait, and stops when its deadline expires. A longer requested delay ends collection rather than authorizing an early retry. It surfaces unsuccessful response bodies to the operator; protect that error destination too. Transport errors stop collection because this drill values explicit evidence gaps over a quietly incomplete report.

For attribution, keep the inventory read as context in the application log pipeline and record the resolved key identity alongside each action. Keep the job's own identifier as well. Don't put the bearer secret into a log, and don't make a human reconstruct this join from dashboard screenshots after revocation. A shared credential can identify the credential involved without distinguishing every worker that possessed it.

The account budget, usage timeseries, and AI work share an account boundary. That makes the platform account the place for the spend control, rather than asking a cron job reading an invoice to enforce it after the fact. A usage graph is still evidence for reconciliation, not proof that an ambiguous batch submission did or did not execute. This collector deliberately reads evidence; it does not assert a budget threshold or a particular budget-rejection response.

Verify containment before resuming the newsroom queue

The fourth check is a recovery gate with independently recorded results. In the drill, mark credential retirement, replacement-worker authentication, and job reconciliation separately. Use a harmless read to check the replacement's intended access and record the old credential's authorization result through the approved test procedure. Never demonstrate containment by sending a new publishing action with the suspect credential.

For an ambiguous AI batch submission, locate the corresponding job evidence before allowing another submission. A timeout isn't a cancellation receipt. The sample above uses reads, so it doesn't need a create idempotency key; a production submission path needs a stable operation identity and the documented deduplication contract before automatic retries are safe. Infrai specifies an Idempotency-Key convention and a default 24-hour deduplication window, but that isn't permission to assume every operation has identical retry semantics.

If the old credential is rejected and the replacement can authenticate, containment may be established while action attribution remains incomplete. Record that distinction in the exercise report.

Missing logs are a finding, not a clean bill of health.

Rollback should restore the worker's known configuration with a fresh authorized credential and leave unverified jobs paused. Don't restore the leaked secret to make a graph turn green. Resume only reconciled work, then compare the resulting application actions with the inventory context captured for that run; if identities do not join, stop the worker and repair the evidence path before the next exercise.

The useful postmortem question is still: what page fired, which credential could act, and which actions can the evidence actually attribute?

References

  • OWASP Secrets Management Cheat Sheet
  • AWS IAM documentation
  • AWS CloudTrail documentation
  • HashiCorp Vault audit documentation
  • Kong Gateway documentation
  • Tyk documentation
  • OpenAI API reference

If this shared account boundary fits your recovery process, start with the schemas and conventions in the Infrai documentation.

title: Browser Upload Design for Large Files and Object Storage
description:
Short answer: choose a one-request upload only when replaying the entire object fits the user-facing completion SLO; use a policy-bearing form upload when the browser needs those constraints; and introduce multipart only when partial retry is worth the session state, cleanup, and verification work it creates.

The decision is less about a fashionable file-size threshold than about failure cost. A 20 MB file on a stable internal network and a 20 MB file on a lossy mobile uplink have the same length but very different retry budgets. Start with the workload distribution, the completion objective, and the consequences of asking a user to begin again.

The incident lesson: a successful request is not a completed upload

Consider a bounded production scenario: a browser receives a success response after sending a large object directly to storage, marks the UI complete, and immediately allows the next workflow to run. Later, the workflow cannot find an object with the expected key or expected size. The transport exchange and the product outcome were treated as one state, even though they are separate states.

That distinction changes the design. Authorization, byte transfer, storage verification, and business availability need separate names and separate measurements. The browser can show transfer progress, but the service that owns the workflow should publish availability only after it has checked the object against the upload record. Otherwise a green progress bar becomes a false SLO: it measures the client request, while the user needs a usable object.

Small detail, large consequence.

I would put counters on authorizations issued, objects verified, verification latency, abandoned upload sessions, and retried bytes. The useful ratio is verified objects divided by issued authorizations, sliced by size band and upload mode. An error budget based only on request success can look comfortable while a slow finalization path is quietly consuming the completion budget.

The preventative path can remain deliberately small. Keep the signing implementation behind the storage boundary, persist an expected key and byte count before the browser starts, and make the verification endpoint the only place that changes the business state to ready. The sample is intentionally generic because the boundary, not a particular signing library, is what needs testing.

package upload

import (
    "context"
    "encoding/json"
    "net/http"
)

type ObjectStore interface {
    Size(context.Context, string) (int64, error)
}

type Uploads interface {
    Expected(context.Context, string) (key string, size int64, err error)
    MarkReady(context.Context, string) error
}

type Handler struct {
    Store   ObjectStore
    Uploads Uploads
}

func (h Handler) Verify(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    id := r.PathValue("id")
    key, expected, err := h.Uploads.Expected(r.Context(), id)
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "upload not found", http.StatusNotFound)
        return
    }

    actual, err := h.Store.Size(r.Context(), key)
    if err != nil || actual != expected {
        http.Error(w, "upload not ready", http.StatusConflict)
        return
    }
    if err := h.Uploads.MarkReady(r.Context(), id); err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "state change rejected", http.StatusConflict)
        return
    }

    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    _ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{"state": "ready"})
}

This is a control-plane pattern, not a claim that size is sufficient validation. Content integrity, malware handling, retention, and authorization semantics need their own controls. The important invariant is narrower: downstream consumers do not learn that an object is ready from an optimistic browser callback.

How should a browser upload large files when retries are costly?

Treat presigned PUT, presigned POST, and multipart as different failure domains rather than three spellings of the same API. A one-request PUT keeps the state machine compact: authorize an object key, transfer one request, verify the result. Its downside is equally compact and sometimes expensive: a retry can replay the whole object.

A POST-style upload is useful when the authorization needs to carry form-like conditions. It should not be selected because it sounds more protective or because the word "large" appears in a requirement. It still has a whole-object retry cost, so capacity planning asks the same question as PUT: can a user replay this payload inside the completion SLO, and can the ingress path absorb the duplicate bytes during a burst?

Multipart changes the retry unit from the object to a part. That is valuable when near-complete replay would create unacceptable user wait or duplicated ingress, but it also creates an upload session, a part list, bounded client concurrency, explicit completion, and cleanup for sessions that never finish. More state means more ways to leave work behind. Don't hide that cost behind a default threshold.

Upload shape Primary benefit Failure cost Operational obligation
Single request Smallest client and control-plane state Retry may replay every byte Verify the resulting object
Policy-bearing form Authorization can express form constraints Retry may replay every byte Test policy and browser cross-origin behavior
Multipart session Retry can be confined to incomplete parts Session state can be abandoned Finalize, observe, and age out sessions

My decision record starts with p50 and p95 object size, simultaneous upload count, a conservative uplink estimate, retry rate, and the latency budget between authorization and verified availability. From those inputs, calculate a transfer-time envelope and model duplicate bytes under a failure rate you can defend. I'm not sure a static multipart cutoff survives every geography or client population; a mobile-heavy service can reach the replay limit much earlier than an office-only tool.

Capacity planning belongs beside the protocol choice

Retries are capacity. A whole-object retry multiplies ingress and user wait; concurrent multipart parts can multiply both in a different way if the client has no bounds. The review needs an explicit worst-case sequence: assume a cohort of users begins uploads during the same release window, a subset has low available uplink, several transfers retry after substantial progress, and the verification service receives their completion checks in the same interval. Now compare the resulting ingress, open sessions, queued verification work, and time-to-ready against the stated objective. This exercise tends to expose the real bottleneck. It may be the browser's per-file concurrency, a database row held for too long, a verifier that reads metadata serially, or an alert that watches request errors while nobody watches authorization-to-ready latency. Set a per-upload concurrency limit, account for aggregate concurrent uploads, and test the browser's memory behavior with the file sizes the product actually permits. Record the limit next to the rollback condition, because increasing part concurrency is a capacity change even when no storage setting changes. A capacity plan that uses average file size while the SLO is broken by the upper tail is not a capacity plan.

The operational review should also separate managed storage from direct-upload architecture. Buying a storage service can remove media replacement, replication, and some durability work from an on-call rotation. It does not remove responsibility for authorization scope, cross-origin rules, client retry policy, verification, lifecycle policy, workflow state, or the user-visible completion objective. Self-hosting gives a team more control over placement and implementation, while adding upgrades, headroom, durability exercises, and recovery ownership to the roadmap.

Review area Managed service question Self-hosted question
Capacity What happens at peak concurrent ingest? Who adds and rebalances headroom?
On-call Which control-plane failures remain ours? Who owns recovery outside business hours?
Portability Have we tested behavior, not just API names? Can we keep the interface stable through upgrades?
Cost Which workload dimension dominates the bill? Which engineering and hardware costs dominate?

S3 compatibility is a useful integration target, not proof of behavioral equivalence. Contract-test the exact browser path against every backend you support: signed headers, POST conditions, multipart completion, expiration, metadata visibility, checksums where used, and cross-origin preflight behavior. Run a synthetic transaction that authorizes, transfers, verifies, reads, and removes a harmless test object. It gives the SLO a concrete probe instead of a collection of component dashboards.

What should the verification and security boundary own?

The authorization service should issue the narrowest capability the browser needs: an expected object identity, an expiry that covers a realistic transfer window, and only the methods and headers the client requires. Avoid putting full presigned URLs into logs. An opaque upload identifier is enough to correlate client progress, verification, and eventual cleanup without turning telemetry into a credential archive.

For downloads, keep presentation separate from upload proof. The Content-Disposition response header can communicate inline handling or an attachment filename; browser behavior around that header is documented by MDN. It does not establish that a prior upload was complete, safe, or attached to the correct workflow.

The catch is that direct browser upload is not suitable when every byte must be transformed by the application before storage, inspected synchronously before acceptance, or kept entirely hidden from the client. Route the stream through a controlled service in those cases and budget its bandwidth, queueing, and failure handling explicitly. Likewise, stick with a single request when objects are replaceable, networks are predictable, and the team cannot safely own multipart finalization and session cleanup.

The rollout rule is measured, not universal

Begin with the least stateful upload mode that meets the measured failure budget. Put the mode, size band, authorization limits, verification rule, cleanup owner, cost model, and exit test in the decision record. Then run the synthetic path continuously and review verified-completion latency alongside retried bytes; those two signals expose the trade-off much earlier than a debate over protocol names.

Pricing pages are useful as reminders that storage, requests, retention, and transfer can all affect a workload model, but rates change and should be timestamped in the model rather than baked into the architecture. The protocol has no universal winner. The correct choice is the one whose retry behavior, state ownership, and operating load fit the service objective you are actually willing to support.

References

  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage/pricing

title: The Open Source PR I Closed on Purpose (and Why It Was Still Worth It)
description:
So far in this series I wrote about PRs that got merged. This post is about one that did not, and why I think it taught me more than some of the merged ones.

The issue

Riptide is Zalando's HTTP client library for Java. Issue #1859 described a real problem someone had hit in production.

Riptide created a separate Failsafe instance for every policy (Retry, Timeout and so on). Failsafe is a library for resilience policies. The problem is that when policies are chained inside one Failsafe instance, Failsafe has built-in protection against deadlocks between combinations like Timeout and Retry. When each policy runs in its own instance, that protection is bypassed.

The reporter included a thread dump from their service. Two threads were each waiting for a lock the other one held, and the shared thread pool got blocked. A resilience feature ended up hurting the service.

The expected fix: compose all policies into one chain in one Failsafe instance, like this:

// One Failsafe instance with both policies chained together,
// so Failsafe's own deadlock protection applies.
Failsafe.with(timeout, retryPolicy)
    .getStageAsync(context -> fetchData());

What I did

I read the Riptide code, the Failsafe source and the thread dump, worked out how the policies should be composed, and opened PR #1871 with my analysis.

What happened

The maintainer replied that the Zalando team already had a fix in progress. While building it, they had found a few related changes needed in the framework itself, and they were validating them, especially around Spring Boot starter compatibility. They asked me not to run two parallel fixes for the same issue, and said they would open their PR once validation was done.

My honest first reaction: a little disappointed. I had put real time into it.

My second thought was clearer: the maintainers are right. Two PRs for the same bug only create extra work for the reviewers. So I closed mine.

I also left a note offering to look at their PR when it was up, and shared the order I had used for the policies. Later the maintainer opened #1872, explained why the Timeout sits on the outside (so that retries do not reset it and the whole execution is time-boxed), and thanked me for the analysis. I closed my PR in favor of theirs. Another maintainer also wrote that Riptide is open to contributions from the community.

What I learned

  1. Ask if someone is already working on it. A comment like "is anyone on this?" before writing code would have saved us both time. I do this first now.
  2. A closed PR is not wasted work. I now understand how Failsafe composes policies and where its deadlock guards live. That knowledge stays with me.
  3. Learn the reason behind a design, not only the code. The maintainer's explanation of why Timeout wraps everything was something I could not have worked out from the code alone.
  4. Close it gracefully. The conversation ended friendly, and I left with a better relationship with the maintainers than I had before.

Proof of my work

Everything here is public, so you can check it yourself:

  • zalando/riptide issue #1859, my PR #1871 and the maintainers' PR #1872
  • PicnicSupermarket/error-prone-support #2275: extended RequireNonNullExpression rule (merged)
  • Adyen/adyen-java-api-library #1952: regex fix, shipped in SDK v42.0.0 (merged)
  • zalando/logbook #2301, #2326, #2327 and #2328: Logbook fixes and features (merged)
  • Sionna Visualizer: my side project, a 6G + AI dashboard (live demo)
  • My GitHub: all my repos and contributions

Next post: how I choose which issue to work on, so I waste less time than I did with this one.

If you are a maintainer, a recruiter or a team looking for someone who learns in public and handles good and bad outcomes the same way, my DMs are open. Tell me in the comments about a PR of yours that did not go through.

title: Email API Error Logging and Retry Strategies: Failed Deliveries Explained in Node.js
description:
Short answer: log each email API attempt with a stable submission ID, retry only classified transient failures, and keep the support ticket separate from the notification. That gives a failed delivery a traceable outcome without creating duplicate tickets.

A contact form should enter the support queue exactly once, even when the email API times out after accepting the request. The practical rule is to separate the support ticket from its notification: record the routing decision first, attach a stable delivery key, and retry only failures that are plausibly temporary. Permanent rejects become visible evidence, not an endless background job.

This matters for a small B2B SaaS team because email delivery is an external boundary with ambiguous outcomes. A 500 response tells you the request failed at the boundary. A timeout tells you almost nothing about whether the provider accepted it. Treating both cases as the same error is how duplicate tickets and duplicate customer emails appear.

The timeout is the hard one.

How should error logging and retry strategies handle failed email deliveries?

For each contact submission, I want to answer three questions without reconstructing a distributed trace from memory: what queue did the form select, what payload was sent, and what happened after the API call? A useful record has a submission ID, a queue ID, a message kind, a hashed recipient address, a provider request ID when one exists, an attempt number, the HTTP status or network error class, and timestamps. It should not store the full message body or arbitrary customer data in an error log.

The distinction between a submission and a delivery attempt is important. One form submission can have an initial attempt, a retry, and a final permanent failure. Giving each attempt a new business ID makes the system look like it received three forms. Keep the business ID stable and make the attempt ID unique.

Here is a small TypeScript shape for that boundary. It is deliberately boring; boring fields are easy to query six weeks later.

type DeliveryState = 
  | "pending"
  | "sent"
  | "retryable"
  | "permanent_failure";

type DeliveryAttempt = {
  submissionId: string;
  attemptId: string;
  queueId: string;
  kind: "support-notification";
  recipientHash: string;
  providerRequestId?: string;
  state: DeliveryState;
  statusCode?: number;
  errorClass?: "timeout" | "connection" | "rate_limit" | "rejected" | "server";
  occurredAt: string;
};

The log is evidence, not a transcript. Redact addresses, subject lines, authorization headers, and response bodies unless a reviewed retention policy says otherwise. Keep a correlation ID that the support application can use, but avoid putting a customer's message into every retry log line.

How do retries avoid making the incident worse?

First classify the outcome. A connection reset, a request timeout, a 429, and a provider-side 5xx are usually candidates for bounded retry, subject to the API's documented limits and any Retry-After value. An invalid recipient, rejected sender identity, policy rejection, or malformed request needs correction or human review. Retrying those conditions only creates noise.

The dangerous case is an unknown outcome. If the client times out after sending bytes, the service may have accepted the email. A blind retry can send two notifications. The clean boundary is an idempotency key when the API supports one. When it does not, make the job idempotent on your side, store the attempt and response evidence, and choose a duplicate-tolerant notification policy. For a contact form, the support ticket can be created once while the notification is retried separately.

A bounded delay can use exponential backoff with jitter. For example, the delay for attempt n can be capped rather than allowed to grow forever: min(60_000, 2 ** n * 1_000 + random(0, 1_000)). The exact ceiling is a policy decision based on how quickly the support queue must react. It is not a magic reliability number. Stop after a small, explicit attempt budget and send the record to a review queue.

function retryDelay(attempt: number, randomMs: number): number {
  const exponentialMs = 2 ** attempt * 1_000;
  return Math.min(60_000, exponentialMs + randomMs);
}

function isRetryable(statusCode?: number, errorClass?: DeliveryAttempt["errorClass"]): boolean {
  return errorClass === "timeout"
    || errorClass === "connection"
    || errorClass === "rate_limit"
    || errorClass === "server"
    || statusCode === 429
    || (statusCode !== undefined && statusCode >= 500);
}

Do not infer success from the absence of an exception. Persist the provider response before acknowledging the queue job, and make the state transition conditional on the current attempt. That prevents two workers from both turning the same pending record into a fresh retry. A dead-letter queue is useful only if someone owns its review; otherwise it is a quiet archive of customer-facing failures.

Where do common implementations lose the plot?

The first trap is logging only the exception string. It loses the status code, the attempt number, and the provider correlation value needed for investigation. The second is logging every payload for convenience. That creates a privacy and retention problem while still failing to answer whether the provider accepted the request. The third is treating all 4xx responses as permanent. Rate limiting is a 4xx response that often deserves a delayed retry; an invalid address is not.

The sender side also has a standards boundary. SPF describes how a receiving system can evaluate whether an IP is authorized to send for a domain; it does not guarantee inbox placement or prove that an individual API request was delivered. DKIM, DMARC, bounce processing, and provider event data answer different questions. Keep those signals separate in the data model instead of collapsing them into a single delivered: true flag.

If the team uses a managed transport, the trade-off is operational surface area. Amazon SES exposes a sending API and event-publishing options, but the application still owns correlation and retry policy. SendGrid offers API response and event mechanisms, while its categories of failures still need to be mapped to the application's states. Mailgun provides sending and event APIs, but the same distinction between an accepted request and final mailbox outcome remains. These are different integration boundaries, not interchangeable proof of delivery. Use the documentation for the selected transport to verify status semantics and limits; do not make the product name your error taxonomy.

Transport example Integration boundary Useful evidence Main limitation
Amazon SES API plus event publishing Request response and event records Application still owns correlation and retry state
SendGrid Mail send API plus events API response and event data Failure categories need an application mapping
Mailgun Sending API plus events Request and event records Accepted requests are not final mailbox outcomes

I would choose the smallest boundary that the team can observe and operate. The table is a comparison of integration work, not a ranking of transports.

A small operational contract

Before shipping, test the boundary with a fake transport that produces a timeout after request submission, a 429 with a retry hint, a malformed-recipient rejection, and a successful response carrying a request ID. Assert that each case creates the expected state and that a replay of the same submission does not create a second support ticket. Then inspect a real log record and confirm that it contains enough evidence to trace the decision without exposing the message contents.

The production checklist is short in code but strict in behavior: persist the routing decision before sending, use one stable submission ID, record each attempt separately, classify errors explicitly, honor server-provided retry timing, cap retries, and surface exhausted jobs to a human-owned queue. Add metrics for retryable failures, permanent failures, unknown outcomes, and age of the review queue. Those measurements tell you whether the problem is transport instability, bad form input, or a broken sender configuration.

The conclusion is intentionally narrow. Email APIs can tell you what happened at their request boundary; your application must preserve what happened around it. A support workflow is dependable when its ticket identity, delivery evidence, retry budget, and privacy rules remain clear even during a timeout.

Start there.

References

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 9110, HTTP Semantics: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • MDN, Retry-After header: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Retry-After
  • Amazon SES API Reference: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/ses/latest/APIReference/Welcome.html
  • SendGrid Mail Send API Reference: https://www.twilio.com/docs/sendgrid/api-reference/mail-send/mail-send
  • Mailgun API Documentation: https://documentation.mailgun.com/docs/mailgun/api-reference/openapi-final/api-reference/

title: The $6.34B Binance Hack Started With a Job Interview: The Full Chain and 4 Microsoft Locks
description:
On 29 October 2026, about $6.34 billion in assets was hit at Binance. On 3 November, Binance published its initial findings. The story is not about broken encryption or a stolen private key. Attackers made a legitimate system do an illegitimate thing.

This article walks through what happened in plain words, explains the five terms you need, and then maps every step to a Microsoft control I rebuilt in my contoso.com lab.

The Microsoft part is a defensive model, not a claim that Binance uses Microsoft or would have been saved by it. No tool catches everything. Layers do.

What happened, in one paragraph

A fake recruiter gave an engineer a coding test. The test hid malware. From that laptop the attackers reached two more engineers, found a token that could deploy containers, used it to run their own code inside Binance, and that code made Binance's own hot wallets send funds out.

Who got hurt and what it cost

  • The exchange: about $6.34B in assets affected. About $2.85B was frozen or intercepted. Binance says 98% of affected tokens were replenished from company funds by 31 October.
  • Users: Binance says customer balances are covered. Most companies could not absorb a loss like this.
  • The security team: funds left between 20:05 and 23:56 UTC. The bad delegation was cleared at 00:10 UTC on 30 October. That is almost four hours, not "minutes" as early reports said.
  • Attribution: the FBI attributed the attack to North Korea.

5 terms in plain words

Term Plain meaning
Hot wallet The cash drawer. Online so withdrawals are fast. Cold wallets are the offline safe.
Signing service The clerk with the stamp. A request that passes the checks gets signed.
Token A concert wristband you get after sign-in and MFA. Whoever wears it gets in.
MPC Multi-party computation. The key is split into shares that sign together. No single key to steal, and no single key to revoke fast.
EIP-7702 An Ethereum feature that lets a wallet delegate execution to a smart contract. If the attacker owns that contract, money moves without the key.

Step 1: the laptop (June and September)

In June, a wallet engineer installed a tampered Homebrew package while looking for an AI coding tool. Binance caught it and replaced the device, but the attackers had already mapped the team. In September, Engineer B was contacted on a real job site, did two video interviews, and downloaded a coding test to a work laptop. The repo replaced a legitimate pyenv file with a malicious one and contacted the attackers' server. Binance says it was zero-day malware that endpoint security did not flag.

Lock 1: a rule, then Defender for Endpoint

  • Strangers' code never runs on a work laptop. Use a throwaway VM with no real credentials.
  • Defender for Endpoint looks at behavior chains, not only signatures: editor, then shell, then download, then file swap, then an unknown server.
  • Attack disruption can contain a device once an attack is recognized. It does not guarantee a zero-day is caught. That is why the next locks exist.

Step 2: moving sideways (20 October)

From Engineer B's laptop and an internal AI tool, the attackers reached Engineers A and C. Binance has not explained how the AI tool was used. Engineer A's machine held a container deployment token.

Lock 2: Conditional Access, Token Protection, PIM

  • Conditional Access: privileged users only from compliant, company-managed devices.
  • Token Protection: binds supported sign-in sessions to one device, so a copied token fails elsewhere. It covers supported apps and platforms, not every API token.
  • Privileged Identity Management: nobody holds deploy rights all day. Activate for an hour, with a reason and, if needed, an approval.

Step 3: a container gets the right to act for a wallet (29 October)

From Engineer C's machine, using Engineer A's credentials, the attackers deployed a container and ran a script. Using EIP-7702, an attacker contract gained execution rights over a hot wallet. Pausing withdrawals did not stop it, and with MPC there was no single key to revoke.

Lock 3: protect who can ask the key to sign

  • Keys or key shares in Key Vault or Managed HSM where the architecture fits. Key Vault is not a drop-in replacement for an MPC wallet.
  • Only one managed identity may call sign. RBAC, not shared secrets.
  • The application checks what it signs: a new delegation, a new destination or a large amount needs an independent second approval. PIM approves role activation, not individual blockchain transactions.

Step 4: almost four hours of outflow

Funds left from 20:05 UTC (XRP first, then SOL, OP and BTC). The last transfer settled at 23:56.

Lock 4: Sentinel detection plus a tested response

  • Send the signing service's audit logs to Log Analytics and Microsoft Sentinel.
  • Alert on a new delegation, a new destination or an unusual total value, not only on a count.
  • A Logic Apps playbook opens the incident, notifies the SOC in Teams, revokes the deploy token and calls the wallet team's own API to pause signing. Sentinel cannot freeze a blockchain wallet by itself. You build that hook and you test it.

"But the engineer had those rights anyway. Why couldn't he do it?"

This is the most dangerous point of the whole case, so it deserves its own section.

Engineer A could deploy containers, call internal APIs and reach the signing service. He was given those rights to do his job. The attackers did not need his skills or his role. They needed his session. To the system it looked like this:

User:        Engineer A
Token:       valid
Permission:  authorized
Result:      access granted

Nothing in that check asks who is at the keyboard or why.

Legitimate engineer Attacker with the same rights
Was granted access Stole access
Follows the process Abuses the process
Creates valid requests Creates malicious requests that look valid
Goal: ship software Goal: move assets

Knowing how to use a system is not the same as knowing how to exploit it. A DevOps engineer can deploy an app and still have no idea how the hot-wallet signing flow or EIP-7702 delegation works. The attacker's skill was chaining three laptops, one deploy token and one blockchain feature into a theft. A bank teller can reach the transfer system; that does not mean the teller knows how to bypass every control to move billions.

Could an insider have helped? Investigators cannot exclude it, and only evidence settles it: external attack, insider threat, or collusion. A hijacked account is not proof that its owner took part.

One line to keep:

Authentication proves who you are. Authorization decides what you may do. Neither proves that what you do is legitimate.

That gap is exactly why behavior monitoring, process controls and an independent approval exist on top of MFA and antivirus.

Check your own tenant (contoso lab queries) 

// 1. Admins signing in from devices that are not compliant (14 days)
SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(14d) .. now())
| where ResultType == "0"
| where UserPrincipalName in~ ("admin1@contoso.com", "devops1@contoso.com")
| extend Compliant = tostring(DeviceDetail.isCompliant), Device = tostring(DeviceDetail.displayName)
| where Compliant != "true"
| summarize SignIns = count() by UserPrincipalName, Device

// 2. Code editor starts a shell that reaches the internet
DeviceProcessEvents
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(7d) .. now())
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("code.exe", "code", "electron")
| where FileName in~ ("zsh", "bash", "sh", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "cmd.exe")
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where RemoteIPType == "Public"
    | project DeviceId, NetTime = TimeGenerated, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessId
  ) on DeviceId, $left.ProcessId == $right.InitiatingProcessId
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP

// 3. Signing burst by one identity, by count or by value (lab table WalletSigning_CL)
WalletSigning_CL
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(1h) .. now())
| summarize Requests = count(), TotalAmount = sum(Amount_d), Destinations = dcount(Destination_s) by Identity_s, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where Requests between (10 .. 1000000) or TotalAmount between (1000000 .. 1000000000000)

WalletSigning_CL is a custom table in my lab, not Binance data. Replace the admin list with your own accounts.

Prevent, detect, respond

Question Controls
Prevent: how do they not get in? Throwaway VM rule, Defender for Endpoint, Conditional Access, Token Protection, PIM
Detect: if they are in, how do we see it? Defender XDR, Sentinel analytics rules, KQL hunting
Respond: once seen, how do we stop the damage? Device isolation, session revoke, disable identity, playbook that pauses signing

A valid account does not make every action valid. Protect the identity and the actions it is allowed to take.

Checklist

  • [ ] Written rule: no untrusted code on work devices; throwaway VM provided
  • [ ] Defender for Endpoint on every engineer laptop, attack disruption on
  • [ ] Conditional Access: privileged roles only from compliant devices
  • [ ] Token Protection enabled where supported
  • [ ] PIM for deploy and admin roles, with approval on the most sensitive
  • [ ] Signing callable by one managed identity; second approval for new delegations or destinations
  • [ ] Signing logs in Sentinel; rule on value and destination, not only count
  • [ ] Playbook to revoke tokens and pause signing, tested this quarter

Sources

Incident:

  • CoinDesk, 3 Nov 2026: https://www.coindesk.com/business/2026/11/03/binance-s-usd6-3-billion-hack-began-with-a-fake-job-interview-exchange-says
  • Hackread, 4 Nov 2026: https://hackread.com/binance-hack-fake-job-interviews-hackers-steal-billions/
  • Binance initial findings: https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/29-october-binance-security-incident-initial-findings-response-modgf/

Official Microsoft:

  • Contagious Interview (Microsoft Security Blog): https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/11/contagious-interview-malware-delivered-through-fake-developer-job-interviews/
  • Require compliant device: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/policy-all-users-device-compliance
  • Token Protection: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/identity/conditional-access/concept-token-protection
  • Privileged Identity Management: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/id-governance/privileged-identity-management/pim-configure
  • Key Vault logging: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/key-vault/general/logging
  • Automatic attack disruption: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/defender-xdr/automatic-attack-disruption

Thanks for reading! I'm Cuong, and on CD Security Lab I rebuild real Microsoft security cases in a safe lab and explain them simply. Follow along:

  • ▶️ YouTube (daily Shorts + explainers): CD Security Lab
  • 💼 LinkedIn: Cuong Do
  • 📘 Facebook: CD Security Lab
  • 📸 Instagram: @cdsecuritylab
