title: Go Email Integration: How to Diagnose DKIM Verification Failures in 2026
description:
For a developer tools service, resolve DKIM verification failures at the sending-domain boundary, and suppress a recipient only when the delivery evidence supports a recipient-level decision. Mixing those two decisions can turn a signing configuration mistake into an expanding list of incorrectly blocked developers.

TL;DR: inspect the actual message signature and the receiving system's authentication result, reconcile the selector with DNS, and then investigate signed-content changes. Keep this investigation separate from bounce classification. The decision below favors a small normalized evidence model because integration effort increases whenever provider-specific authentication labels leak into recipient state.

How should an email service handle DKIM verification failures?

The invariant is simple: a failed authentication check must not, by itself, mark an address invalid. RFC 6376 defines DKIM as a mechanism through which a signing domain claims responsibility for a message; it does not establish that the recipient exists, that the visible author is trustworthy, or that delivery will succeed. SPF evaluates a different identity and authorization relationship under RFC 7208. A passing SPF result therefore does not repair a failing DKIM signature.

Keep those boundaries.

Consider a proposed deployment-notification service that sends build failure alerts to developers. Its evidence record should distinguish a message identifier, recipient, signing domain, selector, authentication result, delivery status, and ingestion identifier. These are separate fields because an investigation may discover a common selector error across many messages while finding an invalid recipient in only one delivery attempt. Storing a single “email failed” flag discards the information needed to reconcile those cases.

An exactly-once mindset belongs at the state-transition boundary: one authenticated event identifier should cause at most one committed transition, with an audit record explaining the decision. It does not justify claiming exactly-once transport. Duplicate delivery, delayed feedback, and a failure between persistence and acknowledgment must remain explicit failure boundaries in the design.

Step 1: collect the signature before changing DNS

Start with a received message's original headers and body, rather than a screenshot of a domain setup page. Under RFC 6376, the signature's d= identifies the signing domain and s= identifies the selector; the public-key lookup uses the selector followed by ._domainkey. and that domain. For the illustrative values d=notify.example.org and s=release, investigate release._domainkey.notify.example.org. Do not substitute the visible From domain merely because it looks related.

Record the receiving system's result alongside that signature. RFC 8601 defines Authentication-Results, including its trust-boundary considerations: an arbitrary header supplied by an untrusted sender is not trustworthy evidence of verification. For this workflow, accept authentication results only from the receiving infrastructure whose assessment you intend to rely on.

The order of investigation matters. First establish whether the receiver found a usable key at the correct owner name. Then compare the published key with the key associated with the sender's active selector. Finally inspect canonicalization and whether signed headers or the body changed after signing. RFC 6376 specifies both body-hash verification and signature verification, so a body-hash mismatch is a reason to investigate message transformation; it is not sufficient evidence that the DNS record is wrong.

A selector is evidence, not decoration.

DNS TXT records also require care: RFC 6376 specifies concatenating character strings within a TXT resource record before use. Treating those strings as separate keys can produce a misleading diagnosis. When a record changes, retain the queried name, observation time, and resolver context in the investigation record; a subsequent observation should establish whether the receiver can see the intended record before the domain is declared healthy. Avoid promising a universal propagation interval.

Step 2: choose where evidence becomes recipient state

The operational decision is where to normalize feedback. This comparison concerns implementation choices for the notification service, rather than commercial products.

Approach Integration work Failure boundary Suitable use
Translate authenticated delivery events into a local evidence model Write and test one adapter per event source; keep application decisions stable Incorrect translation can misclassify a delivery result A service that needs recipient suppression and an explanation for each change
Parse delivery status notifications directly Handle message structure, per-recipient results, and enhanced status codes A message-level outcome can obscure different recipient outcomes Teams that need access to standards-based delivery reports
Maintain suppression manually Build little initial ingestion code; require an operator for each decision Slow or inconsistent updates as event volume grows Small investigations and exceptional corrections

RFC 3464 describes delivery status notifications, and RFC 3463 defines enhanced status codes. The latter distinguishes address status from security or policy status: 5.1.1 means a bad destination mailbox address, while 5.7.1 means delivery is not authorized and the message was refused. Both are permanent-failure codes, but they do not support the same recipient-state transition.

That distinction is the critical integration contract. An adapter should retain the reported status and supporting context instead of converting every permanent failure into “invalid address.” A temporary failure should remain outside permanent suppression, and an unclassified rejection should enter investigation rather than silently acquiring a recipient-level meaning. The narrow rule used below intentionally sacrifices classification coverage for an auditable reason to suppress.

Step 3: implement the critical transition in Go

This complete Go program is a deterministic rehearsal of the decision boundary. Run it as a standalone program: it checks that a DKIM-related policy rejection leaves the recipient eligible, that an explicit bad-mailbox result suppresses it, and that replaying the same event adds no audit entry.

The input is already normalized evidence from a trusted adapter.

The example does not authenticate incoming webhooks or infer a delivery status from a free-text error. Those responsibilities precede this function. The trade-off is reduced classification coverage in exchange for a smaller decision surface: this implementation suppresses only the explicit mailbox-invalid status because treating every permanent failure as address evidence would conflate authentication policy with recipient validity. This approach is not suitable for deployments that require automatic handling of every address-related status; those deployments need additional reviewed classification rules and corresponding evidence fixtures before enabling suppression.

package main

import "fmt"

type Event struct {
    Source    string
    ID        string
    Recipient string
    DKIM      string
    Status    string
}

type EventKey struct {
    Source string
    ID     string
}

type Decision struct {
    Event  Event
    Action string
    Reason string
}

type Store struct {
    Seen       map[EventKey]bool
    Suppressed map[string]bool
    Audit      []Decision
}

func (s *Store) Apply(e Event) (bool, error) {
    if e.Source == "" || e.ID == "" || e.Recipient == "" {
        return false, fmt.Errorf("missing evidence identity")
    }

    key := EventKey{Source: e.Source, ID: e.ID}
    if s.Seen[key] {
        return false, nil
    }

    action := "retain"
    reason := "no recipient-invalidity evidence"
    if e.Status == "5.1.1" {
        action = "suppress"
        reason = "bad destination mailbox address"
        s.Suppressed[e.Recipient] = true
    }

    s.Audit = append(s.Audit, Decision{
        Event: e, Action: action, Reason: reason,
    })
    s.Seen[key] = true
    return true, nil
}

func main() {
    s := Store{
        Seen:       make(map[EventKey]bool),
        Suppressed: make(map[string]bool),
    }
    recipient := "build-owner@example.net"
    policy := Event{
        Source: "delivery-adapter",
        ID: "notification-policy",
        Recipient: recipient,
        DKIM: "fail",
        Status: "5.7.1",
    }
    if _, err := s.Apply(policy); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if s.Suppressed[recipient] {
        panic("policy rejection suppressed a recipient")
    }

    invalid := Event{
        Source: "delivery-adapter",
        ID: "notification-invalid-mailbox",
        Recipient: recipient,
        DKIM: "pass",
        Status: "5.1.1",
    }
    if _, err := s.Apply(invalid); err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if !s.Suppressed[recipient] {
        panic("invalid mailbox was not suppressed")
    }

    before := len(s.Audit)
    changed, err := s.Apply(invalid)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    if changed || len(s.Audit) != before {
        panic("replayed event changed state")
    }
    fmt.Println("policy retained; mailbox suppressed; replay ignored")
}

The two different event identifiers matter. Deduplicating on recipient alone would discard later evidence about the same address. The source is part of the key because independent integrations need not share an event-ID namespace. The adapter contract must additionally require that a replay preserves the event's meaning; a reused identifier with a conflicting payload warrants investigation rather than an unrecorded overwrite.

The durability limitation is deliberate.

This in-memory implementation has no restart durability or concurrency protection. Before deployment, persist the deduplication key, recipient mutation, and audit entry in one transaction, enforce uniqueness on the key, and acknowledge ingestion only after commit. A queue acknowledgment cannot substitute for that transaction. If two workers can accept the same event concurrently, the database constraint must arbitrate their writes.

Use a recipient identifier scoped to the application's tenant and sending policy in that persistent design. The one-recipient example deliberately omits those dimensions; a shared deployment must define them before deciding whether one tenant's delivery result can affect another tenant's notifications. Likewise, checking suppression before enqueueing leaves a race with already queued messages, so the sending worker needs a current suppression check under the application's stated consistency policy.

Step 4: verify recovery and record the rejected shortcut

Deploy the adapter in observation mode first: record proposed transitions, compare them with the underlying delivery evidence, and enable writes only after policy rejections and invalid-mailbox outcomes remain distinguishable. Track authentication failures by signing domain and selector, while tracking suppression decisions by their evidence and reason. A sudden concentration under one selector calls for a signing investigation; it should not automatically change the recipient-validity rule.

Recovery requires fresh evidence.

Send a fresh message signed through the production path and obtain a trusted receiver's verification result. Rechecking DNS alone does not establish that the sender used the intended key or that a later processing stage preserved the signed content. For a build alert, verify both authentication evidence and the delivery outcome.

Neither proves that the developer read the notification.

The rejected shortcut is automatic suppression after every permanent rejection. Its valid use case is narrower: temporarily holding outbound work during investigation, with an explicit release policy and without labeling those addresses invalid. A hold limits sending while evidence is incomplete; permanent recipient suppression asserts something more specific.

Finally, keep the audit trail proportionate. RFC 6376 does not establish regulatory compliance, and authentication evidence alone cannot establish consent, authorization to retain recipient data, or a lawful retention period. Define access, retention, and deletion rules for identifiers and message evidence under the obligations applicable to the service. Preserve the decision reason without collecting complete message bodies by default.

The acceptance criterion is a reconciled transition: a known event, a defensible classification, a durable decision, and enough evidence to explain it later. That criterion keeps DKIM recovery and invalid-recipient suppression independently testable while containing the integration work.

References

  • RFC 6376, DomainKeys Identified Mail Signatures: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6376
  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 8601, Message Header Field for Indicating Message Authentication Status: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8601
  • RFC 3463, Enhanced Mail System Status Codes: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3463
  • RFC 3464, An Extensible Message Format for Delivery Status Notifications: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3464

title: reset() Inside onSubmit Only Half-Resets a React Hook Form. Here's What Stays Behind
description:
You save a form, call reset() in your submit handler, and the inputs go blank. Looks done. Then the user starts typing the next entry and a red "Title needs 3+ chars" shows up while they're still typing, on a form that's supposed to be fresh.

The values were reset. The submission state wasn't.

Why it happens

The React Hook Form reset docs spell this out in their rules: "Avoid calling reset inside onSubmit. handleSubmit updates isSubmitted, isSubmitSuccessful and submitCount after your handler finishes, so a reset there clears the values but not the submission state."

So the order is: your handler runs, reset() clears everything, then handleSubmit finishes and writes "submitted, successful, count +1" back on top. And once isSubmitted is true, the default reValidateMode: 'onChange' kicks in, which is why errors start firing while the user types.

What I ran

I wanted to see the exact state, so I rendered a one-field form in jsdom with Testing Library and drove it with user-event: React 19.3.1, react-hook-form 7.91.0, zod 4.6.7, @hookform/resolvers 7.0.2, Node 20.19.2. The schema is z.object({ title: z.string().min(3) }). I ran three versions: reset() inside a sync onSubmit, inside an async one (awaits a 20 ms timer first), and the useEffect version from the docs.

Here's the state right after a successful save, and after typing "ab" into the now-empty field without submitting:

After save Error after typing "ab"
reset() in sync onSubmit isSubmitted: true, isSubmitSuccessful: true, submitCount: 1 "Title needs 3+ chars"
reset() in async onSubmit isSubmitted: true, isSubmitSuccessful: true, submitCount: 1 "Title needs 3+ chars"
reset() in useEffect isSubmitted: false, isSubmitSuccessful: false, submitCount: 0 none

Async made no difference. And submitCount never really climbs with the in-handler version: after the second save it was back at 1, because reset() zeroes it and handleSubmit adds one. If you use submitCount for anything, like "show the hint after two failed tries", that's quietly wrong.

One thing I couldn't reproduce: errors getting stuck. In every version, a too-short title showed the error and fixing it cleared it. What changes is when validation starts, not whether it works.

The fix

Move the reset into an effect that watches isSubmitSuccessful. This is the docs' "Submit with Reset" pattern, with the schema from my test:

import { useEffect } from 'react';
import { useForm } from 'react-hook-form';
import { zodResolver } from '@hookform/resolvers/zod';
import { z } from 'zod';

const schema = z.object({ title: z.string().min(3, 'Title needs 3+ chars') });
type FormValues = z.infer<typeof schema>;

export function TaskForm({ save }: { save: (v: FormValues) => Promise<void> }) {
  const {
    register,
    handleSubmit,
    reset,
    formState: { errors, isSubmitSuccessful },
  } = useForm<FormValues>({
    resolver: zodResolver(schema),
    defaultValues: { title: '' },
  });

  useEffect(() => {
    if (isSubmitSuccessful) reset({ title: '' });
  }, [isSubmitSuccessful, reset]);

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(save)}>
      <input aria-label="title" {...register('title')} />
      {errors.title && <p>{errors.title.message}</p>}
      <button type="submit">Save</button>
    </form>
  );
}

reset() clears isSubmitSuccessful too, so the effect fires again on every later save, not just the first one. In my run it did: after the second save the state was back to false/false/0.

If save throws, nothing resets, which is usually what you want: in my run the field kept "kept text" after a failing save. handleSubmit passes the error on, though, and here it ended up as an unhandled promise rejection, so catch it inside save and show the user something.

I type-checked that exact component with TypeScript 5.9.3 (strict) and ran it through the same jsdom setup: the field cleared after each save and typing "ab" afterwards showed no error. All of this ran in jsdom, not a real browser. The behavior comes from React Hook Form's state handling rather than the DOM, so I'd expect the same in an app, but I haven't checked that part.

If you've got reset() sitting at the bottom of a submit handler somewhere, it's a two-line move. Worth it just to get submitCount honest again.

title: I built my own password manager because I'm terrible at remembering passwords
description:
Hey everyone!

I've been working on a personal project called GoLock, a desktop password manager built with Go.

The motivation was pretty simple: I'm terrible at remembering passwords. With so many accounts and services, keeping track of all my credentials became a bit of a headache. So I decided to build my own solution.

GoLock allows you to store your credentials in a locally encrypted vault, focusing on security, privacy, and simplicity.

Here are some of the technologies and features I've worked with:

  • Go (Golang) – Application logic and backend.
  • Wails – Desktop application framework.
  • AES-256-GCM – Data encryption.
  • Argon2id – Key derivation.
  • Local storage, keeping user data under their own control.
  • Minimalist interface with dark and light themes.

The project is still evolving, and I have plenty of ideas for future improvements.

I'd really appreciate any feedback, suggestions, or thoughts you might have.

And honestly, I'd also love to get some stars on GitHub! It would mean a lot to see people supporting something I've spent time building.

GitHub: https://github.com/carlosfdsn/golock

Thanks for checking it out!

title: Build a Fine-Tuned Model Training and Serving Pipeline on AWS
description:
From raw training data to production-ready machine learning using Amazon SageMaker.

Building a machine learning model is only the beginning of an AI project.

In a real-world environment, we also need to prepare datasets, fine-tune models, evaluate performance, manage model versions, deploy inference endpoints, and monitor the model after deployment.

Managing these steps manually can become difficult as projects grow.

This is where Amazon SageMaker AI and AWS managed services can help.

In this article, we'll build an end-to-end machine learning workflow on AWS, using a customer support classification use case to understand each stage.

By the end, you'll understand how to move from raw training data to a deployed model endpoint using AWS services.

1. What Is Model Fine-Tuning?

Fine-tuning means taking an existing pre-trained model and adapting it to perform a specific task using your own dataset.

Instead of training a model from scratch, we start with a model that has already learned useful patterns from a large dataset.

We then train it further using task-specific examples.

For example, imagine a company receives thousands of customer support messages every day.

We want to automatically classify each message into one of four categories:

  • Billing
  • Technical Support
  • Account Access
  • General Inquiry

A pre-trained language model can be fine-tuned using labeled customer messages to recognize these categories.

Common fine-tuning approaches include:

  • Full fine-tuning: Updates most or all model parameters.
  • PEFT: Updates a smaller number of parameters.
  • LoRA: Uses low-rank adapters to reduce trainable parameters.
  • QLoRA: Combines quantization and LoRA to reduce memory requirements.
  • Continued pre-training: Continues training on domain-specific data before task-specific fine-tuning.

The right approach depends on model size, dataset, available compute, and performance requirements.

2. AWS Architecture Overview

We'll use AWS managed services to create a repeatable ML workflow.

The high-level architecture looks like this:

Amazon S3
   |
   v
SageMaker Processing
   |
   v
SageMaker Training
   |
   v
Model Evaluation
   |
   v
Quality Check
   |
   v
SageMaker Model Registry
   |
   v
Model Approval
   |
   v
SageMaker Endpoint
   |
   v
Application Predictions
   |
   v
Amazon CloudWatch

Here's what each service does:

AWS Service Purpose
Amazon S3 Stores raw data, processed datasets, and model artifacts
SageMaker Processing Cleans and prepares training data
SageMaker Training Fine-tunes the pre-trained model
SageMaker Pipelines Automates the ML workflow
SageMaker Model Registry Manages model versions and approval
SageMaker Endpoint Serves model predictions
Amazon CloudWatch Collects logs and operational metrics
AWS IAM Controls access to AWS resources
AWS KMS Supports encryption and key management

The goal is to make the complete workflow reproducible and easier to manage.

3. Step One: Prepare the Training Dataset

Let's start with a simple customer support dataset.

Create a CSV file named customer-support.csv:

text,label
"My payment was deducted twice",Billing
"I cannot access my account",Account Access
"The application keeps crashing",Technical Support
"I want to know about your services",General Inquiry
"My invoice contains an incorrect amount",Billing
"Password reset is not working",Account Access

A real production dataset should contain enough representative examples for every category.

Before training, check for:

  • Missing values
  • Duplicate records
  • Incorrect labels
  • Class imbalance
  • Poor-quality text
  • Personally identifiable information

Store the dataset in Amazon S3:

s3://my-ml-project/
│
├── raw-data/
│   └── customer-support.csv
│
├── processed-data/
│   ├── train/
│   └── validation/
│
├── model-artifacts/
│
└── evaluation/

Amazon S3 provides durable storage for datasets, processed files, and trained model artifacts.

4. Step Two: Process the Data with SageMaker Processing

Before fine-tuning, we need to clean and split the dataset.

Amazon SageMaker Processing allows us to execute data preparation scripts through managed processing jobs.

Here's a simple Python example using pandas and scikit-learn:

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

df = pd.read_csv("customer-support.csv")

# Remove missing and duplicate records
df = df.dropna(subset=["text", "label"])
df = df.drop_duplicates()

# Clean text
df["text"] = df["text"].astype(str).str.strip()

# Split dataset
train_df, validation_df = train_test_split(
    df,
    test_size=0.2,
    random_state=42,
    stratify=df["label"]
)

train_df.to_csv("train.csv", index=False)
validation_df.to_csv("validation.csv", index=False)

The stratify parameter helps preserve class proportions across the training and validation datasets.

For larger projects, preprocessing may also include tokenization, text normalization, data validation, and removal of sensitive information.

The processing job can read the raw data from S3 and write the prepared datasets back to S3.

5. Step Three: Fine-Tune the Model

Now let's fine-tune a pre-trained model.

For this example, we'll use Hugging Face Transformers with distilbert-base-uncased.

DistilBERT is a smaller transformer-based model that can be useful for text classification tasks.

The following is an illustrative training script:

import pandas as pd

from datasets import Dataset
from transformers import (
    AutoTokenizer,
    AutoModelForSequenceClassification,
    Trainer,
    TrainingArguments
)

MODEL_NAME = "distilbert-base-uncased"

labels = [
    "Billing",
    "Technical Support",
    "Account Access",
    "General Inquiry"
]

label_to_id = {
    label: index
    for index, label in enumerate(labels)
}

train_df = pd.read_csv("train.csv")
validation_df = pd.read_csv("validation.csv")

train_df["label"] = train_df["label"].map(label_to_id)
validation_df["label"] = validation_df["label"].map(label_to_id)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_NAME)

def tokenize(batch):
    return tokenizer(
        batch["text"],
        truncation=True,
        padding="max_length",
        max_length=128
    )

train_dataset = Dataset.from_pandas(train_df)
validation_dataset = Dataset.from_pandas(validation_df)

train_dataset = train_dataset.map(
    tokenize,
    batched=True
)

validation_dataset = validation_dataset.map(
    tokenize,
    batched=True
)

model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    MODEL_NAME,
    num_labels=len(labels)
)

training_args = TrainingArguments(
    output_dir="./model-output",
    learning_rate=2e-5,
    per_device_train_batch_size=16,
    per_device_eval_batch_size=16,
    num_train_epochs=3,
    eval_strategy="epoch",
    save_strategy="epoch",
    logging_steps=50,
    report_to="none"
)

trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    args=training_args,
    train_dataset=train_dataset,
    eval_dataset=validation_dataset,
    processing_class=tokenizer
)

trainer.train()

trainer.save_model("./model-output")
tokenizer.save_pretrained("./model-output")

This example demonstrates the core fine-tuning process.

For a SageMaker Training Job, adapt the script to the selected training container, dependency versions, input-channel paths, and expected model output directory.

Pin compatible versions of PyTorch, Transformers, and other dependencies in your training environment.

After training, SageMaker can store the model artifacts in Amazon S3.

6. Step Four: Evaluate Model Performance

A completed training job does not automatically mean the model is ready for production.

We need to evaluate its performance.

For classification, useful metrics include:

  • Accuracy
  • Precision
  • Recall
  • F1-score
  • Confusion matrix

Example evaluation code:

from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    precision_recall_fscore_support
)

predictions = trainer.predict(validation_dataset)

predicted_labels = predictions.predictions.argmax(axis=1)
actual_labels = predictions.label_ids

accuracy = accuracy_score(
    actual_labels,
    predicted_labels
)

precision, recall, f1, _ = precision_recall_fscore_support(
    actual_labels,
    predicted_labels,
    average="weighted",
    zero_division=0
)

print("Accuracy:", accuracy)
print("Precision:", precision)
print("Recall:", recall)
print("F1 Score:", f1)

We can save the evaluation results as a JSON file in S3.

Example:

{
  "accuracy": 0.94,
  "precision": 0.93,
  "recall": 0.94,
  "f1_score": 0.93
}

These values are illustrative, not actual benchmark results.

We can define a minimum quality threshold before allowing the model to proceed.

For example:

Minimum F1 Score: 0.90

If F1 >= 0.90:
    Continue to model registration
Else:
    Stop the pipeline

This prevents an underperforming model from automatically reaching production.

7. Step Five: Automate Everything with SageMaker Pipelines

Running every step manually is not a scalable approach.

Amazon SageMaker Pipelines helps orchestrate machine learning workflows.

A typical pipeline includes:

  1. Data processing
  2. Model training
  3. Model evaluation
  4. Quality validation
  5. Model registration

A simplified pipeline structure looks like this:

from sagemaker.workflow.pipeline import Pipeline
from sagemaker.workflow.steps import (
    ProcessingStep,
    TrainingStep
)
from sagemaker.workflow.conditions import (
    ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo
)
from sagemaker.workflow.condition_step import ConditionStep
from sagemaker.workflow.functions import JsonGet

# Configure these objects for your environment:
# processor, processing_args, estimator, training_args,
# evaluation_args, evaluation_report, register_step, session

processing_step = ProcessingStep(
    name="PrepareData",
    step_args=processing_args
)

training_step = TrainingStep(
    name="FineTuneModel",
    step_args=training_args
)

evaluation_step = ProcessingStep(
    name="EvaluateModel",
    step_args=evaluation_args
)

quality_check = ConditionStep(
    name="CheckModelQuality",
    conditions=[
        ConditionGreaterThanOrEqualTo(
            left=JsonGet(
                step_name=evaluation_step.name,
                property_file=evaluation_report,
                json_path="f1_score"
            ),
            right=0.90
        )
    ],
    if_steps=[register_step],
    else_steps=[]
)

pipeline = Pipeline(
    name="FineTunedModelPipeline",
    steps=[
        processing_step,
        training_step,
        evaluation_step,
        quality_check
    ],
    sagemaker_session=session
)

pipeline.upsert(
    role_arn="YOUR_SAGEMAKER_EXECUTION_ROLE_ARN"
)

pipeline.start()

Note: This is a structural example, not a complete executable pipeline. You must configure the processing, training, evaluation, model registration, and evaluation PropertyFile objects. The registration step must be defined before it is referenced in the quality gate.

The key idea is that SageMaker Pipelines can connect all the stages into one repeatable workflow.

8. Step Six: Register and Manage Model Versions

After successful evaluation, we can register the model using Amazon SageMaker Model Registry.

Model Registry helps us manage model versions and track their lifecycle.

For each model version, we can maintain:

  • Model artifacts
  • Training information
  • Evaluation metrics
  • Model package details
  • Approval status
  • Deployment history

A typical lifecycle looks like this:

Model Training
      |
      v
Model Evaluation
      |
      v
Quality Threshold
      |
      v
Model Registry
      |
      v
Manual Approval
      |
      v
Production Deployment

For production systems, manual approval is useful because an ML engineer or authorized reviewer can inspect the model before deployment.

9. Step Seven: Deploy the Model for Predictions

Once approved, we can deploy the model to an inference endpoint.

Amazon SageMaker supports several inference options:

Inference Type Best Use Case
Real-time inference Low-latency online predictions
Serverless inference Intermittent or variable workloads
Asynchronous inference Large requests or longer processing
Batch Transform Large offline prediction workloads

For our customer support classification application, real-time inference may be appropriate when an immediate response is required.

Here's a simplified deployment example:

from sagemaker.huggingface import HuggingFaceModel

huggingface_model = HuggingFaceModel(
    model_data="s3://YOUR_BUCKET/model/model.tar.gz",
    role="YOUR_SAGEMAKER_EXECUTION_ROLE_ARN",
    transformers_version="YOUR_SUPPORTED_VERSION",
    pytorch_version="YOUR_SUPPORTED_VERSION",
    py_version="YOUR_SUPPORTED_PYTHON_VERSION"
)

predictor = huggingface_model.deploy(
    initial_instance_count=1,
    instance_type="ml.m5.large"
)

The framework versions, Python version, instance type, and inference handler must match the selected SageMaker container and model artifacts.

Example input:

{
  "text": "My payment was deducted twice"
}

Illustrative prediction:

{
  "label": "Billing",
  "confidence": 0.97
}

The actual response format depends on your inference handler and model implementation.

10. Step Eight: Monitor the Deployed Model

Deployment is not the end of the machine learning lifecycle.

Real-world data can change over time. Customer language, user behavior, and business requirements may evolve.

A model that performs well today may become less accurate in the future.

Amazon CloudWatch can help monitor:

  • Endpoint invocations
  • Latency
  • Errors
  • CPU and memory utilization
  • Endpoint availability
  • Application-level prediction metrics

You can also capture inference inputs and outputs, subject to privacy and data-retention requirements, for later analysis.

Monitor data quality and prediction distributions to identify possible data drift.

Important: Check the current availability of SageMaker Model Monitor in your AWS account and Region. AWS documentation notes that Model Monitor is no longer available to new customers. If it is unavailable, you can build alternative monitoring workflows using captured data, custom processing jobs, CloudWatch metrics, and your own evaluation logic.

A good monitoring strategy should cover both infrastructure health and model quality.

11. Security Best Practices

Machine learning pipelines may process sensitive customer and business information.

Keep these practices in mind:

IAM least privilege: Use dedicated IAM roles for processing, training, pipeline execution, and inference. Grant only the permissions each component requires.

Data encryption: Encrypt S3 objects and other supported storage resources. Use AWS KMS where appropriate.

Protect sensitive data: Remove or mask personally identifiable information before training whenever possible.

Private networking: Consider VPC configuration and controlled network access for workloads handling sensitive data.

Model quality gates: Require measurable evaluation criteria before registration or deployment.

Model approval: Use Model Registry approval workflows to control production releases.

Cost monitoring: Review training, processing, endpoint, and storage costs regularly.

12. Cost Optimization

The total cost of a fine-tuning pipeline depends on:

  • Training instance type and duration
  • Processing job duration
  • Model size
  • Storage consumption
  • Inference traffic
  • Endpoint configuration
  • Data transfer and monitoring requirements

Some practical optimization ideas:

  1. Start with a smaller pre-trained model.
  2. Use PEFT or LoRA where appropriate.
  3. Use smaller datasets for initial experiments.
  4. Consider managed spot training where supported and suitable.
  5. Choose serverless or asynchronous inference for workloads that do not require continuously provisioned real-time capacity.
  6. Shut down unused real-time endpoints.
  7. Review S3 storage and CloudWatch usage.

Always balance cost against model quality, latency, and availability requirements.

13. Final Architecture

Let's bring everything together:

             Amazon S3
          Raw Training Data
                 |
                 v
       SageMaker Processing
          Data Preparation
                 |
                 v
        SageMaker Training
          Model Fine-Tuning
                 |
                 v
         Model Evaluation
        Accuracy / F1 Score
                 |
                 v
          Quality Check
                 |
          Pass   |   Fail
            |    |    |
            v    |    v
       Model Registry  Stop
            |
            v
      Model Approval
            |
            v
     SageMaker Endpoint
            |
            v
      Application / API
            |
            v
       CloudWatch Monitoring

This architecture gives us a structured and repeatable approach to managing the machine learning lifecycle.

Conclusion

Fine-tuning a model is only one part of delivering a successful AI solution.

A production-ready system also needs automated data preparation, repeatable training, evaluation, model versioning, controlled deployment, and continuous monitoring.

By combining Amazon S3, SageMaker Processing, SageMaker Training, SageMaker Pipelines, Model Registry, and SageMaker Endpoints, we can build a scalable workflow for these requirements.

The same architecture can be adapted for:

  • Customer support automation
  • Document classification
  • Sentiment analysis
  • Fraud detection
  • Product categorization
  • Domain-specific text classification
  • Intelligent enterprise applications

Don't just train a model. Build a complete pipeline that makes it reproducible, measurable, manageable, and ready for production.

Useful AWS Resources

  • Amazon SageMaker AI Documentation
  • Amazon SageMaker Pipelines
  • SageMaker Model Registry
  • Deploy Models for Inference
  • SageMaker Inference Options
  • Amazon S3 Documentation

What does your current ML workflow look like? Are you using SageMaker Pipelines, or are you still managing training and deployment manually? Share your experience in the comments!

title: I built an open-source, self-hosted URL shortener with .NET 10 and React 19
description:
When building modern web applications, URL shorteners are often treated as simple toy projects. But once you consider sub-5ms redirection speeds, high-concurrency traffic surges, dynamic geo/device routing, and strict GDPR privacy, link orchestration becomes a serious engineering challenge.

I wanted to solve this by building LinkLift — an enterprise-grade, self-hosted URL shortener and link orchestration platform built on ASP.NET Core (.NET 10), React 19, and Docker.

⭐ GitHub Repository: github.com/vpritesh/LinkLift (MIT Licensed)

🚀 What LinkLift Does

  1. Sub-5ms Redirection Engine: Hybrid L1 in-memory + Redis L2 distributed caching for instant resolution under heavy load.
  2. Dynamic Conditional Routing: Conditional rules that direct visitors based on:
    • Country (Geo-IP): US visitors to your US store, EU visitors to your EU site.
    • Device & OS: Automatically route mobile users to app stores and desktop users to web portals.
  3. Real-Time Click Telemetry: Live click streaming via SignalR WebSockets and Redis Pub/Sub — no page refreshes needed.
  4. GDPR & Privacy First: Built-in BotShield crawler filtering, daily-salted SHA-256 IP anonymization, and automated 90-day retention purge workers.
  5. Modern Executive Dashboard: Clean Charcoal-Blue theme, collapsible sidebar, global command palette (Ctrl+K), and SVG/PNG QR code generator.
  6. Multi-Server Fleet Switcher: Switch and manage multiple remote LinkLift instances right from the browser.

🏛 Architecture & Tech Stack

LinkLift follows Clean Architecture with strict separation of concerns:

  • Backend: ASP.NET Core 10 Minimal APIs, C# 13, EF Core 10
  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Vite
  • High-Throughput Channels: Bounded System.Threading.Channels queue to asynchronously batch click events to SQLite, Postgres, or SQL Server without blocking HTTP request threads.
  • Cache & Pub/Sub: Redis L2 cache and Redis SignalR bridge.

🐳 Quick Start with Docker

You can test the entire cluster locally in under 60 seconds:

git clone https://github.com/vpritesh/LinkLift.git
cd LinkLift
docker compose up -d --build
  • Dashboard: http://localhost:3000
  • API & Swagger: http://localhost:5000/swagger
  • Default Master API Key: ll_live_master

💬 Feedback Welcome!

The project is completely free and open-source under the MIT license.

I would love to hear your feedback on the architecture, Docker setup, and features. If you find it interesting, please consider starring the repository on GitHub!

title: Logistics Email Failures: API Error Logging and Retry Strategies for Expiring Resets
description:
Short answer: for failed email deliveries from an API, use error logging to preserve the decision context and retry strategies to handle only failures that can plausibly change. Keep the reset template owned by the team that owns the account-security contract, and use a short deadline. A second send must never extend the password-reset token or quietly create a second valid path.

For a logistics operation, this is a practical boundary. A dispatcher may need access before a pickup window closes, but a reset email is still security traffic. The useful question is not “did the API accept my request?” It is “what did we know at each step, and why did we send, retry, suppress, or expire the attempt?”

What does the reset email actually cost to retain?

Start with the billable shape of the work, not with a retry loop. In an illustrative batch of 100,000 reset attempts, one request record per attempt is 100,000 durable records. Retaining a full rendered body, provider response, and repeated payload for every retry can multiply storage and expose more personal data without improving the decision later. The dominant retention term is usually duplicated message evidence, not the small classifier that decides whether a failure is transient.

The change I make is to retain a compact event envelope and a hash of the rendered template, while keeping the reset token out of logs altogether. One attempt can carry an event id, account reference, template revision, request time, expiry time, recipient domain, provider request id when present, normalized error class, and attempt number. The body belongs in a controlled template store with its own access policy; it does not belong in an operational log.

This is a deliberate loss. If an incident needs the exact body sent to one recipient, a hash cannot reconstruct it. The trade is acceptable when the template store is versioned and access is audited. Keeping every payload in the hot log is easier during the first incident and harder during the next privacy review.

The same envelope makes retry accounting cheap and explicit:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Optional


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DeliveryEvent:
    event_id: str
    account_ref: str
    template_revision: str
    recipient_domain: str
    created_at: datetime
    expires_at: datetime
    attempt: int
    outcome: str
    error_class: Optional[str]
    provider_request_id: Optional[str]
    body_sha256: str

The envelope is not a success metric. It is the evidence needed to explain the state transition. Keep retention long enough for the security and operations teams to investigate a reset window, then delete or aggregate it according to the organization’s retention policy.

Keep it boring.

How should error logging guide retry strategies for failed email?

The API response is only one signal. A timeout after the request leaves an ambiguous state: the message may have been accepted even though the client did not receive the response. Retrying immediately can produce two emails. A durable idempotency key, or an equivalent deduplication record at the sending boundary, is therefore part of the retry design rather than an optional convenience.

Classify outcomes by whether the cause can change without changing the recipient or template. A connection timeout, a temporary DNS problem, a rate-limit response, or an SMTP 4.x enhanced status generally belongs in a bounded transient path. A malformed address, an authentication failure, a policy rejection, or an SMTP 5.x status generally belongs in a terminal path. The exact meaning still comes from the sending API and its documented error fields; do not infer it from a human-readable message alone.

HTTP 429 commonly means the caller must respect a limit, while 5xx indicates a server-side failure. Neither status tells you that a retry is safe forever. Honor an explicit Retry-After value when one is supplied, cap the number of attempts, and stop when the reset token expires. Exponential backoff with jitter prevents a fleet of workers from waking at the same instant.

Here is the decision boundary I want in code review. It is intentionally boring.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta
import random


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class RetryDecision:
    retry: bool
    delay_seconds: int
    reason: str


def decide_retry(
    *,
    status_code: int | None,
    smtp_class: str | None,
    attempt: int,
    now: datetime,
    expires_at: datetime,
    retry_after_seconds: int | None = None,
    random_value: float | None = None,
) -> RetryDecision:
    if now >= expires_at:
        return RetryDecision(False, 0, "reset_expired")
    if attempt >= 3:
        return RetryDecision(False, 0, "attempt_limit")

    transient = status_code in {408, 429} or (
        status_code is not None and 500 <= status_code <= 599
    ) or smtp_class == "4"
    if not transient:
        return RetryDecision(False, 0, "terminal_delivery_error")

    base = retry_after_seconds if retry_after_seconds is not None else 2 ** attempt
    jitter = int((random_value if random_value is not None else random.random()) * 3)
    delay = min(base + jitter, 60)
    if now + timedelta(seconds=delay) >= expires_at:
        return RetryDecision(False, 0, "retry_would_outlive_reset")
    return RetryDecision(True, delay, "transient_delivery_error")

The numbers in this example are policy inputs, not universal defaults. Three attempts and a 60-second delay cap may fit a short-lived reset flow; a longer-lived notification needs a different budget. The important properties are visible: no retry after expiry, no unbounded loop, and no second token just because transport was uncertain.

This approach is a poor fit for long-running bulk mail or messages with no meaningful expiry. Those workloads need a separate queue budget, suppression policy, and retention schedule; borrowing a password-reset policy would discard useful delivery opportunities. The limitation is deliberate: a short-lived security flow values a clear stopping point more than maximum eventual delivery, while a newsletter or operational report may reasonably keep trying after this reset window has closed. That is the trade-off.

Choose the policy by message purpose, not by the convenience of sharing one worker configuration.

What should a failed reset attempt leave behind?

Log state transitions, not secrets. At minimum, record queued, submitted, accepted, deferred, delivered when the channel reports it, bounced, rejected, expired, and suppressed. Keep the original provider or SMTP code alongside the normalized class. Normalization supports dashboards; the original value preserves evidence when the classifier turns out to be incomplete.

An event should answer five questions without opening a message body: which account flow was involved, which template revision was selected, which recipient domain was targeted, which attempt made the decision, and which clock caused the next action. Correlation ids should connect the account request, queue job, delivery request, and callback. They should not be the reset token, an email address, or a full provider payload.

I also separate “accepted by the API” from “delivered to the mailbox.” Those are different states. SPF is one part of sender authorization, and the SPF specification itself describes policy evaluation rather than a guarantee that a message reaches an inbox. DKIM and DMARC add other pieces of domain authentication and policy. A passing authentication check cannot turn a deferred or rejected delivery into a success.

Alerting should follow the state machine. A spike in transient failures is an operational signal. A rise in permanent rejects for one recipient domain is a deliverability or data-quality signal. A queue age beyond the reset validity window is a security and usability signal. Putting all three into one “email failed” counter hides the action required.

Who should own the template and the retry policy?

The account-security team should own the meaning of the template: what the user is being asked to do, how long the token is valid, and which link is authoritative. The communications or platform team can own rendering infrastructure, queue mechanics, and delivery telemetry. Ownership of the template revision must travel with the event envelope, so a later retry cannot accidentally render a newer message against an older security decision.

For a logistics password reset, the message should identify the action and its short validity window without putting the secret in a subject line, log field, or analytics label. A worker may retry a delivery attempt, but it should reuse the same security transaction and idempotency key. If the reset has expired, the worker records expired; it does not manufacture a fresh reset as a side effect of a transport retry.

Test this boundary with a small matrix: timeout before response, timeout after apparent acceptance, 429 with Retry-After, SMTP 4.x, SMTP 5.x, malformed recipient, template revision change, and expiry during backoff. Assert both the final state and the retained evidence. The test that only checks for a raised exception misses the duplicate-send case, which is the one users notice immediately.

The least complicated design that remains explainable is a versioned template, a single security transaction, an idempotent delivery boundary, and a bounded state machine. Keep the evidence compact, preserve the original error, and let expiry end the retry path. That gives operations enough context to diagnose delivery without making the log a second copy of every sensitive message.

Further reading

  • RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework (SPF): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7208
  • RFC 5321, Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5321
  • RFC 3463, Enhanced Mail System Status Codes: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3463
  • RFC 6376, DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Signatures: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6376
  • RFC 7489, Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • RFC 7231, HTTP Semantics: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7231

title: How I Built a Static Blog with 50+ Articles and Zero Frameworks: Pure HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
description:
How I Built a Static Blog with 50+ Articles and Zero Frameworks: Pure HTML, CSS, and JavaScript

Every few months, someone asks me the same question: "What framework is your blog built with? Next.js? Astro?" The answer usually surprises them: none. My blog, wuhuajin.com, is a fully static site built with pure HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript — no React, no Vue, no build framework. It has over 50 published articles, and it has held near-perfect PageSpeed scores for over a year.

This is the story of why I went framework-free, how the architecture actually works, and the specific trade-offs you should consider before doing the same.

Why I Dropped Frameworks for a Content Site

Frameworks solve real problems: state management, component re-rendering, routing, and code organization at scale. A blog doesn't have any of those problems. It has one job — serve text and images to readers as fast as possible.

Once I framed it that way, the case for a zero-framework blog became obvious:

  • Speed is the feature. No bundle to download, no hydration to wait for, no runtime JavaScript between the user and the content.
  • Maintenance is nearly zero. No dependency tree to keep updated, no breaking upgrades every six months, no lockfile churn.
  • Total control. Every byte of HTML is mine. I decide how it's structured, how it's cached, and how it's crawled.
  • Longevity. A plain HTML file from 2005 still renders today. I want this blog to outlive whatever the frontend ecosystem does next.

The catch: you lose the scaffolding that frameworks give you. So I built a small, custom toolchain to replace only the parts I actually needed.

The Architecture: Content in Markdown, Pages in HTML

The entire site follows one simple rule: write in Markdown, ship as static HTML. No content is rendered on the client — every article is prerendered into its own standalone HTML file at build time.

wuhuajin.github.io/
├── src/
│   ├── components/        # Reusable UI pieces (navigation, footer, sidebar, feed...)
│   ├── template/
│   │   └── posts/         # Article Markdown, organized by category (20+ categories)
│   ├── css/               # Third-party CSS (highlight.js themes, etc.)
│   └── js/                # Third-party JS (marked, highlight.js, APlayer)
├── scripts/               # Custom Node.js build scripts
├── server.js              # Local dev server (port 8000)
├── index.html
└── package.json

The src/ directory is the source of truth. Each UI piece is a self-contained component — its own HTML fragment, CSS, and JavaScript. Nothing is shared through a bundler's module graph; components are simply assembled into pages by the build scripts.

The Content Pipeline: Markdown → Prerendered HTML

The heart of the system is the prerendering pipeline. Every article lives as Markdown with YAML front matter:

---
title: "My Article"
date: 2026-01-01
category: ["JavaScript"]
tag: ["es6", "async"]
description: "Hand-written meta description (never auto-overwritten)"
top: true
---

A custom Node.js script parses the front matter, renders the Markdown with marked, applies syntax highlighting with highlight.js, and writes out a complete standalone HTML page — including the table of contents, code-block toolbar, and reward card. The result is a page that renders perfectly even with JavaScript fully disabled.

Why prerender instead of rendering client-side?

  1. Crawlers see the full content. Googlebot gets the complete article in the initial HTML. There's no "render the page before indexing it" dependency.
  2. Instant first paint. The browser has nothing to do but paint what's already there.
  3. Resilience. If a CDN edge or a third-party script fails, the content is still on the page.

The Build System: Custom Node.js Scripts, No Bundler

Instead of Webpack, Vite, or esbuild, the build is a sequence of small, focused .cjs scripts:

Script What it does
build-articles.cjs Prerender every Markdown article into posts/<category>/html/
build-feed.cjs Parse front matter → generate the homepage feed data.json
build-home.cjs Generate homepage data
build-sitemap.cjs Auto-generate sitemap.xml from the feed
build-links.cjs Build aggregation and resource-navigation pages
add-front-matter.cjs Backfill missing front matter fields
update-wordcount.js Count real words per article for the feed
watch.cjs File watcher + live reload for development

Each script is idempotent — running it twice produces no diff. That property alone has saved me hours of debugging. And because there's no bundler graph, a broken component fails loudly in the build output instead of as a subtle runtime error in the browser.

For development, a small server.js uses Node's native http module, chokidar for file watching, and a WebSocket connection for live reload. One command (npm run dev) builds once, starts the server at localhost:8000, and hot-reloads on change. No Vite, no webpack-dev-server, no 200MB node_modules.

Bilingual Without an i18n Library

The site is English-first with a one-click Chinese switch. Instead of a heavyweight i18n framework, it uses a lightweight dictionary: a plain JavaScript object mapping English keys to translated strings, plus a runtime function that swaps text nodes and lang attributes when the user switches.

The whole i18n layer is one component (src/components/i18n/) and a few hundred lines. It covers everything a blog actually needs — navigation, footer, buttons, and labels — without the 40KB+ payload of a full i18n solution.

The Performance Numbers

Zero framework doesn't automatically mean fast — you still have to do the work. Here are the results after 20+ rounds of optimization:

Metric Before After Improvement
Homepage HTML size 57 KB 34 KB −40%
Social share image 576 KB 262 KB −55%
CLS (layout shift) 0.37 < 0.1 −73%
Render-blocking CSS 11 KB Async loaded Eliminated
Render-blocking JS 13 files All defer Eliminated

The techniques are mostly boring and reliable: defer on every script, preconnect to the five third-party origins the site talks to, explicit width/height on every image, aspect-ratio locked on cover containers, lazy loading below the fold, and non-critical CSS loaded asynchronously. The biggest single win was prerendering — because the HTML already contains everything, there's almost nothing left to block rendering.

When a Zero-Framework Blog Makes Sense (and When It Doesn't)

Do this if:

  • Your site is content-first — articles, documentation, product pages.
  • You're comfortable maintaining a few hundred lines of build scripts.
  • You want maximum performance with a tiny attack surface.
  • You plan to run the site for years, not months.

Don't do this if:

  • You need complex interactivity — dashboards, real-time collaboration, or app-like behavior. That's what frameworks are for.
  • You want a large team contributing without learning your custom conventions.
  • You value ecosystem leverage — prebuilt components, plugins, and hiring familiarity — over raw control.

There's no shame in using a framework. The point is to choose based on what your site actually needs, not on what's popular.

What I'd Do Differently

Two things, looking back. First, I'd write the build scripts with better error messages from day one — "fail loudly" beats "fail mysteriously" every time. Second, I'd add automated checks earlier: a simple script that verifies every article has a meta description and every image has dimensions before deploy. Both would have saved me real debugging time.

This article is based on the real-world architecture of wuhuajin.com, a zero-framework static blog with 50+ articles running on GitHub Pages and Cloudflare CDN. If you're weighing framework-free options for your own content site, feel free to reach out.

Originally published on wuhuajin.com.

title: Object Storage for Low-Volume Uploads Explained — R2, B2, and S3 for Python
description:
Short answer: For low-volume image uploads and private signed documents, start by testing Cloudflare R2 or Backblaze B2; choose S3 when AWS controls matter most, and test Infrai when one self-describing REST integration needs to cover storage plus other backend capabilities.

For a marketplace that stores user avatars and signed documents, the least complex good answer is private object storage with server-issued signed URLs and a deletion deadline. Cloudflare R2 and Backblaze B2 are strong starting points for low-volume image uploads; Amazon S3 is the broader, more mature choice when the surrounding AWS controls matter more than delivery simplicity.

Infrai belongs in the same experiment when the Python service will also connect storage to other backend capabilities. Its public discovery surface describes request and response schemas and provides runnable examples, so a junior developer can inspect a capability before installing another SDK. One key and one bill across those capabilities can also remove credential and reconciliation work; that is a workflow benefit, not a reason to assume its storage controls beat a specialist.

The decision is access control versus delivery simplicity. I would test that trade-off with a small, reproducible fixture before choosing a vendor. A cheap bucket that cannot express your retention boundary, or that makes browser uploads awkward, is not cheap in the way your application needs.

Which object storage solutions suit low-volume image uploads?

The concrete input is a signed PDF uploaded by a marketplace participant. It must be private, retrievable by an authorized application flow, and deleted at a known deadline. An avatar follows the same access pattern, although it may have a shorter retention period. The experiment does not need a production-sized corpus: exactly three objects are enough to test the control plane, the upload path, and the deletion policy.

I use five pass/fail checks:

  1. A browser or client can upload without receiving permanent storage credentials.
  2. An unauthorized request cannot read the object through a public URL.
  3. The application can issue a time-limited download URL after authorization.
  4. A deletion deadline can be represented with a day-level lifecycle rule or an application-owned deletion job.
  5. The Python integration can report an actionable error instead of silently accepting a failed write.

The decision rule is deliberately plain: pass all five checks with the fewest moving parts, then prefer the option whose operational controls match the document's risk. Do not rank providers by a single request price. At low volume, a missing access-control feature or a second reconciliation job can dominate the bill and the maintenance burden.

Private by default.

Here is a compact Python harness for recording the result and checking the available storage surface through Infrai. It is intentionally small: the same pass/fail cases can be run against R2, B2, S3, or an adapter behind a unified backend API. The request uses the public discovery route and the verified bucket-list route, never a public object URL.

import json
import os
import time
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone
from typing import Callable
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.request import Request, urlopen


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class StorageResult:
    private_by_default: bool
    signed_download: bool
    deletion_deadline_days: int | None
    upload_error_is_visible: bool


def evaluate(result: StorageResult) -> list[str]:
    failures = []

    if not result.private_by_default:
        failures.append("objects are not private by default")
    if not result.signed_download:
        failures.append("downloads are not authorization-gated")
    if result.deletion_deadline_days is None:
        failures.append("no deletion deadline is represented")
    if not result.upload_error_is_visible:
        failures.append("upload failures are not visible to the caller")
    return failures


def deadline(days: int, now: Callable[[], datetime] =
             lambda: datetime.now(timezone.utc)) -> datetime:
    if days < 1:
        raise ValueError("this policy uses a day-level deadline")
    return now() + timedelta(days=days)


def infrai_get(path: str) -> dict:
    key = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
    url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1" + path
    for attempt in range(4):
        request = Request(
            url,
            method="GET",
            headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + key, "Accept": "application/json"},
        )
        try:
            with urlopen(request, timeout=20) as response:
                body = response.read().decode("utf-8")
                if response.status < 200 or response.status >= 300:
                    raise RuntimeError(f"Infrai returned HTTP {response.status}: {body}")
                return json.loads(body)
        except HTTPError as error:
            body = error.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
            if error.code != 429 or attempt == 3:
                raise RuntimeError(f"Infrai returned HTTP {error.code}: {body}") from error
            retry_after = error.headers.get("Retry-After")
            wait_seconds = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
            time.sleep(wait_seconds)
        except URLError as error:
            raise RuntimeError(f"Infrai request failed: {error.reason}") from error
    raise RuntimeError("Infrai request exhausted its retry budget")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    discovery = infrai_get("/discovery")
    buckets = infrai_get("/storage/bucket/list")
    print("discovery capabilities:", len(discovery.get("capabilities", [])))
    print("bucket response keys:", sorted(buckets))
    sample = StorageResult(
        private_by_default=True,
        signed_download=True,
        deletion_deadline_days=30,
        upload_error_is_visible=True,
    )
    failures = evaluate(sample)
    print("PASS" if not failures else "FAIL: " + "; ".join(failures))
    print("delete after:", deadline(sample.deletion_deadline_days).isoformat())

That script proves the decision rule, not a vendor's availability. In the real adapter, keep the object key separate from the user's display name, persist the deadline beside the document record, and test an expired signed URL as well as a valid one. The storage layer should never be the only place that knows a document must disappear.

How do R2, B2, and S3 differ here?

Cloudflare R2 is a good fit when the application already lives close to Cloudflare's edge and the team wants an S3-shaped object store without adding many storage-specific concepts. Backblaze B2 is a practical low-volume option with a straightforward object-storage model and a clear path to larger usage. Both deserve a real trial in the five-check harness, especially for avatar and ordinary file uploads.

Amazon S3 brings the deepest ecosystem: IAM, bucket policies, lifecycle management, event integrations, versioning, and object-lock features are familiar to many operations teams. Those controls are valuable for signed documents, but they also increase the number of decisions a junior developer must get right. S3 is the safer choice when an existing AWS security and audit model is already a requirement; it is not automatically the simplest choice for a small marketplace.

Solution Integration Best fit Main limitation to test
Cloudflare R2 S3-shaped API and SDKs Low-volume uploads near a Cloudflare-based app Confirm the exact browser and retention workflow
Backblaze B2 B2 API or S3-compatible tooling A focused object-storage deployment It is not covered by Infrai's current storage vendor set
Amazon S3 AWS SDKs and REST APIs Existing AWS identity, audit, and retention controls More policy surface for a small team
Infrai storage Self-describing REST API A Python backend already using several unified capabilities No public-read ACL, versioning, object lock, or self-service CORS route

The table is a starting map, not a benchmark. Run the same three-object fixture against the candidates that survive your security review.

The important boundary is the same across these options: private objects and signed access are different from permanent public links. A marketplace should grant access through its own authorization decision, then hand the client a short-lived signed URL. CORS still needs to be tested from the actual browser origin, and the policy must be explicit rather than inferred from a successful command-line upload. MDN's CORS guide is a useful reference for that part of the test.

For an image-only product, the differences may be tolerable. For signed documents, ask one sharper question: what happens when an object is overwritten by mistake? Versioning and object lock are specialist controls. If the provider or integration lacks them, do not claim that the bucket is an immutable archive; keep the authoritative record and any legal-hold workflow outside that narrow upload path.

Where does a unified REST layer fit?

A unified backend API is worth testing when the team is already wiring storage beside AI, databases, scheduling, or notifications. The advantage is discovery: the public API description can expose a capability's request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples, so adding a new backend capability can start with reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. That matters in a notebook-to-prod project where the first prototype is often written by a junior engineer and later moved into a service.

The storage surface includes bucket discovery and creation, object reads and writes, presigned URLs, lifecycle configuration, and deletion. Keep the integration small. A Python service can discover the available capability, create one private bucket, and delegate the actual browser transfer to a presigned URL; it does not need a catalog of every storage route in the article.

This approach removes a concrete integration cost: one authentication and request convention can sit beside the other backend capabilities, while per-call metadata can make cost, latency, vendor, cache status, and request ID visible to the application. That visibility is useful in an eval harness because a passing functional test can still expose an unexpectedly slow or expensive leg.

The recommendation is narrow: try Infrai for the storage leg when your Python service values self-describing discovery, one credential across backend capabilities, and a consistent REST integration, and when its private, signed-access model passes the five checks above. The recommendation is not for a public image host or a compliance archive. There is no public-read ACL, no object versioning or object lock, no conditional If-Match write, and no self-service CORS route; those are material constraints for a browser-heavy or immutability-sensitive design. Its storage vendor coverage also does not include Backblaze B2, so a team specifically standardizing on B2 should integrate B2 directly.

The experiment should record the result, not assume it. Run the same three-object fixture against the chosen direct provider and the unified layer, capture pass/fail plus latency and error details, and keep the one with the clearer ownership boundary. No benchmark result is needed before that test exists.

What should be operationally true before launch?

Use a private bucket. Store only opaque keys in application records, and authorize every download before generating a signed URL. Never attach the backend authorization header to the returned signed URL: it is a separate request with its own signature. Treat the URL lifetime as a delivery detail, not as the document's retention policy.

For deletion, choose a day-level lifecycle rule where the provider supports the needed boundary, or run a scheduled job that selects due records from the database and deletes the corresponding objects. A one-day minimum lifecycle is not an hourly expiry mechanism. Multipart uploads also need an explicit cleanup plan when the storage system does not automatically remove abandoned fragments.

Before calling the work complete, check a failed upload, an expired URL, a missing object, a repeated delete, and a browser-origin request. Record request IDs and provider errors. If the storage API cannot offer conditional writes, coordinate concurrent updates with the database or a queue; do not pretend that last-write-wins is a concurrency policy.

For the signed-document fixture, make the deadline part of the test data rather than a note in a ticket. Create one document record with a deadline 30 days out, one avatar with a shorter policy, and one intentionally expired record. Authorize the first two through the application, generate signed downloads, then attempt the expired path and verify that the application refuses it even if the underlying object has not yet been removed. Next, delete the due object and repeat the delete to observe the provider's real error shape. Finally, send a browser-origin request and inspect the response headers. This sequence catches a common design mistake: treating a valid signed URL as proof that retention, authorization, and CORS are all correct. They are separate controls, so the fixture should keep them separate too.

One last practical distinction: a trial balance that cannot pay for persistent writes is not evidence that the storage path works. Test with the billing state and credentials the production workflow will use. That small detail belongs in the fixture's setup notes, where it can be reviewed instead of becoming a surprise during launch.

If your result is a pass for private uploads, signed delivery, and day-level deletion, start by checking the storage capability details at the Infrai documentation. If the result is a fail on immutability, public delivery, or browser CORS control, choose the specialist that owns that requirement instead.

Further reading

  • Cloudflare R2 documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • Backblaze B2 documentation: https://www.backblaze.com/docs/cloud-storage
  • Amazon S3 documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
  • MDN, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS): https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

title: Replace a headless Claude Code script with Maki to cut token spend
description:
Headless Claude Code scripts are handy: pipe a prompt in, get structured output out, wire it into CI or a cron job. They are also where token spend quietly piles up, because every run re-reads files in full and drags bash output into the context window.

tontinton/maki is an open source coding agent built around one goal: use as few context tokens as possible. Its README says it can run UI-less with output compatible with Claude Code's stream-json format, which makes it a candidate drop-in for existing scripts. This post covers what it does differently, how to install it, and how to point a headless script at it.

Why it uses fewer tokens

Per the README, maki attacks the biggest token sinks directly:

  • An index tool uses tree-sitter to produce a skeleton of a file with the exact start and end lines of each item, so the agent can read only the function it needs. The author reports it adds about 59 tokens per turn but saves about 224 on reads, a net of roughly 165 tokens per turn.
  • A code_execution tool runs a sandboxed interpreter where all other tools are async functions, so data can be filtered or summarized without ever entering the context window.
  • A task tool lets the agent delegate to a weak, medium or strong model from the same provider, think Haiku, Sonnet, Opus.
  • rtk integration. If you have rtk installed, maki uses it to shrink bash output. The author notes bash is only about 12% of total token use and reads are about 65%, which is why the index tool matters more.

Other details from the README: a Rust terminal UI with fast startup, Lua plugins, plan mode, skills and MCP support, a memory tool, and a permission system that parses bash commands with tree-sitter, so git diff && rm -rf / is evaluated as git * plus rm * rather than waved through as one git command.

Install

On Linux or macOS, the README recommends reading the script before running it:

curl -fsSL https://maki.sh/install.sh -o install.sh
cat install.sh
chmod +x install.sh && sh install.sh

The one-liner is curl -fsSL https://maki.sh/install.sh | sh. It installs to ~/.local/bin, and you can override that with MAKI_INSTALL_DIR. Other routes from the README:

brew install maki
nix run github:tontinton/maki
cargo install --locked --git https://github.com/tontinton/maki.git maki

Windows has a PowerShell installer (irm https://maki.sh/install.ps1 | iex).

Pick a provider

Maki supports many providers through environment variables. A few from the README:

  • Anthropic: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY only. The README states that using OAuth is against Anthropic's terms, so use an API key.
  • OpenAI: OPENAI_API_KEY, or OAuth with maki auth login openai.
  • Google: GEMINI_API_KEY. DeepSeek: DEEPSEEK_API_KEY. OpenRouter: OPENROUTER_API_KEY.
  • Local: OLLAMA_HOST (for example http://localhost:11434) or LLAMA_CPP_HOST (for example http://localhost:8080).

Export the key for the provider you want before the first run.

Swap it into a headless script

If your script currently calls Claude Code in print mode, the README's headless flags are the ones to try:

maki --print --output-format stream-json

The README says the output is compatible with Claude Code, so a parser that reads Claude Code's stream-json should keep working. Test it on a low-stakes job first, compare the output side by side, and check your token bill after a week. Note that --yolo disables the permission system, so keep it out of anything that touches a real machine unless the job is sandboxed.

Use it from your editor

Maki also speaks ACP. In Zed's settings.json:

"agent_servers": {
  "Maki": {
    "default_config_options": {
      "model": "deepseek/deepseek-flash"
    },
    "type": "custom",
    "command": "maki",
    "args": ["acp"],
    "env": {}
  }
}

Caveats

  • The benchmark and token numbers are the author's own, from his usage. We have not reproduced them.
  • The author discloses that over 90% of maki's code was written by maki, guided by humans.
  • This walkthrough follows the README and we have not run it end to end.

The step-by-step version lives on our use-case page: replace a headless Claude Code script with Maki. If token spend is your main worry, also see cut token spend in Claude Code with Headroom.
